Ukraine ordered 54% more FPV attack drones this year than in all of 2025, and deliveries jumped almost fourfold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:00:24 UTC
02:00:24 KST

Ukraine’s Defense Procurement Agency has contracted about 5.5 times as many drones of various types in recent months as in the same period of 2025. It is roughly 300% more over the year as a whole, the Defense Ministry said.
Drones are the weapons this war runs on, from short-range strikes to hits deep inside Russia, and Ukraine has raced to build and buy more of them while sparing its troops. The agency contracted for about $8 billion worth of drones in the first half of 2026 alone, double the amount for the same period last year.
The ministry wants to arm the force at every level, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara stresses. Deep-strike drones hit targets far inside Russia, while middle-strike drones kill enemy drone crews and burn logistics and command posts, lowering the risk to Ukrainian soldiers.
“Technology and having enough of these systems raise combat effectiveness and at the same time reduce the risks for our soldiers,” Khmara said.
FPV drones lead the surge
The sharpest growth is in FPV drones, the cheap first-person-view quadcopters that do much of the killing on the front. Contracting for them in 2026 already exceeds the total for all of 2025 by 54%, and deliveries have risen almost 3.7 times, the ministry notes.
International support and the scaling of Ukraine’s own defense industry made the jump possible, Khmara adds. Much of the buying now runs through the DOT-Chain Defense marketplace, where units select what they need, and the agency handles contracts and logistics, cutting the average delivery time for in-stock items to 9 days.
Making supply predictable
The ministry is trying to make deliveries steadier, Khmara explains. It is aligning the front’s needs, purchase planning, and the production capacity of the Ukrainian industry, making supply more predictable.
Predictable contracting lets manufacturers build their production lines step by step, plan logistics and order components in advance, he says. The ministry frames the push as a larger order book for the domestic industry and a way to scale the solutions that work in combat.

Ukraine wants to draft 15 of every 100 workers at its weapons plants. Arms makers say this could slow guns soldiers need
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:48:18 UTC
01:48:18 KST

Ukraine wants to build more weapons at home while making it easier to draft the people who build them. Kyiv has proposed cutting the draft-exemption quota for defense-industry enterprises from 100% of their workers to 85%, while the Ukrainian Council of Arms Manufacturers says the limit should stay at the previous level for qualifying critical plants.
The change would strip the draft shield from 15% of the workers at plants the Defense Ministry has deemed critical to the economy. Those are the people who set production volumes, delivery dates, and new designs, the council argues, so losing them would hit output just as Ukraine pushes to make more of its own weapons.
The draft resolution has already been sent to the Cabinet of Ministers for approval.
“We consider that the proposed reduction of the limit does not account for the staffing needs of defense production,” the council says.
A workforce that takes years to build
Ukraine’s defense industry is still growing, with new plants, expanding capacity, and new technologies, the council adds. Raising the share of Ukrainian-made weapons in the forces, localizing components, and cutting reliance on imports all require more specialists, not fewer.
These teams are built over the years, the manufacturers add. Companies invest in finding and training people who master specific technologies and production processes, and keeping them is what lets firms plan expansion and take on new commitments to the military.
Uncertainty at the worst moment
Cutting the exemption limit would add uncertainty, just as the state expects producers to raise output. The fallout could affect both manufacturers and military units awaiting their weapons.
The council urges the Economy Ministry to drop the cut to 85%and asks the Defense Ministry and the Cabinet to maintain exemptions of up to 100% for qualifying defense workers. It offers to share data on the industry’s staffing needs and help assess how the change would affect defense orders.
The reservation rules must reflect the growth of the defense industry and Ukraine’s need for more of its own weapons, it concludes.

====================================================================================================

Hegseth saw the future of war, but cannot lead the way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:19 UTC
01:44:19 KST

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth got one big thing almost right when he addressed junior leaders of the joint force the other day. Too bad he keeps getting so many other things so badly wrong.
What he got right, and also captured elegantly in a historical analogy, was the direction in which warfare is developing, and in which the Pentagon must go as well, even though it is not set up to do so.
Hegseth labeled the effort Project Agincourt. The name comes from a famous battle in 1415, when the English were badly outnumbered by a French force composed largely of men-at-arms in heavy armor. However, the English showed up with archers carrying longbows and supplied with vast numbers of arrows made by fletchers working near the front lines.
Illustration:Tania Chou
The English won.
Hegseth chose the analogy because it shows the strategic importance of so-called cost-exchange asymmetries. They become a factor when one side — the French in 1415, the US or Russia today — comes to the battlefield with weapons that are sophisticated, but also expensive (“exquisite,” in today’s jargon), such as plated armor and steeds, or F-35s and Patriot interceptors.
The other side — the English then, the Iranians or Ukrainians today — can then counter with weapons that are just barely good enough individually, but devastating in vast numbers, and above all inexpensive and expendable (ie, “attritable”).
The English had their arrows, the Iranians and Ukrainians (and many others) use drones. Those become especially lethal in swarms, and then downright diabolical when networked and guided by artificial intelligence to kill autonomously.
OUT OF STEP
The US’ problem is that its military is out of step with this development. It might still have the world’s most powerful forces, but in the words of Dan Driscoll, who last month quit as secretary of the army, “the US Army in 2025 looked shockingly similar to that of 1975.”
That is, it relies far too much on exquisite weapons that are great for, say, bombing Iranian nuclear facilities out of the blue, as in last year, but are uneconomic against seemingly limitless barrages of attritable Iranian ordnance, as in this year.
As Council on Foreign Relations defense and national security program director Michael Horowitz said, “militaries cannot endlessly block salvos of US$35,000 Shahed-136 attack drones with US$4 million Patriot missiles.”
So the US military needs to shift its procurement and its tactical and strategic models away from exquisite weaponry and toward what Horowitz calls “precise mass.”
That, in a nutshell, is the objective of Project Agincourt. It takes existing initiatives in the Pentagon, reorganizes and turbocharges them, in the hope that the joint force can bring precise mass to the battlefield before, say, the Chinese do the same.
One nuance is that the goal is not to replace the equivalents of plated armor with longbows.
“I am often asked whether the US military should prioritize high-volume, low-cost equipment or exquisite programs,” Driscoll writes; “unfortunately, the answer is both.”
Hegseth calls that a “high-low mix.”
So far, so good — and so intellectually harmonious between Hegseth and Driscoll. To see the Pentagon’s problem, you have to look beyond Hegseth’s speech.
Driscoll published his essay in Foreign Affairs just before Hegseth announced Project Agincourt, which grew out of efforts Driscoll had been coleading, along with other top brass such as General Randy George.
However, George was dismissed by Hegseth in April, and Driscoll resigned just weeks before Hegseth’s address.
GENERAL EXIT
Moreover, Driscoll and George are among a procession of senior leaders whom Hegseth has shoved or nudged out. (In his speech, the secretary boasted that he had reduced the number of generals and admirals by 10 percent and has another 10 percent to go.)
Driscoll met with US President Donald Trump before resigning and told him that Hegseth was damaging the military with all the firings and constant turmoil. Specifically, Driscoll reportedly said that Hegseth was undermining the innovation campaign that Driscoll was pushing — the one now labeled Agincourt — by purging so many of its leaders.
The clashes extend beyond personalities and include substantive differences. Driscoll makes clear that the precise-mass revolution cannot happen without breaking open the oligopoly of defense contractors who today make all those exquisite weapons, each in a deliberate information silo so that it cannot interoperate with any others used by US or allied forces.
He also assigns a huge role to US’ allies, with whom the Pentagon must coordinate.
INDUSTRIAL CAPACITY
“The United States’ greatest deterrent, the foundation of its diplomatic clout and the primary factor in its ability to win on the modern battlefield will be its collective allied industrial capacity and military interoperability,” Driscoll wrote.
His vision is to modernize the military readiness of the entire, united West. That point is lost on Hegseth and Trump, who in word and deed keep antagonizing the US’ allies, in effect pushing partner nations such as Canada toward weaning themselves from the US rather than doubling down on interoperability.
The best that can be said about Hegseth’s announcements is that he has put into catchy words what deeper thinkers such as Driscoll have been saying for a long time. If it takes a bit of plagiarism to prepare the US military for the rest of the century, so be it.
SHOCK AND AWE
What is worse is that Hegseth also proved once again why he is incompetent. At heart, he is still the TV personality and culture warrior who prefers to shock, polarize and divide rather than the leader who unites, rallies and builds.
“We’re no longer the woke department,” Hegseth boasted on that stage. “No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals.”
No secretary of defense before or (presumably) ever again could sound so buffoonish in a role of such responsibility.
Hegseth has grasped where warfare is going because thoughtful people like Driscoll explained it to him. Yet Hegseth keeps ousting every Driscoll in sight. If the US one day loses to tomorrow’s longbow archers, the blame would belong to mediocrities like this secretary of war.
Andreas Kluth is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering US diplomacy, national security and geopolitics. Previously, he was editor-in-chief of Handelsblatt Global and a writer for The Economist. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Michael Mazza On Taiwan: Taiwan Will Fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:17 UTC
01:44:17 KST

Taiwan might just give up. That’s the argument Simon Shuster made in The Atlantic’s October issue. The US is unreliable, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) leadership is aligned with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Taiwan does not have the military capability to defend itself in a prolonged war without help. What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on.
Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. It regularized the arms sales process, enhanced the military-to-military relationship, and treated Taiwan more like a normal diplomatic partner. Despite the announcement of a record arms sale at the end of 2025 and continuing improvements in bilateral military ties, however, Trump’s second term has given Taiwan more cause for concern.
Trump has deferred additional arms sales in order to avoid angering Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), openly echoed Xi’s talking points about Taiwan, and publicly implied that Taiwan is too far away for the US to defend. Considering the larger context — for example, Trump’s refusal to prioritize Russia’s defeat in Europe and his threats to invade Greenland, a territory of NATO member Denmark — responsible Taiwanese national security planners must question American dependability.
Like Trump, current KMT leader Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) has spoken in language reminiscent of Xi’s own. During her trip to China in the spring, she described people from China and Taiwan as sharing a Chinese identity and encouraged Taiwan to embrace Xi’s goal of the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.” Cheng is controversial even within the KMT, but certainly there are elements within the party that see war as simply unimaginable, which in turn has inhibited preparing for it.
That is one reason why Taiwan’s defense modernization efforts are not keeping pace with China’s own advances. In 2026, the opposition in the Legislative Yuan stripped all of the funding for domestic drone production from a special defense budget and later advanced a separate drone bill that arguably did not prioritize the Ministry of National Defense’s need for unmanned capabilities. Taipei has been making important investments in its military, but this year’s challenges are emblematic of a decades-long failure to fund a defense budget that is appropriate for the threats Taiwan faces.
Yet despite these challenges, reports of Taiwan’s impending submission to the CCP are greatly exaggerated. Rather, there are good reasons to think Taiwan will defend itself vigorously if Beijing opts for aggression.
First, most people in Taiwan have embraced a Taiwanese identity. Even those who recognize a shared cultural endowment with People’s Republic of China citizens see Taiwan as distinct from China. This is why three decades of public polling show consistent trend lines: growing identification as “Taiwanese” rather than “Chinese” or “Both Taiwanese and Chinese” and plummeting support for unification. What is more, despite the crisis of confidence facing democracies around the world, an overwhelming majority of Taiwanese believe multiparty democracy is a good way of governing — and they act like it. In the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance’s Global State of Democracy Initiative, Taiwan ranks seventh globally on democratic participation. It is far from clear that, as Shuster argues, “voters in Taiwan can feel the balance of power shifting, and many will choose the side that looks more stable, even at the risk of their own liberties.”
Despite its political polarization, moreover, Taiwan is a country with remarkable social cohesion and an active civil society. When the Matai’an barrier lake overflowed in September last year, numerous nonprofit organizations and thousands upon thousands of individual volunteers leapt into action. Taiwan is a country in which people trust each other, care about each other, and are willing and eager to help each other. They have a proven track record of pulling together during natural disasters. There is not much evidence that they would respond differently during a manmade disaster — like, say, an invasion.
This is backed up by numerous public polls and survey experiments, which show that Taiwanese are willing to defend Taiwan. For example, earlier this year, Academia Sinica’s American Portrait survey found, according to a Taipei Times report, “that 58.7 percent of respondents would be willing to resist Chinese invasion ‘at all costs’ even if the US does not deploy any military forces to help Taiwan.”
To be sure, a war with China is not something to wish for. Taiwan will be outmanned and outgunned, even if it does succeed in kicking its military acquisition and reform efforts into high gear. Energy security is a major weakness, as is economic resilience. The US may come to its aid, but that’s no guarantee of victory.
Even so, Taiwan has three crucial advantages. First, its mountainous island geography favors the defenders. Second, Taiwan’s defenders know that geography well, and their potential attackers do not. Fighting on home territory provides both tangible and moral benefits. But Taiwan’s third and perhaps most important advantage is its people. Taiwanese love their country and do not want to see it swallowed up by a vicious predator. They believe it is worth defending. Their societal characteristics make them well suited to pulling together in service of such a defense.
If China opts for force, the road ahead will be trying. But Taiwan will fight.
Michael Mazza is senior director for research at the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security (formerly the Project 2049 Institute) and a senior non-resident fellow at the Global Taiwan Institute.

US launches probe into Taiwan firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:16 UTC
01:44:16 KST

The US International Trade Commission (USITC) has launched a Section 337 investigation naming Taiwanese technology companies, including Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海), Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) and Quanta Computer Inc (廣達), as respondents. The Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) pledged assistance if needed.
The USITC said on Friday in a statement that it had voted to institute an investigation under Section 337 of the US Tariff Act of 1930 into certain vertical power delivery systems, related components and computing devices incorporating such systems.
The investigation covers 20 companies from Taiwan, China, Germany and the US, the commission said, adding that it has not made any decision on the merits of the case.
Photo: Bloomberg
The probe involves power delivery technology used in artificial intelligence servers, MOEA International Trade Administration (ITA) said.
In addition to the three Taiwanese companies, China-based Luxshare Precision Industry Co (立訊精密) and Foxconn Industrial Internet Co (工業富聯) are also named as respondents, it said.
The ITA said the investigation stems from a complaint filed by Massachusetts-based power technology company Vicor Corp on Sept. 9, with a supplemental filing submitted the following day.
Vicor alleges that vertical power delivery systems, related components and computing devices incorporating the technology infringe its patents when imported into or sold in the US. The company is seeking a limited exclusion order to bar imports of the accused products, as well as cease-and-desist orders to prevent their sale in the US.
The ITA said Section 337 investigations typically take 12 to 16 months to complete. If the complainant prevails, the USITC can issue exclusion and cease-and-desist orders restricting the affected products from entering or being sold in the US market.
The agency described the case as a patent dispute between private companies being handled under US Section 337 procedures. It said the government respects the legal process and would continue to monitor developments, maintain contact with the affected companies and provide assistance if necessary.
The USITC said the case would be assigned to an administrative law judge, who is to hold a hearing and issue an initial determination on whether Section 337 has been violated before the commission conducts its own review.
The commission said it would set a target date for completing the investigation within 45 days after instituting the probe.
Any remedial orders issued would take effect immediately and become final after 60 days unless disapproved by the US Trade Representative, it added.
Delta Electronics said it places great importance on intellectual property rights and compliance with laws in all jurisdictions, and would respond to the investigation through legal procedures to safeguard its rights and interests.
The company declined to comment further because the case is now in legal proceedings, but said its products are not currently affected by the investigation.

‘Winning without a fight’ could spark war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:15 UTC
01:44:15 KST

A Taiwanese friend said that he has never believed that China would attack Taiwan, as winning without fighting has always been Beijing’s preferred strategy.
China would prefer to achieve its objectives without a devastating war. If intimidation, economic pressure and political warfare could persuade Taiwan to accommodate Beijing’s demands, why risk an amphibious invasion?
However, the conclusion that China therefore “will not attack” does not follow, and confidence that Beijing would never use force could contribute to miscalculation.
The important question is not whether Chinese leaders want a major war. They have powerful reasons to avoid one. The question is whether Beijing might conclude that it can achieve its objectives through limited coercion because Taiwan lacks the political will to resist.
Former chief of the general staff admiral Lee Hsi-ming (李喜明) identified this problem. Taiwan’s willingness to fight is difficult to quantify, but persistent domestic attacks on the country’s willingness to resist could create a dangerous impression in Beijing: Taiwan does not want to fight and might collapse once serious pressure is applied.
That goes to the heart of deterrence. Deterrence depends not only on military capability and resolve, but also on an adversary’s perception of them.
Taiwan might possess anti-ship missiles, drones, mines, air defenses and favorable geography, but if China believes Taiwanese society would fracture after several days of a blockade, cyberattacks or military pressure, it could discount those advantages.
Imagine, then, that Beijing does not initially plan an invasion. Instead, it expects Taiwan to fold under coercion.
Large military exercises become a partial blockade. Cyberattacks disrupt communications and financial networks. Economic pressure intensifies. Perhaps China conducts limited strikes while presenting Taipei with political demands.
What if Taiwan refusess?
Beijing would face a choice: Retreat and accept the political consequences of failed coercion, or escalate. A blockade could become strikes; strikes could provoke retaliation; further escalation could draw in the US and Japan. A strategy intended to avoid war could produce one.
History repeatedly demonstrates that wars can begin not because leaders desire prolonged conflict, but because they expect their opponents to collapse quickly. The danger lies in discovering that assumption was wrong only after coercion has begun.
“China will definitely attack” and “China will never attack” are analytically unsatisfactory. Both arguments claim certainty about a decision dependent on changing circumstances, perceptions and calculations. A better question is what could change Beijing’s cost-benefit calculation. One is Taiwan’s political endurance.
The ideal outcome for Washington and Taipei is not for Taiwan to resist heroically until US forces arrive. It is for a war to never begin. That requires Beijing to believe, before a crisis, that Taiwan cannot be rapidly coerced into submission.
Taiwan therefore needs to send Beijing two messages: You cannot easily defeat us and we will not easily quit.
If China truly prefers to “win without fighting,” deterrence requires convincing it of something paradoxical: Without fighting, you cannot force Taiwan to submit. Even with fighting, you cannot be confident of doing so.
The greatest danger in the Taiwan Strait might not be that Beijing has already decided to wage war. It might be that China convinces itself that Taiwan will surrender before a real war is necessary — and discovers too late that it was wrong.
Simon H. Tang is an adjunct professor at California State University, Fullerton, who lectures on international relations.

New Yorkers attend auction for old subway signs, seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:14 UTC
01:44:14 KST

New York’s subway is known for being dirty, noisy and sometimes flooded, but that does not stop people from flocking to grab a seat, sign or other memorabilia at a unique annual auction.
In south Brooklyn, shoppers hoping to get a slice of the city’s transit service waited for hours to trawl through an open-air market organized by city authorities. Each person gets a maximum of 45 minutes to search, allowing others to come in after them.
Nori Juba, 61, found what he was looking for: a large sign bearing the name of Grand Central station, along with the numbers of the subway lines he takes every day.
Photo: AFP
The train system is “old and creaky and it’s outdated,” he said. “But I think that’s what makes it interesting. And this piece of metal is dirty. It smells like a subway station, but there’s something about it that makes it real New York, one of a kind in the world.”
The prices are not cheap: a medium-sized sign cost about US$500, while larger ones can run past US$1,000.
The iconic orange plastic seats from the New York subway go for about US$900 each.
Celebrities are sometimes spotted at the market, and this month, filmmaker Spike Lee was stopping for pictures with fellow shoppers.
He showed off the metal sign he just bought, marked “Penn Station,” the subway stop for Madison Square Garden — the arena where his beloved Knicks basketball team plays.
New York’s Metropolitan Transportation Authority has always resold its signs to collectors, but more recently opened up sales to the public, said Paul Dvoskin, the director in charge of the program.
“Five years ago, an idea was born to hold a garage sale of sorts, and to let people just come in and purchase these items” in person, he said. “We called it a grab-and-go back then, and it just ended up being significantly more popular than we ever thought it would be.”
Officials do not disclose how much the two-day sale brings in, but it draws about 4,000 people each year.
The plastic seats, sold only since last year, are the most popular items.
So are the MetroCards, the small yellow magnetic cards emblematic of the city, which have recently been retired from use. They sell for US$6.

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) set a record for its southernmost deployment of a coast guard vessel as the vessels Chiayi and the Penghu reached Palau’s Pulo Anna Island on Saturday in a cooperative exercise between the two countries.
The island, about 217 nautical miles (401km) southwest of Koror in the Palauan state of Sonsorol and 1,220 nautical miles from Taiwan’s southernmost point, Oluanpi (鵝鑾鼻), is the furthest south a CGA vessel has sailed.
The two vessels are in Palau for the coast guard’s second diplomatic visit to the country.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
They docked at Malakal Harbor on Tuesday last week.
The coast guard ships Hualien and the Taipei visited last year, but did not sail that far south.
Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr and his wife boarded the Chiayi on Thursday for a reception ahead of Double Ten National Day on Saturday.
The Chiayi and the Penghu departed on Friday for a two-day joint patrol of Palau’s exclusive economic zone about 200 nautical miles southwest of Koror, accompanied by Palauan officials.
Personnel from the Palauan Division of Maritime Security and Fish and Wildlife Protection, Lieutenant Jim Kloulechad and Sergeant Gerald Ringang were on the Penghu as part of the patrol, the CGA said.
Kloulechad thanked the CGA for helping Palau patrol its waters, saying the relationship was important to the two sides.
Only five people live on Pulo Anna Island, Kloulechad said, adding that the visit was a valuable opportunity to ensure their safety and well-being.
Taiwan and Palau have continued to deepen cooperation through joint patrols, maritime search-and-rescue exercises and personnel exchanges since signing a coast guard cooperation agreement in 2019, the CGA said.
The joint patrol helped safeguard Palau’s maritime security, and further bolster bilateral maritime law enforcement and emergency response capabilities, it added.
Palau does not have an independent national coast guard, instead relying on its marine law enforcement division and international partners to patrol its exclusive economic zone, combat illegal fishing and conduct search-and-rescue operations. Its maritime fleet includes long-range patrol vessels such as the PSS Remeliik II and PSS Kedam, as well as smaller patrol boats and surveillance equipment.
It works closely with the US Coast Guard, which can enforce maritime laws in Palau’s exclusive economic zone under a bilateral agreement, and receives training and other assistance from Japan.
Taiwan contributes through diplomatic visits and joint patrols, which helped broaden bilateral maritime law enforcement and emergency response cooperation.

Architect fights to save India’s significant historic sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:12 UTC
01:44:12 KST

For three decades, Abha Narain Lambah has pioneered efforts to preserve some of India’s most significant historic sites — from ancient Buddhist caves and Islamic tombs to Hindu temples and Mumbai’s imperial-era Gateway of India.
“My journey began as a concerned citizen,” the 56-year-old architect said. “I felt very strongly about the way heritage was completely left to decay.”
In the world’s most populous nation and one of its fastest-growing major economies, urban development is advancing at dizzying speed.
Photo: AFP
“It’s only in the last 30 years that we’ve managed to have city-wide listings and heritage regulations, and even those are very limited to cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad and Kolkata,” she said. “Historical buildings are neither protected by government, nor do local communities or owners have the funds to look after them.”
Lambah’s career began partly as an activist, after she worked with US architect Joseph Allen Stein, whose modernist buildings in Delhi set concrete and local stone among courtyards and gardens.
“He showed me this interface between old and new,” she said.
After moving to Mumbai in 1995, Lambah encountered a city where hundreds of historic buildings stood outside government protection.
“A lot of colonial heritage was technically considered too young to be declared national monuments,” she said. “The challenge was: What do you do about historic buildings, that are not protected under central government rules and have no funding?”
She has since also supported conservation plans for more than 20 world heritage sites.
That includes a 15th-century Hindu temple at Hampi, Le Corbusier’s 20th century masterpieces in Chandigarh, Rajasthan’s Amer Fort and Bodh Gaya, where Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment.
In Mumbai, where ornate Victorian Gothic facades and geometric Art Deco buildings face salt air, neglect and redevelopment, she turned to the challenge of saving the city’s wider architectural fabric.
“Every city faces this challenge — there is a warp and weft of new and old, and a tug of war between development and conservation,” she said. “These are cultural assets.”
At Mumbai’s 19th-century David Sassoon Library and Keneseth Eliyahoo Synagogue, Lambah helped bring together private donors, foundations and community groups to rescue the Victorian heritage site and the blue-and-white house of worship after their restoration stalled due to lack of funds.
“When people have been working, living and even commuting through these historic buildings, they feel intensely passionate about them,” she said.
Her work to restore Mumbai’s 19th-century Bandra railway station had to be carried out around trains and commuters.
“Random people commuting past would tap me on the shoulder and say... ‘We know what you’re doing — you’re doing it for us.’”
She pointed to her work at Mumbai’s Royal Opera House, once facing demolition, but with its ornate gilt interiors and grand auditorium now intact.
“We could have lost it entirely,” Lambah said. “Instead, its life has been extended and it has become a cultural space that is actively used by people.”
Lambah is also working to conserve Mumbai’s most recognizable landmark, the Gateway of India, built under British rule, but shaped by Indian architectural traditions and embraced by generations since the country’s independence.
People at times ask her why India should conserve “a vestige of colonialism,” to which she responds: “These buildings are as Indian as they get, because they’re built from the stone, tears and sweat of Indians.”
“I have to look at the entire palimpsest of 6,000 years of India’s built heritage. What doesn’t seem convenient can’t be left out or forgotten,” Lambah said.
When she started working in Mumbai, there were only two qualified conservation architects in the entire city, she said.
“Today, there is a larger number of young architects who are studying conservation, who are practicing,” she added.
That growth is welcome, but the task remains enormous, she said.
“We have to catch up,” Lambah said. “It’s a long, arduous road ahead.”

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11

A man charged along with Super Micro Computer Inc co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw (廖益賢) of conspiring to send cutting-edge chips to China in violation of US export controls pleaded guilty, court documents said.
Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun (孫廷瑋), a former outside contractor described by US authorities as a “fixer” who allegedly aided in the sales, pleaded guilty on Thursday at a hearing in federal court in New York as part of an agreement with prosecutors, court filings showed.
Prosecutors claimed the men were part of a scheme to send Nvidia Corp-powered servers to an unnamed Southeast Asian company and then divert them to Chinese customers.
Photo: Lam Yik Fei, Bloomberg
The charges came in a high-profile crackdown on alleged smuggling of restricted artificial intelligence (AI) technology to China. Super Micro said in August, following an independent probe, that its current senior management had no knowledge of the purported scheme.
A sentencing date was scheduled for Sept. 8 next year.
Liaw has pleaded not guilty in the case. The US also charged Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang (張瑞滄), who served as a general manager in Super Micro’s Taiwan office. Chang has not appeared in the case.
The scheme allegedly involved efforts by the defendants and others to evade scrutiny by auditors from Super Micro and the US government — including by falsifying records and setting up “dummy” servers to which they affixed serial numbers with a hair dryer, an indictment said.
San Jose, California-based Super Micro is not named as a defendant in the case. Asked for comment on the guilty plea, the company referred to its prior statements and said it was cooperating with the government’s investigation.
“We have taken action against all identified employees and those parties no longer have any relationship with Supermicro,” Super Micro chief executive officer Charles Liang (梁見後) said in a public letter to stakeholders in March. “Mr. Wally Liaw has also resigned from the company’s board of directors,” he said.
Washington has restricted sales of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The indictment said Nvidia’s B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, were subject to the restrictions.

MOA seeks to standardize pet care training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:07 UTC
01:44:07 KST

The Ministry of Agriculture (MOA) is developing standardized educational materials for pet care professionals to ensure quality of training across institutions, and plans to work with the Ministry of Labor to introduce a pet care technician certificate, an MOA official said.
The growing pet market is driving demand for pet care professionals, but training materials remain inconsistent in quality and content, the MOA said.
To standardize pet care professionals’ expertise, the ministry has commissioned the Chinese Society of Animal Science to compile professional teaching materials covering pet care, physiology and nutrition, it said.
Photo: Yang Yuan-ting, Taipei Times
The materials would be published as early as 2028 for use at high schools, vocational schools and colleges offering programs in animal science, veterinary medicine and related fields, it said.
The ministry previously published guides for dogs and cats focusing on basic care and how to live with pets, including appropriate foods and basic information on the Animal Protection Act (動保法), Department of Animal Welfare Deputy Director Chen Chung-hsing (陳中興) said last month.
The new materials would be professional reference books rather than guides for general pet owners, with the first phase focusing on common pets such as dogs and cats, he said.
Although specific pet businesses engaged in dog or cat breeding, sales or boarding must have at least one staff member who meets one of several qualifications, including completion of 200 hours of professional training and receipt of a certificate of completion, course materials are not standardized, with different schools of thought sometimes offering conflicting guidance and some materials focusing on specialized small-animal veterinary medicine, Chen said.
The new materials would provide standardized references for training pet care professionals and help students develop more advanced professional knowledge, he said.
The Ministry of Labor already has some relevant certifications, including one for pet grooming, and once standardized teaching materials are in place, the ministries would work together to introduce a pet care technician certification, he said.
No launch date has been set as details still need to be discussed, he added.

Military police’s role to be expanded to combat: MND
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:04 UTC
01:44:04 KST

Taiwan is expanding the Military Police Command’s mission from policing to also include combat operations and drastically increasing the size of its forces, disclosures from the Ministry of National Defense (MND) showed.
The military police would be expanded from 5,600 troops to 11,000 troops, the ministry said in the five-year force structure plan.
The command’s mission would be transformed from policing and presidential security to a motorized infantry force to defend the metropolitan Taipei region and critical infrastructure against decapitation strikes, the document showed.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
The military police’s 1st Garrison Combat Team is responsible for defending southern Taipei, including the Boai Special Zone, and would cooperate with the 66th Marine Brigade out of Songshan Air Base and the Army Guandu Area Command, it said.
If Taiwan is attacked, the Military Police Command’s volunteer personnel and conscripts would be tasked with the defense of key government structures in the Boai Special Zone, major roads, bridges and energy infrastructure, it said.
A senior defense official on Sept. 25 said on condition of anonymity that the ministry’s proposed budget for next year indicates the military police’s intended future role.
The military police’s procurement plans are focused on urban fighting, asymmetric warfare and air defense against low-flying drones, with considerable emphasis on the last mission category, they said.
The US-made M-ACE is a mobile anti-drone system consisting of several linked, vehicle-mounted electro-optical/infrared sensors, radar and electronic warfare modules, directed energy effectors and a 30mm Bushmaster chain gun, with a 3km effective range, they said.
The important features of the M-ACE vehicles are the artificial intelligence-driven targeting software’s capability for precision engagement while avoiding firing on civilian structures, the use of air burst shells and the ability to use a jamming device, the official said.
The military police has been given priority for new T112 assault rifle and rifle-mounted Smartshooter smart optics, designed to engage uncrewed aerial vehicles at 400m, they said.
The ministry’s NT$140 million (US$4.39 million) budget for remote-controlled weapon stations carrying anti-tank guided missiles, which are likely to be mounted on light tactical vehicles or Clouded Leopard infantry fighting vehicles with Javelin missiles.
The proposed military police budget also includes assault ladder vehicles and armored personnel carriers.
Funds are earmarked for a presidential command vehicle, disguised as a civilian car, featuring heavy armor protection and a satellite communication system hardened against jamming.
The procurement plans indicate that the military police would take on greater responsibility for combat operations in urban areas without relinquishing their traditional counter-terrorist and presidential protection roles.

EDITORIAL: Chiang’s ship is taking on water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:03 UTC
01:44:03 KST

With the Taipei mayoral election quickly heating up, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) campaign team has finally started to get serious this month, but a major mudslinging initiative and several sloppy mistakes have drawn a larger wave of public criticism, while sporadic municipal issues continue to crop up, raising concerns about whether the city government’s wheels are coming off.
Just a few months ago, Chiang of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) was widely expected to win handily in Taipei, traditionally a political stronghold for the KMT and with no major third-party candidates this year. KMT supporters regarded him as a frontrunner to become a presidential candidate, and they had high hopes that other KMT candidates running for office could ride his coattails to victory, not just in Taipei, but across the country.
However, his main challenger, Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈柏洋), has rapidly gained ground with his unconventional campaign style, becoming a media sensation, a phenomenom named the “Ocean Wave” by Shen’s supporters. The nation’s election spotlight has quickly turned to Taipei, catching Chiang off-guard, with his performance being scrutinized by a nationwide audience.
Taipei City Government departments have had their fumbled handling of many municipal issues in the past few months questioned, including child protection, food safety and infrastructure construction, as well as being suspected of giving preferential treatment to the mayor’s family. Yet Chiang continued to reply to questions evasively, either blaming the central government or giving vague answers such as “the city government is addressing the issue.”
Opinion polls, even from generally pro-KMT organizations, show Shen’s approval rating quickly catching up to Chiang’s, with only a single-digit percentage point gap remaining. Chiang’s campaign has had to shore up its defenses as it shifts tactics from ignoring Shen to aggressive mudslinging, in an attempt to reclaim the narrative and reproduce the successful outcome of his negative 2022 campaigning.
The first sign of Chiang’s shifting tactics was when the campaign announced on Oct. 2 that five of the KMT’s Taipei legislators would become spokespersons. Among them are Lo Chih-chiang (羅智強) and Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯), known for their combative partisan politics. They launched their first “attack” the next day, quoting an article Shen wrote 12 years ago, and misleadingly accusing him of advocating the “decriminalization of illicit drug use” and “giving out drugs in communities.”
Shen quickly clarified that his article was discussing drug prevention policies in many countries, including Taiwan. Chiang and his team continued to try to misrepresent Shen’s stance, in hopes of stirring hostility and public anxiety, as he did in 2022 by distorting and criticizing the government’s COVID-19 response measures, although he had supported many of them himself as a legislator.
It backfired, offending people across a swathe of professions, as health providers, disease-prevention officials, social workers, and firefighters and paramedics voiced their contempt and concern that the vilification of the drug harm reduction programs by Chiang’s campaign would disrupt an effective, evidence-backed public health policy. Chiang’s Facebook post about Shen’s drug stance triggered a record-breaking backlash, garnering more than 400,000 mostly negative comments in less than a day.
Chiang does not seem eager to face the challenge head-on, declining or delaying some interview requests. Although he had resisted Shen’s calls for a public debate, the pair last week agreed to a televised debate on drug policy. In an interview on Friday, Chiang said some voters were “so irrational” during last year’s recall campaign. Later that same day, amid criticism, he said that “one must be humble before the will of the people” and that he respected voters’ judgement.
Meanwhile, Chiang’s campaign and the city government are being criticized for a series of issues, from allegations of misuse of city resources for election ads to continued food poisoning issues in schools and city agencies releasing error-ridden artificial-intelligence-generated materials.
With less than 50 days until the elections, Chiang’s team needs to sail straight, but the continually sloppy and lax attitude of the city government has many residents wondering if Chiang is even competent enough to steer the loose ship he is tasked with leading.

Line platform gives farmers helping hand: institute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:44:00 UTC
01:44:00 KST

The Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute said it has developed a Line-based pest-management platform for rice and cucumber farmers that reduced average query times by at least 90 percent to less than a minute in field tests.
Rice is an important staple crop with an annual output value of more than NT$35 billion (US$1.1 billion), while small cucumbers are harvested repeatedly and require pest and disease control throughout the harvest period, the institute said last week.
It therefore developed the platform to help farmers promptly get information on pest and disease management, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from the institute’s X account
Farmers previously managed pests and diseases based on experience, or by searching for information online or making telephone inquiries, the institute said.
That can be time-consuming and the information is scattered and inconsistent, it said.
The new platform uses Line, which most agricultural workers already know how to use, so they do not need to download or learn another app, it said.
Users can search for pest and disease information by crop and images of damage symptoms, it said.
The platform then recommends pesticides and provides dilution ratios and pre-harvest intervals, the institute said.
The system can retrieve the latest pesticide-use information from the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency’s Web site, it said.
Users can scan pesticide-product barcodes to access safe-use information and use a separate feature to calculate dilution ratios, it said.
Field testing showed that the platform reduced average query times to less than a minute from about 10 minutes with manual data retrieval, a time reduction of at least 90 percent, it said.
It can also assist agribusinesses, grain dealers, agricultural cooperatives or local production and marketing groups in contract farming management and pesticide-use compliance, it said.
The institute said it plans to license the technology to an agricultural information service provider to build, operate and maintain the system for eventual use by agribusinesses and their contracted farmers.

Urban trees more than numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:59 UTC
01:43:59 KST

The number of trees does not necessarily determine how much shade a city has. The most important factor for street shade, urban cooling and the quality of public spaces is the canopy cover built up over years of growth. When mature trees disappear, planting replacements does not immediately restore the shade that was lost. The changes to Taipei’s urban trees in the past few years are not merely a landscaping issue, but a urban environment and public governance matter.
To understand what is happening to Taipei’s tree cover, we can look at two sets of numbers: the number of trees removed and the extent of canopy cover shown in satellite imagery. This reflects the area of ground covered by leaves and branches when viewed from above.
Publicly available data show that Taipei removed 1,425 trees in 2024. That number rose to 3,164 last year — an increase of 1,739 trees, or about 122 percent in a single year. In total 4,589 trees were removed over two years.
Satellite imagery provides the canopy cover data. Shen Sheng-feng (沈聖峰), a researcher at Academia Sinica’s biodiversity research center, uses imagery from the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-2 satellites to analyze urban areas and surrounding mountain forests separately. The results showed that Taipei’s urban tree canopy covered approximately 628 hectares in 2024, falling to about 615 hectares this year. This net decline of approximately 13.7 hectares over two years is equivalent to almost 20 soccer fields.
Canopy covers figures are significant because even planting new trees does not mean that urban shade immediately increases. Newly planted saplings need years to provide a comparable amount of shade to mature trees with large canopies.
The 13.7 hectare decline in tree canopy cannot be directly attributed to trees being cut down by the city government. Tree removal, land development, heavy pruning, transplantation and natural disasters all cause changes in tree canopy.
We do have clear records for some cases. This year, a 40-year-old rosewood tree near Dongmen Market was scheduled to be transplanted, but was instead cut down by a contractor. The authorities penalized the contractor and sought NT$325,000 in compensation.
The number of trees removed annually in Taipei increased by about 122 percent in one year, while during the same period, satellite data showed a decline in urban tree canopy.
Data on each of the 3,164 trees need to be made available. It should be established what their species, ages and trunk diameters were; why they had to be removed; whether safety assessments had been carried out; and which among them could have been transplanted or preserved in place.
Urban tree management should establish a system that can be monitored over the long term. It should include itemized records of tree removals, transplants, assessments and replacement plantings, and publish annual tree-canopy coverage rates and changes for each administrative district. Long-term standard indicators for mature tree canopy should be established, ensuring that different city administrations can be compared with the same standard across the years.
We already know about the 13.7 hectare decline in Taipei’s urban tree canopy over two yearsthrough satellite imagery. Why 3,164 trees were removed, and exactly how much those removals contributed to the decline in tree canopy should be answered through complete and publicly accessible data.
Urban greening should not be measured simply by how many trees have been planted. What matters more is how much mature tree canopy — capable of providing shade, cooling the city, and continuing to grow — the city would have in the years to come.
Hsiao Hsi-huei is a freelancer.

Saudi Arabia yesterday kept its main international airport closed and moved Riyadh schools online as Yemen’s Houthi rebels threatened new airstrikes across the kingdom, a day after a missile attack killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.
Saturday’s strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen’s Iran’s-backed Houthis and the kingdom, and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the US-Iran war. US President Donald Trump said he was considering whether to join Saudi Arabian strikes against the rebels, a scenario that could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through a crucial waterway and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.
The attack was condemned by other countries, with Russia saying hostilities needed to end “through political and diplomatic means,” and German Minister of Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul describing it as “a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation.”
Photo: AP
The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the “heinous attack” and stressed “total solidarity” with Saudi Arabia, saying it would continue “to remain by its side in its defence of its territory and its infrastructure,” calling on the Houthis to cease their attacks.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reaffirmed the country’s commitment to Saudi Arabian sovereignty, and said attacks “targeting civilians and vital infrastructure are utterly unacceptable and pose a serious threat to regional peace and stability.”
The US also said it “strongly condemns” the attacks, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying the attacks “must stop now.”
Saudi Arabian authorities said schools in the capital would hold classes online until the end of the week.
The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
The dead included four Saudi Arabian citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese, a Saudi Arabian statement said.

Stop hostile talk, Taiwan urges China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:58 UTC
01:43:58 KST

Taiwan yesterday urged China to stop its hostile rhetoric toward Taiwan as the US welcomed President William Lai’s (賴清德) commitment to Taiwan Strait stability in his Double Ten National Day speech.
Lai on Saturday described Taiwan as a “city upon a hill” and said that “Taiwan cherishes peace, but we will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said Lai’s speech “disregards facts, distorts the truth, misleads the public and reveals ulterior motives.”
Photo: CNA
Taiwan is part of China and Taiwan’s future “can and must be decided jointly by all the Chinese people, including our compatriots in Taiwan,” it added.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said China has no right to dictate Taiwan’s future, urging Beijing to stop hostile rhetoric that could heighten cross-strait tensions and to abandon the use of force or coercion to change the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait.
The Republic of China (ROC) and the People’s Republic of China (PRC) exist as equals and are not subordinate to each other, a reality recognized by the international community and the consensus among Taiwanese, the ministry said.
Taiwan’s future can only be decided by its 23 million people, and China has no right to interfere, it added.
“Taiwan will continue to collaborate with global democratic partners and remain committed to safeguarding national sovereignty and supporting Taiwan’s sustainable development, as well as preserving peace, stability and prosperity across the Taiwan Strait and the region,” the ministry said.
A US Department of State spokesperson said the US welcomed Lai’s commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait in his National Day address.
Separately, Brookings Institution senior fellow and former American Institute in Taiwan chairman Richard Bush said he was struck by the moderate tone Lai took in his speech while discussing cross-strait relations.
Lai took a pragmatic view of potential threats while remaining open to dialogue, he said.
In Taipei, National Taiwan University political science associate professor Chen Shih-min (陳世民) yesterday said Lai’s speech reflects three main principles: maintaining stability, expressing a clear stance and reiterating Taiwan’s commitment to safeguarding peace.
It also did not provide Beijing with any excuse for military coercion or provocation against Taiwan, he said.
Lai’s statement that Taiwan “welcomes the US and China managing their competition through dialogue and reducing the risk of conflict and war” makes it clear that the nation welcomes a dialogue between the US and China, he added.
The president reiterating that Taiwan is a protector of peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait and that enhancing defense capabilities is not a provocation but to deter war also demonstrated that Taiwan would not be the first to use force and that it opposes all forms of violence, Chen said.
That dispels China’s narrative that “Taiwan is a disturber of peace and stability or a provocateur in the Taiwan Strait,” he said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) during a meeting last month with US President Donald Trump said China and the US fought together against Japan in World War II, Chen said.
Lai in his speech set the record straight, saying that it was the ROC government that fought alongside the US during the war, he added.
The president also detailed Taiwan’s economic achievements, and the figures demonstrated that as the nation reduces its dependency on China, its economy boomed and it became more connected to the world, Chen said.
National Chung Cheng University Department of Political Science professor Tsai Jung-hsiang (蔡榮祥) said Lai’s speech reiterated the definition of peace, rectified historical facts and formed alliances with the international community.
Lai emphasized that peace must be maintained through strength, while providing a clearer definition of what that means: developing asymmetric weapons, enhancing national defense capabilities and aligning with the combined strength of Indo-Pacific nations, he said.

Military quadbot exhibited at tech forum in Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:57 UTC
01:43:57 KST

A military-use quadruped robot dog was presented at the Taiwan-Japan Future Technology Forum in Taipei yesterday, by the event’s organizer, the Indo-Pacific Strategy Thinktank.
The robot is built on the Vision 60 platform developed by US-based Ghost Robotics, which has been adopted by the US Marine Corps, Army and Air Force. In addition to autonomous reconnaissance and surveillance, the robot can be armed and engage targets, and has been used in Japanese Self-Defense Forces military exercises.
The Vision 60 has an IP67 protection rating, allowing it to withstand immersion in one meter of water for 30 minutes. It operates at temperatures from minus-40°C to 55°C.
Photo: Chen Yu-fu, Taipei Times
Powered by an Nvidia Jetson system, the robot can carry a 10kg payload and operate for more than three hours per charge, compared with about 90 minutes for similar products. Its modular design allows a malfunctioning leg to be replaced quickly.
Wu Jung-tsan (吳榮燦), deputy general manager of Tansimo Robotic Manufacturing, said mission-specific equipment allows the platform to perform tasks ranging from inspections and search and rescue to security and detection.
The robot can be equipped with light detection and ranging (LiDAR) technology for autonomous navigation and obstacle avoidance across complex terrain, including indoor and underground environments without GPS signals. With a wireless charging station, it can return to recharge independently, supporting extended monitoring missions while reducing maintenance needs.
A six-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic arm can open doors and handle objects, including ammunition. With a gripping force of up to 11.3kg, it can move objects weighing up to 3.75kg, making it suitable for explosive ordnance disposal, disaster response and other hazardous tasks.
Imaging options include a low-light camera capable of operating at 0.0001 lux and a pan-tilt-zoom camera with 33x optical zoom, 360° horizontal rotation and infrared night vision at distances of up to 50m. A security payload combines target detection and tracking with low-light and thermal imaging, while AI-powered image recognition can support personnel management at industrial facilities.
Wu said the Vision 60 took part in a Japanese military exercise in the first quarter of this year, demonstrating that quadruped robots have moved beyond the laboratory into practical use.
Deploying unmanned systems for some high-risk tasks can improve operational efficiency and reduce risks to personnel, he said.

CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) said on Saturday that it would leave its gasoline and diesel prices unchanged this week, despite volatile international crude oil prices last week.
Formosa Petrochemical Corp (台塑石化) matched CPC’s price adjustments for this week, information posted on the company’s Web site yesterday showed.
It would be the fourth consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have kept their domestic fuel prices unchanged, even though crude oil prices rose last week amid concerns over supply disruptions caused by military tensions in the Middle East.
CPC said under its floating fuel price mechanism, which tracks a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai crude and 30 percent Brent crude, the average international crude oil price rose to US$114.65 last week from US$112.54 per barrel the week before.
However, a stronger New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$31.810 against the US dollar last week, compared with NT$31.850 the week before, helped CPC lower its oil purchasing costs to some extent, the company’s data showed.
State-run CPC said it is leaving retail fuel prices unchanged in line with government price stabilization measures meant to ease inflationary pressure and keep fuel cheaper than in neighboring markets to improve Taiwan’s competitiveness.
Retail gasoline prices this week are to remain at NT$31.2, NT$32.7 and NT$34.7 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would stay at NT$29.9 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.7 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

Palestine postpones legislative elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:51 UTC
01:43:51 KST

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11 next year, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA said.
Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
Photo: AP
The move leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority’s credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas’ party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas’ presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The Palestine Liberation Organization’s Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in east Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, adding that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs Gideon Saar wrote on X that Abbas’ “attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability.”
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi said earlier this week.
Hamas called the postponement “a step in the right direction” and said further talks should focus on rebuilding Palestinian institutions and holding elections at a later date.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year.
Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas’ Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election, but behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan.
“Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership,” Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan’s faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

====================================================================================================

France’s students feel disowned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:50 UTC
01:43:50 KST

When adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outside France might have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought: “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or “That’s just the French being French.”
However, the situation that has provoked the high-school walkouts and teenage anger is most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations.
In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development education rankings; schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms, and, in a school in Bagnolet, no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 to more than 30 today; and half of primary and high schools missing teachers at the start of the school year — many of them with no substitutes or replacements.
Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, said that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for 1 hour and 45 minutes each way between Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers — all for 2,100 euros (US$2,353) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only 56 percent of what they are in Germany — even as more than 200 billion euros in public subsidies finds its way annually to businesses.
So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt; instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first.
They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw — all from police munitions. Hundreds more have been injured in some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little more than a week, almost half the number of arrests made during the months of yellow vest protests from 2018 to 2020.
It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high-school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. However, the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer garbage fires with police charges.
“Sure some people were burning trash cans,” said Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycee Paul Eluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.”
On the other hand, she and her fellow students certainly felt the tear gas that the police launched in response.
Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mold, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Sylla Wague would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police.
However, she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable with May 1968, to take part.
“If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions, and so this is for the next generation of students and teachers,” she said.
I cannot imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021, The Lancet found that 75 percent of French 16-to-25-year-olds exhibited signs of “eco-anxiety,” telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workers actively dislike artificial intelligence and feel pessimistic about the future it portends.
As for Sylla Wague, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, in France and elsewhere.
For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading.
Centralized policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools.
A far-right government, the kind Sylla Wague said she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, right-wing politicians have called for harsher sentences and more law and order, but this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been.
Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen — it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own. On n’est pas mal eduque, on n’est pas ecoute (“We’re not poorly educated; we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign brandished at Paris’ Place de la Republique on Tuesday last week.
Responding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered the example of how thoughtful architecture could have more impact than one might expect.
The technical high school he previously worked in — Gabriel Peri, in an extremely poor area — reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction, which, Richards said led to a calmer climate for students and teachers.
“Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he said.
However, a real answer does not stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During French President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard.
“Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us,” Sylla Wague said.
Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness,” the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with.
Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. He is the author of Generation Desperation.

Reports of elder-abuse exceed 26,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:50 UTC
01:43:50 KST

More than 26,000 cases of domestic violence against elderly people were reported last year, Ministry of Health and Welfare data showed, highlighting the need to protect Taiwan’s 4.67 million people aged 65 or older.
Reports of suspected domestic violence against elderly people rose to 26,684 cases last year from 20,182 in 2022, Department of Protective Services data showed.
There were 14,292 cases in the first half of this year, with psychological abuse accounting for 44.1 percent, physical abuse 37.9 percent, and stalking or harassment 25.5 percent, with some cases involving multiple forms of abuse, the department said.
Photo: Chiu Chih-jou, Taipei Times
Nearly 58 percent of the cases involved the elderly person’s descendants, while 27.1 percent involved a spouse or partner, it added.
Economic abuse was recorded 362 times last year, up from 161 in 2022, it said.
In the first half of this year, 188 entries were recorded in the economic-abuse classification, or 1.32 percent of the total number of reported cases, the department said.
Elder abuse is often associated with family dynamics and the distribution of family resources, department Director Kuo Tsai-jung (郭彩榕) said yesterday.
Supporting families and helping them improve their relationships are important in preventing this kind of domestic violence, she said.
The ministry has worked with local governments to promote public awareness of elder abuse as well as the 113 hotline for domestic violence, while bolstering reporting mechanisms, Kuo said.
Economic abuse often involves psychological and physical violence as well, stemming from the pressures of long-term care and family dependency, especially when older people cannot work, she said.
In some cases where adult children depend on money from their parents, they might have feelings of low self-worth due to employment setbacks or health issues, and could turn to emotional manipulation and verbal and physical abuse to control their parents, she said.
If family conflicts are not addressed, more serious violence could occur if parents lose their ability to care for themselves, household resources become scarce or their children have substance abuse problems, she added.
In cases such as these, social workers usually conduct interviews and provide psychological support to help parents establish financial and emotional boundaries, while guiding parents toward legal resources to protect themselves, Kuo said.
One way to prevent elder abuse is to ease the caregiving burden on family members by utilizing long-term care services, Providence University adjunct associate professor of social work Wang Hsiu-yen (王秀燕) said.
It is important to improve communication and caregiving skills by deepening an understanding of the physical, psychological and social aspects of aging, as well as proper care for people with dementia, she said.
In addition, older people who are still mobile should be encouraged to take part in activities to prevent them from becoming socially isolated, Wang said.
Elderly people and their families should report any abuse and seek help, she added.

Manila opens largest OFW service center in Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:48 UTC
01:43:48 KST

The Philippines yesterday opened its largest overseas Filipino worker (OFW) service center in Taipei, with hopes of establishing two more in central and southern Taiwan over the next two years, the country’s Overseas Workers Welfare Administration said.
The OFW Global Center-Taipei is the third such facility worldwide, following centers in Hong Kong and Kuala Lumpur, Administrator Patricia Yvonne Caunan said.
It is the largest to date, she added.
Photo: CNA
The center is in the same building as the Manila Economic and Cultural Office (MECO), the Philippines’ de facto embassy in Taiwan, in Taipei’s Neihu District (內湖).
It is designed as a one-stop hub where Filipino migrant workers in Taiwan can access government services, welfare assistance and training without returning to the Philippines.
The facility includes training spaces, a cafe offering free coffee, a karaoke room and areas for government services.
Planned activities include Mandarin classes, financial literacy programs, computer and artificial intelligence training, and courses on content creation and entrepreneurship, Caunan said.
“Skills are the best protection for migrant workers. You can never take away skills,” she said, adding that the training can help workers pursue new career opportunities or start businesses after returning to the Philippines.
She also highlighted the emotional challenges faced by migrant workers living away from their families, saying the center would provide counseling and opportunities for social interaction to help address feelings of homesickness.
“Just walk in and make sure that you make yourself comfortable in our cafe,” Caunan said when asked how Filipino migrant workers can access the center’s services.
Regarding plans to expand the service network in Taiwan, Caunan said the administration hopes to establish similar centers in Taichung and Kaohsiung over the next two years, with feasibility studies under way.
“We don’t want our OFWs in Kaohsiung to travel all the way to Taipei just to experience this,” she said, adding that the proposed centers would likely be near MECO’s offices.
The new center in Taipei reflected the Philippine government’s commitment to supporting its citizens overseas, MECO Chairperson Corazon Avecilla-Padiernos said.
“Wherever our Filipinos may be, the care and support of our government must remain within their reach,” she said in her remarks at the opening ceremony.
Among those welcoming the center was Geraldine G. Domingo, 54, a Taipei-based caregiver who has worked in Taiwan for 12 years.
“This is very convenient now because everything is here already, what a Filipino overseas worker needs,” Domingo said.
She was particularly interested in Mandarin classes to help Filipino workers communicate with Taiwanese employers and friends, and also supported opening centers elsewhere in Taiwan.
Judith Vidal Mendoza, 37, another Taipei-based caregiver who has worked in Taiwan for eight years, said the facility would make Philippine government services more accessible.
“For me, as an OFW, it is very important for us to have access,” Mendoza said, referring to document processing services that Filipino workers need while living abroad.
Migrant workers often have to take time away from their jobs to handle administrative procedures and hoped the center would offer faster document processing and additional services, she said.
About 191,000 Filipino migrant workers were living in Taiwan as of the end of August, including more than 61,000 in Taipei, New Taipei City and Taoyuan, the Ministry of Labor said.
