Hurricane Simon turns into a level 4 storm near Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:45 UTC
01:43:45 KST

Hurricane Simon strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm and was expected to make landfall or skirt the coast of west-central Mexico yesterday, the US National Hurricane Center said.
Fluctuations in strength are expected until the core of Simon reaches the coast, with a maximum wind speed of 249kph, the center said.
“Significant or catastrophic wind, surge, and rainfall appears likely over portions of west-central Mexico” on Saturday night and yesterday, it added.
Photo: Reuters
“Preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion shortly in the hurricane warning area,” it said.
It comes as Florida assesses the damage from Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which killed at least four people in the southeastern US.
Simon is the latest in a busy hurricane season in the Pacific, where the powerful El Nino is weakening wind shear, allowing the storms to gain in strength.
Mexico’s navy had evacuated about 100 people from settlements along the country’s west coast due to the storm.
In the Pacific tourist resort of Puerto Vallarta, the skies were cloudy on Saturday, but the sea was still relatively calm.
The government of Jalisco state, where Puerto Vallarta is located, declared a red alert for several municipalities.
The airport has also suspended operations.
However, residents of Puerto Vallarta, which sits on a huge horseshoe-shaped bay that helps defuse the power of a hurricane, appeared largely unfazed by the threat.
While shop owners sandbagged the entrances to their stores and boarded up the doors and windows, there was little sense of impending disaster.
“What people are most scared of is that the water will reach a tall height... like it did with Hurricane Kenna,” furniture shop owner Paulina Perez said, in reference to the 2002 storm that killed at least four people.
She put up a sign in her shop that read: “Simon, be brief, be peaceful.”
“Simon says: ‘Everything is going to be alright,’” someone had spray-painted on a board, in a play on the name of a popular children’s game.
Moises Villasenor said he was “a little worried” as he filled sandbags to protect his small hotel, situated about three blocks from the seafront.
On the whole, “we’re very positive,” he said.
Tourists also exuded calm.
“We’re going to enjoy it as much as we can, even if it’s just for today,” said Edna Morales, 41, who arrived on Friday with her husband.
Authorities said they would order residents to take shelter starting at 5pm.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林： Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:45 UTC
01:43:45 KST

1. 他手術醒來時並不覺得痛。
ˇ He felt no pain when he awoke from surgery.
χ He felt painless when he awoke from surgery.
Photo: AdobeStock l 照片:AdobeStock
註：painless 是「無痛的」、「不使人感覺痛苦的」，用於事物，如 painless death（善終）。說人覺得痛或痛苦，須用 to feel a pain；說人不覺得痛或痛苦，該用 to feel no pain。
2. 恐懼與自我懷疑是創意的死敵。
ˇ Fear and self-doubt are the deadly enemies of creativity.
χ Fear and self-doubt are the dead enemies of creativity.
註：dead 是「已經死去」的意思。表示「致命的」、「勢不兩立」、「極端的」，應該用deadly。deadly 通常作形容詞，例如：deadly poison（劇毒）、deadly hatred（深恨）、deadly enemy（死對頭）等。
3. 他做事很認真負責，頗受同事尊敬。
ˇ Being a conscientious worker, he is respected by his coworkers.
χ Being a conscious worker, he is respected by his coworkers.
註：conscious 是「有知覺的」、「神志清醒的」。例如：
He is conscious of his responsibility. 或
He is conscious that he has a responsibility.
（他感到他有責任。）
表達「認真負責的」、「按良心辦事的」應用 conscientious。此外，當代美語裡，除律師、學者外，使用「同事」一詞時多用 co-worker，少用 colleague，以免讓人覺得自命不凡。
4. 我一想起這件事總是感到慚愧。
ˇ The very thought of it made me ashamed.
χ The very thought of it made me shameful.
註：ashamed 是「（感到）羞恥」或「慚愧」，用於人；shameful 是「可恥的」，指事情或行為。試觀察下列句子：
This is really shameful, and I feel ashamed of it.
（這事真可恥，我感到慚愧。）
5. 「真討厭！」他帶著鄙夷的語氣說。
ˇ “What a nuisance!” he said with a contemptuous snort.
χ “What a nuisance!” he said with a contemptible snort.
註：contemptible 是「可鄙的」、「無恥的」、「下賤的」，例如：
He is a most contemptible fellow.
contemptuous 是「傲慢的」、「瞧不起人的」，例如：a contemptuous look, a contemptuous remark 等。
Exercises
A. 他認為這是一種可恥的行為。
He considers this kind of conduct to be completely __________ .
1. ashamed 2. shameful 3. shamefaced 4. shame
B. 因為有打麻醉劑，拔牙時她不覺得痛。
Because she had been given an anesthetic, she __________ when her tooth was pulled out.
1. felt not pain 2. felt painless 3. felt no pain 4. spared no pains
Answers:
A. 2 B. 3

Notes from Central Taiwan: Beijing’s intimidation tactics in Taiwan and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:44 UTC
01:43:44 KST

Cognitive warfare, says the Ministry of National Defense (MND), is the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) use of “political, economic, cultural, military and legal means, with the intent to divide internal unity and undermine social stability” in Taiwan. Last week offered several examples.
PRC media in October last year reported that the Chongqing Municipal Public Security Bureau had opened an investigation into Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the DPP’s mayoral candidate for Taipei in next month’s election, for “Taiwan independence” activities. This was a cognitive warfare ploy, designed to unsettle the targeted person and to establish the idea that it has legal jurisdiction over Taiwan and its people.
Last week Taipei prosecutors argued for an 18-month prison term for a private investigator Cheng Yung-chin (鄭永津), who was charged with violations of the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法), along with fellow investigator Hsieh Yi-chen (謝乙辰) and two others over the surveillance of Shen. Cheng was said to have accepted NT$360,000 (US$11,299) from two Hong Kong residents to surveil Shen.
Photo: Tien Yu-hwa, Taipei Times
The purpose of this steady drip-drip of PRC threats (recall that PRC officials have said that Taiwan independence activists will be imprisoned) against Shen is intended to instill fear into the candidate. It is also intended to put pressure on others who might be tempted to adopt his political stances.
Another kind of warning was also the subject of a trial last week. Japanese activist in Taiwan Yaita Akio, who was attacked in Taichung in July, said on Twitter that the Taichung District Prosecutors Office was seeking a five-year sentence for the perpetrator, Liao Gangfa (廖港發), after finishing their investigation. The Taichung District Prosecutors’ Office indicted Liao on Tuesday on charges of assault, public insult and participation in a criminal organization.
TRANSNATIONAL PRC REPRESSION
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Yaita said that violence on the PRC’s behalf is occurring regularly in democratic countries. He pointed to the surveilling of the son of President William Lai (賴清德) in the US, the attack on a Chinese restaurant named “Xi Jinping” in South Korea (vandalized by four Chinese nationals) and the vandalism against the Kami Comedy Club because a performer had publicly mocked PRC dictator Xi Jinping (習近平). He could have added a string of other incidents, including the planned ramming attack on the car of Taiwan Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) in Prague in March of 2024.
All of this is a form of cognitive warfare, designed to suppress speech and actions inimical to PRC imperialism against Taiwan, and fill the targets with anxiety and fear.
This month also saw the US arrest of a woman acting as an unregistered agent of China and surveilling President Lai’s son and his family near Seattle in September last year. It was amusing to watch pro-PRC types on Twitter claim that the purpose of the surveillance was to highlight the fact that Lai’s son lives in the US (a common issue with Taiwan’s elites is that their children are citizens of other countries). But the PRC’s allies in Taiwan, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and its sock puppet, the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), have already done that. It is a staple of their election attacks on Lai.
Photo: Hsu Kuo-chen, Taipei Times
Hence, the claim that the surveillance existed to highlight where Lai’s son lives was itself a form of cognitive warfare. It was designed to conceal and downplay the actual reason for the surveillance by shifting the issue to what Lai was doing, not on what the PRC was doing.
The purpose of the surveillance was simple, though many commentators who do not have children did not get it: nothing messes with a target’s head more than threats to their children. I know this from personal experience, as my children were regular targets of threats in my blogging days. The surveillance existed to remind Lai that his children could easily be targeted, to stress him out with fear and anxiety. Action against leaders’ children, from medieval kidnapping of Kings’ sons through George Washington’s authorized but abandoned plot to have Prince William kidnapped in 1782, to the 1944 German kidnapping of the son of Hungarian Dictator Miklos Horthy to force Hungary to stay in the war on the German side, is a common policy in history.
Lai is well aware of the leverage his son represents. It should be noted that the team hired to surveil Puma Shen also tracked his daughter’s movements.
PRC COGNITIVE WARFARE IN TAIWAN
Television host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) appeared to be the target of cognitive warfare last week. A PRC-military-affiliated account, called “Junzhengping” (鈞正平), attacked Tsai on social media after he attended the opening of Puma Shen’s campaign headquarters on Sunday. The post, though it did not attack Tsai by named, appeared to accused him of “reaping profits in mainland China while flirting with Taiwan independence,” saying people like him would “pay an unbearable price.” The attack, along with other social media comments, suggests that the PRC may leverage Taiwanese business activities in the PRC to silence them.
The staunchly pro-KMT United Daily News (UDN) put out a commentary warning that Tsai could face “dual political and social death” in the PRC, showing how the local pro-PRC papers are quick to reinforce the latest Beijing cognitive warfare claims. UDN later took down the commentary.
Another element of Beijing’s cognitive warfare was on display in a South China Morning Post article on how Beijing would govern a post-annexation Taiwan (Amber Wang, “Beijing’s policy advisers map out how post-reunification Taiwan could be governed,” Oct. 6, 2026). The piece mapped out various policy proposals by PRC “scholars.” The key point of the piece from the cognitive warfare perspective is the continuing insistence that Taiwan will be governed as Hong Kong is. Thus, anyone forwarding a comparison of annexed Taiwan to current Hong Kong is forwarding PRC propaganda.
The major goal of PRC cognitive warfare is to get Taiwan to surrender without a fight. It has two main axes of attack. On one hand the PRC insists that annexation is inevitable, that PRC power is overwhelming and will continue to grow, and that Taiwan has no chance of resistance. On the other hand, it dangles the possibility that annexation will not be so bad — if accepted without resistance, the PRC “scholars” say, it can be like Hong Kong. The SCMP article followed that latter approach, saying that Taiwan’s future status under PRC control will depend on how much resistance there is to annexation.
The reality, as many have noted, is that PRC promises cannot be trusted. Moreover, the proper model for Taiwan governance by the PRC isn’t Hong Kong but its treatment of the other would-be nations it has subjugated, Tibet and East Turkestan (Xinjiang).
The idea that these ideas come from “scholars” also provides them with a veneer of legitimacy that will enable actual scholars and journalists to comment on them as if they were sincere and not propaganda, helping to further spread them. Of course, they also plausibly buttress the nattering of PRC supporters and shills who claim that Taiwan will be in the same position as Hong Kong — assuming they “make a deal” — just surrender by another name.

Indonesia releases eight orangutans rescued from fires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:43 UTC
01:43:43 KST

Eight orangutans rescued in over the past weeks from blazes that tore through Borneo Island have been released into a protected forest, Indonesian authorities and rescuers said yesterday.
The apes were saved from several locations razed by fires — mostly plantations near their forest homes — in the West Kalimantan Province on the Indonesian side of Borneo last month, the Indonesian Ministry of Forestry and the YIARI wildlife rehabilitation foundation said in a statement.
The orangutans, three mom and baby pairs as well as two male teenagers, were relocated on Friday to the Batu Nyambu Protected Forest in West Kalimantan, a 23,000-hectare reserve with primary and secondary forest cover.
Photo: AFP / Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation
YIARI CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the animals to a new location was a “necessary step” when their habitat was no longer safe.
“Protection of habitats will always be a top priority to ensure orangutans continue to have safe forests to live in, but as long as their habitat remains threatened, rescue is one of the best options we can take to help them survive,” Sanchez said.
The reserve was chosen due to availability of food and water sources as well as its connectivity to other forests, YIARI operational director Argitoe Ranting said.
“We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat,” Argitoe said.
Indonesian authorities and YIARI rescued 46 orangutans from threats of fires between August and Friday, local natural resources agency head Murlan Dameria Pane said.
Orangutans are critically endangered, and about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, the World Wildlife Fund said.
Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned fires were burning in habitats containing 52 percent of Borneo’s orangutan population.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but the fires have intensified this year because of the El Nino, set to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.

South Korea completes Arctic shipping route trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:42 UTC
01:43:42 KST

A South Korean container ship yesterday returned from a trial voyage through the Arctic, testing an alternative route opened by melting sea ice as conflict in the Middle East disrupts global shipping.
The PanStar Acro made the round trip to Europe in less time than the conventional route through the Suez Canal, officials said, but the initiative has drawn concerns that increased traffic could accelerate Arctic ice loss.
The Arctic route could also expose operators to sanctions-related risks, because it runs along Russia’s northern coast.
Photo: Yonhap via Reuters
“The PanStar Acro, which embarked on a trial voyage along the Arctic shipping route on August 22, docked at Jaseongdae Pier in Busan Port,” the South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said in a statement.
The vessel sailed through the Arctic’s Northern Sea Route before making port calls at Felixstowe in the UK, Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Gdansk in Poland, and returning via the same route.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung hailed the successful voyage, saying it “shortened the one-way sailing time by 10 days compared with the conventional route via the Suez Canal.”
“It also allowed us to gain valuable experience operating a South Korean container ship in polar waters and to collect navigational data,” Lee wrote on X.
The Middle East conflict, sparked by US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, has roiled global shipping, prompting governments and operators to explore alternative routes.
However, environmental advocates warn that expanded commercial shipping along the Northern Sea Route could threaten the fragile Arctic ecosystem.
Major shipping companies have pledged to avoid Arctic routes, citing environmental concerns.
The Northern Sea Route is generally more accessible during the warmer months, when reduced sea ice makes navigation easier, although ice conditions remain unpredictable and some vessels still require icebreaker assistance.
Without making any reference to the environmental concerns, Lee said the successful trial mission would help his country “prepare for the era of Arctic shipping routes.”
“We will transform Busan and the southeastern region into a ‘southern maritime capital region’ and ensure that this new sea route becomes a new engine of growth,” he added.

16:43:42 UTC
01:43:42 KST

A technology worker developed a bald patch after months of overtime and late nights, but showed improvement after four months of treatment and lifestyle adjustments, a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) practitioner said on Saturday.
A 32-year-old project manager in the tech industry developed a coin-sized bald patch on the back of his head after six months of working overtime and staying up late under significant stress over the launch of a major company project, traditional Chinese medicine practitioner Chuang Ke-chun (莊可鈞) said.
He was diagnosed with alopecia areata, a prevalent non-scarring form of hair loss, which typically presents as clearly defined round or oval smooth bald patches, often without visible redness, inflammation or scaling on the scalp, she said.
Many people only discover the condition when looking in the mirror, styling their hair or being told by others, Chuang added.
The condition is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy hair follicles, disrupting normal growth cycles, she said.
While high-stress environments, emotional trauma and irregular sleeping habits might be associated with the onset of the condition, genetic predisposition and other autoimmune disorders can also increase risk, she said.
Hair loss should not be attributed solely to psychological stress without medical evaluation, she added.
In traditional Chinese medicine, treatment approaches are tailored to each patient’s physical constitution, sleep quality and emotional state, she said.
Common TCM therapies aim to tonify the liver and kidneys, nourish and move the blood, soothe the liver and calm the mind, she said, adding that acupuncture might also be incorporated into the regimen.
People are advised to make lifestyle adjustments, such as maintaining regular routines, ensuring adequate sleep and managing stress through exercise, meditation or yoga, Chuang said.
A balanced diet should include high-quality proteins such as fish, meat, eggs and beans, alongside foods rich in iron, zinc, vitamin D and B vitamins, while avoiding extreme calorie restriction, she said.
The scalp should be washed gently, using the fingertips to massage rather the fingernails to scratch, and excessive heat should be avoided when drying the hair, Chuang said.
As hair growth takes time and response rates vary, people should attend regular follow-up appointments rather than becoming overly anxious about short-term results, she said.
Anyone noticing sudden patchy hair loss should seek prompt medical evaluation, she said.
Chuang cautioned against applying irritants such as raw ginger or garlic to the scalp, warning that such folk remedies can cause contact dermatitis and aggravate scalp conditions.

Shen holds first campaign motorcade; Chiang urges debate coordination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:41 UTC
01:43:41 KST

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) held his first campaign motorcade in the capital yesterday, while incumbent Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) urged Shen’s camp to discuss arrangements for a televised election debate or debates.
Shen’s motorcade event started in Datong District (大同) yesterday afternoon and drew thousands of supporters, some of whom followed the procession on scooters, carrying campaign banners.
In Taiwan, campaign motorcades are a common feature of local elections, allowing candidates to greet voters along neighborhood streets while serving as a public show of support for them.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Accompanied by his supporters, Shen arrived at Dalongdong Baoan Temple, a local Taoist temple and religious center, where he was greeted by crowds of wellwishers.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the motorcade, Shen reiterated his call for four debates, saying a single event would not allow enough time for detailed discussions of individual policy issues. He also said his campaign would send staff to Monday’s coordination meeting.
Earlier yesterday, Chiang was asked about Shen’s proposal to hold four debates during an event in Taipei.
Photo: Chen Chih-chu, Taipei Times
The DPP candidate had made the proposal to Chiang in person when the two met at a temple event on Saturday evening.
Chiang said the focus should be on actually holding debates, rather than turning them into a campaign talking point, adding that calling for more debates did not necessarily mean winning an election.
He said both camps have agreed in principle to broadcaster TVBS holding a televised debate or debates and signed consent forms, with the broadcaster scheduled to meet representatives of both sides today to discuss the details.
Chiang said his campaign team would attend and urged Shen’s representatives to do the same.
The local elections will be held on Nov. 28.
The elections are also known as the “9-in-1” elections because voters in Taiwan’s 22 cities and counties will cast ballots for candidates vying for nine different local government posts, including city mayors, county magistrates, and city and county councilors.
Also up for grabs are seats for township chiefs and chiefs of Indigenous districts in municipalities, township councilors and Indigenous councilors in municipalities, and ward chiefs. In total, elections will be held for 11,051 officials at all levels of local government.

Athletes open up for mental health day talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:37 UTC
01:43:37 KST

Karl-Anthony Towns has been traded from Minnesota, lost the conference finals and won the NBA title for his childhood team — and still feels he is in the period of grief that began six years ago.
Just 10 days before the New York Knicks’ banner-raising celebration, the All-Star big man marked World Mental Health Day by sharing his ongoing emotional journey following the death of his mother to complications from COVID-19.
Entering the first game of this year’s NBA Finals, he said he felt “this very big calm” wash over him. He was taken back to amateur youth games with crowds so small he could spot his mom from anywhere.
Photo: AP
“I felt like it was kinda just me, her and the game of basketball,” he told the audience gathered on Saturday by the nonprofit Project Healthy Minds. “I was able to be like an artist out there. I was able to have my paint brush and have a canvas with the court. And I was able to just paint a beautiful picture for her about the love I have for the game. The love I have to show the world because of her.”
There was a time when he had lost that love for the game. Towns, whose bright smile became a constant image of the Knicks’ championship run, said basketball “felt hollow” after his mother’s death. “I didn’t know if I wanted to do it anymore,” he said.
However, Towns found some solace in Arnie Kander, a well-known strength and wellness coach.
“Just to be heard, to be able to talk to someone you can trust, be able to really unload all that pain onto it and allow them to understand your feelings and articulate your feelings the right way, it makes life much lighter,” he said. “And I felt myself getting lighter every time we kept talking.”
Project Healthy Minds hopes Towns’ example would inspire others to seek mental health care. The tech nonprofit runs a free online marketplace for finding therapy, psychiatry, support groups and other services. Its annual World Mental Health Day festival in New York offers an all-day schedule of yoga, art therapy and speakers.
Speaking on Saturday with Towns was Boardroom chief executive officer Rich Kleiman, the longtime manager for NBA superstar Kevin Durant and a new member of Project Healthy Minds’ board.
Kleiman said that these sorts of conversations are growing more prevalent among athletes. DeMar DeRozan and Kevin Love kick-started the conversation eight years ago when DeRozan tweeted about depression and Love then published a first-person essay about anxiety. Kleiman recalled trading stories about anxiety attacks with Love for several hours one night shortly afterward.
Most players would not feel that comfortable constantly telling their story, Kleiman said. Mental health is not a topic of discussion in the locker room, but he said players are certainly more aware of its impact.
“They just carry so much weight and speak to so many people,” Kleiman said before the panel. “I think it says a lot that Karl Towns is feeling comfortable enough right before the season starts to be able to be so open about it.”
Another panel brought together former NFL wide receiver Brandon Marshall and Gotham FC forward Midge Purce for a conversation about finding purpose outside of performance. Marshall, a six-time Pro Bowl player who publicly shared his borderline personality disorder diagnosis in 2011, said therapy showed him how to “connect with his brain.” He even started taking his therapy sessions in the cafeteria to normalize it for others.
Purce discussed her evolving definition of “tough.” Raised by her dad, she said she grew up believing toughness meant “no tears.” However, she credited her teammates with teaching her “it’s OK to feel sad and upset.”
“I think tough is being able to feel all those things that are touching you and touching your heart, but still finding that resilience to go forward while living all of it,” she told the crowd.
Saturday’s sports focus offers a glimpse into Project Healthy Minds’ future programming.
With interest in women’s sports growing and live sports remaining a powerful convener in an otherwise fragmented media landscape, Project Healthy Minds chief executive officer Phil Schermer finds that athletes are well suited to bring their message to the masses.
Athletes, according to Schermer, also shape the US public’s notions of strength. It makes sense to him that they could then model that “it is strong to talk about your emotions.”
“There need to be more men — and more men who are archetypes of strength — being vulnerable,” Schermer said. “Being willing to talk about these things. And role modeling that it can serve as fuel for your greatest success.”
The Knicks championship run became a rare moment of monoculture, Schermer said.

Microsoft calls for AI ‘emergency brake’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

Microsoft Corp chief executive officer Satya Nadella said companies should treat powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models as potential insider threats, assume they could be compromised and create an “emergency brake” system to prevent agentic models from going rogue.
Nadella said that those deploying advanced AI should not rely on assurances from model makers.
“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” Nadella wrote on Saturday in a post on X. “Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”
Photo: Bloomberg
The statement comes as Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Inc have disclosed a spate of incidents in the past few months involving their AI models acting in unintended ways, ranging from behaviors such as an Anthropic model submitting a false tip in a police homicide case, to several hacks of third-party Web sites. These disclosures have fueled concerns about the security risks of cutting-edge AI and renewed conversation about a so-called AI kill switch.
Microsoft’s AI researchers released a set of guiding tenets that place limits on the company’s development of its most advanced models on Sept. 14, following calls from industry leaders for slowing down frontier models and focusing on safety.
The guidelines said AI models should not have rights or legal personhood, be engineered to escape human control or deceive users, or complete a task that would require violating their governing principles.
Nadella’s safety tips include not relying on a single AI model for critical decisions, keeping tamper-proof records of agents’ actions and subjecting AI systems to independent audits. He also called for disclosures of major AI failures or breaches and for enterprises to share details about what went wrong so others can bolster their safeguards.
“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behavior we can observe, limits we can test and actions we can always contain.”
“In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it,” he added.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has so far taken a largely hands-off approach, but Trump’s newly launched AI task force on Friday said that developers are required to report and resolve security incidents or face potential unspecified consequences.
“Companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm,” the group, dubbed the Super Intelligence Force, said in a statement following the disclosure of a breach by Anthropic. “Delayed notification, inadequate corrective action and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated.”
Debate over how to mitigate AI risks has accelerated following a spate of alarming breaches along with a now-viral essay from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that warned of the technology’s catastrophic risks. Amodei and other AI leaders have called for additional government regulation and industrywide coordination to help mitigate the risks, prompting some pushback from other tech and policy officials.
Unlikely allies Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) and former US Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan have argued for robust use of existing laws to prevent the dire outcomes that AI safety advocates warn about. At the same time, Khan has criticized having industry police itself, calling it “a recipe for disaster” and indicating there is room for future AI legislation.

Only Russia is responsible for the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said yesterday as he vowed to press ahead with strikes on Russian oil refineries, despite criticism from US President Donald Trump, who blamed him for high diesel prices and said he should be replaced.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack yesterday shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskiy wrote on X.
Photo: Reuters
“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do so,” he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump’s comments, writing on X that Zelenskiy was leading the country through a war for its independence.
“He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well,” Sybiha wrote.
Trump on Saturday said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskiy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
The US president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskiy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices.
Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.

Paul Seixas makes cycling history at just 20 years old
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:32 UTC
01:43:32 KST

France’s rising cycling talent Paul Seixas made history at the Tour de Lombardy when he became its youngest winner ever on Saturday after riders protested safety concerns.
The 20-year-old Seixas broke away with about 20km left to win the one-day race in northern Italy that had been dominated by the currently injured Tadej Pogacar for the previous five years.
“I had the feeling today would be a great day. It feels like a dream,” Seixas said.
Photo: AP
He savored the winning feeling after racing for nearly six hours.
Spanish Vuelta winner Enric Mas was second at 48 seconds behind, followed by Italian Giulio Ciccone.
The Tour of Lombardy started in 1905. It is one of cycling’s elite one-day Monument races.
Seixas finished this summer’s Tour de France fourth overall in his debut.
Also this season, Seixas became the youngest winner of the Fleche Wallonne at 19 and finished runner-up to Pogacar, a five-time Tour champion, at the Strade Bianche and Liege-Bastogne-Liege.
The start of the race was delayed for about five minutes when riders did not begin as scheduled in a protest to denounce unsafe racing conditions and the recent death of a cyclist.
Star rider Remco Evenepoel spoke for the peloton at the start line in Bergamo.
“Unfortunately, we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague, so we want to make this statement to show the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do,” Evenepoel said.
“So this is why we want to spend five minutes more still to make our statement towards organizations, to the public, to everybody that is following cycling, because we cannot accept the fact that people are dying.”
British rider Finlay Tarling died following a serious incident in the Volta a Portugal race in August when the 19-year-old was run over by a car that entered the road. The driver reportedly missed the signs from stewards and entered the road going in the opposite direction of the race.

Japan should sell arms to Taiwan: ex-army chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:32 UTC
01:43:32 KST

Japan should include Taiwan among the destinations eligible for arms sales, former chief of staff of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force Kiyofumi Iwata said at a conference in Taipei yesterday.
Japan had abolished restrictions on arms sales, allowing it to provide weapons to 17 countries with which is has defense and technology agreements, which excludes Taiwan, Iwata told the Taiwan-Japan Future Technology Forum hosted by the Indo-Pacific Strategy Thinktank.
Taiwan should be included in the future, he said, calling Japan and Taiwan an inseparable community with a shared destiny.
Photo: CNA
The First Island Chain serves as a crucial breakwater, preventing Chinese military expansion into the Western Pacific, he said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) “China dream” aims for dominance in the western Pacific, making Taiwan, situated at the core and strategic center of the First Island Chain, a pivotal point, he said.
If Taiwan fell under Chinese control, Xi’s dream would come true, he said, calling it an unfortunate outcome that must be prevented at all costs.
If Beijing uses Taiwan as a springboard to push the Chinese naval and aviation forces into the western Pacific, Japan would be forced to make major shifts in its security strategy, he said.
Taiwan’s strategic importance extends to energy security, as shipping routes through the South China Sea are indispensable to Japan and could be constrained if China gained control over Taiwan, he said.
The Japanese government fully understands Taiwan’s importance and is drawing up contingency plans for an emergency involving Taiwan, he said.
In March last year, the Japanese government drafted plans for evacuation drills in the event of a regional security emergency, he said.
An evacuation would involve about 120,000 people, including approximately 110,000 residents of the Sakishima Islands, and tourists in the area, to Kyushu and Yamaguchi Prefecture, he said.
A full-scale drill is scheduled for next month, reflecting the Japanese government’s preparations for a Taiwan contingency, he added.
Maintaining the “status quo” in Taiwan is of vital national interest for Japan, he said.
Late Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe had said “a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency,” while his wife, Akie Abe, reversed the phrase, saying “if Taiwan is safe, Japan is safe,” Iwata said, calling her statement accurate.
The shared destiny between Japan and Taiwan is highlighted as they both face economic coercion from Beijing, he said, citing China’s Jan. 6 decision to tighten export controls on dual-use items heading to Japan.
Commenting on reports that China shipped containers of dual-use materials to Russia and Iran via rail, he said Taipei and Tokyo should join hands to counter Beijing’s tactics.
Japan has lifted restrictions on arms sales in five categories, making it possible in principle to supply weapons internationally, he said.
While arms sales remain limited to 17 countries, there are no restrictions on dual-use components, he said, calling for mutual assistance between Taiwan and Japan in this area.
Drones would be the most promising area for defense industry cooperation, he said, particularly in dual-use technologies.
The Japanese drone market is dominated by Chinese manufacturers, which account for about 90 percent of the market, he said, calling it “a very serious problem.”
Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry in December last year proposed establishing domestic production facilities capable of manufacturing 80,000 drones annually by 2030, he said.
The plan includes domestic production of key components, such as motors, batteries, communications modules and flight-control chips, as well as cooperation with countries such as Taiwan, he said.
Japan is moving to reduce its dependence on China and has an urgent need to develop a drone supply chain, analysts said.
Taiwan has strong manufacturing capabilities, a solid information and communications technology sector and a trusted non-red supply chain, they said.
In July, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ Global UAV Academy and the Japan Drone Consurtium signed a letter of intent in Tokyo to cooperate on non-Chinese supply chains, certification and talent cultivation.
Iwata said he hoped Japan and Taiwan could soon expand their drone cooperation to establish a production system capable of manufacturing tens of thousands of units.
The cooperation model developed through drones could be applied to other sectors, he said, adding that such efforts should serve their shared goal of reducing dependence on China.

Lodging fines total NT$143.389m this year, data show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:29 UTC
01:43:29 KST

There were 1,600 unlicensed lodgings across Taiwan in the first nine months of this year, while accommodation-sector fines totaled NT$143.389 million (US$4.5 million), Tourism Administration data showed.
Currently, 3,270 general hotels are operating nationwide, a slight decline from the same period last year, the administration said, attributing the decline to individual business decisions regarding the market.
Of the 1,068 unlicensed hotels and daily rental suites, Taipei had the highest number at 275, all of which were daily rental suites, followed by Taichung with 195 and Yilan County with 181, the data showed.
Photo: Huang Yi-ching, Taipei Times
The remaining 532 unlicensed lodging establishments were guesthouses.
The number of unlicensed hotels and short-term rental suites rose compared with the same period last year, mainly due to an increase in short-term rental suites in urban areas and more inspections by local governments, which led to more lodgings being listed for monitoring or closed, the Tourism Administration said.
As of the end of last month, authorities had conducted 4,054 inspections of licensed hotels and daily rental suites, with Taipei recording the most at 988, followed by Kaohsiung with 666 and Taichung with 480, it said.
Of the 733 fines issued, Taipei topped the list with 204, followed by Tainan with 130 and Taichung with 129, it added.
Of the NT$121.265 million in fines, Tainan accounted for the most at NT$29.75 million, followed by New Taipei City with NT$21.75 million and Taipei with NT$19.16 million, the agency said.
Meanwhile, the number of licensed guesthouses reached 12,872, an increase of about 400 compared with the same period last year, it said.
As guesthouses are typically operated as side businesses using spare rooms in private residences, they are less likely than hotels to suspend or cease operations due to business costs, it said.
There were 532 unlicensed guesthouses registered for monitoring, fewer than a year earlier, the agency said, attributing the decline to more inspections by local governments.
As of the end of last month, authorities had conducted 9,247 inspections of guesthouses, with Yilan County recording the most at 1,945, followed by Penghu County with 1,296 and Taitung County with 1,274, it said.
Of the 277 fines issued to guesthouse operators, the most were in Taitung County at 63, followed by Tainan with 31 and Pingtung County with 27, it said.
Guesthouse-related fines totaled NT$22.124 million, with Taitung County accounting for the most at NT$4.83 million, followed by Pingtung County with NT$2.974 million and Yilan County with NT$2.27 million.

DPP depriving Taiwan of future: KMT head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) accused the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) government in an interview of championing Taiwan’s identity while depriving Taiwan of its ability to shape its own future, saying that Taiwan should pursue peace and propose practical solutions to reduce cross-strait risks.
The interview with Japanese digital news outlet Shincho QUE, published on Friday last week, covered cross-strait relations, Taiwan’s exchanges with Japan and the US, and how Taiwan can take the initiative amid shifts in the international situation.
The KMT has been falsely labeled regarding its positions, Cheng said.
Photo: Taipei Times
Since taking office as party chair, she has expanded communication with the international community, helping people in Japan, Europe and the US understand the KMT and the importance of peace across the Taiwan Strait, she said.
The KMT pursues stable cross-strait relations to safeguard Taiwan’s democracy, freedom and prosperity, Cheng said, adding that the KMT should play an active role in promoting peace.
Taiwan must safeguard its democratic values and should not make unilateral concessions, she said, adding that stable cross-strait relations must be built on mutual respect and understanding.
Trips to Beijing this April and the US this June were important steps for the KMT to explain its position to the international community, the party chair said.
The KMT advocates easing tensions in the Taiwan Strait and resuming cross-strait dialogue based on the so-called “1992 consensus,” she said.
The “1992 consensus” refers to a tacit understanding between the KMT and the Chinese Communist Party that both sides of the Taiwan Strait acknowledge that there is “one China,” with each side having its own interpretation of what “China” means.
The DPP rejects the “1992 consensus,” saying that Beijing does not recognize the Republic of China and acceptance of the understanding would imply agreement with China’s claim over Taiwan.
This would enable Taiwan to improve its own situation rather than wait for major powers to decide its future, she added.
Although the DPP champions Taiwanese subjectivity, its governing has led people to lose faith in Taiwan’s ability to shape its own future, Cheng said.
Without that initiative, Taiwan risks becoming a bargaining chip in the power struggles between major countries, she said.
Cheng voiced concerns about how Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (台積電) expansion in the US might impact Taiwan’s strategic value, citing Taiwan’s key role in the global high-tech industry.
Easing cross-strait tensions would help integrate regional talent, technology, markets and capital, she said, adding that the US could continue to play a leading role in the region while promoting cooperation.
The DPP has stirred anti-China sentiment, but this strategy is losing its effectiveness as people become increasingly aware of the risks of war, Cheng said.
No country wants to go to war with China and any military conflict in the Taiwan Strait would have far-reaching consequences for the world, Cheng said.
“If everyone can share in the benefits of peace, who would want to start a war?” she said.
The KMT would continue to pursue peace, stability and prosperity for Taiwan through dialogue and communication with the international community, she added.
In response, the DPP yesterday said President William Lai (賴清德) in his National Day address on Saturday outlined how Taiwan, in 10 years of DPP rule and amid upheavals in the global landscape, has worked with democratic allies and leveraged its technological strengths to improve its footing and engage with the world.
Rather than worrying about Taiwan losing its say, Cheng should focus on whether she, as KMT chair, still has control over her own party’s strategy in next month’s local elections, the DPP said.
Additional reporting by Chen Yun

ECCT chair urges agility in software and energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

Taiwan is known for its strength in hardware manufacturing, but new European Chamber of Commerce Taiwan (ECCT) chairman Frank Grunert sees considerable potential in software as well.
A hardware engineer typically starts with a defined product and works backward through the steps needed to build it, Grunert said in an interview on Monday last week.
“When you write software, you often don’t know [what you’ll have] in the end,” he said. “You have a rough idea of what you want to have, but you have a lot of agile changes in between.”
Photo: CNA
Software development also requires connecting information across sources and breaking down data silos, he said, describing the process as “a kind of co-creation with your customer, with your environment.”
Grunert praised Taiwan’s engineering precision and said he was impressed by its software startups. Agility is important to success in the software business, he added.
Grunert took over as chair of the ECCT on Sept. 1 after assuming leadership of Siemens Taiwan Ltd in August 2024. He previously served as Siemens AG’s global head of grid control, a role involving software used to manage electricity networks.
Siemens Taiwan vice president and head of communications Ray Jui (芮家楹) described Grunert as eager to acquire new knowledge and well versed in artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.
Grunert also advocated a more agile approach to electricity infrastructure projects, saying that Taiwan needs to expand power generation capacity and upgrade its grid to meet rapidly growing demand.
Once authorities identify the need for a substation, power plant or grid upgrade, budgeting and procurement must precede construction, he said. The entire process could take five to seven years.
“That is much too long,” Grunert added.
He proposed dividing projects into smaller pieces and eliminating unnecessary administrative steps to accelerate implementation. Authorities should also be able to adjust budgets as circumstances change during construction, he said.
Public procurement could become more efficient through digitization, he added. Companies bidding for large contracts still have to print extensive documentation and submit multiple copies.
In his inaugural message to ECCT members, Grunert identified energy supply and costs, labor and talent shortages, and deeper European-Taiwanese economic ties as issues that would shape business conditions into the next decade.
“Our chamber should think on that horizon, not only the next advocacy cycle,” he wrote.
During the interview, Grunert said European equipment, chemicals and materials suppliers complement Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. A bilateral investment agreement could provide businesses on both sides with a clearer framework and greater investment certainty.
On offshore wind, canceled projects, slower development and companies withdrawing from the market were thinning the pipeline of new projects, Grunert said.
Overlapping or conflicting responsibilities between central and local authorities could delay permits, he said. For developers financing construction with bank loans, that can delay revenue while scheduled payments still have to be made.
He urged Taiwan to examine financing arrangements used elsewhere and improve permitting coordination to help developers and suppliers remain in the market.
Renewable power generation also increases resilience by reducing reliance on imported fuel, while battery storage helps balance fluctuations in wind and solar power, he said.
For electricity infrastructure more broadly, Grunert urged a change in how projects are implemented.
“We need to be able to slice projects in smaller pieces,” he said.

Mswati arrived in Taiwan on Friday last week for his 20th visit to the country since he was crowned king in 1986, primarily to attend the Republic of China National Day celebrations.
Lai and the monarch yesterday visited Army Aviation and Special Forces Command’s Flight Training Command, a Tainan-based training center where army aviators learn to fly.
Photo: Screen grab from the Presidential Office’s Flickr page
During the visit, Mswati and his wife Inkhosikati Make Zuma were shown military helicopters on display in a hangar. Both got a chance to operate a military helicopter flight simulator, while the king sat in the cockpit of a Black Hawk helicopter.
In his remarks during the visit, Lai said Taiwan donated two retired UH-1H helicopters to Eswatini in 2020. Between 2019 and 2020, the Tainan-based command trained 11 Eswatini pilots and maintenance personnel to fly and maintain the helicopters.
Lai expressed his gratitude to the personnel involved in the mission for their contributions to diplomatic ties between the two countries.
Mswati thanked Taiwan for donating the helicopters and assisting in the training of Eswatini’s pilots.
The helicopters, which were formally handed over to the Umbutfo Eswatini Defence Force air wing, have already played a crucial role, including medevac flights to transport casualties in urgent need of advanced medical care, the king said.
Mswati said that during this visit to Taiwan, he saw the continued development and progress of Taiwan’s aviation sector. He said he looked forward to deepening exchanges and sharing expertise and experience between the two countries.
The king’s itinerary includes observing a joint ground-air military exercise and a visit to an agricultural research center. He attended an investment dinner hosted by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) on Friday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
Mswati’s Taiwan visit is expected to conclude on Oct. 17.

A deadly airstrike hits a Sudan-Egypt border gold mine, killing at least 13 miners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Breadcrumb
Deadly airstrike hits Sudan-Egypt border gold mine, killing at least 13 miners
An airstrike killed at least 13 artisanal miners in a border area between Sudan and Egypt where artisanal and small-scale gold mining is widespread, a medical group said Sunday.
The strike Saturday in the Border Triangle Area between Sudan, Egypt and Libya, and also wounded at least 28 others, according to the Sudan Doctors Network, which tracks the conflict in Sudan.
It wasn’t immediately clear who was behind the strike. The network, however, said the miners were repeatedly warned by Egyptian authorities to evacuate the area, which is reportedly part of Egypt.
Gold has played a central part in the war in Sudan, with the insurgent paramilitary Rapid Support Forces smuggling out thousands of tons of gold from the Darfur and Kordofan regions to fund themselves.
Abdel-Aziz Yousef, a survivor, told The Associated Press that an unknown aircraft struck an artisanal gold mine in a mountainous area Saturday morning.
He said that many people were killed or wounded, and others fled the area for fear of further strikes.
The medical group said the death toll is likely to increase given that some of the wounded have suffered from serious injuries and limited access to healthcare facilities.
In June, Egyptian security forces detained hundreds of people, including foreigners, on the border with Sudan, accusing them of illegal gold mining and smuggling.
More than 50% of gold mined in Sudan was smuggled out of the country, according to a U.N. Panel of Experts Report in 2024.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

NEW DELHI: CPM Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas on Sunday wrote to Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and President Droupadi Murmu, Rajya Sabha Chairman CP Radhakrishnan alleging that he was assaulted by Delhi Police personnel while speaking to the media during protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. He sought urgent intervention, an independent investigation and accountability, alleging a breach of parliamentary privilege.Brittas said the incident took place while he was exercising his democratic duty and interacting with the press."While peacefully interacting with journalists in connection with the ongoing democratic protests demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, Shri Gyanesh Kumar, I was forcibly dragged away, bodily lifted by police personnel, assaulted inside a police vehicle and subsequently abandoned on the roadside. The incident raises grave questions concerning personal liberty, the right to peaceful expression, police accountability and compliance with the constitutional safeguards that this Hon'ble Court has time and again upheld and reaffirmed through its authoritative judgments," he said in his letter."The Government cannot intimidate democracy into silence. It cannot deploy the police as an instrument of political retaliation.
It cannot substitute the force of the baton for the force of argument. And it cannot expect the people to surrender their constitutional freedoms merely because those in power find dissent inconvenient. Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution protect freedom of speech and peaceful assembly, while Article 21 safeguards life and personal liberty. Any restraint or detention must have a lawful basis, and any use of force must be necessary, lawful and proportionate. The brutal assault, the circumstances in which I was taken away, and the manner in which I was released demand urgent scrutiny under these constitutional guarantees and the applicable laws and Rules governing police conduct and detention," he added.
Brittas also wrote separate letters to President Murmu and vice president, Rajya Sabha chair CP Radhakrishnan, while refering to Supreme Court directions. "The police atrocities raises serious questions under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution, which protect freedom of speech and peaceful assembly, and Article 21, which safeguards life and personal liberty," he wrote in letter to the president.Meanwhile, addressing the Rajya Sabha chair, he cited "authoritative publication Rajya Sabha at Work" and said, "The matter, however, extends beyond the personal indignity and physical harm inflicted upon me. It raises a question of privilege and of the dignity and authority of the Rajya Sabha itself. I do not contend that membership of Parliament confers immunity from law. My submission is that the forcible manhandling and assault of a sitting Member, in circumstances where I was peacefully discharging my role as a public representative and had repeatedly identified myself, must be considered in the light of established parliamentary precedents concerning the treatment of Members by law-enforcement authorities,"The allegations came amid a fresh round of protests in the national capital on Sunday, when more than 200 demonstrators were detained as they attempted to march towards Jantar Mantar. The INDIA bloc is set to hold a march on Monday, with opposition leaders stepping up their criticism of the police action.The protests followed a security clampdown on Saturday, when thousands of demonstrators and several opposition leaders were detained as police prevented them from reaching Jantar Mantar. More than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the capital as part of the security arrangements.
The demonstrations have been called by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and backed by opposition parties seeking Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The allegations have been denied by officials.

Saudi Arabia is unlikely to back down in the face of the Houthis following an attack on Riyadh’s airport that killed 12 people and wounded 309, with the kingdom likely stepping up its military campaign against the Iran-backed terror group, regional experts told The Jerusalem Post.
The attack, which marked a significant escalation in the Houthis’ campaign against Saudi Arabia, has exposed the kingdom’s vulnerability to strikes against civilian infrastructure. Bernard Haykel, a senior fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies (FDD), said Saudi Arabia had long understood the Houthis’ ability to carry out such attacks, particularly with what he described as support from Iran and Iraqi Shiite militias.
“My sense is that they’re not going to buckle. They’re not going to just capitulate to the Houthis because of this,” he explained.
Haykel said Riyadh now faces a choice between reaching an accommodation with the Houthis or intensifying its military campaign against them, adding that he expects the Saudis will pursue the latter course and rely more heavily on Yemeni forces opposed to the group.
“I think that they’re going to ramp up against the Houthis,” he said.
The attack comes as Saudi Arabia faces the consequences of a broader regional conflict that Riyadh had sought to avoid. According to Haykel, Saudi leaders opposed the war against Iran and made considerable efforts to prevent it, but now recognize that they will have to bear some of its costs.
“They realize that they have to pay a price,” he said.
Former ambassador says attack shocked Saudis
Michael Ratney, former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia and senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said the scale and audacity of the attack had shocked the Saudis, even though they were familiar with the Houthis’ military capabilities.
Ratney noted that the Houthis had already carried out several strikes against airports, including in Riyadh, during the preceding week, while the latest was the most serious of those incidents. “I think they were shocked, but in a way understood that this is what the Houthis are all about,” Ratney explained.
He identified the targeting of civilian airports as a particularly significant escalation. In the past, the Houthis had generally focused on military installations and energy infrastructure, including Saudi military bases and energy facilities.
“For them to target civilian airports with the expectation of civilian casualties is really a new escalation for the Houthis,” Ratney said.
The attacks put Riyadh in a difficult position as it seeks to achieve its military objectives in Yemen without triggering a wider escalation that could expose additional Saudi infrastructure to retaliation.
Ratney said Saudi Arabia’s immediate military priority was to help the Yemeni army retake positions along the coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that the Houthis had seized the previous month.
“They’re determined to get the Houthis off of the Bab el-Mandeb,” he said, adding that Riyadh would probably then look for a way to de-escalate the conflict.
Riyadh growing concerns over lack of American assistance
Both experts pointed to Riyadh's concerns about the limits of American military assistance, especially as Washington deploys forces and resources across the region.
Haykel said Saudi Arabia was disappointed that the United States was not better prepared to help defend the kingdom against attacks from the Houthis and Iran, particularly given the potential shortage of missile-defense systems.
“I think there’s disappointment that the Americans are not better prepared and better able to help in fighting the Houthis and the Iranians,” he said.
At the same time, Haykel said Saudi leaders understand that American military power has limits, particularly when US forces are already heavily committed across the Persian Gulf.
Ratney said the United States was providing some assistance behind the scenes, including intelligence sharing, targeting and operational planning. But he added that Riyadh would prefer more direct American involvement in airstrikes.
“Clearly what they would like is US support on airstrikes, and I think there is some frustration,” he said.
The attack could influence Washington’s willingness to provide more overt military support, Ratney said, although he cautioned that Trump’s response was difficult to predict.
Still, Ratney said neither Saudi Arabia nor the United States appeared eager to escalate the conflict further.
Saudis worried about further strikes on civilian infrastructure
The concern is that intensifying military operations against Iran or the Houthis could provoke disproportionate retaliation, with civilian infrastructure rather than military targets bearing the consequences.
“None of them really want to escalate at this point because they see the result,” Ratney said.
The attack also raises questions about whether Israel could play a greater role in helping Saudi Arabia counter the Houthi threat, given Israel’s experience confronting Iranian-backed groups and its advanced intelligence and air-defense capabilities.
“The political risk of that outweighs any kind of military benefits that they might derive,” Ratney said, explaining that Saudi leaders are reluctant to see Israeli politicians publicly highlight or take credit for cooperation between the two countries.
Haykel was more skeptical about Israel’s ability to deliver a decisive military blow against the Houthis, particularly through intelligence-led operations targeting the group’s leadership.
He said Israel had developed extensive intelligence capabilities against Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing it to target the organization’s senior figures and commanders. He does not believe Israel currently possesses a comparable level of intelligence on the Houthis in Yemen.
“If the Israelis had the intelligence on the Houthis to, say, destroy the leadership of the Houthis and the second-, third-tier commanders, you know, what they did to Hezbollah, basically, if they could do that in Yemen, that would be an incredible service and help in this war,” Haykel said.
For Riyadh, the immediate challenge remains how to deter further Houthi attacks without becoming trapped in another prolonged and costly conflict in Yemen. Both experts agree that it will be hard.

Hundreds join 'I'm not Jewish, I'm a Zionist' trend, 'Post' analysis finds - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:37:00 UTC
01:37:00 KST

A social media trend in which non-Jewish users publicly declare themselves non-Jewish Zionists has spread rapidly across X, with a Jerusalem Post exclusive analysis identifying more than 600 matching posts from nearly 550 accounts over the course of just over a week.
The posts follow a recognizable formula: "I'm not Jewish. I'm [nationality, religion or identity]. And I am a Zionist."
The Post wrote a code to analyze X and ascertain where the trend started and who is amplifying it. This analysis uncovered 613 posts published between October 4 and October 11, with relatively little activity during the first several days before the trend accelerated sharply on October 9.
The dataset contained just three matching posts from October 4, followed by 13 on October 5, 10 on October 6, 22 on October 7, and 26 on October 8.
That number then jumped to 131 on October 9, roughly five times the number captured the previous day. Another 270 matching posts were published on October 10, followed by 138 captured on October 11 as of the time the data was collected.
In total, 539 of the 613 posts analyzed, or approximately 88%, were published from October 9 onward.
From scattered declarations to a viral formula
Declarations of support for Zionism by non-Jewish users predate the current trend, and the earliest posts located by the Post do not yet display the standardized format that has now become more widespread.
Among posts found on October 4 were broader declarations such as, "I'm not Jewish, but I am a Zionist."
By October 5, however, users had begun inserting their national identity into the declaration. One early example read, "I'm not Jewish. I am Irish, and I am a Zionist."
An October 6 post similarly stated, "I'm English, I'm not Jewish, but I am a Zionist."
By October 7, the three-part structure began appearing more frequently, including variations identifying the poster as American, Canadian or Iranian before declaring support for Zionism.
One example posted by Dutch writer Bart Schut on October 11 read, "I'm not Jewish. I'm a Dutch atheist. And I am a Zionist."
The Post's dataset included posts referencing a wide range of national identities, including Iranian, American, Canadian, German, Finnish, Irish, Italian, New Zealander, English, Polish, Australian, British, Dutch, Czech, Japanese, Portuguese and Nigerian, among others.
Some users went further, combining national and religious identities. References to Christians, Catholics, atheists, Muslims, Hindus and agnostics all appeared in the posts analyzed.
Hundreds of accounts join trend
The 613 posts collected by the Post came from 549 separate X accounts, indicating that the volume captured in the analysis was not primarily produced by a small number of accounts repeatedly posting the same phrase.
Most accounts appeared only once in the dataset.
The available data does not establish that the posts were centrally coordinated or part of an organized campaign. Rather, it demonstrates the rapid replication and adaptation of a common linguistic template across hundreds of accounts.
The timing suggests that the phenomenon changed significantly around October 9, just two days after the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks.
After the Post captured 74 matching posts in total between October 4 and October 8, another 539 appeared from October 9 onward.
The trend had also begun drawing attention from users on X itself by that point, with posts explicitly referring to the growing number of "I'm not Jewish, but I'm a Zionist" declarations as a trend.
For example, on October 9, user Oren Barsky wrote: "the 'I’m not Jewish, but I’m a Zionist' trend is one of the most moving things I’ve seen on this platform."
By October 11, Barsky said the trend is "basically [his] whole feed."
How the Post analyzed the trend
The Jerusalem Post collected public X search results using multiple variations of the phrases "I'm not Jewish" and "Zionist," covering posts published between October 4 and October 11.
Duplicate post URLs were removed, leaving 613 posts from 549 unique accounts for analysis.
The dataset is not an exhaustive record of every post participating in the trend. The figures instead provide a snapshot of the trend visible through public X search results and demonstrate its growth within the period analyzed.
Either way, amid the widespread hostility toward Israel and Zionism, the emergence of a trend centered on expressions of solidarity with Israel and the Jewish people's right to self-determination marks a notably positive shift in the social media discourse.

The Guardian view on mental health: overdiagnosis is not the problem facing young people | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:27:06 UTC
01:27:06 KST

Perhaps the single most important finding of the independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism in England, published last Friday, is that mental distress across the population, and particularly young people, has substantially worsened. Its chair, Prof Peter Fonagy, told the BBC that the former health secretary Wes Streeting had been “completely wrong” to suggest that conditions and disorders were being overdiagnosed.
Mr Streeting acknowledged his mistake. But some rightwing politicians and commentators have leapt on the notion that medicalisation of ordinary states of mind is behind the huge rise in young people seeking help. This review should bury that idea. Instead, this should be a moment to face facts. First, that the rises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes. Second, that current services are not up to what is being asked of them.
Fifteen years after the phrase “parity of esteem” gained prominence – the idea being that people with mental ill health have equivalent entitlements to those with physical illnesses – it is a long way from being realised. Years-long queues for mental health care and neurodevelopmental support are not even included in official waiting-list figures.
The difficulty comes in deciding what to do about this, particularly given the fiscal rules under which the government has chosen to operate. One proposal already accepted by ministers is for stronger regulation of ADHD and autism assessments. Currently, many of these are delivered by private providers, with no common standards in a market with low barriers to entry; such a situation should never have been allowed, though long waiting lists have driven the demand for their services.
There is no straightforward fix to the wider set of problems. The experts are right to say that access to services should be based on need, not labels. It is reasonable to challenge the way that a diagnosis has become a “door to support”, both in mental health and special educational needs contexts. But the more important question is how this situation came about. The answer is that demand overwhelmed services, and diagnosis-based thresholds became a form of triage. On the critical question of resources, the report has less to say.
It recommends stronger accountability for mental health in the Department of Health and Social Care – an excellent idea, and probably a precondition of improvement – and suggests that this and other proposals should be incorporated in the upcoming mental health strategy. Beyond that, it argues for a 10-year plan, one aim of which would be to roll mental health and neurodevelopmental support into one service.
This is an ambitious agenda, which deserves a serious response. But while Prof Fonagy may be right that some reordering of waiting lists could be managed at relatively little cost, it is inconceivable that broader reforms can be achieved without new funds. And while the report refers repeatedly, and rightly, to the need for investment, it does not explicitly state that budgets should increase as a proportion of overall health spending; nor does it make the case for waiting list targets.
Did the authors fear that such demands would be ignored? So far, Yvette Cooper has followed her predecessor as health secretary in saying relatively little about mental health and young people. Now is the time to show that she is listening.

English adjectives as adverbs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

English adjectives as adverbs?
« previous post |
Some of the comments on "Filthy comfortable" (10/9/2026) related to the issue of an adjective being used as an adverbial intensifier, which is a fairly common though always irregular development.
We can start with very, for which Wiktonary gives the etymology
From Middle English verray, from Old French verai (“true”), from Early Medieval Latin vērāgus, from Classical Latin vērāx, derived from vērus, from Proto-Italic *wēros, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros.
According to the OED, the purely intensive adverbial use of very developed in the 16th-17th centuries.
The page on real from Merriam-Webster's Concise Dictionary of English Usage starts like this:
The adverb real, which is used only as an intensifier, developed from a use of the adjective to modify compound noun phrases like good turn. By the 18th century the real was apprehended as an intensifier modifying good alone, and its independent use grew from then. It was a development that took place, apparently, outside of mainstream British English; the OED identifies it as chiefly Scottish and American, and we have some slight Irish evidence. It has been from the start primarily a spoken use.
We covered the regional use of wicked as an intensifier back in 2014.
And scary as an intensifer in "scary smart" seems to have started around the turn of the century, as Google ngrams shows us.
A typical example:
[link] He made it to Wall Street because he’s scary smart — and you want him on your team — but he’s so socially awkward it’s painful.
And another one, in Doonesbury:
The same period seems to have seen the development of "crazy good":
And similarly, "sneaky good":
The phrase "silky smooth" seems to have been developing over a longer period:
But this kind of adverbialization is not something that you can (felicitously) apply wherever you like: *bewildering(ly) odd, *total(ly) flat, *strange(ly) lacking, etc.

The Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifies | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:25:39 UTC
01:25:39 KST

On Friday, Donald Trump drove home his belief that might is right and the rule of law is an obstacle rather than an essential foundation stone of international order. First came the escalated assault on the international criminal court (ICC), sanctioning the body itself. Then he announced a deal with Russia to buy diesel.
The US has long chafed at the notion of being bound by the rule of law that it espoused publicly. That hypocrisy now appears as a lesser vice. The president has declared that “my own morality” is all that constrains him. His brazen flouting of the law, embrace of dictators and rhetorical attacks all undermine global standards.
Weeks before the midterms, Mr Trump blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities for high diesel costs. It is his own unlawful war on Iran that has raised prices. The weekend’s attacks on Riyadh’s international airport, suspected as the work of Tehran-backed Houthis from Yemen, underscored that he cannot simply park that conflict when it suits him.
The Moscow deal is unlikely to produce significant shipments; the Russian military runs on diesel. But Ukraine is supposed to heed its message to make life easier on Vladimir Putin. It is Mr Putin (for whom the ICC has issued a warrant) who launched the illegal war, and whose troops launched lethal attacks on civilians this weekend. But in a world turned upside down, Mr Trump blames Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to cut a peace deal and says the democratically elected leader should go.
It is similarly perverse to wield measures designed to target human rights abusers and war criminals against those who seek to defend their victims. Mr Trump’s attack on the ICC was fuelled first by its Afghanistan investigation – though it has suspended consideration of US actions there – and then the issuing of arrest warrants for Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant. The court has been preparing for these measures. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said that companies have six months to wind down ties and that US allies must rein in the court: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”
In stark (and intentional) contrast, the Nobel committee on the same day announced that this year’s peace laureate is Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and chair of the UN commission which last year concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. It was not only a recognition of a remarkable career that began in apartheid‑era South Africa, but a reminder that institutions defending universal principles are under increasing pressure, and must be defended. “Peace requires justice,” the committee said.
As the ICC says, it cannot stand alone. The UK, EU and others too were right to criticise the US decision and declare their commitment to the court; invoking blocking statutes against sanctions would add heft to the rhetoric. They must show similar resolve in standing with Ukraine.
The nakedness of Mr Trump’s hostility to the rule of law has one benefit: no one can explain it away, or assume it is narrowly bounded. The war on Iran, kidnapping of Venezuela’s president, extrajudicial killings of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and threats over Greenland and Canada have shown how far he will go, and overturned assumptions that allies will be safe. It is clear that the problem is not a “rogue court”, as Mr Rubio has claimed, but a rogue superpower.
