Saudi Arabia: second strike on Riyadh airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:24:00 UTC
01:24:00 KST

Saudi Arabia: Second strike hits Riyadh airport
Published October 11, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was struck by an "unidentified projectile" for the second time in two days on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
"King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement, adding that it "resulted in injuries, and the assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities are still under way."
Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki also said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available.
The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."
A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.
Sunday's strikes came as Riyadh airport remained closed following an attack on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured over 300 more — the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade.
On Sunday, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed that one of its citizens died after being wounded in Saturday's attack.
"It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today," read a statement posted on social media. "We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased."
Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia
It also came just hours after the Houthis warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports.
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted.
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Why are Saudi airports being targeted?
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks?
The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."
The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.
The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.
The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.
While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.
How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."
Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.
On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."
Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.

Saudi Arabia: Second strike hits Riyadh airport
Published October 11, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was struck by an "unidentified projectile" for the second time in two days on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
"King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement, adding that it "resulted in injuries, and the assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities are still under way."
Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki also said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available.
The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."
A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.
Sunday's strikes came as Riyadh airport remained closed following an attack on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured over 300 more — the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade.
On Sunday, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed that one of its citizens died after being wounded in Saturday's attack.
"It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today," read a statement posted on social media. "We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased."
Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia
It also came just hours after the Houthis warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports.
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted.
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Why are Saudi airports being targeted?
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks?
The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."
The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.
The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.
The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.
While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.
How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."
Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.
On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."
Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.

El-Sisi in Jakarta: Trade promises, a Nile pledge and an outdated Palestine formula
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:17:29 UTC
01:17:29 KST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi landed in Jakarta on Saturday evening, 10 October 2026, at the end of an Asian tour that began in South Korea and passed through Malaysia.
The route tells a story. Cairo is looking east for money, technology and friends while its own region burns. Jakarta wants a firm partner at the far end of the sea route linking Asia to Europe.
The two presidents had met only a month earlier at the BRICS summit in New Delhi. BRICS is a club of large developing economies that both countries have joined. Meeting again so soon signals hedging: spreading bets across many partners so that no single power has too much control.
In April 2025 the two leaders agreed to raise relations to a “strategic partnership”, a promise of long-term cooperation. On Sunday their foreign ministers signed an action plan to give that label real tasks.
Smaller agreements covered visa-free entry for officials, shared statistics and fisheries. The fisheries deal matters: both nations lose money to illegal boats and can share ways to track them.
The economy is the weak point. President Prabowo Subianto said both sides will work toward an Economic Partnership Agreement, a deal that cuts taxes and rules on goods crossing the border. He also welcomed a joint investment fund.
Egypt badly needs foreign investment. Indonesia wants new buyers in Africa and the Arab world, and Egypt could be the gateway. Yet no figures were announced, so these remain intentions.
Defence may be the most commercial item. The leaders agreed to deepen defence industry cooperation. Egypt is a major arms buyer, and Indonesian state companies building ships, aircraft and ammunition want export orders.
Education supports this. Egypt offered more scholarships in medicine, engineering and science, adding to the thousands of Indonesians already at Al-Azhar University. They are the future carriers of the relationship.
OPINION: Israel and Indonesian vice president Gibran prove the powerful can break rules and walk free
Security shaped the mood. A day before the talks, an attack on Riyadh’s main airport killed 12 people, while fighting in Yemen grew near the Bab al-Mandab, the Red Sea’s southern gate.
Ships that avoid it sail around Africa, raising costs for Indonesian exporters and cutting Egypt’s Suez Canal income. The leaders’ call for calm is about trade as much as morals.
The boldest step was on water. Prabowo declared that Indonesia will back Egypt’s efforts to secure its rights to the Nile. Egypt gets nearly all its fresh water from the river and fears Ethiopia’s giant dam upstream will reduce the flow.
For a country that normally avoids picking sides, this is a real departure. It buys trust in Cairo, but Ethiopia is also a BRICS member and a growing market. Indonesian diplomats must now remain a friend to both.
On Palestine, both leaders condemned Israeli settlements, and el-Sisi repeated the two-state formula based on the 1967 borders. That formula is obsolete. Thirty years after Oslo, settlements have swallowed the land and real talks stopped long ago. Defenders say it is the only plan with United Nations backing, but a goal that cannot be reached is not a policy.
Jakarta and Cairo would help Palestinians more by calling instead for one Palestinian state, with equal citizenship and one vote for everyone between the river and the sea.
Both leaders also pledged to help rebuild Gaza. Without a real political solution, there is little point. Concrete without a political answer only pays for the next ruins.
Prabowo invited el-Sisi to treat Indonesia as a second home, and Indonesian officials often recall that Egypt was the first country to recognise Indonesia’s independence. History opens the door; strategy must walk through it.
By el-Sisi’s next visit, are trade talks under way, is there money in the fund, is Indonesian equipment in Egyptian hands, and is there a more honest position on Palestine? If so, this weekend mattered. If not, it was only ceremony.

Verstappen wins Singapore GP as Antonelli closes in on F1 title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:16:44 CST
01:16:44 KST

By F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SINGAPORE, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Red Bull's Max Verstappen continued his late-season resurgence with a commanding victory at the Singapore Grand Prix on Sunday, while Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli strengthened his grip on the 2026 Formula 1 world championship with third place.
Starting from pole position for the 50th time in his career, Verstappen led every lap around the Marina Bay Street Circuit to finish ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, with Antonelli completing the podium after a late charge through the field.
The victory followed Verstappen's triumph at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend and Saturday's Singapore Sprint, extending the Red Bull driver's winning streak to three races across the two weekends.
"It has taken a while [to win in Singapore], but I think this race was very good," said Verstappen, who had never previously won any race at the venue before Saturday's Sprint.
"The last few races have been really positive for us. It's just great to see, and we gave a lot of motivation to the team to deliver even more results.
"It's a really good group of people, I really enjoy working with them, and hopefully we can have a bit more fun to the end of the year."
More significantly for the championship, Antonelli extended his advantage over Mercedes teammate George Russell to 89 points with just 150 still available, leaving the Italian within touching distance of his maiden world title.
Russell, who had crashed out of Saturday's Sprint while leading, recovered from 19th and last on the grid to finish ninth, but now faces an increasingly improbable task to overhaul his teammate.
Verstappen's victory was built on a decisive defensive move at the start. Despite a sluggish getaway, the Dutchman moved across to cover Leclerc's challenge into the first corner and retained the lead, with Lewis Hamilton holding third ahead of Antonelli and the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.
Leclerc initially kept the pressure on, remaining within a second of Verstappen through the opening laps, but the Red Bull gradually pulled clear as Ferrari struggled to match its rival's pace.
Hamilton, the highest-placed driver to start on medium compound tyres, was the first frontrunner to stop, switching to softs on lap 19 in what appeared to be an aggressive two-stop strategy.
Leclerc followed six laps later, emerging narrowly ahead of his teammate on medium tyres. Despite Hamilton having the faster compound and repeatedly requesting more pace, Ferrari kept the pair in position as they pursued different strategies.
Verstappen, meanwhile, extended his opening stint until lap 33 before switching from soft to medium tyres, retaining the lead comfortably as his rivals completed their stops.
A second virtual safety car on lap 39, caused by Lance Stroll stopping with a clutch problem, presented Ferrari with another strategic opportunity. Leclerc pitted for fresh soft tyres, as did Antonelli, but Hamilton made what would prove a costly decision to stay out on his increasingly worn set.
With a substantial tyre advantage, Leclerc swept past Hamilton for second on lap 46 and began reducing Verstappen's lead, although the gap remained too large to mount a serious challenge.
Verstappen had a worrying moment on lap 52 when he briefly ran wide at the final corner, but continued to maintain a comfortable advantage over the Ferrari.
Behind them, Hamilton's race unraveled as his soft tyres lost performance. Antonelli, Norris and Piastri all closed rapidly on the seven-time world champion, who had little grip left to defend his position.
Hamilton ran wide while defending against Norris on lap 54, allowing Antonelli to pass the McLaren driver for fourth. The Italian then overtook Hamilton for third on the following lap, with Norris also passing the Ferrari driver to take fourth.
Piastri, who had made an additional stop after suffering a slow puncture, completed Hamilton's late collapse by passing him on the final lap to claim fifth.
Hamilton eventually finished sixth, having started third, while Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson took seventh ahead of Audi's Nico Hulkenberg. Russell finished ninth, with Isack Hadjar completing the points positions after starting from the pit lane following problems on Saturday.
Antonelli's podium came after the Mercedes mechanics were forced to rebuild part of his braking system on the grid after a sensor problem emerged before the start.
The result also underlined Mercedes' contrasting fortunes, with Russell having been forced to start from the back after exceeding his permitted allocation of power unit components.
Yet while Verstappen celebrated another victory, the championship picture increasingly favored Antonelli, whose latest podium moves him another step closer to becoming Formula 1's youngest ever world champion.
The next round of the 2026 Formula 1 season is the United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, on October 25. ■

World Insights: Transatlantic divides over security, development, climate emerge at Arctic assembly
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:16:12 CST
01:16:12 KST

By Xinhua writers Zhu Haochen, Zhang Yuliang and Zhang Zhaoji
REYKJAVIK, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The United States and its European and Canadian allies displayed diverging priorities on Arctic security, resource development and climate policy at the 2026 Arctic Circle Assembly, highlighting growing strains in transatlantic relations
As the three-day gathering concluded Saturday in Reykjavik, Iceland, discussions revealed contrasting approaches to the region's future, with Washington emphasizing military capabilities and resource development while its allies placed greater weight on sovereignty, local interests and environmental protection.
HOW TO ENSURE SECURITY?
Founded in 2013 by then-Icelandic President Olafur Ragnar Grimsson, the Arctic Circle holds its annual assembly in Iceland every October and serves as a major international platform for dialogue on Arctic affairs.
Security featured prominently at this year's gathering, but Washington and its allies differed in their priorities. While U.S. officials insisted on expanding military capabilities and infrastructure, European and Canadian officials emphasized sovereignty and autonomy as their paramount concerns.
At Thursday's opening ceremony, Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy said the United States was investing billions of dollars to strengthen its military presence in the state. He also outlined plans to work with allies on Arctic ports, airports and shipping networks that could serve military needs.
For some U.S. allies, however, concerns over Washington's respect for their sovereignty have complicated security cooperation.
Since returning to the White House in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his intention to take control of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark. Despite a new security agreement reached by the United States, Denmark and Greenland in September, trust among the allies has yet to recover.
In Reykjavik, Greenland's Foreign Minister Mute Egede said Greenlanders had endured enormous pressure and uncertainty, reinforcing the importance of autonomy in determining their future. "We will not be spectators to our own future," he stressed.
U.S.-Canada relations have also deteriorated due to Trump's threats to make Canada the "51st state" and his sharp tariff increases on Canadian goods.
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand stressed that the Arctic was not merely a strategic frontier, but also "home" to local people. She said Canada was strengthening "middle-power diplomacy" with Nordic countries and other partners to safeguard peace, security and respect for sovereignty in the Arctic.
Zhao Long, director of the Center for Marine and Polar Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told Xinhua that Arctic affairs were increasingly being securitized amid growing geopolitical rivalry.
He said Washington and its allies did not entirely share the same perceptions of external security threats, making it increasingly difficult for the United States to coordinate a common position amid new tensions among them.
HOW TO SHARE DEVELOPMENT BENEFITS?
As global warming opens up the Arctic and makes shipping routes and natural resources increasingly accessible, questions over how to develop the region and distribute the economic benefits have gained prominence.
At the assembly, U.S. officials enthusiastically promoted plans to expand energy development and infrastructure construction, emphasizing the Arctic's strategic and economic value, while Washington's allies placed greater weight on local communities' right to shape development and share in its benefits.
Dunleavy said the Trump administration has been seeking to transform Alaska's development model to support both defense needs and resource exploitation. Thomas Dans, chairman of the U.S. Arctic Research Commission, described U.S. investment in the region as "unprecedented."
Meanwhile, representatives from Greenland, the European Union (EU) and Canada emphasized that Arctic communities should make their own development choices.
"The future of the Arctic cannot be shaped solely by what the world wants to get from the Arctic. It must also take into account what Arctic peoples themselves want," Egede said.
He stressed that development must create opportunities for local residents rather than allow external investment and security infrastructure to override their choices.
Anand also highlighted the Arctic's enormous potential in critical minerals, energy and transportation, but stressed that the key was to ensure that "local people benefit."
HOW TO TACKLE CLIMATE CHANGE?
Climate change emerged as another major point of divergence between Washington and its allies at the assembly.
European and Canadian representatives prioritized climate action and environmental governance, warning that rising temperatures, thawing permafrost and changes in marine ecosystems were already threatening the region.
Asked whether climate change or military threats concerned him more, Egede chose climate change, saying it was "changing the way local people live."
Anand warned that declining sea ice and thawing permafrost were affecting Arctic ecosystems, food security and local livelihoods. She said climate governance should stand alongside military security and economic development as one of the three major issues facing the Arctic.
European Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela said tackling climate change would remain a central pillar of the EU's Arctic strategy, with environmental protection integrated into every Arctic-related policy.
By contrast, U.S. officials placed less emphasis on climate issues. Dunleavy acknowledged that his discussions with the White House had focused mainly on energy, defense and infrastructure, while climate issues had received "relatively less" attention.
Trump has long dismissed global warming as a "hoax" and announced U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement during both of his presidential terms.
Zhao said Trump's decision to withdraw from the agreement in 2025 had further widened climate policy differences between Washington and its European allies. He warned that downgrading climate cooperation would continue to undermine multilateral governance and scientific cooperation in the Arctic.
Finnish Arctic affairs expert Lassi Heininen said environmental cooperation played an important role in easing military tensions and maintaining geopolitical stability in the region.
He emphasized the importance of preserving such cooperation amid growing strategic competition in the region. ■

Feature: Whom does Japan's government protect? Documentary sparks debate
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:16:09 CST
01:16:09 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- "The interests of the United States are being placed above the human rights of Japanese people and Japan's national sovereignty."
Hiroyuki Oba, a reporter with Japan's Mainichi Shimbun newspaper, made the remark in an interview with Xinhua in Tokyo on Saturday, following the release of a documentary examining low-altitude flights by U.S. military helicopters over central Tokyo.
Titled "300 Meters Above Tokyo," the documentary takes its name from a Japanese aviation safety rule that generally requires aircraft to maintain a vertical distance of at least 300 meters from the highest obstacle in densely populated areas. Yet a special law enacted in connection with the Japan-U.S. Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) exempts U.S. military aircraft from this restriction.
The film goes beyond the skies over Tokyo, examining alleged crimes involving U.S. military personnel, victims' struggles for justice and the Japanese government's response.
Why are different rules applied under the same sky? The question sparked heated discussion at a post-screening event on Saturday, raising a broader issue: Whom is the Japanese government protecting?
LEGAL PRIVILEGES, LIMITED ACCOUNTABILITY
Signed by Japan and the United States in 1960, SOFA governs the legal status of U.S. forces stationed in Japan. Under the agreement, the United States has the primary right to exercise jurisdiction over offenses committed by U.S. service members in the performance of official duty, while Japan generally has the primary right to exercise jurisdiction over offenses committed outside official duty.
However, when a suspect is in U.S. custody, U.S. authorities generally retain custody until Japanese authorities formally bring charges, under the agreement's provisions on custody and the transfer of suspects.
In practice, the arrangement can complicate Japanese investigations and delay the transfer of suspects to Japanese custody. Critics argue that the special treatment afforded to U.S. personnel weakens accountability and makes it more difficult for Japanese authorities to investigate alleged crimes.
At the post-screening discussion, Oba said Japanese police could request to question suspects but faced limitations if they could not maintain continuous control over their whereabouts.
Each interrogation requires coordination, and the time available is limited, Oba said. Meanwhile, it is difficult for the public to know how suspects are managed or treated inside U.S. military bases.
These constraints have repeatedly fueled frustration among victims and local residents, particularly in Okinawa Prefecture, which hosts a large concentration of U.S. military facilities in Japan.
On Oct. 3, a 39-year-old Japanese woman was found dead at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa. A 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, identified as Devin Jacob Ballard, was arrested by Okinawa police the following day on suspicion of murdering the woman and stealing her wallet and other belongings. Ballard has denied the allegations.
The incident prompted the Okinawa prefectural government to protest and call for effective measures to prevent similar crimes, as well as a fundamental review of SOFA.
At the central government level, however, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and other officials have confined their public responses to expressing regret, lodging protests and demanding full cooperation with the investigation and measures to prevent a recurrence. They have not raised the prospect of revising SOFA in their public statements.
According to Okinawa Prefecture statistics, more than 6,400 criminal cases involving U.S. service members and military-affiliated personnel were recorded between 1972 and 2025. The prefecture has also reported an upward trend in cases involving U.S. military personnel in recent years.
Over the decades, several cases have left a lasting impact on Japanese society.
In 1995, three U.S. servicemen stationed in Okinawa abducted and raped a 12-year-old girl, triggering widespread public outrage. In 2016, a military-affiliated individual killed a 20-year-old Okinawan woman and dumped her body. In 2023, a U.S. service member stationed in Okinawa abducted and sexually assaulted a girl under the age of 16.
"I am really angry because these incidents have never stopped," Ai Takahashi, a woman who attended the screening, told Xinhua.
Takahashi said she had recently joined a protest outside the U.S. Embassy in Japan over the death of the Okinawan woman. While demonstrators gathered outside, music from a party being held inside the embassy could be heard, she said.
"The stark contrast was really painful to see," she said.
QUESTIONS OVER TRANSPARENCY
Another chapter of the documentary, titled "Who Lets the Perpetrators Escape?" examines a further source of public distrust: cases in which the Japanese government did not promptly disclose serious alleged crimes involving U.S. military personnel, leaving the public to learn of the incidents only through media reports.
"Choosing to cover things up despite all these problems is itself a problem," a man in his 60s told Xinhua at the discussion.
The issue, the film suggests, extends beyond the handling of individual criminal cases to broader questions of transparency and accountability in the relationship between the two countries.
Oba also recalled the difficulties he encountered while investigating noise pollution around U.S. military helicopter facilities. Finding Japanese residents willing to speak publicly about the issue was surprisingly difficult, he said.
Even residents who strongly opposed the flights were often reluctant to be interviewed. Some feared that publicly criticizing the U.S. military could expose them to scrutiny, while others worried that doing so might affect their children's future employment prospects.
More than 80 years after the end of World War II, the privileges enjoyed by U.S. forces stationed in Japan continue to affect the lives of local communities. For those seeking changes to the existing arrangements, the documentary's central question remains unresolved: When the interests of the alliance appear to conflict with the rights of Japanese citizens, whose interests will the government put first?
As the film and the voices surrounding it suggest, changing the status quo may still be a long road ahead. ■

Ian Berry obituary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:11:16 UTC
01:11:16 KST

On 21 March 1960, a crowd gathered outside a police station in a Transvaal township, part of a nationwide protest against apartheid pass laws used to control where black South Africans could live, work and travel. A young British photojournalist pushed his way to the front and took a few pictures of police across the fence who were standing atop their armoured personnel carriers. With nothing much happening, he turned back and headed for his car. Then – without warning – there was the sound of heavy gunfire.
The photographer, Ian Berry, who has died aged 92, captured images of the carnage, which soon became known around the world as the Sharpeville massacre. Dozens of demonstrators were killed, many shot in the back as they fled, and hundreds were injured in what turned out to be a turning point in the country’s history.
Berry and his colleague, the Drum reporter Humphrey Tyler, had ignored police warnings that they would be arrested, and were the only journalists there when the shooting started. It was the first time Berry had been shot at, or seen others killed, but it would not be the last in a career that took him to the Congo crisis following independence in 1960-65, the Vietnam war, the Aberfan disaster of 1966, in which coal waste engulfed a Glamorgan village, and the six-day war between Israel and its neighbours in June 1967.
He was tenacious, but his edge was his eye for human moments, capturing the people behind the headlines, often photographing scenes that were off-centre, and yet told a story better by focusing on individuals.
In 1968, when Magnum’s Paris bureau asked if he would go to Prague as Soviet tanks encroached, he took a plane to Munich, rented a car and drove to the Czech border, only to find that journalists were being turned away. With typical guile, Berry talked his way through, persuading a Russian officer that he was on his way to an architects’ conference, which he had read about on the flight. He captured memorable images of peaceful resistance during the first days of the invasion, then smuggled them out in the hubcaps and door panels of his rented Volkswagen Beetle for publication in Paris Match.
Born in Preston, Lancashire, Ian was the son of Walter, who owned garages, and Ethel (nee McKimmings), a housewife. He was a boarder at Rossall school, on the coast at Fleetwood, and from an early age had wanderlust. A postwar assisted emigration scheme took him to South Africa in 1952, when he was 17.
In Johannesburg he worked for a family acquaintance, Roger Madden, who had recently returned home from assisting the photographer Ansel Adams in the US. Madden taught Berry to use a large-format camera and to print in the darkroom, but he would find his own path using a diminutive Leica, the camera favoured by prominent visual journalists of the day.
Berry moved on to studio work and small-town editorial assignments, and worked for the Rand Daily Mail, covering the beginnings of the treason trial in 1956 that included Nelson Mandela as a defendant. After hearing that Tom Hopkinson, the former editor of Picture Post in London, was coming to edit Drum, a newly established South African weekly aimed at a black readership, Berry persuaded him to give him a job. A few months later, Hopkinson sent him to Sharpeville.
He was called to give evidence at the trial of the wounded, who had been charged with obstruction. The pictures also brought him to wider international attention, and through Hopkinson he became acquainted with Magnum Photos, the agency with whom he remained until his death.
When Berry moved to Paris in 1962, he met Henri Cartier-Bresson, one of Magnum’s co-founders, and became a full member five years later. By then, he had left Paris for London to become a contract photographer for the Observer, travelling abroad on reportage assignments while shooting members of the British arts scene for the paper’s weekend magazine.
He photographed actors, film people and artists, including John Gielgud, Dusty Springfield, Lindsay Anderson and Henry Moore, and gained a reputation for his observational portrait stories.
Berry’s magazine assignments were accompanied by projects pursued over years, and it is for these that he will be best remembered. In 1972, the Whitechapel Gallery in London commissioned him to photograph its East End neighbourhood, and two years later, an Arts Council bursary (said to be the first ever given to a photographer) led to the publication of The English (1978), a collection that observed class, ceremony and everyday leisure activities.
That seamless transition between commissioned journalism and self-directed work reflected the Magnum model, which allowed photographers to earn a living from magazines while retaining control of their pictures and developing subjects beyond an editor’s brief.
Travel assignments for Life, Paris Match, National Geographic, Geo and others took Berry across the world, and often fed into longer studies. His continuing engagement with apartheid South Africa resulted in Black and Whites: L’Afrique du Sud (1988) and Living Apart (1996), while other projects examined changing daily life in China and the former Soviet Union.
In later years, a commission to photograph Greenland’s retreating glaciers developed into Water, an examination of how water sustains life and how its scarcity, pollution and destructive force expose humanity’s impact on the planet. Drawing on 15 years of work, it was published in 2023, accompanied by an essay by his second wife, Kathie Webber, whom he had married in 1973.
Berry’s first wife was Shirley, a South African, with whom he had a daughter, and he had a son from another relationship; both children predeceased him. He is survived by Kathie.

Saudi Arabia can fight the Houthis, it may not be able to defeat them.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:06:06 UTC
01:06:06 KST

Saudi Arabia can afford a long war. It can buy aircraft, missiles, drones, air-defense systems and intelligence. It can absorb losses that would bankrupt a poorer state. Yet that does not mean it can defeat the Houthis. That distinction has become impossible to ignore. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly called Donald Trump twice last week and urged Washington to strike the Houthis directly. Trump declined, although Washington agreed to provide intelligence and targeting support. The episode is revealing not because Saudi Arabia lacks military power, but because Riyadh appears to recognize that the Houthi problem is no longer one that firepower alone can solve.
The timing matters. The Houthis have seized Mocha on Yemen’s Red Sea coast and moved toward strategically important islands at the mouth of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. At the same time, attacks attributed to Iran-aligned forces have disrupted Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, the very infrastructure designed to give Riyadh an alternative route around the Strait of Hormuz. This leaves Saudi Arabia facing a strategic problem that is much harder than defeating an insurgency. It must protect an economic system built around a handful of extraordinarily valuable and geographically exposed nodes. The Houthis do not need to conquer Saudi Arabia. They only need to make Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure sufficiently vulnerable, costly and unpredictable.
Saudi Has the Firepower
On paper, the balance is overwhelmingly in Saudi Arabia’s favor. Riyadh spent an estimated $83.2 billion on its military in 2025, making it the world’s eighth-largest military spender. It possesses advanced fighter aircraft, precision weapons, sophisticated air defenses and extensive access to Western intelligence and technology. The Houthis, by comparison, are a much poorer non-state actor operating from one of the Middle East’s most difficult physical environments. Yet the conventional balance has never translated into decisive strategic victory.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen’s war in 2015 with overwhelming airpower and a clear political objective: prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen and restore a government friendly to Riyadh. Years of airstrikes imposed enormous damage and slowed Houthi advances, but they did not produce the political outcome Saudi Arabia wanted.
The lesson is that airpower is poorly suited to solving a political problem when the adversary can disperse, regenerate and operate below the threshold of conventional war. The Houthis have spent the past decade adapting precisely to that imbalance. According to ACLED, they conducted nearly 1,000 rocket and missile attacks and more than 350 distinct drone attacks against Saudi and Emirati territory between 2015 and the April 2022 truce. More importantly, the character of those attacks changed. Guided missiles accounted for just 15 percent of Houthi rocket and missile events in 2015, but 89 percent by 2022. Drone attacks also increasingly outnumbered missile attacks.
That evolution points to a fundamental strategic mismatch. Saudi Arabia has generally sought to punish the Houthis by destroying military assets and degrading their operational capacity. The Houthis, meanwhile, have increasingly sought to deny Saudi Arabia the ability to operate securely and predictably. That is the difference between punishment and denial. A military power can destroy a missile launcher. It cannot easily destroy the political and economic incentives behind a dispersed missile force. It can intercept a drone. It cannot guarantee that the next drone will not find another vulnerability. It can strike a command center. It cannot bomb away the geography that gives an adversary access to a strategic maritime chokepoint.
The 2019 attack on Abqaiq and Khurais illustrated the problem dramatically. The assault temporarily knocked out more than half of Saudi oil production and almost 5 percent of global oil supply.
Whether the attack was launched from Iranian or Iraqi territory or claimed by the Houthis, its strategic lesson was unmistakable that a relatively inexpensive asymmetric attack could impose enormous costs on one of the world’s most heavily armed states. That is why Saudi Arabia’s military superiority should not be confused with strategic invulnerability.
The Houthis Are No Longer Fighting Only for Yemen
The most important change in 2026 is that the Houthi threat is no longer primarily territorial. It is increasingly geographic and economic. The seizure of Mocha and the Houthi advance toward Perim Island and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait have altered the strategic map. Bab al-Mandeb is not simply another battlefield. It is one of the world’s principal maritime chokepoints, linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Reuters reported that Houthi forces reached the strategic island of Perim on September 11, putting them closer to the maritime gateway through which energy and commercial traffic moves between the Middle East, Europe and Asia.
READ: Saudi Arabia says 3 killed in attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid airport
That development matters enormously for Saudi Arabia. For years, Riyadh has invested in reducing its dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The East-West Pipeline is central to that strategy because it allows Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea port of Yanbu without passing through Hormuz. But the geography of the current conflict is beginning to turn that strategy against Riyadh. Hormuz is under pressure from Iran. Bab al-Mandeb is increasingly exposed to the Houthis. And the East-West Pipeline has itself been disrupted by drone attacks attributed to Iran-aligned forces in Iraq. Reuters reported that the pipeline outage could threaten as much as 4 percent of global oil supply, while Saudi crude production had already fallen sharply from earlier levels.
This is no longer a conventional war in the familiar sense. It is a contest over the reliability of economic geography. That distinction is critical.
Iran and its aligned forces do not need to seize Saudi oil fields. They do not even need to shut down every shipping lane. They only need to increase the risk attached to the routes through which Saudi energy reaches the global market. This is chokepoint warfare. The objective is not necessarily to control every inch of territory. It is to acquire leverage over the narrow points through which enormous volumes of trade must pass.
That is precisely why Houthi capabilities matter beyond Yemen. ACLED has documented how the group previously used drones and missiles against airports and hydrocarbon facilities rather than concentrating solely on battlefield targets. From 2018 to early 2022, 43 percent of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia targeted civilian airports and energy infrastructure. The logic is brutally efficient that attack what the adversary cannot afford to lose. For Saudi Arabia, that means oil infrastructure, ports, pipelines, airports and increasingly maritime routes. The Houthis therefore do not have to win a conventional war. They only have to make the cost of maintaining normality rise faster than Riyadh’s ability or willingness to absorb it.
Can Saudi Afford to Defeat Houthis?
This is where the question of Saudi military capability becomes inseparable from the question of Saudi economic strategy. Riyadh can certainly retaliate. It can intensify airstrikes, deploy more intelligence assets, expand missile defenses and work with regional partners. Saudi Arabia has enough resources to impose substantial costs on the Houthis. The harder question is whether escalation would actually solve the problem. A heavier Saudi campaign could force the Houthis underground. It could destroy launch sites and command infrastructure. But it could also generate the very response Riyadh wants to avoid: more attacks against oil facilities, cities, ports and shipping. That is the escalation paradox.
If Saudi Arabia restrains itself, the Houthis may consolidate their position around Bab al-Mandeb and strengthen their bargaining power. If Saudi Arabia escalates dramatically, the Houthis may retaliate against the infrastructure that makes Saudi Arabia economically powerful but strategically exposed. The request to Trump therefore makes more sense in this context. MBS was not necessarily asking Washington to fight Saudi Arabia’s war for it. He was seeking to alter the cost-benefit equation by adding American military power to the deterrence equation. Trump’s refusal to authorize direct strikes, while allowing intelligence and targeting support, exposes a new strategic reality that Riyadh cannot automatically assume that Washington will absorb the escalation risks associated with every Saudi security problem.
That leaves Saudi Arabia with a difficult choice. It can fight the Houthis alone. But a war of indefinite containment would consume resources and expose critical infrastructure. A campaign designed to achieve decisive victory could be even more dangerous because it would invite retaliation against precisely those assets Saudi Arabia is trying to protect. The central problem, therefore, is not Saudi Arabia’s military weakness. It is Saudi Arabia’s strategic exposure. The Houthis possess less firepower, less money and fewer sophisticated weapons. Yet they can exploit a fundamental asymmetry, the cost of launching an attack can be tiny compared with the cost of defending every potential target.
A cheap drone can force the deployment of expensive interceptors. A single strike on a pipeline can disrupt millions of barrels of potential exports. A credible threat to shipping can raise insurance premiums even without sinking a single tanker. A temporary closure of a chokepoint can create economic consequences far beyond the battlefield. This is why the Houthi challenge should not be measured by the territory the group controls or the number of weapons it possesses. It should be measured by the amount of strategic uncertainty it can impose.
Saudi Arabia therefore faces a paradox that extends far beyond Yemen. It has sufficient military power to fight the Houthis, but military superiority does not guarantee strategic immunity. Riyadh can degrade the group, deter some attacks and impose painful costs. What it cannot easily do is eliminate the geography, economic exposure and asymmetric incentives that make the Houthi strategy possible.
That is the real lesson of the current crisis. Saudi Arabia does not need to become militarily stronger simply to defeat the Houthis. It needs to become strategically harder to coerce. That means diversifying energy routes, hardening critical infrastructure, improving integrated air and missile defense, strengthening maritime security, expanding regional intelligence cooperation and, above all, reducing the number of single points of failure on which its economic model depends. The Houthis have exposed a vulnerability that money and military technology alone cannot solve. Saudi Arabia can win battles against them. But unless Riyadh changes the strategic geometry of the contest, the Houthis may not need to win the war.

The eviction operations carried out by the state security forces began shortly after 8:00 am on the Guano beach in Ceuta, where around 400 migrants were still present following the wave of illegal immigration from Morocco that brought more than 70,000 people at the end of July.
The operation was made up largely of officers from the National Police, the Spanish riot units, immigration staff and members of the Civil Guard and local police. The procedure was similar to the two previous clearances on Tarajal and Trampolín beaches.
The migrants were grouped together and taken by bus to the Centro de Atención Temporal de Extranjeros (CATE), where their details will begin to be registered. Afterwards, they will be housed in one of the camps set up by the government, such as the one at the port.
On the two previous occasions, not all the migrants cooperated with the procedure, and many fled into the hills, only coming down when food was distributed. This morning, many gathered up their belongings and left the area before the police arrived.
Minors separated from adults
During the eviction, officers found numerous minors. They were assembled separately and will be transferred apart from the adults.
Several of them were carrying signs asking to be taken to a centre for minors. According to local media, many of the children on this beach had already tried to be registered previously but ran away.
On 20 August, the transfer of migrants from Trampolín beach to temporary reception centres in Loma Margarita and El Embolsamiento began. Some migrants later returned to the beach, as happened when the camp at the port of Ceuta was opened.
Clean-up and assessment of the settlement
Once the site had been emptied, cleaning crews moved in to remove tents, rubbish and all kinds of debris. The work will continue throughout the day, as there is still much to do in a place that has served as a camp for a long time. The ecological damage is significant and will have to be assessed by environmental experts in contact with the Ministry of the Environment.
The camp has left behind serious incidents, including the deaths of two people, as well as brawls, thefts and fights. A parallel life also developed there, with street markets and a way of life of its own.
The eviction comes ahead of the visit by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, scheduled for 13 October. The royal couple will preside in Ceuta over a tribute to those who died at sea during the mass crossing at the Tarajal border. After spending the night in the autonomous city, they will travel on to Melilla. It will be the first time a Spanish monarch has spent the night in Ceuta since the visits by Alfonso XIII in 1904 and 1927.

Pope says to be operated in 'coming days' for lung nodule

"During recent medical checks, a nodule on my lung was found. It has been detected at a very early stage and is very localised," the 71-year-old said in a weekly address in St Peter's Square.

Chicago-born Leo became the first US pope last year, after his Argentine predecessor, Francis, died on April 21, 2025, at age 88.
Francis spent weeks at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where popes traditionally go for medical treatment.
Leo was elected leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics on 8 May 2025.
The former Robert Francis Prevost, less ebullient than his predecessor, has gradually imprinted his style on the Catholic Church's leadership, finding his voice as he takes on some of the world's most pressing issues, from bloody conflicts to artificial intelligence.
After the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, the pope became a high-profile critic of the war.
He condemned US President Donald Trump's threat to destroy Iran as "truly unacceptable" and urged Americans to demand that US lawmakers "work for peace".
Trump slammed the pontiff as "WEAK on Crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy", to which Leo replied that he had a "moral duty to speak out".

Paris motor show: Macron calls for European preference against China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:03:27 UTC
01:03:27 KST

On Monday, the French president will open his final Paris Motor Show, pushing his "Made in Europe" agenda: tying state aid for this key industry to genuinely EU-based production.
Emmanuel Macron is bidding farewell to the Paris Motor Show. The French President will head to the Paris event this Monday, a biennial gathering he has never missed, for his final visit as head of state. It will be an opportunity for the man who declared in 2023 that he "loved" cars to take stock of his record in this strategic sector.
Macron insists that the car industry is "at the heart" of French manufacturing, providing 400,000 direct jobs nationwide. The presidency particularly points to ramping up electric vehicle production and the emergence of a national battery industry.
Before 2017, electric car production in France was still marginal and relied almost entirely on a single flagship model: the Renault Zoe. At the start of Emmanuel Macron's term, a presidential source recalls, the country had "no battery factories at all, obviously".
Electrification and "Made in France"
Since then, output has taken off, but it is still not enough to meet domestic demand. In 2025, according to Insee (source in French), 331,000 new electric passenger cars were registered in France, compared with 216,000 produced in French factories.
But six out of ten electric cars made in France are exported, notably to the United Kingdom and other European markets. In the end, only 26% of new electric vehicles bought in France are manufactured on national soil. Car makers, therefore, have to rely heavily on imports to supply the French market.
France remains far off the target (source in French) set by the government of producing two million electric vehicles a year by 2030. The Élysée nonetheless highlights progress in the electrification of the car fleet and welcomes the opening of four battery plants in the north of the country.
As for every edition, the presidential trip to the show will be preceded, on Sunday evening, by a dinner at the Élysée bringing together representatives of the automotive sector, the presidency has confirmed. Around 60 stakeholders are expected, including carmakers, equipment suppliers, battery manufacturers and companies specialising in rare earths, both French and European.
The presidency notes that no brand boss or Chinese exhibitor will attend the dinner. The show itself, however, will host numerous Chinese manufacturers.
The following day, Emmanuel Macron will stroll through the aisles of the Motor Show, with stops scheduled at the stands of Stellantis, Renault and equipment supplier Valeo. The visit will end with a roundtable devoted to autonomous cars.
A strict European preference
While China has an export capacity of 55 million vehicles of all types, compared with 12 million for Europe, Paris wants the EU to "finally support what it produces" in the face of the wave that is coming.
When it comes to electric cars, France argues that European public subsidies should more strongly favour vehicles produced within the 27 member states. The aim is to establish a "genuine" European preference that covers the entire value chain, from batteries to spare parts.
Even though Paris remains open to "high-quality" Chinese investment in Europe, notably including technology transfers, France wants to avoid the creation of "screwdriver factories", where only "the last bolt is tightened in Europe" while all the other components are made elsewhere.
This is a position Paris needs to align with Berlin, which "is not easy", as France and Germany have "very different" models, the Élysée points out.
"Germany is a country that exports far more vehicles than France, so the interests are inevitably not entirely the same," says a source at the presidency of the Republic.
In practice, Berlin fears retaliatory measures against its own manufacturers, which are highly dependent on Chinese customers, if access to the European market were to be restricted for Beijing, whether through a strict European preference or environmental criteria.
Talks with Germany still ongoing
German business and finance daily Handelsblatt reported on Wednesday that an agreement had been reached between France and Germany: Paris would agree to further relax the European target for cutting CO2 emissions from new cars by 2035, lowering it from 90%, as proposed by the European Commission, to 80% compared with 2021. In return, Berlin would back stricter "Made in Europe" rules.
The Élysée has denied this ahead of the Motor Show: "There is no agreement", but "talks" are indeed under way over European preference.
After a day reserved for the press, featuring the president's visit, the Paris Motor Show, one of the oldest and best-attended in the world, will open its doors to the public from 13 to 18 October at the Porte de Versailles exhibition centre.

At least five people missing as flash floods in Nepal sweep away houses
Authorities urge villagers to move to safer places after a river bursts its banks in the central part of the country.
Flash floods have hit central Nepal, sweeping away houses and leaving at least five people missing, according to officials, weeks after devastating flooding in the country that killed hundreds.
A landslide in Chumnubri village in Gorkha district, about 100km (62 miles) west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River on Saturday, leading to downstream flooding, authorities said.
Two women and three men were unaccounted for, and there are no reports of casualties, said the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
According to the agency, at least 82 people, including nine foreigners, have been rescued from the affected areas.
The flood swept away about a dozen houses and two suspension bridges and damaged a hydroelectric project camp, carrying some of the construction equipment away, authorities said.
A muddy torrent washed away a highway bridge connecting Gorkha with the neighbouring Dhading district, said NDRRMA Chief Executive Dharam Raj Uprety.
Evacuation order
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing.
“We have asked villagers living along the riverbanks downstream to evacuate and remain safe,” said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, Gorkha district’s most senior bureaucrat.
National disaster authorities alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood.
“Please help ensure that people in at-risk areas are moved to safe locations in time and assist search and rescue operations as needed,” the NDRRMA said in a social media post.
Officials said army and police rescue personnel had reached the area and were also monitoring the situation from a helicopter.
“The flood looked similar… It was very scary, and it still feels like a nightmare for us,” said local official Laxmi Gurung of Chumnubri rural municipality.
“Our house is gone, we have no electricity… but there have been no casualties.”
Heavy rainfall in late September also triggered floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the disaster agency.

How extreme boredom can push people toward aggressive behavior
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:00:45 UTC
01:00:45 KST

Boredom might be more than just a fleeting annoyance; it could actually drive people toward aggressive behavior. A new paper suggests that experiencing intense boredom increases the desire for sensation and stimulation, which in turn can lead to both physical aggression and support for military conflict. These findings were published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Psychologists usually define aggression as any behavior explicitly aimed at harming or injuring another living being. Over the decades, researchers have identified biological factors like hormone levels and environmental factors like social rejection that contribute to hostile tendencies.
Recently, some psychologists have begun to explore the role of boredom in aggressive acts. Previous research has linked boredom to everyday sadism, which is the derivation of pleasure from inflicting suffering on others.
It remained unknown whether boredom also drives non-sadistic aggression, which does not require the aggressor to feel pleasure from someone else’s pain. People often experience boredom as an unpleasant emotional state defined by a lack of meaning and an inability to engage with their current environment.
Heng Li, a researcher at Sichuan International Studies University in China, designed a series of studies to test the boundaries of boredom and aggression. Li proposed that boredom acts as a psychological signal prompting people to seek out highly arousing experiences to restore a sense of meaning.
This pursuit of high-arousal experiences is known in psychology as sensation seeking. Because sensation seeking can reduce a person’s inhibitions and narrow their focus to immediate thrills, Li suspected it might push bored individuals toward aggressive actions.
To establish a baseline connection, Li first surveyed 180 Chinese university students and 190 Vietnamese university students. The participants completed standardized questionnaires measuring their general tendency to experience boredom in daily life, as well as their hostile tendencies.
The survey assessed physical aggression, verbal aggression, anger, and hostility. By studying both Chinese and Vietnamese populations, the research expanded beyond the Western, industrialized nations that typically dominate psychology samples.
Li found a positive association between the propensity to experience boredom and aggressive traits. In both groups of university students, those who reported feeling bored more often also reported higher levels of trait aggression. The relationship held true across all four subcomponents of hostile behavior.
Because surveys only measure self-reported tendencies, Li conducted a second study to test physical behavior. This experiment involved 124 non-student adults in China.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two video-watching conditions. In the boredom group, people watched a monotonous 25-minute video of a man repeatedly folding laundry. In the control group, participants watched an engaging 25-minute documentary about a local park.
After watching the videos, participants filled out a questionnaire designed to measure their current desire for sensation seeking. A researcher then escorted them to a separate room with a punching bag and provided boxing gloves.
The researcher told the participants to punch the bag for as long as they wanted, explaining that they would evaluate the punching experience afterward. A concealed camera recorded the activity, and independent raters later evaluated the force and comfort level of the punches.
The results showed that participants in the boredom condition delivered more punches than those in the control group. The bored participants also punched the bag harder, appeared more comfortable doing so, and reported enjoying the activity more.
Statistical analyses revealed that sensation seeking mediated this effect. The tedious laundry video increased participants’ desire for stimulation, which directly predicted their increased physical aggression toward the punching bag.
A final experiment tested whether this mechanism applies to real-world political aggression. Li recruited 277 American adults through an online platform, ensuring a mix of liberal and conservative voters.
As in the previous experiment, participants were randomly assigned to watch either a boring video of a water wall or a more engaging documentary. They then answered questions about their current sensation-seeking desires.
Following the video and sensation-seeking survey, the participants read hypothetical scenarios involving international conflicts. They were asked to imagine themselves as the commander-in-chief and rate their level of support for aggressive military action against Iran.
The scenarios included situations where foreign military entities trained insurgents or blatantly disregarded the international community. Higher agreement on the survey indicated a stronger endorsement of violent military solutions.
Li found that conservatives generally exhibited more support for military strikes than liberals. However, the boredom manipulation increased support for war across the entire political spectrum.
Both liberal and conservative participants who watched the boring water wall video reported higher sensation-seeking scores and greater support for military aggression than those who watched the documentary. Once again, sensation seeking served as the bridge linking the tedious experience to the hostile response.
While the experiments demonstrate that boredom can cause aggressive behavior in laboratory and hypothetical settings, human decision-making relies on many other variables. A person’s baseline level of self-control may alter how they respond to a lack of stimulation.
People with high self-control might resist aggressive impulses even when they feel intensely under-stimulated. Future studies could test whether diminished self-control worsens the aggressive responses seen in bored individuals.
It is also easy to misinterpret these results as proof that boredom inevitably leads to violence. Aggression is just one possible pathway people use to escape an existential void.
Other research shows that people often cope with boredom through positive or neutral behaviors, such as engaging in creative hobbies, physical exercise, or nostalgic daydreaming. Providing people with constructive, high-arousal activities can help channel sensation-seeking urges away from hostility during times of extreme monotony.
The study, “Bored to battle: The relationship between boredom and aggression,” was authored by Heng Li.

Johan Segertoft, head of Saab’s Gripen business unit, said: “The cooperation agreement we have now signed lays the foundation for establishing GKN Aerospace as Saab’s partner in engine-related matters for Gripen E/F. For Saab, being able to contribute to strengthening Sweden’s fighter aircraft capability and domestic industrial capacity is of utmost importance.”
The two already work together on the engine for the earlier Gripen C/D, and this agreement extends that arrangement to the E/F.
The Gripen E/F is powered by the F414, an American engine built by GE Aerospace, and a country operating a fighter on a foreign powerplant depends on the supplier for support, upgrades and spares across the aircraft’s life. Building domestic depth in engine expertise reduces how much of that sits outside national control.
GKN Aerospace has substantial operations in Sweden at Trollhättan, where it has long worked on military engine components and support, and the company also has a significant British footprint.

Prominent Republican senator says Trump's Russian diesel deal may be illegal
Oct 11 - Republican US Senator Thom Tillis on Sunday said President Donald Trump's diesel supply deal with Russia may be illegal and will put American lives at risk, adding to bipartisan criticism of the arrangement announced by the president on Friday.
Trump said that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” said Tillis, an influential Republican from North Carolina who is retiring from the Senate at the end of his term in January.
Prices for diesel — used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking — are near record highs and could hurt Trump's fellow Republicans in next month's congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain their thin majorities in Congress.
Analysts have said Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the Trump administration will follow through with the deal using existing legal authority, adding that the agreement was good for the American people and would bring prices down.
"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have. So, you know, anyone in Congress who says whether it's an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill (that) prohibits us from doing it is wrong," Bessent told the "Fox & Friends" program.
Trump last month signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," to honor the South Carolina Republican who died in July. Graham, a longtime Russia hawk, was a staunch backer of the legislation.
Tillis is not the first Republican to criticize the deal. Retiring Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska said on X on Friday that "propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities."
Mike Pence, Trump's former vice president, called his decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil a "betrayal" of Graham’s legacy and urged the president to "rescind" it.
"The president's actions and his comments over the last 24 hours are the exact opposite of the intent of that bill," Tillis said, adding, "I will guarantee you at the first opportunity (Russian President Vladimir) Putin has to embarrass or undermine President Trump, he will."
As Trump's poll numbers have cratered, congressional Republicans have increasingly distanced themselves from the president, on matters ranging from the conflict in Iran to the trade war with Canada.
The Senate's No. 2 Republican, John Barrasso of Wyoming, defended the diesel deal on Sunday, telling CBS' "Face the Nation" that Trump is focused on bringing costs down for consumers, ranchers, farmers and truckers.
"The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said. REUTERS

Saudi authorities have not identified those responsible for the attacks, although the Houthi militia announced Thursday that it had targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile.

Privacy Authority orders police review of how Yahalomi footage, personal information reached media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:57:35 UTC
00:57:35 KST

The Privacy Protection Authority instructed Israel Police’s internal privacy inspector on Sunday to examine how footage and sensitive information about Mali and Liel Yahalomi reached the media after the mother and daughter were found in Argentina, and what privacy considerations police weighed before authorizing publication.
The authority said its review of media reports indicated that at least some of the information may have come from the police. It has not determined that a privacy violation occurred.
The pair were found on a bus in Argentina on August 14 after a weeklong search. Police released footage of an Israeli police representative approaching them.
Israeli media reports included Yahalomi mother, daughter's sensitive detail
The authority cited later reports that included details from the investigation, such as private correspondence, searches using artificial intelligence tools, the women’s financial situation and transactions, their movements and location, and their expected arrival date in Israel.
The authority said the public should be informed when missing women are found and safe, but raised concerns about publishing footage of them in vulnerable moments and exposing personal details after they had been located.
“The importance of reporting that missing women have been located and are safe is clear to all,” Privacy Protection Authority head Gilad Semama said.
“But there is real difficulty in publishing videos of them in vulnerable moments and exposing their personal details, movements, location and financial transactions after they have already been found.”
Police leak may have seriously infringed on the women’s privacy, watchdog says
Semama said the reports appeared to have originated in the police investigation and may have seriously infringed on the women’s privacy without legitimate justification or in line with police procedures.
Semama wrote to Police Commissioner Daniel Levy and the police’s internal privacy inspector, George Kevorkian, directing the inspector to use the supervisory powers granted under the Privacy Protection Law to conduct a comprehensive review.
The inspector is to examine how the footage and personal details reached news outlets, whether police procedures were followed, and what criteria, if any, were considered before publication was authorized.
The inspector is also to develop lessons for handling privacy issues when police share information with the media in similar cases and provide the findings to the Privacy Protection Authority. The review is being conducted by the police’s internal privacy inspector. No findings have been announced.

EU Parliament adopts resolution calling for Muslim Brotherhood to be added to terror list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:57:14 UTC
00:57:14 KST

The European Parliament has adopted a resolution calling for a coordinated European approach to addressing “Islamist entryism and Muslim Brotherhood networks" and for the Muslim Brotherhood to be added to the EU terror list.
Resolution P10_TA(2026)0342 was adopted on Thursday with 381 votes in favor, 167 against and 15 abstentions.
The resolution refers to Islamist entryism as an "unacceptable form of covert and malicious interference aimed at weakening democratic institutions, the rule of law and the neutrality of public institutions."
It condemns Islamic entryism for "spearheading efforts to roll back women’s rights and gender equality, sexual health and reproductive rights, LGBTIQ+ rights, equality between women and men, freedom of conscience, freedom of expression, public order and social cohesion."
The resolution then stresses the Parliament’s opposition to legitimizing networks that seek to undermine established civil institutions.
Calls for a common European approach to identifying Islamist entryism
The text calls on EU Member States to develop a common European approach to identifying signs of Islamist entryism, including what it describes as the use of "doublespeak" in religious and political discourse. It also calls on the Council to include entities and individuals linked to the Muslim Brotherhood on the EU list of terrorist organizations.
The text also calls for greater scrutiny of European funding and stronger safeguards to prevent EU financial resources from reaching individuals or organizations that may threaten democratic institutions and fundamental freedoms. It specifically singles out Qatar and Turkey for increased scrutiny over foreign funding.
Massad Boulos, Trump's Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs, welcomed the resolution's adoption.
He wrote on X/Twitter that the United States is taking decisive action against Muslim Brotherhood chapters involved in terrorism and destabilizing activities, and that it encourages "continued cooperation with our European partners to combat terrorism, disrupt violent extremist networks, and protect our shared security."

Launch is part of “broader mensch campaign”

According to the group, conference organizers told him that the messaging was inappropriate before security guards and staff escorted him from the auditorium and took away his pass to block him from attending subsequent votes.
