In Ukraine, they propose limiting mobilization deferments for relatives of people with disabilities: who will be affected by the changes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:56:26 EEST
00:56:26 KST

In Ukraine, they propose limiting mobilization deferments for relatives of people with disabilities: who will be affected by the changes
Kyiv • UNN
The legislative proposals could tighten the conditions for deferments for relatives of people with disabilities and eliminate the grounds for relatives of the third degree. For now, this is only a draft; the current rules remain in effect.
The Office of the Military Ombudsman has prepared legislative proposals that envisage tightening the requirements for obtaining a deferment from mobilization for parents of children with disabilities, husbands and wives, and other relatives of people with disabilities. This was reported by former Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Lyudmyla Denisova, UNN writes.
Details
According to Denisova, the Ukrainian Human Rights Protection Center received from the Office of the Military Ombudsman the text of the draft law, a comparative table, and an explanatory note. The proposed changes could narrow the existing guarantees for a number of categories of persons liable for military service.
In particular, they propose introducing additional conditions for parents of children with disabilities under the age of 18. If a family has one child with a disability and both parents, the right to a deferment on this basis could be lost. For husbands and wives of people with Group I and II disabilities, as well as for people whose parents have such disabilities, they propose establishing mandatory permanent-care requirements.
What other changes are being proposed
Additional restrictions could affect parents of children with serious illnesses without an established disability, second-degree relatives, and guardians of legally incapacitated persons. They propose eliminating the separate ground for a deferment for third-degree relatives.
Denisova criticized the initiative, emphasizing that people with disabilities may need help from close relatives even without an officially established need for permanent care. According to her, the proposed restrictions could deprive some families of the support they need.
At the same time, she emphasized that these are only legislative proposals, not an adopted law. The current grounds for deferment remain in effect. The Ukrainian Human Rights Protection Center is preparing an appeal to the relevant committee of the Verkhovna Rada with comments on the proposed changes.

How to tackle serious safeguarding gaps in nurseries | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:52:49 UTC
00:52:49 KST

Your editorial on early years provision (The Guardian view on nurseries: some things are going right for under-fives, 4 October) ends by referring to the horrifying case of Vincent Chan, who worked at Bright Horizons nursery in north-west London. We write as the MP representing the constituency in which the nursery is situated and as the parent of children who attended the nursery and were victims of Chan. We believe his case exposed serious gaps in the safeguarding system that urgently need addressing by government.
First, CCTV should be mandatory in nurseries. When used with appropriate safeguards, it can provide both a deterrent and an important source of evidence when allegations are made.
Second, implementing a “flare” system that goes beyond Disclosure and Barring Service checks, allowing parents, carers and nurseries to report safeguarding concerns, and connecting allegations and relevant employment information across early years settings and over time.
Third, the law governing sexual and exploitative images of children needs examination. One family affected by this case has discovered that photographs of their child found on Chan’s devices did not meet the existing legal threshold for an indecent image. We should ask whether current legislation adequately protects children from exploitative or sexualised imagery that falls short of this threshold.
Finally, early years settings need clear, enforceable standards governing electronic devices, backed by Ofsted inspection. Nurseries hold large quantities of photographs and other sensitive digital information about vulnerable children. The rules governing how devices are used should reflect that responsibility. Had this been in place, Chan could have been caught sooner.
We urge the urgent attention of the prime minister and the government on these matters. 
Tulip Siddiq MP Labour, Hampstead and Highgate, Parent A Parent of children who attended Bright Horizons, Finchley Road, London

A two-tier food system for people living in poverty | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:52:34 UTC
00:52:34 KST

Charlotte Hill (While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution, 6 October) conflates two separate problems. One is food waste; the other is domestic food insecurity. If, as she suggests, we use the former to address the latter, we are simply creating a two-tier food system where people living in poverty do not have the dignity of making their own choices.
While the work of food-waste charities such as the that one Hill heads is commendable as a sticking plaster, in the long term it entrenches poverty and removes any incentive for large corporations to tackle the food waste they create.
The right to food, established in the United Nations charter, includes the right of individuals to acquire food by socially acceptable means – in effect, having enough income to buy it in the same way as everyone else. The question we should be asking is not how can we use up surplus food, but how we can ensure that no one has to rely on charity in order to eat.
People on low incomes are not there to make large corporations feel good about themselves via charitable donations. Hill says that “unavoidable surplus food” is generated in our farming system. If this is the case, then consider coming to an arrangement with schools, hospitals and prisons, but please don’t view people struggling to make ends meet as a repository for your waste products.
In a country with food surpluses, we should be battling against the institutionalisation of food aid, not encouraging it.
Jane Middleton
Bath

Why plan for judge-only trials in fraud cases is wrong | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:51:55 UTC
00:51:55 KST

The government is right to abandon David Lammy’s main proposal to replace some jury trials with judges sitting alone (Ministers drop plans to cut jury trials in England and Wales after outcry, 4 October). There are other ways to reduce the appalling backlog of criminal cases and to protect victims. However, the government is wrong to proceed with its plan for judge-only trials in some fraud cases. As a circuit judge, I presided over fraud trials with juries, including a Ponzi fraud worth £48m and a Russian identity fraud with more than 40,000 documents. The juries were totally on top of both trials and delivered sensible, rational verdicts – in both cases guilty on some charges and not guilty on others. My experience is that the key issue in fraud cases is frequently whether the defendant acted dishonestly. That is not a technical question. It is something that juries are much better able to decide than judges.
Nic Madge
St Albans

Yemen in the Middle East’s energy equation: From natural resources to the right to development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:44:20 UTC
00:44:20 KST

In a mountainous area of Yemen, solar-powered pumps changed how families obtained water. Households that had spent hours collecting it gained access to a system carrying water through tanks at different elevations to their homes. Documented in a World Bank report on electricity access, the experience delivered benefits visible in everyday life: time saved, accessible water and greater opportunities for work and education.
Local electrification projects and the opening of Aden’s solar power plant raise a broader question: how can energy partnerships grow from individual projects into lasting economic capacity?
Yemen’s oil and gas resources, strong solar potential and maritime access provide a basis for economic development. Energy partnerships should connect these assets with domestic production, reliable services and local employment. The terms of investment will determine how much value stays within the country.
Yemen’s share of resource value
Yemen has decades of experience in oil production. The Yemen LNG project’s historical overview records output of approximately 300,000 barrels a day in 2010. This indicates the industry’s past scale; estimating present revenues requires updated production, cost and reservoir data.
Service contracts surrounding extraction determine part of Yemen’s return from oil. Purchasing from domestic suppliers, training technicians and commissioning Yemeni firms to undertake maintenance circulate revenues locally and build skills that can outlast a project. Local content commitments covering these activities can retain more value within Yemen, provided they have measurable targets and effective oversight. A general promise of “technology transfer” offers little basis for assessing delivery.
Refining decisions should begin with markets, feedstock and operating costs. Capital-intensive facilities without dependable sales and maintenance capacity can tie up scarce development funds for years. Assessments should also examine contributions to fuel availability, lower supply costs and domestic services.
Balhaf’s two liquefaction trains have a combined design capacity of 6.7 million tonnes a year, but assessing their economic contribution requires an appraisal of equipment condition, feedstock availability and operating arrangements. Design capacity cannot be treated as current output.
Future decisions should weigh gas export revenues alongside the value of supplying electricity and industry. Reliable power supports workshops and cold storage and enables new investment, while exports generate foreign currency. Infrastructure costs and returns from each use should guide allocation. Agreements with foreign partners need clear information and commitments to support that assessment.
READ: Yemen humanitarian crisis ‘sharply worsens’ as fighting displaces over 200,000: UN
Electricity for services and production
A small system powering lights, a fan and a phone charger may count towards electricity-access statistics, as the World Bank notes in Yemen’s case. It may nevertheless fall short of the power and operating hours required by a health centre or production facility.
Investment planning should begin with the consumer: which equipment must operate, for how many hours and at what affordable cost? The answers determine generation, storage and network requirements. Buying capacity without these connections increases the risk of poor returns.
International cooperation should cover the working life of a project. Equipment suppliers need to provide training and spare-parts access; investors and electricity buyers need clear arrangements for payments, repairs and currency risk. Power purchase agreements (PPAs) must reconcile the project’s revenue requirements with the buyer’s ability to pay. Without maintenance funding, the value of the original investment can deteriorate within a few years.
Solar power: From natural potential to local markets
According to Yemen’s profile published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), approximately 51 per cent of the country’s land falls within a potential annual solar-output range of 1,900–2,000 kilowatt-hours per kilowatt of installed photovoltaic capacity. These estimates help identify promising areas, with site conditions, dust and maintenance requirements shaping project-level performance.
Small solar systems can expand markets for installers, repair technicians and equipment suppliers. Purchase financing and after-sales services matter: abundant sunlight alone cannot help a household unable to afford the upfront cost. Mini-grids can provide shared generation and storage for groups of consumers, particularly where extending the main grid is expensive.
At a larger scale, the UAE-funded Aden Solar Power Plant began operating in July 2024. Its performance can inform subsequent partnerships. Delivered electricity costs, service quality and local maintenance capacity offer useful measures of success.
Diversifying this mix requires attention to the maturity of each option. IRENA’s data show geographical variations in wind resources, making local measurements essential, while geothermal potential identified in Yemen’s Technology Needs Assessment requires further study. Yemen has no nuclear electricity generation; any long-term consideration would require economic, grid and institutional assessments consistent with the International Atomic Energy Agency’s infrastructure framework.
The right to development as a measurable commitment
The UN Declaration on the Right to Development emphasises people’s participation in development and the fair distribution of its benefits. For energy projects, this has contractual implications: service provision, employment and domestic procurement commitments should be specified, with performance information available for assessment.
Yemen’s ports can facilitate equipment imports, energy trade and industrial services. Investment in skills and domestic firms would increase the value of that maritime position. Negotiations with international partners should incorporate these connections from the outset.
Greater exports, accompanied by reliable electricity and productive opportunities, can help reduce poverty and strengthen economic capacity. The credibility of energy diplomacy will ultimately be measured by people’s share of the value generated from their resources—a share visible in incomes, skills and the quality of services.

Rescuers have been battling to rescue people affected by the flash floods in Nepal that swept 45 houses and left five people missing.
Flash floods hit central Nepal on Sunday, sweeping away houses and leaving at least five people missing, officials said, weeks after devastating flooding that killed hundreds.
Videos circulating online showed a dark, debris-filled river surging through the hills in Gorkha district.
"What we know is that a dry landslide had blocked the river and then it burst to cause the flood", said national disaster agency chief Dharam Raj Uprety.
Some 45 houses were swept away, with the flood also damaging three hydropower projects and four bridges.
According to the disaster agency, at least 82 people, including nine foreigners, have been rescued from the affected areas.
"Five people are unaccounted for", Uprety said.
Four helicopters were deployed to support rescue and evacuation efforts as water levels in the Budhi Gandaki continued to rise.
Authorities earlier issued an alert, urging residents to move away from the river to safer areas.
Nepal still recovering from latest flooding
The latest flooding comes with Nepal still recovering from devastating floods, triggered by a mountain glacial collapse on August 26, which killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.
"The flood looked similar... It was very scary, and it still feels like a nightmare for us," said local official Laxmi Gurung of Chumnubri rural municipality.
"Our house is gone, we have no electricity... but there have been no casualties."
The Kathmandu‑based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said the floods highlight the "range of hazards capable of generating destructive floods in Himalayan river systems".
"While response efforts must remain the immediate priority, understanding what triggered this flood, will be critical for reducing future risks and strengthening resilience," ICIMOD's director general Pema Gyamtsho said in a statement.
Heavy rainfall in late September also triggered floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the disaster agency.

Successive Israeli attacks on the occupied West Bank have caused over $3 million worth of losses to the agricultural sector, the Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture reported on Friday.
The report from the ministry states that between 1 and 8 October, there was a marked surge in attacks on the Palestinian agricultural sector.
The attacks include the uprooting, burning, and destruction of trees as well as stealing crops, targeting agricultural facilities and water sources, and bulldozing land.
Many Palestinian farmers have also been prevented from accessing their land, while settlers construct roads and expand outposts which encroach on the land and homes of residents.
A spokesperson for the ministry said their teams have documented agricultural losses worth around $3,678,000, spanning various areas, noting that areas of Jenin and the northern West Bank had suffered the most damage.
“Israeli attacks are no longer limited to isolated incidents, but have now include field attacks, official measures, and settlement expansion,” the spokesperson said.
“What is happening to the Palestinian agricultural sector represents a continuous targeting of the foundations of production, food security, and the resilience of farmers,” the ministry said in a statement.
According to figures released by the ministry, during the attacks, agricultural losses in Jenin had amounted to $2.63 million, followed by Ramallah, and then Hebron.
The Ministry of Agriculture called on UN institutions, rights groups and the international community to take action and provide Palestinian farmers and their land with protection.
The developments come as the Palestinian olive harvesting season commenced in October, and has since seen dozens of Israeli army and settler attacks targeting farmers.
Every year, settlers steal crops and damage olive trees, some of which are hundreds of years old and are a key part of Palestinian identity as well as provide income for families.
The Palestinian Authority’s Commission against the Wall and Settlements announced that over 45,000 trees have been cut down or damaged in the occupied West Bank in the first half of this year, including more than 26,000 olive trees.
Despite initiatives such as the 2026 Olive Harvest Campaign introduced by the Ministry of Agriculture, and support from activists, Israeli attacks have continued.
On Saturday, ten Palestinians, including journalists, were wounded by rubber-coated metal bullets, and dozens suffered from tear gas inhalation during an attack carried out by settlers and Israeli forces in Deir Abu Mash’al, located west of Ramallah.
Jamil Atta, the head of the town’s village council, told The New Arab that “farmers were accompanied by foreign solidarity activists, they went to their land to pick olives in the southern area of Deir Abu Mash’al village, but settlers attacked them and called on Israeli forces, who then opened fire and used tear gas to assault people and expel them from the area”.
Hassan Mleihat, a supervisor at the al-Baydar human rights organisation, also told The New Arab that in recent weeks, dozens of Palestinian farmers were stranded at the gates to their land in Qalqilya after Israeli forces closed them.
He noted that settlers carried out attacks while under the protection of Israeli forces.
Official Palestinian figures state there are around 750,000 settlers residing in around 194 settlements and 400 outposts in the occupied West Bank.

Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street.
Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had.
Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”
His comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the hugely consequential referendum vote.
Burnham did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote.
A report by parliament’s intelligence and security committee in 2020 criticised the government and intelligence agencies for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum.
The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts.
It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election.
The committee also said that whether a hostile state had sought to influence a democratic process was important regardless of whether those efforts had succeeded.
Burnham said Britain needed to be more open about attempts by hostile states to interfere in its politics, particularly as European leaders grapple with the rise of the far right.
Last month the prime minister attacked Russian information warfare during a speech to the UN general assembly, saying there was evidence Moscow had tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.
Burnham told the podcast: “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.
“I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that, actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”
He said he had discussed the threat posed by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, on a visit to Berlin this week. Burnham said Merz raised concerns about the party’s links to Russia.
“One thing I did say to Chancellor Merz … is we need to support you in taking on the threat that you face and particularly the type of politics that you’re facing,” he said. “You know, he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia – funded, I believe.”
He added: “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation, that is emanating from Russia into German politics.”
Last month Burnham opened the door to Britain eventually rejoining the EU, saying his government would examine all options for the country’s future relationship with Brussels.

Ukrainians greet it with doubt
The reaction in Kyiv was wary. Trump already declared an energy ceasefire once, and Putin broke it within five minutes, said Andrii Kovalenko, former head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, asking whether Trump was now “announcing it to himself.”
Meanwhile, lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak called for an explanation, warning that Trump’s “energy ceasefire” might mean Ukraine stops hitting Russian refineries and tankers while Russia merely promises not to strike Ukrainian oil tankers it would struggle to find in the first place.

Ukrainians with accounts in EU banks will be checked under new rules — what will change
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Ukrainians with accounts in EU banks will be checked under new rules — what will change
Kyiv • UNN
EU banks will verify citizenship, check sanctions lists, and review clients’ virtual IBANs. The rules may take effect after approval by the European Commission.
The European Union is preparing common rules for checking customers of banks and other financial institutions, which will also apply to Ukrainians. The new requirements provide for clarifying citizenship details, checking sanctions lists, and monitoring virtual bank accounts. UNN reports this, citing the European Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA).
Details
On October 1, AMLA announced the completion of the technical standards and the submission of the documents to the European Commission for approval. Their aim is to introduce harmonized customer verification procedures in all 27 EU countries.
In particular, financial institutions will have to collect information about customers’ citizenship, check them against sanctions lists while taking into account different spellings of names, and identify users of virtual IBANs and the accounts associated with them.
When will the new rules come into force?
According to AMLA, the standards are proposed to apply six months after they enter into force. Before that, the documents must be approved by the European Commission and published in the Official Journal of the EU.
For Ukrainians who already have accounts with European banks, this may mean providing additional clarification of their personal data. At the same time, information on existing customers will be updated gradually, depending on the level of risk.
The new requirements are part of a reform of the European anti-money-laundering system. The EU’s main regulation in this area is scheduled to apply from 2027.

The Makkah Alliance has been called defensive. Now it has to prove it.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:26:46 UTC
00:26:46 KST

When Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Makkah Alliance for Defence in August, most of us read it as a statement of intent. It took barely two months for that to change. On October 5, ministers and commanders met in Riyadh and agreed to activate collective deterrence measures and send forces and capabilities to the Kingdom at speed. The same meeting appointed retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood, a Pakistani, as the alliance’s first secretary-general for three years.
Then came Thursday. Two Houthi attacks hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, one on the facilities and one on a Saudia aircraft. Three Saudi citizens died, among them a pilot, and people of several nationalities were wounded. Hundreds of flights were cancelled, and European regulators widened their no-fly advisory. By Friday the airport was running normally again. The signal had still been sent: the capital is within reach.
I think this is the moment the alliance has to answer a question it has so far dodged. The pact is modelled on NATO’s Article 5, so an attack on one is treated as an attack on all. Yet all three governments describe it as purely defensive. Both statements can be true only if someone explains where the line sits.
This is not only about Yemen
It helps to remember what kind of war this is. Reuters ties the escalation to the wider US-Iran confrontation. Iranian attacks have choked traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which makes the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait far more valuable than usual. A month ago the Houthis took ground along that coast. Saudi Arabia has answered with a growing air campaign, Sanaa included, and Yemeni government forces backed by Riyadh have launched a large offensive that their government says is meant to retake everything the Houthis have conquered. The coalition says it hit 324 targets and gave those forces air cover.
So the state this alliance is rushing to protect is also a state on the attack. That does not make Saudi Arabia’s position illegitimate, because it is being struck hard. But it does mean “defensive” cannot be assumed. It has to be shown.
Where the language starts to strain
Prince Khalid bin Salman said the committee would act against the attacks and “all those responsible for them”. I keep coming back to that phrase. It could mean the Houthis. It could mean their sponsors. The statement does not say.
Islamabad has been more careful. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif says Pakistani and Turkish forces are in a supportive role while only Saudi troops fight, and he has described that support as including reconnaissance. His test for the pact to apply is unprovoked aggression or spillover from Yemen into Saudi territory, which is a fair standard. And on October 9 the Foreign Office spokesman said allied forces would not attack from or inside Yemen, dismissing reports of Pakistani strikes as speculation.
I take those statements at face value. Nothing in the public record puts Pakistani or Turkish soldiers in combat in Yemen. But “supportive” covers a lot of ground, and some of the reporting is awkward. Middle East Eye, citing Reuters, says Pakistan flew four plane loads of weapons to Aden for the Saudi-backed government. I could not find any official Pakistani confirmation, so that stays an unverified report for now. If it is accurate, though, it is hard to square with the Foreign Office line. Guarding Saudi cities from missiles is one thing. Arming one side of a ground offensive is another, and people in Pakistan are entitled to know which one their country is doing.
How many troops, exactly?
The numbers in circulation come from reporters, not from the government. In May, Reuters reported that Pakistan had sent 8,000 troops, a fighter squadron and an air-defence system. On October 2 it quoted a Pakistani official saying 30,000 to 40,000 troops were helping guard Saudi land borders and intercept drones and missiles.
The army’s spokesman has now confirmed that Pakistani forces are in the Kingdom in “multiple capabilities and domains” and have been for decades. That is accurate, and it is also a little convenient. A decades-old training and advisory mission is a very different thing from a force of tens of thousands on border defence. Nobody in government has told the public which description fits.
I understand why troop positions are kept quiet. Revealing them can get people killed. But the overall size, purpose and limits of a commitment this large are a matter of public policy, and they should not be treated as an operational secret.
READ: Turkiye completes preparations to submit Mecca defense pact to parliament: Foreign minister
Ankara has not finished its homework
The pact brings together NATO’s second-largest army, the Muslim world’s only nuclear-armed state and the leading Gulf power. On paper that is formidable. In practice, the three are not at the same stage. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Turkiye is still assessing how it can help, and the Turkish parliament has not ratified the agreement. Reports say the government plans to take it to parliament, which would clear the way for a deployment. Until that happens, Ankara’s role rests on executive decisions alone, and a pact that lacks legislative backing at home will be hard to sustain once casualties rise.
Pakistan’s difficult position
Pakistan has the most to balance. Years ago its parliament voted unanimously against sending combat troops into the Yemen conflict, and nobody has formally revoked that stance. Pakistan also has a long border with Iran, which supports the Houthis, and a large Shia community at home. Any sense that the country is slipping from defence into offence would carry costs inside Pakistan as well as abroad.
And Islamabad is not short of other worries. India on the eastern frontier, Afghanistan on the western one, and militancy in Balochistan all take up men and money. The economy is fragile, too. A new $1.2 billion IMF deal comes with a warning that the Middle East conflict is weighing on growth, and the families who depend on Gulf remittances feel every escalation directly.
None of this is an argument for walking away from Riyadh. The bond is old and deep, built on faith, history and shared interest. It is an argument for a commitment that Pakistan can actually carry.
On adding new members
People keep asking whether other Muslim countries will join. The Foreign Office has said expansion is “not on the cards” at the moment. I read that as a pause, not a refusal. A bigger alliance is not automatically a stronger one, since every new member brings its own threat perceptions and its own limits on using force. The pause is reasonable, but only if the three founders can make their own arrangement work first.
Defence is not the same as victory
Say the air defences work perfectly. Yemen’s war would still be there. Missiles can be shot down, but the political, territorial and sectarian quarrels behind this conflict will not be solved by interceptors. The danger is a slow slide: an alliance created to protect civilians gradually becomes responsible for a campaign with no clear end. That slide is most likely if Saudi offensive goals, like taking back the Red Sea coast, start to be treated as the alliance’s own.
What I would ask of the alliance
I would start with three things. First, publish a short statement of what the alliance defends, what triggers collective action and what it will never do. It should cover cross-border operations and arms supplied to forces inside Yemen. Second, brief the legislatures. Pakistan’s parliament should hear in closed session what the troop levels and rules of engagement are, and Turkiye should finish its ratification. Third, say plainly that all this military readiness is meant to bring about talks, and back that with real work through Oman, the UN and regional partners alongside it.
How we will know
The alliance began with the promise that regional powers can look after their own security. Thursday’s attack shows how badly that is needed. But I will not judge it by troop numbers or by how many flags appear at the next meeting. I will watch whether Riyadh’s airports stay open, whether civilians are safer, whether the war stays contained, and whether the governments involved can tell their own citizens, honestly, what they have signed up for.
If they can, this could become a template for regional cooperation. If they cannot, it will be remembered as an alliance that promised more than it defined.

The Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed on Sunday that one of the 12 killed in Saturday's strike was an Indian national.
Despite the airport's temporary closure, the Saudi Energy Ministry said a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Sunday.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Sunday's projectile had targeted Terminal 4 of the airport, without elaborating.
Earlier, the Houthis had said in a statement on X:
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina."
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Houthis warn, 'Worse is yet to come,'
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said later on Sunday that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
International energy conference still going ahead
A five-day WPC Energy Congress is taking place this week at a convention center some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport. State TV said more than 70 ministers, 300 company executives and representatives of over 25 international energy organizations had confirmed their attendance.
It was not immediately clear whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to go ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available.
Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the 12 dead included 4 Saudis, 2 Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said.
Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

Report exposes details on post-WWII Nazi entry into Canada following B'nai Brith legal victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:18:59 UTC
00:18:59 KST

The Canadian government released an unredacted version of a 1986 historical report uncovering details about how Cold War American intelligence operations facilitated the entry of individuals with suspected Nazi backgrounds into Canada following a Federal Court ruling siding with B’nai Brith Canada in September.
The report, titled “Nazi War Criminals in Canada: The Historical and Policy Setting from the 1940s to the Present,” was authored by researcher Alti Rodal as a foundational background report for the Deschênes Commission on war criminals in Canada.
Key sections detailing inter-agency friction and security screening breakdowns remained heavily redacted by Ottawa for decades before the recent declassification.
The release followed a prolonged legal battle spearheaded by B’nai Brith Canada, which has fought since the 1980s to compel Ottawa to divulge Holocaust-era records in national archives.
In early September, the Federal Court sided with B’nai Brith, ordering the government to remove almost all redactions from the 618-page report pursuant to the Access to Information Act.
After the Department of Canadian Heritage chose not to appeal the decision, the Library and Archives of Canada provided B’nai Brith Canada with an advance copy of the declassified report at the beginning of October.
New details show proof regarding a covert US resettlement scheme
According to B’nai Brith Canada and reporting by The Canadian Press, details from the newly unredacted passages bring to light archival proof regarding a covert US resettlement scheme.
The report showed that Canadian officials discovered an active and organized program operated by the Research and Resettlement Branch of the US Army, known as USAREUR, which served as a cover used by the CIA and other American intelligence services to relocate defectors and former agents who had provided services to the US.
According to reporting by The Canadian Press on the contents of the declassified sections of the report, a USAREUR official confided that the resettlement scheme included individuals with criminal records, encompassing cases of moral turpitude, a category that historically included Nazi collaborators.
The newly unredacted text discloses that the US official provided Canadian authorities with a list of roughly 35 to 40 individuals who had already entered Canada with the assistance of the covert American program.
Subsequent checks by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police led investigators to conclude that nearly all of those individuals would have been rejectable on security grounds.
As detailed in reporting on Rodal’s unredacted version, American intelligence personnel were uniquely positioned to provide these individuals with falsified documentation and assure Canadian visa officers during routine checks that there were no adverse findings.
A 'historic outcome'
Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s chief executive officer, called the release a historic outcome following the September court victory.
“We are pleased this information has been made available to historians, survivors of the Holocaust and their descendants, and the public,” Wolle said on Thursday. “The time has finally come to obtain justice for the Jewish people, for Canadians to learn from the past, as well as to pursue truth and accountability in Canada.”
B’nai Brith Canada said that the fight for accountability is ongoing as the organization continues its push to secure the release of Part II of the Final Report of the Deschênes Commission.
That portion has remained entirely suppressed by the government since 1986 and is believed to contain sensitive investigative names and findings regarding suspected Nazi war criminals who settled in Canada.

Daycare aide sentenced to 10 years for abusing eight toddlers in Hod Hasharon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:18:52 UTC
00:18:52 KST

A Central District Court judge sentenced Ruan Abd al-Hai to 10 years in prison on Sunday for repeatedly abusing and assaulting eight toddlers at the “Gan Shel Sigal” daycare in Hod Hasharon, where she worked in the nursery group.
The court also ordered her to pay a total of NIS 450,000 in compensation to the children’s parents.
The offenses took place between May and July 2023, when the children were between eight months and a year and a half old. Abd al-Hai was convicted on April 19, after a trial, of 277 offenses: nine counts of abusing a helpless minor under her care, 146 counts of assault causing actual bodily harm and 122 counts of aggravated assault.
The court’s judgment described recurring violence against children who depended on her for care. It found that Abd al-Hai hit, shook, pinched, and threw them onto the floor or mattresses, sometimes while they were crying.
In one incident, the judgment said, she kicked a child lying on a mattress and then struck the child’s head and back. In another, she hit an eight-month-old girl while holding a phone in one hand.
The court also found that Abd al-Hai sometimes fed the children food that had fallen on the floor and, in one incident, forced food into a child’s mouth.
When children cried or approached her, she sometimes ignored them and continued drawing or using her phone. On several occasions, she left children alone in a room with the door closed while she was elsewhere with other children.
Verdict followed trial with video footage
The verdict followed a trial in which the court examined video footage from the daycare. Abd al-Hai’s defense did not ask to cross-examine witnesses and agreed to the submission of evidence and videos, but argued that there was a real dispute over how some footage should be interpreted.
The court acquitted her of 64 allegations, finding in some cases that the conduct did not amount to a criminal offense or that the footage was too unclear to determine what had happened.
The prosecution asked for 14 years in prison, within a sentencing range of 13 to 17 years, citing the number of offenses, the repeated violence and the children’s complete dependence on their caregiver. The defense argued that Abd al-Hai had accepted responsibility and saved court time by not challenging witnesses. It also asked the judge to consider her lack of a criminal record and personal circumstances.
The judge set a sentencing range of nine to 13 years and imposed a 10-year term. She cited the repeated violence against very young children and the need to deter abuse that can be difficult to uncover because the victims cannot describe what happened. She also took into account Abd al-Hai’s lack of previous convictions, her expressions of remorse, and her participation in a treatment group for daycare workers who had harmed children.
The parents’ accounts to the court described lasting effects on the children and their families, including sleep and eating difficulties, anxiety and fear. The judge acknowledged that the families’ concerns about the children’s future would continue after the case ended. She also told parents who had expressed guilt that they could not have known what was happening, according to the judgment.
The NIS 450,000 compensation will be paid in 25 monthly installments beginning December 1. Abd al-Hai is to report to prison on October 18 to begin serving her sentence. The judgment says she may appeal to the Supreme Court within 45 days.

Pakistan imposes emergency rule in Imran Khan's provincial stronghold
Pakistan placed a northern province under emergency rule on Sunday, the president's office said, following anti-government demonstrations by supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and militant violence in the northwest.
Thousands of Khan's supporters have been marching in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province to demand his release and air anti-government criticism fuelled by harsh economic conditions.
Shortly after the measures were announced, Junaid Akbar, a lawmaker from Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, said on X that the province's chief minister, Sohail Afridi, had been arrested along with the provincial president.
A government spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the PTI provincial leader detentions. The country's law minister confirmed the provincial government had been disbanded, saying at a news conference that incidents of militancy had increased during its tenure.
PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan called the emergency declaration "an extremely alarming and grave political mistake and an undemocratic measure".
"The people will never accept such actions against their rights," he posted on X.
The declaration, invoked under two articles of Pakistan's constitution dealing with security, grants the federal government sweeping administrative powers over the province.
President Asif Ali Zardari signed the order after cabinet recommendations "regarding the law and order situation, and the failure of negotiations with government delegations", his office said.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's office said earlier the decision had been taken over the "deteriorating law and order situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and... from the provincial government's deliberate indifference in the war against terrorism".
'Held hostage'
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is a stronghold for Khan's party, and the PTI-led government there will be sidelined under Sunday's extraordinary constitutional measures.
At a later news conference, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar confirmed that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's provincial government would be "non-functional until the situation improves", outlining arrangements for the province to be administered directly by its governor, assisted by an advisory council.
Intense security was deployed in the provincial capital of Peshawar on Sunday, with large numbers of personnel around the chief minister's residence, an AFP reporter said, while mobile phone networks in the area appeared to be disrupted.
Public transport services were suspended, and roads in other cities in the province were also closed.
"All the roads are blocked. We have a democratic government here, with members of the provincial and national assemblies being held hostage," Abdur Rehman, 32, told AFP in Peshawar.
"If they impose an emergency, it would amount to stealing the mandate of our Pashtun people. This should not happen," he added, referring to the ethnicity of the majority of the population in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
PTI supporters began "long march" demonstrations, led by the province's chief minister, between towns and cities throughout Khyber Pakhtunkhwa a week ago with plans to eventually reach the Pakistani capital, as talks with the government broke down.
Show of force
Khan, a hugely popular former cricket star, has been behind bars since August 2023, facing scores of charges ranging from corruption to inciting violence, following widespread anti-establishment riots in May that year.
He and his legal team reject the allegations, branding them as politically motivated.
Once backed by the country's powerful military establishment during his rise to power, Khan fell out over key appointments and foreign policy issues before the parliament ousted him in a vote of no confidence in 2022.
He has publicly accused the military leadership, including Army Chief General Asim Munir, of orchestrating his removal. The military denies meddling in politics.
Facing the threat of civil unrest in recent weeks, the government sought to avert the opposition party's street protests through talks with its leaders, tying negotiations over PTI's demands to agreement on ramped-up security measures in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
The protesters' demands included access to Khan by his doctors. Talks broke down on 4 October, prompting the demonstrations.
In a separate security challenge, Pakistan has blamed an increase in attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the southern border province of Balochistan on militancy emanating from Afghanistan.
The Taliban government in Kabul denies such claims and criticises Pakistan for violating Afghanistan's sovereignty and killing civilians in strikes Islamabad says target militants.
The accusations have sparked a bitter rift and armed conflict between the neighbouring countries this year.

How the ICC can be saved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:15:35 UTC
00:15:35 KST

How the ICC can be saved
Hoping for ‘dialogue’ with the US over its sanctions on the ICC is meaningless. Action is needed to protect the court.
The sanctions the United States has imposed on the International Criminal Court threaten to degrade its capacity to function, leaving it to die a slow institutional death. Its continued operation as an international organisation, let alone a court of law, would become impossible.
The international community has responded with weak statements of condemnation. States Parties have had more than 20 months since US President Donald Trump came to power to prepare for this move. Efforts should have been made to strengthen the court’s institutional resilience.
Still, it is not too late to act. The grace period offered by the US should be used not to engage in fruitless negotiations, but to undertake immediate measures to protect the court.
Impact of sanctions
The sanctions block the ICC’s assets and other property interests in the US or in the possession or control of US persons. Subject to exemptions and licences issued by the US Department of the Treasury, US individuals and companies are prohibited from doing business with the court.
US banks, insurers, IT firms, and other businesses cannot supply the ICC with goods or services or receive payments from it without risking penalties. Many non-US businesses will overcomply and withhold their services out of fear of being sanctioned themselves.
Cutting the court off from suppliers and service providers could paralyse its investigative and prosecutorial activities across all situations.
The sanctions, however, come with a “grace period” of 180 days to allow for maintaining or winding down the ICC operations. This covers States Parties’ payments to the ICC, salary payments, health insurance, and medical services for its employees or contractors, and payments for rent, utilities, and routine services. Separate licences permit the provision of certain telecommunication, cloud and software services, the processing of ICC pension payments, and services needed for the benefit of specified ICC detainees.
Washington has presented the “grace period” as an opportunity for States Parties “to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions” addressing US objections. Yet, in essence, it is an instrument of overt political coercion designed to force States Parties into compliance.
No space for ‘dialogue’
After the sanctions announcement, numerous States Parties once again reaffirmed their support for the court and criticised the US. At this point, however, the ICC cannot be defended with statements alone.
Performative support rings hollow unless accompanied by a coherent, coordinated strategy for countering US coercion and protecting the ICC’s independence. Declarations will not prevent banks from closing ICC accounts, insurers from withdrawing coverage, tech companies from discontinuing their services, or other businesses from abandoning the court out of fear of US retaliation.
The European Union has repeatedly affirmed that the ICC is a cornerstone of international justice and that its independence from external pressure must be protected. On October 10, EU High Representative Kaja Kallas reiterated this position, calling attacks or threats against the court, its officials, and those cooperating with it “not acceptable”.
Beyond these statements, however, the EU has remained passive, seemingly out of fear of further antagonising Trump and triggering US tariffs.
It is troubling that some States Parties and the EU have welcomed the humiliating “grace period” as creating “scope for dialogue” and “space for diplomacy” with Washington. What meaningful compromise is possible when the US objective, stated in unequivocal terms, is to destroy the court?
Over the past 20 months, the US has steadily escalated its war on the ICC. For States Parties and the EU to expect a different outcome now is an exercise in self-deception that betrays, in equal measure, obsequious deference to Washington and a lack of self-respect. Appeasing bullies only emboldens them.
Dialogue under such coercive conditions opens the door to pressure on the ICC to retreat from its mandate in Palestine in exchange for sanctions relief. Accepting US demands, in particular sacrificing the Palestine investigation to appease the rogue regime in Washington, would destroy the court as an independent and impartial institution.
It would reinforce the perception that international justice operates selectively, depending on the political power of those within its purview. Betraying the ICC’s mandate and victims’ pursuit of justice would mean an intolerable loss of legitimacy for the court and discredit the very idea that no one is above the law.
Urgent action needed
Meaningful action is long overdue, but it is not too late for it. States Parties must now make a principled choice and stick to it. They must defend the ICC and secure its ability to function – not pursue fruitless dialogue with a hostile non-party state, beg it for mercy, and offer concessions neither they nor the court can afford.
They must publicly commit to increasing the ICC’s budget and provide it with the resources and facilities it needs to withstand political and economic pressure. They must adopt effective legal measures, blocking legislation and safeguards against financial de-risking, to shield the court, its officials, and those cooperating with it from the extraterritorial effects of US sanctions. These protections must extend equally to Palestinian civil society organisations, targeted for supporting the court’s investigations.
The EU should immediately activate its Blocking Statute to prohibit EU operators from complying with US sanctions. Although no silver bullet, this measure would go some way towards shielding the ICC. A growing number of Member States and MEPs have called on the European Commission to extend this legislation to the anti-ICC sanctions and ensure that protections would be in place in the event of court-wide sanctions. This step can no longer be postponed.
In parallel, States Parties must urgently finalise arrangements for alternative banking, payment and digital infrastructure to ensure the court’s uninterrupted access to essential services. The measures must form a coordinated, structural response, going beyond declarations of solidarity and temporary fixes.
If the international community stands by as the US dismantles the ICC, the ability of any international court — or even any national court — to operate without fear or favour will become impossible.
The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

German 'lawfare': When lawsuits become a political weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:14:00 UTC
00:14:00 KST

German 'lawfare': When lawsuits become a political weapon
October 11, 2026
A verbal slip, an attempted quip, a lawsuit: Things can move fast in the rancorous atmosphere that currently rules German politics.
The brief exchange happened on a political TV talk show shortly after the Berlin election on September 20, won by the socialist Left Party. The show's host, Maybrit Illner, quickly corrected herself after accidentally saying of the Left Party's Berlin mayoral candidate, "Elif Eralp says she is an antisemite…. She is not an antisemite."
One of her guests, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), responded immediately: "Na doch" (or, "well, yes she is"). In the angry fallout, the Left Party's lawyers jumped on these two words, and have filed a lawsuit, arguing that this amounted to defamation of Eralp, as it falsely suggested that the Left Party politician did indeed consider herself antisemitic.
Not only that, the suit stated, Dobrindt's remark would "undermine her integrity as a political officeholder" and hinder her attempts to form a government in Berlin.
It was not the first time the Left Party has got its lawyers involved following its election victory, as it gets bombarded by accusations of antisemitism from the center right, especially over an incident at an election campaign event in Berlin when a rapper chanted "Death to the IDF" — the Israel Defense Forces, or the Israeli army.
Economy Minister Katherina Reiche also angered the socialist party by giving a speech in which she said that the party was now "openly embracing antisemitism." A video of the speech was posted on the Economy Ministry's Instagram account.
Power of the lawsuit
The lawsuit has become an increasingly popular weapon in German politics in recent years, usually by deploying sections 185, 186 and 187 of the German Criminal Code, which cover offenses including insult, defamation and "intentional defamation," which means knowingly asserting or disseminating untrue facts about others. Theoretically, the punishment can be a fine or up to a year in prison.
In September 2025, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) pressed defamation charges against ChancellorFriedrich Merz after he said that the far-right party's policy of remigration amounted to "ethnic cleansing."
Similarly, the Green Party in Berlin brought hate speech charges against Merz last year, when he said "we still have this problem in the cityscape" when describing the presence of immigrants.
In another case, the Green Party's own Robert Habeck was sued in 2024 by the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason(BSW) for claiming that the new upstart party was "buying votes" on the internet by building up "troll armies." Prosecutors dropped the case after Habeck agreed to pay €12,000 ($13,500) to three charities without admitting any wrongdoing, on the grounds that there was only limited public interest in a criminal procedure.
But charges like these, especially when politicians claim defamation, have little chance of success. "Prosecutors usually dismiss such cases very quickly due to a lack of sufficient grounds for suspicion," media lawyer Christian Solmecke, of the firm WBS Legal, told DW in an email.
"The Federal Constitutional Court has consistently held that, in the political arena, the boundaries of what is permissible are significantly wider than in the private sphere," Solmecke added. "Anyone who voluntarily enters the political arena must also be prepared to endure sharp, polemical, exaggerated and hurtful criticism."
Felix Zimmermann, editor-in-chief of the legal affairs outletLegal Tribune Online (LTO), agrees, because German law makes a careful distinction between an opinion and a false statement. "'Antisemitic' or 'not antisemitic' is an opinion, especially at the moment, when people have very different definitions of it," Zimmermann told DW.
Lawsuits as PR
That hasn't deterred politicians from trying it more and more often. "We are undoubtedly observing a new level of intensity and scale of this practice," said Solmecke. "Political culture has become harsher and more polarized. The threshold for no longer merely engaging political opponents through debate, but instead outright criminalizing them, has dropped dramatically."
The danger, Solmecke argues, is that this often amounts to the "misuse" of law enforcement agencies as political instruments.
But lawfare appears to be effective as a political tactic, not least because it's a guaranteed headline. "From the point of view of the parties filing the complaints, they are highly effective as a PR strategy," said Solmecke. "The political benefit arises entirely independently of the legal outcome."
In the Left Party's case, Zimmermann thinks it certainly pays to show you won't stand to be called antisemitic — not least because Eralp has repeatedly underlined her commitment to the Jewish community in Berlin.
"I think it's mainly about the fact that the Left Party wants to form a coalition in Berlin and Ms. Eralp wants to become mayor," Zimmermann said. "So of course it's good if you're insulted to challenge it, as a signal."
When lawsuits have a constitutional point
The motion against Katherina Reiche, on the other hand, may have much better chances — because she chose to post her inflammatory speech on the Economy Ministry's official social media channels. This could, Zimmermann said, well be seen as a violation of the "principle of neutrality," a constitutional rule that forbids the state from vilifying any particular political party.
"That is of course difficult for a politician, because if they say it on their own account they're allowed, but if they say it on the ministry's account they're not allowed," said Zimmermann. "It's a little absurd, because you're effectively splitting one person into two."
But even though the Left Party filed the complaint against Reiche as an urgent motion, the Constitutional Court may take several weeks, if not months, to actually decide the case — by which time the coalition negotiations in Berlin may have long since finished and Reiche's speech has had its effect.
The consequences for Reiche, in other words, will be limited — even if her ministry is forced to take down the post and the Left Party can eventually claim a victory.
Edited by: Rina Goldenberg

Her father was killed on 9/11; on October 7, Jamie Pila fought for Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:11:39 UTC
00:11:39 KST

Throughout her military service as a combat intelligence soldier in the IDF, Jamie Pila, 24, carried a small locket containing a photograph of the father she never knew. Engraved on it were the words "Daddy's Angel." "He was always with me and gave me strength," she says, looking at his picture.
Her father, James Gartenberg, was murdered in the September 11 terrorist attacks on New York's World Trade Center in 2001. At the time, her mother was three months pregnant with Jamie, while her older sister was just two and a half years old.
More than two decades later, Jamie would find herself facing terrorists on another day that changed history, October 7, 2023, while serving as an Israeli soldier near the Gaza border.
"The locket reminds me that I've already paid the highest price for terrorism, and that I have to be here and do my part in the fight, even if it's a small one," she says.
On the morning of September 11, 2001, James arrived at his office on the 86th floor of the North Tower of the World Trade Center. It was supposed to be his final day at the company before moving to a new job, and he had come to pack up his belongings. "After that day, he was supposed to leave for good," Jamie says.
When a hijacked plane struck the tower several floors above his office and fire broke out on his floor, James tried to contact his wife, Jill. "He left her a voicemail saying he didn't know if he would make it out, and that he loved her and my sister," Jamie recalls.
When Jill realized the scale of the disaster, she broke down in the street. "Nobody understood what had happened to her, but she already knew he wasn't going to get out."
As she grieved for her husband, strangers approached her, and she began telling them through tears about the baby she was carrying. "My mom ended up telling people the two most opposite things in the same conversation, the greatest joy and the greatest pain," Jamie says.
‘My parents thought I'd change my mind’
Although she never met her biological father, Jamie feels a deep connection to him. "Everyone tells me I'm exactly like him, both in personality and facial features. Sometimes people look at me and say, 'Wow, you are your father.' Over the years, I've gotten to know who he was. He was a good person, someone who always cared about others and who really loved New York."
Two years after her husband's death, Jill remarried a man named Jay, and the family settled in New Jersey. Jamie gained a father who raised her, along with a brother and sister from his previous marriage. "He's my dad in every sense," she emphasizes.
Her childhood was comfortable and peaceful, far removed from the life she would eventually choose. "We had a quiet life. I had everything. After high school, everyone went off to college on their own path. I played a lot of sports, mainly snowboarding and ice hockey. In high school, I moved to a boarding school where I trained in snowboarding."
Jamie was preparing to begin college when the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted her plans. "When classes moved to Zoom, I realized that wasn't really for me, so I decided to wait a year until we could go back to studying in person," she says.
While looking for something meaningful to do during the break, she learned through her mother about a program run by Masa Israel Journey, which brings young Jewish adults from around the world to Israel.
She decided to go. "I felt like I'd arrived somewhere I didn't know anyone, but people welcomed me with open arms. I just felt at home."
The connection surprised her. "Everywhere I'd traveled before, I thought it was the most beautiful place in the world. But Israel was the first place in my life where I actually wanted to learn about its history. I felt that I had to be part of it."
One particularly emotional moment came when she visited the September 11 memorial in Jerusalem, the only memorial outside the United States that bears the names of all those killed in the attacks.
Standing at the site overlooking the city, she found her father's name engraved in Jerusalem stone. "I was standing at a lookout over all of Jerusalem, and I saw my dad's name carved into the stone," she recalls. "I'm on the other side of the world, standing in front of my father's name, with this incredibly beautiful view behind it and silence all around."
By the summer of 2021, Jamie had made up her mind. She would return to Israel on her own and enlist in the IDF as a lone soldier, the Israeli designation for service members without immediate family support in the country.
"My parents thought I'd get over the idea, that I wasn't serious," she says. "I told them that this time was different."
"They tried to convince me there were lots of ways to support Israel. That I could volunteer and do things for the country, and that I didn't have to enlist. But I knew I had to serve in the IDF."
In May 2022, Jamie enlisted at Michve Alon, an IDF training base that helps new recruits, including immigrants, prepare for military service. She subsequently began training as a combat intelligence collection soldier.
"I researched all the units, and that was exactly where I wanted to go," she recalls. "At first they told me my Hebrew wasn't good enough, but I promised I'd learn. There was nothing that could stop me."
After completing her demanding training, she was assigned to Battalion 727, serving along Israel's border with Egypt. Six months later, on October 7, 2023, she was sent into the fighting near Gaza.
‘I just hoped I would stay alive’
"On October 6, we went out on a nighttime operation and got back at 6:30 in the morning," Jamie recalls. "We were planning to shower and go to sleep. But as soon as we returned, the sirens started."
By midday, her unit had been called to the Gaza border communities, where Hamas terrorists had launched an unprecedented attack. "As we got closer to Gaza, there was this strange silence, the kind that tells you something terrible has happened."
Jamie decided not to tell her family what was unfolding. "I thought to myself, if I text my mom that I love her, it'll sound like a goodbye message, and that could scare her. So I decided not to write to anyone, and I just hoped I would stay alive."
Her team of female combat soldiers reached the area near the Sufa military outpost, close to the Gaza border. "It was a shock," she recalls. "People were bleeding, screaming for help."
The unit split into smaller groups. Some soldiers helped locate people using a drone, while Jamie joined a team accompanying an officer who was evacuating the wounded.
The soldiers were instructed to treat everyone they encountered with suspicion. "They told us to suspect everyone. 'Even when you think it's a soldier, it could be a terrorist.'"
The situation was especially frightening because of how exposed the small group was. "There were only four of us, four female combat soldiers, with wounded soldiers behind us that we had to protect."
Then she heard gunfire. "I heard shots behind me. In the United States, when there's gunfire, you learn to run. But in that situation, I told myself, 'If I get up, I'm dead. I just have to stay where I am.'"
Despite the courage and composure she displayed that day, Jamie does not dwell on the danger she faced. "I don't think about the fact that I risked my life," she says. "I think about how I could have done more."
Her father's memory remained with her throughout her service, connecting the tragedy that had shaped her life before she was born with the violence she encountered as a soldier.
Jamie completed her military service in January 2025 and was discharged from the IDF. Today, she lives in Herzliya with her partner, who also served as a combat intelligence soldier, and is beginning her studies in Israel. Her parents and siblings remain in the United States.
Sometimes, she wonders what James would have thought of the path she chose. "I sometimes wonder what my dad would think if he heard that he had a daughter who was a combat soldier in the IDF," she says. "He was never in Israel, but everyone, his friends and my family, is incredibly proud."
Despite the distance from her family in New Jersey, and despite missing the sports that were such a big part of her life in the United States, Jamie is certain about where she belongs. "I hate the heat. Snowboarding was my whole life. But every time I leave here, I'm just waiting to come back."
For a young woman whose life began in the shadow of September 11 and whose military service brought her face to face with the horrors of October 7, the decision to stay in Israel is deeply personal. "I came here, enlisted and fought terrorism," she says. "And now I just can't bring myself to leave."

The drugs are estimated to be worth Rs 50 crores in the international market."WY" methamphetamine refers to Yaba, a highly addictive combination of methamphetamine and caffeine pressed into pills. The tablets are usually orange or green and are frequently stamped with the letters "WY"."They typically contain a mixture of methamphetamine, caffeine, and binders. The term "Yaba" comes from the Thai word for "crazy medicine." The 'WY' stamp is widely associated with illicit production networks in the Golden Triangle region of Southeast Asia, particularly Myanmar," a senior officer said.
Acting on intelligence inputs, NCB smeuths intercepted two suspicious trucks in Guwahati.
"Because it combines a potent central nervous system stimulant with caffeine, it causes intense stimulation, followed by a severe crash, addiction, and significant long-term physical and mental health risks," the official added.The breakthrough comes as part of a wider, intensified crackdown on narcotics trafficking across the North Eastern region.
Acting on intelligence inputs, NCB smeuths intercepted two suspicious trucks in Guwahati.A search of the vehicles uncovered specially fabricated concealed cavities cleverly built inside the fuel tanks -- a sophisticated method designed to evade law enforcement checkpoints. Officers recovered the massive consignment of methamphetamine on the spot. Both arrested suspects are residents of Bishnupur, Manipur.Preliminary investigation revealed that the multi-crore drug consignment originated from Myanmar. The NCB is aggressively pursuing the wider network to identify international suppliers, domestic receivers, financiers, transporters, and other handlers to dismantle the entire supply chain from source to destination.The agency said the operation continues and it is committed to dismantling drug networks, tracking financial trails, and fulfilling the national vision of a Nasha Mukt Bharat (Drugs-Free India).Emphasizing a zero-tolerance approach, the NCB said its operational strategy extends far beyond individual seizures, prioritizing the destruction of financial and logistical syndicates."To combat the organized nature of these cartels, NCB Guwahati zone is maintaining coordinated intelligence-sharing with state police, the Anti-Narcotics Task Forces (ANTF), Assam Rifles, BSF, CRPF, SSB, Customs, DRI, NIA, and the Enforcement Directorate (ED)," an officer said.

Protesters called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Government to impose a complete and immediate arms embargo on Israel.
The demonstration was organised by the Palestine Coalition, comprising the Palestinian Forum in Britain, Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC), Muslim Association of Britain (MAB), Stop the War Coalition, Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) and Friends of Al-Aqsa.
The march set off from Victoria Embankment and passed through central London before concluding with a rally and sit-in on Whitehall, near Downing Street. Participants carried Palestinian flags and placards demanding an end to British arms supplies to Israel and accountability for its crimes.
Chants of “Free Palestine”, “Stop Arming Israel”, “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” and “Stop the genocide” rang out along the route. Students, healthcare workers, trade unionists, academics and artists joined the demonstration.

A ring depicting one of the Seven Wonders of the World was found on the seabed in Egypt
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:04:49 EEST
00:04:49 KST

A ring depicting one of the Seven Wonders of the World was found on the seabed in Egypt
Kyiv • UNN
Egyptian underwater archaeologists discovered a bronze ring depicting the Lighthouse of Alexandria. The artifact was likely used as a seal.
Underwater archaeologists have discovered a bronze ring depicting the legendary Lighthouse of Alexandria—one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The find was recovered from the bottom of Alexandria’s submerged ancient harbor in Egypt. La Brújula Verde reports, writes UNN.
Details
The artifact was found by a joint expedition of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities and the European Institute of Underwater Archaeology on the submerged island of Antirhodos, which was once part of the city’s eastern harbor.
Scientists suggest that the ring was used as a seal. It could have been used to leave an imprint of the lighthouse in wax or soft clay, seal letters or amphorae, or authenticate documents.
What is known about the legendary lighthouse
Egyptian archaeologist Hisham El-Leithy noted that the engraving on the ring resembles depictions of the Lighthouse of Alexandria on coins from the 2nd century AD.
The lighthouse itself was built approximately between 297 and 284 BC. According to researchers’ estimates, it stood about 120 meters tall, making it one of the tallest structures in the ancient world.
The lighthouse survived for many centuries, but powerful earthquakes in 1303 and 1323 led to its destruction. Some of the stone blocks still lie underwater in Alexandria’s harbor, where archaeologists continue their research.

An equally irate Trump warned that Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukraine’s society to chose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to bow down to US demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” sixty-day ceasefire.
Zelenskyy says ceasefire 'was news for me' but Kyiv would accept it if Moscow does
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said the “energy ceasefire” was news to him.
He told the news outlet Axios that he was not aware of an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia announced by  Donald Trump, but added that if Moscow agreed to such a ceasefire, Kyiv would accept it.
“The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If president Trump negotiated it with Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it,” Zelenskiy was quoted as saying by Axios.
Just hours before Donald Trump claimed the two sides had agreed a ceasefire on energy strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy rebuffed his demand that Ukraine stop bombing Russian oil refineries.
Zelenskyy demanded Moscow has to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on Ukraine and its energy infrastructure.
Ukraine’s president said any deal to end his country’s long-range drone strikes on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to stop attacks on energy infrastructure
Donald Trump has claimed Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an ”energy ceasefire”, though the US president gave no details of the purported agreement.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social network.
Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social account shortly after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told ABC on Sunday that Ukraine was ready for a ceasefire, including on energy infrastructure.
This announcement follows Trump’s criticism of Zelenskyy for attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which he blames for global shortages.
