Russia’s Yandex Under Fire as Drones Hit Third Data Center in Four Days
Russia’s technology giant Yandex has suffered its third reported drone strike in just four days, with an attack on a major data center in Vladimir on October 11 triggering a fire, shutting down operations, and disrupting dozens of digital services across Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to OSINT monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 11, drones targeted the Yandex facility in Russia’s Vladimir region overnight, with footage circulating online showing a fire at the site. Yandex subsequently confirmed that the data center had been taken offline following the attack.
The disruption reportedly affected more than 80 Yandex Cloud services, including computing infrastructure, databases, data storage systems, and artificial intelligence tools such as the YandexGPT API.
Popular consumer services were also affected, including the Alice voice assistant, Yandex Music, Telemost video conferencing, and Yandex Smart Home. The attack also disrupted electricity supplies beyond the facility itself.
Vladimir regional governor Alexander Avdeyev confirmed that drones had struck infrastructure outside the city, causing a fire and forcing two electrical substations offline. Approximately 5,000 residents were left without power.
The targeted facility is part of one of Yandex’s largest data center complexes, with a reported power capacity of approximately 56 megawatts.
In March 2026, the company commissioned an additional data center in Vladimir, designed to accommodate 2,800 server racks and provide 40 megawatts of power capacity.
The infrastructure supports Yandex Cloud, which provides businesses with computing resources, application hosting, data storage, and other digital services.
The latest attack follows two other reported strikes against Yandex infrastructure in less than a week.
On October 9, drones targeted one of the company’s largest data centers in Russia’s Kaluga region. The facility was designed to accommodate more than 3,800 server racks, with a projected power capacity of 63 megawatts.
Just a day earlier, on October 8, another Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region, was struck. That facility has a declared power capacity of 12 megawatts.
The three attacks have reportedly affected Yandex facilities across three separate Russian regions within four days, raising questions about the vulnerability of the country’s major digital infrastructure to drone strikes.

6E 6115 was diverted to Hyderabad after smoke was detected from a customer’s PED
NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight operating from Delhi to Chennai Sunday had to be diverted to Hyderabad after a the battery of passenger’s personal electronic device caught fire. The crew put the PED in water and then the aircraft safely diverted to Hyderabad.“6E 6115 was diverted to Hyderabad after smoke was detected from a customer’s PED. The cabin crew responded promptly and the situation was brought under control. In line with established protocols, the pilots diverted the flight and landed safely at Hyderabad,” an IndiGo spokesperson said.
The personal electronic device with the lithium ion battery or power bank, whatever it is that caught fire, was kept in the overhead baggage bin. Many countries, including India, mandate that the same be kept in front of passengers so that they can quickly spot when and if they start emitting smoke and/or catch fire. The idea is to avoid any delay. However despite announcement to the effect, most passengers simply ignore this instruction and have the power bank or PED in bags and put them in overhead bin.The biggest scare on this front remains airlines taking cabin bags from passengers at boarding gate to be kept in baggage hold of aircraft. These cabin bags may have PEDs, power banks and if a fire breaks out in them in the belly baggage hold, the same won't even get detected easily. The aviation ministry is aware of this issue and is working to resolve it.

Iran, Turkmenistan emphasize expansion of parliamentary, economic cooperation
TEHRAN- Farzaneh Sadegh, Iran’s Minister of Transport and Urban Development and Chair of the Iran–Turkmenistan Joint Economic Cooperation Committee, met Dunyagozel Gulmanova, Speaker of the Assembly of Turkmenistan.
According to the news website of the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development, at this meeting, held in the city of Awaza, Sadegh emphasized the expansion of inter-parliamentary cooperation and the strengthening of sustainable relations based on the principle of good-neighborliness, and stressed the need to increase the volume of trade exchanges.
Other axes of the Iranian Minister of Transport and Urban Development’s talks included developing transport infrastructure, strengthening cooperation in the field of transit, and exporting Iran’s technical and engineering services to Turkmenistan.
She also emphasized the necessity of following up on the resolutions of the joint committee, especially in the key sectors of energy and transit.
At this meeting, Dunyagozel Gulmanova, Speaker of Turkmenistan’s Parliament, while expressing appreciation for Sadegh’s presence and valuable remarks at the international conference “The Role of Women in Maintaining Peace and Achieving Sustainable Development,” emphasized the importance of enhancing relations with neighboring countries.
The Speaker of Turkmenistan’s Parliament, stating that the country emphasizes synergy and the expansion of international cooperation, said: In this regard, developing relations with the parliaments of neighboring countries is essential and strengthens friendship among countries.
At the end, she noted: Turkmenistan seeks sustainable development and increased participation in its country and is ready for economic cooperation with other countries.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, referring to the agreements made during the trip to Turkmenistan, announced plans to begin construction of the Gumdag–Atrak road within the next one to two months and said: The expansion of rail and road cooperation and the follow-up of transport agreements have been among the main axes of the two countries’ negotiations.

Referring to previous meetings between Turkmen officials and officials of the Islamic Republic of Iran, she added: After the trip of the National Leader of Turkmenistan to Iran to attend the funeral of the martyred leader, issues related to relations between the two countries were also raised in his meetings with the President and the Speaker of the Islamic Consultative Assembly, and following up on the agreements was placed on the agenda.

Given Turkmenistan’s role in the transfer of cargo entering the country, expanding this cooperation is of particular importance.

Based on the agreement reached, the executive operations of this route are to begin within the next one or two months.

Zack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:00:29 UTC
00:00:29 KST

Zack Polanski has signalled a potential overhaul of the Green party’s cherished grassroots democracy, calling for leaders to have greater control over strategic direction after a divisive vote equating Zionism with racism.
The Green party leader has also questioned whether political parties should seek to define what members believe, in his strongest criticism yet of a motion that has provoked bitter divisions, international condemnation and calls for his resignation.
Writing for the Guardian after his defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, Polanski suggests the party’s focus on defining Zionism has been misguided, even though he agrees with the substance of the motion.
Appearing to accept criticisms of his leadership over the issue, he admits his priority was “fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party” and accepts that his own colleagues and members may feel “let down” by his decision to not make an intervention last week.
He adds: “I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.”
Polanski says the party’s rapid growth means its democratic structures need to change, including giving leaders more responsibility for setting its political direction.
“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he writes.
His intervention marks the clearest indication yet that he believes the party’s internal structures need reform, after senior Greens raised concerns that its system of policymaking gives disproportionate influence to a small minority of members.
Under the Greens’ existing rules, policy is decided by members at party conference rather than by its leadership, a system that has increasingly come under scrutiny as membership surged.
The controversy intensified last weekend when 1,022 members representing about 0.4% of the party’s total membership voted in favour of a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism and backing a single Palestinian state.
The motion, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813, was opposed by four of the party’s five MPs and prompted criticism from the European Green party, whose position supports a two-state solution.
Ellie Chowns, the Greens’ Westminster leader, said the party must not become vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists, arguing the vote demonstrated the urgent need to modernise its policymaking structures.
Polanski, who is Jewish and grew up in a Zionist household, writes: “It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.
“This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the Holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.
“At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up with identity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.
“There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with, such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.”
The comments go beyond Polanski’s previous objections to elements of the motion, which largely centred on its call for a single Palestinian state rather than leaving Palestinians to determine their own political future.
The controversy exposed divisions within the Greens and raised questions about the party’s ability to manage its rapid expansion under Polanski’s leadership.
The Guardian previously reported that senior Greens feared the existing structure allowed a small number of highly motivated activists to determine policy for the wider membership. Some argued members should set broad political priorities while smaller bodies developed detailed policies.

Yes, it’s been a tough week for the Greens: but don’t lose sight of how we’re transforming British politics | Zack Polanski
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

When I stood for leader of the Greens in 2025, our party was at a crossroads. The transformative leadership of Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay had taken us to an electoral success we’d never seen before. I knew we had even greater potential – and that the country was crying out for the bold politics we could offer.
We have seen unprecedented wins this year – from our first ever parliamentary byelection win to our landslide council and mayoral victories in former Labour strongholds.
Those victories have moved Labour. Our electoral successes helped topple Keir Starmer, seeing him replaced by a prime minister unarguably to his left. They forced a change in tone in the government’s relations with Israel. The government has even rowed back on some of its cruel anti-migrant policies.
Our work isn’t done. But the next phase for our party takes place in a landscape that is clearly more challenging for us. Andy Burnham is enjoying a honeymoon phase, and hasn’t yet had to make the “difficult decisions” that will reveal exactly who will lose out under his government – unpopular choices he will probably start making at his fast-approaching first budget.
Of course I wanted to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. But our result shows, as the polling expert John Curtice has said, that our party represents a greater threat to Labour in places like this than ever before. We tripled our vote share in a seat that Labour has comfortably held since 1983 and forced it to campaign hard in a constituency it would once have taken for granted.
We have transformed the electoral landscape and, as the first nationwide serious threat to Labour on its left in modern political history, we are here to stay.
The result also came at a difficult moment for our party. A motion voted through at our conference, “Zionism is racism”, has stirred up strong feelings among many members and the wider public too. And I know there have been questions about my approach to the motion.
I’m a Jewish man who grew up in a Zionist household. The story I was told about Israel was one of destiny and safety: a land without a people for a people without a land. But since then I have learned about the people who did live on that land – and what has happened to them. The Palestinians driven from their homes; slaughtered en masse; and those who remain, living under an apartheid system that denies them fundamental rights, including that of self-determination.
It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.
At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up with identity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.
There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with – such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.
Before the vote, I made it clear that there were amendments I would like to see made, and I am disappointed that those did not pass.
I have been asked why I was not present for the vote. The answer is that my priority was fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party. I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.
My responsibility now is to bring our party together to achieve our full potential. This starts with an assurance from me: under my leadership, I will not tolerate antisemitism. No one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith or where they worship. I will meet any group within our party that fears victimisation to understand exactly what they need in order to feel safe and welcome.
Second, our party has grown to a size none of us could have anticipated when I became leader. Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible.
Above all, that unity must be deployed in the service of changing this country for the better. This government is on course to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times. Energy bills are expected to rise again this winter; rent increases are forecast to speed up. Meanwhile, Burnham is offering no concrete support for bills and ruling out any controls on rents, and Reform UK is still using cost of living pressures to stir up division in our communities.
The Green party’s bold, principled ideas have never been more needed. From an emergency brake on rents to full public ownership of water companies, we are offering solutions that this government won’t go near unless we force it to. We have work to do – and I will bring my party together to get it done.
- Zack Polanski is the leader of the Green party of England and Wales and a member of the London assembly

Swiss pharma giant Roche presents positive data on eye disease drug
Basel-based pharmaceutical company Roche has presented new data on vamikibart, its experimental treatment for macular oedema associated with uveitis, a condition in which inflammation causes swelling in the macula.
The data show that the treatment delivers sustained improvements in vision and reduces retinal swelling over a 52-week period.
More
How a clash with Roche exposed cracks in Swiss drug pricing system
The results were presented on Saturday at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology in New Orleans, Roche said.
The data come from two identical Phase III trials. In both studies, a higher proportion of patients treated with vamikibart saw an improvement in vision compared with those in the control group. Around two-thirds of patients did not require any further injections after the initial treatment phase.
More
Big Pharma steps up race for AI-discovered drugs
The drug has not yet been approved. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted Roche’s application and is expected to make a decision by July 2027. Applications have also been submitted in the European Union, China and Japan.

Russia has redeployed military personnel to Belarus to participate in CSTO exercises: what is known about the maneuvers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:59:44 EEST
23:59:44 KST

Russia has redeployed military personnel to Belarus to participate in CSTO exercises: what is known about the maneuvers
Kyiv • UNN
CSTO exercises involving more than 1,500 military personnel from five countries have begun in Belarus. The troops are practicing peacekeeping operations and countering biological threats.
Joint military exercises of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), "Indestructible Brotherhood-2026" and "Barrier-2026," began in Belarus on October 11. More than 1,500 military personnel from five countries, including Russia, are taking part in the maneuvers. The military will practice conducting peacekeeping operations and countering biological threats, UNN reports.
Details
The opening ceremonies of the exercises took place in Vitebsk and Staryya Darohi. The main phase of the maneuvers is scheduled for October 12–16.
Military contingents from Belarus, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan are taking part in the exercises. Units of law enforcement agencies, the national guard, and operational groups of the CSTO Joint Staff are also involved. In total, more than 1,500 military personnel and over 300 units of weapons, military equipment, and special equipment have been deployed in the maneuvers, including approximately 80 drones of various types.
The command-and-staff exercises "Indestructible Brotherhood-2026" involve practicing the preparation and conduct of a peacekeeping operation by CSTO collective forces. At the same time, as part of the special exercises "Barrier-2026," the military will practice eliminating sources of biological threats, as well as organizing radiation, chemical, and biological protection and medical support. The exercises will take place at the Losvido and Starodorozhsky training grounds.
The core of the Russian contingent consists of units of the Russian Armed Forces' Central Military District, including motorized rifle, reconnaissance, and medical units, military signalers, electronic warfare specialists, and operators of unmanned systems. The CSTO leadership emphasizes that the exercises are planned and allegedly are not directed against third countries.
Context
The Collective Security Treaty Organization comprises Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Armenia. At the same time, Armenia has frozen its participation in the organization's activities.
In 2026, Russia holds the CSTO chairmanship. The organization's stated priorities include increasing the readiness of collective forces, developing military-medical cooperation, and improving mechanisms for responding to security threats.
Reminder
At the beginning of October, Russia and its allies conducted exercises involving the seizure of territories and the creation of a security zone outside the country. Forty-seven thousand military personnel took part.

Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove lung nodule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:59:38 UTC
23:59:38 KST

Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove lung nodule
The 71-year-old religious leader told pilgrims during his weekly Sunday blessing at St Peter’s Square.
Pope Leo has said he will undergo surgery in the next few days to remove a small lung nodule recently discovered during a health check.
The 71-year-old leader of the Roman Catholic Church told pilgrims during his weekly Sunday blessing that “it was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed”.
“The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it,” he said at St Peter’s Square during remarks delivered in Italian.
The Vatican later said that a week of recovery time is expected after Leo’s surgery, though spokespeople did not say whether the nodule is believed to be malignant.
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than five percent of lung nodules ultimately become cancerous, although the risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking.
“Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign,” said Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in the United States and division chief of hematology-oncology at Washington, DC’s MedStar Georgetown University Hospital.
The pope has no previously known health problems and is considered physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
Latin American tour
The pope has a major trip planned November 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It’s unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he planned to go.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished the pope well after receiving the news, saying in a statement, “I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days.”
“The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it [today] …are reassuring,” the prime minister added.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88. He was hospitalised several times and grew frail in his later years. He did not usually announce his hospital visits in advance, sometimes sparking intense media speculation about his health.

Norwegian nonprofit Fritt Ukraina is allocating NOK 10 million (about $1 million) to strengthen air defenses around Chornomorsk, a key Ukrainian port on the Black Sea, the organization announced on 9 October.
Russian attacks on port infrastructure and civilian vessels are threatening Ukraine’s maritime trade and agricultural exports, putting pressure on a vital source of revenue for the country and disrupting shipments of food to international markets.
The funding will support Ukrainian State Border Guard Service and Armed Forces units defending the region against Russian attack drones. It is being delivered through Dronefall, a project run by the Ukrainian Come Back Alive Foundation, which equips military units with interceptor drones and the equipment needed to operate them.
Fritt Ukraina, whose name means “Free Ukraine,” is a Norwegian nonprofit organization that supports Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s full-scale invasion. The donation is part of its Odins Ravner 2.0 fundraising campaign, which provides military assistance to Ukrainian forces.
Interceptor drones and equipment to protect port infrastructure
The support includes STING, Blyskavka and P1-SUN interceptor drones, alongside ground control stations, communications equipment, generators, charging stations, laptops, tablets and vehicles, according to the organization.
The interceptor drones are already operational, according to Fritt Ukraina. The equipment helps Ukrainian personnel detect and intercept Russian attack drones, while vehicles allow crews to move quickly and operate from different positions.
Fritt Ukraina Secretary General Natalia Golis said effective air defense requires more than interceptor drones alone. Communications systems, reliable power supplies and mobility are also essential to ensure units can use their equipment effectively.
The organization is supporting Dronefall for the third consecutive year and has become the Come Back Alive Foundation’s largest foreign partner. The latest donation was matched by a donor affiliated with the Ukrainian foundation.
Russian attacks threaten Ukraine’s maritime exports
More than 90% of Ukraine’s agricultural products, including grain and vegetable oils, are exported through three ports in southern Odesa Oblast. Russian attacks have targeted port infrastructure and civilian vessels, increasing security risks for commercial shipping and driving up freight and insurance costs.
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, more than 1,000 Ukrainian port facilities and over 200 civilian vessels have been damaged or partially destroyed, Fritt Ukraina reports. The disruption threatens Ukrainian export revenue and international food supplies.
“The attacks on Ukraine’s ports do not only undermine the country’s defense capabilities. They also threaten a vital part of its economy and its ability to export food to the rest of the world,” Golis said.
Dronefall aims to expand Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones using dedicated interceptor aircraft and supporting equipment. According to Fritt Ukraina, participating units have destroyed more than 53,000 Russian drones, accounting for approximately one in five unmanned aerial vehicles entering Ukrainian airspace.
The NOK 10 million contribution is part of Fritt Ukraina’s broader Odins Ravner 2.0 campaign, which provides more than NOK 60 million in support to Ukrainian forces.

Israeli settlers attack Palestinian olive harvesters across occupied West Bank
Israeli settlers and soldiers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives across the occupied West Bank overnight and into Sunday, with reports of tear gas being fired at women picking olives, agricultural equipment being stolen, and trees destroyed.
The attacks targeted communities around Nablus, Ramallah and Jerusalem as Palestinians worked to gather a crop central to their agricultural livelihoods. They followed at least 18 settler attacks recorded across nine West Bank governorates on Saturday, according to the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission.
In Yatma, south of Nablus, five Palestinian women, including an elderly woman, suffered from tear gas inhalation after Israeli forces fired canisters at them while they were picking olives, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The women were then prevented from leaving the land, according to Wafa, with Israeli forces citing its location in Area C — the part of the occupied West Bank placed under full Israeli security and administrative control under the Oslo Accords.
East of Ramallah, settlers reportedly accompanied by Israeli soldiers raided agricultural land in the village of al-Mughayir and stole equipment used for the olive harvest.
Local sources told Palestinian media that settlers also stole harvested olives. The raid came a day after the village faced what the sources described as "continuous attacks" by settlers, who destroyed a number of trees.
In neighbouring Ein Yabrud, settlers reportedly seized a vehicle as well as agricultural equipment, further disrupting Palestinians’ work during the harvest.
Another incursion was reported on Sunday in Mikhmas, north of Jerusalem, where a group of settlers entered land planted with olive trees.
The theft of crops and equipment, alongside attacks on farmers and the destruction of trees, threatens both the immediate harvest and the livelihoods of families dependent on their groves.
Attacks across nine governorates
The latest incidents followed a wave of attacks documented on Saturday by the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission, which recorded at least 18 settler attacks across nine governorates, including Ramallah, Nablus, Jerusalem and Hebron.
The reports from several villages described attacks on Palestinians while they were working their land, with Israeli soldiers reportedly protecting settlers during the incursion into al-Mughayir.
Separately, Israeli forces carried out overnight raids and arrests across the occupied West Bank.
Soldiers arrested three Palestinians in Hebron, three in Bethlehem governorate and six in Jenin governorate, including one who was injured in Qabatiya.
In Tulkarm, Israeli forces arrested nine Palestinians, among them people who had previously been detained.
Israeli forces also delivered an evacuation order to a Palestinian family living in Qalandiya village, north of Jerusalem, citing a lack of the required paperwork for their residential building following a judicial decision.
Palestinians and human rights groups say Israeli authorities use planning and permit requirements to force Palestinians from their homes in occupied territory.

Netanyahu condemns deadly Saudi airport attack: ‘On behalf of Israelis, I offer condolences’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:52:35 UTC
23:52:35 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued an unusual public condemnation on Sunday of a deadly missile attack on Saudi Arabia's main international airport, offering condolences on behalf of Israelis after a strike blamed on Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed 12 people and wounded 309 in Riyadh.
"I condemn in the strongest possible terms the shocking terrorist attack at Riyadh airport," Netanyahu said in a statement. "On behalf of the citizens of Israel, I extend our deepest condolences to the families of those murdered and wish the injured a full recovery."
"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with determination," he continued. "Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East, one that stands united against threats, protects its people and builds a future of security, cooperation and prosperity for all the peoples of the region."
The unusually direct message of solidarity came as the Houthis threatened further attacks across Saudi Arabia and a new projectile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday afternoon, less than a day after Saturday's deadly attack.
Houthis threaten further strikes as Riyadh airport remains closed
The Saudi-led coalition reported that another projectile struck Terminal 4 on Sunday, triggering a fire. It also reported intercepting a separate cruise missile. Around the same time, reports emerged of an attack on the airport in Sanaa, Yemen's Houthi-controlled capital.
Earlier Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree reaffirmed the group's intention to enforce what it described as an aerial blockade of Saudi Arabia, warning international airlines, airport employees and passengers against using the kingdom's airports and airspace.
The facilities, he warned, had become "theaters of operations for our forces."
Saree said the Houthis remained determined to enforce their declared principle of "airport for airport, blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation" until their objectives were achieved.
He accused Saudi Arabia of bearing responsibility for the consequences of failed attempts to intercept Houthi missiles and urged the public to take the group's warnings seriously.
The spokesman said all areas of Saudi Arabia were potential targets except Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities. The clarification followed Saudi accusations last month that the Houthis had fired toward Mecca, home to the Kaaba, one of Islam's most sacred sites.
An aviation industry source in Saudi Arabia told AFP on Sunday morning that operations at Riyadh's international airport remained suspended. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported that the shutdown had been extended, with flights not expected to resume before midnight Sunday local time.
Twelve killed, hundreds injured in deadliest Gulf attack since Iran war began
Saturday's missile struck the area housing terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid International Airport, which serve domestic flights.
Saudi aviation authorities said the dead included four Saudi nationals, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Sudan and the Palestinian territories.
Among the 309 wounded, several were reported to be in critical condition, with hospitals across the Saudi capital treating large numbers of casualties.
The strike was the deadliest attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war involving Iran began in February.
Western sources said information gathered after the attack suggested there had been no advance warning and that no warning sirens sounded before the missile struck.
The attack came just two days after another deadly Houthi strike on the same airport killed three Saudi nationals, including a pilot, and damaged at least one passenger aircraft that was empty at the time.
Several other attacks targeted airports in Riyadh and Abha earlier in the week, killing three more people.
The growing focus on Saudi airports marks a significant escalation in the conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which is supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government with extensive airstrikes against rebel-held territory.
Trump weighs military intervention as international condemnation grows
U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Houthis, although he emphasized that no decision had been made.
Trump later described the attack on Riyadh airport as "terrible" and "unacceptable."
The possibility of direct American involvement comes as the conflict in Yemen increasingly intersects with the broader war involving Iran, a longtime backer of the Houthis.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed deep shock over the deadly strike, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned what she called a dangerous escalation. Germany also joined the international condemnation.
Why the fighting in Yemen is escalating
The renewed confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began in July, ending roughly four years of relative calm in Yemen's civil war, which erupted in 2014.
The latest escalation followed Houthi attempts to break the Saudi-imposed air blockade on rebel-held territory, coinciding with renewed fighting involving Iran.
Last month, Houthi forces launched a rapid offensive that brought strategic coastal areas of southwestern Yemen under their control, strengthening their position around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The narrow waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and forms part of a vital shipping route between Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal, carrying approximately 12% of global trade.
Although the Houthis already possessed the ability to strike ships in the Red Sea using missiles and drones, their territorial gains gave them greater control over the strategic passage.
Its importance to Saudi Arabia has increased dramatically because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula, during the war with Iran.
Earlier last week, Yemeni government forces backed by Riyadh launched a major ground offensive aimed at pushing the Houthis out of their newly captured territory and restoring control over Bab el-Mandeb.
Saudi Arabia has provided extensive air support for the operation, carrying out heavy bombardments of Houthi positions.
Reports indicate that pro-Saudi forces have made advances near the strait, although the extent of those gains remains unclear. The Houthis deny claims by Yemen's internationally recognized government that its forces have already regained control of Bab el-Mandeb.
The intensifying conflict has now brought Saudi Arabia's civilian aviation infrastructure directly into the fighting, while Netanyahu's condemnation and Trump's consideration of military intervention underscore the widening regional repercussions.

The province, which borders Afghanistan, was ruled by former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.

In the United States, a way to restore damaged cartilage has been found: scientists are talking about treating arthritis without surgery
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:46:16 EEST
23:46:16 KST

In the United States, a way to restore damaged cartilage has been found: scientists are talking about treating arthritis without surgery
Kyiv • UNN
Blocking an age-related protein restored cartilage in old mice and human tissues. The method still requires clinical trials.
American scientists from Stanford University have discovered a way to stimulate the regeneration of articular cartilage, which usually barely regenerates. The experimental treatment has already shown results in animals and human tissues. ScienceDaily reports this, citing Stanford Medicine, writes UNN.
Details
Researchers found that blocking a certain protein, whose levels increase with age, can trigger the regeneration of cartilage tissue. Its gradual deterioration is one of the main causes of osteoarthritis.
During experiments on older mice, the treatment helped restore lost cartilage. In addition, it reduced the risk of developing osteoarthritis after knee joint injuries.
Will people be able to avoid joint replacement?
Scientists also tested the approach on human cartilage tissue obtained during knee replacement surgeries. After the inhibitor was applied, the cells began forming new functional cartilage tissue.
Researchers believe the discovery could become the basis for treating osteoarthritis without complex joint replacement surgeries.
At the same time, the method remains experimental for now. Its effectiveness and safety for patients still need to be confirmed in clinical trials.

The risk tolerance is low and non-existent."
"I would also share with you a reflection: the way that it appears to me that the IDF and other security professionals view threat. Normally, our doctrine tells us we view threat…as capability plus intent. What I have noticed now is that they reflect threat as capability. That many IDF security professionals view capability as equal in a threat, I think they're reflecting some of the policy guidance they receive and some of the societal pressures that they feel. But in this regard, it's helping to understand this environment," he noted.
In other words, Salene, while sympathetic to Israeli trauma after October 7, was telling his Israeli audience that going to the extreme of always focusing on the worst-case scenario of what enemy capabilities are is counterproductive and problematic.
While he wanted to support Israeli military officials in some respects, he challenged them to consider whether politicized policy guidance and social pressures, rather than expert judgment, are shaping their professional assessments.
Salene warns Hamas threat extends far beyond Gaza, West Bank
Next, he warned that the threat of Hamas itself is also much broader than its immediate forces on the ground confronting Israel.
"Hamas is then not confined just to one place. It's not confined to just Gaza. It's not confined to Judea and Samaria. It exists in Jordan and in Syria, and in Lebanon, and we have financiers in Florida, and in Europe. So this understanding is priority number one for counterterrorism: a broader view of Hamas as an ecosystem," stated the US general.
Here, Salene encouraged Israeli political and defense officials to look beyond the obvious physical battle space before them to think of Hamas as a movement, idea, and series of relationships which extend across the globe, and cannot be shut down by more force in Gaza and the West Bank alone.
In addition, Salene specifically complimented IDF Central Commander Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth, saying, "You have an incredibly principled leader. An incredibly principled leader in IDF Central Command. Very difficult environment inside of your society. I'm speaking as a military officer to see another military officer attempting to enact his policy with the instruments he had, which now touches your political level."
With these remarks, Salene laid bare problems which Bluth and the Shin Bet have highlighted in terms of a lack of support from the political echelon and from the police in cracking down sufficiently against Jewish extremist violence and terror in the West Bank, even as all Israeli forces have worked well together to keep the larger Palestinian terror problem down.
Discussing security coordination with the PA, he said, "Security coordination. What is it then the United States can do to support the security coordination? There are two parts. The first part, respect and understand what exists and not get in the way."
"The second part is when that begins to break down and becomes very difficult. Where is it the United States can step in in order to assist if it gets difficult, there's tragedies this summer you can tell," he added.
Moreover, Salene said, "Tragedy. How is it that it didn't spiral? I will just share with you. There was effective security coordination. There was communication. There was an effort to de-escalate and contain the crisis so it did not spread. Why? If I zoomed out for a moment and said that if the crisis has spread and destabilized, would the destabilization only be confined to Judea and Samaria?"
Continuing, he asserted, "A destabilization is likely to affect the stability of Jordan. As a US Central Command officer, the stability of Jordan matters. It's important to you. It's important to us. It's important to the bigger picture, to the wider strategic question, which remains open."
Salene highlights role of Israeli-Palestinian security coordination in preventing escalation
Here, Salene was arguing that when Israeli and Palestinian security officials work well together, his office can just stay out of the way, but when they are not, he has stepped in at crucial moments to calm tense situations which could have blown up into much larger unnecessary conflicts.
Salene also reminded everyone that a destabilized West Bank can have concrete national security implications with Jordan, which has been an invaluable ally in counterintelligence against Palestinian terror.
Trying to convince some of the skeptical Israelis listening that US and Israeli security coordination with the PA pays off, he said, "21 years ago, we received funding from my government to provide police forces non-lethal training…we're not paying for an army. We don't support an army. We support police forces, and I offered that there were questions about what it is for the IDF and the security services."
He said that his office helps "enable the training, in accordance with international standards, human rights, and the rule of law, of a security partner to counter Hamas and terrorist threats. This is a particularly difficult conversation today. It's a particularly difficult conversation to have in this environment, but it is a necessary one."
He then asked rhetorically: "Because what is the alternative? What is the alternative? Is the alternative that the security forces in Judea and Samaria are not on the field? Would the gap remain open, or would it be filled? And if it be filled by a terrorist organization, or it be another command upon the IDF."
Realizing how hard it might be to convince some Israelis of the necessity of a US coordinator is necessary to help train PA forces, he volunteered that skeptics exist in the US as well, noting, "There are folks in my own government who say, 'Why should we spend another dollar? Over here in the Palestinian Authority, that's a corrupt institution. Yes, there is corruption. This is the instrument that we have. I am not a politician.
This is a political discussion, and it will quickly get to the political. I will speak to the practical and the technical."
Continuing, he stated, "In a practical and technical institutional capability in accounting, I will share with you that there are people on the other side who work on de-radicalization, who push on education, who know that their structure is wrong."
These comments hit Netanyahu at his most sensitive point. Of all of the aspects of the October 2025 ceasefire which Netanyahu did not like, but signed on to get the Israeli hostages back, allowing PA police into Gaza, trained by the US, Egypt, and Jordan, was the provision he opposed most vehemently.
Yet, where Netanyahu viewed creating a new Gaza police force associated with Fatah as strengthening PA military power which could confront Israel in the Strip, Salene said that any other alternative will lead to Hamas or Palestinian power brokers who disregard human rights and any vision of a stable future for Gazans.
Next, he revealed strengths and weaknesses of the process of the US and other countries coordinating with the PA.
He said that these allies are "a coalition of nations who also support the security of Israel, even when the political place gets very difficult at the technical place, at the military place to maintain this military architecture together for the day when the political winds have shifted, but the architecture remains for the support for defense of Israel."
"Now, the coalition that we lead has nine other nations inside this coalition. The United States coordinates inside this coalition to ensure it is not too far left, not too far right, down the middle to align these efforts. Other actors are on the stage who are not in our coalition. I want to argue there are other actors that have a relationship with the Palestinian authorities that's not in our interest. Russia and China would come to mind," he cautioned.
Salene urges negotiations, de-escalation to counter Hamas recruitment
Waxing philosophical, Salene then asked some additional rhetorical questions about some of the x-factors which go to the heart of the counterterrorism mission, "Back to the fundamental question: Which way is the terrorist ideology the people who are being marketed to being recruited, which way are they going to go? I would argue it is in our interest for those people to stay with the negotiation track, de-escalation, coordination to support a future negotiation, not to succumb to Hamas and the call to jihad."
Next, he stated, "So in this case, the provision of basic social services…undermines the Hamas' argument, which then helps us in the wider picture in a struggle with the movement, which extends far beyond this country."
"These are the ways that we do at the security system to disrupt, coordinate capability, legitimacy, and order, to get to a more durable stability, to one day open the stage for a larger conversation," he added.
Here, Salene tried to convince Israelis that providing a better life to Gazans is in Israel's interest since more stability will bring less conflict.
While a hard sell to Israelis after October 7, Salene argued there is still no real alternative.
CENTCOM and Lt.-Gen. Salene's office declined to comment regarding the article.

Where are the pilots who saved us? Flydubai survivor questions crew’s role in attack - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:43:35 UTC
23:43:35 KST

Eleven days after helping to overpower the co-pilot accused of trying to crash a flydubai flight bound for Israel, passenger Asaf Rajuan wants two flight attendants who were on board to be investigated. He has also called for the two additional pilots who were traveling and who landed the aircraft in Saudi Arabia to be questioned.
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post on Sunday, Rajuan said he suspected the attendants had assisted the attacker. He described confrontations with passengers, objections to filming and exchanges between the two men that left him afraid the danger had continued after the co-pilot was restrained.
The September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the co-pilot attacked the captain with an aircraft emergency axe.
His allegations remain unsubstantiated. The UAE’s account on Friday credited a flight attendant with helping subdue the attacker. It said the co-pilot had confessed to acting alone, while making clear that investigators were still checking for accomplices and other connections.
Rajuan wants Israel involved in establishing what happened. In our conversation, he kept returning to the crew’s behavior and the difficulty of knowing whom to trust while the aircraft was still airborne.
He had been returning from Phuket, Thailand, with his wife and their two daughters, approaching 12 and 14. He was seated in 7D when a woman ran down the aisle shouting that someone had a knife. He looked toward his family and saw them thrown into the air.
He thought he was watching his daughters die.
He ran toward the front. The captain’s resistance had already weakened the attacker, Rajuan said, making it easier for passengers to overpower him. He suffered a small head wound and emerged covered in blood, much of which, he said, was not his own.
The suspicions about the attendants
Rajuan made his most specific accusation in an interview with N12’s Ulpan Shishi, broadcast Friday. He alleged that one attendant began loosening the attacker’s restraints after passengers had subdued him. Several passengers noticed and challenged the man, he said.
He also described an attendant approaching the wounded captain with a tablet while the captain was receiving medical treatment. Rajuan said passengers intervened because they could not understand why someone would try to give him a pill in that condition.
“I have no proof,” he said when asked whether the attendants had cooperated with the attacker.
In the interview with the Post, Rajuan described grabbing, pulling at clothing, and repeated confrontations with the attendants. One asked whether he was a police officer. He remembered their physical strength and their determination to stop passengers filming. He feared someone would produce another weapon.
There was uncertainty even about where the aircraft was heading. Passengers checked GPS locations and offered competing answers: Iraq, Jordan, Saudi Arabia. Rajuan wondered whether they were still being hijacked.
“I became paranoid,” he said.
He acknowledged that he had begun suspecting everyone. Yet he wanted investigators to examine the specific encounters he and other passengers remembered, including the attendants’ interactions with those guarding the attacker. He described an atmosphere of mutual fear and pressure that persisted after the immediate struggle had ended.
The pilots who took over
Rajuan also wanted to know what had become of the two additional pilots. He said he had looked for their public accounts and had not found them. On N12, he recalled last seeing the pilot who saved the aircraft as he disembarked.
Their presence aboard Flight FZ1073 has an explanation we reported on September 30.
There were four pilots: the captain who was attacked, his co-pilot, and a second flydubai cockpit crew traveling in the passenger cabin. The additional captain and co-pilot were available to operate the return flight from Israel.
A person familiar with the arrangement told the Post that possible regional diversions could add hours to the flight and leave the operating crew beyond its permitted working hours. The additional pilots had been assigned as a staffing precaution, without advance warning of an attack.
When I interviewed Tal, an Israeli businessman aboard the flight, at Tel Aviv’s Carlton hotel on October 1, he described having to get those men forward while other passengers fought the attacker.
“I had to shake them to get them to move to the front and take control of the plane,” he said.
Tal recalled an interval when the cockpit was empty. One pilot eventually took control; the other, he said, took longer to recover from the shock. We have not independently established the duration of that interval or the precise sequence inside the cockpit.
The UAE’s account described the relief captain noticing unusual movements of the cockpit door, entering with an access code and helping passengers and a flight attendant overpower the attacker. He and his co-pilot then restored control and landed in Tabuk.
It did not address Tal’s account of their initial hesitation or the empty cockpit.
The relief pilots have spoken to investigators: prosecutors said they had taken statements from both men. The statement did not name them.
Our interviews have reconstructed the emergency from the passenger cabin: people fighting at the front, an injured captain being treated, two other pilots being urged toward the controls. Rajuan wants the men who eventually flew the aircraft to give their own account, including what they saw of the attendants’ conduct.
“I hope that Israel will investigate it as it should be,” he said. “Because it’s something that needs answers.”

Jewish students join "Nonnegotiable" campaign against El-Sayed over antisemitism, safety concerns

Unknown Publisher

14:43:24 UTC
23:43:24 KST

University of Michigan students have joined the Nonnegotiable Michigan campaign, expanding the grassroots effort onto college campuses as young voters express growing anxiety over Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's past rhetoric and refusal to address community concerns.
The students, who identify as Democrats and are connected to the initiative through the Jewish Caucus of the College Democrats of America, stated that they feel disappointed by their options in the Michigan Senate race.
Lacking a candidate who addresses their baseline needs as liberal and progressive Jewish Americans, these student leaders have signed onto the Nonnegotiable petition to help build a political home within the Democratic Party while organizing their peers on campus.
The inclusion of campus leaders marks a broader generational expansion for a campaign that was initially launched with Michigan rabbis, cantors, and synagogue lay leaders representing approximately 40,000 Jewish Michiganders.
Previous waves of endorsement have drawn prominent figures, including a University of Michigan Regent, a sitting state representative, former state lawmakers and mayors, and nine executive board members of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus.
The campaign's momentum builds on mounting community frustration that previously led faith leaders to write to former Vice President Kamala Harris ahead of her Michigan visit, noting that El-Sayed had declined to address their basic needs.
That correspondence pointed to past remarks from El-Sayed characterizing Israelis as bloodthirsty and American support for Israel as stemming from purchased loyalty, alongside his continued reticence to affirm Jewish sovereignty.
Urge for El-Sayed to affirm five core commitments
The student leaders are publicly and privately urging El-Sayed to affirm five core commitments: that Jewish safety, including the safety of Zionist Jews, must be guaranteed; that the right of Jews to define their own identities must be respected; that Jewish sovereignty in Israel must be recognized; that the full participation of Jews, including Zionist Jews, in American political life must be upheld; and that an affirmative vision for a better future for the Middle East must be offered.
While framing the initiative as an open invitation rather than an ultimatum or an endorsement of either Senate candidate, Nonnegotiable campaign leaders argue that El-Sayed's refusal to respond is deepening anxieties as Election Day approaches.
Nonnegotiable said that according to their compiled data there are 8,057 first-time Jewish voters in Michigan this year.
With new polling showing that the race is within the margin of error, and with high stakes for the future of the Democratic Party, organizers said that El-Sayed's affirmation of the bare minimum needs of Jewish Democrats would go a long way for a voting bloc that has overwhelmingly supported the party for generations.

The side-by-side comparison shows both men with blood on their faces and their right fists raised in the air. The resemblance has attracted attention on social media, offering an unexpected moment of humor following the attempted hijacking.
Trump's original photograph, taken by Associated Press photographer Evan Vucci on July 13, 2024, captured the then-presidential candidate moments after a bullet grazed his ear during a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.
Surrounded by Secret Service agents, Trump raised his fist and shouted "Fight!" as an American flag flew behind him.
The photograph quickly became one of the defining images of the 2024 presidential campaign, appearing on newspaper front pages and the cover of Time magazine.
Trump's iconic raised-fist photograph becomes viral internet meme
It also became an internet phenomenon. According to the meme-tracking website Know Your Meme, social media users produced countless adaptations, parodies, and illustrations of the raised-fist photograph. One early post by Elon Musk attracted well over 176 million views and three million likes.
Now, more than two years later, the image has found an unlikely Israeli counterpart.
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post on Sunday, Rajuan laughed about the comparison.
"I didn't plan it," he said.
In a separate interview with Channel 12, Rajuan acknowledged that the comparison was circulating online, describing the resemblance as amusing and emphasizing that his own gesture had been completely spontaneous.
Rajuan's viral photograph taken midair after struggle with flydubai co-pilot
Rajuan said his photograph was taken while the aircraft was still airborne, following the struggle with the co-pilot who allegedly attempted to crash the September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
He had sent it to family and friends, barely noticing the blood covering his face.
"People told me to touch my face. I didn't even understand what they were talking about," he told the Post.
The Israeli father of two had rushed toward the cockpit after watching his wife and daughters thrown into the air as the plane plunged.
"I saw the end of their lives before my eyes," he recalled.
The photograph captured a moment of relief after a terrifying confrontation. Its resemblance to Trump's famous pose has since given Rajuan an unexpected place in the online afterlife of an iconic American image.

FEDA urges UN and European Parliament to take urgent action to protect hunger-striking detainees in Egyptian prisons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:42:56 UTC
23:42:56 KST

The Families of Egyptian Detainees Association (FEDA) has called on the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) to take urgent action following reports of hunger strikes and collective protests among detainees in several Egyptian prisons, particularly during 7th–9th October. The association warned of potential risks to detainees’ lives and health amid reported restrictions on fundamental rights and concerns over access to medical care.
In an urgent appeal dated 10th October 2026, FEDA urged the UN Working Group to seek clarification from the Egyptian authorities regarding the reported hunger strikes and the grievances behind them, and to take appropriate steps within its mandate to protect detainees from death, serious injury, ill-treatment, and reprisals for participating in peaceful protests.
As part of its international advocacy efforts concerning the situation of detainees in Egypt, FEDA has also sent similar letters to the European Parliament, urging urgent attention to detainees’ conditions, action to protect hunger strikers, and efforts to end reported violations in Egyptian prisons. The association called for respect for detainees’ fundamental rights, particularly the rights to life, healthcare, family visits, and a fair trial.
According to information received by FEDA, which the association says it is continuing to verify, the protests have been linked to deteriorating detention conditions, repeated alleged violations of detainees’ basic rights, and the absence of effective remedies for their complaints. Reports have referred to protests in several places of detention, including Minya, Abu Zaabal, Badr, the Tenth of Ramadan, and New Valley prisons. FEDA stressed that the level of available information and documentation varies between facilities.
Restrictions on family visits, exercise, and medical care
FEDA identified the main grievances reported by detainees and their families as the denial or severe restriction of family visits, deprivation of outdoor exercise and sunlight, obstruction or delay of necessary medical treatment, and prolonged pretrial detention in cases reportedly extending beyond applicable legal limits.
The association also expressed concern that despair arising from years of detention and repeated legal proceedings without a final resolution has led some detainees to resort to hunger strikes as a means of protesting their conditions and demanding that their grievances be addressed.
READ: Detainees to begin hunger strike in Egypt prisons
FEDA warned that hunger strikes can cause serious health complications, particularly for detainees with chronic illnesses or those denied adequate medical monitoring. It also called for scrutiny of reports of security interventions, detainee transfers, communication restrictions, and confiscation of personal belongings, stressing that such measures must not be used to punish individuals for peaceful protest.
Postponement of the new Criminal Procedure Code adds to detainees’ concerns
FEDA linked the growing frustration among detainees to prolonged pretrial detention and the postponement of Egypt’s new Criminal Procedure Code, Law No. 174 of 2025. The Code had been scheduled to enter into force on 1 October 2026, but its implementation was postponed for one year, until October 2027, according to the information cited in the appeal.
The association said that some detainees had hoped the new Code’s provisions concerning pretrial detention would lead to a review of their legal status or their release. The postponement, it argued, has deepened frustration among those who have already spent extended periods in custody.
FEDA stressed that postponement of the new Code should not justify detention beyond the limits established by the legislation currently in force. It called for the review of cases in which detainees may have exceeded applicable legal limits and for scrutiny of any use of successive cases or repeated proceedings to circumvent those limits and prolong detention.
FEDA concluded its appeal by urging urgent action to prevent further harm and address concerns regarding arbitrary and prolonged detention in Egypt. It also called on international and human rights institutions to monitor the situation of hunger strikers and work to ensure the protection of their fundamental rights.

Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire – Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:39:03 UTC
23:39:03 KST

Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire – Trump
US President Donald Trump has said Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire. The announcement comes just days after Trump’s phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, during which the two leaders agreed on a deal aimed at easing the global fuel crisis through Russian diesel exports.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday, adding that “both parties have agreed” and urging Moscow and Kiev not to “break it.”
Ukraine's Vladimir Zelensky later confirmed on X that he discussed Trump’s announcement with NATO chief Mark Rutte, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, adding that Kiev supports the initiative.
On Friday, Trump and Putin held a phone call, shortly after which the US Treasury Department announced a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing the fuel to be sold, delivered, and imported into the US until April 7, 2027.
According to Trump, Moscow agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November and one million more shortly thereafter. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak also confirmed the figures and said Moscow would begin lifting diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule “immediately.”
The US president allegedly struck a deal with Moscow after Zelensky ignored Washington’s requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, Axios reported on Saturday. Trump has blamed Ukraine, and Zelensky personally, for exacerbating the global fuel crisis, saying that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have driven up fuel prices, including for American consumers.
On Saturday, Trump once again accused Zelensky of seeking to “make problems for the world” and ignoring US requests, suggesting that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” The Ukrainian leader hit back by demanding a two-month-long total ceasefire to hold the vote.
“If President Trump really wants to have some changes during elections… please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” he told ABC on Sunday.
Russia considers Zelensky illegitimate, as his presidential term expired more than two years ago and he has not called a new election, citing martial law.
Ukraine has ramped up long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including civilian and energy infrastructure such as oil refineries, amid continued setbacks at the front. Zelensky has recently threatened to intensify attacks on Russian refineries in particular. Moscow has denounced the attacks as acts of terrorism and vowed to intensify strikes on Ukrainian military-related facilities, including drone and missile warehouses, while maintaining that it never targets civilians.

Djiboutian authorities continue search and recovery operations as fears grow for those still missing. About 82 people survived the shipwreck, according to a statement issued by the United Nations migration agency on Sunday.
The latest boat accident is one of many similar deadly calamities that have occurred in Djibouti's Red Sea coast area. In most of these incidents, desperate East African migrants attempted to cross the dangerous route, hoping to reach the Middle East via war-torn Yemen, with the main destination being Yemen's northern neighbor, Saudi Arabia. ■

Namibia detects foot-and-mouth disease in second region

WINDHOEK, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has detected foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) in the Zambezi Region, marking the second region affected by the outbreak after cases were reported in the southern Kharas Region, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform said Sunday.
The disease was detected at Kalala Island in Kabe Constituency, where veterinary officials observed 20 cattle showing clinical signs on Oct. 5. All 12 samples collected from the animals tested positive for FMD virus on Oct. 7, according to a public notification from the ministry.
The ministry said emergency vaccination had commenced in the affected area, while intensive surveillance was underway to establish the full extent of the outbreak.
Movement of all cloven-hoofed animals and their raw products has been suspended throughout the Zambezi Region. Marketing and trade, including livestock auctions and other animal-gathering events, have also been halted, while slaughter at local abattoirs and informal markets has been suspended, it said.
The Directorate of Veterinary Services has activated the national FMD contingency plan and established roadblocks to enforce movement restrictions, while allowing slaughter at export abattoirs under commodity-based trade for quarantined cattle with satisfactory traceability.
The latest detection comes as Namibia intensifies containment efforts in the southern Karasburg Veterinary District, where Agriculture Minister Inge Zaamwani recently inspected control operations and met affected farmers.
Construction of a veterinary cordon fence along farms bordering the Orange River has commenced and is expected to be completed within four months, the ministry said in a separate statement on Sunday.
Construction of another fence around the containment zone is expected to begin during the week of Oct. 12, it added.
Vaccination teams are also preparing to deploy to the Karasburg outbreak epicenter, with vaccination expected to begin once schedules are agreed upon by relevant stakeholders.
The ministry urged livestock owners to comply with animal movement restrictions, cooperate with veterinary officials, and report suspected cases to the nearest state veterinary office. ■

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
22:38:24 CST
23:38:24 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Mingde Strategic Dialogue 2026, which concluded in Beijing on Sunday, brought together scholars and strategic thinkers from around the globe to explore the new opportunities China's development offers the world.
Over the six-day event, themed "Resilience and Vitality: New Opportunities China's Development Brings to the World," international participants took part in field visits and public discussions.
Hosted by Renmin University of China (RUC), the dialogue took participants to Xinyu in east China's Jiangxi Province and Wenzhou in east China's Zhejiang Province before they gathered in Beijing to discuss China's resilient growth and explore new approaches to global economic recovery and sustainable development.
Speaking at the forum in Beijing on Sunday, Jennifer Shipley, former Prime Minister of New Zealand, said in her keynote speech that when reflecting on who has contributed to global growth in the last two decades, global growth statistics would be "somewhat miserable without China's momentum."
"At a time of volatility, we all look for stable anchors upon which we can rely and pathways that will lead to mutual prosperity," she said, adding that China has made an outsized contribution to both over a sustained period of time.
When attending the 2026 Wenzhou Business Development Forum -- Zhejiang Belt and Road Think Tank Dialogue in Wenzhou, Shipley told Xinhua that China's large consumer market and growing middle-income group offer opportunities for industrial development and international trade.
Rejecting the view that China's development has peaked, she said that through development planning, strategic investment and decisive leadership, China has built new industries in relatively short periods and made significant progress in areas such as electric vehicles, while continuing to advance in robotics.
Mulatu Teshome, former President of Ethiopia, said in his keynote speech on Sunday that China has made renewable energy more accessible and affordable, a shared opportunity to build a sustainable planet.
John Ross, former director of economic and business policy for the mayor of London, the United Kingdom, and a senior researcher with Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies of RUC, noted that China's open-source AI models could help make AI more accessible across the Global South, highlighting another area in which China's development could benefit other countries.
Reflecting on their entire trip in China, including visits to lower-tier cities, a steel manufacturer and a lithium mining company, many participants described the visits as "eye-opening."
"China has made significant advances in areas including artificial intelligence, automation, infrastructure, batteries and renewable energy," said Glenn Diesen, professor at the University of South-Eastern Norway.
George Galloway, a former member of the United Kingdom Parliament, was deeply impressed by a visit to a steel factory in Xinyu, Jiangxi, where he saw steel so thin it could be torn by hand.
On what lessons the world could draw from China's remarkable development, Richard Caplan, professor of international relations at the University of Oxford, said in an interview with Xinhua that China offered an alternative to development models historically promoted by international institutions.
"China's experience has attracted considerable interest from developing countries, particularly in Africa, where some countries see it as a model worth studying and potentially adapting to their own circumstances," the professor said.
Radhika Desai, a professor of political studies at the University of Manitoba in Canada, said on the sidelines of Sunday's forum that one lesson the rest of the world could draw from China's development path is the importance of overall planning, even in economies with a large private sector.
Looking ahead, cooperation will remain key to addressing shared economic challenges. Diesen said European concerns about industrial competitiveness, the automotive sector and technological sovereignty could be addressed through cooperation with Chinese companies.
For Ethiopia, Mulatu said, deeper cooperation with Chinese enterprises in mining, agriculture, manufacturing and infrastructure is needed. He also pointed to China's zero-tariff treatment for eligible African countries as an opportunity to expand exports. ■

Chinese golfer Liu makes history as first amateur to win women's China Open
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
22:38:23 CST
23:38:23 KST

SHANGHAI, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Beijing teenager Liu Yujie made history on Sunday as the 16-year-old became the first amateur to win the Women's China Open, securing a four-stroke victory at the national championship.
Starting the final round one stroke off the lead in sunny but breezy conditions at the links-style PGA Anying Golf Club Yangtze Dunes course on Shanghai's Chongming Island, Liu closed with a three-under-par 69 for a 54-hole total of seven-under 209. It was the third CLPG Tour victory in two years for China's top-ranked female amateur against professional fields.
"The thing I'm especially happy about is that I won my first tournament after being away from competition for two months. I'm a player who really loves competing, and I usually play tournaments consecutively rather than taking such a long break," said Liu, the daughter of former table tennis world champion and Olympic gold medalist Liu Guoliang.
"To come back and achieve such a good result feels great. I think it shows that I've matured as a player and become better at adapting to different situations."
Cui Jinghan added to a strong showing by Chinese amateurs at the CLPG Tour's flagship event, with the 15-year-old Beijing native carding an even-par 72 to finish tied for second with overnight leader Shi Yuli, who shot 74. As the leading professional, Shi collected the 180,000 yuan winner's purse.
Playing in the final group, Liu drew level for the lead at the first hole after making par while Shi opened with a bogey. Liu then birdied the second to move into the outright lead.
Shi birdied the 150-meter fifth hole to draw level, but the seventh proved pivotal as Liu made birdie and Shi bogeyed for a two-shot swing. Shi dropped another stroke at the eighth to fall three behind, while Liu reeled off 10 consecutive pars before sealing victory with a birdie on the final hole.
"Overall, I felt good about my game today. My driving, approach shots, and shots around the greens were all pretty steady. I was able to maintain a consistent scoring level throughout the three rounds. Even with a two-shot advantage heading into the final hole, nothing is certain until the ball drops into the cup. I knew I had to stay patient and concentrate on what I needed to do," said Liu, 16th in the World Amateur Golf Rankings.
"The 18th hole was definitely the highlight of my day. It was the final hole, and there were more spectators there than anywhere else on the course. It was great to play such a beautiful hole in front of everyone, and I was really happy to make a birdie."
Shi, last year's inaugural points ranking winner, lamented a missed opportunity to claim her second career title after winning the season-ending CLPG Tour Championship in December.
"My game wasn't in great shape during the first half of the year as I was sick quite a bit. This week, I felt like I was getting back into form, so it was a bit of a shame that I couldn't quite finish the way I wanted to on the final day," said Shi. "I struggled to find my rhythm today, and my tempo felt a little off, particularly with my putting. I was probably a bit too aggressive on the greens."
Cui, 79th in the World Amateur Golf Rankings, started the day two shots behind Shi but was unable to mount a sustained challenge for the lead while playing in the final group. Her round included three birdies and three bogeys, with the last bogey coming on the final hole.
"I played pretty well today, especially on the back nine where I holed a few long putts. On a few holes, particularly the first two or three, I didn't judge the wind quite right, which affected my distance control," said the teenager.
"This result will give me more confidence moving forward. When I play in bigger tournaments in the future, I'll feel more confident setting higher goals for myself. It'll also encourage me to keep practicing and improving my game."
Ren Yijia, the CLPG Tour points ranking leader, shot a one-over 73 to finish fourth, five strokes off the pace. Thailand's Nook Sukapan finished a further shot back in fifth after carding a 67, the lowest round of the tournament.
Pang Runzhi, last year's champion, closed with a 77 to finish tied for 29th, 15 strokes behind Liu. ■
