News Analysis: Israel's Arab vote could decide next premier, despite political exclusion
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
22:38:15 CST
23:38:15 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Israel's Arab citizens could help decide who will govern after the Oct. 27 election, yet neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main challenger, former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is willing to bring Arab parties into his coalition.
ELECTORAL STAKE
The upcoming parliamentary vote will be the first since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attack and wider regional conflict.
Forming a government typically requires a coalition controlling 61 of the Knesset's (parliament) 120 seats.
An Oct. 4 poll by Israeli public broadcaster Kan projected 51 seats for Netanyahu's right-wing bloc and 52 for four predominantly Jewish opposition parties spanning the political spectrum from right to left. Arab parties were projected to win 13 seats, with four going to a party outside either bloc. Even with those four seats, the opposition would remain five short of an outright majority in the Knesset.
For Arab citizens, roughly one-fifth of Israel's population and descendants of Palestinians who remained in 1948, the paradox is stark: their votes could shape the next government while their representatives are excluded from it.
POLITICS OF EXCLUSION
Netanyahu, on trial for three counts of corruption charges he denies, has made Arab support for his rivals a campaign weapon, portraying these votes as a national threat.
Eisenkot, a former army chief who served in Netanyahu's wartime cabinet, rejects Netanyahu's rhetoric while preserving the political exclusion.
Although he has accused Netanyahu of portraying Arab politicians as "traitors," he sets conditions that effectively exclude them from his own coalition, including a requirement that parties representing Israel's Palestinian minority embrace the country's identity as a Jewish state. In a recent interview on Israel's Ynet news site, he said no Arab party meets his conditions.
The Joint List is the political alliance of Arab-majority political parties in Israel. It was originally formed by Hadash, Balad, Ra'am and Ta'al ahead of the 2015 election. In August, Hadash, Ta'al and Balad reached an agreement to run together in the 2026 Israeli legislative election, while Ra'am chose to run separately.
Political psychologist Prof. Eran Halperin argued in a recent interview on Israel's Ynet news site that Eisenkot's tougher stance was aimed at courting right-wing voters opposed to Arab political participation, but it is an "implausible fantasy" for Eisenkot to secure 61 parliamentary seats without Arab parties.
He proposed including the Arab-majority party Ra'am in a coalition and seeking outside support from other Arab parties, arguing that Jewish-Arab political cooperation was also essential to rebuilding trust between the two communities.
In 2021, Netanyahu's camp sought Ra'am's support, but the Arab party joined the centrist coalition with crucial seats that ended Netanyahu's 12-year hold on power, underscoring the political stakes in Netanyahu's efforts to delegitimize Arab parties as potential partners for his rivals.
Late last month, Israel's Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of Balad, from running in the Knesset elections with support from Eisenkot's Yashar party and Yair Golan's left-wing Democrats, despite Golan's commitment to Jewish-Arab partnership.
Abu Shehadeh withdrew after Supreme Court judges indicated they would uphold the ban.
The move sparked criticism from Israel's Arab community. Ahmad Tibi, lawmaker and leader of the Ta'al, called the vote "a slap in the face of the entire Arab public," while human rights group Adalah accused the process of seeking to "turn racism against Palestinians into election propaganda."
THE ARAB PARTIES' LEVERAGE
Arab parties, however, are seeking to use their parliamentary leverage to secure political gains. They can recommend a candidate to the president and influence a government's confidence vote by supporting or abstaining.
Yousef Jabareen, chairman of the Joint List and leader of Hadash, announced on Saturday that his party was ready to back any government that replaces Netanyahu, subject to negotiations.
"According to all the data, an alternative government cannot be formed without negotiating with the Joint List," he said in a video statement.
His demands include a funded program to tackle crime in Arab communities, an end to house demolitions, and a political path toward Palestinian statehood. He ruled out supporting budgets for wars and settlements.
Arab voters have their own priorities. A September Israel Democracy Institute poll found that a party's position on crime in Arab society is ranked most important among Arab voters.
In a May survey by the Moshe Dayan Center and the Konrad Adenauer Program for Jewish-Arab Cooperation at Tel Aviv University, 77.2 percent of respondents supported the inclusion of an Arab party in the next government coalition, and 63.7 percent believed in or favored an Arab-Jewish political partnership. ■

Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:34:15 UTC
23:34:15 KST

Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties
Trump has long criticised US military support for Ukraine and has lambasted Zelenskyy since his first term.
United States President Donald Trump has called for the removal of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after blaming the Ukrainian leader for rising diesel prices, which have put pressure on the Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections.
The criticism on Saturday came as tensions between the US and Ukraine have increased after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Saturday, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump added.
Zelenskyy on Sunday pushed back, vowing to continue striking Russian oil refineries. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
This is not the first time Trump has lambasted Zelenskyy. Their tense relationship goes back to Trump’s first term as president, when he pressured Zelenskyy to investigate his rival, Joe Biden, and his son, Hunter Biden.
Here’s a timeline of some of the occasions when Trump has been critical of Zelenskyy:
October 2026: In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticised Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason, he never does,” Trump added.
Trump, who has been urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure for weeks, struck a deal with Putin on Friday to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices.
The deal marked a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Russia over its full scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said every additional $1bn Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries.
Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished, he added.
April 2025: On April 15 , Trump criticised Zelenskyy and implied Kyiv had started the war against Russia, saying the Ukrainian leader was “always looking to purchase” US missiles. “You don’t start a war against someone 20 times your size and hope people give you some missiles,” Trump said.
Then on April 23 , he criticised Zelenskyy for making “very harmful” statements after the Ukrainian president pushed back against the idea of ceding occupied Crimea to Russia in a potential peace deal.
Zelenskyy had ruled out ceding any territory, declaring, “There is nothing to talk about – it is our land, the land of the Ukrainian people”.
In a post on his social media platform, Trump accused Zelenskyy of stoking tension by “boasting” that Kyiv would not legally recognise ceding Crimea to Russia.
“This statement is very harmful to the Peace Negotiations with Russia,” Trump said, adding that Russia invaded the Crimean Peninsula and annexed it back in 2014 “without a shot being fired”.
“It’s inflammatory statements like Zelenskyy’s that makes it so difficult to settle this War,” Trump said. “He can have Peace or, he can fight for another three years before losing the whole Country.”
Despite the tension, the two leaders held a private meeting at the Vatican on April 26, 2025, during Pope Francis’s funeral.
Feb 28, 2025: During their fiery Oval Office meeting, Trump and Vice President JD Vance clashed with Zelenskyy over rare earth mineral agreements, security assurances and peace negotiations with Russia.
Trump warned Zelenskyy, “You’re either going to make a deal [on ending the war with Russia] or we’re out,” and accused the Ukrainian leader of having “disrespected” the United States and “overplayed his hand”.
The US president and Vance also berated Zelenskyy for lacking gratitude and refusing to compromise to end the war, with Trump arguing that Zelenskyy was unready for peace.
The meeting devolved into a shouting match and Zelenskyy departed the White House abruptly.
February 19, 2025: A month after returning to power for a second term, Trump called the Ukrainian president a “dictator without elections” and accused him of wanting to keep the “gravy train” of US military support going while Washington tries to end the war with Russia.
In a lengthy and scathing post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump accused Zelenskyy of taking US money and embroiling the country in an endless conflict.
He later doubled down on those comments, telling an audience at an investment summit in Miami that Zelenskyy had “done a terrible job, his country is shattered, and millions and millions of people have unnecessarily died”.
“A dictator without elections. Zelenskyy better move fast or he’s not going to have a country left. Gotta move. Gotta move fast cause that war’s going in the wrong direction,” Trump said on stage at the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute summit.
“In the meantime, we’re successfully negotiating an end to the war with Russia. Something I’ll admit that only Trump is going to be able to do and the Trump administration – we’re going to be able to do it. I think Putin even admitted that,” he said.
“Biden never tried. Europe has failed to bring peace and Zelenskyy probably wants to, maybe he wants to keep the gravy train going. I don’t know what’s the problem, but he has been able. He’s very upset,” he added.
Trump had been critical of Biden’s financial and military support to Ukraine during the war. He had vowed to end the war within 24 hours of his taking office, but later said he was being “sarcastic”.
2024 Campaign trail: On the 2024 US presidential election campaign trail, Trump repeatedly criticised Zelenskyy for not trying hard enough to end Russia’s war on Ukraine. In September, at an election rally speech in North Carolina, Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy for refusing to negotiate, stating that even the “worst deal” or giving up a small amount of territory would be better than ongoing death and destruction.
July 2019: During his first term, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to work with Rudy Giuliani and the US attorney general to investigate Democratic political rival Joe Biden. That is according to a five-page memo summarising the July 25 call.
At the time of the call, the Trump administration was also withholding from Ukraine nearly $400m in congressionally approved security assistance, prompting speculation the US president was using the money as leverage to get his desired investigations.
Zelenskyy expressed willingness to look into new cases and cooperate with US investigations, though he and Ukrainian officials later maintained they did not feel directly threatened or pressured during the conversation itself.

From global economic power to hosting the Olympics
PM Modi outlined India's ambitions, including becoming one of the world's three largest economies, emerging as a global manufacturing hub and sending an Indian to the Moon. He expressed confidence that collective efforts would help the country realise these goals.The Prime Minister also referred to India's sporting ambitions. He said the country was working towards hosting the 2030 Commonwealth Games and pursuing its ambition to stage the 2036 Olympic Games.
Growth in higher education
The Prime Minister highlighted the expansion of higher education since 2014. He said the number of universities had increased from 750 to more than 1,300, while colleges had grown from 38,000 to over 52,000.He encouraged students to remain curious and continue learning, stressing the importance of education, innovation and new ideas in building a developed India.
‘Make in India’, ‘vocal for local’ benefiting Tamil Nadu
Earlier in the day, PM Modi said India's overall progress depended on the development of its states. He reaffirmed the Centre's focus on strengthening manufacturing, infrastructure and job creation, highlighting the role of Tamil Nadu in the country's industrial growth.
"We need to strengthen the states to strengthen the nation, and therefore, the central government is promoting manufacturing in states like Tamil Nadu. The campaigns of the central government, be it 'Make in India' or 'Vocal for Local', are benefiting Tamil Nadu as well," he said.The event marked 50 years of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School and its contribution to education in Tamil Nadu.

Transcript: Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir, on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 11, 2026

Transcript: Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir, on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 11, 2026
The following is the full transcript of the interview with Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 11, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by the Chief Technology Officer of Palantir, Shyam Sankar. Welcome to Face the Nation.
SHYAM SANKAR: Thank you for having me, Margaret.
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's good to have you here in person. We've been talking a lot about technology, artificial intelligence, and public perception of it right now, and that's where I want to start with you because our polling shows there's a problem here. 50% of those polled by CBS say AI will create more problems than it solves. 29% say it'll solve more than it creates, and 21% just really don't know. Like 45% of Americans want the government to restrict use and development of AI. Is your position there should not be any guardrails at this moment?
SHYAM SANKAR: No, not at all. That's not my position. I think the- the burden is absolutely on the technology industry to show the American people that there are real benefits to AI and not kind of ephemeral sort of benefits like it can help me schedule travel, but actually meaningful benefits that result in job growth and prosperity for the American people. I think one of the things that's really complicated in the current discussion, is that there's an unseen force driving the narrative around AI safety, and it's- it's really this millenarian doomsday cult meets messianic complex called effective altruism. The most famous effective altruist that most Americans know is Sam Bankman-Fried, and the effective altruists are, it's almost like a religion that they've been thinking about doomsday scenarios from AI since the early 2000s.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He was–he is jailed. He was the crypto investor—
SHYAM SANKAR: Correct.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who defrauded investors. But this sounds very academic. Like, what makes you so focused on this?
SHYAM SANKAR: Because there's only really roughly 2,000 AI researchers in America, and the vast majority of them believe in this sort of worldview around effective altruism. And if you hear someone like Jacob Coxon telling you that AI has a 10% chance of ending humanity, and you believe—
MARGARET BRENNAN: A researcher who had this warning recently.
SHYAM SANKAR: Yes, correct. And you believe he's speaking as a technically informed individual who does this work, it's a scientific critique. I think the American people would be right to be quite panicked and worried about what's going on here. But if you understand that it's actually a theological critique, then you can- you can kind of weigh it against the empirical facts of what is actually happening out there. You know, I take—I think there's a profound truth to Pascal's saying that every human has a god-shaped hole in their heart, and it's important to understand that many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine God of AGI. And I mean, there's so many interesting stories around this. Like, for example, so many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI. I believe so much— (CROSSTALK)
MARGARET BRENNAN: What? That makes no sense. What do you think—
SHYAM SANKAR: I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I will—I'm showing you my chips are all in. So there is kind of this mass psychosis, social delusion around it, and I think it's getting in the way of actually what is happening with AI. Where is it meeting the American worker in industry? What are the results of doing that, and the doomsdayers have basically been wrong. Everything they predicted, they- they told us that ChatGPT 2.0 was too dangerous to release. They told us at this point in the timeline, we'd already have mass unemployment and job displacement, and the economists see that actually we're having job growth in areas that we wouldn't have predicted doing exactly that. So the technology industry has two burdens. One is to show very clearly to the American people that- that AI is going to result in economic prosperity and security for the nation. And two, to actually do and absorb the burden of engineering. You cannot abdicate this idea that designing safe products is your job. You can't hand wave around it. If you look at the kind of narratives that come out of the doomsdayers, they seem like two contradictory narratives. One narrative is this technology is going to end humanity.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SHYAM SANKAR: And simultaneously, they say, "But I believe it has some chance of creating utopia." So at first blush, this seems contradictory, but it has one thing in common, which is that you, as a human, have no agency. The machine god is going to decide the future, and only perhaps a small number of us can try to avoid the horrible outcome. And I think it obfuscates the more profound reality that we have a huge amount of human agency over how we're going to use this technology to deliver the outcomes the American people expect.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well let's talk about that because the other part of this argument would be, and no one who wants- the people who don't want guardrails are simply in it for commercial reasons. They want to keep selling chips, or they just want access to market. So that would be the counter argument to the idea that you know what you're saying, which is an ideological opposition to guardrails.
SHYAM SANKAR: Maybe we could just back up and who's on the side of no guardrails?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when- I want to get into the specifics here, because even just defining what guardrails is seems really complicated, and there's not even common agreement on that right now. But Jay Clayton, who is the new DNI and the new AI czar, said this week the focus is on control and monitoring of technologies with the potential to do harm. So, what does that look like to you? Because it sounds like he's not even sure yet.
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I think there's a very clear view that we should be regulating the application of the technology. So if you're going to use this in medicines, you know the FDA- As a republic, we have 250 years of rich laws and history on how to manage liability. I don't want to trivialize the metaphor, but you know, if I buy a car and the car is defective, that's the car maker's problem. If I then use that car to go drive into my neighbor's house, that's my problem. And you know, this sort of obfuscation. The narrative is this technology is a total difference of kind. I don't think so. I think it's a difference of degree.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, in that humans aren't in control of it, it would be a different kind.
SHYAM SANKAR: No, humans are in control of it. Even if we look at the kind of salacious reporting around Hugging Face, the models did not do anything they were not instructed to do. You know, they were- the- the real first, you have human error. They- they were not in a sandbox. They had access to the internet. It was a horrible cybersecurity configuration. Then, from that perspective, they were asked to- to- succeed at a specific benchmark, and they were not given constraints on how to do that. And they said, "Oh, the best way to succeed at the benchmark is to get the answers to the test, and to do so.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, for that, who should take action to--
SHYAM SANKAR: --I think it's a defective product. Like, if--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Is it up to the Justice Department to then bring suit, like on the programmers, like who's liable for the technology not, you know, staying within the sandbox--
SHYAM SANKAR: --The AI companies of course. In that, in that specific case, it would be the AI companies. If another company had licensed that technology to use in another in an application, and the product worked as expected, but you misused the product, then it would be you that are responsible for that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you believe that, am I understanding you, the existing laws on the books should be able to handle technology as it develops?
SHYAM SANKAR: I think it is a massive running head start. I think the laws on the books speak to a lot of the current considerations. Might we need a few more things on the margin? Sure, but I think we'll figure that out as we go through it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So let's talk about some of those things because you were with the president when he summoned some of these AI leaders recently, and he asked them all to sign a pledge to implement robust internal controls, partner with an external auditor and establish a committee to evaluate reports from auditors. That was Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia, Elon Musk. They all signed it. Palantir, your company didn't. Why?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, those accords were for companies that actually make AI models, which we do not, so–
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you help to use them and build out platforms. Like you don't see a reason for constraints there.
SHYAM SANKAR: Oh, we- we do have those constraints. In fact, that- part of that's our entire business, is how do you safely deploy these models in specific use cases. We're just not a party that- we weren't asked to be a part of the accord.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you were there at that meeting.
SHYAM SANKAR: I was.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, what happened? Like, what was the conversation?
SHYAM SANKAR: The conversation was really an assertion that the American people expect AI to generate economic prosperity and to do so securely, and that we as companies have an affirmative obligation to deliver on exactly those things, and that we have existing laws to look at this, and that we should be all taking this quite seriously, very productive conversation.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because it sounded like the White House was saying something more should be done, and now you have this new AI Czar Jay Clayton going out to Silicon Valley this week. He said he's launched this 120-day review of AI policy. What do you hope comes from that, or is this another one of these like blue ribbon commissions that doesn't produce any--
SHYAM SANKAR: --No, I think a lot will come up to it, which is really focus and energy, and using the existing agencies and regulatory apparatus to make sure we're on top of this stuff and providing support where it's needed. I think one of the challenges, going back to my comments on effective altruism is, today, the so-called independent research organizations that are overseeing this are not really independent. They have conflicts with the labs. They are made up of people with a singular worldview around effective altruism, looking for the doomsday scenarios. You know, you have evaluators who are essentially pointing a loaded gun at a target, saying, "I can't believe the gun worked." When they should really be saying, "What guardrails do we have in place? You know- are you know are these products working to the specifications we designed, and what- what are the opportunities for misuse?
MARGARET BRENNAN: So I've spoken to people, for example, in the financial industry who say we did need some regulation here, but there's the SEC, there is you know the CFTC, they oversee certain operations here. Don't you think within the current institutions there could be some sort of entity that oversees technology?
SHYAM SANKAR: I think there's going to need to be an incident response and reporting regime that creates more visibility and transparency into what you're learning in the testing, well ahead of product launches that give visibility and transparency to the government of how people are doing and implementing exactly the existing laws.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who does that, or who could do that?
SHYAM SANKAR: I will defer to Director Clayton on that, but I think that's one of the things that I- I suspect they will be driving towards.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He's got to figure that out. Well, we look at the last administration- President Biden and Xi Jinping came to like, a very limited agreement, but at least on one principle, which was humans, not AI, should retain control over decisions to use nuclear weapons. Would it be sensible--
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, that seems obvious.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, that seems terrifying, first of all, that they had to come to a conversation about that, but shouldn't that be expanded elsewhere in the defense space? Would you agree with that? Is that one of the areas--
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, the current part of the policy is there's two parts of it. There's the kind of military doctrine, which is that a human is always accountable for every decision that's made, and the other part of it is that humans are in- in the decision-making processes that- that relate to lethal force here.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But in terms of the things where you think there should be more guardrails, is the defense space one of them? Biotech, I've heard others.
SHYAM SANKAR: All spaces need to- need to have a thought around safety of application.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But that's still- who does that and how?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I think the Department and the Congress should do it with defense. The Department of Transportation should do it with transportation. The FDA should do it with medicines.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But so, watch for that possibly happen. Because you know, I hear from people in the technology space this argument that we need to just go so furiously forward to compete with China. China is pushing for AI to be integrated into all of its industries, but they have the ability to also delay things to get government- governance to catch up, they've done that. They've tapped the brakes themselves before. So, do you think the U.S. should also consider tapping the brakes in certain areas, just slow things until they have some idea of the guardrails?
SHYAM SANKAR: You know, we have this beautiful, messy process in America, but I would argue, as frustrating as it might look, it's kind of working. So, we have frontier models now that have not been released because people have realized maybe we're not ready to release them. That would have been an unimaginable thought a year ago. And so as people are starting to wrap their heads around whether it's the labs, government- I think it is a consequence of our messy process and the discussions that people are having that we're evolving how we're doing this, and the pace is naturally changing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Let's talk a little bit about DOD, the Department of War, Department of Defense. SHYAM SANKAR: Well, the- the Department today has a wide range of model providers, everything from XAI and OpenAI to open-weight models like Nemotron from NVIDIA, so I don't think- I don't- there's been no operational impact from that. I think there's a kind of a broader statement which really has been powering the growth of our commercial business, which is companies are realizing, and it equally applies to the government, that you're not going to pick any one model provider. That actually, your sovereignty and agency as an institution comes down to your ability to kind of control, decide which models you're going to use in what context, have the ability to switch models, to be able to control the weights themselves, where you need to feel that control over them. MARGARET BRENNAN: So you don't know yet who's going to replace them, but you don't see a big impact from this kind of decision. It was certainly a huge story for Silicon Valley and the defense space to hear that--
SHYAM SANKAR: It's already been replaced. It's already been replaced, and users who are building AI applications get to pick the models that they're using. It's a suite of models that are available from, you know, Google, from XAI, from OpenAI. And what was the second part of your question there, sorry?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, I was asking about the impact. It sounds like you don't think it's- it's a big one. Look, I can move on here.
SHYAM SANKAR: No impact.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You have said recently that the war in Iran is the first major conflict where AI played a central role, particularly for targeting. Do you see risks for that?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, you know, targeting is this- is kind of this very salacious word. Really, targeting is a process, and if you think about military operations, you know, the ability to execute 1000 strikes in a single day would have taken two weeks of planning by 50 people before, and being able to do that with one person in four hours provides you a significant battlefield advantage against your adversaries. So, it's really not about, you know, people jump immediately to something like AI picking the targets. That's not what's happening. It's really given a set of effects that you want to create- I want to be able to take out the enemy's air defenses. Okay, what targets relate to that? Okay, how do I then push them through a process where I understand are any of these targets on the no-strike list? Are any of these targets too close to civilian infrastructure? How do you do all the things that are so susceptible to human error under the time crunch- what's doing in a way that has much higher repeatability and accuracy, so you can get more throughput to the system?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, that goes to a broader argument about the elimination of some of the people who were involved in mitigating civilian impact from strikes. Bloomberg reported some personnel relied too much on the AI in the Maven system made by Palantir using AI-enabled software. Have you determined what happened there?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, we should wait for the final report. But what I can say is that reporting is inaccurate.
MARGARET BRENNAN: The reporting from Bloomberg, you're saying, is inaccurate?
SHYAM SANKAR: Yeah, it's inaccurate, and actually, the likely cause is human error. And then- and quickly following that, we actually built additional AI agents that did more checking. That's part of the process we don't own, but responding to the urgency of the moment, we built additional AI that actually double checks more of the work outside the process that we own to ensure things like that couldn't happen again.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you're suggesting it was outdated intelligence or human error that fed information into the computer system. Is that what you're saying?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, we should wait for the final report, but I think we will find--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you know when that'll be released?
SHYAM SANKAR: I don't.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because the initial reports have been widely reported on, including by this network. Do you see a harm in that being made public soon, or is it helpful to what you say are improvements you want to make?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I- I will defer to the Department on the- on the timing of how- I have no control over that. But yeah, I would love the- the truth to get out there.

SHYAM SANKAR: I would defer to the Department on that. That's- that's not our place.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But it is because you are such a- Palantir is such- so interwoven with the U.S. government. I mean, it's billions of dollars of government contracts right now, do you think more information should be briefed to Congress about the benefits along with the risks?
SHYAM SANKAR: Sadly, I'm just a technologist. I mean, on these policy issues, I would defer to others.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I want to quickly ask you before we go about the modernization efforts, which you are part of. I understand you are lieutenant colonel in the Army Reserves in the Army Executive Innovation Corps.
SHYAM SANKAR: Correct.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which is new.
SHYAM SANKAR: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: There are also executives from Meta and OpenAI. So, what are you working on there?
SHYAM SANKAR: My principal role is to help with Army human resourcing in the G-1 department here. So, strategies on how do we, you know, the Army is drowning in talent, what we would call green suiters who actually know how to code, and they're- they're- they're exceptional. You might have an E-4 who's an exceptionally good coder. There's not an obvious career path for them within the Army. The Army doesn't know how to manage that talent. SHYAM SANKAR: That's right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So for people who look at that and say these big corporations could have a conflict of interest because they're also doing business with the U.S. government. How do you respond to that?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, it's carefully managed by- by the- the lawyers in the Department. We're only allowed to work on projects where we don't have conflicts.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And do you think--
SHYAM SANKAR: I would just say, more broadly, I mean it is the greatest honor to be able to serve in our U.S. military. The Singapore Grand Prix nearly broke its attendance record despite dangerous air pollution
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:29:47 EEST
23:29:47 KST

The Singapore Grand Prix nearly broke its attendance record despite dangerous air pollution
Kyiv • UNN
The Singapore Grand Prix was attended by 301,294 spectators — the second-highest figure in the race's history. The PSI in the city reached 192 points.
More than 301,000 spectators attended the Singapore Formula One Grand Prix, despite severe air pollution caused by large-scale forest fires in Indonesia. This was the second-highest attendance figure in the history of the race in the country, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
According to the organizers, Singapore GP Pte Ltd, 301,294 people attended the three-day event, held from October 9 to 11. This was the second-highest figure since 2008, when Singapore first hosted a round of the Formula One World Championship.
The historical record was set in 2022, when around 302,000 spectators attended the race. The event took place after pandemic restrictions had been lifted. This year's attendance was also the highest since the configuration of the Marina Bay Street Circuit was changed in 2023. For comparison, last year's Singapore Grand Prix attracted 300,641 spectators.
Significant interest in the race remained despite the serious deterioration in air quality. Due to large-scale forest and peat fires in Indonesia, Singapore was among the cities with the highest levels of air pollution in the world. According to Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA), on October 9 the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in the central part of the city reached 192 points. This figure falls into the category of air that is unhealthy for the population.
Over the weekend, pollution levels fell somewhat but remained elevated. As of the evening of October 11, the PSI in different areas of Singapore ranged from 112 to 155 points. The pollution was reportedly caused by smoke from fires on the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Kalimantan, which was carried by the wind toward Singapore. The situation was exacerbated by dry weather associated with the El Niño climate phenomenon.
Despite the environmental situation, the organizers did not cancel the race or the scheduled entertainment events. Concerts by international performers, including Lana Del Rey, Janet Jackson, and other artists, were held as part of the Grand Prix. At the same time, the International Automobile Federation (FIA) had previously warned that outdoor entertainment events could be restricted if air quality deteriorated further.
Context
Singapore authorities continue to monitor the spread of the smog. Local residents were advised to limit prolonged strenuous physical activity outdoors, especially people with chronic heart and lung conditions, children, and older people.
Singapore's Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, Grace Fu, reported having contact with Indonesian representatives regarding possible cooperation in combating fires and transboundary air pollution.
The National Environment Agency warned that the smog could persist in the coming days due to unfavorable weather conditions and the continued fires in the region.
Recall
The Singapore Grand Prix took place on October 9-11 in the new sprint format on the grueling Marina Bay circuit.

In a televised interview with ABC News broadcast, Zelensky reiterated Kyiv’s conditional readiness for an energy armistice, while noting that reaching a verifiable deal required mutual commitments.

“To stop Putin – and I think this is the main goal, to stop him, this is the main deal, to stop this war ... we count on American support,” Zelensky told ABC News. “Then, and of course, we count on our European partners, and I hope that we will save this unity, Europe and the United States.”
Zelensky highlighted the severity of recent Russian bombardments against civilian life-support systems, reporting that Russian forces had carried out 196 strikes targeting Ukraine’s electrical sector alongside 20 strikes against oil and gas infrastructure over the preceding week, resulting in 153 civilian deaths.
Neither the Ukrainian government nor the Kremlin immediately issued formal statements confirming the operational parameters, verification mechanisms, or start time of the ceasefire announced by Trump.
Sanctions disputes
Trump’s ceasefire proclamation arrives after days of public friction between the White House and Kyiv surrounding energy markets and leadership in Ukraine.
On Friday, Oct. 9, Trump announced a commercial arrangement under which Moscow agreed to deliver commercial diesel fuel onto international markets, prompting the US Treasury Department to issue a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 2027.
The administration defended the measure as a step to lower retail fuel costs ahead of the November US midterm elections.
The commercial deal drew criticism from Ukrainian officials, who described the timing as counterproductive while peace consultations were underway in Miami with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
On Saturday, Trump criticized Zelensky for continuing long-range drone attacks on Russian refineries, claiming the strikes drove up fuel prices and asserting that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Responding to Trump’s comments on ABC News, Zelensky defended Ukrainian sovereignty, stating that leadership decisions belong exclusively to Ukrainian voters.
He added that if the US administration sought wartime balloting, Washington should press Moscow for a comprehensive 60-day ceasefire to enable safe voting under martial law.

Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:25:03 UTC
23:25:03 KST

Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
Repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Airport reveal the limitations of even the most high-tech air defences.
Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), are hitting deep inside Saudi Arabia with waves of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times by the Houthis since their new military campaign against the kingdom began in September.
An attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded 309, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority was forced to suspend operations and diverted all flights, while the United States and United Kingdom issued new travel warnings for citizens.
The Houthis claimed two other attacks on the air hub earlier this week and on Sunday warned people to avoid Saudi airports.
Houthi weaponry
Saudi Arabia possesses one of the best-equipped militaries in the world, boasting advanced, multilayered air defence systems.
Saudi warplanes have pummelled Houthi positions across Yemen in the past week, seeking to roll back the Iran-backed group’s recent advances against the Yemeni government army, which Riyadh supports.
The Houthis’ own arsenal has come a long way since the group seized control of Sanaa from the government in September 2014.
Their drones and missiles have reached as far as Israel and, as their accuracy has shown, can hit particular targets such as Saudi airports and oil facilities.
Here’s what we know about the Houthis’ weaponry, how their tactics have changed and why Saudi air defences are struggling to keep pace.
How advanced is the Houthi arsenal?
The exact type of weapon used to attack Riyadh airport is unknown, but the Houthis have fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the 2015 intervention. The Iran-backed group has also targeted Israel and allegedly Israeli-linked vessels since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
The group has used its weapons in concert, mixing drones and missiles of varying speeds to confound air defences. The same mix has shaped Yemen’s ground war, with the Houthis pounding government positions for weeks before seizing the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month.
Among the group’s most advanced options are medium-range ballistic missiles such as the Palestine-2, a two-stage solid fuel missile believed to have a range of 2,000km with hypersonic capabilities. Another is the Toufan, which appears to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr missile, thought to have a range of between 1,350km and 1,950km.
The reach of those missiles – some carrying cluster warheads – has allowed the Houthis to breach Israel’s air defence network, some 2,000 km from Yemen.
The Houthis also maintain a number of short-range missiles, such as their Burkan and Badr series. They are also believed to be of Iranian origin and have been used in cross-border strikes into Saudi Arabia.
According to Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at Kings College War Studies Department, the Houthis’ missile arsenal is essentially derived from Iranian weaponry, with some Chinese technological influences.
“The Houthis have demonstrated little evidence of significant indigenous technological innovation,” he said. “Their domestic capabilities are largely confined to producing certain lower-end missiles and drones.”
Last month, Yemen’s government forces alleged that the Houthis have been receiving help from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to develop a new capability – loitering cruise missiles.
Why are Saudi defences struggling to keep up?
Saudi authorities say their forces shot down a number of projectiles over the past week, including a pair of ballistic missiles aimed at the capital on Thursday. But they failed to intercept the projectile that hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.
Nawaf Obaid told Al Jazeera that occasional penetration of Saudi air defences is to be expected, given the size of the kingdom and its border with Yemen.
“As much as you can have a multi-layered air defence system, one will always come through,” he said, pointing out that dozens of Houthi attempts are thwarted for each successful attack.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy and defence analyst, told Al Jazeera that the main focus of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defence system was countering threats from Iran.
However, as the attacks from the Houthis increase, he views it as likely that the Saudis are re-orienting some of these defences towards Yemen.
There is also the issue of interceptor stocks. Saudi Arabia – along with many of the United States’ regional and global allies – has struggled with limited stockpiles of Patriot and THAAD munitions. These were rapidly expended by the US and its allies during the early months of the war with Iran.
Last month, Riyadh had reportedly reached out to a number of friendly countries to deploy air defence or other support to help defend against attacks by the Houthis.
Limitations
However, the Houthis are also fighting under serious constraints. The group is under a UN-mandated arms embargo, a years-long Saudi blockade, as well as fighting on several fronts across Yemen.
“Militarily, the Saudi-led coalition has the upper hand, but the Houthis can still dominate the headlines with occasional strikes against Saudi Arabia,” Obaid said.
“As the world’s largest crude oil exporter and a G20 economy, Saudi Arabia carries global responsibilities that make such attacks disproportionately visible.”
The exact size of the Houthis’ missile arsenal is unknown, calling into question the group’s ability to sustain attacks on Saudi Arabia, while simultaneously fighting a fierce ground war where missiles and drones have been used by the Iran-backed group.
Obaid said that Saudi Arabia’s air campaign in Yemen has focused heavily on targeting the group’s missile depots, underground installations and drone production facilities. The group is “inflicting enormous damage” on the Houthis’ military capabilities, he added.
Pusztai told Al Jazeera that the Houthis likely have just a limited number of short-range ballistic missiles left.
This would mean they would be incapable of launching saturation attacks, where multiple missiles and drones are fired at targets, such as in Saudi Arabia.
Instead, they could focus on aiming single missiles at less-defended civilian targets “to maximise the strategic impact of these attacks, in this case to disrupt civilian air traffic”.

Ukraine’s ‘secret cargo’ sparks scandal in EU state – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:24:52 UTC
23:24:52 KST

Ukraine’s ‘secret cargo’ sparks scandal in EU state – media
A scandal is brewing in Austria over a secret Ukrainian intelligence shipment reportedly allowed to cross the country unchecked, with opposition politicians demanding to know what it contained and who authorized its passage.
A Volkswagen van belonging to Ukrainian intelligence carried 200 kg of undeclared “special cargo” through Austria in January, Kronen Zeitung reported on Saturday. The shipment was reportedly linked to the Ukrainian delegation attending the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, where Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky was present.
The case emerged after the right-wing opposition Freedom Party of Austria (FPO) obtained a diplomatic note requesting permission for the van to cross Austrian territory. The Foreign Ministry later confirmed the note’s existence in response to a parliamentary inquiry, according to the outlet.
The cargo reportedly passed through Austria without customs clearance or security screening. Its contents remain unknown.
FPO Secretary-General Christian Hafenecker demanded to know what Ukrainian intelligence transported and why the authorities allowed it.
“What was in those 200 kilograms? Cash, gold, weapons, documents, or something else entirely?” he asked, as cited by the newspaper. “Austria is not a lawless transit corridor for foreign intelligence services. We are still a neutral state!”
Asked about the shipment, the Foreign Ministry declined to elaborate, telling Kronen Zeitung it receives hundreds of diplomatic notes daily and that it forwarded the request to the Interior Ministry.
The FPO plans another parliamentary inquiry to determine who authorized the shipment, why it escaped inspection, and what it contained.
A transit hub for Kiev’s billions?
Hafenecker already questioned the authorities over suspicious shipments to Ukraine earlier this year.
In May, he demanded that the Finance Ministry explain how nearly $22 billion in cash and gold has been transported from Austria to Kiev since 2022 without triggering money-laundering concerns or regulatory scrutiny. The figure emerged from an FPO parliamentary inquiry to Finance Minister Markus Marterbauer, which revealed 1,011 cash export declarations for shipments from Vienna to Kiev from 2022-2026.
Hafenecker noted Austria’s anti-money-laundering rules, which require individuals withdrawing as little as €12,000 ($13,400) from inherited accounts to prove the money’s origin, while anyone crossing the EU’s external border with more than €10,000 in cash must declare it.
The Austrian Financial Market Authority described the shipments at the time as routine banking operations, citing Ukraine’s widespread use of foreign currencies. Hafenecker nevertheless demanded full disclosure of the transfers, a regulatory audit, and a parliamentary report from Austria’s Money Laundering Reporting Office.
His Euroskeptic FPO party previously demanded an end to Austrian financial aid to Ukraine, branding the country a corrupt “bottomless pit” amid high-level embezzlement scandals.
Kiev’s ‘war mafia’ cash convoy in Hungary
Hafenecker’s demands in May followed a separate scandal over cash and gold shipments transiting Hungary en route to Ukraine.
The diplomatic row erupted in March when the Hungarian authorities seized two trucks belonging to Ukraine’s state-owned Oschadbank near Budapest, confiscating $40 million, €35 million, and 9 kg of gold in a money-laundering investigation. The shipment originated from Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank.
Hungary said the convoy was supervised by a former general of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), with other escorts reportedly having military backgrounds. All seven were deported to Ukraine, and the vehicles and assets remained in Hungarian custody. Kiev called the seizure “state banditism” and blackmail.
The Hungarian authorities questioned the money’s origin and purpose. Then-Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto suggested that the convoy could be linked to a Ukrainian “war mafia” and raised suspicions that the cash was intended to influence Hungary’s April 12 parliamentary elections against then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban, a longtime critic of Kiev.
Hungary ultimately returned the seized assets in May, after Orban lost the election to Peter Magyar’s pro-EU Tisza party. Kiev maintained that the shipment was a routine bank transfer but did not publicly explain the origin of the assets or why such a large sum was being transported through Hungary.

Hochvogel mountain at risk of major collapse as 400,000 cubic metres of rock threatens to break away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:23:36 UTC
23:23:36 KST

The Hochvogel sits on the border between Germany and the Austrian region of Tyrol. It is part of the Allgäu High Alps and stands at 2,592 metres high.
Around 2,000 cubic metres of rock broke away from the Hochvogel mountain in the Allgäu Alps in June. Now researchers are warning that another major collapse could be imminent, potentially sending up to 400,000 cubic metres crashing down the mountainside.
The summit itself is at risk of breaking apart, with a fissure that has existed since the 19th century steadily widening. Records suggest the crack was once about shoulder-width, but the gap is now several metres across.
Scientists have been monitoring the hotspot for twelve years, initially on field trips and, since 2018, with permanently installed sensors and measuring equipment. A drone with a laser scanner has also been deployed to the area.
In spring, measuring instruments recorded movement rates of up to five millimetres per week. In geological terms, that is extremely fast; normally the Alps shift by an average of around 1.8 millimetres per year. Readings from the early-warning system are now prompting the researchers to raise the alarm.
Hochvogel
The Hochvogel sits on the border between Germany and the Austrian region of Tyrol. It is part of the Allgäu High Alps and stands at 2,592 metres high.
The mountain has been closed to climbers approaching from the Austrian side for some time, but the ascent from Germany remains open.
At the beginning of October, a team led by geology professor Michael Krautblattler from the Technical University of Munich (TUM) climbed the peak once again to inspect the terrain and measuring instruments.
Krautblattler specialises in debris flows and rockslides and wants to "equip areas that are dangerous with intensive early-warning systems and thus be able to read properly the warning signs the mountain gives us," as he said in an interview with the German Alpine Club (DAV) in February.
Instruments transmit data around the clock
There are now more than 30 sensors on the Hochvogel, measuring the entire summit to millimetre precision and documenting movements.
In 2024, TUM described the main fissure as up to six metres wide, around 35 metres long, and about 60 metres deep.
A new crack on the south-west ridge is now regarded as a key weak point where the highest rates of movement are recorded. The scientists refer to this hotspot as "Fissure 6."
According to Krautblatter, similar early-warning systems are currently in use at only two other locations - the Partnach Gorge and the Höllental Gorge.
"There we are learning in great detail which signals the mountain gives off and how long in advance. Often, it is just days or hours. Systems like this will be vitally important in high mountain areas, because there things are going to change dramatically, beyond anything we know from experience," Krautblatter told DAV.
The researchers receive the data from the instruments systematically, several times an hour, in their offices. Krautblatter hopes the technology will help keep the Alps accessible while allowing authorities to close off danger areas before disaster strikes.
Hochvogel rockslide could be imminent
Researchers believe the mountain could be reaching a critical point and that between 250,000 and 400,000 cubic metres of debris could break away and crash down the mountainside.
Scientists believe extreme weather could be partly behind increasing movements on the mountain.
On the Hochvogel, "we can see a clear influence from heavy precipitation events, in other words intense rainfall, thunderstorms and snowmelt," Johannes Leinauer from the TU Munich team told Deutschlandfunk.
"And these thunderstorm events are currently becoming more frequent and more intense as a result of the climate change, and that can of course affect how quickly and how often such rockfalls occur," he added.

Victor Mair and Benjamin Franklin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:21:01 UTC
23:21:01 KST

Victor Mair and Benjamin Franklin
« previous post | next post »
Wikipedia’s article on Benjamin Franklin starts this way:
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath active as a physicist, philosopher, statesman and inventor.
The article goes on to list (some of) his other achievements, including his role as a writer, and as the founder of institutions such as the American Philosophical Society and what became the University of Pennsylvania. It omits many other things, including his contributions as an orthoepist and phonetician.
Franklin did none of this because he was trained to do it or hired to do it, but because he was curious about the world around him, and followed up in unexpected and consequential ways on chance encounters both common and rare.
Victor Mair was also active throughout his life in many different intellectual and cultural and physical areas. For regular readers of this blog, I don’t need to make a list — but I learned several new things about his history at yesterday's memorial service.
And Victor’s diverse activities were Franklin-esque. Like Franklin, he was involved in the world around him; curious about both ordinary and unique aspects of his experiences; and able to turn that curiosity into insights, discoveries, communications, and organizational support.
This pattern is less common among today’s academics than perhaps it should be, but Victor’s example shows us what’s possible.

How Freelancers in Ukraine Can Protect Their Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Freelancers working in any part of the world need to keep a close watch on their own privacy, since they don’t have the benefit of a large company with its own cybersecurity protocols and team to keep employees safe, but freelancers in Ukraine face a unique threat.
Alongside the everyday risks of working online, the risks of wartime threats to digital infrastructure and an unstable internet and power infrastructure mean that protecting your own data – not to mention your clients’ data – is particularly challenging.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Here are some practical ways to secure your data and prevent your livelihood from being disrupted.
Utilise a VPN for research
By now, most of us are aware of what a VPN is and (perhaps roughly) what it does. In a nutshell, it masks your real IP address from the websites you visit and encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, helping protect it from interception on the local network. However, a VPN does not prevent tracking through cookies, logged-in accounts, or other tracking technologies, and it does not protect against every online threat.
This is particularly important for Ukrainian freelancers to understand, since blackouts and power outages mean that many have to move their work to local cafes and unsecured hotspots. While they may seem legitimate, it is impossible for you to identify whether a bad actor is using the connection to hijack your private activity and data.
HTTPS already encrypts data exchanged with websites that use it. A trusted VPN can provide an additional layer of protection, particularly on unfamiliar networks, but it is not a substitute for other security measures. You can usually try a VPN free to get to know the tool before you sign up for a subscription – for instance, details on CyberGhost’s free trial are on their official page for those interested in trying the service.
Secure Your Accounts with 2FA and Regular Updates
Two-factor authentication is a strong line of defense against bad actors. Even if someone obtains your password, a second authentication factor adds another barrier to accessing your account. Depending on the service, this may involve a code generated by an authenticator app, a security key, or confirmation on a trusted device. The level of protection varies by method; no method should be described as impossible to bypass.
If you receive a prompt for 2FA on your phone that you don’t believe you have triggered via a normal login attempt, don’t click it or give approval. Instead, check the account’s security by opening its official app or typing its official website address into your browser yourself, rather than following a link in the unexpected notification.
Similarly, keep your devices up-to-date. Updates don’t just bring new emojis and UI features – they also keep software patched against vulnerabilities.
Use Freelancer-Friendly Payment Platforms
Unfortunately, invoicing scams are all too common these days. If you’re in a rush – or in a rush to be paid that week – you’re not always going to check things over as thoroughly as you should. Unfortunately, thanks to AI, it’s easier than ever for bad actors to put together a highly convincing invoice for payment and send it straight to your inbox.
Don’t send your banking details unless you are sure about the person on the other end.
Don’t Fall Victim to Social Engineering
This refers to tactics that involve bad actors using you as a point of entry, rather than, say, a vulnerability in the IT infrastructure. It’s the difference between someone trying to break in through a window, versus someone knocking on the door and convincing you to let them in – say, by pretending to be a police officer.
Common social engineering techniques include phishing emails, fake client queries, vishing (voice phishing, which may include using AI to imitate another person’s voice during a phone call) along with fake charities and, during wartime, fake relief programmes.

Only Russia is responsible for the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday in a TV interview, responding to criticism from US President Donald Trump, who blamed him for high diesel prices and said he should be replaced.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday his country could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire, pushing back against US counterpart Donald Trump's call for Ukraine to pick a new leader.
"First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader", Zelenskyy told ABC News in a televised interview, a day after Trump said Ukraine needed a new president who would agree to end the war.
Zelenskyy said he told Trump's team that if they really wanted Ukraine to hold elections, "please tell Putin to give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections".
"We want peace, we are ready for a ceasefire, we are ready to begin with any kind of steps of de-escalation", Zelenskyy told ABC in a TV interview.
"And if the Russians want us not to attack their diesel, their refineries, etc., we are asking President Trump to give them a signal not to attack the energy infrastructure of Ukraine".
'Don't kill our children, we will stop attacking your diesel'
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data centre run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so", Zelenskyy said on X, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
"Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel. And I think it's a fair deal", he added.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well", Sybiha wrote.
Trump vows for 'new leader' in Ukraine
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does", Trump said.
The US president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.

Palestinian election delay fuels anger over political legitimacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:17:30 UTC
23:17:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Abbas' Palestinian election delay fuels anger over political legitimacy
The postponement of Palestinian elections until September 2027 has reignited questions over political legitimacy, accountability and the willingness of Palestinian factions to relinquish power, with citizens in Gaza questioning who benefits from another year without a vote.
The decision came after the Central Elections Commission announced it had completed its technical and administrative preparations to receive applications for candidacy for legislative elections scheduled for November 28, 2026.
On Saturday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas subsequently issued a decree cancelling the previous arrangements and setting 11 September 2027 as the date for simultaneous presidential and legislative elections.
According to the Palestinian news agency WAFA, the decision followed consultations with political factions and a recommendation from the Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO).
The presidency cited Israeli restrictions on movement, the inability of election officials and observers to access Gaza and East Jerusalem, and the failure to complete arrangements for an international stabilisation force, deploy Palestinian police in Gaza, and begin reconstruction following Israel's withdrawal.
The PLO Executive Committee reaffirmed its commitment to elections, arguing that the new date would help ensure the participation of Palestinians across Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank, and Gaza.
However, the announcement has revived concerns about a political division that has persisted for nearly two decades, particularly after the 2021 legislative elections were also postponed.
For many Palestinians, the question is whether another year will create the conditions for meaningful democratic participation or simply extend the tenure of an entrenched political leadership.
Palestinians question who benefits
Tayseer Abu Shahla, a resident of Jabalia in northern Gaza, doubts elections alone could bring meaningful change amid the current political fragmentation but argues that postponement offers no solution either.
"Fragmentation, division and the absence of a genuine vision for citizens' futures could produce representatives driven by self-interest rather than a common national project," he told The New Arab.
Abu Shahla said Israeli restrictions and military checkpoints across the occupied territories would already have complicated participation, but stressed that these obstacles did not justify indefinitely delaying Palestinians' right to choose their representatives.
In Gaza City, Salah Abu Warda believes those most likely to benefit are political factions and officials concerned about losing their positions or facing a fresh test of public support.
He argued that the delay gives incumbent leaders more time to consolidate their influence, avoid internal competition and pursue political arrangements without direct electoral accountability.
Young candidates and electoral lists are also affected, he added, while Palestinian institutions face a deepening legitimacy crisis.
Riyad Issa, a resident of Al-Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza, offered a more blunt assessment.
"Those who fear the people's voice benefit from postponing elections, while the people themselves pay the price," he told TNA, arguing that Palestinians had been deprived of their right to choose and hold their leaders accountable.
"We are tired of slogans, speeches and promises. We want to know who governs us and who makes decisions on our behalf without consulting us. The homeland is not anyone's private estate, and our votes do not belong to factions or parties," he added.
Hamas calls for dialogue as divisions persist
Hamas welcomed the postponement as a "step in the right direction", arguing that the necessary conditions for free and fair elections across the Palestinian territories, including Jerusalem, were absent.
The movement called for a comprehensive national dialogue to agree on a political strategy and to reform Palestinian institutions, including the Palestinian National Council and the Legislative Council.
It also expressed readiness to participate in talks producing binding outcomes.
However, previous reconciliation efforts have failed to overcome political divisions, raising questions about whether renewed dialogue will yield concrete results.
The Democratic Reform Current within Fatah, led by Mohammed Dahlan, also remains part of the wider debate over the Palestinian political system and the future of the Palestinian Authority, amid continuing disputes over leadership and representation.
For Gaza-based political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim, the postponement effectively gives the Palestinian leadership another year without renewing its popular mandate.
Despite their disagreements, factions often converge when political processes threaten their positions and interests, Ibrahim argued, leaving citizens waiting while leaders remain absorbed in internal power struggles.
He said the crisis extends beyond factional disputes to the question of who has the right to represent Palestinians without a renewed electoral mandate or meaningful accountability.
Postponement, he added, would prolong rather than resolve the legitimacy crisis.
Gaza's needs must come first
Political researcher Tayseer Abdullah, also from Gaza, told TNA that the cancellation of the previous electoral arrangements should not become a pretext for denying Palestinians their constitutional and legal right to vote.
Although initially hesitant about holding elections while Gaza was enduring such devastation, he ultimately supported the process as a right delayed for 16 years.
Abdullah argued that the additional year should be used to prioritise urgent humanitarian needs rather than allow factions to consolidate their internal positions or escape electoral pressure.
He called for addressing the plight of displaced families living in tents, providing medical care for the wounded and people with disabilities, repairing schools and hospitals, restoring essential infrastructure, and ensuring access to clean water and electricity.
He also urged the opening of crossings to facilitate travel and the entry of essential goods and equipment, alongside social protection for Palestinians struggling with poverty and destitution.
In the coming period, he said, it should demonstrate whether political factions are prepared to place citizens' interests above their own.
For Palestinians facing the consequences of war, displacement and political paralysis, the central question remains whether September 2027 will bring a genuine opportunity for democratic renewal or another missed chance to reclaim their political voice.

chen wei on the dance floor as a stage for imagined ecstasy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:15:26 UTC
23:15:26 KST

chen wei on the dance floor as a stage for imagined ecstasy
in his guest essay, the artist reflects on the elusive nature of ecstasy, drawing from nightlife, staged photography, personal memories, and stories shared by friends to examine how pleasure is performed, imagined, and reconstructed.
Ecstasy
A gigantic image of a beautiful woman portrayed from the chest up was plastered on a public bus that drove by slowly in front of me; her hair shampooed in foam, her eyes closed, eyebrows lifted and lips half open. This shampoo advertisement is about ecstasy and pleasure. It is also the safest and the most appropriate kind of inebriation modeled on mass experience, that champions cliché performance and apparent pretense. Ecstasy embodies the highest level of enjoyment. As poetic as it may be, it is also not trustworthy. For a long time, I was fascinated by this condition, the system it creates, the state it may reach and its relationship to performance.
I began to review my own experience of enjoyment from my memories. From frequenting disco clubs and roller skating clubs in the 1990s, to performing in all kinds of bars and outdoor venues with my music band at the beginning of the new millennium, pogoing with the audience, and my solo performance of noise on stage, either I could not remember or perhaps I have never reached the ecstatic state. I had to take on a more realistic search, looking for the sources by frequenting all kinds of nightclubs, hanging out and talking with friends, sometimes even dancing among a sweaty crowd. Ecstasy was like a catalyst that pierced through layers and layers of the poster wall, which allowed me to step over spilt drinks on the floor, to go across the dance floor, bringing me back to midnight again.
In the Waves
Hundreds of extras scattered around in a film studio. They are told that they will be part of a photograph where they will have to pretend to dance and act as if they were inebriated on the dance floor. The rehearsal begins under intense lighting, and without any prior consensus, the extras exhibit the same kind of look as the woman in the shampoo advertisement. Orders are amplified through the loudspeaker, and they begin to lose their minds, their bodies stiffen, they become unsure of how to perform a state of intoxication. It must be extremely tiring and annoying to stay in one fixed position over a long period of time. The smoke generator continues to pour out thick fog at them periodically.
Well, they do not look quite right actually. Are they dancing or doing something else, are they enjoying it? They gather together in the fog, some even seem somewhat at loss and restless. We captured this series of group photos and portraits.
‘I, a boat lost under the hair of coves, hurled by the hurricane into the birdless ether.’ – Arthur Rimbaud, The Drunken Boat
Fiction
In recent years, I am often asked, ‘Do you go to nightclubs, do you dance?’ This is certainly not the case, because I neither have the time nor the energy to do so. Except for work reasons, I go very rarely. But I have a lot of friends, and friends’ friends, who have rather diverse experiences at nightclubs. For me, these are very precious sources, because they describe the atmosphere on the dance floor in a spectacular fashion. Their stories are the fundamental literary references of dance floors, real or fictional, for me to recreate in my studio, and I try my best to visualize these remnant fragments from their memories.
Even though these efforts may have been spent in vain, they allow reality and fiction to come together. It is like the old game of charades, where people provide different types of descriptions of the same subject. My interest, however, is not in the differences in iterations. Because the dance floors are indeed different now. The use of artificial fog and lighting, mirroring reflections and fluorescent materials, all kinds of monotonous designs and installations, are, in my opinion, to create a disappearance of space. This allows us, as consumers, to be isolated quickly from the so-called space. As we follow the DJ and ride on the music, being there induces us to wander and to escape without a destination, neither is one necessary… We revel into the wee hours of the night or even until the sun rises, and we would come up from that semi-basement dance floor, and wave for a taxi on a wet sidewalk. Perhaps, this in itself is the fictional component of life.
Of course, we would once again step into midnight, and return to the same fictional component.
Chen Wei (b. 1980, Zhejiang, China) lives and works between Beijing and Tokyo. His artistic work began in Hangzhou, China, where he was initially involved in experimental music performance and sound art before turning to photography, video, and installation. His work is known for carefully staged images, meticulously constructed sets, and a theatrical approach to space. Moving between reality and fiction, the everyday and the dreamlike, he examines the complex realities and psychological states of contemporary life. In recent years, he has increasingly extended this approach into the exhibition space, using video, sound, installation, and other materials to reshape the relationship between images, narrative, and spatial experience.
Recent solo exhibitions include Sweet Dreams, Fotografiska, Shanghai (2024); Make Me Illusory, West Bund Museum, Shanghai (2021); Good Night, HOW Art Museum, Shanghai (2021); The Club, Centre for Contemporary Photography, Melbourne (2017); and Noon Club, JNBY Art Space, Hangzhou (2016).
His work has also been presented at M+, Hong Kong; Centre Pompidou, Paris; Tokyo Photographic Art Museum, Tokyo; Gwangju Biennale; Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein; Asia Society, Houston; Museum Folkwang, Essen; 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa; and UCCA Center for Contemporary Art, Beijing.
