Yaroslava Mahuchikh’s name immortalized in space: an asteroid near Jupiter named after the Ukrainian athlete
Kyiv • UNN
Asteroid (57915) Mahuchikh was named after Olympic champion Yaroslava Mahuchikh. The celestial body belongs to the Jupiter trojans.
An asteroid moving near Jupiter’s orbit has been named after Ukrainian Olympic champion and high-jump world-record holder Yaroslava Mahuchikh. The celestial body received the official name (57915) Mahuchikh in August 2025. The Athletics Federation of Ukraine reported this, citing the WGSBN bulletin, UNN writes.
Details
The asteroid was discovered on March 9, 2002, at Mount Bigelow in the U.S. state of Arizona during research conducted as part of the Catalina Sky Survey project. It was initially designated 2002 EB110.
The international astronomical catalog noted the Ukrainian athlete’s main achievements: Olympic gold at the 2024 Paris Games, bronze at the Tokyo Games, and the high-jump world record of 2.10 meters.
What is known about the Mahuchikh asteroid
The celestial body belongs to the L4 group of Jupiter trojan asteroids. They orbit the Sun near the gas giant’s orbit, approximately 60 degrees ahead of it.
Interestingly, Mahuchikh is not the first Ukrainian athlete whose name has been given to a space object. Earlier, asteroid (212723) Klitschko was named after brothers Vitali and Wladimir Klitschko.
In addition, on October 7, 2026, a symbolic star honoring Yaroslava Mahuchikh was unveiled in Kyiv on the "Walk of Stars."
Reminder
In Kyiv, stars honoring Yaroslava Mahuchikh, Hryhorii Kriss, Serhii Dzinziruk, and Oleksandra Kononova were unveiled . Mahuchikh thanked Ukraine’s defenders.

DHS did not address questions from the Guardian seeking the name of the officer who struck Parra-Hernandez and whether he was equipped with a body-worn camera, which ICE policy requires.
Parra-Hernandez’s hospitalization came with ICE facing criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for the agency’s aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.
More than 30 people have died in 2026 during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September.
On Friday morning, a 72-year-old man shot an off-duty ICE official who was “intoxicated and agitated” and was accused of attacking the man and his daughter on their property in Fresno, California.
On Thursday, in New York City, an ICE agent shot a man who was in his vehicle with a five-year-old child, mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.
Markwayne Mullin, the Trump administration’s homeland security secretary, later said on CBS’s Face the Nation that ICE took the time to learn the “pattern of life” of the man shot in New York on Thursday – but “we didn’t know the five-year-old was in the vehicle”.
The Harris county precinct 4 commissioner, Lesley Briones, alluded to those various other cases in a statement on Saturday, saying: “Under the Trump administration, ICE has brought chaos and destruction to communities across our country.”
Briones described herself as “horrified” after Parra-Hernandez’s case on Saturday and called for ICE to release any relevant video to the sheriff’s office.
DHS did not immediately respond to the Guardian when asked for comment on Sunday.

Finally, a helpful intervention in the ‘overdiagnosis’ wars. But where’s the money to answer this tragedy? | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:10:35 UTC
23:10:35 KST

Back in late 2025, when Keir Starmer’s grip on the Labour party was loosening and Reform UK was still in its pomp, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, commissioned what the government called its “Independent review into prevalence and support for mental health conditions, ADHD and autism”.
Here, it seemed, was not just an inquiry into England’s ever-extending waiting lists for the diagnosis of mental illness and neurodevelopmental conditions, and the dire lack of support for people who experience one or both of them. The review would also dovetail with two other huge issues: mounting claims of “overdiagnosis”, which Streeting had appeared to partly endorse, and the government’s drive for the reform of so-called welfare. An apparently well-briefed piece in the Times seemed to speak volumes: work led by the renowned psychologist Peter Fonagy, it said, was commencing just “as Labour seeks a fresh crackdown on welfare spending” amid diagnoses “which have become the most common reason for a sickness benefit claim”.
Last Friday saw the publication of the 600-page final report Fonagy had co-authored with Gillian Baird – a specialist in paediatric neurodisability – and the psychiatrist Simon Wessely. And, as so often happens with such inquiries, its interpretation suggested the media’s equivalent of a Rorschach blot. One of the Guardian’s headlines was “No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real”. The Mail, by contrast, yelled out a rather different message – “Rush to diagnose ADHD and autism can damage children” – while the Telegraph went for “ADHD surge fuelled by benefits, report warns”.
Such are the perils of producing a very nuanced mixture of analysis and recommendations. When he appeared on Radio 4’s Today programme, Fonagy said that Streeting had been “completely wrong” to agree with suggestions of the common overdiagnosis of mental health disorders. When it comes to autism and ADHD, he and his colleagues’ report says that “if present trends continue we are clearly entering a phase in which the balance of risks is changing, from previous merited concerns with under-recognition and underdiagnosis towards an increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis”. But it also insists that right now, “we cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”, and points out that any data that might settle this festering argument “largely do not exist”. This is not the kind of stuff that suits a world that craves simple binaries and polarised shouting, but it speaks an undeniable truth.
For the most part, in fact, it is hard to disagree with what the review points out. But among its conclusions lies one troubling proposal – that provision for both mental illness and so-called neurodivergence can and should often be led by observations of need rather than formal diagnosis. In making that suggestion, I have no doubt that Fonagy and his colleagues’ intentions are benign. But our systems of power and politics and the government’s increasingly anxious view of public spending could yet make it very dangerous indeed.
First, though, the undeniable positives. In a very elegantly written and often moving introduction, Fonagy – who is 74 – completely rejects the popular idea of a new generation of wilting wimps falsely claiming to be suffering from mental ill-health. “The cacophony of voices now available to a young person – most of them digital, many of them confident, few of them accountable – has made the ordinary developmental process of understanding oneself far harder than it was for me,” he says. He goes on: “Young people today are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”
These are mental health issues. When it comes to autism and ADHD, Fonagy and his two colleagues’ insistence that overdiagnosis is currently not happening “at scale” and that “the evidence does not show that people presenting today are less impaired than those presenting previously” is very important indeed. When Streeting commissioned the review, among the most in-vogue books was The Age of Diagnosis by the neurologist and epilepsy specialist Suzanne O’Sullivan, which made the absurd suggestion that the overdiagnosis of autism might have reached the point where it was partly to blame for rising rates of anxiety and depression among the young, linked to her claim that “the stigma of autism has been associated with low self esteem among children”. (If autism is still stigmatised, O’Sullivan publicly calling it an “illness” is hardly helpful.)
The review, by contrast, is altogether more calm and evidence-based: for a bundle of reasons, it says that overdiagnosis and misdiagnosis may well be a future risk, but we can guard against those dangers by more closely regulating private diagnostic clinics (which are often partly NHS-funded) and stop them advertising their services. These are proposals that many autism and ADHD insiders agree with.
On a different subject, Fonagy and his co-authors also do us all a favour by emphasising the correct meaning of the ubiquitous term “neurodiversity”: whereas O’Sullivan says that it “has a biologising, pathologising effect”, the report rightly understands that the word means the complete opposite: it crystallises the plain fact that “variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour is part of natural human diversity rather than pathology or disorder”.
But what do we do when faced with genuinely diagnosable conditions that are debilitating and entail intensive support? One bit of first-person testimony in the report is heartbreaking. “When she was 12,” says an unnamed parent, “our daughter was put on ADHD medication, which lowered her mood, leading her to self-harm. She was referred to CAMHS [child and adolescent mental health services] who turned her down. Within the next month we ended up in A&E due to taking an overdose. She was then finally accepted by CAMHS, who suggested an autism assessment.
“Two years later, after receiving an autism diagnosis, little changed. School would not make any adjustments until an EHCP (education, health and care plan) was accepted, and social care said she did not meet their threshold for support because she did not have a learning disability. Our daughter was broken and unsupported and was admitted to inpatients at 15 years old.”
Herein lies one of the review’s few dangers. By way of lessening an increasingly frightening crisis that is partly centred on pitifully long waits for formal diagnoses that can easily be ignored, it suggests moving towards a more “needs-based” approach, which echoes the government’s plans for special needs education. “There should be a fundamental shift from a diagnosis-dependent system to a needs-led plus diagnosis system,” it says. Such a change, the report says, would require “increased capacity, transformation through digitally enabled care, clearer national standards and sustained investment”.
They are my italics, with very good reason. The government responded to the report by saying that the health and social care secretary, Yvette Cooper, “has asked NHS leaders to urgently examine how people can access advice, assessments and treatment more easily”. But without sufficient money, “needs-based” help is likely to amount to very little at all. Coincidentally, the Fonagy review arrived on the same day as reports that the prime minister and the chancellor had rebuffed Cooper’s requests for money to fund a pay rise for NHS staff including nurses, porters and midwives. So what chance of a huge cash injection to tackle what the report so starkly highlights?
Meanwhile, the Department for Work and Pensions still has a culture built around crackdowns and pushing people into work. Councils repeatedly fail to meet their responsibilities for the care and education of neurodivergent people. And, in the absence of properly funded change, both they and people suffering mental illness only stand even a faint chance of pushing their way through an almost impossible mess of bureaucracy and obstruction if they have pieces of paper confirming that their condition – or conditions – are real and true.
This is what makes politicians who talk of “overdiagnosis” look so crass, and the likely fate of such a definitive and in-depth report so tragic. It is an all too familiar story, indicative of our current defining national predicament: the government simply cannot afford what it proposes, so one of our cruellest modern crises looks set to grind on.
- John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,930 Troops, 39 Artillery Systems in One Day

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, the latest figures bring Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,552,840.
Russian forces also lost six armored combat vehicles during the latest reporting period, raising cumulative losses to 12,408 tanks and 25,521 armored vehicles. Another 39 artillery systems were added to the tally, bringing the overall estimate to 51,039, while four multiple-launch rocket systems and one air defense system brought those totals to 2,205 and 1,701, respectively.
Ukraine also reported 1,531 operational-tactical UAVs lost over the past day, pushing the cumulative total to 558,457. Another seven unmanned ground systems were recorded as lost, raising that category to 2,924.
Russia’s estimated aviation losses remained unchanged at 443 aircraft and 356 helicopters, while cruise missile losses stayed at 5,126. Naval losses also remained unchanged at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 557 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost, bringing the cumulative figure to 161,503, while the total number of special equipment losses stood at 4,812. Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 221 times across the front during the latest reporting period, according to Ukraine’s General Staff on October 11.
The heaviest fighting was reported in the Pokrovsk and Huliaipole sectors, where Russian forces launched 25 and 21 attacks, respectively. Another 18 attacks were recorded in the Kostiantynivka sector, while Ukrainian forces repelled 10 assaults each in the Southern Slobozhanshchyna and Lyman sectors.
Russian forces also conducted six attacks in the Sloviansk sector and three in the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors. No offensive operations were reported in the Kramatorsk, Oleksandrivka, or Orikhiv sectors.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Air Force reported that Ukrainian forces destroyed more than 4,700 Russian aerial targets and neutralized over 48,000 tactical-level drones in September 2026. The military also conducted more than 1,600 aviation sorties, including missions to intercept aerial threats and strike Russian positions.

Anthropic's artificial intelligence invented a murder witness and sent false information to U.S. police
Kyiv • UNN
During testing, an Anthropic agent sent police a fabricated report about a murder witness. The company discovered the incident two months later.
An AI agent of the American company Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, independently sent the Philadelphia police fabricated information about an unsolved murder. The incident occurred during automated system testing, but the company discovered it only two months later. BBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
On July 18, the artificial intelligence used a website through which citizens can report information about crimes to law enforcement. The agent claimed that it had allegedly seen a person matching the description of someone connected to the case. In fact, this information was entirely fabricated.
The police system automatically flagged the report as spam, so it did not reach investigators and did not affect the investigation.
Anthropic did not know about the incident for more than two months
The company discovered the violation only on September 28 and stopped the relevant testing. At the same time, the Philadelphia police were informed about the incident only on October 7. Law enforcement officials called the delay unacceptable and urged developers to strengthen security measures.
As it turned out, this was not the only instance of uncontrolled activity by Anthropic's AI agents. During other tests, they interacted with U.S. government websites, including submitting 20 incomplete visa applications through the State Department's website.
The company has already published a study of the unintended actions of its AI systems. The incidents raised concerns about the safety of autonomous agents that can independently interact with government institutions.

Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:09:12 UTC
23:09:12 KST

Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on.
Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.
The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.
The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.
However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.
So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?
What did Eritrea and Ethiopia say at the UN?
Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.
In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.
He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking.
Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”.
He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.
The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”.
“The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.
Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts.
“Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said.
“The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.”
What is the latest fighting about, and how is Eritrea allegedly involved?
Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city.
In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.
Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.
It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.
Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims.
The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development.
Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified.
The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement.
That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger.
The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated.
Has Ethiopia sent troops north towards Eritrea?
Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday.
Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city.
Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops.
Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat.
Are Ethiopia and Eritrea inching towards war?
Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation.
BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.”
He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”.
Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours.
Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera.
“The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted.
“It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.”
Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said.
“The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control.
“A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.

Grace Wu's tribute to Victor Mair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:06:54 UTC
23:06:54 KST

Grace Wu's tribute to Victor Mair
« previous post | next post »
I spent yesterday afternoon at the Memorial Service for Victor Mair, where many of his relatives, friends, students, and colleagues told stories about Victor and his influence on their lives.
Because Grace Wu was not able to attend, she sent me a tribute to read on her behalf, which I've reprinted below.
I have always been deeply grateful to Professor Mair and to his extraordinary contributions to Taiwanese language education. In fact, Penn’s Taiwanese language program, which began in 1993, would not have existed without his advocacy. More than 30 years ago, at a time when there were not yet any Taiwanese language courses being offered even in Taiwan, he had the vision to establish Taiwanese at Penn. I often think about what a remarkable idea and commitment that was.
Over the years, Professor Mair also wrote extensively about Taiwanese in Language Log. For example, on 6/16/2018, in a post with the title “Mother tongue is like mother’s milk”, he mentions the Taiwanese dictionary that my father helped compile.
And on 10/16/2009, in “National Language vs. Mother Tongue”, he led with a photo that I sent him, and discussed the campaign to replace topolects with Putonghua.
But the essay I love most is “How to Forget Your Mother Tongue and Remember Your National Language”.
There is one passage that has always been especially meaningful to me:
“The simplest way to make speakers of a language feel that their tongue is inadequate is to stigmatize it as sù 俗 (‘vulgar’), lǐyǔ 俚語 (‘slang’), tǔhuà 土話 (‘earthy speech’), and so on. Once such evaluations are accepted by the speakers of a given language themselves, the psychological impact is tremendous. Subjected to such indoctrination, they lose confidence in their mother tongue and may become acutely embarrassed when outsiders hear them speaking it.”
This idea was a real revelation to me. Having grown up under a Mandarin-centered language system, I had never fully understood how deeply the stigmatization of Taiwanese during the martial-law era had affected our attitudes toward our own language.
Professor Mair helped me understand this history and, more importantly, helped me feel proud of my own language. His work also taught me to be more respectful of my students’ accents and to approach dialects and language varieties with greater openness, empathy, and understanding.
I will always be grateful for Professor Mair’s lifelong dedication to East Asian scholarship and Taiwanese language education, and for the profound humanistic spirit with which he approached language, culture, and the people who speak them. His intellectual work touched many lives, including mine, and his influence will continue through generations of students and teachers.
Above is Grace Wu's tribute to Victor Mair, composed for his 10/10/2026 Memorial Service.

Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
IRGC warns against ignoring the ‘security and rules’ of the strategic waterway as US CENTCOM says it disabled vessel trying to run naval blockade.
US bombs cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman 'trying to run Iran blockade'
Tehran, Iran – Strikes around the strategic Strait of Hormuz have picked up again as mediated efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran remain deadlocked.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Saturday night that an unnamed crude oil supertanker hit a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route in the waterway with navigation systems turned off. In a statement, it warned of a similar fate for any oil tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.
On Sunday, a senior Iranian army official told state television that the country’s forces remain prepared for both defensive and offensive operations, more than seven months since the United States and Israel started the war by attacking Iran on February 28.
“We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” said Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint coordinator of the army.
His comments came after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several incidents of military action or warnings against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman over the past day. It said ship masters in the vicinity of Ras al-Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), had been directed via radio broadcast overnight to move from their anchorages. And on Sunday afternoon, UKMTO reported an unidentified projectile had struck a tanker heading outbound through the Strait of Hormuz.
Separately, the UAE said its coastguard had rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out at an unnamed tanker close to its shores, although it did not identify the cause of the blaze.
Early on Sunday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) released footage of a fighter jet bombing the stern of a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman and disabling its propulsion to enforce its naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports.
Since the US reimposed the blockade in mid-July, CENTCOM says its forces have disabled four commercial vessels, turned around 135 ships and destroyed 10 tankers linked with Iran. Washington says Tehran has exported no oil through the blockade line.
This comes as at least a dozen ships were attacked over the week ending on October 5, the highest number since the war began. At least one was hit off the north coast of Qatar, signalling that the danger extends beyond the immediate Hormuz passage as Iran and the US vie for control.
The ship attacks appear to have decreased energy flows that had surpassed pre-war levels at the start of the month. Kpler data cited by CNBC on Friday showed that average crude passing through the strait for the week ended October 7 was 8.5 million barrels per day, roughly 40 percent below the normal level.
To reopen the strait and reach a resolution to the war, Iran has demanded a return to a now-collapsed memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June, as well as Washington’s backing of an already finalised Iran-Oman deal that designates temporary coordinated entry and exit routes for vessels transiting the strait.
Messages continue to be exchanged between the two sides through mediators, although no breakthrough is expected in the coming weeks leading to the US midterm vote, set to take place on November 3, and Israel’s election, due on October 27.
US Vice President JD Vance said last week that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the war, signalling a potential easing of the oft-repeated US demand that zero enrichment must take place on Iranian soil.
Tehran has said a nuclear agreement potentially involving diluting its high-enriched uranium can be part of the later stages of talks, but has emphasised it will not abandon enrichment altogether.
“The achievements of our indigenous nuclear industry cannot be stopped,” Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said during a speech on Sunday, pointing to electricity generation as a main use case.
He also renewed criticism against the International Atomic Energy Agency for not condemning repeated US threats to again bomb Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, told reporters on Sunday that authorities plan on using military and diplomatic avenues to get what they want.
“The Islamic Republic will decisively pursue the country’s interests,” he said. “If those interests can be secured through diplomacy, that is much better, but if not, we will secure them in the field of battle”.

Antidepressants in pregnancy not tied to extra autism or ADHD risk beyond maternal depression, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:00:29 UTC
23:00:29 KST

Children whose mothers had a recorded depression diagnosis around the time of pregnancy were slightly more likely to need special educational support in school, and those whose mothers were also prescribed antidepressants had a small additional increase in risk. However, the researchers could not rule out that this extra risk reflects more severe depression rather than the medication itself. The research was published in PLOS Medicine.
Expectant mothers often face difficult decisions regarding mental health treatment, especially given concerns about how medications might affect fetal brain development. Fears about potential side effects lead some pregnant women to stop taking prescribed antidepressants, which can leave both mother and child vulnerable to the harms of untreated depression. In an educational setting, a special educational need refers to situations where a child requires additional support at school to help with learning, communication, physical, or behavioral challenges compared to their peers.
Early observational studies fueled worries about medication safety during pregnancy. A 2016 study reported that taking antidepressants during pregnancy was associated with an increased risk of autism spectrum disorder in children. Follow-up research, however, suggested that the mother’s underlying depression and shared family traits might actually explain the connection.
Studies that accounted for those factors often saw the link fade. For instance, a 2018 systematic review found that apparent risks of autism and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder largely shrank or disappeared when researchers properly accounted for the mother’s mental health history. Similarly, a 2017 study using sibling comparisons showed that links to neurodevelopmental conditions, which affect how the brain develops, such as autism and ADHD, largely disappeared when comparing exposed children to their unexposed siblings, pointing to shared family factors rather than the drugs themselves.
Recent research covered by PsyPost in 2025 also found that children exposed to antidepressants in the womb showed no increased risk of anxiety or depression once maternal depression was factored in, while another study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicated that population-level risks are largely driven by shared genetic and family factors.
To help address this ongoing debate, Saraid McIlvride and her colleagues at the University of Glasgow evaluated both depression and antidepressant use side by side in a large population. The authors sought to separate the potential side effects of the medications from the developmental effects of the illness itself.
“Women want to have confidence in their decision to take medication during pregnancy and know that long-term studies investigating potential effects have been carried out,” study lead author Saraid McIlvride, a Daphne Jackson Research Fellow at the University of Glasgow, told PsyPost. “Many studies have focused on pregnancy and neonatal outcomes, but fewer studies have looked at longer-term outcomes, particularly for newer or less common antidepressants, and there have been conflicting results.”
“This dataset, which linked child education and health records with their mother’s health records across the whole of Wales, allowed us to follow children up during primary school and gave a large enough sample size to look at some individual antidepressants and other educational outcomes beyond ASD and ADHD.”
Because this was observational research, the scientists analyzed existing health and education databases rather than assigning treatments to participants. The dataset linked primary care, maternity, and school records for 167,447 children born in Wales between 2009 and 2016. By tracking the children through 2022, when they were just under 6 years old on average, the team could identify any special educational needs recorded by schools.
Children were grouped by two separate measures: whether their mother had received at least one antidepressant prescription during pregnancy or in the month before conception, and whether she had a depression diagnosis recorded by her family doctor in the two years before giving birth. Overall, 7.6 percent of the children were born to mothers who had a recorded depression diagnosis but received no antidepressant prescriptions. Another 4.2 percent were exposed to both a maternal depression diagnosis and antidepressant prescriptions, while 3.6 percent were born to mothers prescribed antidepressants without a recorded depression diagnosis. The remaining children, who formed the comparison group, had neither exposure recorded.
The researchers adjusted their models for factors such as child sex, age, ethnicity, maternal age, smoking habits, and the level of deprivation in the family’s neighborhood. The analysis indicated that both untreated maternal depression and antidepressant prescriptions were associated with higher odds of a child developing a special educational need. Among children with neither exposure, the baseline rate of requiring special educational support was 20 cases per 100 children. For children whose mothers had untreated depression, this rate rose to 23.6 cases per 100 children.
Children whose mothers had both a depression diagnosis and antidepressant prescriptions had a predicted rate of 26.5 cases of special educational need per 100 children, while those whose mothers were prescribed antidepressants without a depression diagnosis had a rate of 26.3 per 100. When examining the additional risk linked to medication, the gap depended on whether the mother had a depression diagnosis. Prescriptions were associated with an extra 6.3 cases per 100 children among mothers without a recorded depression diagnosis, but only 2.9 additional cases per 100 children among mothers who had a recorded diagnosis.
The authors note that the smaller gap reflects the already elevated rate among children whose mothers had untreated depression, meaning the higher risk linked to maternal depression cannot be attributed solely to medication. Compared with unexposed children, both maternal depression and antidepressant exposure were associated with higher odds of autism, ADHD, learning difficulties, and behavioral, emotional, and social difficulties.
But when children of mothers with treated depression were compared with children of mothers with untreated depression, the differences for autism and ADHD were not statistically significant; only learning difficulties and behavioral, emotional, and social difficulties showed small differences, of about one additional case per 100 children each.
The researchers also looked at different types of antidepressants. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the standard first-line antidepressants, which include drugs such as sertraline and fluoxetine, made up about 83 percent of prescriptions and followed the same general pattern as the overall results.
Two less common classes, tricyclic antidepressants, an older type of medication, and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, showed a larger gap between treated and untreated depression, with about 8.8 extra cases of special educational need per 100 children for each. Because relatively few children were exposed to these drugs, the estimates were imprecise, ranging from roughly 3 to 15 extra cases per 100.
The tricyclic result is consistent with a 2026 meta-analysis, which found that tricyclic antidepressants were the only class where links to neurodevelopmental conditions persisted after accounting for maternal mental health, though that study also could not rule out underlying illness severity.
“Maternal depression during pregnancy was associated with an increased chance of children having special educational needs,” McIlvride said. “Taking antidepressants during pregnancy was linked to a small increase in this risk, compared to untreated depression, but we weren’t able to show if this increase is due to these women having more severe depression or an effect of the medication. Untreated depression can have a serious impact on the well-being of both mother and baby so it is vital to keep taking antidepressants if they are needed.”
Independent specialists reviewing the research for the Science Media Centre emphasized that the modest differences in risk should be interpreted with caution. Asma Khalil, a professor of obstetrics and maternal-fetal medicine at City St George’s, University of London, who was not involved in the study, said in her comments that the work provides helpful context but cannot determine causation.
Khalil pointed to the gap of roughly three cases per 100 children between mothers with treated and untreated depression. “That difference is worth studying, but it does not show that antidepressants caused it,” Khalil said. “The researchers could not measure how severe the mothers’ depression was, and women prescribed medication may have differed in important ways from those who were not. A prescription also does not establish that a medicine was taken throughout pregnancy.”
“The main outcome was a broad measure of special educational needs, which is not the same as a clinical diagnosis,” Khalil added. “This study adds valuable evidence about the needs of children and families, but it cannot tell an individual woman whether taking or stopping an antidepressant would change her child’s developmental risk.”
McIlvride similarly emphasized that population-level statistics do not translate directly into an individual pregnancy’s personal outcome.
“This study has estimated an association at a population level and so can’t tell an individual about their personal risk,” McIlvride noted. “It gives women and their families information which could potentially benefit their child’s development by identifying a need for support earlier. This study also shows that antidepressant use during pregnancy is increasingly common – around 1 in 12 women were taking antidepressants in our study, and we can expect this figure to be even higher today – therefore this is an area which deserves more research.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The biggest limitation is that the researchers had no data on how severe each mother’s depression was. Because doctors typically prescribe medications like tricyclic antidepressants for more severe or treatment-resistant depression, the higher risks seen with these specific drugs might simply reflect the fact that the mothers prescribed them were experiencing a more intense form of the illness.
“This study does not show that depression or antidepressant use during pregnancy causes autism or ADHD in children – it shows an association, which could be due to many different reasons,” McIlvride emphasized. “The increased risk associated with antidepressants we observed in our study could be due to more severe disease, as it is likely that women who are taking antidepressants will have more severe depression.”
Angelica Ronald, a professor of psychology and genetics at the University of Surrey who was not involved in the study, said in comments to the Science Media Centre that shared genetic influences could account for part of the link, while describing the large sample size and linked records as notable strengths of the study.
“There is evidence from a range of sources that depression and neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism and ADHD share some genetic influences,” Ronald said. “This means we expect autism, ADHD and depression to run in the same families to some degree. This new study does not account for the fact that autism, ADHD and depression share some inherited (genetic) influences. Shared genetic influences might explain some of the associations found here between maternal depression in pregnancy and maternal use of antidepressants in pregnancy and offspring special educational needs.”
David Curtis, an honorary professor at the UCL Genetics Institute at University College London who was not involved in the research, questioned in his comments to the Science Media Centre whether the depression link reflects any harm in the womb at all.
“Although this study shows that children of mothers who suffered depression or took antidepressants have increased rates of special educational needs, we cannot assume that this represents a causal relationship,” Curtis said. “In fact, for me it seems somewhat implausible that a mother being depressed in the two years before birth would somehow cause the child to be at subsequently increased risk of having learning difficulties. Typically, a depressive illness per se does not produce profound physiological changes such as might be expected to substantially disrupt fetal development. Alternative explanations seem more likely.”
“A mother depressed in the years before delivery would be more likely to have subsequent episodes of depression and these subsequent episodes might impact a child’s psychosocial development,” he explained. “A mother with a previous diagnosis of depression might have more contact with support services which could result in a higher probability of problems with the child being detected.”
The researchers also lacked some data. The group of women prescribed antidepressants without a recorded depression diagnosis likely included many with unrecorded depression or anxiety, as well as some treated for other conditions, such as migraine and chronic pain, for which tricyclic antidepressants and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are also prescribed. The researchers did not have data on maternal alcohol or illicit drug use, nor could they account for the mental health of fathers or the potential influence of breastfeeding.
McIlvride pointed to several next steps for expanding on this line of inquiry. “The average age of children in our study was just under 6 years old, so it would be of interest to follow the children up for a longer period,” she said. “Further research is needed to answer questions around the dose of medications or how taking medication while breastfeeding could affect children’s development.”
Future studies that include detailed measures of depression severity, environmental factors, and longer follow-up windows could help better explain the relationship between maternal mental health care and long-term child development.
The study, “Prenatal exposure to maternal depression and antidepressants and neurodevelopmental outcomes: A population cohort study,” was authored by Saraid McIlvride, Neha Rao, Sarjit Singh, Scott M. Nelson, Jill P. Pell, and Michael Fleming.

====================================================================================================

The most successful people I meet are often the ones struggling most | Darren Lee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

Some of the most successful people I meet as a psychiatrist are also some of the most dissatisfied with life. They don’t necessarily look unwell. They are executives, entrepreneurs, doctors, lawyers and high achievers. They run companies and families. They are the people others depend on when something goes wrong. Often, they are exceptionally good at coping. Until they aren’t.
Holly* came to see me after years of depressive symptoms and worsening substance use, both of which she had largely managed to conceal from family, friends and colleagues. Her GP recommended a residential treatment program. In her early 40s, she held an executive position in a demanding organisation. She was ambitious, respected and known for her extraordinary work ethic. She was also exhausted.
Outside work, things were beginning to unravel. She was struggling to sleep and increasingly used alcohol to switch off at night. There were periods of profound sadness and numbness. But Holly kept working.
In fact, work was the one place she still felt energised. She would often be in the office 12 hours a day. She told me that when she was busy, she didn’t have to think. There was always another meeting, deadline or problem to solve. Achievement gave her a sense of control and, temporarily, a sense that she was doing well in her life.
Holly’s story is something I see regularly – often the characteristics we celebrate as resilience in society can also be ways of coping.
In therapy, we began to understand why achievement had become so important to Holly. Her childhood had been unpredictable. She learned early to monitor the moods of the adults around her, avoid causing problems and become fiercely independent. Academic success brought praise and, crucially, higher self-esteem. So she became very good at succeeding, but this meant being harder and harder on herself when she failed.
None of this meant her ambition wasn’t genuine. Nor does being ambitious mean someone has experienced trauma in their life. But for Holly, achievement had become tangled up with something deeper.
She told me in one of our earlier sessions: “If I am successful enough, useful enough and busy enough, I know I will feel better about myself.” This can be one of the more difficult manifestations of unresolved trauma to recognise because, from the outside, it can look remarkably functional.
Fear of failure can contribute to perfectionism. Difficulty resting can be mistaken for drive. Becoming highly attuned to other people’s moods can make someone appear very emotionally perceptive.
Nobody stages an intervention because you’re answering emails at 1am or volunteering for another project. In fact, you may be promoted for precisely the behaviours that are exhausting you. The difficulty comes when achievement stops being something you pursue and becomes something you need. For some people, slowing down creates an uncomfortable silence. Without the next deadline or accomplishment, difficult emotions may have more room to surface, and the person can feel flat or depressed. So they keep working. Until a relationship ends. A parent dies. There’s a redundancy. A child is born. The body simply becomes exhausted. Or the strategies being used to manage the feelings – alcohol, drugs, compulsive exercise or relentless work – begin creating problems of their own.
This was where Holly found herself.
Treating her depression was important, but so was understanding what sat beneath her relentless productivity. Over time, she began recognising that some of the qualities that had once helped her cope earlier in life were also masking deeper difficulties with self-esteem, safety, intimacy and identity.
The goal of our sessions wasn’t to strip her drive or trace every achievement back to childhood pain. Ambition can come from curiosity, passion, purpose, competitiveness and genuine enjoyment. Instead, I raised questions such as: What happens when you stop? Can you rest without feeling guilty? Can you fail without feeling worthless? Can you say no without fearing rejection? Can you feel valuable when you aren’t achieving anything? For Holly, these questions were surprisingly difficult.
After starting to address her depression and substance use, she began creating space in her life that had previously contained almost none. She learned to sit with her feelings rather than immediately working through them or suppressing them. This helped her separate her sense of worth from her role and productivity. She remained successful. But success was now less determined by external factors.
Sometimes the behaviours that helped us survive become so embedded that they mask our past traumas and adversity. The challenge isn’t necessarily to give them up. It’s to understand what drives them – and realise we are more than them.

Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked when the Secretary of State expected to receive endorsement of the revised programme baseline, with reference to the Brimstone 3 entry in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority Major Projects Annual Report for 2025 to 2026.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The revised baseline of the Brimstone 3 programme was approved on the 19 June 2026 and carries an Initial Operating Capability forecast of November 2026.”
The last schedule the department gave publicly came in a written answer of 30 April 2025, which said Brimstone 3 was scheduled to be fielded on Protector in the fourth quarter of 2025 and on Typhoon in the fourth quarter of 2026. November falls inside that Typhoon window.
Final safe separation trials were completed in the United States in June and further testing followed in Britain during August. Clearance on Protector was still outstanding in September, when the department said the results were undergoing analysis, and Mr Pollard said at that point that “previous delays have been overcome through a revised plan of combined USA and UK based testing.”
The programme began on 1 July 2017 and carries an approved end date of 30 April 2029. Its delivery confidence rating fell from amber to red in the March 2023 figures, which the department attributed at the time to difficulties resourcing suitably qualified and experienced people, and recovered to amber by the final quarter of 2023 to 2024 following a formal review.

WHO: Cause of Siberian Plague Lab Worker’s Death Still Unclear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:53:00 UTC
22:53:00 KST

The World Health Organization (WHO) stated that the cause of pneumonia that killed an employee of an anti-plague research center in Siberia remains undetermined, though no cases of plague have been confirmed and no evidence of secondary transmission has been detected, Reuters reported.
According to a statement issued by the UN health agency, Russia’s consumer health regulator, Rospotrebnadzor, reported that diagnostic tests conducted on the deceased researcher and individuals who came into contact with her returned negative for tested high-consequence pathogens.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The WHO noted that none of the monitored contacts have developed symptoms, and no secondary cases of severe respiratory illness linked to the incident have been identified.
“The main uncertainty remains the lack of a confirmed diagnosis for the deceased worker,” the WHO said, while confirming that it found no indication of ongoing community spread.
Russian authorities informed the organization that the employee was vaccinated in accordance with mandatory laboratory safety protocols, and that post-mortem testing did not detect microorganisms associated with her occupational duties.
Russian officials stated that active medical monitoring of all quarantined contacts concluded on Oct. 8, with the findings transmitted to the WHO.
Siberian institute quarantine
The case centers on the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, a state biological research facility in the Irkutsk region.
Can Trump Sidestep Russia Sanctions as the Midterms Loom?
The deceased researcher, identified in independent Russian media reports as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, died overnight between Oct. 1 and Oct. 2 after being hospitalized with acute, rapidly progressing pneumonia of undetermined etiology.
The incident prompted unverified reports in regional media suggesting potential accidental exposure to pneumonic plague within the research facility.
Russian health authorities rejected reports that a plague infection occurred, classifying the fatality as an isolated case of severe “community-acquired pneumonia.”
Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev previously announced that regional authorities conducted nearly 5,000 diagnostic laboratory tests on biological samples collected from approximately 200 individuals placed in isolation following the fatality.
According to regional officials, all tests returned negative for dangerous infectious agents.
Precautionary measures introduced following the death included the temporary quarantine of a hospital in Shelekhov alongside several municipal clinical wards in Irkutsk.
A precautionary mask-wearing requirement was also enacted at the Irkutsk Aluminum Plant. Regional authorities lifted the quarantine measures on Thursday, Oct. 8, asserting that the risk to public health had passed.
Global surveillance
The WHO’s updated statement follows earlier calls by the agency for greater diagnostic clarity and data transparency from Moscow.
During a media briefing on Wednesday, Oct. 7, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus noted that while Russian authorities had notified the organization of the precautionary quarantine of 200 contacts and reported zero confirmed plague cases, the global health body had requested comprehensive laboratory data to verify the findings.
The agency sought specific details regarding the methodology used in laboratory screenings, the exact clinical factors prompting the extensive localized quarantine measures, and verification concerning reports of a potential second employee hospitalized with acute respiratory symptoms.
“As we don’t yet have the full picture of this event, we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” Tedros said at the time, reiterating that transparent data sharing is essential for evaluating international health risks.
While Rospotrebnadzor maintained that it provided complete technical information to international regulators, Russian authorities have not publicly identified the specific pathogen responsible for the fatal pneumonia.

Palestinians have not elected a president for over 20 years: Abbas postpones elections again

President of the Palestinian Authority Mahmoud Abbas has postponed the parliamentary elections scheduled for November 2026 and set presidential and parliamentary elections for September 11, 2027. The last time Palestinians elected a president was in 2005, and a parliament in 2006. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Abbas signed the relevant decree on October 10. He cited Israeli restrictions, the difficult security situation, and the lack of conditions for free voting as the reasons for the postponement.
In particular, this concerns Israel's military operations, the expansion of settlements, and restrictions on movement in the West Bank. In the Gaza Strip, according to the Palestinian authorities, the holding of elections is hindered by the humanitarian crisis, the presence of Israeli troops, and problems with access for international observers.
Abbas remains in power after the end of his presidential term
Mahmoud Abbas has headed the Palestinian Authority since 2005. His presidential term ended in 2009, but since then he has continued to govern by decree.
According to Reuters, the decision to postpone the elections was made after consultations with Palestinian political forces. Representatives of Fatah and Hamas agreed to postpone the vote during a meeting in Cairo.
Israel criticized Abbas's decision. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar called his explanation an attempt to avoid responsibility for the absence of elections for two decades.
At the same time, France emphasized the need to hold the vote. Abbas had previously promised to organize elections as part of political reforms supported by international partners. Whether they will be held in September 2027 will depend on the security situation in the Palestinian territories.

South Africa to seek court oversight of asylum ruling amid anti-immigration protests

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
21:50:37 CST
22:50:37 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The South African government will ask the courts to oversee the implementation of a Constitutional Court ruling on asylum applications, as anti-immigration protests continue in parts of the country, the Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) on Migration said Sunday.
The immediate trigger for the country's latest round of anti-immigration protests was a Sept. 28 directive issued by the Department of Home Affairs following the Constitutional Court's July 7 judgment in the Scalabrini Center of Cape Town case.
The directive outlined procedures for processing asylum applications, but anti-immigration groups viewed it as an attempt to regularize the status of undocumented migrants. Protests in Durban and Soweto turned violent, with vehicles set alight. The department withdrew the directive on Friday.
Briefing the media on Sunday, IMC Chairperson and Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development Mmamoloko Kubayi said the government decided to seek a supervisory order to clarify how the ruling should be implemented. The order could include a suspension period to give the Department of Home Affairs time to strengthen its administrative capacity and improve its handling of asylum applications.
"The objective is not to delay compliance, but to ensure effective and sustainable compliance that serves both the administration of justice and the broader public interest," Kubayi said.
She stressed that the government remained legally bound to comply with the existing court order while seeking further guidance from the courts.
Meanwhile, the Department of Home Affairs plans to introduce a new registration and appointment system for asylum applications by Nov. 10. The government is also moving ahead with plans to relocate refugee reception centers to ports of entry, starting with Beitbridge by December.
The IMC said 30 people had been arrested since Thursday, including 25 in KwaZulu-Natal and five in Gauteng, on charges including public violence and illegal gathering, and called on the public to exercise restraint and resolve grievances through lawful channels.
"Matters relating to asylum, migration, and border management must be addressed through lawful processes and not through misinformation, intimidation, incitement, or acts of violence," Kubayi said. ■

22:50:06 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Chinese veteran Zhang Shuai and Katerina Siniakova of the Czech Republic finished runners-up in the women's doubles at the 2026 China Open on Sunday, falling to Canada's Gabriela Dabrowski and Brazil's Luisa Stefani in straight sets.
Dabrowski and Stefani needed just 59 minutes to defeat Zhang and Siniakova 6-1, 6-2 and claim their seventh title as a pair. It was their fifth title of the season, following triumphs in Dubai, Strasbourg, Eastbourne and Sao Paulo. The pair also finished runners-up at Wimbledon this year.
"Obviously today's performance was like a really great culmination of the entire week, which was awesome for us," said Dabrowski. "We have had such a fun time in Beijing. We really enjoyed it. Tomorrow we have a day off. We are really excited. Definitely going to celebrate maybe later. Then tomorrow, hopefully, some tourist stuff. It really is well-earned."
The victory marked Dabrowski's 25th career tour-level doubles title and her seventh at a WTA 1000 event. Stefani claimed her 18th career doubles title and fifth at WTA 1000 level. The pair improved their tour-level record as a team to 75-19.
"I have a lot of pride. I'm very grateful for everything that we've been accomplishing and how well we've been playing, and how we've improved together since the beginning of the year," said Stefani.
"I think it's really cool to see that come to light in how we execute and how we perform. Then we get results from it. I think it's kind of cool to be in the middle of this process and living it in real-time. To be healthy and playing well, winning a title here, also means a lot. It's really special to, yeah, just still feel good at this point in the season," she added.
For Siniakova and Zhang, the Beijing final was their sixth tour-level event together. They first partnered at the 2024 Guangzhou Open, where they won the title, and have since added two more championships, in Adelaide and Toronto, both this year.
Their defeat in Beijing marked their first loss as a team this season, ending a 13-match winning streak. They now hold a 19-3 record as a pair.
"I am of course also very happy to be on the same side with Shuai, especially here in Beijing. It was a very tough week for me, but I was really happy to share it with you," Siniakova said to Zhang at the press conference. "Definitely, it's a great tournament, great two weeks. Even if it was not meant to be today, I really enjoyed it. As you said, we did play our best - or we tried. Maybe it wasn't our best today, but our opponent just played amazing."
"I really treasure the time here, every tournament, every event. We see those people, local people, trying their best to try to support these events. That makes me want to stay in the sport," Zhang said.
"I have the motivation to continue to stay on the tour, to continue to try my best in this sport. I feel the urge and passion for it. See you in Wuhan," she added. ■

Wildlife park confirms tiger will not be euthanised after man mauled to death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:48:21 UTC
22:48:21 KST

A wildlife park in Yorkshire has confirmed the tiger that mauled to death a man who entered its enclosure will not be euthanised.
A man, who has not yet been named, was seen entering a tiger enclosure at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, located near Doncaster, before police were called at 1.35pm on Saturday.
South Yorkshire police said the tiger “subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury” and despite the efforts of emergency services, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.
In a statement on Sunday, the wildlife park thanked those who had expressed concern after the “tragic incident” and said their “thoughts and heartfelt sympathies” remained with the family of the man who lost his life.
“The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support,” the statement read. The park also confirmed that the tiger, named Altai, was “safe and well and will not be euthanised” after the incident.
The foreign secretary and MP for Doncaster North, Ed Miliband, said he was “deeply saddened” and sent his “thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died”.
“I am very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded,” Miliband added.
One visitor at the park, Marie Miller, wrote in a Facebook post that she had seen the man before the incident and he was “happily enjoying” his visit. Miller said the man had asked a stranger to take a picture of him.
“The man who I saw on the bridge with his earpods in dancing was happily enjoying seeing the tiger,” the post read.
“He asked a total stranger to take a picture of him with the tiger in the background.”
Another visitor, who did not want to be identified, told the South West News Service that it was “frightening and confusing” when the park was evacuated after the incident.
She said: “At first, we were all scared and confused because we had no idea what was going on. Different routes had been closed off, and staff were positioned around the park directing visitors where to go.
“The scariest part was not knowing what was happening.”
The visitor said she heard people saying the man was 22, but was unable to confirm this. “As we walked past the police near the tiger enclosure, we saw officers surrounding a young man in the tiger enclosure,” she said. “We saw an air ambulance outside the park, although, from what we observed, it didn’t take anyone away.”
South Yorkshire police said the man’s family was made aware of the incident on Saturday and were being supported by specialist officers. The force has encouraged people not to share videos of the incident that have been circulating online.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is on a purpose-built 2-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.

Archaeologists unearth medieval convent’s heating system during renovations in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:43:36 UTC
22:43:36 KST

A well-preserved medieval stone-chamber heating system was found during renovations of a property in Basel, Switzerland, the Canton of Basel-Stadt announced in late September.
The system had once belonged to the now-excavated Gnadental convent for women, established in around 1231 outside of Basel’s city walls, and was found beneath what had once served as the dining hall in the east wing of the convent.
It is almost completely preserved, and is one of the most significantly known examples of heating systems of its type in both Switzerland and Europe at large.
Based on the sites’s architectural history, archaeologists have estimated that the heating system was built between the 13th and 14th centuries.
The underground chamber where the heating system was found contained fieldstones which served to store heat, typical of stone-chamber heating systems. After removing the stones, archaeologists were able to study the firing channel beneath.
Made up of ashlar blocks, the channel also revealed two pointed arches standing in their original position.
Additionally, eight closable openings were still carefully preserved. Warm air would exit through these openings, rising from the heating chamber into the dining hall once the smoke from lighting the fire had cleared.
After uncovering the chamber, the Archaeological Soil Research Basel-Stadt created a 3D model of the find for additional documentation in research. The find will be added to the Petersgraben 52 renovation project and be subject to further study down the line.
What is the Gnadental convent?
Gnadental convent was built outside the city wall for Franciscans around 1231, later becoming a temporary home for several orders while their own convents were built inside the city or before they left.
Some 20 years after construction, the Franciscans moved from Gnadental convent to the newer Barfüsser Monastery, founded in what is now Barfüsserplatz. From then on, the older convent buildings housed several women's orders, including the Cistercian nuns and the Order of Poor Clares.
In 1279, lay sisters from Gnadenthal near Niederwil (AG) moved in, after whom the convent received its name. They were incorporated into the Poor Clares and lived there until the Reformation and the dissolution of the convent.
After the convent was abandoned, the buildings continued to be partially used. In 1573, building materials were taken from the convent to be reused into a granary.
Watercolor paintings done by Johann Jakob Schneider from the 19th century still depict the older convent buildings. However, towards the end of the 19th century, the granary was demolished to make way for a vocational school at the site.

Nepali authorities urged villagers on Sunday to move to safer places after a flood in a river in the central part of the country swept away several houses and infrastructure, but there were no reports of any casualties.
Two women and three men were out of contact, the national disaster authority said. The army said a further 49 people, including a foreigner, had been rescued. They did not give the person's nationality.
A landslide in Chumnubri village in Gorkha district, about 100 km (62 miles) west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, leading to downstream flooding, authorities said.
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing.
"We have asked villagers living along the river banks downstream to evacuate and remain safe," said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, the Gorkha district's most senior bureaucrat.
The flood swept away about a dozen houses and two suspension bridges and damaged a hydroelectric project camp, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.
The flooded river carrying muddy sludge was rising and had washed away a highway bridge connecting Gorkha with the neighboring Dhading district, said Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the Authority.
Authorities alert citizens about flood
National disaster authorities alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood.
"Please help ensure that people in at-risk areas are moved to safe locations in time and assist search and rescue operations as needed," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in a social media post.
Officials said army and police rescue personnel had reached the area and were also monitoring the situation from a helicopter.
