Lebanon ports join IMEC, but can they compete with Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:42:13 UTC
22:42:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Beirut and Tripoli join IMEC Ports Club: Can they compete in regional trade?
The ports of Beirut and Tripoli have joined a network linked to the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), giving Lebanon a potential foothold in regional trade while raising questions over whether the crisis-hit country has the infrastructure and connectivity to compete with hubs such as Israel’s Haifa port.
The administrations of the Port of Beirut and Port of Tripoli signed a joint declaration in New Delhi on 6 October to join the IMEC Ports Club, launched the same day.
"The participation of Beirut and Tripoli in the IMEC Ports Club places Lebanon inside the conversation, as a new trade architecture linking India, the Middle East and Europe is being shaped," Lebanon’s Public Works and Transport Minister Fayez Rasamny told The New Arab.
He said the aim was to turn the two ports into gateways for transit, logistics and regional trade by connecting them to inland transport networks, border crossings and markets beyond Lebanon.
"That is where the real economic value is created: in cargo movement, storage, logistics services, investment and jobs," Rasamny said, pointing to plans for a logistics corridor linking Beirut with the Bekaa Valley and the Syrian border to the east, as well as a proposed railway connecting Tripoli with Abboudieh in northern Lebanon.
"Geography gives us an advantage; connectivity is what will turn that advantage into economic power."
However, joining the Ports Club does not mean Lebanon has formally become a signatory to the original IMEC framework announced in 2023, nor does it guarantee that the corridor’s main route will pass through the country.
Rasamny said the club nevertheless offered Lebanese ports a platform to build partnerships, improve supply-chain and digital connectivity, and position themselves to attract future trade flows.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the inclusion of Beirut and Tripoli, describing it as a major achievement that had not received the media attention it deserved, had even been met with scepticism.
Israel, with which Lebanon has no formal diplomatic relations and is still at war with, is part of IMEC’s original framework. Haifa port – its largest – is expected to play a role in the proposed corridor, placing the two Lebanese ports’ potential involvement in a wider network that also includes Israel.
'It depends on connectivity'
The prospect of Lebanon playing a role in the network raises questions about whether its ports could compete with Haifa for shipping and logistics business, or instead serve complementary routes and markets.
Recent figures point to significant activity at Lebanon’s ports, although the picture is mixed. Beirut handled around 6.4 million tonnes of freight in 2025, an increase of 18.4 percent on the previous year, while container throughput reached approximately 944,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs).
In September 2026, Beirut received three large container ships in a single day, including a 366-metre vessel. Yet total freight volumes fell by 10.1 percent year on year in the first seven months of 2026, even as container throughput continued to rise.
Tripoli has also demonstrated its ability to accommodate larger vessels. In June, it received the CMA CGM Eugénie, a container ship more than 360 metres long with capacity for around 15,000 TEUs, reported to be the largest container ship ever to dock at the port.
But the milestone has not translated into an overall increase in freight activity. Tripoli handled 674,000 tonnes of freight in the first five months of 2026, down 32.1 percent year on year, according to Credit Libanais.
The figures highlight the distinction between being able to accommodate large ships and attracting sustained cargo traffic.
Yeghia Tashjian, regional and international affairs cluster coordinator at the Issam Fares Institute for Public Policy and International Affairs at the American University of Beirut, told The New Arab that Lebanon’s inclusion was meaningful, but "more modest than some headlines suggest."
The Ports Club, he said, is "an open platform for port-to-port dialogue and cooperation" rather than a new institutional structure, making Lebanon’s participation "a foothold rather than state-level membership" of IMEC.
Tashjian said Lebanon could realistically seek to become a "secondary Mediterranean transshipment and logistics node," rather than a central land bridge within the corridor.
Beirut and Tripoli could compete with Haifa for some cargo and logistics activity, but joining the club does not mean they will automatically handle the same routes or markets. Their ability to attract business will depend on whether they can offer shippers commercially viable services and reliable connections to destinations beyond Lebanon.
Tripoli could have a particular role because of its proximity to Syria, Tashjian said. If cross-border routes reopen and Syria becomes stable enough to support trade towards Iraq and the Gulf, the northern port could become a link between maritime shipping and regional markets.
But this would require substantial improvements to Lebanon’s transport infrastructure. Tashjian highlighted the lack of adequate connections between ports and inland markets, including the need for north-south rail links to move goods through Syria and onwards to Iraq, Jordan and beyond.
The proposed Tripoli–Abboudieh railway and Beirut’s planned logistics corridor could help address those gaps, but their potential depends on implementation and the development of reliable cross-border routes.
Geopolitical obstacles
Lebanon also faces broader obstacles to attracting investment and cargo. The Port of Beirut continues to bear the legacy of the devastating 2020 explosion, while the country’s fiscal and institutional difficulties and recurring regional conflict risk making shipping companies and investors cautious.
Security and political developments in Syria will also be critical. Without reliable overland connections to regional markets, Lebanon’s ports may struggle to attract the cargo volumes needed to establish themselves as logistics hubs, regardless of their ability to receive larger vessels.
There are also geopolitical complications. Lebanon’s participation in a network that includes Israel does not itself amount to normalisation or formal cooperation between the two countries. But with Haifa part of IMEC’s original plans, Beirut and Tripoli will need to establish what distinct commercial role they can play within the wider network.
The eastern Mediterranean is already the focus of competing efforts to strengthen trade and transport links, with countries including Cyprus, Greece and Egypt seeking to consolidate their positions. Lebanon’s participation in the Ports Club could also feed into wider domestic debate over its engagement with other infrastructure initiatives, including China’s Belt and Road Initiative, IMEC’s main rival.
Ultimately, joining the IMEC Ports Club gives Beirut and Tripoli a platform to develop partnerships and seek a greater role in regional trade. Whether that translates into new investment, jobs and cargo flows will depend less on the declaration itself than on Lebanon’s ability to deliver infrastructure projects, strengthen cross-border connections and provide the stability and governance needed to attract long-term commercial interest.

Creating a ghost town: Lives in limbo behind Israeli gates and checkpoints
Israeli restrictions in Hebron have made life for Palestinians from the city a daily ordeal.
Hebron, occupied West Bank – Badr al-Tamimi, 60, lives in Hebron’s Old City, where Israeli checkpoints, iron gates and road closures turn the simplest tasks into a dispiriting daily ordeal for Palestinian residents.
The situation goes beyond mere restrictions on movement. Israel has created a ghost town in parts of Hebron, where residents feel they are being driven out. This is most pronounced in an area known as H2, where Israel has complete control and Palestinians are subject to the dictates of the military.
A few days ago, Israeli authorities installed three iron gates across a 200-metre (656-foot) stretch of Hebron’s Old City – amounting to just 0.2 dunams (200 square metres) – as part of Israel’s apparent attempts to restrict Palestinians’ freedom to move around the city.
Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Al Jazeera that one gate was erected on al-Zahid Road, the only route accessible to vehicles reaching the Old City entrance. A second was placed at the start of al-Shalala Street, which leads to shops connecting to the Bab al-Zawiya area in the city centre. A third towers over another section of al-Shalala Street, a thoroughfare used by pedestrians to access the shopping area.
They are part of a wider web of travel restrictions across the occupied West Bank, but Hebron, which has a strong settler presence, has suffered more than most Palestinian cities.
Approximately 40 percent of the 89 checkpoints in the West Bank and 11 percent of all 925 movement obstacles are located in the H2 area of Hebron, which is under tight Israeli control, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
About 7,000 Palestinians in an area of Hebron where hundreds of settlers live are affected by the latest travel restrictions. Since October 2023, when the genocidal war on Gaza began, only Palestinians with specific identification numbers could enter this area. Checkpoints at the entrance to this zone are generally only open from 7am to 8pm.
Al-Tamimi, who lives in the al-Sheikh neighbourhood adjacent to the city’s famed Ibrahimi Mosque, owns a shop in the Old City.
Palestinians can be kept waiting for hours at the checkpoints, and the mood of a soldier manning one can decide the commute time of a Palestinian. Worshippers attempting to enter the Ibrahimi Mosque can be held up for hours by soldiers.
“They might allow a limited number of people to enter while others are forced to wait, whereas resident movement comes to a halt during incursions, Jewish holidays, and the associated security measures,” he added.
Repeated closures have paralysed economic activity in Hebron, making it increasingly difficult for shops and companies to do business.
“Our presence in the Old City is a matter of steadfastness, not the availability of the elements needed for economic life,” al-Tamimi said.
Even after Israel’s occupation of the city in 1967, Hebron was once a bustling city with lively shops and markets. Residents could move more freely between neighbourhoods, which helped with economic life in the city.
Things changed in 1994, the year of the Ibrahimi Mosque massacre, when a US-born Israeli settler murdered 29 Palestinian worshippers.
From that point, the Old City’s geography changed, becoming isolated from its surroundings, al-Tamimi said.
He points to Shuhada Street, once a vital artery for transport and commerce in the city before road closures and restrictions transformed the area’s reality.
“They committed the crime, yet they continue to punish us for it,” he said.
In 1997, the Hebron Protocol was signed between the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) and Israel, dividing the city into two zones: H1, which was under relative Palestinian jurisdiction, and H2 – an area which includes the Old City, the Ibrahimi Mosque, and illegal settlements – remained under Israeli security control.
Issa Amro, coordinator of the Youth Against Settlements group, said Israeli prohibitions intensified with the outbreak of the second Intifada in 2000 when Hebron became a centre of the uprising.
During this period, vast areas of the city were sealed off, shops were forced to close, and residents often remained confined to their homes or neighbourhoods.
Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, the number of checkpoints has risen to 32, while other obstacles impeding Palestinian movement now exceed 130.
The “closed zones”, designated by Israeli authorities as areas of military activity with restricted access to Palestinians, have expanded around the Ibrahimi Mosque and the illegal settlements that lie in the heart of the city.
“The movement restrictions are effectively holding residents as hostages,” Amro said.
Mayor al-Jabari said approximately 10,000 Palestinians in the Old City and the surrounding closed zones are affected by these measures.
Some parts of Hebron are inaccessible to vehicles, and Palestinian residents are subject to curfews two or three days a week, usually over the weekend.
He believes these restrictions are aimed at hindering Palestinians’ ability to return home and stifle life in parts of Hebron.
Meanwhile, Israeli authorities have helped settlers expand in the area, imposing a new suffocating reality for Palestinians in the city.
Al-Jabari said Israel’s current government could be doing this to curry favour with settlers ahead of this month’s election.
Control of Hebron, its Old City, and the Ibrahimi Mosque is a key issue for settlers, and politicians in this group occupy key posts in the Israeli government.
This has coincided with a concerted effort by Israeli authorities to cement the settler presence in and around the city.
“The seizure of buildings and land, along with the installation of gates, is a continuation of Israeli policies that have been in place for decades,” al-Jabari said.
“These include the closure of Shuhada Street and the shutting down of over 500 shops, as well as the establishment of settlement outposts and military positions within the Old City.”
He has seen more restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement over the past month, measures that will undoubtedly appease settlers.
Hebron municipality has responded to this by filing lawsuits in Israeli courts, despite its scepticism about the impartiality of the judiciary.
With these measures continuing, life for Palestinians is getting worse, making work, life and education a daily struggle.
Israel cites the security situation as a pretext for erecting more checkpoints and iron gates in Hebron, but there are no such restrictions on settlers.
Since 2015, Israel has limited the number of Palestinian residents of closed zones who can pass through these checkpoints. Students and teachers frequently have their bags searched by Israeli soldiers or are detained.
Ayat al-Jabari, a 40-year-old science teacher, worked for a year at Qurtuba School, located near the closed Shuhada Street, before transferring to her current position at Al-Fayha School, near the Ibrahimi Mosque.
Although reaching Qurtuba School from her home should have been a five-minute journey, it often took an hour.
On her unsettling morning route through a nearby cemetery, often in darkness during the winter months, settlers and soldiers often appear in the graveyard to block the path of Palestinians or abuse them.
“Every day, I was forced to take a long route and walk through a cemetery to avoid passing the checkpoint, as I don’t hold a [special identification card] number. Even those who do hold numbers are sometimes forced to take this path to escape the soldiers’ moods,” she said.
After moving to Al-Fayha School, al-Jabari hoped her commute would improve, but the situation is no better than before.
“Whenever Jewish holidays arrive, these schools are closed because all the students live in areas subjected to a total lockdown, to the point where residents are even forbidden from opening their front doors,” she said.

IDF advances Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, Palestinian reports say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:40:22 UTC
22:40:22 KST

According to reports from Gaza, IDF forces operating in the Gaza Strip have pushed the Yellow Line forward by dozens of meters. Three years after the October 7 massacre, the IDF controls approximately 64% of the Gaza Strip, with two divisions deployed across a broad area and about 30 military outposts.
Israeli defense officials say the military's defensive lines have been completely overhauled since the massacre and the failures that preceded it. Pushing the Yellow Line forward serves several operational purposes. It allows the IDF to improve its operational control in areas where it detects significant Hamas efforts to regroup or indications that terrorists intend to carry out attacks or launch terrorist operations from those locations.
"Even if Hamas tries to do something, it will encounter IDF forces positioned on the front line. Our defense does not begin at the border fence but deeper inside the territory," a senior defense official told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth.
Since October 7, holding territory has become a cornerstone of the IDF's offensive defense strategy across most fronts, particularly in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon. The idea is not to wait for the enemy to reach Israeli communities but to establish a buffer zone where threats can be identified, intercepted and confronted before they reach populated areas.
The IDF did not always embrace this approach. For years leading up to October 7, 2023, Israel's defense doctrine was built around intelligence and technological superiority. Oct. 7 exposed the limitations of a doctrine focused primarily on preventing surprise attacks. The failure went deeper than the lack of an intelligence warning and the inability to prevent the surprise assault: The IDF was not prepared to fight such an attack once it was underway. That lesson is now being applied in different ways across all fronts.
In Gaza, the IDF has shifted from a defense strategy centered on defending the border to one focused on shaping the territory beyond it. The military controls key routes, operates outposts and forward positions and continues efforts to locate and dismantle underground infrastructure in areas under its control.
This marks a dramatic departure from the defense doctrine that prevailed before the massacre, when the military's instructions were to defend the border and enter Gaza when necessary. The question today is not simply how much territory the IDF holds, but how long it can maintain control, at what cost and with how many troops.
The military is pursuing a similar approach on other fronts, including Lebanon and Syria. The lesson drawn from the failures of three years ago is the need to establish defensive depth and maintain a presence on the ground, creating a security buffer of roughly 10 kilometers (6 miles), while conducting operations aimed at pushing threats farther away and preventing hostile forces from reestablishing themselves.
This new defense strategy also requires a larger deployment of forces. Some 40,000 reservists have been added to the military's personnel roster since the start of the war, tens of thousands of reservists have been reassigned, approximately 30 battalions have been added to the military's operational force structure and mandatory military service has been extended to 32 months.
New formations have been established, additional battalions and rapid-response units have been created and drone and remotely piloted aircraft capabilities have been expanded. Intelligence-gathering and firepower capabilities have also been strengthened, while new formations have been established to provide greater military strength within each operational sector.
Beyond the operational costs, holding territory also carries a price on the international stage. Israel is already facing U.S. pressure to withdraw from areas it captured in southern Lebanon. The IDF's new strategy is also hampering normalization with Arab countries, which are increasingly alarmed by what they perceive as a "plot to expand Israeli territory at their expense."

Hurricane &quot;Isaias&quot; claimed the lives of four people in the United States, leaving hundreds of thousands without power

Hurricane "Isaias" claimed the lives of four people in the United States, leaving hundreds of thousands without power
Kyiv • UNN
Hurricane “Isaias” claimed at least four lives in Florida and Alabama. The storm also left hundreds of thousands of customers without power and halted some oil and gas production.
At least four people were killed as a result of the powerful Hurricane "Isaias," which struck the southeastern coast of the United States. UNN reports this, citing Reuters and the Associated Press.
The storm caused widespread destruction and left hundreds of thousands of consumers without electricity. The states of Florida and Alabama were hit hardest.
Details
Hurricane "Isaias" reached the U.S. coast on the night of October 10 near the city of Destin, Florida. At the time it made landfall, it was a Category 2 storm on the Saffir–Simpson scale, with sustained winds reaching 169 km/h.
According to local authorities, the storm claimed the lives of at least four people. Two were killed when trees fell onto residential buildings in Florida and Alabama. Another man died of carbon monoxide poisoning after a generator was used in a garage. The fourth death was linked to a traffic accident caused by a tree that had fallen onto a road.
According to the monitoring service PowerOutage.us, as of midday on October 10, about 670,000 consumers in four states remained without electricity. In particular, approximately 420,000 consumers were without power in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia, and 17,000 in Mississippi. Meanwhile, according to updated information from the Associated Press, about 396,000 consumers in northwestern Florida and southern Alabama remained without power on the morning of October 11.
Strong winds knocked down trees and damaged power lines, the roofs of residential buildings, and infrastructure facilities. In the city of Pensacola, the hurricane damaged a hotel and the local airport. Commercial flights were temporarily suspended due to the storm's aftermath. Some communities experienced problems with drinking-water supplies. Authorities also reported flooded roads and damage to transportation infrastructure. About 16,000 utility workers were prepared to restore power in Florida.
How the hurricane affected oil and gas production
The storm also had a significant impact on the operations of the U.S. oil and gas industry. According to the relevant U.S. federal agency, as of October 10, about 69% of oil production and 57% of natural-gas production in the Gulf of Mexico had been suspended. Personnel were evacuated from 113 offshore production platforms. Shell and Chevron began gradually returning workers to facilities to resume production.
Amid disruptions to energy supplies, the U.S. Department of Energy authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of oil from the country's Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
The threat of flooding remains
After making landfall, "Isaias" gradually lost strength and weakened into a post-tropical cyclone. However, U.S. meteorologists warn that hazardous weather conditions will persist in a number of regions. In particular, the hurricane's remnants are moving toward the Appalachians and the Mid-Atlantic states, where heavy rain, localized flash floods, and gusty winds are forecast.
U.S. President Donald Trump approved federal emergency declarations for Florida, Alabama, and Georgia. This will make it possible to mobilize additional resources to deal with the consequences of the natural disaster.
It should be noted that "Isaias" became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, which was characterized by unusually low storm activity.

From ancient clay to living tradition: the enduring art of Iranian pottery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:36:09 UTC
22:36:09 KST

From ancient clay to living tradition: the enduring art of Iranian pottery
TEHRAN - Pottery is among the oldest forms of human craftsmanship, transforming ordinary clay into vessels and objects of practical use and artistic expression.
In Iran, this ancient art has evolved over thousands of years, reflecting the country's changing civilizations, cultural exchanges and artistic traditions. From prehistoric earthenware to elaborately decorated ceramics of the Islamic period, Iranian pottery offers a glimpse into the country's long history of innovation and craftsmanship.
The craft involves shaping clay by hand or on a potter's wheel, followed by drying and firing. Depending on the raw materials, techniques and intended use, finished pieces may retain the natural colors of the clay or receive decorative coatings and glazes. Across Iran, potters have developed distinctive styles, forms and motifs, creating a diverse tradition that remains alive in several parts of the country.
Although the precise beginnings of pottery in Iran remain uncertain, archaeological evidence places its origins in prehistoric times, possibly as early as the eighth to fifth millennia BC. Regions including Gilan, Kordestan and Sistan-Baluchestan have played important roles in the development of the craft. The emergence of painted pottery on the Iranian Plateau also demonstrates how early communities combined practical skills with an increasingly sophisticated sense of design.
During the Achaemenid period (c. 550–330 BC), pottery production developed alongside other artistic traditions. Vessels took on varied shapes, while rhytons, drinking vessels often fashioned in animal forms, became part of the broader repertoire of ancient Iranian craftsmanship.
Pottery continued to develop during the Parthian period (247 BC–224 CE), when different production techniques and decorative styles circulated across a vast geographical area. Excavations at the Anahita Temple in Kangavar, western Iran, have yielded evidence of both unglazed vessels and glazed pottery. The latter included pieces with red, gray and greenish finishes, reflecting the range of materials and techniques available to potters of the time.
Under the Sassanids (224–651), pottery makers produced bowls, jars, jugs, figurines and animal-shaped objects. Some vessels featured geometric and vegetal patterns, carved designs and raised decorations. Others carried inscriptions in Middle Persian, also known as Pahlavi. Glazed pieces decorated with fish and animal motifs were among the characteristic products of the period.
Sassanid artistic conventions also influenced pottery produced in subsequent centuries. Winged animals, mythical birds, arabesque-like patterns and the Sassanid eagle became part of a visual vocabulary that continued into the Islamic period. Some later ceramics decorated with motifs associated with pre-Islamic Iran became known as Gabri ware, a historical term used for certain types of pottery. Examples of pottery from different periods are preserved in the National Museum of Iran.
The arrival of Islam brought further changes, as potters adapted earlier decorative traditions and experimented with new techniques. Iranian ceramic production reached a notable level of technical sophistication during the Seljuk period (11th–13th centuries), often regarded as a golden age of Persian ceramics. Craftspeople employed methods including incising, relief decoration, pierced designs, painting beneath or over glazes, gilding and enameling. These techniques enabled the production of vessels with intricate patterns and a wide range of finishes.
Ceramic production continued to evolve under the Safavids (1501–1736). Shah Abbas I encouraged artistic and commercial links with China, including efforts to develop Iranian porcelain production. Chinese ceramics influenced the tastes and practices of Iranian workshops, illustrating how pottery traditions developed through both local innovation and international exchange.
Over time, pottery became an established profession in many Iranian communities, with skills and techniques passed from one generation to the next. Despite the introduction of modern equipment and changing markets, some workshops continue to rely on traditional methods, preserving distinctive regional practices.
One notable example is Kalporgan village in Sistan-Baluchestan, where pottery-making traditions are often associated with techniques believed to have ancient roots. Women potters in the village are particularly known for shaping vessels by hand without using a conventional potter's wheel, while distinctive geometric designs are applied to the surfaces. The resulting earthenware reflects a close relationship between local materials, inherited knowledge and everyday life.
Other important centers include Lalejin in Hamadan province, widely recognized for its pottery and ceramics, as well as Shahreza in Isfahan province and communities in Gilan. Their products range from plain household vessels to colorful jugs, bowls and decorative objects sold in local markets and beyond.
For researchers, these regional traditions help connect archaeological discoveries with contemporary craftsmanship. Iranian pottery is more than a record of ancient domestic life: it is a continuing cultural practice in which materials, techniques and designs preserve memories of the past while adapting to the needs of the present.

‘A Hawaiian son’: Honolulu honours Sun Yat-sen as his landmarks vanish

Eddie Flores pressed the button at a pedestrian crossing on King Street, then pointed across the road.

“It’s no longer there,” said Flores, chairman of the restaurant chain L&L Hawaiian Barbecue. “But we can more or less point out where the building is.”

Trump's diesel deal with Putin: How much, how long, and will It cut prices?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:34:28 UTC
22:34:28 KST

Trump's diesel deal with Putin: How much, how long, and will It cut prices?
TEHRAN - On October 9, US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the US and global markets, paired with a temporary 6-month US sanctions waiver. The move is aimed at easing record-high US diesel prices weeks before the November 3 midterms. Initial volumes are modest relative to consumption, so analysts expect limited and mostly psychological price effects — unless larger follow-on deliveries materialize and Russian refineries recover.
What exactly was agreed?
Trump said the deal was reached in a phone call with Putin and described it as highly successful. In his words, "vast amounts" of fuel would flow, and he publicly thanked Putin.
Putin confirmed Russia's "readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and world markets."
Operationally, the agreement has two parts:
Physical volumes in phases, as outlined by Trump:
300,000+ tons immediately — roughly 2.25 million barrels
500,000 tons in November
1 million tons shortly after
3 million tons more "in a short period," conditional on the state of Russian refineries
Total nominal volume: over 4.8 million tons.
A legal window to deliver it. The US Treasury's OFAC issued a temporary general license allowing the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian-origin diesel. The authorization runs for about six months, until April 7, 2027, covering cargoes loaded during that window.
This is the largest fuel-related sanctions relaxation since the Ukraine war began in February 2022. Previous licenses in the context of the ongoing US-Iran conflict were typically 30-day extensions.
How big is this in market terms?
Put in context, the first shipments are small:
The US consumes about 3.6 to 3.8 million barrels of diesel per day and exports about 1.5 million barrels per day. The first 2.25-million-barrel tranche equals roughly half a day of US consumption.
Global diesel demand is around 30 million barrels per day. The early Russian volumes equal 72,000 to 124,000 barrels per day — a fraction of one percent.
The 800,000 tons expected by end-November equals about 6 million barrels, or less than two days of US use.
That is why most market analysts describe the deal as a redirection of existing flows rather than major new net supply: if Russian barrels go to the US, current buyers of Russian diesel must source from elsewhere, leaving global balances broadly unchanged.
Looking back: how did we get here?
US sanctions history: Since 2022, the US has banned imports of Russian oil and petroleum products and, together with allies, imposed price caps and shipping restrictions to limit Moscow's energy revenues.
Only three weeks before the diesel announcement, Trump signed a sweeping bipartisan sanctions law targeting Russia's oil and gas income. The new diesel license therefore represents a sharp, if temporary, reversal — a pause, not a repeal.
Russia's export position: Russia imposed its own restrictions on diesel exports in July after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged several refineries. The International Energy Agency has estimated Russian diesel output fell by about 30%.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow would begin lifting those restrictions ahead of schedule starting in October, adding that the domestic market remains "fully supplied." Russian officials have framed the US deal as a normal commercial operation that also helps stabilize world markets.
Why US diesel is at record levels: Two overlapping disruptions explain the price spike:
Refinery losses in Russia from the Ukraine war, reducing global diesel availability.
Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and Middle East refining amid the eight-month US-Iran conflict, which has raised freight, insurance and replacement costs.
The result: US average diesel hit a record $6.53 per gallon on September 22, easing only slightly to $6.28 by October 9, according to AAA. A year earlier it was about $3.68. Futures prices dipped modestly on the announcement, but pump prices did not move.
Trump had already tried domestic tools — including a proposed ban on diesel exports and authorization for off-road, tax-exempt diesel use — before turning to external supply.
Why now? The political calendar
The timing is inseparable from US domestic politics. The midterm elections are on November 3, with fuel prices and inflation ranking as voters' top economic concerns. Farm states such as Iowa have been hit particularly hard by diesel costs during harvest season.
Trump has stated the goal explicitly: lower costs for "farmers, ranchers and truckers" as his top priority. Supporters present the deal as pragmatic — using every available barrel to protect consumers. Critics in Congress, including Democrats Chuck Schumer, Jeanne Shaheen and Elizabeth Warren, as well as some Republicans such as Michael McCaul, argue it contradicts the intent of the sanctions law passed weeks earlier and provides revenue to Moscow while the Ukraine war continues.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a "weak decision" and a "gift to Putin."
Energy analysts, regardless of political view, converge on a narrower technical point: volumes are too small to transform prices, though they could shave the peak off futures and provide localized relief on the US East Coast — New York-New Jersey and Philadelphia — where Russian-origin cargoes would most plausibly land.
What happens next? Three scenarios
Base case — partial delivery, limited price impact:
Russia delivers the first 1.8 million tons (300k + 500k + 1m tons) while keeping the conditional 3 million tons under review. Global diesel futures ease modestly, US retail diesel falls by cents, not dollars. This is the consensus among analysts at Eurasia Group, CSIS and Columbia University.
Prerequisite: Russian refineries stabilize and Hormuz-related freight costs do not worsen.
Upside case — full delivery plus refinery recovery:
If all 4.8+ million tons arrive in November-December and Russian refineries return toward normal throughput, combined with a seasonal demand softening, US diesel could retreat more meaningfully from record highs. Even then, analysts note, prices would remain far above 2025 levels because Middle East refining and shipping constraints persist.
Downside case — logistics and politics interrupt flow:
Tanker availability, insurance disputes, port restrictions, Congressional pressure, or a new escalation in either Ukraine or the Gulf could delay or shrink deliveries — particularly the conditional 3 million tons. In that case, the price effect would be almost entirely symbolic, while the political controversy would remain.
The key variable to watch is not announcements but loadings: how many vessels actually load Russian diesel in October-November, where they discharge, and whether OFAC extends or narrows the license after April 2027.
Bottom line
The agreement opens a narrow, time-limited corridor in an otherwise sanctions-constrained relationship. Economically, it is best understood as a short-term buffer — potentially helpful at the margins, but not a structural fix for a diesel market strained by two conflicts at once. Politically, it signals that in an election season, energy prices can temporarily outweigh sanctions logic.
Whether drivers feel it at the pump will depend less on diplomacy and more on refineries, tankers and the Strait of Hormuz.

Flu season arrives earlier than usual in England, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:32:58 UTC
22:32:58 KST

Flu is striking earlier than usual in England, experts have said, insisting that vaccination is the best way to blunt its impact.
According to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), flu is at low levels, but various metrics, such as the proportion of positive tests and GP consultations for influenza-like illness, suggest it is on the rise, with the number of emergency-department attendances for influenza-like illness above seasonally expected levels.
“Flu activity throughout September has been higher than in the same period during all past four winter seasons,” UKHSA reported, adding that flu trends had been rising since August.
Prof Sir Andrew Pollard, the director of the Oxford Vaccine Group, said: “There is one simple action for all those who are at risk because of age or their underlying health conditions, which is to get vaccinated as soon as possible and before we reach the peak of transmission.
“Everyone can benefit from being vaccinated but free vaccines are only available for children and those in higher-risk groups.”
He added that those who were not eligible for a free flu vaccine via the NHS might be able to access them for free through their workplace, while vaccines were also available privately for anybody able to pay for them.
A private flu vaccination costs about £20 at most high street pharmacies, and some retailers offer them for under £10 as part of membership schemes.
Pollard said an earlier flu season did not necessarily mean a worse flu season. “We don’t know for certain why the timing varies each year.” He believed an early rise was due to a combination of factors, including the weather, the particular strain of the virus that is around and its ability to spread, the immunity of the population to the circulating strain, and aspects of behaviour – for example, the number of close contacts people have.
Antonia Ho, a professor of infectious diseases at the University of Glasgow’s Centre for Virus Research, said it was important to get vaccinated as soon as possible as it took a few weeks for the vaccine to provide full protection.
“An early rise in influenza cases may indicate a more intense influenza season overall, because earlier onset is associated with a longer period of community transmission and higher cumulative case numbers,” she said. “However, onset timing alone doesn’t determine severity.”
Data from UKHSA has suggested the increase in flu is being driven by cases among young people aged 18 to 24, and that a mix of two flu A subtypes – H1N1 and H3N2 – is circulating in England. “The flu vaccine covers both subtypes and also influenza B,” said Ho.
While UKHSA has noted that the H1N1 subtype of flu A appears to have changed or “drifted” a little from the strain that was used to make this year’s flu vaccine, Ho said it was too soon to say if that would affect how well the vaccine worked.
According to data from UKHSA, the vaccination programme in England last winter is estimated to have prevented about 100,000 hospital admissions and 7,000 deaths, despite the flu season again starting earlier than usual.
John Tregoning, a professor of vaccine immunology at Imperial College London and author of the book Infectious: Pathogens and How We Fight Them, said: “Last year is a good example where [we] also had an early start to the flu season, and then because of that, probably people slightly changed their behaviours and went and got vaccinated, and then it comes down again.”
Experts have urged those eligible for a Covid jab to get vaccinated, with UKHSA data suggesting levels of Covid are rising. Tregoning also emphasised the importance of vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
Ho said that while vaccination against respiratory diseases was important, there were additional measures people could take if they started to feel unwell.
“If you have flu-like symptoms, ideally stay at home, practice good hand hygiene, avoid contact with others,” she said.

Forgotten Safavid-era village discovered in southern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:30:50 UTC
22:30:50 KST

Forgotten Safavid-era village discovered in southern Iran
TEHRAN – Researchers have identified and documented the remains of an abandoned village believed to date back to the Safavid era in the Dasht-e Barm forest area of Kazerun county, Fars province, southwestern Iran.
The village, named Royin, had been deserted for years and was not mentioned in any of the accessible databases reviewed by researchers, according to Mohsen Abbaspour, a cultural heritage researcher and activist.
Speaking to ISNA, Abbaspour said the discovery emerged from a year-long research project examining historical settlements in the oak forests of Dasht-e Barm, which lie within the Arjan-Parishan Biosphere Reserve.
Researchers identified the village's name by studying inscriptions on gravestones in two historic cemeteries and collecting ethnographic information from neighboring villages. Some inscriptions included the name Royini as part of the names of people buried there.
The oldest legible gravestone documented so far records the death of a woman in Jumada al-Awwal 1110 AH, corresponding to the late Safavid period. Abbaspour said comparisons between the village's surviving houses and architectural patterns in other Safavid-era settlements in the Kuhmareh region of Fars also support the conclusion that Royin dates back at least to that period.
The research documented the remains of the residential area, two cemeteries situated on opposite sides of a seasonal river, and approximately 21 hectares of terraced gardens.
Based on comparisons with other historical villages in the region, researchers believe residents relied on livestock raising and cultivated fruit trees suited to the local climate, including figs, plums and walnuts.
Pottery fragments examined during the study further support the proposed dating and suggest that the settlement once sustained an active community. Residents used pottery with simple decorative finishes, along with stone tools, for everyday activities, Abbaspour said.
The research also examined the village's layout, place names, surviving architecture, energy sources and historic gravestones. The findings have been documented in a research paper.
Abbaspour expressed hope that efforts to register and introduce the village would encourage further academic research and attract visitors interested in Iran's historic rural settlements.
Dasht-e Barm lies about 30 kilometers north of Kazerun, along the road connecting the city to Shiraz. The forest area contains several other historical remains, including a caravanserai, sections of an ancient southern route, historic cemeteries, old mills and abandoned or historic villages.

Pentagon raises US-Iran war toll to 21 killed, over 800 wounded
The US Department of War has raised the death toll of US personnel in its war on Iran to 21 killed and 865 wounded in an acknowledgement that losses faced during the conflict were greater than previously admitted.
The Pentagon added two non-combatant deaths, including one Major who died in Kuwait on 6 March and a Navy suicide from September, according to The Washington Post.
The publication previously reported in September that the department's internal figures counted 23 service members as having died since the start of the war on 28 February.
The admission is a firm rebuttal of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who previously labelled the reporting of a higher death toll as “a complete lie", as well as a correction of previous reporting by the Pentagon, which has underreported the toll since the start of the war due to Trump's own claims that the war has ended.
In a bid to mark deaths in the region tied to continued war with Iran, the department created a new category for those killed after Trump’s declaration.
The Pentagon told The Post in a statement that, rather than correcting its own figures, it is making revisions to how it reports casualties.
The number of US casualties in its war on Iran have been contentious, with US media outlets revealing larger casualty figures than admitted to by the Pentagon throughout the war.
Despite US and Israeli airpower decapitating Iran's leadership and destroying vast swathes of Iranian military assets, Iran's quick response saw ballistic missiles and drones targeting US bases, alongside Iran's Gulf neighbours and Israel.
Iranian attacks on US bases have left the 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and Al Udeid Air Base, the largest US airbase in the region, severely damaged.
Iranian attacks also damaged or destroyed US radar used to track ballistic missiles and aircraft on the ground.
The extent of the damage has led the Department of War to mull pulling troops and withdrawing from bases in the Gulf.
However, in recent weeks, Trump ordered new plans to be drawn up for renewed strikes against Iran, as negotiatons between the two reach an impasse.

“Not a single radio-controlled platform passed the tests without being affected by our systems,” Phantom Defense told Militarnyi.

While specific drone models and competing manufacturers involved in the evaluations were not publicly disclosed, US evaluators invited Phantom Defense to participate in subsequent testing cycles and technical demonstrations under the program.
Streamhunter system
The company presented several electronic warfare configurations tailored for varied operational echelons during the US trials.
For fixed positions, the company demonstrated the Specter PRO, a directional and omnidirectional dome-type jamming complex engineered to protect platoon strongpoints, brigade command centers, and critical infrastructure installations from loitering munitions and tactical reconnaissance aircraft.
Interview: Georgian Conductor Nikoloz Rachveli on Music, Ukraine and Solidarity
For frontline tactical formations, Phantom Defense evaluated its compact mobile systems – including the Specter L, Specter X, and Specter XL.
These variants are designed for vehicle mounting and dismounted fire teams operating in electronically contested sectors near the forward edge of battle.
The trials also featured Streamhunter, a dedicated signal-interception system capable of capturing and decoding live video feeds transmitted by adversary drones. Data gathered by Streamhunter and the Specter jammers were fed into a unified C2 management system, which provided real-time situational awareness and automated jamming protocols.
Phantom Defense noted that testing inside the US took place under strict regulatory constraints on radio frequency emissions, which differed from the operational parameters encountered under electronic warfare conditions in Ukraine.
The manufacturer reported that its equipment has an established combat record in Ukraine, with company-tracked systems recording the detection of more than 11,000 reconnaissance and strike drones and confirming more than 7,000 video-verified neutralizations.
Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program
The evaluations form part of Gauntlet II, an assessment stage within the US Department of Defense’s $1 billion Drone Dominance program. The initiative aims to procure small unmanned aircraft and counter-drone systems over a two-year timeframe, with projected acquisitions exceeding 200,000 units through 2027.
The participation of Phantom Defense highlights expanding technical collaboration between the Ukrainian defense-industrial sector and the US armed forces.
In a related procurement under the Drone Dominance initiative, the US military ordered an additional 1,320 F10 combat strike drones from Ukrainian manufacturer F-Drones, extending the first commercial export of Ukrainian-produced strike drones to the Pentagon.
The contract followed an initial batch of 2,000 F10 drones shipped to US defense authorities in July under an official permit issued by Ukraine’s State Export Control Service.

Cultural officials reject Rubio’s remarks on Persian history at Athens’ Acropolis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:23:51 UTC

Cultural officials reject Rubio’s remarks on Persian history at Athens’ Acropolis
TEHRAN – Joining Iranian political officials, several senior cultural figures, including the tourism minister, the head of the Iranology Foundation and the director-general of the National Museum of Iran, have criticized US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s remarks on ancient Persian history, saying historical civilizations should not be used to justify political hostility or threats of war.
The reactions followed a speech Rubio delivered in Athens on October 7, in which he referred to the Greco-Persian Wars and the Persian army’s campaign against Athens in 480 BC. Speaking against the backdrop of the Acropolis, he said the forces of Persian king Xerxes had burned sanctuaries and destroyed parts of the ancient city.
In separate statements, the three Iranian officials challenged Rubio’s interpretation of history and emphasized Iran’s longstanding cultural and civilizational contributions.
Tourism Minister Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri said Iran should be addressed with respect as a living civilization and a great nation with an enduring place in world history.
In a statement issued late Friday, Salehi-Amiri said a nation’s identity could not be reduced to a single war, king or government, describing Iran as one of the world’s oldest continuous civilizations and a major contributor to the development of culture, knowledge, social order and coexistence.
“Iran cannot be defined by one war, one king or one government,” he said.
The minister also rejected the notion that Greek civilization belonged exclusively to the United States, pointing to the philosophical legacy of Socrates and Plato and their emphasis on justice, ethics and restraint.
“Greek civilization is not the exclusive property of the United States either,” Salehi-Amiri said.
He argued that political power was temporary compared with the historical memory and cultural identity of nations, adding that Iran had drawn strength from its civilizational heritage and the spirit of its people through periods of war, sanctions and what he described as historical distortion.
“Those who have considered themselves superior, unrivaled and entrusted with a historic mission have always overlooked one truth: powers come and go, but nations that stand firm on their memory, culture and identity endure,” he said.
Ali Akbar Salehi, head of the Iranology Foundation and a former Iranian foreign minister, also responded to Rubio’s remarks, drawing attention to repeated threats by US President Donald Trump to destroy a civilization.
“Secretary Rubio, the land of Cyrus the Great, who freed captives and respected the followers of other faiths, is not an enemy of civilization,” Salehi wrote.
“Now that you spoke of civilization, what is your opinion on Trump's threats, who repeatedly threatened to destroy a civilization and return it to the Stone Age?” he asked.
Salehi’s remarks invoked Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire, whose rule is widely associated with the history of ancient Persia and its imperial policies toward conquered peoples.
Jebrael Nokandeh, director general of the National Museum of Iran, focused on the use of heritage sites in political discourse, saying the Acropolis and other properties inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List should serve as places of peace and coexistence rather than platforms for hostility.
“The Acropolis of Athens and all sites inscribed on the World Heritage List are realms of peace and peaceful coexistence for all the people of the world; they are not platforms for hate speech or the justification of warmongering,” Nokandeh said.
Addressing Rubio directly, he urged the US official to respect the significance of World Heritage sites and refrain from using them to justify confrontational policies or issue threats against Iran.
Nokandeh also criticized what he described as politically motivated interpretations of history, arguing that historical accounts should be grounded in scholarship and expertise rather than political objectives.
“History cannot be manipulated to suit political whims through personal and non-expert interpretations,” he said, adding that the study and narration of history required knowledge, expertise and integrity.
He further said Iran’s Persian civilization had made contributions to human history that could not be diminished by political rhetoric, noting that its significance was well established among scholars and experts worldwide.
Rubio’s speech drew parallels between the ancient Greco-Persian Wars and contemporary challenges facing the West, presenting the United States as the successor to the ancient Western civilization associated with Greece.
His remarks have prompted criticism in Iranian political and cultural circles, where officials have challenged the use of ancient conflicts to frame present-day relations and have called for greater respect for Iran’s historical identity and cultural heritage.

Dengue death toll tops 300 mark in Bangladesh as infections near 100,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:23:33 UTC
22:23:33 KST

Dengue-related deaths in Bangladesh rose to 303 since January this year, as health authorities reported four more fatalities across the country and nearly 2,200 new hospitalisations.
With the latest admissions, the total dengue caseload stood at 99,275, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) on Sunday.
October has recorded 58 deaths so far, while September saw 148.
Of the total hospitalised patients, 92,803 have been discharged after recovery.
Bangladesh usually experiences its dengue season between June and September.
The mosquito-borne disease has shown a sharp rise in infections and related deaths compared with the corresponding period last year.
There were 225 deaths and 53,606 dengue cases recorded by health authorities in the corresponding period of 2025, according to DGHS data.
Infected mosquitoes transmit dengue to humans through bites. There is no specific treatment for the viral infection.
The South Asian nation of 175 million recorded its highest-ever annual number of dengue deaths in 2022, when 281 people died.
Meanwhile, health authorities also reported seven more deaths involving measles-like symptoms and over 1,200 new infections.
The total number of deaths linked to measles infections rose to 1,162 since mid-March. Of these, 104 have been confirmed as measles deaths.
Symptomatic measles cases reached 205,028, while confirmed cases stood at 22,421.
The health ministry has immunised around 20 million children in response to the outbreak, in addition to routine vaccinations and a catch-up campaign launched in late September.

He warned that the students’ future must not be used as “a bargaining chip” in migration negotiations.
“I am sincerely saddened for these 13 young adults,” Prevot added.

At least 139 migrants dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:22:12 UTC
22:22:12 KST

The UN's IOM agency says tens of thousands of migrants travel from the Horn of Africa through Djibouti each year as they look to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and eventually reach the Gulf countries.
At least 139 migrants died after a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti earlier this week, the UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday, with 84 others still missing.
The vessel had been carrying 305 people from Djibouti to Yemen when it sank near Guhere, north of the town of Obock, per the IOM. The incident occurred on the night of 8 to 9 October.
The death toll climbed from 109 after 30 more bodies were recovered. Among the 109 bodies initially recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women, and 15 were children, including nine girls and six boys, the IOM said in an earlier statement, adding that more than 80 people had survived the shipwreck - all Ethiopian nationals.
"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” Alexandre Coissac, the IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said. "Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance. This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."
Search and rescue operations are ongoing, and the IOM and local authorities are providing assistance to survivors.
According to the IOM, tens of thousands of migrants travel from the Horn of Africa through Djibouti each year as they look to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and eventually reach the Gulf countries.
"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," the IOM said.
In March, another shipwreck off the coast of Djibouti left nine migrants dead and 45 others missing as they attempted to make the crossing to Yemen.
"Since 10 September, more than 20,000 incoming movements to Djibouti from Ethiopia have been observed by IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix," the IOM added on Sunday.

Russia to cut spending in real terms but boost defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:19:07 BST
22:19:07 KST

Russia has allocated 17.1 trillion roubles to national defence in its draft budget for 2027, around 35 per cent of all federal government spending, while planning a real terms reduction in overall spending, according to the latest Defence Intelligence update on the war in Ukraine.
The assessment, published on Friday, said: “Russia’s spending plans for 2027 almost certainly represent a real-terms reduction compared to 2026. But military spending is set to increase. On 30 September 2026, the Russian government submitted its proposed 2027 budget to the Duma (the lower house of the state legislature). Compared with updated expected spending for 2026, the plan forecasts a nominal spending increase of 0.5 per cent, well short of inflation, which the Bank of Russia estimates at 6.3 per cent. Spending on education, healthcare, and social policy are all highly likely set to decrease by between 6 and 7 per cent compared to 2026 in nominal terms.”
“The draft 2027 budget allocates 17.1 trillion rubles (USD $202.6 bn) towards national defence, which is around 35 per cent of total federal government spending. This is a 40 per cent increase compared to what was initially planned in 2026. However, Russia will almost certainly overspend on defence by at least 4-5 trillion rubles (USD $47-59 bn) in 2026 (included in updated 2026 total spending plans). As a result, the actual increase in defence spending will almost certainly not be as high as 40 per cent.”
“The 2027 budget forecasts that the budget will be less reliant on oil revenues than in previous years. Oil revenues are forecast to amount to 16 per cent of total federal revenues in 2027 compared with 22 per cent in 2026. This change is down to a reduction in the oil-price threshold at which Russia saves additional revenues into its National Wealth fund: USD $50 per barrel in 2027 down from USD $59 per barrel in 2026.”
Defence Intelligence writes its assessments against a published probability yardstick, in which “almost certainly” carries a 95 per cent or greater likelihood and “highly likely” sits between 80 and 90 per cent.

Ukrainian drones hit Yandex, third data centre targeted
Overnight into Sunday, Ukrainian drones attacked Russian technology giant Yandex's data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow in the third reported attack on the firm in days.
The company said the centre's infrastructure had been damaged and its operations completely halted. According to the latest information, there were no casualties in the attack.
Yandex added that it is continuing to assess the state of the infrastructure and cannot yet say how long repairs will take. This is already the company's third data centre to be attacked in October.
Yandex, often dubbed "Russia's Google", runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as food-ordering and taxi apps used by tens of millions of people.
Governor Aleksandr Avdeyev confirmed (source in Russian) the UAV attack in Vladimir and the ensuing fire. He said residential areas had escaped destruction. Residents of the houses closest to the attack site have begun to be evacuated.
In Vladimir, two substations supplying electricity to 5,000 residents were switched off. An hour later, the governor said that 80% of the power supply had been restored and heating and water supplies were back to normal.
Preliminary reports suggest that a supercomputer housed at the Vladimir data centre was damaged. An identical machine is located at the Yandex data centre in Ryazan that was also targeted.
Taxi and navigation disruption
In the wake of the attack, users experienced widespread disruptions to the company's services. People were unable to order taxis in Moscow, St. Petersburg, Perm, Krasnoyarsk, Vladivostok, Ulan-Ude, Yekaterinburg and other Russian cities.
"I can't get anything to work at all", said Yevgeny, a 69-year-old sitting behind the wheel of a Yandex-branded taxi near Moscow.
"I've never seen anything like this before. It hasn't happened in the last five years. Now I don't know what to do", he said.
Similar problems were reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia. Drivers say they cannot log into the app or are facing navigation failures, while passengers see no available cars. There have also been reports of outages across many of the company's other services.
On 9 October, drones attacked (source in Russian) Yandex's data centre in Kaluga. On the morning of 8 October, the Ukrainian armed forces struck (source in Russian) a Yandex data centre near Ryazan. The Civic Democrats, the largest opposition party in the lower house, performed poorly.

Five candidates secured more than 50% of the vote in Saturday’s Czech Senate elections, winning their seats in the upper house without the need for a runoff next weekend.
They include Grolich of the Christian Democrats, Jan Grulich of TOP 09, Jan Sobotka of the Mayors and Independents, Tomas Fiala of Our Czechia, and Zbynek Linhart of the Mayors and Independents, who won by a wide margin.
Among candidates advancing to the second round of voting for one-third of the Senate’s 81 seats, the Mayors and Independents and ANO each secured 13 places, while the Civic Democrats won nine, with around 90% of votes counted.
Christian Democrats wins most seats in municipal elections
Christian Democrats were the most successful party in municipal elections with nearly 2,000 councillors elected. It was followed by the Mayors and Independents, government leaders ANO and the Civic Democrats, according to Radio Prague.
Turnout at national level was reported to stand at 47%.
In the capital Prague, the Mayors and Independents came first with 23% of the vote. They came just ahead of Together for Prague, an alliance of the Civic Democrats and TOP 09, that secured 22%.
Prague Together came in third with 18%, while ANO came fourth in the capital with 14%.
Petr Hlavacek, the electoral leader of the Mayors and Independents in Prague, ruled out forming a city government with ANO, saying his party would hold talks with Together for Prague, Prague Together and the Pirates in the coming days.
ANO came first in six of 13 regional capitals.
The outcome of the municipal elections is expected to become clearer once local governing coalitions are formed, while the final composition of the Senate will be determined after next weekend's runoff elections.
Nearly 190,000 candidates competed for around 62,000 seats on local councils, while 154 candidates contested 27 seats in the upper house of parliament.

Saudi's civil aviation authority said the latest Riyadh airport attack caused injuries and that damage assessments are underway.
There were no immediate details about the latest strike at King Khalid Airport, which hit the same complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights.
Saturday's strike at the airport, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.
The airport remains closed on Sunday and Saudi Arabia moved Riyadh schools online amid the Houthis' latest threat. Flights were diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the U.S., Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
Earlier on Saturday, the Houthies threatened new attacks on the kingdom's airports, except for the holy sites of Mecca and Medina, warning passengers not to travel.
"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," Saree wrote on X.
He urged "everyone to take our warnings seriously."
On Sunday, the Houthis said the airport under their control in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again. They blamed the Saudis but provided no details.
The attack on Riyadh's airport on Saturday drew condemnation from the United Nations and world leaders, including President Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks by Iran's proxies are "pushing the region into a spiral of violence."
"They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes," she wrote on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday condemned "in the strongest possible terms" the attack on King Khalid Airport and extended his condolences.
"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve," he said in a statement shared on X. "Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East—one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, cooperation, and prosperity for all the peoples of our region.
The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the 309 people injured, some in serious condition.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.

Dengue deaths surpass 300 in Bangladesh as infections near 100,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:12:12 UTC
22:12:12 KST

SM Najmus Sakib
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
Dengue-related deaths in Bangladesh rose to 303 since January this year as health authorities on Sunday reported four more fatalities across the country and nearly 2,200 new hospitalizations.
With the latest admissions, the total dengue caseload stood at 99,275, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
October has recorded 58 deaths so far, while September saw 148.
Of the total hospitalized patients, 92,803 have been discharged after recovery.
Bangladesh usually experiences its dengue season between June and September. The mosquito-borne disease has shown a sharp rise in infections and related deaths compared with the corresponding period last year.
There were 225 deaths and 53,606 dengue cases recorded by health authorities in the corresponding period of 2025, according to DGHS data.
Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. There is no specific treatment for the viral infection.
The South Asian nation of 175 million recorded its highest-ever annual number of dengue deaths in 2022, when 281 people died.
Meanwhile, health authorities also reported seven more deaths involving measles-like symptoms and over 1,200 new infections.
The total number of deaths linked to measles infections rose to 1,162 since mid-March. Of these, 104 have been confirmed as measles deaths.
The number of symptomatic measles cases reached 205,028, while confirmed cases stood at 22,421.
The Health Ministry has immunized around 20 million children in response to the outbreak, in addition to routine vaccinations and a catch-up campaign launched in late September.

13:06:00 UTC
22:06:00 KST

European intelligence agencies have warned executives at defense manufacturing companies across Europe that Russia has intensified plots to assassinate industry leaders in an effort to disrupt military supplies to Ukraine.
Accoring to the Financial Times, citing officials from five European intelligence services, the Kremlin ordered an expansion of hybrid operations and kinetic sabotage across the continent to weaken Western backing for Kyiv.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Intelligence officials stated that targeting European civilians – previously considered an operational line avoided by Russian intelligence – has become an integral component of Moscow’s covert planning.
The warnings indicate that senior defense executives, as well as leaders of smaller enterprises specializing in unmanned aerial vehicles and drone components, have been designated as potential targets for Russian intelligence agents.
In Germany, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) has expanded security consultations with defense contractors, advising senior staff and executive leadership to contract private close-protection details, a BfV official confirmed.
“Russia is engaged in the targeted planning of acts of violence against individuals by state or state-controlled actors,” BfV Vice President Sinan Selen warned German lawmakers.
“We are observing a further evolution of these actions in terms of targets, methods, and the actors involved, notably the use of organized crime structures.”
Can Trump Sidestep Russia Sanctions as the Midterms Loom?
Several European defense executives confirmed to the Financial Times that they have upgraded personal security protocols over the past six months following specific guidance from national security agencies, while others noted they enact specialized protective measures primarily during international travel.
GRU operational methods
Western intelligence assessments attribute primary responsibility for the targeted assassination plots to Russia’s military intelligence directorate, the GRU.
Intelligence officials explained that Russian case officers have increasingly turned to transnational organized crime networks to execute operations.
Rather than relying solely on low-level individuals recruited through online platforms for financial bounties, Russian handlers are structuring specialized cross-border cells that divide surveillance, logistical staging, mission planning, and tactical execution among separate operational layers.
Security officials reported that several active plots have been identified and disrupted before execution. In other instances, security teams detected suspicious surveillance operations tracking the daily routines of targeted defense personnel at private residences and commercial facilities.
Intelligence coordinators stressed that the broader objective of the Russian campaign remains psychological coercion, noting that threats and surveillance alone serve to generate intimidation.
“The primary goal from the Russian perspective is still psychological,” an intelligence official stated. “The mere fact that people feel they might be targeted achieves the desired effect. They want people to think twice before doing business with Ukraine.”
European visa clampdown
The intelligence alerts arrive as European governments and security services move to restrict operational avenues utilized by Russian agents across the EU.
The European Commission is finalizing proposals to tighten Schengen visa regulations for Russian citizens visiting the EU as tourists, aiming to present a legislative package in January following sustained pressure from member states including Sweden, Poland, and Estonia.
Proponents of the measure argue that open travel channels provide hostile intelligence agencies with conduits to conduct surveillance, arson, and industrial sabotage.
Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer warned that existing travel frameworks expose the continent to hostile infiltration, stating that the EU must address structural vulnerabilities exploited by foreign adversaries.
Frontline European governments plan to elevate the visa debate during a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council on Monday, Oct. 12, where ministers will also consider travel curbs on accredited Russian diplomats moving between member states.
Estonia has concurrently advocated for an EU-wide entry ban targeting roughly 650,000 former Russian military combatants, warning that individuals with military training could be mobilized by Russian intelligence services to execute sabotage or penetrate European criminal networks.
The intensified security posture across Europe follows widespread investigations into state-sponsored hybrid operations over recent months, including arson attacks against logistics warehouses, GPS jamming affecting regional aviation, and reconnaissance operations directed against critical defense infrastructure.
