India’s crackdown on youth protesters: What next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:06:00 UTC
22:06:00 KST

India’s crackdown on youth protesters: What next?
India’s Cockroach youth movement and student groups have said protests will continue despite detentions.
India’s capital is bracing for a second day of protests after thousands of people, including the leaders of the “cockroach” youth movement and opposition politicians, were detained amid a major crackdown on demonstrators.
Abhijeet Dipke, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader, called Prime Minister Narendra Modi a “bully” shortly after he was released on Sunday. Thousands of other protesters, some of whom are members of left-wing student groups, were released on Sunday after the Supreme Court called their detention “illegal”.
“Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” Dipke said in a post on X.
The protesters are demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over a revision of voter lists that they say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Modi’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Millions of voters, including Muslims, have been deleted from the rolls in a process marred by technical errors and a perceived lack of transparency.
The protests erupted across several Indian cities after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper found that two election commissioners objected to many of Kumar’s decisions. India’s Election Commission is a constitutional body with three members, and decisions are taken by majority.
What was the scale of the government crackdown?
Ahead of Saturday’s protests, the capital, New Delhi, was turned into a fortress with tens of thousands of police and paramilitary forces deployed, trains and metros suspended, and markets and major roads blocked, to prevent protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar – a designated protest site close to India’s parliament. Jantar Mantar was sealed off.
Jantar Mantar was the site of the July protest that led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmesh Pradhan. That protest, also led by the CJP, was triggered by a string of exam paper leaks.
Security forces also set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points across the city of 20 million people, checked buses and inspected vehicles searching for protesters.
Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes.
More than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, according to local media, and mobile internet services were suspended across several areas of the capital to stop people from online mobilisation efforts by the CJP and other youth groups.
Police detained CJP founder Dipke, as well as his associates, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, from an airplane upon arrival in New Delhi from Mumbai.
Dipke shared a video on his Instagram channel, showing a team of police officers entering the Air India plane after it landed. As they came closer, he said: “I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys.”
In another video shared by Ranka, Dipke said: “This is dictatorship”.
Delhi police also detained YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a leftist group affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist).
Some opposition politicians, as well as former chief ministers – Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala – were also detained, television channels showed.
Despite the unprecedented crackdown, small protests took place elsewhere in the city, including at the popular crafts market “Dilli Haat”. But police also ended up quashing these protests and detaining journalists trying to cover the demonstrations.
Besides New Delhi, some 600 people were also arrested in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, over the protests, according to the ANI news agency.
Have protesters been released?
On Sunday, police officials said all detainees had been released.
The CJP leaders were released on the condition that there would be ‘no breach of peace’ for a year.
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in New Delhi on Sunday afternoon after their release, Saurav Das, the group’s co-convenor, slammed the police for “arriving like mafia dons” and “abducting” them on their plane.
After his release, Rathee said he was “KIDNAPPED.”
Several journalists from news outlets, including Scroll.in, Newslaundry and others were detained. They have all since been released, but Newslaundry said some of their reporters’ media equipment was seized during the detention.
The Committee to Protect Journalists told Al Jazeera on Saturday that it was deeply concerned by reports of journalists being temporarily detained.
“Just as police personnel are doing their jobs, journalists are also doing theirs. A free and independent press is essential to democracy,” Kunal Majumder, the CPJ’s Asia Pacific programme coordinator, said.
How were detainees treated?
Aban Raza, a 37-year old visual artist based in New Delhi who was detained on Saturday, said the “entire experience has left her shocked and angry”.
“We are protesting for the right to vote. It affects all of us. So why is the police suspicious of us and treating us with so much aggression? This makes me angry,” she told Al Jazeera.
Together with three other protesters, including economist Jean Dreze, Raza managed to get close to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning.
“As soon as we reached close enough to the protest site, we started unfurling our banners which called for the resignation of Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar and for free and fair elections. But within minutes, police officials approached us, began tearing our banners and dragging us towards a bus to detain us,” she told Al Jazeera.
“We tried to resist as the police dragged us inside the bus. Both my arms feel very sore today,” she said.
Raza says that some of those detained were not even protesters.
“They were people who had just been picked up whilst they were going about their day. One person was going to the Gurudwara, another was going to meet his wife and they got detained. Most of these people were working class people,” she said.
Raza, who was released on Saturday night, said she is going back to protest on Sunday.
Will the protests continue?
Youth leaders have struck a defiant note, pledging to keep up protests in New Delhi. Some members were detained on Sunday.
The group’s co-convenor Saurav Das, who was released from detention on Sunday, said in a post on X: “After Modi-Shah [Amit Shah, India’s home minister] turned Delhi into a fortress and unleashed what can only be described as a war against their own citizens, one thing has become abundantly clear: Gyanesh Kumar is at the very heart of this government’s survival.”
“But we the young generation will continue to demand accountability. We shall neither be intimidated nor silenced. We are not backing down. We are returning with full strength!” he added.
The CJP has also announced protests in other Indian cities including Mumbai for Sunday evening.
Meanwhile, Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association, began a protest on Sunday afternoon in central Delhi.
“Our peaceful protest has started at RK Ashram. Join us here and stand with us!” she said on X.
But shortly afterwards, Bora and several others were detained.
Are India’s opposition parties backing the protests?
The INDIA Bloc – India’s opposition alliance led by the Indian National Congress – has participated in protests alongside the youth-led groups, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Kumar.
The Bloc is expected to hold a protest on Monday in the capital.
“Yesterday, we held a comprehensive meeting with various leaders to prepare for this march,” Congress general secretary K C Venugopal told reporters on Saturday.
“Gyanesh must go. There will be no backing down,” he added.
Congress party leader and the leader of the opposition in parliament, Rahul Gandhi, has been spearheading a campaign against the election commissioner for months. He was briefly arrested last week over the election protest in New Delhi.
“Modi government has turned the ‘Mother of Democracy’ into a ‘Muzzled Democracy’!” Congress party president Mallikarjun Kharge posted on X.
“Detentions, arrests, jails, lathis [batons] and pellets cannot deter the people of India. Since the days of our freedom struggle, the youth have been at the forefront of shaping the nation’s destiny.”
Why is India’s government refusing to talk to the protesters?
The protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last month that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar’s revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.
The BJP says that of the 130 million names deleted from voter lists, 28 million are dead, 63 million have relocated, 10 million are duplicates and 30 million could not be traced by officials.
The ruling party has also said its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation.
But these protests have become a larger question of democracy and the right to dissent under the Modi government.
While the government had briefly engaged in talks with the youth groups during the July 2026 protests, it has taken a much more hardline stance against demands targeting constitutional and electoral authorities.
The BJP’s officials have also characterised the protests and online opposition as a concerted political effort to destabilise the government rather than highlight legitimate public grievances.
On Saturday, BJP spokesman Sambit Patra dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements” and said that “their flop show has been completely demolished”.
“What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India’s story. India is calm and going ahead under good governance,” he told reporters.
Critics and analysts interviewed by Al Jazeera argue that conceding to demands for the election chief’s resignation would validate opposition accusations of vote theft and project weakness for a prime minister sensitive to his political aura.
But Sanjay Kapoor, editor of Hard News Magazine and a political analyst, told Al Jazeera on Saturday that most people coming to the protests do not want Modi’s BJP to continue to govern.
“Modi’s government has begun to lose a lot of credibility at the moment,” he said.
“BJP is afraid that the ground has shifted dramatically against them and they would find it very difficult to come back to power.”
What has been the global reactions to the protests?
On Saturday, the United Nations Human Rights Office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
“We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled,” UN Human Rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in a statement.
He also urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
Amnesty International told Al Jazeera that the detentions signal the Indian government’s desperate attempts to “suppress critical voices”, while Human Rights Watch said that “instead of addressing legitimate citizen concerns, institutions expected to uphold rights appear to be under the stranglehold of rising authoritarianism.”
The Indian mission to the UN in Geneva, however, called the global concerns “misplaced” and said they constitute “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India’s Constitution.
“As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order.”
What next?
As youth leaders have pledged to continue the protest against the election commissioner, analysts say the movement is “not going to die”.
“I don’t think the Modi government realises the extent of public anger,” Jayati Ghosh, a former professor from the Jawaharlal Nehru University, told Al Jazeera.
Ghosh said that the way the government is responding to the protests is making things much worse. “And more and more people feel alienated and oppressed by the government,” she said.
“So I don’t think this is going to end quickly, unless the government changes tack and actually starts listening and behaving like a normal democratic government.”
Veteran journalist Sanjay Kapoor says the government believes that the protests are aimed at “toppling the government”.
It may or may not happen, he added. But Prime Minister Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, he says, see the protest similar to “the colour revolutions that swept parts of eastern Europe and protests in India’s neighbourhood [Nepal and Bangladesh].”
Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst, compared the current protests to the mass protests in the 1970s that led to the declaration of the state of emergency by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
“Every time there is unrest, calling elections and the change of regime has happened,” Kidwai told Al Jazeera.
“Stopping the protests and detaining people will prolong the protests. What I am foreseeing is chaos and uncertainty.”

Hamas quickly endorsed Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas’s decision to postpone the Palestinian Legislative Council elections, originally scheduled for November 28, to September 11, 2027.
The delay would give the group time to rebuild its support base and strengthen its political position while fueling criticism of its main rival, Fatah, Prof. Kobi Michael, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) and the Misgav Institute, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
In a statement late Saturday, Hamas reaffirmed the need to “put our affairs in order through a democratic process of free and fair elections,” but said that the postponement is necessary “given the absence of the necessary political, security, and on-the-ground conditions” across the Palestinian territories, including east Jerusalem.
“We affirm our readiness to engage in comprehensive dialogue to reach clear outcomes that are binding on all parties,” the statement said.
“These should include mechanisms for putting Palestinian affairs in order, particularly with regard to the Palestinian National Council and the Palestinian Legislative Council; agreement on a comprehensive national strategy encompassing the political program and the management of the transitional period; confronting serious Zionist threats targeting our national cause; and saving our people wherever they are, particularly in the Gaza Strip, which is facing a war of extermination and forced displacement.”
Abbas said the postponement was necessary because of the security situation in Gaza and alleged Israeli obstacles to holding elections in east Jerusalem. Israel’s foreign minister denied the latter claim.
Michael, who had long predicted that the elections would be postponed, said Hamas’s endorsement of the decision was unsurprising, as the group understood that the delay would give it time to rebuild its legitimacy and support base in Gaza.
Poll shows declining support for Hamas, Fatah, falling confidence in war outcome

“Time is working in their favor,” Michael said, noting that anger over the postponement was being directed almost entirely at Fatah, potentially damaging its public standing ahead of what could be a critical vote for Hamas.
Hamas seeks to retain political influence through Palestinian elections
The group has already committed to handing over control of the Gaza Strip to the Board of Peace, Michael noted. Winning seats in the PLC through its allied list could give Hamas a way to retain political influence while promoting an image of democratic legitimacy to the international community.
“By attacking and criticizing Abu Mazen (Abbas) over the postponement of the elections, building and strengthening its political alliance with Dahlan, Hamas can position itself as the ultimate alternative to the PA and Abu Mazen,” he said.

Shin Bet to establish Islamic studies program to address Oct. 7 intelligence failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:05:33 UTC
22:05:33 KST

The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) is preparing to establish a new Islamic studies program as part of an initiative led by agency chief David Zini to address intelligence failures exposed by investigations into the October 7 massacre, particularly the failure to understand Hamas's ideology and religious extremism.
The new program will operate alongside the Shin Bet's long-established Arabic language institute, which provides language training for personnel across various positions within the organization. The institute is considered to maintain exceptionally high professional standards and periodically also trains IDF personnel.
Zini's initiative will bring together lecturers, subject-matter experts, and senior current and former officials to provide comprehensive instruction on Islam.
He has also decided that the program will incorporate research into Islam, with curricula tailored to the Shin Bet's operational challenges across different arenas. The goal is to strengthen and deepen understanding of the religion and its various interpretations among personnel working in different professional fields.
Lack of understanding of Islam deemed failure of Oct. 7
One of the central conclusions drawn by Israel's intelligence community from the failures of October 7 was a fundamental lack of understanding of Islam, its various branches and interpretations, Palestinian culture, particularly in the Gaza Strip, and broader developments across the Middle East.
This failure was especially significant given the extraordinary volume of high-quality intelligence available regarding Hamas's intentions to launch an incursion into Israeli territory.
The intelligence community's findings also highlighted a failure to understand Hamas's ideology, the growing radicalization of the organization following Yahya Sinwar's release from prison, and the incorporation of Sheikh Ahmed Yassin's vision into Hamas's organizational strategy.
Another critical gap involved the failure to recognize the disconnect between the organization's day-to-day conduct and the deeply held beliefs instilled in Hamas operatives from kindergarten onward.
According to intelligence community sources, as intelligence gathering became increasingly precise through advances in signals intelligence (SIGINT) and cyber capabilities, the perceived need for a fundamental understanding of Islam gradually diminished.
These technological capabilities enabled intelligence agencies to intercept telephone calls, radio communications, WhatsApp messages, and emails, providing increasingly detailed information about their targets.
However, the growing reliance on technological intelligence came at the expense of expertise in Islamic studies. The need for specialized centers dedicated to understanding radical Islam declined, and over time, the professional expertise of intelligence specialists, including their understanding of the enemy, deteriorated.
Against the backdrop of wartime investigations and intelligence gathered during the conflict, a senior intelligence official recently told Walla that Israel had fundamentally underestimated the depth of Hamas's hatred and ideological extremism.
"We did not understand how much Hamas hates Israel. How unwilling it is to accept any compromise. How extreme it is, and how prepared it was before October 7 to justify atrocities such as rape and the kidnapping of children, even though the writing was on the wall. The legitimization of suicide bombings more than 40 years ago was a preview of what was to come," the official said.
Effort to improve employment conditions
In parallel with the initiative to strengthen the Shin Bet's professional expertise, Zini is undertaking a major effort to improve employment conditions for agency personnel.
Working conditions have deteriorated over the past decade despite the growing scale and complexity of the challenges facing the organization.
There is an expectation that progress will be made in negotiations with the Finance Ministry following the elections, particularly regarding salary levels and pay increases, to encourage a new generation of highly qualified recruits to join the Shin Bet.

====================================================================================================

How Israel's pager operation shattered Nasrallah’s aura of invincibility - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:05:31 UTC
22:05:31 KST

The second anniversary of the pager operation is a reminder that the first thing to explode on September 17, 2024, was not thousands of small devices. It was the carefully cultivated aura of invulnerability that Hassan Nasrallah had built around himself.
For years, the Hezbollah leader had appeared from his hideout, boasting about missiles, tunnels, and “surprises,” asking the Lebanese to believe that his disappearance was strategic brilliance. The terrorist group could see without being seen, strike without being touched.
Then an old-fashioned device exposed the reality. The organization that had cowed Lebanon through fear had been compromised through its own supply chain. Its leader, who threatened to bury his enemies, did not know his men were carrying booby-trapped devices.
This was not simply an intelligence coup worthy of a spy thriller. Israeli intelligence had constructed a false reality in which Hezbollah operated with complete confidence. Public investigations and the book In the War Room trace the idea’s origins to 2002-2006, during Meir Dagan’s tenure.
Around 2014, Mossad and Israeli military intelligence began introducing wireless devices into Hezbollah’s network, monitoring them while retaining the option of detonation. In 2022, they turned to pagers: devices operatives would carry rather than leave in an office or warehouse.
Front companies, licensing arrangements, dummy websites, and stores gave a battery unavailable on the open market a convincing commercial identity. A Taiwanese brand and a supply chain stretching from Hungary to Hong Kong supplied the cover. The Mossad did not simply intercept a shipment. It created the product, marketed it, built its reputation, and cut the price until Hezbollah’s procurement officials chose the trap themselves.
This was the difference between penetrating an organization and shaping the choices it believed were its own. The procurement process offered the appearance of control while delivering precisely what the adversary wanted.
They thought they were vetting a product. In reality, the product was exposing the organization.
Explosives were built into the batteries
A Reuters investigation found that explosives and a concealed detonator were built into the battery, allowing the devices to pass Hezbollah’s security checks. Even when officials noticed that batteries drained faster than advertised, distribution continued.
The message and alert were designed to make recipients bring the device toward their faces and use both hands. The alert tone and explosive charge had been tested to produce the intended response. The Mossad had choreographed the movements of those carrying its bombs.
The bitterest irony was that Nasrallah himself helped the operation. In February 2024, he called mobile phones more dangerous than spies and urged his men to smash them, bury them, or lock them in metal boxes. Hezbollah accelerated its adoption of pagers. His warning did not create the operation, but it drove more men toward the prepared device. The leadership’s fear had become a predictable procurement decision. Hezbollah had chosen its own poisoned remedy.
I see something deeper here than a procurement mistake. An entire security doctrine collapsed: secrecy supposedly meant switching off a phone, while the enemy was manufacturing the alternative.
At 3:30 p.m. on September 17, the devices began to ring. Roughly 3,000 exploded. The next day came the wireless devices, some held by Hezbollah for nearly a decade. Dozens were killed and more than 3,400 wounded. Devices had been distributed among fighters, commanders, support personnel, and affiliated medics. The penetration even reached Iran’s ambassador. The target was the infrastructure that enabled an Iranian-backed militia to operate as a state within Lebanon.
More important, in my view, was the assault on trust. Anyone still carrying a device had reason to fear its battery. Those who watched colleagues fall simultaneously understood that the enemy had helped build the walls behind which they sheltered. The equipment meant to connect the organization had become a source of fear. Replacing it could restore communication, but could not erase the discovery that trusted channels had carried the enemy inside.
Two former Mossad officers described the intended psychological impact. Wafiq Safa, a close Nasrallah associate, later recounted that the attacks left him deeply shaken and barely eating for almost a day. The man who had spent his life instilling fear in the Lebanese discovered, days before his death, that fear had reached his own hideout.
The operation also opened a military campaign. On September 20, Ibrahim Aqil and Radwan Force commanders were killed. Strikes expanded to weapons depots, facilities, and positions. On September 27, Nasrallah was killed beneath the headquarters he had regarded as an impregnable fortress.
Intelligence derives its real power from turning secrets into paralysis and confusion at the moment military force can exploit them. Without the subsequent strikes, the explosions would have remained an extraordinary intelligence feat. Their succession made the operation the opening phase of a broader dismantling.
Nasrallah had built his authority on the belief that obscurity proved knowledge, disappearance meant immunity, and questioning the leadership betrayed resistance. The farther he withdrew, the more formidable he appeared. Secrecy became wisdom beyond scrutiny.
The pagers exposed what that mythology concealed. His disappearance was isolation. His secrecy hid ignorance of what entered his warehouses. His speeches promised deterrence while his security apparatus was already penetrated.
That is the weakness of closed ideological organizations. They confuse loyalty with competence and treat questions as betrayal. Eventually, the leader’s word becomes a vulnerability no one dares challenge. A professional intelligence service could engineer the environment around its target; a terrorist militia had mistaken suspicion and obedience for security.
Two years later, Hezbollah can buy devices, change intermediaries, and rebuild parts of its network. It cannot turn the clock back to before the first ring.
The militia that claimed to protect Lebanon could not even protect its own supply chain. The leader who threatened to bury his enemies was himself buried beneath the concrete, along with the project he had built. And the Shi’ite community asked to believe in divine protection saw that an aura of sanctity could neither stop a signal nor reveal a compromised battery.
The most devastating part was that Hezbollah’s own leadership had led its men, step by step, to the very tool Israel designed to reach them. In doing so, it shattered the image of Nasrallah as an infallible leader.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

Russia enlists criminal groups to carry out attacks on the heads of European defense companies – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:03:23 EEST
22:03:23 KST

Russia enlists criminal groups to carry out attacks on the heads of European defense companies – FT
Kyiv • UNN
Russian special services are preparing attacks on the heads of European defense companies, enlisting organized criminal groups. The goal is to intimidate businesses and weaken support for Ukraine.
Russian intelligence services have intensified preparations for assassination attempts targeting executives of European defense companies involved in the production of weapons and military equipment, including for Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing the Financial Times.
Details
According to the publication, which spoke with representatives of five European intelligence services, the Kremlin is stepping up sabotage activities in Europe in an attempt to weaken military support for Ukraine. Potential targets of Russian intelligence services may include executives of major defense corporations, as well as smaller companies producing drones, components, and other military equipment for the Ukrainian army.
European intelligence services are particularly concerned about the change in methods used to conduct Russian operations. According to FT's sources, Russian military intelligence is increasingly involving members of organized criminal groups in preparing acts of sabotage and possible assassinations.
Previously, recruits approached via the internet and offered financial rewards were actively used to carry out such tasks. Now, according to intelligence assessments, the organization of operations is becoming more complex, with individual stages of preparation potentially being carried out by different groups in several countries.
The publication's sources claim that European law enforcement and intelligence agencies have already detected and thwarted individual plots. There have also been cases of suspicious surveillance of potential victims near their homes and workplaces. Amid the rising threats, a number of European defense companies have introduced additional security measures. Some executives are under round-the-clock protection, while during trips abroad they use the services of specialized security teams.
According to FT's sources, the aim of such actions is to intimidate Europe's defense industry. The constant threat of attacks could increase companies' security costs and complicate their cooperation with Ukraine.
Context
One of the best-known cases was the reported preparation of an assassination attempt against Armin Papperger, CEO of the German defense contractor Rheinmetall. In July 2024, Western media reported on a Russian plan to kill him. In January 2025, NATO official James Appathurai confirmed that there had been a threat to the life of the company's head and also reported other similar plots against representatives of the defense industry.
In addition, on October 5, 2026, the heads of Germany's intelligence agencies warned during hearings in the Bundestag about an intensification of Russia's hybrid operations. In particular, they referred to threats of sabotage, acts of violence, and attacks on the defense industry and critical infrastructure.
On October 7, Denmark's Security and Intelligence Service also reported attempts to carry out sabotage against Danish companies supplying weapons to Ukraine. According to the agency's assessment, Russian entities are increasingly directing their operations against production facilities whose activities directly affect the Ukrainian army's military capabilities.
Reminder
U.S. prosecutors exposed an alleged global network of Russian intelligence services, whose members are accused of preparing assassinations and acts of sabotage in the United States and Europe. The U.S. Department of Justice charged five individuals, who remain at large.

Wang Manyu poses for a selfie during the awarding ceremony of the women's singles at 2026 World Table Tennis (WTT) China Smash in Beijing, China, Oct. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Han)
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- China's Wang Manyu successfully defended her women's singles title after defeating Japanese chopper Hitomi Sato 4-0 at the 2026 WTT China Smash on Sunday.
In the men's singles final, world No. 1 Sora Matsushima edged Chinese Taipei's Lin Yun-ju 4-3 in a seven-game thriller.
Wang had a 6-1 head-to-head record against Sato, although their most recent meeting, and their only previous encounter in the WTT Series, saw Sato win 3-0 in the round of 32 at the 2026 WTT United States Smash three months ago.
Wang stormed to an 11-2 win in the opening game. With the top seed leading 9-8 in the second, the expedite rule came into effect, under which the server must win the point within 13 strokes or the receiver is awarded the point.
Wang then won two consecutive points to take the second game 11-8 before prevailing 11-3, 11-9 to secure her fourth WTT Grand Smash title.
Despite the defeat, Sato made history as the first chopper to contest a WTT Grand Smash final.
"I had not expected the score to be 4-0. I had a stable mindset and resolutely executed my tactics in the match," Wang said.
Earlier in the day, Matsushima saw off home player Zhou Qihao 4-2, while Lin edged Brazil's Hugo Calderano in a seven-game thriller.
As the 11-day tournament came to a close, China won two of the five titles, with Wang also successfully defending the women's doubles crown alongside Kuai Man.
"I carried my momentum after the Asian Games into the China Smash, while facing difficulties and challenges during this process. Thanks to my coaches and teammates for their support, which helped me embrace these challenges with a positive mentality," Wang said.
South Korea's Lim Jong-hoon won two doubles titles, partnering Shin Yu-bin in the mixed doubles and Oh Jun-sung in the men's doubles. ■

22:02:41 KST

Some 82% of French people now disapprove of the president. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella are weakened by Mediapart's revelations about antisemitic texts attributed to the young RN leader.
Protests by secondary-school pupils, a fuel crisis and a budget debate getting off to a bad start in the National Assembly, where there is no majority, the government is facing a string of difficulties that are being reflected in opinion polls.
Seven months before the end of his second term, Emmanuel Macron’s popularity has fallen to its lowest level since he entered the Elysée Palace in 2017, according to a new barometer published at the weekend.
According to the Ipsos BVA-Cesi survey (source in French) for La Tribune Dimanche, only 15% of those questioned have a favourable opinion of the French President, one point down from a month earlier.
The backlash is hitting the president harder than his Prime Minister. Sébastien Lecornu’s popularity has edged up slightly, gaining two points in a month: 22% of French people now view his performance positively.
Purchasing power remains the French public’s main concern, cited by 54% of respondents, a stable figure. The future of the welfare system comes second, at 44% (+4 points), ahead of the level of public debt, which worries 33% of those surveyed (+3 points).
Three far-right figures in the top five
Among the political figures seen as possible successors to Emmanuel Macron, far-right leaders Jordan Bardella and Marine Le Pen continue to dominate the rankings, with 33% and 32% favourable opinions respectively.
Their ratings have, however, slipped compared with the previous month: Jordan Bardella is down three points and Marine Le Pen four.
This fall comes in the wake of revelations by Mediapart about antisemitic and conspiracist messages attributed to Jordan Bardella, posted from an old Facebook account. The President of the Rassemblement national has denied the accusations.
The online survey was carried out on 7 and 8 October among 1,000 adults, a few days after Mediapart published its first article on the affair, on 28 September.
Behind Bardella and Le Pen, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe takes third place, with 20% satisfied, up one point.
Sarah Knafo, a leading figure in Reconquête, the nationalist party led by Éric Zemmour, and François Hollande, the former Socialist President, round out the top five. Both receive 18% favourable opinions. Neither has yet declared a presidential bid.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the radical left’s candidate, comes next with 17 % favourable opinions, level with centrist Gabriel Attal and the Republicans’ leader, Bruno Retailleau.
The leader of La France Insoumise party nevertheless stands out for an exceptionally high rejection rate: according to the study, 69% of French people say they would be unhappy if he were to move into the Elysée.

Poland’s security services have held an urgent meeting after receiving “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
At the time of writing, no details have been released regarding where and how the alleged attacks were expected to take place, who might be behind them, nor what the source of the information was.

On Sunday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, first announced that the police had received “information…regarding a possible assassination attempt” on Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz, who, as well as serving as defence minister, is also a deputy prime minister.
Dobrzyński revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW), police and State Protection Service (SOP), which provides security for high-ranking officials, would meet to discuss the potential threat.
Speaking after that meeting, interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka confirmed that the threat had first been identified by SOP, which passed the information on to the police.
“We are taking this matter extremely seriously,” added Dobrzyński, speaking alongside her. He criticised “pseudo-experts” in the media who had expressed doubt about the announcement of a possible assassination attempt.
“We’re talking about threats directed at the most important people in the country,” he added. “This information is so serious and credible that we’ve decided to share it with you now…We are talking about a high probability that these threats will be carried out.”
Dobrzyński did not divulge any details about the nature of the attack nor where the warnings had come from, but said that he would be able to provide further information once the police and security services had carried out further investigation.

Another source within the intelligence services told the newspaper that the threat was treated more seriously than others because it contained information about addresses linked to Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Also in September, the security services detained three teenagers who were accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them was additionally charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school.

Russia equips Geran attack drones with image-based navigation using Google map imagery, reducing reliance on satellite navigation that Ukraine can jam, defense adviser warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:01:50 UTC
22:01:50 KST

Russia is developing new navigation systems for attack drones and missiles that could make its strikes against Ukrainian cities harder to stop, as Moscow adapts its weapons to counter Ukrainian electronic warfare defenses, Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said.
The shift poses an additional challenge for Ukraine as Russia continues to attack cities and critical infrastructure with drones and missiles. Systems that can navigate without relying on satellite signals may be harder to disrupt electronically, increasing the importance of other defenses, including interception and physical destruction of incoming weapons.
Image-based navigation could make Russian strike drones harder to jam
Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on defense technology development, said image-based navigation systems would see wider use in 2027, including in medium- and long-range strike drones and inexpensive cruise missiles.
The technology allows drones to navigate by comparing images captured by an onboard camera with stored photographs of the terrain. Even basic navigation can use publicly available satellite or ground imagery from services such as Google, Beskrestnov said.
Unlike satellite navigation, which can be disrupted by electronic warfare, image-based navigation relies on visual recognition of the terrain. This makes drones using the technology more resistant to jamming and could allow them to continue toward their targets even when satellite navigation signals are unavailable.
Russia already uses image-based navigation on attack drones
Beskrestnov said Russian forces were already using the technology on several types of unmanned aircraft, including Molniya, V2U, and Lancet drones.
He also reported that similar systems had recently been identified on the Russian Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones, using a flight controller called Susanin.
The Geran series includes Russian attack drones used in strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The introduction of image-based navigation could make some variants more difficult for Ukrainian forces to counter using electronic warfare.
Russia adapts its weapons to Ukrainian defenses
The development reflects Russia’s broader effort to adapt its weapons as Ukraine improves its air defenses and electronic warfare capabilities. By reducing reliance on satellite navigation signals, Russian drones can become less vulnerable to one of Ukraine’s key methods of disrupting incoming attacks.
Beskrestnov warned that image-based navigation would expand beyond individual drone models, with broader adoption expected next year across different categories of strike weapons.

‘It’s not just about circling things on a map’: how our journalists use and corroborate satellite imagery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:00:27 UTC
22:00:27 KST

How to bear witness when you can’t physically go there? Journalists have always grappled with this. Whether it’s because of armed conflict, repressive regimes or prohibitive terrain, some places remain too dangerous or difficult for reporters to access.
Enter low-orbit satellites. As the technology has evolved and proliferated, satellite imagery has become increasingly indispensable. But as with all reporting tools, it requires professional judgment and painstaking work to verify things.
“When satellite images show that something on the ground has changed, there’s a lot that needs to be corroborated,” says Kaamil Ahmed, a reporter on the Guardian’s global development team who used extensive satellite imagery for an investigation we published last week into the destruction of Rohingya villages in Myanmar. “For instance, we could see from the images that people had been displaced, but we needed to verify the images, we needed to be sure about what actually happened and who was behind it, and also whether the villages we were looking at were really Rohingya villages. None of that was straightforward.”
“We have to treat satellite imagery in exactly the same way as any other type of data we look at, or any human source we speak to,” adds Ashley Kirk, the Guardian’s senior editor for visual journalism. “It goes back to basic journalistic principles of second-sourcing and triple-sourcing information. So that might involve checking that we can still see the same thing in images obtained from another satellite provider, or cross-checking things with information from the ground, such as social media posts or witness testimony, and speaking with experts.”
Kaamil has been reporting on the persecution of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority group from western Myanmar, for more than 10 years. Myanmar has been accused of orchestrating an ethnic cleansing of its Rohingya population after a military crackdown from 2016 to 2017 led to about 700,000 people seeking refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh.
Last week’s investigation mapped the more recent destruction of Rohingya villages in western Myanmar since 2024 by a group of insurgents. It also examined the construction of detention camps and labour camps. “We’d heard for a couple of years that things were happening in that particular area, but it was very hard to stand up,” says Kaamil. “Phone lines and the internet have been down for years so there’s so little evidence coming out of the area. Often, we’d have to simply wait for people to go to Bangladesh as refugees before we could hear their testimony. So that’s why satellite imagery has been so useful.”
Indeed, it was shortly after Kaamil published another satellite-led investigation back in March – which examined attacks on a village in Darfur as part of the ongoing war in Sudan – that a source contacted him and suggested he apply the same reporting techniques to a particular area in western Myanmar.
“One of the challenges was that this was a very remote area. Satellite providers weren’t passing over it regularly so, to begin with, we were really struggling to get the quality of images we needed. There’d be big gaps in the timeframe, there weren’t images from the right day, or they weren’t the right resolution.”
All these things can hamper journalists’ efforts to make informed comparisons.
Ashley recalls facing similar issues over the summer when we used satellite imagery to assess the impact of the wildfires across Europe. “We needed to look at historical images to see the burn scars and assess how certain landscapes had changed,” he explains. “But quite often we are restrained by whenever a satellite goes around Earth and captures images of a very specific area. You’ve got to hope that it’s the right time of day and exactly the right area, and also that there are no obstructions such as cloud cover or smoke obscuring the landscape too much – which in the case of the wildfires would often happen.”
Even when our data and visual journalists manage to source clear images of a specific area on a specific day at a specific time, there is still a lot of corroboration to be done. Kaamil offers an example from his investigation into the attacks in Sudan: “There’s a lot of destruction in Darfur, but some of the satellite images of burnt landscapes were actually related to agriculture rather than the war, so we have to be very careful about checking and not making assumptions.”
Ashley points to another example from his team’s extensive use of satellite imagery to report on the destruction of Gaza over the past three years. “You would see a circular object and you might think it’s the dome of a mosque. But a circular pattern could also indicate a crater. So then, for example, we’d use images from other times of the day to see if there are any shadows that suggest a building.”
For last week’s story about the Rohingya villages, Kaamil corroborated the satellite imagery using eyewitness testimony from some of the sources he has kept in touch with during his years of covering their plight, as well as other sources of data. “For instance, on top of satellite imagery, we also used fire data from Nasa, which has sensors that detect every fire of a certain size. That helped us to verify that fires actually happened in these villages on the dates that people said that they happened. We also used conflict data because it was very important for us to be sure that these villages were not destroyed as a side-effect of shelling during battles between the insurgents and the military – that they were actually systematically destroyed. The conflict data showed us that there were actually very few battles during the period of destruction indicated by the satellite imagery, because at that point the insurgents had complete control of that particular region.”
Gathering all this supporting evidence isn’t just about corroborating things. The interactive article we published last week presents some of those eyewitness testimonies, together with photographs and video clips, alongside the satellite imagery. The result is a more immersive experience that gives audiences a fuller picture of what has been happening on the ground.
“One of the big limitations of satellite imagery is that it’s literally very distant from the human story on the ground,” says Anna Leach, a visual projects editor who also worked on the investigation. “But of course this is a very human story about the displacement of people, and we always try to show that human element in everything we do.”
“We tried to make sure the article remained connected to the people affected,” adds Prina Shah, a senior digital designer on the Guardian’s visual team who also worked on the project. “So we included photos of villagers’ faces and other images to show that people actually live here and it’s not just about circling things on a map.”
Ashley highlights another example from our coverage of the war in Gaza. Published in December, the article in question used satellite imagery alongside on-the-ground photography to chart a woman’s two-year search for safety in the ruins of Gaza. “We tried to show all of the different places that she was displaced to and how each of those places got destroyed, and so she just had to keep on fleeing,” he says. “Combining the satellite imagery with more traditional reporting techniques meant we could tell her story and also contextualize it. We showed the human story, but the satellite imagery allowed us to show, for example, all of the other tents that surrounded her tent and so you immediately see that her story is just one of thousands. Satellite imagery is really effective for giving people a sense of the scale of what’s happening alongside what’s happening to individuals.”
Given that our satellite-based interactive articles often contain multiple perspectives and narratives, our visual journalists also put a great deal of effort into honing the experience of scrolling down as you read them and see the visual evidence. “We’re thinking about how we explain quite complex imagery in a digestible way to an audience that might be viewing it on a mobile phone,” says Prina. “This can entail things like ensuring different elements pop up when they’re meant to and fall back when they need to because the audience’s attention needs to be focused on different aspects of the satellite imagery, for example, or on the personal accounts that are presented simultaneously.”
This process involves a lot of testing and fine-tuning before the article is published. “Certain issues only come to light when you’re playing with the actual interactive and refining interactive elements and animation and transitions to improve focus or understanding.”
Having spent so many years reporting on the Rohingya, Kaamil really appreciates the team’s efforts to bring the story to life: “We’ve tried to go beyond satellite images that just show destruction. People might get immune to that,” he says. “Also, the Rohingya refugee population has existed for so many years now, it can seem like a stagnant situation. Presenting things in a fresh and different way is part of how we try to make people care and ensure that our reporting has impact. So these forms of journalism help us to report on things that aren’t always on the news agenda.”
The investigation into the erasure of Rohingya villages was part of the Guardian’s Global development series, which is supported by theguardian.org.

Women on hormonal birth control view their romantic traits more positively
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:00:22 UTC
22:00:22 KST

Women who use hormonal contraceptives tend to evaluate their own romantic and social qualities more favorably than women who do not use them. A recent set of psychological evaluations suggests that synthetic hormones in birth control might inadvertently boost how women perceive their desirability to potential partners. These findings were recently published in the journal Human Nature.
To understand how people navigate romantic relationships, psychologists often study a concept called mate value. A person’s mate value is a summative evaluation of the characteristics that make them an attractive partner. For women, these qualities historically include physical markers of fertility, as well as social skills, loyalty, and potential parenting ability. People tend to seek out romantic partners whose mate value roughly matches their own. Because of this matching process, having an intuitive sense of one’s own mate value helps individuals successfully navigate the dating market.
Hormonal contraceptives suppress natural fertility by disrupting the normal production of ovarian hormones. Because fertility is a primary component of mate value, some evolutionary psychologists hypothesized that women taking birth control might subconsciously perceive their own mate value as lower than they otherwise would.
However, there is a competing hypothesis based on how synthetic hormones interact with the brain. Hormonal contraceptives contain synthetic versions of progesterone and estradiol. When these synthetic hormones bind to receptors in the brain, they mimic physiological states that naturally promote social bonding and maternal behavior. Animal research has shown that administering these hormones can prime nurturing behaviors. Because sociality and parenting capacity are also major components of mate value, it is entirely possible that hormonal contraceptives could boost a woman’s self-perception in these areas.
Juliana E. French, a psychology researcher at the University of South Florida, worked with a team of researchers to test these competing ideas. They designed a series of evaluations to see whether women on birth control viewed their romantic traits more positively or more negatively than naturally cycling women.
In the first evaluation, the research team recruited 94 unmarried, undergraduate women. The participants reported whether they used a hormonal contraceptive, such as a daily pill, a patch, or an implant. The researchers also gathered data on the naturally cycling women’s menstrual cycles to estimate their natural conception risk on the day of the study.
The participants then completed a widely used psychological survey that measures self-perceived mating success. Instead of directly asking the women to rate their own attractiveness, this survey asks them to evaluate their success in attracting partners. For example, participants rated how much they agreed with statements about whether people they like tend to reciprocate those feelings.
The researchers found that women using hormonal contraceptives reported higher self-perceived mating success than the women experiencing natural menstrual cycles. This positive association remained consistent even when the researchers adjusted their statistical models to account for the natural fertility fluctuations of the non-users.
The team then designed a second evaluation to see if this pattern held true for older, partnered women. They recruited 91 newly married women for a two-year longitudinal study. The researchers assessed the women at the beginning of their marriages and then checked in annually for the next two years. During each assessment, the participants reported their contraceptive use and completed the same mating success survey.
Because the participants were newly married, the researchers removed survey questions that implied seeking outside sexual partners. They also asked the couples to report how often they had engaged in sexual intercourse over the previous month.
The results of the second evaluation mirrored the first. The married women using hormonal birth control consistently viewed their mating success more highly than the naturally cycling married women. By accounting for the frequency of sexual activity in their statistical models, the researchers demonstrated that the higher self-perceptions were not simply the result of having a more active sex life.
Despite these consistent results, the mating success survey primarily measures romantic opportunities rather than underlying personal traits. To address this limitation, the team conducted a third evaluation using a broader measurement tool. They recruited 178 unmarried university students who were participating in an upcoming speed-dating event.
Before the event, the women completed a survey evaluating themselves on 29 different traits related to romantic desirability. These included short-term desirability traits, such as physical attractiveness and a fun personality, as well as long-term traits, such as loyalty, educational ambition, and social reputation.
Once again, the women using hormonal contraceptives rated themselves more positively across this broader spectrum of traits. The researchers noted that the majority of the contraceptive users in this specific group reported taking birth control for reasons other than preventing pregnancy. Many used the medications to manage acne or regulate their menstrual cycles. This detail helps rule out the idea that highly desirable women simply take birth control in greater numbers to manage an abundance of dating opportunities.
To confirm the stability of their findings, the researchers combined the data from all three evaluations with the results of a previous, independent paper whose results were not statistically significant. The aggregated data revealed an overall positive link between hormonal contraceptive use and self-perceived mate value.
While the findings represent a consistent pattern, the research relies entirely on observational data. The study tracks existing habits rather than assigning medical treatments to participants. Because of this design, the results do not prove that hormonal contraceptives cause women to view themselves more favorably. It remains possible that an unidentified psychological factor leads women with higher self-perceptions to seek out hormonal birth control in the first place.
To determine if the synthetic hormones are directly responsible for the psychological shifts, future research will need to employ experimental designs. Scientists could randomly assign participants to take either a hormonal contraceptive or a placebo and measure any changes in their self-perception over time.
Additionally, the current paper did not separate the participants based on the specific type of birth control they used. Different formulations of oral pills, implants, or rings deliver varying doses of synthetic hormones. Some methods use a combination of progestin and estradiol, while others rely on progestin alone. Investigating how these specific formulations interact with a woman’s psychology will require more detailed medical tracking in future studies.
The study, “Hormonal Contraceptives and Women’s Mate-Value-Related Traits and Outcomes,” was authored by Juliana E. French, Elizabeth Barron, Emma E. Altgelt, Maryanne Fisher, and Andrea L. Meltzer.

‘Citizen Osama’ turns life under bombardment into urgent, intimate cinema
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

At barely 70 minutes, Ahmed Hassouna’s Citizen Osama feels much larger than its running time. Not because it drags, but because of how much life, death and uncertainty it compresses into a short span. Events arrive with the relentlessness of a permanent emergency. Buildings are bombed, people are pulled from rubble, colleagues are killed, food becomes harder to find, and humanitarian aid appears only to prove painfully insufficient. Between these episodes, Osama Al-Ashi goes home to his wife, his young child and his anxious parents.
The result is a film in which public catastrophe and private life can no longer be separated.
That perspective gives Citizen Osama a striking place beside NAZA, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary, which has recently drawn significant international attention. Where NAZA examines Israeli military systems through testimony from Israeli personnel, Hassouna remains on the ground with those living beneath their consequences. The films approach the same historical moment from radically different positions.
Premiering in Venice Open at this year’s Venice Film Festival, Citizen Osama follows Al-Ashi, once an artistic photographer and now a war documentarian living in northern Gaza. Hassouna shot the film himself; Denis Le Paven edited it, while Rasmus Steen composed its restrained score. The documentary has also been selected as Palestine’s submission for the 2027 Academy Awards.
There is little distance here between journalism and filmmaking. Osama’s camera exists first because there is something that urgently needs to be documented. Yet the accumulation of those images, and Hassouna’s shaping of them, gradually transforms reporting into cinema. The distinction becomes almost irrelevant. Recording events is at once a professional duty, a means of producing evidence, an act of memory and, eventually, storytelling.
Some of the film’s most difficult passages show people trapped beneath destroyed buildings and the desperate collective effort to reach them. Elsewhere, the deaths of journalists puncture any illusion that the word “PRESS” printed across a protective vest can offer real security. The killing of Al Jazeera journalist Ismail al-Ghoul, one of the colleagues mourned in the film, becomes another reminder that Osama can leave home to work and simply not return. Al-Ghoul and cameraman Ramy El Rify were killed in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City in July 2024.
But Citizen Osama understands that catastrophe is experienced not only through explosions and death. Sometimes it is measured in flour.
Osama searches for basic food for his family and finds flour contaminated with mold and worms: technically available, but barely fit for consumption. Diesel is another constant problem. These details are small compared with the scale of the destruction, and that is precisely why they matter. Hassouna shows what happens when the tasks that ordinarily structure everyday life — buying food, moving around, caring for a child — become precarious logistical operations.
A similarly memorable sequence observes humanitarian aid falling from airplanes. Some packages appear to land in the sea, prompting people to enter the water to retrieve them; those that reach land are immediately surrounded by crowds. Hassouna does not need to stop and explain the absurdity of these images. The aid is visible, desperately needed, and, at the same time, clearly inadequate to the need around it.
The film’s tight editing is crucial. Citizen Osama could easily have become a succession of horrors, each image attempting to overwhelm the previous one. Instead, Le Paven repeatedly returns the film to Osama’s family and colleagues. His parents worry about both Gaza’s future and the immediate possibility that their son might not come home. His wife and child embody another responsibility, one that exists uneasily beside his determination to continue working.
And then, remarkably, people still laugh.
In one deceptively minor scene, Osama and other journalists trade terrible jokes. They are not especially funny, which is part of what makes the moment so affecting. Humor becomes less an escape from reality than another way of continuing to exist inside it. Citizen Osama repeatedly notices these fragments of ordinary behavior without sentimentalizing them.
“Resilience” is a word so often applied to Palestinians that it risks becoming an abstraction. Hassouna makes it physical. It means digging through ruins to help another person. It means finding something to eat. It means going back to work. It can also mean telling a bad joke when almost nothing around you provides a reason to laugh.
This creates the film’s central tension: between agency and inevitability. Osama is constantly acting — filming, moving, providing, helping, protecting — within circumstances over which he possesses almost no control. Hope therefore does not emerge from any suggestion that conditions are about to improve. Citizen Osama offers little basis for that kind of optimism. What survives instead is the refusal to surrender every remaining form of agency.
Hassouna largely avoids turning the documentary into an exercise in political exposition. There are no lengthy explanatory passages instructing viewers how to process what they are seeing. The images and Osama’s circumstances carry the argument. Its graphic moments can be extremely difficult to watch, but sanitizing them would produce a different and considerably less truthful film. The spare use of music works for the same reason: the film rarely needs to tell us when an image is devastating.
In the film’s press notes, Hassouna describes Osama as more than an individual protagonist, someone through whom he could express something of his own experience and that of others who have lived through the war. He calls the film an attempt to preserve what they have lived through and to safeguard their humanity. In the same notes, he describes Venice as an opportunity to tell their story in their “own voice and through our own images.”
That phrase may provide the clearest key to Citizen Osama. The camera cannot stop the destruction surrounding Osama. It cannot guarantee his safety, find food for his family, or bring his colleagues back. What it can do is preserve evidence that these lives existed in all their fear, exhaustion, affection, absurdity, and stubborn humanity.
That is also why the comparison with NAZA matters. One film interrogates military systems from within Israeli society; the other records what life looks like underneath their consequences. Citizen Osama may not yet have received comparable attention, but it belongs fully to the same cinematic reckoning — not as an accompanying document, but as a work in its own right.
For its rather brief duration, it turns the act of looking into an act of survival.

Zermatt glacier slopes reopen after heatwave closure
From Wednesday, skiers will once again be able to hit the slopes on the Theodul Glacier above Zermatt, in canton Valais. The area, which normally remains open throughout the summer, was forced to close temporarily because of the heatwave and rapidly melting snow.
The ski area, which extends to nearly 4,000 metres above sea level, will reopen to the public on October 14, according to Zermatt Bergbahnen. Recent snowfall and lower temperatures have significantly improved conditions, the operator said, although it noted that not all slopes are open yet.

In Saas-Fee, some ski lifts on the Allalin Glacier have also reopened after being shut since mid-August. Keeping them running requires a considerable effort, Simon Bumann, director of Saastal Bergbahnen, told Swiss public broadcaster SRF. The slopes are being prepared using snow stored from last winter.

Russian forces strike Kharkiv with guided bombs, killing woman and injuring eight
As reported by Ukrinform, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov and Head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration Oleh Syniehubov said this on Telegram.
“Kharkiv has been attacked with enemy guided aerial bombs – a residential area in the Nemyshlianskyi district is under attack. There is a fire at the site of the strike. We are establishing the details,” Terekhov wrote.
He later reported that a strike hit the grounds of a car service station near private homes, some of which were damaged.
The mayor reported three people injured, two private houses completely destroyed and around 15 more damaged by the blast wave. Several cars also caught fire.
Terekhov later clarified that the person rescued from under the rubble of a damaged house was a 35-year-old woman. Despite the efforts of medics, she died from her injuries.
For his part, Head of the Regional Military Administration Oleh Syniehubov reported that a guided aerial bomb struck a private residential building in Nemyshlianskyi district. A fire broke out, and parked cars also caught fire.
“At this point, we know of three injured people, including a child, and one woman killed,” the regional governor wrote.
State Emergency Service units and emergency medical crews are working at the site of the strike.
Syniehubov later reported that eight people had been injured.

A Living Canvas: The Ukrainian Museum in New York at 50
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Few art exhibitions can succeed in bringing works as disparate as embroidered shirts and lithographs into conversation.
Yet visitors to “A Living Canvas,” the Ukrainian Museum’s 50th anniversary exhibition in New York, encounter precisely this unexpected juxtaposition: ritual cloths (rushnyky) and women’s blouses bearing traditional Borshchiv embroidery hang from the ceiling alongside prints by the avant-garde artist Alexander Archipenko.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the shirts, black thread is worked into pale hemp cloth to produce intricate linear and floral patterns; the contrast between the dark embroidery and the unembroidered fabric is what gives the designs their structure. In Archipenko’s lithographs, black and white likewise establish relationships between form and empty space.
Although the works differ in medium and purpose, both invite us to consider how complex forms can emerge from a restricted palette and, perhaps more importantly, how decorative art and modernist abstraction can reveal similarity despite the vastly different artistic traditions from which they originate.
The exhibition, on display until Nov. 8, continues in this vein, organizing its collection thematically around color, form, geometry, texture and line, rather than chronologically. In doing so, it challenges the conventional hierarchy between folk and fine art. The village workshop emerges not merely as a source of inherited motifs for the modern artist, but as a site of artistic experimentation in its own right.
US Proposes Economic Incentives to Russia for Limited Truce
The exhibition’s emphasis on continuity is particularly fitting for an institution born of the Ukrainian diaspora. Founded in 1976 by the Ukrainian National Women’s League of America, the museum traces its collection to 1933, when the organization purchased 600 folk-art objects for the Ukrainian pavilion at the Chicago World’s Fair.
These objects, acquired at a time when Ukraine lacked an independent state, became the nucleus of a collection dedicated to preserving its artistic heritage.
Half a century later, that mission has acquired renewed urgency.
Russia’s full-scale invasion has endangered Ukraine’s cultural heritage, with UNESCO having verified damage to 560 cultural sites, including 43 museums, as of Sept. 23, 2026. Against this backdrop, “A Living Canvas” offers an opportunity to consider how artistic traditions persist despite displacement, how cultural memory is sustained despite war, and how a museum might preserve a culture without turning it into a collection of obsolete relics.
Nowhere is this preservation of memory more poignant than in a traditional woven kilim, or rug, depicting geometrized “Tree of Life” symbols with bright reds, yellows and whites. Woven by Anton Krashok for his daughter Ahafiia and donated by his granddaughter Anna Suhy, the rug accompanied the family through the various vicissitudes of the 20th century: Soviet occupation, displacement to the Donbas, the Second World War and eventual immigration to the United States in 1945.
What began life as an ordinary household furnishing became a repository of family history. Its survival across continents and successive waves of displacement speaks to the significance of material culture in sustaining belonging and identity.
The kilim’s inclusion in a subsection of the exhibition devoted to the “Tree of Life” extends its significance beyond the history of a single family. A recurring motif in Ukrainian folk art, the Tree of Life embodies ideas of regeneration as well as the interconnectedness of successive generations.
Here, the woven textiles appear alongside ceramics and contemporary interpretations of the motif, including a pastel by Irma Osadsa where twisting, almost bodily forms move up and circle around a thin trunk; celestial spheres in either corner situate the tree within a cosmic order. The juxtaposition reveals the persistence of aesthetic traditions through which later generations have understood their place in their culture.
On the opposing wall, Christian iconography offers another meditation on the relationship between material objects and spiritual continuity. Here, the visual conventions of Ukrainian religious art are reinterpreted in a strikingly modern style.
In one painting by Christina Saj, depicting the Last Supper, golden circles immediately recall Byzantine icons, in which halos signify holiness, but the figures are stripped of almost all individual attributes. There are no recognizable faces, no elaborate garments, nor identifying inscriptions. Instead, block colors and a stripped-back simplicity transition the beholder into the realm of the spirit.
The proximity of these two subsections reveals a shared preoccupation with the relationship between the earthly and the eternal: both invest material surfaces with meanings that transcend their immediate physical existence.
Yet the exhibition’s commitment to bringing these objects to life is not only confined to the relationships between them: Their physical arrangement transforms the visitor’s encounter with the collection.
Traditional garments hang suspended from the ceiling rather than being confined to mannequins or displayed flat against walls. Woven textiles project into the galleries on angular wooden supports, exposing their folds and undersides. Silhouettes can flicker as visitors can move around them, encountering objects that might otherwise be appreciated only for their decorative surfaces
A similar dialogue unfolds in the section devoted to texture and materiality.
Here, the thickly worked and highly saturated surfaces of Mykhailo Moroz’s canvas recalls the experiments of the Post-Impressionists. Nearby, traditional Hutsul lizhnyky, heavy woollen blankets rooted in the sheep-herding traditions of the Carpathian Mountains, offer another expression of texture. A hanging Hutsul hunia, a thick woollen shepherd’s cloak, makes this relationship between material and labor particularly apparent. Suspended from the ceiling, its shaggy surface projects outward, exposing individual fibres and the garment’s underlying construction.
Areas of mending interrupt its surface, preserving evidence of its previous life. Rather than presenting the cloak as an immaculate example of traditional costume, the display allows its history of use and repair to remain visible.
There is something especially fitting about this approach in an exhibition devoted to cultural preservation. The museum’s collection is not composed exclusively of objects produced for aesthetic contemplation. Many were worn, handled, repaired and inherited before eventually entering its holdings. Their accumulated traces of use form part of their historical significance.
By exposing their construction and allowing visitors to examine them from different angles, the exhibition makes the labor of their makers and the lives of their former owners more readily apparent.
A central gallery provides the exhibition with a final flourish, celebrating the vibrant colors of Ukrainian visual culture.
In contrast to the opening monochrome subsection, the rich palette of traditional costume and decorative art finds counterparts in modernist and contemporary painting. Three hand-woven panels separated by a meter of space hang from the ceiling in the centre of the room.
Jaroslava Lialia Kuchma’s 1997 “My Father’s Grove” is suspended to allow the visitor to move around and between, to view all sides and angles as if, quite literally, moving through a forest. On a side wall, a collection of oil paintings by Ilona Sochynsky.
These exuberant abstractions seem almost unable to contain themselves. Sweeping ribbons of saturated color twist across the canvas, while neighboring compositions burst beyond the conventional rectangular frame, their irregular edges transforming painting into something approaching sculpture.
The forms suggest petals, bodies, even cosmic landscapes without settling into any single representation. Vibrant colors and rhythmic patterns associated with traditional decorative arts are in this way liberated from recognizable motifs and reimagined as abstract movement.
The exhibition’s greatest achievement is perhaps its refusal to present cultural preservation as an exercise in nostalgia. Its unusual arrangements encourage visitors to discover new relationships between objects separated by centuries and artistic purpose.
Traditional garments become sculptural forms; household textiles become interlocutors for modernist abstraction. The open-plan nature of the space allows for free movement between otherwise disconnected subsections.
The emphasis, as the exhibition’s title suggests, is on life not as completed but as an ongoing, dynamic process of “living.” Ukrainian cultural heritage is far from a completed inheritance, but a tradition continually remade, possessing a vitality that persists across time and geography, and even in the face of war.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
