Paris airport protest won't harm Israeli security. But it could complicate things for Elbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:57:39 UTC
21:57:39 KST

Behind the protest at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris on Thursday, which caused the delay of a shipment of components for Israeli defense giant Elbit Systems, lies a complex reality. While relations between the Israeli and French governments are at a nadir, French companies continue to supply components to the Israeli defense industry.
In April, the French newspaper Le Monde published a report documenting hundreds of shipments that arrived in Israel during the October 7 war from 14 French companies, led by defense giants Thales, Safran and ADR. When it comes to weapons, planes or helicopters, you won't find French brands used by the Israel Defense Forces, but many electronic components manufactured in France are integrated into the systems produced by the Israeli defense industry.
According to French government data, the volume of these sales to Israel amounts to only tens of millions of euros per year. However, even trade of limited financial scope can stir up a media storm and cause reputational damage.
On Thursday, French labor organizations reportedly prevented the loading of a shipment of components destined for Elbit via an Air France flight from Charles de Gaulle Airport to Ben-Gurion International Airport, in protest of events in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. Three labor organizations, which include aviation workers in France, pointed to the shipment delay as an achievement. In cooperation with pro-Palestinian organizations, including Urgence Palestine, they called for the prevention of cargo transfers on El Al flights as well.
The shipment included chips and other electronic components. Its delay has no real significance for Israel's security, as some of the stalled goods are intended for products exported from Israel to foreign customers. However, it could damage Elbit's reputation. Shipment delays like the one on Thursday could prompt the company's clients to question whether Elbit can deliver products on schedule.
Such damage could benefit Elbit's French competitors in the international arms market. However, it would also exact on an economic cost to France. The shipment delay harms local companies that supplied components to their Israeli customer and could also lead to a loss of revenue for Charles de Gaulle Airport.
The incident is another sign of the nadir in relations between the Israeli and French governments. In June, the French government restricted the participation of Israeli defense companies at the Eurosatory defense exhibition near Paris, and prevented some companies from exhibiting at all, even after they modified their displays to meet the organizers' demands. "We invested tens of thousands of dollars, flew 12 employees here, and it was all for nothing," said Richard Hecht, marketing manager for Controp, at the time. According to a representative of the Israeli-based OSG company, French government officials made the decision to disqualify the displays.
The French government holds stakes in the company that manages the airport and is also responsible for regulatory oversight of its operations. French authorities could have acted quickly to curb the crisis over the goods destined for Israel. However, in the current political climate, it seems that France was even willing to incur damage to French companies rather than intervene.
Between boycotts and mega-deals
The sanctions by cargo workers at the Paris airport are currently no more than symbolic on an economic level. However, they raise concerns about whether the Israeli decision not to end the war in Gaza and Lebanon will lead to similar actions at other ports worldwide.
Until a year ago, during a period of high-intensity fighting in Gaza and the north, there were more reports of ports refusing to allow Israeli goods to pass through their territory. These incidents have almost ceased in the past year with the perception that the war has ended.
As of today, Israeli industries continue to benefit from the surge in demand for weapons in international markets and have announced mega-deals in the Gulf states, Greece, Germany, India and elsewhere. While Israeli real estate and food companies were blacklisted by the United Nations two weeks ago due to their activities in the West Bank, Israeli defense companies remain unaffected by such sanctions. The IDF may use these products in its operations in the West Bank and Gaza, but as long as the weapons are not manufactured in Nablus or Hebron, the UN has no issue with them.
In the same week that components destined for Elbit were delayed at the Paris airport, Israeli defense giants featured prominently at the Marrakech Air Show 2026 in Morocco, a country that is home to some 40 million Muslims. While Israeli defense companies had to contend with restrictions and even closure of their pavilions at the French exhibit in June, they had no such problems in Morocco where eight Israeli defense companies showcased their wares.
The Marrakech exhibition featured loitering munitions, AI-based robotic systems, autonomous navigation capabilities for drones, laser guidance for FPV drones and satellite communication. The Israeli companies displayed both their defensive and offensive products without being required to specify where they are employed. In fact, the Moroccan defense minister and chief of staff even visited the Israel Aerospace Industries pavilion.

Britain to fly hypersonic target from Hebrides range
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:55:51 BST
21:55:51 KST

A target vehicle able to replicate threats travelling at more than five times the speed of sound is being built under Project Bowline, with a live flight demonstration planned at the MOD Hebrides Range in 2027, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State to set out the full requirements of the hypersonic target to be delivered under the project.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State at the Ministry of Defence, said: “Project Bowline is delivering a hypersonic target capability to support the development, evaluation and testing of missile defence systems against advanced threats. The programme will design, manufacture, qualify and test a target vehicle capable of replicating emerging high-speed threats travelling at speeds in excess of Mach 5.
“The capability will provide a realistic test environment for missile defence research, development and experimentation, supporting the United Kingdom’s contribution to allied air and missile defence. A live flight demonstration of the capability is planned at the MOD Hebrides Range in 2027.
“Details of the full technical requirements are commercially and operationally sensitive and therefore will not be released.”
Testing an interceptor against a realistic hypersonic threat requires something to shoot at, and few countries have one. A target that flies above Mach 5 lets designers prove tracking, discrimination and engagement against the kind of manoeuvring, high-speed object that current air defence radars and effectors were not built to handle.
The choice of the Hebrides range is of course coupled with an announcement made this week, when Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard signed an agreement with QinetiQ at the site covering the first design stage of a multimillion-pound investment to develop it for the testing of hypersonic missiles and other advanced technologies. That work was announced as part of Project Safari, the joint Ministry of Defence and QinetiQ programme opening test and evaluation facilities to smaller companies.

Deutsche Bank chief warns German election results worrying foreign investors
BERLIN, Oct 11 - The head of Germany's largest bank warned that foreign investors may be driven away following victories in state elections last month by parties on the political extremes.
The AfD, which wants to restrict immigration and send asylum seekers home, scored some of its biggest-ever wins in eastern Germany last month. At the same time, the Left Party scored its biggest win in the election for the city government of Berlin, pledging to expropriate holdings of property companies.
"This poses a significant risk to Germany, and it should not be played down," Christian Sewing, chief executive of Deutsche Bank, told the Bild daily in an interview, referring to the rise of political extremes.
"You can't expect a foreign investor to immediately draw a distinction between a state government and Germany as a whole," he said. "It's seen as Germany as a whole and I think that from an investor's point of view, that's understandable."
In the state of Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD, which is classified by security services as extremist in some regions, only narrowly fell short of an absolute majority in the state parliament, and it followed up two weeks later by taking first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The AfD has been accused by economists of fostering a climate that will drive away badly needed skilled workers and foreign investors.
The Left Party, meanwhile, vowed to tackle Berlin's soaring housing costs by expropriating the holdings of residential property companies.
"And whether it's Saxony-Anhalt with the AfD or what's happening here in Berlin, it's anything but conducive to economic growth. And it's anything but investment-friendly," Sewing said.
He urged the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz to carry on with reforms to revive the economy.
"That is the only response we have to the far-right and far-left extremists in this country," he said. REUTERS

European Commission wants to tighten visa issuance for Russians in 2027 — newspaper

2026-10-11
12:42:37 UTC
21:42:37 KST

BRUSSELS, October 11. /TASS/. The European Commission is preparing a plan to tighten Schengen visa issuance for Russians starting in January 2027, citing certain Russian "hybrid threats," Politico reported.
According to the newspaper, the European Commission intends to propose "tighter visa rules for hundreds of thousands of Russians who visit EU countries as tourists each year." Politico pointed out, citing its sources, that Brussels is thus attempting, in particular, to prevent 650,000 veterans of the special military operation from entering the EU.
The newspaper noted Sweden, Poland, and Estonia actively support these restrictions, stating that Russian tourists pose a hybrid threat to the European defense industry, which produces weapons for Ukraine.
The specifics of the restrictions have not yet been disclosed.
EU visa policy is not within the European Commission’s jurisdiction; it remains a priority for the bloc’s member states. The European Commission can only issue recommendations on changing visa issuance rules. For this decision to become binding on all EU countries, it must be approved by all member states in the EU Council at the interior minister level.
Despite the restrictions, according to Eurostat data, the number of Schengen visas issued to Russians increased by 10.2% in 2025 compared to 2024, reaching 620,000. Of these, 478,000 were tourist visas, and the remainder were issued for family reunification and other travel purposes.

Hive Dwellers vs. Screen Players: Anatomy of Two Societies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:40:03 UTC
21:40:03 KST

This question has puzzled many wise individuals in the West—and echoed through the stunned minds of Trump and Netanyahu alike: Why, following the assassination of the leadership, did the Iranian government not collapse like other countries?
In the first week, a thoughtful friend in the West posed this question to me via email. To answer it thoroughly and achieve a precise understanding by invoking Shia history and Imam Hussain might well prove incomprehensible to a Western mind. Therefore, I tried to frame my answer using concepts drawn from Western literature itself. I wrote to my friend recounting a research book by Maurice Maeterlinck, titled The Life of the Bee, which a kind neighbor gifted to me in my youth before the revolution.
The point I am about to share may make the aforementioned question easier for a Western reader to grasp. Maeterlinck notes that before a real-world experiment, all researchers assumed the sovereign ruler of the hive was the queen, and that everything existed to serve her and her desires. Consequently, they set up an experiment: they placed a ring at the entrance of a beehive through which worker and soldier bees could pass easily, but which the queen, due to her larger body, could not traverse.
They then staged a mock attack on the hive. Following their natural instinct, the bees mobilized to save the queen first. Since the only exit from the besieged hive was through that ring, the queen became stuck in it while trying to escape. After some time, her protective guards assumed she was refusing to leave. They stung her to death, selected another larva capable of becoming a queen to replace her, and established a new hive with a young queen elsewhere.
 
The scientist's conclusion is profound and fascinating. From then on, he stripped the title of "God of the Hive" from the queen, redefining that supreme force as the "invisible spirit of the hive."
This is precisely what happened in Iran, with one difference: the true executioners this time were real aggressors, yet once again, their aggressive methods failed to conquer the invisible spirit of the hive.
I will elaborate on the difference between a nation whose god is the invisible spirit of the hive and the populations of other countries with more precise explanations. I have a filmmaker friend named Seyyed Reza Mirkarimi, the director of several monumental works in Iranian cinema whose name and films you can look up. He offers a striking interpretation of those countries surrounding Iran that have only been independent for a few decades. He compares them to cinematic backlots during the production of grand Hollywood epics.
To better understand his analogy, imagine a film about the era of Alexander the Great being shot on a set in Cinecittà in Rome—thousands of extras, towering props, and magnificent scenery.
Viewed from the camera angle, on the big screen, or even in IMAX, we marvel at its grandeur. Even the actors, deeply immersed in their roles through rehearsal, believe in their characters for a time. Yet once the false glamour of the screening subsides, or filming concludes, they realize they merely stepped out of their true selves for a brief spell to live in someone else's skin.
Once shooting wraps, all those grand sets are dismantled and replaced by another set of deceptive facades. That is the sum total of a magnificent, dazzling life lived in a cinematic backlot devoid of true identity. Perhaps the very next day after filming ends, even the lead actor is not permitted to enter, wander around, or reminisce about the past.
The disparity between many newly established Arab states—filled with heterogeneous racial populations like Pakistanis, Indians, and others—and the original indigenous
 
Ahmadzadeh Haj Habib: Arab inhabitants mirrors precisely the role of these film extras. Their sole reason for presence is to collect a paycheck and grab a slice of that fleeting fame and profit for tomorrow, without leaving any lasting impact on the future of that cinematic backlot.
 
Yet the Iranian nation—and even the leadership that was assassinated—believe in the spirit of the hive. That is why, for two hundred and twenty days, men and women, young and old, have stood steadfastly in the public squares and streets.   
In closing, I recommend that you, the reader of this essay, seek out and read the legendary Persian tale The Conference of the Birds by the Iranian poet Attar of Nishapur. The plot is briefly as follows: a flock of birds from across the world gathers to find a mythical bird named the Simurgh atop Mount Qaf and make him their leader. On the final day of the journey, atop Mount Qaf, only thirty diverse birds remain; the rest have fallen behind along the way for various excuses. They do not behold a mythical Simurgh; instead, they realize that the legendary Simurgh is, in fact, their own collective gathering. They no longer need to wait for a miraculous bird to lead them.

Denmark tests humanoid robots in supermarkets to help to ease staff workload at night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:37:05 UTC
21:37:05 KST

Picking up products, placing them on shelves and repeating the same movements for hours. At a Føtex supermarket near Copenhagen, robots are learning to perform one of the most time-consuming jobs in retail.
Developed by Danish start-up Hive Robots and built by China's Unitree, the machines have been training since June. For now, human operators guide every movement, helping the artificial intelligence learn how to handle different products.
The ambition is to have them restocking shelves independently by early 2027, working mainly at night when the supermarket is closed.
The experiment is part of a wider trial with Salling Group, Denmark's largest retailer, which has more than 2,000 stores in six European countries.
According to Føtex, workers spend between 40 and 50 per cent of their time replenishing shelves. The retailer hopes robots will eventually take on some of this repetitive physical work, giving employees more time to assist customers.
The machines could later check expiry dates, identify empty shelves and spot misplaced goods. But they still work more slowly than people and need close supervision.
Danish law would also have to change before robots could operate autonomously among shoppers. For now, the focus remains on night-time work and tasks away from customers.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s worst diplomatic nightmare just got closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:36:05 UTC
21:36:05 KST

Ukraine’s worst diplomatic nightmare just got closer
On the evening of October 9, the presidents of the United States and Russia spoke by phone. The announcement that followed was straightforward: Russia would sell the US 1.8 million metric tons of diesel over the next three months, followed by a million tons a month, and the US would issue temporary licenses authorizing the shipments.
The news drew a furious, bordering on hysterical, response from Kiev and stunned silence from Europe.
Let’s look at why this deal matters, what it has to do with Ukraine, and what might come next.
The tug-of-war championship
Ever since US President Donald Trump returned to office, the central aim of Russian diplomacy has been to separate relations with the US from the Ukraine issue. The White House is open to the idea, too: The US needs Russia as a counterweight to China, and there are substantial economic opportunities. But as we explored in an earlier piece, until recently, neither side managed to pull it off.
Ukraine and its supporters in Europe and the US, meanwhile, have pursued the opposite goal: keeping US-Russia relations tied to the Ukraine conflict.
In February and March 2025, Trump relieved America of responsibility for Ukraine’s fate and handed the job of financing it squarely to Europe. The US retained just three commitments: the relatively modest military supply programs already approved under former President Joe Biden, intelligence sharing, and weapons sales for cash, with Ukraine waiting in line like any other customer.
This maneuver cemented a status quo that neither Europe and Ukraine on one side nor Russia on the other would allow to change, with their respective allies in the US also weighing in. Everyone tried to bring Trump over to their side on Ukraine. Nobody succeeded.
This is why the understandings reached in Anchorage went nowhere: Ukraine’s supporters torpedoed them. It is also why those supporters failed to use Trump to escalate the conflict. Russia prevented deliveries of Tomahawk missiles, the expansion of Starlink coverage over Russian territory, and so on.
Despite the apparent stalemate, Russian officials kept talking to Witkoff and Kushner. The aim was to maintain a channel to Trump and deny Ukraine’s supporters an opening to drag the US back into the war on their side or steer him back onto Biden’s course.
This is why Russian officials at every level distinguish between US and European actions, often explicitly contrasting the two.
A few numbers on oil
Russia is one of the world’s largest diesel exporters, supplying just under 40 million metric tons to the global market in 2025. On July 8, 2026, Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries prompted a temporary ban on diesel and gasoline exports.
Since then, Russia’s refining situation has improved considerably. Gasoline remains in short supply, but a domestic diesel surplus has emerged, and the export ban has begun to loosen in practice. According to Reuters, diesel deliveries to Central Asian countries were already up 19% in September.
Rising diesel production was only part of the story. The end of the harvest season also reduced demand. And as the seasons change, Russia switches to winter-grade fuel, traditionally selling off its remaining summer-grade stocks to countries with warmer climates.
One way or another, seaborne diesel exports were heading toward a restart. Trump had also raised that possibility, publicly linking it to Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.
The Krivoy Rog school of diplomacy
Back to geopolitics. Until yesterday, Russia had been unable to separate its relationship with the US from the Ukraine issue. Even the war with Iran failed to do the trick, despite keeping oil and petroleum product shipments from the Persian Gulf blocked for more than six months.
Help came from an unexpected quarter. Hoping to bring US diesel prices down at least a little before the congressional elections, Trump asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian refineries.
Zelensky responded by demanding a sweeping energy truce. We’ll stop hitting refineries, he effectively said, if Russia stops attacking our energy infrastructure and blockading our ports. And you, Trump, have to supply us with missiles for our Patriot systems, and so on.
Getting nowhere with Zelensky, Trump struck a deal directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who offered to supply diesel in exchange for a suspension of sanctions, without any preconditions.
The transaction itself is not particularly consequential. Yes, it could cool speculative trading ahead of the elections and push prices down somewhat. But the 1.8 million metric tons due to arrive over three months will cover just three or four days of American consumption.
For Russia, the US is an ordinary customer in purely commercial terms. Moscow will make some money selling to America, but it could just as easily have sold these volumes elsewhere. Petroleum products are in short supply worldwide, while Russia has a diesel surplus.
Yet the deal gave both sides what they had been seeking since February 2025: a bilateral relationship detached from Ukraine. So far, that applies to just one specific issue, but getting started is the hard part. Zelensky tried to twist Trump’s arm, pushing him to make Putin stop bombing Kiev, and overplayed his hand. Now Kiev can be bombed relentlessly, and Trump has no reason to care. He got what he wanted.
This does not mean sanctions are finished or that the two powers are entering an era of warm friendship. Oil sanctions are probably here to stay, and as soon as global market conditions change, Washington will turn them back up to full blast. But the sanctions wall can now be taken apart brick by brick, restoring ties wherever both sides stand to gain: launching new energy projects in the Arctic, for example, jointly taking over the surviving Nord Stream 2 pipeline, or resolving the sale of Lukoil’s overseas assets. Ukraine no longer has anything to do with that process or any influence over it.
The art of the backroom deal
Cynics insist that the Trump administration is a complete mess, with the right hand oblivious to what the left is doing. The way this agreement came together suggests otherwise.
After the campaign of long-range strikes against Russia went badly off script, Zelensky once again tried to secure a ceasefire through Trump. He has been trying since early 2025, with no success, but he still held out hope.
Trump could have publicly given Zelensky the boot again. But on Ukraine, he faces opposition not only from Congress but also from parts of his own administration. And an election is just around the corner.
Instead of staging a public showdown, Trump’s team spent more than two months visibly engaged in intensive talks with Ukraine about an energy truce. His envoys, Witkoff and Kushner, traveled to Kiev, and Trump himself showered Zelensky with compliments. In reality, all of it proved to be a screen for a quiet, swift, informal deal with Moscow.
It has since emerged that the first tanker carrying diesel to the US left St. Petersburg on September 22 and is expected to reach the US any day now. In other words, the deal was already well advanced three weeks ago, and both sides were confident it would go through.
That takes some skill. This episode shows that Trump keeps a firm grip on his team and can prevent leaks when he needs to. Even Rubio, prone to breaking ranks, played his part exactly as the boss wanted.
And once the deal was done, there was no longer any need to smile at Zelensky in public. The masks came off. For the first time, Trump publicly declared that Ukraine needs a new president and must hold elections.
The liberal media will inevitably say that Trump is repeating Russian propaganda narratives. In fact, he was saying what he thinks.
***
The diesel deal does not mean Moscow and Washington will now live in perfect harmony. The differences between them are deep and fundamental, and the recently enacted ‘Graham law’ makes lifting any sanctions impossible for at least the next five years.
But this Friday, Putin and Trump finally managed to get past Ukraine and leave it behind. US-Russia relations now depend on Russia and the US alone.

Berlin dringt an der Spitze einer Gruppe von sechs Ländern auf einen sparsameren EU-Haushalt. Zu der Gruppe gehören Schweden, Dänemark, die Niederlande, Finnland und Österreich. Die sechs Länder tragen zusammen 40 Prozent zum EU-Haushalt bei.
Der Vorschlag der EU-Kommission für den nächsten Siebenjahreshaushalt beträgt knapp 2 Billionen Euro.
Die schwedische Europaministerin Jessica Rosencrantz bezeichnete Irlands Vorschlag als „völlig unerschwingliche Erhöhung“, da der Gesamtbetrag immer noch über dem aktuellen Haushalt liegen würde.
Die österreichische Europaministerin Claudia Bauer erklärte, der neue Haushalt sei nach wie vor „meilenweit von einem österreichischen Ja entfernt“.
Der Haushalt wird auch Thema beim Gipfeltreffen der EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs am Donnerstag und Freitag in Brüssel sein.
Die EU-Regierungen wollen bis Ende des Jahres eine Einigung erzielen – bevor die Wahlen in Frankreich, Italien und Polen im Jahr 2027 die Verhandlungen zu gefährden drohen.
Die EU ist gespalten zwischen sparsamen Ländern, die auf Kürzungen dringen, und einem rivalisierenden Lager aus süd- und osteuropäischen Staaten, die sich gegen Kürzungen bei Agrarsubventionen und der regionalen Wirtschaftsförderung aussprechen. Diese Bereiche machen fast die Hälfte des Gesamtbudgets aus.
Der Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

Israel brings a balloon-borne radar to the U.S. Army show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:28:00 UTC
21:28:00 KST

- Israel Aerospace Industries will unveil POINT@AIR, a compact, mobile aerostat-mounted AESA radar based on its ELM-2083 family, at AUSA 2026.
- IAI did not disclose the radar’s range, operating altitude, price or any customers.
Israel Aerospace Industries will show a new radar carried by a small tethered balloon at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, aimed at giving ground forces a mobile, elevated view of low-flying drones, aircraft and other targets.
The system, called POINT@AIR, puts an active electronically scanned array radar on a compact aerostat, a tethered, helium-filled balloon that can hold a sensor high above the ground for long periods. IAI says the radar can detect and track multiple air, sea and ground targets, prioritize them, and feed the data to command-and-control systems. The company says it can be moved quickly and does not need permanent infrastructure. IAI did not disclose the radar’s range, the balloon’s operating altitude, how long it can stay aloft, the size of the crew or the price, and it has not announced a customer.
Raising a radar off the ground lets it see past hills, buildings and the curve of the Earth, which block ground-based radars from spotting low-flying targets until they are close. POINT@AIR is based on IAI’s ELM-2083 radar family. Its radar steers its beam electronically in both directions and also rotates mechanically to give 360-degree coverage, according to the company.
“Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense. The more persistent and comprehensive that view becomes, the better equipped forces are to understand what is unfolding, anticipate threats and act with confidence. IAI is increasingly developing the next-generation capabilities that expand the boundaries of situational awareness and provide our customers with greater visibility, flexibility and time to respond,” said Guy Bar Lev, president and CEO of IAI.
The original ELM-2083 is a larger L-band early-warning radar carried by aerostats and derived from the Green Pine radar used in Israel’s Arrow missile defense system. IAI’s ELTA Systems subsidiary has supplied it to several countries, including India. POINT@AIR is meant to bring the same idea to a smaller, more mobile setup that can move with forces.
“Our goal was not simply to reduce the size of an existing solution, but to rethink what an aerostat-based radar could achieve. By combining advanced AESA technology, long-range detection and 360-degree coverage in a compact configuration, POINT@AIR gives operators the ability to establish persistent awareness where fixed infrastructure may not be practical,” said Dror Bar, CEO of ELTA Systems and an executive vice president at IAI.
Aerostat radars have a mixed history with the U.S. Army. The service used smaller camera-carrying aerostats to watch over bases in Iraq and Afghanistan, but it canceled the much larger JLENS cruise missile defense program after one of its aerostats broke loose from its mooring in Maryland in 2015 and drifted over Pennsylvania.

Sweet protein brazzein shows promise in reducing blood sugar spikes: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:23:37 UTC
21:23:37 KST

Sweet protein brazzein shows promise in reducing blood sugar spikes: Study
Study shows that the sweet protein Brazzein could help reduce blood sugar spikes caused by eating ice cream.
A new study has shown how the sweet protein brazzein could help reduce blood sugar spikes, the Science Alert news outlet reported.
Brazzein is a natural protein originally found in the West African oubli plant, but now largely produced through a fermentation process. It is known for its intense sweetness and has long been eyed as a potential sugar alternative.
Researchers at Russia’s Federal Research Centre of Nutrition, Biotechnology and Food Safety conducted a test on 101 adults living with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The condition, where fat builds up in the liver, is often associated with diabetes and obesity.
The study, published in the Clinical Nutrition ESPEN journal, was a randomised trial that focused on ice cream.
Participants ate a 100 gram vanilla ice cream serving on three separate days: one with sugar, one with brazzein, and one day with brazzein and a fibre called inulin.
Post-meal blood sugar spikes were lower when participants consumed the brazzein or brazzein and inulin versions, compared with the sugar-sweetened version, the study showed.
The reductions in sugar spikes were most notable in participants with type 2 diabetes, according to the study.
“Longer-term studies are needed to determine whether repeated substitution of sucrose-containing desserts with brazzein-sweetened alternatives translates into sustained metabolic, hepatic, microbiome, or behavioural benefits,” the researchers wrote.
The negative health effects of sugar have been widely researched and debated over the years.
The World Health Organization advised in 2023 against the use of non-sugar sweeteners for weight control, and released guidelines warning of “potential undesirable effects” from their long-term use, such as an increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

KYIV — Russia's Vladimir Putin is preparing for a broader confrontation with Europe amid an uptick in the Kremlin's hybrid attacks on the continent, Ukraine's former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba has warned.
In an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Kuleba, who was Ukraine's foreign policy chief from 2020 to 2024, said that Russia's continued war preparations and anti-European propaganda are signs that Putin is planning attacks on other European countries.
"Anti-European hysteria is being fueled in Russia, which I interpret as the preparation for a broader conflict with the rest of Europe," said Kuleba, before adding: "We [Ukrainians] don't have to drag you — Putin will drag you into the war."
Advertisement
European officials say Moscow has upped its hybrid campaign across the continent in recent months, using cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to disrupt critical infrastructure and weaken support for Ukraine.
Kuleba said the failed drone attack on the Leipzig airport in Germany in August was a sign of "growing preparation" for an offensive on the continent. "They see how your intelligence operates. They see how your security forces operate. They see how you react and they draw conclusions," he added.
In the aftermath of the incident, the German government concluded that Moscow was responsible for the attack, and ordered a review of security around sensitive locations.
However, Kuleba, who stood down as Ukraine's foreign policy chief in September 2024, does not think Russia is preparing a full-scale offensive beyond Ukraine. In his view, Moscow is more likely to launch an attack on NATO countries involving drones targeting key infrastructure that would test the alliance's unity and preparedness.
"The truth is that Russia does not need 400,000 more people to wage that war. It needs five drones," he said, adding that in the event of an attack, "[Europeans] can call for NATO consultations... can call for restraint. But this will only encourage Putin to make the next step ... He will always have enough drone and missile capabilities."
Kuleba no longer believes Putin can be persuaded to end the war through negotiations. "He's not looking for a solution, for a pause, and there will be no moment when he will start looking for it," he said, concluding: "Putin is a guarantee of war: anyone after Putin is a chance for peace."
Advertisement
According to Kuleba, any attempts at negotiating with Putin, or pushing for peace, are a waste of time. "The sooner we come to terms with reality, the better policies we can develop to address it," he said.
He noted that while Europe’s political culture is based on "a win-win approach" in which both sides can benefit, Putin’s outlook is very different: “For him, a solution that benefits both sides is not the best option. For him, the world works on the principle of victory and defeat. One side has to win and the other has to lose,” said Kuleba.
The former foreign minister also warned that Ukraine would face its worst ever winter as Moscow ups its attacks against civilians in a bid to break their spirit.
In recent months, Russian strikes have hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and transport links, including bridges over the Dnipro river, as well as homes and civilian sites such as bus stops, schools, postal depots and internet providers. The attacks have disrupted power, transport and daily life as winter approaches.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in a Russian attack on two buses in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Kuleba explained why he believed Moscow has now sharply escalated its airstrikes: “The bombing of cities is a direct consequence of Russia’s failure to defeat Ukraine on the battlefield.” He continued: “The main target of Russian drones and missiles is the Ukrainians’ will to resist — but also the will of Ukraine’s friends abroad to keep supporting it.”
Advertisement
He added:“They don’t just want to turn out the lights in Ukraine. They want to paralyze the country.”
Kuleba described the worst-case scenario in Ukraine as “the collapse of the systems that make life in a big city possible,” such as electricity, water and drainage services.
Could Russia succeed? “I believe Ukraine is too large, too mobile and too adaptable. That’s why I think we’ll get through this winter," said Kuleba.
"The price will be much higher than last year's."

Once considered “taboo,” Russian assassination plots against European defense executives are escalating as its hybrid warfare grows bolder, intelligence agencies warn – FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:21:35 UTC
21:21:35 KST

Russia is expanding efforts to target European defense industry leaders as part of a broader campaign of sabotage and hybrid operations aimed at weakening support for Ukraine, the Financial Times reported on 11 October, citing officials from five European intelligence agencies.
The warnings come amid a wider increase in Russia-linked sabotage and other covert operations targeting European defense companies and critical infrastructure. Moscow is expanding its so-called hybrid warfare campaign against European countries as they continue to support Ukraine, using covert networks, intimidation, and suspected sabotage to undermine security and deter further assistance to Kyiv.
The FT reported that assassinations of civilian targets in Europe, once considered "taboo" even within Russian intelligence services, are becoming an increasingly prominent part of the Kremlin’s plans.
Russian operatives target defense industry leaders
European intelligence officials told the FT that Russian operatives are targeting chief executives and senior employees at defense companies, including smaller firms manufacturing drones and drone components.
The campaign comes as Russia seeks to undermine European backing for Ukraine amid a battlefield stalemate and mounting pressure on the Russian economy.
The warnings have prompted defense companies to strengthen security around senior executives. Some have increased personal protection, while others have relocated production sites in response to suspected Russian threats, according to the FT.
Germany's domestic intelligence service, the BfV, has stepped up contact with employees and management at German defense companies and recommended that some use privately contracted close-protection teams, an agency official told the newspaper.
BfV chief Sinan Selen warned German lawmakers that Russia was deliberately planning acts of violence against individuals through state or state-controlled actors. He said the operations were evolving in their targets, methods, and use of organized crime networks.
Russia adapts its methods to carry out attacks
According to the intelligence officials cited by the FT, Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, has adapted its methods by working more closely with criminal groups and dividing surveillance, logistics, planning, and execution among different operatives.
Officials said some plots had been disrupted, while other cases involved surveillance of targets at home and at work.
The campaign's intended effect extends beyond any individual attack. One European intelligence official told the FT that the threat is psychological, designed to make people reconsider doing business with Ukraine.
Although some Russian operations remain amateurish and have been detected early, the resulting uncertainty forces companies to devote more resources to security. Smaller firms, which may have fewer resources to protect their personnel and facilities, could be particularly vulnerable.
Plot against Rheinmetall CEO raised alarm in 2024
European defense executives have been on heightened alert since 2024, when US and German intelligence agencies uncovered a Russian plot against Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger, a prominent advocate of supplying weapons to Ukraine.
Papperger has said he now receives round-the-clock protection from private security personnel and police.
The FT reported that European intelligence agencies now view threats against defense industry leaders as part of a broader effort to disrupt the production and supply of weapons to Ukraine, rather than isolated plots against individual executives.

Hotels account for most of Taiwan’s illegal lodging fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:16:45 UTC
21:16:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Unlicensed hotels accounted for most of the NT$143.39 million (~US$4.49 million) in fines imposed on illegal accommodation businesses across Taiwan from January through September this year.
The Tourism Administration recorded 1,600 unlicensed businesses, including 1,068 hotels and 532 guesthouses, per CNA. Hotel fines totaled NT$121.27 million, compared with NT$22.12 million for guesthouses.
Tainan led hotel fines with NT$29.75 million, while Taitung County recorded the highest guesthouse fine total at NT$4.83 million, per UDN.
The number of unlicensed guesthouses fell by 41 from a year earlier, but unlicensed hotels increased by 132. Daily apartment rentals made up 760 of the unlicensed hotels, including all 275 listed in Taipei.
Local inspections helped identify more unlicensed hotels, the administration said, while daily apartment rentals also increased in urban areas. Authorities conducted 4,054 hotel inspections and 9,247 guesthouse inspections nationwide.
Taiwan had 16,142 licensed accommodation businesses: 12,872 guesthouses and 3,270 hotels.
Higher statutory penalties contributed to the fine total, the administration said. Changes introduced on April 2, 2025, raised the maximum fine for operating an unlicensed hotel to NT$2 million and an unlicensed guesthouse to NT$1 million.
Fines of up to NT$1.5 million also apply to advertising illegal accommodation on social media, websites, or elsewhere.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Australia’s Northern Territory Legislative Assembly established a Parliamentary Friends of Taiwan group on Friday.

The Northern Territory’s group will strengthen support for Taiwan across Australia and help bring greater international recognition to its contributions, he added.
Fan said Taiwan and the Northern Territory could deepen cooperation in technology, energy, agriculture, education, tourism, culture, and Indigenous affairs.

‘Putin will drag you into the war,’ former Ukrainian foreign minister tells Europeans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:16:13 UTC
21:16:13 KST

KYIV — Russia's Vladimir Putin is preparing for a broader confrontation with Europe amid an uptick in the Kremlin's hybrid attacks on the continent, Ukraine's former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba has warned.
In an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Kuleba, who was Ukraine's foreign policy chief from 2020 to 2024, said that Russia's continued war preparations and anti-European propaganda are signs that Putin is planning attacks on other European countries.
"Anti-European hysteria is being fueled in Russia, which I interpret as the preparation for a broader conflict with the rest of Europe," said Kuleba, before adding: "We [Ukrainians] don't have to drag you — Putin will drag you into the war."
Advertisement
European officials say Moscow has upped its hybrid campaign across the continent in recent months, using cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to disrupt critical infrastructure and weaken support for Ukraine.
Kuleba said the failed drone attack on the Leipzig airport in Germany in August was a sign of "growing preparation" for an offensive on the continent. "They see how your intelligence operates. They see how your security forces operate. They see how you react and they draw conclusions," he added.
In the aftermath of the incident, the German government concluded that Moscow was responsible for the attack, and ordered a review of security around sensitive locations.
However, Kuleba, who stood down as Ukraine's foreign policy chief in September 2024, does not think Russia is preparing a full-scale offensive beyond Ukraine. In his view, Moscow is more likely to launch an attack on NATO countries involving drones targeting key infrastructure that would test the alliance's unity and preparedness.
"The truth is that Russia does not need 400,000 more people to wage that war. It needs five drones," he said, adding that in the event of an attack, "[Europeans] can call for NATO consultations... can call for restraint. But this will only encourage Putin to make the next step ... He will always have enough drone and missile capabilities."
Kuleba no longer believes Putin can be persuaded to end the war through negotiations. "He's not looking for a solution, for a pause, and there will be no moment when he will start looking for it," he said, concluding: "Putin is a guarantee of war: anyone after Putin is a chance for peace."
Advertisement
According to Kuleba, any attempts at negotiating with Putin, or pushing for peace, are a waste of time. "The sooner we come to terms with reality, the better policies we can develop to address it," he said.
He noted that while Europe’s political culture is based on "a win-win approach" in which both sides can benefit, Putin’s outlook is very different: “For him, a solution that benefits both sides is not the best option. For him, the world works on the principle of victory and defeat. One side has to win and the other has to lose,” said Kuleba.
The former foreign minister also warned that Ukraine would face its worst ever winter as Moscow ups its attacks against civilians in a bid to break their spirit.
In recent months, Russian strikes have hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and transport links, including bridges over the Dnipro river, as well as homes and civilian sites such as bus stops, schools, postal depots and internet providers. The attacks have disrupted power, transport and daily life as winter approaches.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in a Russian attack on two buses in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Kuleba explained why he believed Moscow has now sharply escalated its airstrikes: “The bombing of cities is a direct consequence of Russia’s failure to defeat Ukraine on the battlefield.” He continued: “The main target of Russian drones and missiles is the Ukrainians’ will to resist — but also the will of Ukraine’s friends abroad to keep supporting it.”
Advertisement
He added:“They don’t just want to turn out the lights in Ukraine. They want to paralyze the country.”
Kuleba described the worst-case scenario in Ukraine as “the collapse of the systems that make life in a big city possible,” such as electricity, water and drainage services.
Could Russia succeed? “I believe Ukraine is too large, too mobile and too adaptable. That’s why I think we’ll get through this winter," said Kuleba.
"The price will be much higher than last year's."

Details
Laura Loomer spoke out against purchasing Russian energy resources, saying that such transactions could help finance the Iranian regime, which openly demonstrates hostility toward the United States.
Buying Russian oil sends money back into the coffers of Iran’s Islamic regime, which chants "Death to America." We know this

In his view, additional revenues from energy sales could help Moscow continue its war against Ukraine.

Abbas postpones Palestinian legislative elections another year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:13:00 UTC
21:13:00 KST

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas attends the inauguration ceremony of the Innovation and Excellence Compound in the West Bank city of Ramallah, Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (AP Photo)
President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority’s credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas’ party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas’ presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met on Oct. 10 to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization’s Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in east Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar on X said that the “attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability.”
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.
Hamas called the postponement “a step in the right direction” and said further talks should focus on rebuilding Palestinian institutions and holding elections at a later date.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas’ Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority’s control are both regularly reported.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's (R) campaign has accused Meta of suppressing his social media posts ahead of a runoff election vote. (AFP Photo)
The campaign of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has accused tech giant Meta of election interference after his social media content was allegedly blocked on the company’s platforms.
The leftist leader is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in the Oct. 25 runoff, where he will face Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.
In a statement, Lula’s campaign reported instances where platforms owned by Meta, the parent company of Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, allegedly restricted the distribution of his content.
The campaign claimed that in recent days, Meta “prevented President Lula’s profile from promoting Instagram feed posts,” while a post from his official account “experienced an interruption in view counts, which affected its reach.”
It also said that prior to Oct. 4’s first round of voting, in which Flavio Bolsonaro finished first, the profiles of Lula and other leftist leaders “suddenly disappeared from Instagram’s search function.”
“The series of technical issues...raises strong suspicions that Meta’s actions constitute an attempt to interfere in the Brazilian electoral process to the benefit of Flavio Bolsonaro’s candidacy,” the statement added.
Meta’s Brazil office denied the charges, calling them “simply false” and “not supported by the facts.”
“Many of the technical issues mentioned did not affect only Brazil or specific accounts,” Meta told AFP in an email.

Feature: Hairatan railway port emerges as trade hub linking Afghanistan to overseas markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:09:57 CST
21:09:57 KST

HAIRATAN, Afghanistan, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Hairatan-Mazar-i-Sharif Railway, locally known as the "Hairatan railway," has emerged as an important trade center connecting landlocked Afghanistan with Central Asian countries and other overseas markets.
The 75-km single-track freight railway connects Afghanistan with Uzbekistan, facilitating the movement of goods from regional markets to the country and providing access to broader trade networks extending to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, China and Europe.
The railway and associated port facilities have helped Afghan traders transport goods and expand their businesses, while the growing volume of cargo has created employment opportunities for local residents, according to traders and railway officials.
"We transport our goods from China by freight train via Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and receive them at Hairatan port," local businessman Ahmad Agha told Xinhua recently at the port.
In 2016, the first cargo train from China reached Hairatan as part of a pilot project. In 2019, Afghanistan sent its first export train to China, carrying several containers of talc powder.
While waiting to receive his goods, Agha said trade with Chinese businesspeople offered promising opportunities. He expressed the hope that further development of railway networks would strengthen commercial ties with Kazakhstan, Russia and European countries in the coming years.
He added that the growing volume of cargo handled at Hairatan port has provided jobs for many local residents, with hundreds of workers handling containers daily to support their families.
Currently, between 280 and 300 wagons arrive at Hairatan railway port daily from Central Asian countries, reflecting the route's importance in Afghanistan's import and export activities, an Afghan railway official said.
"Our trade transactions have increased this year. On average, around 280 to 300 wagons reach Hairatan railway port daily from Central Asian countries," Sayed Qadim Karimi, head of railway transportation at Hairatan port, told Xinhua recently.
Karimi said the railway serves as a major channel for bringing goods into Afghanistan, including clothing, medical equipment, machinery, electrical equipment and other products, noting that trade with China had increased in recent years.
Afghan businessman Ahmad Farid Fardan also welcomed the railway connection, saying it had contributed to stronger trade ties between Afghanistan and China.
"As a businessman who imports goods from China, I can say that the railway connection has strengthened trade relations in the region, particularly between Afghanistan and China, over recent years," he said.
Fardan, who imports women's clothing and colorful fabrics, expressed the hope that further development of the railway network would help Afghanistan expand its trade and economic relations with China and other countries in the region. ■

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's renowned Angkor Archaeological Park is poised for a recovery in international tourist arrivals following government-led efforts to eradicate online scam networks, a scholar said on Sunday.
The UNESCO World Heritage site recorded 510,528 foreign tourists during the first nine months of 2026, marking a 27.6 percent decline year-on-year, according to a report by the state-owned Angkor Enterprise.
This slump dragged down ticket sales revenue to 24.23 million U.S. dollars during the January-September period, representing a 25.9 percent drop compared to the same period in 2025.
Currently, the United States, the United Kingdom, and China remain the largest sources of international visitors to the ancient park.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, expressed optimism that international visitor numbers -- including Chinese arrivals -- will rebound in the coming years.
He noted that the kingdom continues to spare no effort to dismantle online scams to restore its international reputation and regain the confidence of global travelers.
"The steady recovery will be heavily driven by enhanced bilateral cooperation, expanding direct flight routes, and targeted promotional campaigns," he told Xinhua.
"As we lower travel barriers and actively address safety concerns, Angkor's deep cultural and spiritual appeal will undoubtedly continue to draw back both first-time and repeat global travelers," Mengdavid said.
Located in the northwestern Siem Reap province, the 401-square-kilometer Angkor Archaeological Park is Cambodia's premier tourist destination, encompassing 91 ancient temples built between the 9th and 13th centuries.
Cambodian Minister of Tourism Huot Hak recently attributed the downturn in international tourist arrivals to negative publicity, online scam concerns, border friction, and conflicts in the Middle East that have raised fuel costs and dampened global travel enthusiasm. ■

====================================================================================================

Hackers use security cameras to track troops, military targets in Israel, Ukraine - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:05:52 UTC
21:05:52 KST

Internet-connected security cameras and webcams around the world are increasingly being hacked and turned into military intelligence tools, allowing countries including Israel, Iran, Russia, and Ukraine to monitor troop movements, track targets, and assess attacks, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
The growing threat has emerged across multiple conflicts, including those involving Israel and Iran and Russia and Ukraine, as governments and hackers exploit vulnerabilities in devices originally intended to protect homes, businesses, and public spaces.
According to the report, an estimated 1.2 billion internet-connected cameras operate worldwide, creating an enormous network of potential intelligence-gathering devices. Many are inadequately secured, making them attractive targets for cyber operations.
One incident highlighted in the investigation involved a poultry farmer in northern Israel who discovered that the language settings on a camera overlooking his chicken coop had unexpectedly changed to Arabic during the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran earlier this year.
The farmer contacted the Israel National Cyber Directorate, which determined that hackers had compromised the Chinese-made device. The camera's position provided a view of Israeli security activity near the Lebanese border, giving the intruders potential access to military intelligence rather than simply images of the farm.
The directorate subsequently helped the farmer improve the camera's security and change its viewing angle to prevent the surveillance of military operations, according to the WSJ.
Civilian surveillance becomes military intelligence
The incident illustrates a growing challenge for military and civilian cybersecurity authorities: Cameras installed for routine security purposes can become intelligence assets when hostile actors access them.
In Israel, the threat has already prompted warnings from the National Cyber Directorate about the vulnerability of residential and commercial surveillance equipment.
During the June 2025 Israel-Iran war, the directorate urged homeowners and businesses to secure their cameras, warning that hostile actors could exploit compromised devices to gather intelligence and identify security vulnerabilities.
The agency identified weak passwords, outdated software, and cameras directly exposed to the internet as common security weaknesses.
Israel National Cyber Directorate chief Yossi Karadi subsequently revealed that Iran had infiltrated parking and road cameras during the June conflict to monitor the movements of prominent Israelis.
Speaking at a cybersecurity conference in December 2025, Karadi said Iranian hackers had sought to track Israeli figures for potential attacks.
He also disclosed that Iranian operatives had accessed a street camera overlooking the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot shortly before an Iranian ballistic missile struck the institute during the conflict.
The incident demonstrated how compromised surveillance systems could potentially contribute to both intelligence collection and the assessment of military strikes.
In March 2026, Karadi again warned about Iranian efforts to compromise Israeli surveillance cameras, describing the devices as a valuable intelligence-gathering resource. He said the directorate had blocked 50 camera-hacking attempts that could have enabled broader network intrusions.
Israel also exploited Iranian surveillance networks
The intelligence value of compromised cameras works both ways.
Israel reportedly infiltrated Tehran's traffic camera network to monitor senior Iranian officials and collect information used in planning military operations against the Islamic Republic.
According to a Financial Times investigation published in March, Israeli intelligence agencies used hacked traffic cameras and artificial intelligence to establish patterns of movement among senior Iranian figures ahead of the operation that killed then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei.
The reported operation demonstrated the potential military value of combining widely available surveillance infrastructure with advanced data-processing capabilities.
Rather than relying exclusively on satellites, reconnaissance aircraft, or intelligence operatives, security services can potentially exploit networks that already monitor streets, intersections, and buildings.
Iranian officials have publicly acknowledged concerns about foreign access to the country's surveillance infrastructure.
In November 2025, Gholamreza Jalali, then head of Iran's Passive Defense Organization, alleged that Israel and the US were exploiting Tehran's surveillance systems for intelligence operations.
Jalali claimed that foreign code had been discovered in Iranian systems that redirected camera footage to external servers. The allegations were not independently verified.
Russia, Ukraine exploit the same vulnerabilities
The WSJ investigation also described how Russia and Ukraine have used compromised surveillance systems to obtain battlefield intelligence.
According to the report, both sides have exploited cameras to monitor military activity and improve their understanding of enemy positions and operations.
The same vulnerabilities extend beyond active battlefields. Russian-linked cyber actors have reportedly targeted surveillance cameras in European countries to monitor military movements.
The widespread availability of internet-connected cameras creates opportunities for intelligence collection far from conventional military installations.
Artificial intelligence can increase the usefulness of compromised video networks by helping operators process large amounts of footage, identify relevant activity, and recognize patterns that would otherwise require extensive manual monitoring.
Security warnings for camera owners
Cybersecurity specialists warn that many connected cameras are installed without adequate safeguards or ongoing technical maintenance.
Unlike computers and smartphones, which often receive regular security attention, cameras may operate for years with outdated firmware, weak login credentials, or insufficient protection against unauthorized access.
The growing number of cameras connected to private and commercial networks also creates potential entry points for attacks extending beyond the devices themselves.
Israeli cyber authorities have recommended replacing default passwords with strong, unique credentials, enabling two-factor authentication where available, installing security updates, and monitoring devices for unauthorized access.
The risks are especially high near military facilities, transportation routes, government installations, and other sensitive locations, where a seemingly ordinary camera may capture operationally valuable information.
As warfare increasingly combines conventional military operations with cyberattacks and digital intelligence collection, the WSJ investigation underscores how civilian surveillance infrastructure has become another contested element of modern conflict.

Greeting the participants and wishing the event success, Erdoğan expressed his pleasure that the gathering, which he personally announced during a youth meeting in May, was being held in Türkiye.

Erdoğan also congratulated his ruling Justice and Development Party’s (AKP) Directorate for Relations with Turkic States and everyone involved in organizing the gathering, which brought together young people from across the Turkic world under the motto “Shared Heritage, One Heart.”
“I would like to emphasize that our partnership goes far beyond the borders drawn on maps,” he said. “Our journey together is built on a deep-rooted history, a rich culture and very strong bonds of affection,” he added.
“In this regard, I consider it very important that the children of Anatolia come together with you, my young brothers and sisters from different regions of the Turkic world. On Oct. 3, Erdoğan marked Turkic States Cooperation Day in a post on social media.
“On this path of brotherhood... I wish for our unity, togetherness and solidarity to endure,” he wrote.
The agreement, signed on Oct. 3, 2009, established the Cooperation Council of Turkic Speaking States, known as the Turkic Council. Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan were its founding members.
The council grew out of a series of summits of Turkic-speaking countries launched in 1992 after the breakup of the Soviet Union. Uzbekistan joined in 2019, bringing membership to five.
The group adopted its current name, the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), at a summit in Istanbul in November 2021. Hungary, Turkmenistan and Turkish Cyprus hold observer status.

====================================================================================================

People smugglers are still profiting from small boats. Can the UK fix the crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:00:27 UTC
21:00:27 KST

The smuggler works quickly. Using a small shovel, he digs up a dinghy buried in a sand dune on a beach not far from Boulogne-sur-Mer, assembles it and affixes a motor in record time.
“I never saw anyone work like this,” says Amad, from Iraq, one of a group of about 30 asylum seekers waiting to cross the Channel. “The UK government wants to stop the smugglers, but they are smart. They have plan A, plan B and plan C, so there is always a way for them to get people across this sea. For as long as asylum seekers will pay them, there is too much money involved for them to give up.”
The wind has dropped, the waves are flat and there are no French police in sight. The conditions are perfect as the smuggler rushes everyone into the dinghy as it moves away from the shore.
Amad is one of several asylum speakers who spoke to the Guardian this week from the area of northern France known as the Jungle. They were hoping to cross the Channel to the UK in the next few days.
“This place is busier than ever,” says another asylum seeker, Omar, from Yemen. “So many refugees and so many smugglers are here. Everyone wants to cross.”
Some who have already been forcibly removed from the UK are hoping to return. They were sent to France under the “one in, one out” scheme, where one small-boat arrival is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another asylum seeker brought legally to the UK.
Now, after moving approximately 1,500 people in both directions across the Channel, the scheme has been brought to an end. Beset with problems, it could not be effectively scaled up, the British government concluded.
NGOs working on the ground with asylum seekers in northern France were unsurprised by the outcome and say the end of “one in, one out” must prompt a wider discussion about how to deal with the crisis in the Channel.
The UK government has shown little sign it is contemplating a radical shift in attitude. A Home Office spokesperson pointed the Guardian to an announcement about a refugee resettlement scheme that is likely to assist only a few hundred refugees a year and is highly unlikely to stop people crossing the Channel in small boats.
The spokesperson said: “Just last week, the home secretary announced the reopening of the UK resettlement scheme for new referrals, providing genuine refugees with a safe and legal route to the UK.”
The agencies calling for a different approach hope at least to expand the parameters of the debate.
According to workers in the Jungle, living conditions there are appalling. Those at Utopia 56, which witnesses police interventions on French beaches where asylum seekers try to board dinghies, say that since the UK increased its funding to France earlier this year on a payment-by-results basis, police violence against migrants has increased significantly.
Utopia 56 estimates a 40% increase in police violence from April to August 2026 compared with the same period the previous year. That coincided with an agreement for the UK to pay France £660m over three years to ramp up “stop the boats” initiatives.
Sophie McCann, of Médecins Sans Frontières UK, said: “The government’s increasingly brutal efforts to stop people trying to reach the UK by boat are failing. MSF’s medical and mental health teams in Calais and Dunkirk witness the serious physical and psychological harm caused by violence and harassment meted out by French police, largely funded by the UK, on people who have already fled war, persecution and extreme hardship.
“People will continue to risk their lives crossing the Channel in search of safety in the UK until the government provides safe and accessible routes.”
The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union, which has many Home Office staff among its members, has worked with the refugee charity Care4Calais to draw up a blueprint to introduce a refugee visa-to-travel scheme for asylum seekers to travel legally to the UK.
The plan would still require asylum claims to be considered on merit and for those whose claims are rejected to be removed from the UK. But they say it would eliminate people smugglers from the equation and save lives. According to the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IMO), at least 225 people have died while trying to cross the Channel since 2018.
The scheme would be unlikely to halt irregular arrivals entirely, but Care4Calais says it could dent the smugglers’ business in a way that other initiatives have failed to do.
Charlotte Khan, of Care4Calais, said: “Consecutive governments have focused on border security measures that have only made Channel crossings more dangerous, resulting in a shocking number of lives lost, while completely ignoring the only solution that will work – safe routes.”
The PCS general secretary, Fran Heathcote, called for safe routes to be significantly scaled up. “Our members deal with the human impact of the asylum system on a daily basis and their voices must be heard. The only way to truly undermine criminal smuggling gangs is to remove the demand through a Ukrainian-style visa system, allowing people fleeing war and persecution to travel safely and legally to claim asylum.”
The Labour government has arguably made more efforts than any other to try to prevent asylum seekers from reaching the UK in small boats.
Previously, people travelled less visibly, in the backs of lorries or on planes, and so attracted less public attention. Images of black dinghies overcrowded with people in orange lifejackets, monetised for social media clicks by far-right agitators, have generated mounting hostility from some who say they are evidence that the government has lost control of its borders.
But desperate people continue to clamber into dinghies. In the six days between 2 and 7 October, 1,739 people arrived in 23 boats. Along with the now terminated “one in, one out” pilot, which government trumpeted as “groundbreaking” when it announced it in July 2025, the Home Office and the National Crime Agency make regular announcements about smugglers being intercepted and dinghies seized “upstream”.
There has been a reduction of more than 40% in small boat arrivals so far this year compared with the same period last year, probably due to a combination of UK government initiatives, windy weather and a drop in irregular migration to Europe overall. According to data published by the IMO, there has been a 39% reduction this year in these arrivals to Europe – from 98,040 during the same period last year to approximately 60,000.
Despite the reduction in arrivals, far-right agitators wearing masks and black paramilitary clothing continue to protest on the streets and try to block small boat arrivals.
None of the policy roadblocks appear to have dented the resolve of asylum seekers who want to reach the UK.
Sohrab, from Afghanistan, has been sleeping on the streets of Paris and is making his way to the Jungle. “I want to live and I will do anything to save my life from death,” he says. “I have already spent a bad day in jail in France after police caught me trying to get into a lorry heading for the UK. The smugglers are very violent, but there is no other way for me to reach the UK apart than to go to the Jungle.”
Despite the failure of “one in, one out” to deter small boat crossings, Emily Graham, of the Future Governance Forum, believes it is the way forward.
“The ‘one-in, one-out’ pilot proved cooperation based on responsibility-sharing is right in principle and has the potential to deliver results,” she said. “To reduce the number of people arriving by small boat, the government should build on the previous pilot and seek a new ‘routes for returns’ deal with European partners.”
Amad has another idea. “We would much prefer to give our money to the UK government if they allowed us to come here legally, rather than to the smugglers,” he says. “No asylum seeker would pay smugglers who beat and exploit them, or risk our lives on a dinghy, if there was another way.”
