Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:00:26 UTC
21:00:26 KST

A high-altitude desert plateau traverses Argentina, Bolivia and Chile. I am on the Chilean side, sitting in a Jeep along with two other researchers. The afternoon air is thin and brisk but the sun is piercing – a combination I am familiar with from years of living and travelling in South America’s Andean range.
The landscape is a study in contrasts and contours: broad basins suddenly cut off by sweeping curves; flat expanses sliced by near vertical ascents. The Licancabur volcano looms large above us. Vegetation and humidity levels change rapidly with the rising altitude, bringing cooler temperatures, wetter air and denser plant life.
We are driving to the Salar de Atacama – the Atacama salt flats – the largest of several dozen salt flats in northern Chile, and the third largest in the world. The brilliant white flat lies in a high basin 7,500ft above sea level, enclosed by the even higher Andean mountains to the east and the Domeyko mountains to the west.
This striking landscape – the salt flat, the flamingos, and the neighbouring Indigenous communities – is under threat from a counterintuitive source: our efforts to save the planet from catastrophic climate change. Just beneath my feet is nearly one-quarter of the world’s lithium reserves, suspended in water saltier than the ocean.
Lithium is essential to addressing the climate crisis. It is a key ingredient in the rechargeable batteries that play a starring role in eliminating carbon emissions from transportation and energy – the two highest emitting sectors. But extracting this lithium will come at escalating social and environmental costs. It is this dilemma that has brought me to the salt flat.
When it does rain in the Atacama, it’s hard to overstate the intensity of the floods. I once found myself caught in what is called invierno boliviano, or Bolivian winter, a paradoxical name for a weather phenomenon that occurs during the southern hemisphere’s summer months. These rainy fronts originate in the Amazon and travel up the steep slopes of the Andean mountains, where Bolivia’s high-altitude winds then drive them up and over the ridges, until their torrents drench the Chilean high plateau.
The scientific term for closed basins like the Atacama is “endorheic” (etymologically, “inside” and “flow”), for water can flow down into the Atacama basin but it cannot leave – except by evaporation. And this is the key to Atacama’s extraordinary lithium brine.
After deluges like the one I experienced, water pours down the surrounding mountains; during the long dry spells between storms, it trickles down ravines from the precious mountain springs. As it flows, the water leeches lithium from the volcanic rock, picks up wind-scoured lithium dust, and carries it down to the nucleus, or centre, of the salar. This pooled surface water can only escape through evaporation, and with every drop of water that evaporates, the concentration of lithium in the remaining brine increases. Without the parched and sun-blasted Atacama’s extraordinarily high evaporation rate, lithium concentrations would not reach the “economical” levels prized by mining companies.
Yet further lithium enrichment takes place out of sight. Remaining water gradually seeps into the ground, creating underground wells of lithium-rich brine. These wells are linked to complex hydrothermal systems. Then the heat of magma, especially near the Andes’ active fault lines, drives circulations of subsurface brine through fissures and porous geological strata, dissolving even more lithium out of the subsurface rock.
The resulting brine deposits anywhere from four to 200 feet below the Atacama’s salty crust represent a potential bonanza to corporations. The Atacama’s singular coincidence of climactic, geological, geothermal and hydrological conditions makes it one of the least expensive places on Earth to mine lithium.
And at each step, the process of “mining water” is intimately related to the very environmental conditions that formed the valuable deposits in the first place: miners pump the underground brine to vast evaporation ponds on the surface, where natural evaporation concentrates the brine yet again, increasing its lithium levels 40-fold, from approximately 0.15% to a whopping 6%. One cycle of the process can take 10 to 24 months, depending on brine quality and weather conditions.
But this relatively low-cost, low-tech and supposedly low-impact extractive process nonetheless imperils the species and communities that call the Atacama desert home. And it is a microcosm of a planetary phenomenon: the expanding extractive frontiers of green capitalism. Everywhere that mines are dug up to provide raw materials for the energy transition, global climate action comes into conflict with local environmental protection.
Mining always transforms, in many ways irrevocably, the landscapes in which it occurs. In remaking the earth in the image of extractive capital, physically and chemically separating what is deemed valuable from often toxic waste, mining evokes the image of terraforming so central to science fiction.
But if terraforming is supposed to make a lifeless planet as verdant as Earth, mining, to the contrary, often leaves parts of Earth itself uninhabitable. While the environmental impacts of mining brine are less obvious to the naked eye than, say, mountaintop removal, extracting the lithium-rich liquid does in fact threaten a fragile, desert water system, along with the ecosystems and people that depend on it.
The world’s oldest, driest desert may appear bereft of life. Ecologists call it a “polyextreme” environment, given its altitude and high direct solar radiation, its intense aridity, its huge diurnal temperature swings and its densely saline lakes. Those who study such polyextreme environments alternately describe them as low-diversity, with relatively simple webs of life, or astonishing in their biodiversity. It all depends on perspective. Plants and animals have evolved to make do with less and saltier water and, above all, the abundant energy of relentless sun. Extremity stimulates nature’s creativity.
Artemia, or brine shrimp, thrive in hypersaline lakes that would be intolerable to most species. These tiny creatures are a key node in the plateau’s food chain. The brine shrimp eat bacteria and phytoplankton (microscopic plants) and are, in turn, food for Chilean flamingos. The flamingos, too, have adapted to the saline lagoons, evolving a filter in their bills akin to the lamellar membranes of oysters or whales to strain the microscopic plants and animals from the brine.
The flamingos are a barometer of wetland health. As the birds travel the salt flats in search of food and mates (attracted through a courtship ritual of synchronised dancing), they link together the saline lakes into a web of habitats. And as these habitats suffer, so do flamingo populations: all three of the Atacama salt flats’ endemic flamingo species are in decline.
The distinct drivers of this population loss reveal the compounding harms afflicting this fragile environment. Warmer average temperatures due to climate change evaporate surface water faster, reducing the blue-green algae essential to flamingo and Artemia diets. And the noise and traffic associated with mining operations appear to directly disrupt the flamingos’ breeding.
Researchers are struggling to predict the overall direction of the multiple processes changing the Atacama. Science can only play catchup, documenting the impacts long after the harm has occurred. Lithium extraction’s threat to the liquid supporting its ecosystem is a slow-motion disaster, with planetary causes and consequences.
This fact raises existential questions for the planet’s zero-carbon future.
In the Atacama, global supply chains intersect with local food chains, webs of economic production undermine webs of life, and colonisation and postcolonial state-building erase ancient histories of continuous Indigenous settlement. And these unexpected entanglements are just the beginning of the story. In more ways than I could have imagined when I first stepped foot on the Atacama salt flat on that blustery day, this extractive frontier is a portal into our planetary future.
The task of achieving a globally just energy transition is daunting. But it is possible. Achieving it requires understanding supply chains in reverse, starting from what we produce and consume and working backwards to their material inputs and, further still, to the relentless scramble for new extractive frontiers. Policies that promote alternatives to car use, reduce sprawl, encourage more compact batteries and require recycling would all reduce the scale of mining needed for carbon-free transportation.
We can start by demanding supply chains organised around justice for everyone they touch, rather than profits for just a few. Just as any workplace is simultaneously a site of exploitation and locus of worker power, and any mine is at once a setting for extraction and a potential scene of community resistance, the supply chains of green technologies are both a means of domination – of people and of nature – and fertile ground for making the world anew.
- This is an edited extract from Extraction: The Frontiers of Green Capitalism by Thea Riofrancos, published by Icon Books at £20 in the UK. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Rapid showers and no flushing toilets: drought pushes Lundy island to the brink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

Tom Carr was peering up at the clouds scudding around the island of Lundy, 10 miles off the coast of north Devon. “That one’s definitely got rain in it,” he said. “The mainland will be wet at the moment. And look over at Wales – it’s getting a real soaking just now.”
But above Lundy the sky was, stubbornly, blue. No significant rain has fallen here since the start of May, leading to perilously low water levels. Restrictions have been put in place, visitor numbers limited and there has been talk of the island – home to 28 people – being evacuated.
“It’s been a challenge,” said Carr, a conservation farmer who looks after sheep, cattle and ponies. He has been here more than 20 years and reckons the combination of the climate emergency and the topography of the granite outcrop, which soars out of the Bristol Channel, is the problem.
“Climate change is here, it’s happening. We’re having hotter, drier summers. And when the rain clouds do come in, they tend to split as the approach the island and we stay dry.”
The three-mile long island, famed for its puffins and its pirate past, relies on rainwater and five boreholes. The biggest rain catchment area is in the south. From there – when it does rain – water tumbles down to a collection tank near the harbour. It is then pumped up to an array of tanks and a purification plant near the old lighthouse.
The island manager, Matt Scantlebury, said a fortnight ago the tanks were at 13% capacity – only enough water to keep the island going for about a week. Tonnes of water was being brought over in 1,000 litre containers on the island boat, the MS Oldenburg, to top up the supply.
The campsite, which is popular with climbers once the cliff-nesting seabirds have gone, was shut. The toilets at the island pub, the Marisco Tavern, were closed. Bath plugs in holiday lets – up to 110 people can stay here – were taken away and people were asked to think twice before flushing toilets.
Happily, on the day the water reached its low point, the island received confirmation that the water in one of its freshwater pools – called Pondsbury – was of a good enough quality to be used.
About 12,000 litres of water has been taken from there every day since and the levels are back up to 22.5%. But now the pond is starting to run dry. “And still no proper rain is forecast,” said Scantlebury. “We know we have to find ways of future proofing ourselves.”
To that end, a new 300,000-litre water tank has been ordered. The idea of a desalination plant – seawater is one thing the island is not short of – has been suggested but Scantlebury said it would be expensive and would probably need more energy than the island was capable of producing.
Tristan Howes, the island’s engineer, said finding ways of conserving the little water Lundy had was crucial. “A dripping tap can lose a lot of water,” he said. A broken pipe would be a disaster.
Staff have got used not only to having a rapid shower but catching the water they use in a bucket and using it to flush the toilet. “It’s about being as efficient as we can.”
Luckily, visitors to Lundy, which is owned by the National Trust and managed by the Landmark Trust, tend to be the sort who don’t mind a little bit of hardship.
Michelle Phillips, an animal lover keen to see the island’s ponies, and her husband, Fred Bullinaria, arrived for a day trip with 1.6 litres of water, four Lucozades and a tube of hydration tablets in their backpacks. “I think that will keep us going,” she said.
Vick and Ed Crane were staying on Lundy for a few days to celebrate their 10th wedding anniversary. They had bought wet wipes to limit their water usage. “We don’t mind roughing it,” said Vick. “That’s part of the Lundy experience. It’s an adventure.”
The residents are positive, always looking for the bright side.
Tara McEvoy-Wilding, assistant warden on the island, said some creatures had done well from the hot summer. “It’s been a good year for butterflies and moths.”
And it has also been a good summer for the Lundy cabbage, a primitive brassica that grows only on the island. “It’s quite a pioneering species and likes dry bare ground where there isn’t much vegetation,” said McEvoy-Wilding. “Hundreds of tiny cabbage plants have started to establish in areas where they wouldn’t normally. So that’s positive, at least.”
McEvoy-Wilding said residents had become accustomed to using less water. “You’re more mindful – you only have a short shower and you don’t always flush the toilet. In a way it’s not a bad thing. It makes you think about how much water you could be saving every day by just making very small changes.”
But that doesn’t mean that McEvoy-Wilding is not hoping for rain. “It’s amazing how little rain we’ve had. We had one day in August when it rained for an hour. Absolutely torrential. I was caught in it and got drenched but the ground was so dry it just poured off the island.
“I’ve got an allotment and it’s been hard to keep my vegetables alive. The pumpkins aren’t anywhere near as big as normal. Some nice, steady rain would be perfect.”

How to make pumpkin soup – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

Pumpkin soup, so delicious in theory – sweet, velvety, lightly autumnal – is so often disappointing in reality. Thin in flavour and consistency, thanks to squash’s high water content, it’s likely to make even the most conscientious cook regret not chucking those Halloween offcuts on the compost heap when they had the chance. This, I hope it goes without saying, is not that sort of pumpkin soup.
Prep 20 min
Cook 1 hr
Serves 4-6
About 1½kg pumpkin or winter squash (eg, crown prince, sugar pumpkin, kabocha), washed
Oil
Salt
2 litres light chicken stock, or vegetable stock
1 large red or yellow onion, peeled and chopped
1 celery stick, cut into small dice
2 small carrots, peeled and cut into small dice
1 small red chilli, chopped, or a sprinkle of chilli flakes (optional)
Sugar (optional)
2 tbsp butter (optional)
4 sage leaves, roughly torn, or the leaves from 2 thyme sprigs (optional)
1 handful grated parmesan, or gruyere or similar (optional)
Nutmeg (optional)
1 A note on the pumpkin
The single most important step here is your choice of pumpkin. Look for something that feels heavy for its size. I like the dense, fudgy crown prince or a nutty kabocha, but, if all else fails, a butternut squash will do nicely. Asian, African and Caribbean grocers often stock a wider variety than supermarkets, as will your local greengrocer or farmers’ market.
2 Skin the pumpkin
Pumpkins can be as much as 90% water, so it’s worth roasting the flesh to concentrate its flavour. Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Wash the pumpkin, then cut off some skin from one end so it will sit firmly on a board. Use a Y-shaped peeler or sharp knife to remove the rest of the skin and put the trimmings in a medium saucepan.
3 Deseed and chop the pumpkin
Cut the pumpkin into quarters, then remove the seeds (and the flesh around them). Add all but a spoonful of the seeds to the pan with the skin, and set aside the rest for now. Cut the flesh into large, evenly sized cubes and put these on a baking tray (use a second tray if there are too many to fit comfortably in one layer).
4 Roast the pumpkin
Drizzle the cubes with a little oil (olive is nice, but anything not too strongly flavoured will do) and toss with a little salt. Bake for about 40 minutes, until soft and beginning to brown. If the cubes are colouring unevenly, turn around the tray halfway and remove any that look as if they might burn before the rest are done.
5 Roast the pumpkin seeds
Wash the reserved spoonful of pumpkin seeds, if necessary, to remove any flesh clinging to them, then blot dry with a clean tea towel or kitchen paper. Put the seeds on a fresh tray and toss with a little oil and salt, then put them in the oven for the last 10 minutes of the pumpkin cooking time. Set aside to crisp up.
6 Boil the pumpkin offcuts
While the pumpkin is cooking, put the stock in the peelings pan – a good fresh chicken stock is my favourite, because it’s richer and more neutral than vegetable stock, but most varieties will do, as will plain water. Bring to a boil, then turn down the heat and simmer gently for 30 minutes.
7 Start the soup base
Put two tablespoons of oil in a large saucepan on a medium-low heat, then add the onion, celery, carrots and a good pinch of salt, and fry, stirring regularly until soft but not brown. Stir in the chilli, if using, and fry for another minute or so (if the soup base is ready before the pumpkin is roasted, take the pan off the heat).
8 Add the roast pumpkin
Stir the roast pumpkin cubes into the soup base, then strain in the pumpkin-skin stock (discard the trimmings). Bring to a simmer and cook for about 10 minutes, or until the pumpkin is very soft. Puree with a stick blender or in a jug blender (if using the latter, let the soup mix cool slightly first), then taste and adjust the seasoning, adding a little sugar or diluting the soup with water, as necessary.
9 Finishing touches
If serving with browned butter (a drizzle of cold pumpkin oil is a good vegan alternative), heat the butter until golden, stir in the sage and decant immediately into a heatproof bowl or jug. Serve the soup topped with cheese, if using, a grating of nutmeg, a drizzle of the brown butter and sage or oil, and a few roasted seeds.

Where you direct your attention may shape your body’s inflammatory response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:00:21 UTC
21:00:21 KST

Focusing your mind on physical sensations in your skin might help your body tamp down sudden inflammation, according to a new investigation. Researchers found that when individuals deliberately paid attention to a localized skin reaction rather than distracting themselves, the resulting swelling and redness were substantially smaller, and the swelling subsided faster. The findings, published in Nature Human Behaviour, suggest that voluntary thought processes can influence physiological defenses that were previously viewed as purely automatic.
Acute inflammation is the rapid, protective response the body mounts against injury or irritation, characterized by localized heat, swelling, and redness. In laboratory settings, scientists often test this process using histamine, a chemical the body releases during allergic reactions that causes blood vessels to widen and leak fluid. Applying a droplet to the skin and piercing the surface triggers a raised, fluid-filled bump called a wheal and a surrounding patch of redness called a flare. In this type of challenge, a smaller, faster-settling reaction is viewed as a sign of better-regulated immune activity, reflecting a body that resolves swelling without overreacting.
The research was led by Nofar Mizrachi and Liron Rozenkrantz of the Azrieli Faculty of Medicine at Bar-Ilan University in Israel, where Rozenkrantz is an assistant professor and principal investigator of the Psycho-Biology of Beliefs Lab. The team wanted to explore whether conscious awareness plays an active role in how the body manages sudden immune challenges.
“We’ve known for a long time that attention changes how the body feels. When we distract ourselves from pain or an itch, it feels less intense,” Rozenkrantz told PsyPost. “What has not been tested before was whether attention also changes what the body does in response, specifically whether it affects immune regulation.”
“Inflammation is usually treated as an automatic process, one that is not dependent on or affected by cognition,” she continued. “My lab studies how cognitive processes, such as beliefs and perceptions, influence biological function, so the question was natural for us: is our experience of the body a passive process, or is it part of regulation itself?”
To ground this question in existing biology, the researchers drew upon predictive models of brain-body communication, an idea known as allostasis. In a 2015 theoretical paper, neuroscientists proposed that the brain constantly anticipates bodily needs and adjusts internal biological processes before problems escalate. Another biological pathway of interest is the inflammatory reflex; a 2009 review outlined how the vagus nerve, a major neural highway running between the brain and internal organs, helps suppress excessive inflammation. The authors reasoned that intentionally attending to bodily signals might sharpen the brain’s internal monitoring systems and engage these calming nerve pathways.
To test this idea, the researchers designed three pre-registered experiments, meaning they publicly recorded their hypotheses and analysis plans in advance. In the first experiment, 37 healthy adults received a histamine prick on their forearm during two different sessions. In one session, participants were told to keep their gaze on a screen while focusing all their attention on the physical feelings of itching or burning occurring at the skin site. In the comparison session, participants watched engaging video clips on the screen to distract their attention away from the arm, while skin responses were tracked for 20 minutes.
The person measuring the skin did not know which condition each participant was in during any given test. Session order was balanced across participants, and participants were not told the study’s purpose; when asked to guess at the end of the experiments, only 14 percent correctly identified it.
The team found that focusing attention internally resulted in markedly smaller inflammatory reactions. At the 20-minute peak, the swelling bump averaged 3.5 millimeters under internal attention compared to 5.0 millimeters during distraction, representing roughly a 1.5-fold increase under distraction. The surrounding redness averaged 10.6 millimeters under internal attention compared to 14.0 millimeters during distraction, though unlike the swelling, it did not fade on a different timeline.
About 90 percent of the participants showed a larger swelling reaction when their attention was directed away from the arm. In an additional analysis that was not part of the pre-registered plan, nearly 90 percent of participants showed swelling that had stopped growing or begun to shrink by the 20-minute mark during internal focus, compared to 46 percent during distraction.
Because the video clips in the first experiment introduced different visual stimulation and mental demands, the scientists conducted a second experiment with 20 new participants. In this trial, every participant viewed the identical visual slideshow of 37 abstract geometrical shapes. In the internal attention condition, each new shape served as a mental reminder to bring focus back to the itching sensation in the arm. In the distraction condition, participants spent the time mentally evaluating whether each shape could plausibly exist in real life.
Even with identical visual input and matched mental effort, the immune divergence persisted. Swelling bumps and redness were roughly 1.6-fold smaller when participants paid attention to their arm sensations rather than assessing the abstract shapes. Once again, 90 percent of participants developed larger reactions under distraction. Interestingly, participants reported that the itching and burning felt stronger when they paid attention to it, showing that heightened awareness of discomfort coincided with a smaller physical immune response.
“What I find most surprising is that a process as basic and fundamental as acute peripheral inflammation is affected by cognition at all,” Rozenkrantz observed. “Inflammation is generally thought of as an autonomous physiological process, largely independent of cognition, so finding that something as voluntary as where we direct our attention can participate in its regulation really challenges that separation between cognition and basic bodily regulation. In a sense, this is exactly why we asked the question in the first place: to understand how deeply cognitive processes are embedded in physiological regulation.”
The finding that attention made the itch feel stronger led the researchers to test whether sensory feedback from the skin is required for the brain to regulate the swelling. In a third experiment, 17 participants from the earlier experiments returned for an additional session where a topical numbing cream, lidocaine, was applied to dull nerve signals at the test site. With sensory feedback dampened, the peak swelling bump averaged 4.0 millimeters, which was larger than the 3.1 millimeters seen during internal attention with intact sensation in their earlier visit. The numbing cream also hindered the later recovery phase, meaning the swelling did not drop toward baseline as quickly.
Despite this sensory blunting, the response under numbing cream remained smaller than the 4.9-millimeter average observed under ordinary distraction. This suggests that sensory signals from nerves help the body resolve inflammation in its later stages, while attention may still regulate the response through other routes when local sensation is reduced. Perceived itching ratings between the numbing condition and the distraction condition did not differ in a statistically significant way, suggesting that sensory experience alone did not dictate the outcome.
To explore how the brain might be communicating with the skin, the researchers recorded measures of the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate and sweating. Measures tied to its “fight or flight” branch, including skin conductance (a sign of sweating), heart rate, and skin temperature, showed no differences between conditions, and participants’ self-reported anxiety scores did not differ in a statistically significant manner.
However, heart rate variability, the natural beat-to-beat fluctuation in heart rhythm and an indirect indicator of activity in the calming “rest and digest” branch carried by the vagus nerve, was modestly higher during internal attention. This difference persisted even when the skin was numbed, which the authors interpret as consistent with inward focus engaging the vagus nerve’s anti-inflammatory pathway independently of incoming sensory signals.
“It appears that focusing attention towards the part of the body where a chemical has challenged the immune system leads to a great visible reduction in its effects on the skin, compared to focusing away from the site,” Warren Mansell, director of the LEx Mental Health Research Group and a professor of mental health at Curtin University in Australia, who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost.
“This raises the possibility that through willingly attending to unpleasant feelings in our bodies, we may support our body’s immune reaction to it. It also raises the possibility that chronically distracting ourselves from distress in our body may undermine our immune system. None of these generalizations can be concluded from this study, but the study sets the stage for research that could.”
Mansell noted that the results might seem to clash with common advice to distract oneself from discomfort, as well as with the view that dwelling on bodily sensations worsens worry, panic, and pain. But he argued that reading the findings as contradicting that advice would be a mistake.
“Distraction can still be an effective short-term strategy to manage unpleasant feelings, even if it is not helpful for long-term physiological restoration,” Mansell explained. “Also, the focus on the body that happens in worry, panic and chronic pain is typically involuntary unlike the voluntary attending in this study, and is often elaborative and ruminative regarding thoughts about the bodily feeling, not the feeling itself.”
“The work is consistent with earlier work on the beneficial impact of techniques that include focused attention on the body such as Gendlin’s focusing and interoceptive exposure,” he added. Gendlin’s focusing is a therapy method built around tuning in to subtle bodily feelings, while interoceptive exposure, used to treat panic disorder, has people deliberately bring on feared sensations such as a racing heart.
The authors raise a related point in their paper. They suggest that habitually turning attention away from unpleasant bodily sensations might carry a physiological cost in some situations, and they note that attention-based treatments such as mindfulness, which involve sustained focus on the body, have been linked to improvements in inflammatory markers, though whether avoidance itself prolongs pain or inflammation remains untested.
“I think the main takeaway is that these findings may change how we think about the relationship between cognition and physiological regulation – and more specifically, that our subjective experience of the body may be more biologically consequential than we usually assume,” Rozenkrantz said. “We tend to think of sensations like itch or burning as simply reflecting what is happening in the body. Our findings suggest a fascinating attention-perception-regulation loop: signals from the body shape what we feel, attention changes how we perceive those signals, and that perception may in turn help regulate what is happening in the body.”
“I think the conceptual significance is more important at this stage than the practical significance,” Rozenkrantz added. “This is an initial demonstration in a very specific experimental model, not yet something we can translate into a clinical recommendation.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study examined an allergy-like skin reaction triggered by histamine in healthy young adults. Because of this specific setup, it remains unknown whether voluntary attention would exert similar effects on infectious diseases, long-term autoimmune conditions, or full-body illnesses.
Mansell expressed confidence in the experimental rigor while stressing the need for caution in interpreting the reach of the findings. “I have great confidence in the results owing to the controlled experimental design, the pre-registration and replication,” Mansell noted. “However, the results are modest and specific as opposed to the various interpretations of the results, which are not directly supported by this study.”
Rozenkrantz similarly cautioned against overstating the practical reach of the data. “I think this is crucial: these findings should not be immediately generalized,” Rozenkrantz emphasized. “We studied a small, localized, acute inflammatory response in healthy people. We cannot assume that the same effect occurs in chronic inflammation, disease, wound healing, or other physiological processes, and this is not evidence that people can simply ‘think away’ inflammation or illness.”
There are also practical realities regarding the immune system to keep in mind, as smaller inflammatory responses are not always ideal when fighting off an active pathogen. In addition, the scientists did not measure the immune cells or signaling molecules involved, which leaves the fine-grained biochemical steps unmapped. The numbing cream may not have blocked every type of sensory nerve fiber, and heart rate variability is only an indirect gauge of vagus nerve activity.
The experiments were also small, with 37 and 20 participants in the first two experiments and 17 returning participants in the third, most of them young women, and the numbing-cream session’s order was not balanced against the other conditions.
When considering future directions, Mansell highlighted the need for broader testing. He stated that he would most want to see tested “the impact of more extensive training on more global and enduring indices of immune functioning.”
“What excites us most is how many new questions this opens up,” Rozenkrantz said. “If attention can participate in regulating inflammation, what other physiological processes might it influence? When does this happen, for whom, and under what conditions? And eventually, how might we harness it clinically?”
Even with remaining questions, the findings provide evidence that voluntary attention does more than simply filter our conscious experience of physical discomfort. In this specific laboratory model, paying attention to bodily sensations was linked to smaller, faster-settling skin reactions and to signs of greater vagus nerve activity, offering a fresh perspective on how mental states and physical responses interact.
The study, “Voluntary attention regulates acute immune responses in humans,” was authored by Nofar Mizrachi, Menachem Rottem, and Liron Rozenkrantz.

Leading Chinese mathematicians unite behind use of AI in research
Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau, who is leading the project, warned that the country is lagging behind the US in using the technology
Leading China’s mathematicians joined forces in Beijing on Sunday to launch an alliance aimed at integrating artificial intelligence into mathematical research.
The Yau Laboratory Alliance for Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence is being spearheaded by Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau, who warned that China was lagging behind the United States in using AI to advance frontier science.
It will bring together eight leading institutions and aims to create a network of more than 1,000 scientists.
The alliance will focus on developing specialised AI models for mathematics, using the technology to generate conjectures and formalise proofs, and building systems whose reasoning could be more easily interpreted.

48 lakh calls in four years: India turns to Tele-MANAS as WHO flags mental healthcare gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:58:35 UTC
20:58:35 KST

Since its launch in October 2022, Tele-MANAS has received almost 48 lakh calls, highlighting a crucial demand for accessible mental health support.
NEW DELHI: Exam stress, workplace pressure, anxiety, sleep problems and relationship difficulties are among the concerns for which people are turning to India’s national mental health helpline, Tele-MANAS, which has received nearly 48 lakh calls in four years. The figures offer a glimpse of the need for accessible mental health support, even as a new World Health Organization (WHO) guide warns that the global shift from hospital-centred care to community-based services remains far from complete.Released ahead of World Mental Health Day, the WHO guide found that 81% of countries continue to provide mental health services in psychiatric hospitals, while only 9% have completed the transition to community-based care. Another 53% remain at an early stage of the shift.The gap is particularly striking in the WHO South-East Asia region, where 63% of countries are still at an early stage of transition and none has completed it, according to the report’s regional assessment. The figures are regional and do not represent India’s individual status.The consequences of hospital-centred care are reflected in the duration of admissions.
The report found that 28% of people admitted to psychiatric hospitals stay for more than six months, while 16% remain for over a year. It also estimates that 47% of mental health expenditure goes to psychiatric hospitals, although this figure is based on data from only 49 countries.The WHO calls for mental healthcare to be delivered closer to people’s homes, supported by community services, rehabilitation, housing and continued clinical care. It cautions that deinstitutionalisation cannot mean simply closing hospitals or discharging patients without follow-up. Without adequate planning and support, people risk being neglected or losing access to care.In India, Tele-MANAS has received 47,75,644 calls since its launch on October 10, 2022. Of the 13.35 lakh caller profiles analysed by the Union Health Ministry, 73.2% belonged to people aged 18-45.
Men accounted for 54.18% of the profiles and women 43.78%.The free, confidential service is available round the clock on 14416, through 53 operational cells covering all 36 States and Union Territories. The government has also sanctioned the District Mental Health Programme in 767 districts and integrated mental health services into more than 1.83 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Pope Leo to have surgery to remove nodule on his lung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:55:26 UTC
20:55:26 KST

Pope Leo XIV has said he will undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a nodular lesion on his lung that was recently discovered during medical checks.
The 71-year-old said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or well localised. The Vatican later said Leo would undergo surgery in the first days of this week, with an expected recovery time of a week.
The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3cm (1in) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is considered physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The pope has an extensive trip planned to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November. It is unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery will affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks on Sunday that he planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check “doctors found a small, localised nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it.
“The surgery is already scheduled for the coming days. Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers.”
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died on 21 April 2025 of a stroke after a long hospitalisation brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs.
The Italian premier, Giorgia Meloni, who was among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalisation, expressed her support and that of the Italian government to Leo “as he faces this challenge in the coming days”. In a statement, she added that “the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it” were reassuring.

Protests continued in India's capital, New Delhi, on Sunday as authorities released three leaders of a youth movement, including founder Abhijeet Dipke. Protesters are demanding the resignation of the country's election chief over allegations of electoral manipulation. Police detained thousands of demonstrators on Saturday, while security forces restricted access to parts of the city to prevent gatherings.
The demonstrations centre on demands for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign over a nationwide revision of electoral registers.
Protesters accuse the Election Commission of removing voters in ways that favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Election Commission figures cited by the party indicate that approximately 130 million names have been removed from voter lists during the verification exercise. These include 63 million people recorded as having relocated and 30 million whom officials were unable to trace.
Opposition parties allege that the process disproportionately affects Muslims and other minority communities. The Election Commission and BJP reject allegations of manipulation, maintaining that the revisions seek to remove duplicate, deceased and ineligible voters.
The dispute intensified after the Indian Express reported in September that two election commissioners had raised concerns internally about voter registration procedures, digital systems and revisions to electoral rolls. Saturday's demonstrations faced restrictions after police refused permission for a gathering at Jantar Mantar, a protest venue in central Delhi.
Authorities deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel, erected barricades and restricted transport services. At least 45 metro stations closed, while internet access was suspended in parts of the capital.
Reuters reported more than 2,000 detentions, while the BBC cited media reports placing the figure as high as 7,000. Most detainees were released on Saturday night.

India's Supreme Court held a hearing on Sunday concerning restrictions and detentions. The court directed authorities to restore internet access and transport services unless public order required restrictions. Reuters reported that the government assured judges that journalists and lawyers would be allowed to perform their duties.
The United Nations Human Rights Office urged India to respect the right to peaceful assembly. India's foreign ministry rejected the intervention as interference in domestic affairs.
The CJP emerged in May after Dipke responded to remarks by India's Chief Justice comparing unemployed young people to cockroaches. The movement subsequently organised protests over education and unemployment. It is not registered as a political party.
The demonstrations come ahead of state elections scheduled to begin in early 2027.

Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove lump on lung
October 11, 2026
Pope Leo XIV said Sunday that he will undergo surgery this week to remove a lump on his lung.
"During recent medical checks, a nodule on my lung was found. It has been detected at a very early stage and is very localized," the 71-year-old said during his weekly address in St Peter's Square in the Vatican.
"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it. The operation is already planned in the coming days," he added.
What do we know about the pope's condition?
This is his first major health scare since the 71-year-old American became pope in 2025.
A lung nodule is a small, contained lesion that is smaller than 3 centimeters (1 inch) and can be benign.
According to the American Thoracic Society, fewer than 5% of lung nodules turn out to be cancerous.
The American Cancer Society says the nodules sometimes appear on CT scans of the chest or abdomen during searches for trauma or lung infections that are unrelated to cancer screenings.
Leo is younger than most popes. His predecessor, Francis, was five years older when he assumed the role, while Francis' predecessor, Benedict XVI, was 78 at the start of his tenure.
Leo is not known to have had any previous health issues, and leads a relatively active lifestyle.

Israel unearths 2,000-year-old section of Jerusalem aqueduct that brought water to Temple Mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:34 UTC
20:47:34 KST

A 300-meter-long section of Jerusalem’s Lower Aqueduct, originally constructed in the Hasmonean period, was recently unearthed south of Kibbutz Ramat Rachel, near the capital, the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) announced on Sunday.
The aqueduct was part of a sophisticated ancient water system that carried spring water from the Gush Etzion area to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem through Solomon’s Pools.
Hasmonean architects designed the aqueduct so water could flow by gravity alone, adapting the route to move smoothly across hills and bedrock. They installed cleanout points along the system, providing access to the channel for blockages or routine maintenance.
"The Lower Aqueduct was an impressive engineering project, probably built in the time of the Hasmonean kings to supply water to Jerusalem, explained IAA Excavation Directors Dr. Benyamin Storchan and Gil Freid. “The system was so well planned that it remained in intermittent use until about 100 years ago.”
“The aqueduct runs about 21 km from Solomon's Pools, south of Bethlehem, to Jerusalem. Along most of the route, the water flowed along a very gentle gradient, dropping just one meter in elevation per kilometer."
Section exposes ancient water system's history
The newly exposed section, located in an area slated by the Israel Land Authority for a new neighborhood, reveals several stages in the water system’s history.
Initially, the water flowed through a built and plastered channel. However, about 500 years ago, during the Ottoman period, they installed ceramic pipes within the original aqueduct.
At the same time, the outer wall was plastered, and small stones were pressed into it while the plaster was still wet, creating a distinctive surface that accompanied the aqueduct along its route.
These repairs reflect the aqueduct's importance and the ongoing effort to maintain Jerusalem's water supply.
"The aqueduct is an engineering marvel. Even today, with all our modern technology, building such a system would require extensive planning and effort,” said Dr. Amit Re'em, IAA Jerusalem district archaeologist. “The thought that about 2,000 years ago they managed to bring water to Jerusalem this way is astonishing, and we want the public to be able to appreciate this achievement up close.”
“The dream and vision of the Israel Antiquities Authority is to create a continuous park that will allow people to walk alongside the aqueduct from southern Jerusalem to the Old City, and we are already advancing this initiative together with the Jerusalem Municipality and other partners."
Aqueduct to be incorporated into new neighborhood
The ILA and the IAA are planning to preserve the aqueduct and incorporate it into the main entrance of the new neighborhood.
According to Yehuda Eliyahu, acting director of the ILA, "The spectacular discovery of the ancient aqueduct in the heart of the area planned for the new neighborhood in Jerusalem reminds us that we are continuing a glorious chain of generations of building and development.”
“The Israel Land Authority is pleased to lead extensive modern development while showing national responsibility and carefully safeguarding our historical heritage assets,” Eliyahu said. “Integrating the aqueduct into the entrance of the new neighborhood will give residents and visitors a direct connection to Jerusalem's rich history and to the deep bond of the people of Israel with its eternal capital."
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu echoed the sentiment, adding that "The aqueduct, whose construction is attributed to the days of the Hasmonean kings, tells of a leadership that knew how to think ahead: to expand Jerusalem's capacity to absorb residents, pilgrims, and public life around the Temple.”
“Integrating the aqueduct into the new neighborhood today continues this story: the city is growing, and we are glad that its integration into the new neighborhood will allow future generations to get to know this heritage up close."
The research on Jerusalem's Lower Aqueduct will be presented at the 19th "New Studies in the Archaeology of Jerusalem and Its Region" conference, held in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv and initiated by the Israel Antiquities Authority, Tel Aviv University, the Hebrew University, and Tagliyot – Israel Institute of Archaeology.

The Ben-Gvir effect exposes the West’s discomfort with Jewish power - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:32 UTC
20:47:32 KST

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has become a sort of political lightning rod, drawing high-voltage tension and intense global as well as domestic criticism.
While the obvious reasons for this widespread antipathy concern firstly his positions – death penalty for terrorists, voluntary emigration of Gazans, expansion of Jewish settlement, opposition to Palestinian statehood, to name but a few – they do not explain by themselves this peculiar phenomenon.
However “radical” one may consider them to be, these substantial positions, backed by a long-standing ideology, remain political stances that can be supported, opposed, or debated on their own terms.
Beyond his political program, it is also Ben-Gvir’s manner (or lack thereof) that is being targeted: the theatrical provocations, the confrontational language and the social media stunts. From suggesting a moat of crocodiles around a prison holding Hamas terrorists to publicly humiliating the Gaza flotilla terror supporters, Ben-Gvir understands the power of an image.
And he uses it as a method, a method whose impact is reaching far beyond Israel’s borders, making the debate around him more existential than political. All these, combined with his unapologetic Jewish pride and his rejection of political correctness, trigger a revealing reaction, the “Ben-Gvir effect.”
The recent statements by U2 band member Bono about the Israeli minister illustrate the reach of this effect.
The Irish singer not only compared Ben-Gvir’s remarks about Gazans to the rhetoric of Heinrich Himmler, the architect of the Nazi extermination machinery, but he also claimed that the leader of Otzma Yehudit had put Judaism “in the shade.”
Whatever one thinks of Ben-Gvir’s words, this shift from criticizing a politician or a specific policy to conflating them with Judaism itself deserves scrutiny, because it goes deeper than the standard debate over extremism.
Understanding the criticism directed at Itamar Ben-Gvir
Ben-Gvir may be a lightning rod, and a convenient one, but he did not create the storm that has been gathering above Israel and the Jews since October 7.
He was democratically elected to the Knesset, and his party, which recent polls put at around eight seats in the upcoming elections, is an important component of the current coalition. His critics on the Left see a threat to democracy and the rule of law, and the ones on the right view his provocations as a liability to quieter diplomacy.
He and his party, treated as pariahs for many years, are now part of the political mainstream, whether one likes it or not. In fact, their ideology is not far removed from the historic Right. The core difference lies in language and the Jewish part of the equation.
The new generation of the modern national-religious camp has left the European reference point and its anxieties behind.
Instead, they return to a native Jewish and religious character, rooted in the reality of being here, with no regard for convention or the sensibilities of Western audiences – whom Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is so familiar with.
The national security minister feels no need to moderate his tone when speaking about Jewish sovereignty or particularism.
The backlash against Ben-Gvir thus often shifts from moral objection to personal attack, at times even evoking historical, antisemitic caricatures of the Jew. Yet Ben-Gvir, who, to some extent, projects this image of himself, uses it as a tool of political deterrence. Focusing on the image, however, obscures what matters more.
Beyond aesthetics, the “Ben-Gvir effect” exposes an ancient anxiety: the Western world tolerates the Jew under subjection, but hates and fears the Jew who exerts sovereign power. While this hostility does not make all criticism antisemitic, it does seem to derived from it.
Abroad, Ben-Gvir is often collapsed with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich into a single patronizing category, the “Ben-Gvirs and Smotriches,” Israel’s convenient symbol for a threatening extreme.
By reducing him to a caricature, one avoids having to engage with the real ideas he embodies, ideas that are an integral part of Israel’s democratic political landscape.
Ultimately, the disproportionate rage surrounding him exposes the global and domestic difficulty of accommodating a specific, unapologetic figure: the Jew on his own land, claiming spiritual attachment, possessing raw political power, and refusing to apologize for any of it.
BEHIND BEN-GVIR’S positions lies a strong national-religious conception of Israel that has acquired a larger audience since October 7, as many Israelis are asking questions about identity, sovereignty, and security with a renewed sense of urgency.
Thus, the visceral secular reaction to Ben-Gvir hides something even deeper than just an aversion to his bad manners and alleged racist positions. The problem lies with what he represents: a loud, proud, nationalist religious Jew.
And this Jew, for many in Israel and abroad, is difficult to come to terms with. He is the antithesis of the “court Jew,” the cosmopolitan and universalist Jew who has had to master the codes of the surrounding society to survive, a Jew not necessarily unproud but careful about particularism, and accommodating about his identity.
He is also quite different from the “New Hebrew,” the socialist and secular pioneer, symbol of the building of the country. But this evolution is not simply about style; it is a transformation of the Jewish character itself.
And this Jewish part of the equation is unsettling to secular culture. Beyond beliefs, it is the very existence of a visibly religious person that inevitably raises questions that modern European tradition has relegated to the private sphere: God, transcendence and meaning. And although these questions never disappeared, they were toned down within Israel’s secular-Zionist tradition.
This friction could help explain the discomfort surrounding Ben-Gvir. He is not simply promoting a national-religious agenda; he wears his Jewish identity and attachment to the land openly, refusing to translate them into a universalist vocabulary. He brings his faith out of the private sphere, thrusting it into questions of sovereignty, land, national identity and political power.
While the place of religion in the Jewish state has been a fault line in Israeli society since its creation, and has been dividing Israelis long before October 7, it has become a very raw existential battlefield as it occupies more space within the public debate.
Considering the Jewish particularity of Israel, this conversation needs to happen. But for it to happen, Israel and its citizens need to allow for an accepting, tolerant, and inclusive space, without knee-jerk reactions, without violence, and with a genuine will to understand the other. From his newly gained position, Ben-Gvir himself could actually be helping to bridge these differences.
The Ben-Gvir effect has brought front stage a long-muted Jewish nationalism, attracting intense animosity but also discreet curiosity from Western leaders seeking strategies against radical Islamism and terror.
To capitalize on this attention, Ben-Gvir must change his method from mere provocation to more mature communication, and adopt a syntax that speaks to the international community without compromise or accommodation.
This gives the national-religious camp an opportunity to assert their ideology into the mainstream as an impossible-to-ignore reality in Israel and abroad. Ultimately, the fierce reaction Ben-Gvir triggers reveals as much about those responding as it does about the man himself.
The author holds a PhD from Tel Aviv University and is a regular contributor on Zionism, Israeli society, and Jewish identity.

US Army urges adoption of Israeli battlefield medicine as IDF cuts casualty deaths by half - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:16 UTC
20:47:16 KST

The US Army is recommending that American military medical teams study and adopt Israeli battlefield medicine techniques after the IDF reduced the mortality rate among combat casualties by more than half, Fox News reported, citing IDF data and an official US Army report.
Advances in combat medicine developed by the IDF in recent years have helped significantly reduce deaths among soldiers wounded in battle. The US military is now urging a closer examination of these Israeli methods ahead of future conflicts.
According to data presented to Fox News, the mortality rate among combat casualties stood at approximately 15% during the Second Lebanon War in 2006, compared with 7.1% during the Swords of Iron War.
The US report cited nearly identical figures, showing a decline from 14.8% in 2006 to 7.1% in 2024, despite a significant increase in the proportion of wounded soldiers suffering severe injuries.
One of the most important changes has been a dramatic reduction in the time required to deliver advanced medical treatment to wounded soldiers.
According to a senior IDF combat medicine expert, during the Second Lebanon War, it took between 15 and 20 minutes for advanced medical care to reach a wounded soldier. Currently, such treatment can be administered immediately or within just four minutes.
Positioning medical personnel closer to combat troops, rapidly evacuating casualties by helicopter, and making medical decisions directly on the battlefield are considered key factors behind the improvement.
IDF expands use of blood units on battlefield
The IDF has also expanded the use of blood products on the battlefield, according to the Fox News report. Since 2013, greater emphasis has been placed on rapidly treating hemorrhages, including administering plasma at the point of injury.
Blood units are transported to forward positions in refrigerated containers carried by medical teams, allowing treatment to begin before wounded soldiers are evacuated to a hospital.
In its 78-page report, titled "Israeli Defense Force Medical Lessons Learned," the US Army warned that Israel had been forced to make painful adjustments during active combat, but that the American military now has an opportunity to learn from that experience in advance.
"The time to prepare is now," the report stated, emphasizing that clinical and tactical knowledge alone is insufficient.
The authors recommended studying Israel's medical evacuation systems, medical data collection, preventive medicine practices, and ability to continue providing advanced medical treatment under high-intensity combat conditions.

Could Egyptian military deployment in Somalia upset Horn of Africa balance of power? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:05 UTC
20:47:05 KST

Egyptian technical military teams, including advisors, trainers, and officers, are reportedly preparing for the deployment of troops to Somalia, in the first such move since the signing of a joint military cooperation agreement between the two sides in 2024, The New Arab reported on Friday.
This potentially important development comes as Pakistan and Turkey may also be deploying forces to Saudi Arabia to support the Kingdom’s defenses against the Houthis.
The report at The New Arab says the deployment to Somalia could come “in light of bilateral security and military cooperation between the two countries and within the African Union Mission, widely known as AUSSOM.” It also comes as Turkey has forces in Somalia. However, despite the support, this has not stabilized Somalia enough.
The report added that “the Egyptian troops will reportedly be positioned in the Ceelcade region which used to house the Cisiley Airfield on the immediate northern outskirts of Mogadishu, within the Middle Shabelle region - in the low-lying semi-arid coastal hinterland just north of the Banaadir administrative boundary, around 400 kilometers from the nearest point to Ethiopia's shared border with Somalia.”
Any deployment could tip the balance of power in the Horn of Africa. In early October, Egypt reached out to leaders in Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia. Egypt is concerned about the spiraling military conflicts that are taking place to the south of Egypt. It’s worth understanding this. Egypt’s military met Somali Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi in September.
Houthis advance to Bab el-Mandeb strait, target Saudi airports
This all comes amid many developments. On one side of the Red Sea, the Houthis advanced in September to the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Then Saudi Arabia backed a Yemeni government offensive against the Houthis. Now the Houthis are targeting Saudi airports. Riyadh is a friend of Egypt.
Egypt and Somalia have four other major conflicts. Ethiopia's conflicts involve the federal government in Addis Ababa, led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and several regional movements. The most devastating recent conflict was the Tigray war, fought from 2020 to 2022 between federal forces and their allies, including Eritrean troops, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). On September 21, seven rebel groups in Ethiopia formed a new alliance. Egypt has opposed the Ethiopian Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
In Sudan, Egypt backs the Sudanese army. The army is fighting a civil war. The US has tried to push for a ceasefire and banned Sudan from the UN General Assembly. Sudan's civil war began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), commanded by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, commonly known as Hemedti.
The SAF represents Sudan's established military institutions and is associated with the internationally recognized state authorities. The RSF emerged from paramilitary networks linked to the Darfur conflict and has developed its own military, economic, and territorial power. Support for both sides fuels Sudan's conflict. For instance, Sudan’s military accuses the UAE of backing the RSF. This conflict has likely destabilized Ethiopia.
Meanwhile, in Somalia, the government is fighting terrorist groups such as al-Shabaab. Somalia’s government also doesn’t control most of the country. Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025. Puntland also operates as an autonomous state. Egypt sending forces could change things in Somalia and also potentially affect Ethiopia. It could also change Eritrea’s calculations.
Libya split between Turkey-backed GNU, Egypt-backed Haftar
Libya, a bit farther away in North Africa, borders Egypt and Sudan. As such, it also has a role to play.
In western Libya, the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) is one part of the mosaic of the country. In eastern Libya, Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar commands the Libyan National Army (LNA), also known as the Libyan Arab Armed Forces. His coalition controls much of eastern and southern Libya and is aligned with the rival eastern-based political authorities.
In the past, Turkey backed the GNU while Egypt, the UAE and others backed Haftar. In September, The New Arab reported that Saddam Haftar, Khalifa's son, went to the UAE for meetings. Whether true or not, what these reports indicate is intense interest in the Horn of Africa by media in the Gulf.
These four conflicts - Sudan, Somalia, Libya, and Ethiopia - are increasingly interconnected. Ethiopia's renewed fighting and tensions with Eritrea threaten wider instability in the Horn of Africa. Sudan's war involves cross-border armed networks, while Somalia's security depends partly on neighboring countries' military commitments. Libya remains influenced by competing interests from the Mediterranean, the Gulf, and elsewhere. Any change in the balance could reverberate to the Red Sea, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Indian Ocean.

Kuwait, Lebanon, Syria leading options for Abraham Accords expansion, CSA report assesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:00 UTC
20:47:00 KST

The Council for a Secure America (CSA) has ranked Kuwait as the Middle Eastern country most likely to join the Abraham Accords, followed by Lebanon and Syria, as changing political and security conditions reshape prospects for normalization with Israel.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
CSA released its “Abraham Accords Expansion Opportunities: Middle East Analysis” report on October 8, assessing nine Muslim-majority countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel: Kuwait, Lebanon, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Iraq, Yemen, and Iran.
More than 80% of Israelis surveyed by CSA in June 2026 support the Abraham Accords, which established relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan in 2020.
CSA Executive Director Jennifer Sutton said recent events have “reinforced the need for America's continued engagement in the region.”
The rankings were based on expert analysis, primary and secondary sources, and CSA polling. Researchers examined domestic political power, government structures, public opinion, statements by political leaders, relations with Israel and the United States, regional alliances, economic and energy interests, and ongoing conflicts. CSA said the rankings measure both governments’ willingness and political ability to normalize relations and could change as regional conditions evolve.
Kuwait thought to be closest to normalization with Israel, CSA survey shows
Kuwait ranked first despite its longstanding opposition to normalization and laws barring trade with Israel. CSA pointed to
Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah’s growing authority since suspending parliament in May 2024, closer ties with the UAE, and strong security ties with Washington. Kuwait also came under Iranian attack during the 2026 Iran War. Israel’s ambassador to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, said in September that Kuwait could join the accords within six months. 
Lebanon placed second following significant diplomatic activity with Israel. The countries signed a US-brokered “Trilateral Framework” in June under which Lebanon recognized Israeli sovereignty for the first time, followed by additional talks. CSA polling found 41% of Lebanese believed peace with Israel was likely, although only 32% supported normalization. Hezbollah’s continued presence and failure to fully disarm remain major obstacles.
Syria ranked third after talks with Israel accelerated following the fall of the Assad regime. President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in September that the countries had “almost reached agreements on 90%” of their outstanding issues, with a security agreement potentially preceding peace negotiations. CSA found 54% of Syrians believed peace was likely, 53% supported a security arrangement and 46% supported normalization. The dispute over the Golan Heights remains a key obstacle.
Saudi Arabia, previously seen as a leading candidate for normalization, has moved further away since October 7, 2023, and the 2026 Iran War. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in November 2025 that he was prepared to work toward joining the accords, but CSA said the Iran war and concerns over Israel’s regional alliances have made Riyadh increasingly wary.
Oman has also become less likely to normalize despite a history of contacts with Israel. Sultan Qaboos bin Said hosted several Israeli leaders, but under Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, Oman has repeatedly rejected normalization and strengthened its role as a mediator with Iran and other regional actors.
Full normalization with Qatar dependent on peace agreement with Palestinians
Qatar maintains working contacts with Israel and serves as a mediator between Israel and Hamas, but says full diplomatic relations depend on an Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement. CSA said Doha’s ties with Iran and support for the Muslim Brotherhood make accession to the accords unlikely in the near term.
Iraq remains an unlikely candidate because of Iranian influence and a 2022 law criminalizing normalization with Israel. CSA singled out Iraqi Kurdistan as an exception, citing its longstanding contacts with Israel and greater public openness toward diplomatic relations.
Yemen’s continuing civil war makes normalization highly unlikely. The Iran-backed Houthis are actively hostile to Israel, while other Yemeni factions have previously expressed openness to relations. CSA said a future postwar government could reconsider the issue, but little movement is possible while the country remains divided.
Iran ranked last. Relations with Israel ended after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, and decades of hostility have developed into direct warfare. CSA concluded that normalization is not possible under Iran’s current regime.

Zohran Mamdani and the limit New York’s Jews must set - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:46:42 UTC
20:46:42 KST

On the third anniversary of October 7, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani gave the victims of the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust one sentence of grief. He named Hamas and its war crimes. Then he turned.
“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he wrote, and the rest of his statement, more than twice as long, was an indictment of Israel: genocide, occupation, apartheid, American tax dollars, and arms shipments.
Jewish organizations responded with outrage, as they have many times before. It is not enough. Outrage is what a provocateur wants. Every condemnation confirms that he holds the power to wound, and he pays nothing for it.
Anyone who has worked with someone who tests limits knows you do not contain that person by shouting. You set a calm, consistent boundary and attach a consequence to it.
First, though, the pattern has to be seen clearly. As a psychoanalyst who has spent decades studying the minds of perpetrators and those who sympathize with them, I look at the structure of a statement rather than its slogans. The structure says more.
The grief was short. Mourning requires the capacity to stay with another person’s pain without needing to change the subject.
The mayor could not stay. When grief for Jews becomes intolerable to someone, it is usually because it threatens a story he needs to believe, in which Jews are never the victims.
The word “Jews” is missing, as the ADL’s Jonathan Greenblatt pointed out. To name the victims as Jews would be to admit why they were killed.
Hamas did not murder 1,200 people and drag 251 into Gaza because of a policy dispute. It did so because they were Jews.
Erasing the word erases the motive, and erasing the motive clears the way for a reversal: within a few lines, the victim becomes the perpetrator. This is projection in its plainest form.
The wish to annihilate is lifted off the actual killers and placed onto those who defended themselves. Once that move is made, the anniversary no longer belongs to the dead. It belongs to the accuser.
Jewish New Yorkers asked for one day. Not agreement with Israeli policy, not silence on Gaza; just one day on which their dead could be their dead. The mayor of the city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel could not give them that.
Since a mayor’s words set the city’s emotional temperature, this is about more than hurt feelings. Those who already hate hear that their hatred is righteous. The rise in attacks on Jews in New York did not happen in a vacuum.
So what must be done now?
The boundary should be this: Jewish institutions in New York, including the federations, synagogues, major agencies, and Jewish elected officials, should agree that the mayor will not be invited to Jewish community events, not be given photo opportunities, and will not speak from Jewish platforms.
This holds until he meets one public condition: he must name the victims of October 7 as Jews and acknowledge that they were murdered because they were Jews. The condition is stated once and is not negotiated.
Mamdani needs the image of Jewish acceptance in order to claim he is not hostile to Jews. The community can stop providing it.
Two further steps give the boundary weight. First, the community should hold its own civic October 7 memorial, with the Governor, Council members, and non-Jewish allies standing beside it, so that the city’s memory of that day no longer belongs to the mayor.
Second, every antisemitic incident in New York and the city’s response to it should be documented and sent each month to the City Council, Albany, and the Justice Department. Outrage fades. A record does not.
This asks something of Jewish leaders that outrage does not: discipline. A boundary that one federation honors and another breaks for a ribbon-cutting is worse than none, because it teaches the mayor that the community can be divided.
The limit works only if it is held together.
One sentence of grief followed by a long accusation is not mourning. It is the appropriation of mourning.
Jewish New Yorkers do not need to argue with it. They need to stop lending it their presence.

Saudi Arabia extends Riyadh airport closure after deadly strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:43:08 UTC
20:43:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia extends Riyadh airport closure after strike kills 12
Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport will remain closed until at least midnight local time on Sunday following a strike that killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the latest in a series of deadly attacks on the Riyadh transport hub.
The closure was extended until midnight local time on Sunday, according to a notice to air missions, or NOTAM, issued by Saudi aviation authorities. Flights have been cancelled or diverted while officials assess damage to the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis for Saturday’s attack. The dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt. Some of the injured remain in critical condition, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree renewed the group’s warning on Sunday against using Saudi airports. His statement, which exempted Mecca and Medina, described other airports as "potential targets and sites for operations by our forces" and urged airlines, airport workers and travellers to take the warning seriously.
The statement also said Saudi Arabia "bears responsibility for any failed interceptions".
Earlier attacks on the airport this week killed four people and damaged a Saudia aircraft on the ground, according to Saudi authorities. The repeated strikes have made the protection of passengers and airport staff an immediate concern alongside the disruption to flights.
Questions remain over whether those inside the airport received an actionable public warning before Saturday’s strike, and what procedures were in place after the earlier attacks.
Saudi Arabia already operates a National Early Warning Platform. The Saudi Civil Defence says it uses cell-broadcast technology to send emergency messages, accompanied by a distinctive tone, to phones connected to mobile networks in the affected area. Its purpose is to warn the public and explain what action people should take to protect themselves.
That public-alert function is distinct from intercepting an incoming missile -- the questions concern both whether a threat was detected and whether information reached people in time to act.
During Iranian attacks in March, at the onset of the war launched by the US and Israel, residents of Riyadh received Arabic- and English-language messages warning of a "hostile aerial threat" and instructing them to remain indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors. Reporting on a 18 March incident, however, placed the alerts shortly after explosions were heard.
The Civil Defence also issued mobile warnings for Riyadh and nearby Al-Kharj on 19 September amid escalating Houthi attacks, followed by all-clear messages – showing how the platform has been used during the current escalation.
The attacks come as Riyadh hosts major international energy meetings. The WPC Energy Congress, running from Sunday to Thursday, is proceeding as scheduled, while organisers previously said the Future Investment Initiative would go ahead from October 26 to 29. The latter announcement preceded the latest deadly strike.
The US embassy has meanwhile urged American citizens to avoid King Khalid International Airport and its surrounding areas, and to exercise extreme caution when using other major Saudi airports.
