Thousands rally in London to halt UK arms sales to Israel (VIDEO)
Thousands of people took to the streets of London on Saturday, calling on the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel and boycott trade with the country over its actions in Gaza, which protesters say amount to three years of genocide against Palestinians.
Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza three years ago in response to the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas, in which about 1,200 Israelis were killed and 250 taken hostage. The United Nations estimates that around 1.98 million people, or 90% of Gaza’s population, have been displaced by the operations since then, while much of the enclave’s water and sanitation infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Video footage from central London shows crowds of demonstrators gathering along the Victoria Embankment, with many wearing keffiyehs, carrying Palestinian flags, and holding placards reading ‘End the genocide’, ‘Free Palestine’, ‘Disarm Israel, save lives’, and ‘Make empathy great again’ as they marched towards Parliament. A bride and groom also appeared to be among those taking part.
The protesters urged the British authorities to step up efforts “make much more strident efforts” to force Israel to comply with international law, journalist and political commentator Syed Mohsin Abbas, who was at the scene, told RT. The Deep Dive Perspective podcast host stressed that demonstrators were calling for more concrete steps against Israel wherever possible.
“The realistic demands are really that the arms to Israel should be stopped altogether, trade with Israel should be boycotted,” Abbas added.
There are already some UK restrictions on arms exports to Israel, including the suspension of licenses for equipment that could be used by Israeli forces in Gaza. Britain has also taken steps to restrict trade with Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territories. London has said it will refuse export license applications for goods that could materially contribute to the occupation, while other trade restrictions target settlement-linked activity.
Protesters view those measures as limited steps that fall short of bringing about meaningful change for Palestinians. Ismail Patel, head of the UK-based campaign group Friends of Al-Aqsa (FOA), criticized the restrictions for targeting trade linked to Israeli settlements rather than taking broader action on arms exports and commerce with Israel, accusing the British government of adopting a “performative” stance instead of meaningful action to protect Palestinian rights.

Russia steps up assassination attempts targeting defence company executives in Europe, FT says
European intelligence services have warned executives at defence companies across Europe that Russia is stepping up attempts to assassinate them in an effort to intimidate Ukraine's partners.
Source: Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Representatives of five different European intelligence services said the Kremlin has ordered an expansion of sabotage and hybrid operations in Europe to significantly weaken support for Kyiv in the coming months.
Intelligence officials say the killing of European civilians, once considered taboo even for the Russian secret services, is becoming an increasingly important part of these plans.
According to the warning, Kremlin agents could target executives and other senior employees at defence companies. Executives of smaller companies are also at risk, particularly those involved in manufacturing drones or their components.
A representative of Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) said the agency has significantly stepped up its engagement with employees and executives at German defence companies, including recommending that they hire private close-protection teams.
"Russia is engaged in the deliberate planning of acts of violence against individuals by state or state-controlled actors. We are observing a further development of these actions in terms of the targets, the methods and the actors involved, including the use of organised crime structures," BfV head Sinan Selen warned German lawmakers.
Several defence company executives told the Financial Times that they have stepped up their personal security over the past six months on the advice of the government's security services. Others said they took such measures only when travelling abroad.
Responsibility for potential assassination attempts is largely attributed to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence agency .
According to intelligence sources, Russian officers are increasingly working with organised crime groups, using cross-border agent networks and dividing intelligence gathering, logistics, planning and execution among different cells or individuals, rather than relying on "disposable" agents recruited online for money.
In some cases, active plots have already been uncovered and thwarted. In others, suspicious activity has been observed, including surveillance of individuals' daily routines at home and at work.
"The main goal from the Russian perspective is still psychological. Just by making people feel they might be a target, they are having their effect. They want individuals to think twice before doing business with Ukraine," one intelligence official said.
Background:
- Executives at Europe's largest arms manufacturers have been on heightened alert since early 2024, when US and German intelligence services uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German company Rheinmetall.
- In January 2025, NATO officially confirmed that Russia had intended to kill Papperger.
- In early August, a Russian couple were detained in Sweden after setting up camp near a property where a person under personal protection lived. It later emerged that the person in question was Micael Johansson, CEO of the Swedish defence company Saab.

Can Trump Sidestep Russia Sanctions as the Midterms Loom?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:38:00 UTC
20:38:00 KST

US President Donald Trump faces a deadline to implement tougher Russia sanctions just 16 days before Americans vote in midterm elections that could strip Republicans of their congressional majorities.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed on Sept. 18, sets an Oct. 18 deadline for many initial measures. But it also gives him considerable latitude to waive penalties, choose tariff rates and shape enforcement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump cannot lawfully treat mandatory provisions as optional. He can, however, use the law’s exemptions and waiver powers to limit how much additional pressure Russia faces.
Republicans face a serious risk of losing Congress
As of its Oct. 4 update, Decision Desk HQ’s forecast gave Democrats a 76% chance of winning the House, compared with 24% for Republicans.
The Senate forecast was considerably closer: 56% for Democratic control and 44% for Republicans.
The likely loss of a House majority and the tight contest for the Senate impacts sanctions oversight.
A Democratic House could investigate implementation, seek administration records and question officials about exemptions even if Republicans retained the Senate. Congressional committees have investigative and subpoena powers, although disputes over compliance can delay access to information.
A Republican election defeat would not immediately transfer control of sanctions policy to Democrats. Trump would remain president, and the newly elected Congress would take office in January. But decisions made before the midterms could become the subject of scrutiny afterward.
Ukraine Ready to Halt Refinery Strikes for Energy Truce, Zelensky Says
The political pressure also cuts in different directions. Strong enforcement could help Trump demonstrate toughness toward Moscow. Sweeping tariffs could expose him to criticism over costs for American businesses and consumers. The election creates incentives to manage both risks rather than necessarily choose the harshest available measures.
Democrats were divided over the law, not simply over Ukraine
The House passed the legislation on Sept. 16 by 262 votes to 159. Support came from 203 Republicans, 58 Democrats and one independent; seven Republicans and 152 Democrats opposed it.
The Senate had approved it 86 to 11, with 36 Democrats joining the majority. The contrast between the chambers makes it misleading to describe the legislation as either uniformly backed or uniformly opposed by Democrats.
House Democratic objections centered on the tariff powers and discretion given to Trump. Richard Neal, the senior Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, summarized the distinction:
“We are for Ukraine. We are against giving this president more tariff authority.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries also argued that the legislation contained loopholes allowing Trump to avoid sanctions while imposing tariffs that could raise Americans’ living costs, Roll Call reported.
That gives Democratic critics an argument if enforcement proves weak: they can say they warned that the law gave Trump too much discretion. Democrats who supported it, meanwhile, can demand that he deliver the pressure they voted to authorize.
Ukraine’s MAGA outreach helped change the political backdrop
Notably, the law’s passage followed Ukraine’s efforts to rebuild relations with influential conservatives and challenge the assumption that supporting Kyiv was incompatible with Trump’s America First movement.
In “Inside Ukraine’s MAGA Breakthrough,” Kyiv Post documented outreach through conservative media, congressional offices and visits to Ukraine. The effort included Ben Shapiro’s interview with President Volodymyr Zelensky and Laura Loomer’s subsequent visit.
“When they come to Ukraine, they understand,” Ukraine Freedom Project founder Steven Moore told Kyiv Post. “Ukraine is a story of freedom, and Americans respond to freedom.”
The reporting also cited a June survey commissioned by Razom for Ukraine and the Ukraine Freedom Project in which tougher Russia sanctions attracted support from 81% of likely Republican primary voters and 83% of Trump voters. Loomer subsequently urged Republicans to pass Graham’s legislation.
While those developments do not prove that outreach alone secured passage, they do show why Trump cannot assume that his political base uniformly favors restraint toward Russia. Kyiv had gained advocates within the conservative coalition before Congress approved the law.
What Trump must do, and where he has discretion
Much of the legislation requires initial reviews and sanctions within 30 days of enactment. Its targets include Russian financial institutions, foreign military suppliers and the shipping networks supporting Russian trade.
The Morgan Lewis analysis notes that the law expands restrictions and makes numerous measures mandatory, while also codifying existing sanctions. Consequently, compliance could involve both new penalties and preservation of restrictions already in place.
The tariff provisions allow additional duties of up to 500% on Russian imports and up to 100% on imports from qualifying countries buying Russian energy or facilitating sanctions evasion. The maximum rates do not take effect automatically.
For the relevant third-country tariffs, Congress must receive written justification at least 10 days before imposition. Duties beginning Oct. 18 would therefore require that submission by Oct. 8.
Trump’s most significant flexibility comes from Section 115. It permits waivers after he certifies to Congress that relief serves the US national interest and submits an explanation. Treasury also retains licensing authority. Sullivan & Cromwell’s analysis identifies those powers as important determinants of the law’s practical effect.
Using those provisions would be legally different from ignoring the law. It could nevertheless leave a substantial gap between the pressure supporters of Congress promised and the additional costs Moscow actually faces.
Three paths before the election
Broad enforcement would combine meaningful new sanctions against Russia’s commercial networks with substantial tariffs on qualifying countries. Politically, that would allow Trump to claim he had delivered on the legislation, while accepting the diplomatic and economic consequences.
Selective enforcement would target particular suppliers, banks and vessels while limiting tariffs or granting justified waivers elsewhere. This would let the administration demonstrate action while preserving room for negotiations and avoiding some disruption to trade.
Extensive relief would use waivers, licenses and lower tariff rates to keep additional pressure limited. That could satisfy some procedural requirements without producing the economic impact the law’s strongest supporters expect.
Ignoring the law vs. weakening its impact
An outright refusal to perform mandatory duties would raise a compliance dispute. The legislation’s waiver process gives Trump a more defensible route to restraint, but it also requires him to explain that restraint to Congress.
For Ukraine, the important evidence will therefore be the decisions accompanying implementation: which previously unrestricted networks are targeted, which countries face duties, what rates apply, and who receives relief.
With Republicans facing a likely House loss and a closely contested Senate, Trump may soon have to defend those choices before a less accommodating Congress. The law gives him room to soften sanctions. The midterms could make that room considerably less comfortable.

Over 130 dead after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti coast
October 11, 2026
The United Nations International Organization for Migration (IOM) on Sunday said that at least 139 people were killed when a migrant boat carrying an estimated 305 people capsized off the coast of Djibouti in northeastern Africa.
At least 84 people remained missing in what is thought to be one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
In a statement, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac called the loss of life "devastating," adding, "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and reach Gulf countries.
"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," according to the IOM.
IOM representatives said, "Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing."
Djibouti to Yemen a dangerous crossing
The IOM says it has detected more than 20,000 crossings from Djibouti to Yemen — which is currently in the middle of a raging civil war — in the past month. More than 900 migrants were killed attempting the passage in 2025.
The IOM says most of those attempting to cross are from Ethiopia and Somalia. The 80 survivors from Saturday night's capsizing were all Ethiopian nationals.
The IOM on Sunday urged "donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance."
Of the bodies so far recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women and 15 were children.

At least 109 dead, over 100 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti

At least 139 dead, 84 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
Search and rescue operations conducted after vessel carrying more than 300 people capsizes near Guhere.
At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died and 84 are missing after a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti, according to the United Nations migration agency.
In a statement on Sunday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) quoted survivors as saying that the incident happened near Guhere off Djibouti’s eastern coast in the Gulf of Aden near the Bab al-Mandeb strait from Thursday night to before dawn on Friday.
The boat was heading from Djibouti to Yemen with more than 300 people on board. More than 80 people – all Ethiopians – survived the shipwreck while Djiboutian search and rescue operations continued.
“Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance,” IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac said, lamenting the “devastating loss of life”.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won’t be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the Associated Press.
“This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities,” Coissac added.
Undeterred by instability
Crossing Bab al-Mandeb, a waterway that measures just 20km (12.4 miles) at its narrowest points between Djibouti and Yemen, is a popular but dangerous route for thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa.
Many embark on this journey in search of employment and safety in Gulf countries, undeterred by the rising instability in the region due to the US-Israel war on Iran and the resumption of fighting in Yemen between government forces and Houthi fighters last month.
The IOM said it had recorded “more than 20,000 incoming movements to Djibouti from Ethiopia” since September 10. Last year, more than half a million people tried to move along this route into Yemen, and at least 900 people died or are missing, according to the agency.
Djibouti is not only a place where migrants depart from, but several thousand people are also fleeing to the country from Yemen due to the renewed conflict.

High-tech companies discuss ways to boost ties at 3rd Russia-Iran ICT Forum
TEHRAN – Leading Iranian and Russian companies have explored ways to expand bilateral cooperation in advanced technologies at the third Russia-Iran Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Forum.
The forum brought together officials, diplomats, and public- and private-sector representatives from both countries. The participants met on the sidelines of the second Global Digital Forum, held in Moscow from October 8 to 10, IRNA reported.
During the meeting, Alexander Shoitov, Russia’s deputy minister of digital development, communications and mass media, said the participation of Iranian companies in the Global Digital Forum offered a valuable opportunity to exchange information and establish new partnerships.
He noted that Iran and Russia had significant potential to expand bilateral cooperation, particularly in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.
Shoitov also reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to deepen bilateral ties and develop joint infrastructure in the ICT sector.
For his part, Iran’s ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, highlighted the importance of fostering strategic cooperation between Iran and Russia in the expansion of digital exchanges within a governmental framework. The enhancement of ties helps strengthen the country’s capacity for participation in regional and global markets.
Highlighting the expertise and knowledge of Iranian technology companies in the localization of IT infrastructure equipment, Russian companies can establish joint ventures with reliable partners in Iran, gaining access to the country’s IT and artificial intelligence services market.
Moreover, Iranian and Russian representatives of high-technology companies showcased their latest cutting-edge accomplishments and presented their comprehensive plans and operational proposals for the promotion of cooperation in advanced technologies.
Exchanging best practices and technological solutions, holding B2B meetings, expanding business networks, and exploring opportunities for joint projects were among other key parts of the Forum. Particular attention was given to practical mechanisms for Russian and Iranian companies to enter new markets and develop cooperation with partners from third countries.
The second Global Digital Forum was held at the Mechta multifunctional complex in Gorky Park. As many as 760 delegates from 120 countries took part, including deputy prime ministers, digital development ministers, senior government officials, diplomats, IT company heads, experts, researchers, and representatives of international organizations from Africa, Asia, the Gulf region, Europe, and Latin America.
Sessions were held on artificial intelligence, digital sovereignty, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, and global cooperation. Participants reviewed global trends in digital transformation, the integration of modern products into national digital systems, and prospects for cooperation between countries in the technology sector.
MOUs to bolster ICT ties
In December 2025, top tech Iranian and Russian companies signed five memoranda of understanding (MOUs) on artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, smart government, blockchain and fintech, regulators, technology parks, and post services, to promote cooperation in the information and communication technology (ICT) sector.
The MOUs were signed in Russia during the fifth Iran-Russia ICT Forum held from December 6 to 7, IRNA reported.
An Iranian delegation led by the deputy ICT Minister for Technology and Innovation, Meysam Abedi, attended the forum.
Referring to the strategic partnership between Iran and Russia, Jalali said the two countries have a high capacity, and the expansion of collaborations will be beneficial to both sides.
For his part, Shoitov said the memoranda of understanding and the agreements reached today are the result of ongoing efforts over the past few years.
“Today, we are celebrating the results of our hard work over many years with the companies collaborating. We can confidently say, cooperation is definitely going on.
So far, the two countries have signed many memoranda of understanding, but there are still new areas of cooperation opening up in our interactions that benefit the people of the two nations,” Shoitov further noted.
Abedi, for his part, said the reached agreements are the result of three years of continuous cooperation between the ICT ministries of the two countries.
He called on Iranian and Russian companies to seriously follow up on the implementation of the MOUs and agreements, and to remove probable obstacles with the help of the government departments of the two countries.
The official went on to propose locating a third country as the joint market for Iranian-Russian products on the agenda, expressing hope that the two countries would sign MOUs on a joint market by the sixth forum.
In May, Russian Presidential Aide Andrei Fursenko emphasized the significance of promoting partnerships and collaborations with Iran in emerging technologies.
It is a fact that focusing on already established technologies will not be beneficial for the two countries. So, it is essential to put on the agenda the technologies that have not (fully) developed yet, which is a much more difficult task, IRNA quoted Fursenko as saying.
For his part, Safarinia said Iran is committed to promoting international scientific cooperation, highlighting that Russia is among the top countries with which Iran is willing to expand ties.

20:33:53 KST

At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.
Another 84 people are still missing after the incident, which, according to survivors, happened near Guhere, north of the fishing town of Obock, during the night of 8-9 October when the boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen.
Eighty-two people, all Ethiopian nationals, survived the capsizing, the UN agency said.
It described the incident as one of the deadliest boat disasters recorded on a migration corridor between the Horn of Africa and the Arab peninsula known as the eastern route.
“This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” said Alexandre Coissac, the IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti.
The organisation is providing healthcare, psychosocial, food and other assistance to 64 survivors at its Obock migrant response centre.
The IOM is working with local authorities to provide emergency assistance. Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, and local authorities are providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for those who died.
The eastern route is one of the busiest migration paths in the world. Hundreds of thousands of people a year, mostly Ethiopians and Somalis, use it to reach Gulf countries, mainly Saudi Arabia. Some have been forced out of their communities by conflict and natural disasters, and others move to seek work and other economic opportunities.
The route accounts for most of the migratory movement from the Horn of Africa. The other main ones are the northern route to north Africa and Europe, and the southern route to southern Africa.
The eastern route is also one of the most dangerous globally, with some people dying from walking long distances in searing heat and others from the capsizing of boats that smugglers have crammed them on to in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
Coissac said: “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.”
In 2025, more than 900 people died or went missing along the route, according to the IOM’s missing migrants project, while the number undertaking the journey increased by 18%. In March, nine people died and 45 went missing after a migrant boat capsized.
This week’s tragedy shows the movement is happening despite fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group and Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast.
The violence has forced more than 3,800 people to cross to Djibouti to seek protection, according to the country’s office for assistance to refugees and disaster victims (Onars).

Iran’s Medical Council urges global health bodies to act over US sanctions
TEHRAN – The Iranian Medical Council has called on the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and the World Medical Association (WMA) to take immediate action against the use of patients’ lives as a tool of political and military pressure.
In an official letter to the three international organizations, the council said the US government was violating international humanitarian and criminal law through inhumane measures, including economic blockade and pharmaceutical sanctions against Iran, turning patients’ lives into an instrument of political and military coercion.
Mohammad Raiszadeh, head of the Iranian Medical Council, urged the leaders of international health organizations to respond promptly and responsibly to what he described as inhumane acts and the weaponization of medical resources in armed conflicts.
He cited previous reports of direct attacks on healthcare facilities, medical infrastructure, and pharmaceutical facilities, adding that the US attack on the Touska, a vessel carrying medicines and, in particular, vital supplies for dialysis patients, was another clear example of directly endangering patients’ health and lives.
Raiszadeh said Iran’s medical community expected the WHO, WMA, ICRC, and other relevant international bodies to respond appropriately and responsibly to the use of medicines, healthcare facilities, medical shipments, and patients’ lives as instruments of warfare.
He also called for effective measures to ensure safe, rapid, and unhindered routes for the delivery of medicines, medical equipment, and pharmaceutical raw materials.
An effective response from institutions whose very purpose is to protect human health, life, and dignity would represent the fulfillment of their moral and historic responsibilities to humanity, he added.
Raiszadeh stressed that Iran’s medical community and people would not forget these events and would pursue accountability, in accordance with international law, for both those responsible for the actions and institutions that remained silent in the face of them.
As of March 27, data compiled from WHO, the Iranian Red Crescent, and national health agencies reveal a targeted erosion of medical neutrality. A total of 292 medical and relief centres, including hospitals, pharmacies, and primary health clinics, have been damaged or destroyed.
This destruction has forced 13 hospitals completely out of service, while another seven have been fully evacuated under duress because of proximity to danger zones.
The emergency response capacity has been further crippled by the destruction of 48 ambulances and rescue vehicles, as well as an emergency medical helicopter.
The assault on health care is not merely incidental but systemic. Under the Geneva Conventions and the UN Charter, medical personnel and facilities must be protected at all times unless used for military purposes. Yet, verified reports indicate US–Israeli attacks on health facilities and the killing of at least eight health-care workers, doctors, nurses, and emergency first responders in Iran.

DOE advances conservation efforts for reptile and amphibian species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:30:18 UTC
20:30:18 KST

DOE advances conservation efforts for reptile and amphibian species
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) is developing national conservation programs for priority reptile and amphibian species, with a focus on deploying modern monitoring technologies, strengthening local community engagement, and providing ongoing training for experts.
The plan primarily targets salamanders, marsh crocodiles, spider-tailed horned vipers, and Talysh toads through new methods of monitoring, census, and conservation measures, IRNA quoted Peyman Ashouri, an official with the DOE, as saying.
Razi University in Kermanshah province has already estimated the population of the yellow-spotted salamander using artificial intelligence (AI), and a census of the marsh crocodile is planned to be conducted from February 20 to May 21, he added.
The official elaborated on adopted measures to address human-wildlife conflicts, stating that a project is currently underway to mitigate threats, reduce conflicts, and restore the habitats of the Lorestan newt and Talysh toad; the initiatives include installing signage, producing wildlife awareness posters and brochures, organizing educational programs for tourists and local communities, and removing waste from the habitats.
Referring to spider-tailed horned vipers, Ashouri said the DOE is drafting a conservation plan for the protection of the species, which will be implemented soon.
Data-driven strategies to strengthen biodiversity conservation efforts
The DOE is implementing a comprehensive range of conservation, scientific, legal, and operational initiatives to strengthen the protection of wildlife species and habitats across the country based on a targeted and strategic approach, with priorities guided by data and scientific research.
According to Peyman Valizadeh, an official with the DOE, the DOE focuses on a more scientific approach to develop and implement conservation efforts tailored to the specific needs of each species and habitat, IRNA reported.
It has so far prepared plans for the preservation of 25 endangered species, with thirteen more plans being developed. The plans provide a clear framework for species conservation by delineating the species’ status, major threats, conservation priorities, necessary actions, and assessment indicators, he noted.
However, the DOE faces some challenges in implementing these measures at national and provincial levels. One of the biggest challenges is securing funding to implement the plans. Developing specialized capacity to preserve species is the other problem. Lack of trained, specialized forces has made it difficult to implement the conservation action plans effectively. Therefore, training specialized personnel, developing experts’ capacities in provinces, and strengthening scientific and technical capabilities of the headquarters are put on the agenda, the official highlighted.
Referring to adopted measures to combat wildlife trafficking, Valizadeh said to foster greater coordination among the responsible agencies, the DOE has established a national committee on combating wildlife trafficking; the committee has held three expert meetings so far. Furthermore, the drafting of a comprehensive plan to combat and prevent wildlife trafficking is nearing completion. Furthermore, a comprehensive program to combat and prevent wildlife trafficking is being drafted.
To manage human-wildlife conflicts, efforts have been made to shift the approach from a reactive posture to the identification of critical hotspots, understanding the drivers of conflict, and implementing preventive measures. The DOE has identified some conflict hotspots for species like leopards, black bears, and herbivores; collecting data on black bears in Hormozgan and Kerman provinces is underway.
Moreover, the DOE has signed an agreement with the National Environment Fund and the Agricultural Products Insurance Fund to support local communities and compensate their losses, Valizadeh further noted.
Accurate information on species distribution, habitats, movement paths, and ecological corridors makes conservation efforts more effective, he added.
In this regard, the DOE, in cooperation with Shiraz University, has carried out research to prepare comprehensive distribution maps to identify migration and movement corridors for herbivores and carnivores.
The maps will serve as a management tool for habitat conservation, prevention and management of human-wildlife conflicts, development of conservation priorities, and proper use of smart monitoring and conservation programs, thereby providing a more accurate basis for conservation decision-making, Valizadeh said.
The official went on to say that the DOE will secure funds, train skilled human forces, and foster intersectoral cooperation to establish an integrated system that benefits from scientific information, field data, capacities of local communities, and the capabilities of executive agencies to develop and implement conservation plans for each species and habitat.

“Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:28:27 UTC
20:28:27 KST

“Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”
TEHRAN – World Migratory Bird Day serves as an opportunity to highlight the vital role these birds play in maintaining ecosystem balance and the need to protect their habitats. These tireless travelers cover thousands of kilometers each year to survive, yet face mounting threats, including drying wetlands, habitat destruction, illegal hunting, and climate change.
World Migratory Bird Day is a global observance aimed at raising awareness of the importance of conserving migratory birds and their habitats. It was first established in 2006 through an initiative by the Secretariat of the Agreement on the Conservation of African-Eurasian Migratory Waterbirds (AEWA) and the Secretariat of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), with support from the United Nations.
The observance seeks to draw public attention to threats such as habitat destruction, environmental pollution, illegal hunting and climate change, while underscoring the need for international cooperation to protect migratory birds.
World Migratory Bird Day is observed annually on the second Saturday of May and the second Saturday of October, coinciding with the main bird migration seasons in the Northern Hemisphere. In 2026, the observance falls on May 9 and October 10.
This year’s theme, “Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”, highlights the role of citizen science and public participation in migratory bird conservation. The initiative emphasizes the value of field observations recorded by birdwatchers, researchers, local communities and nature enthusiasts in understanding migration patterns, monitoring population trends and identifying threats affecting different species.
Iran plays a particularly important role in migratory bird conservation due to its geographical position in West Asia and its location along the seasonal migration routes of numerous species. The country’s wetlands, lakes, coastlines and other natural habitats serve as stopover, feeding and resting sites, as well as wintering grounds, for large numbers of waterbirds and shorebirds throughout the year.
Anzali Wetland, Miankaleh, Gori Gol and Shadegan wetlands, along with aquatic habitats in the Lake Urmia basin, are among the areas where continuous monitoring can provide valuable information on species occurrence, relative abundance, arrival and departure dates, and seasonal population changes.
Recording observation dates, bird numbers, geographic locations, habitat conditions and evidence of threats can help improve ecological assessments, particularly when data are collected using standardized methods over extended periods. Such records make it easier to compare findings over time and identify ecological changes. In this context, public participation in documenting bird sightings can complement professional bird census and monitoring programs nationwide.
On World Migratory Bird Day, the theme “Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!” serves as a reminder that effective conservation requires not only expertise and planning but also informed public participation and the transformation of individual observations into reliable, usable data.
Every accurate observation can help reveal a larger picture of the status of migratory birds and the vital routes they depend on — a picture that is essential to protecting this shared natural heritage.

Three Years After October 7, This former Israeli Soldier Still Wakes Up at 6:29 A.M. every Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:20 UTC
20:26:20 KST

Shalev Ben Simon wakes up every morning at the same time. He opens his eyes, looks at his mobile phone and sees – 6:29 A.M. "It doesn't matter what time I go to sleep. Even if I fall asleep at six, after half an hour I wake up and can't go back to sleep. It's this urge, I feel haunted."
Three years have passed since that hour was seared into the collective memory of Israelis. But unlike most other Israelis, Ben Simon was actually there, at 6:29 A.M., in uniform, not far from the border fence near Gaza. "I was actually trying to get out of Shabbat duty that weekend," he admits. "I told all sorts of stories hoping they'd let me go home, but my request wasn't approved. The truth is I wanted to go to Nova," he says, referring to the music festival near Kibbutz Re'im, where hundreds of Israelis were murdered on October 7. "So I would have been screwed either way."
He returned alive after that Saturday, but it is hard to say he returned to life. "I see blood on my hands, hear gunshots, feel my heart pounding. It doesn't go away, I can't shake the sights."
Ben Simon, who is 22, enlisted in Battalion 51 of the Golani Brigade in March 2022. He was trained for combat, served in Hebron in the West Bank, completed a squad commanders course and then returned to his company. Two weeks before October 7, he was promoted to sergeant first class, with his company responsible for the Kissufim sector in southern Israel.
Ben Simon and his comrades were sent to a small outpost, made up of a combined combat team in a wooded area, near the Gaza border. Eight infantry soldiers in an armored personnel carrier and four armored soldiers in a tank – this was the force manning the border outpost that weekend.
"On Friday evening, we all made Kiddush together," he says, referring the recital of the blessing over the wine on the eve of Shabbat. "We stayed up until 2 A.M., it was the time of our lives." At 5:30 A.M., Ben Simon woke his soldiers for a routine round at sunrise. "Five of us entered the armored personnel carrier, sat and talked a bit, and then I decided to nap and asked one of the soldiers to listen to the radio."
The 6:29 Wake-up
At 6:29 A.M., he woke up. "My soldier tells me there's 'purple rain' [code for rocket and missile fire]. I didn't understand what was happening, I asked if they said the word 'chicken' [code for drill] on the radio." The soldier replied in the negative.
"I immediately yelled at the rest of the soldiers to get into the armored personnel carrier," Ben Simon says. Five minutes later, a mortar shell landed near them, creating a crater in the ground. After a few more seconds, another mortar shell hit, this time striking the APC itself. "Everything shook," he recounts. "I immediately called my officer to try and understand what was happening. He told me: 'It looks like there's going to be a hell of a war now. Get the guys ready, follow me.'"
Until then, they had never moved the APC from its spot. "Not even in drills," he says. This was the first of many times that day that Ben Simon was to perform actions he had never practiced. But in real time, there was no time to think about it. They had to act, and fast.
A few minutes after they started driving, Ben Simon opened one of the APC's hatches – and a drone appeared above it. "It was huge, enormous. It cast a shadow over the entire APC. I told the soldiers: 'Listen, I don't know why we got into this, but everyone has to be alert and focused. Load your weapons, and shut up.'"
A few more minutes passed until they reached the breached border fence. "We saw a huge number of motorcyclists just streaming in endlessly," Ben Simon recalls. "Bullets hit the APC again and again, there was also RPG [rocket-propelled grenade] fire. The tank with us went up to a position (a high earthen rampart), and we secured it and started taking down militants with the 'lethal weapon' [a firearm mounted on military vehicles]." At one point, Ben Simon noticed the tank's engine cover was on fire. Get ready to dismount, he told his soldiers. But just before they exited into the chaos, he saw the tank move backward, and he stopped them from exiting.
"Follow me," the armored officer in the tank ordered him. The destination was a path dense with vegetation, which the army anticipated would be used by militants to infiltrate in case of an attack. However, even the most extreme scenario they had trained for did not prepare the small force for what happened next. "We trained for an infiltration of six militants, maybe 10. Not hundreds," he explains. On their way, they joined up with another small force from the battalion, and were immediately ambushed. Bullets were fired from all directions, one hitting the abdomen of a soldier. Ben Simon took out the stretcher and placed the wounded soldier inside the APC. Then they got a new order: "Drive to the kibbutz."
When they reached the entrance gate of Kibbutz Kissufim, located a mere 1.5 kilometers (less than a mile) from the Gaza border, Ben Simon was stunned. Militants on motorcycles moved in one after another. One of them aimed an RPG at the APC and fired. Ben Simon ordered his driver to run him over. As they continued into the kibbutz, the chaos only intensified.
"The APC was just taking insane amounts of fire, I felt it was a miracle it kept moving," Ben Simon recalls. "We drove around the kibbutz and tried to understand what was happening, but it was impossible — there was fire from all directions. I didn't understand where to dismount, where I could drop off the wounded. Even distinguishing between our forces and the enemy was difficult. Some of them were in uniform." Only their Kalashnikov assault rifles gave away their identity, he says.
Ambushed again and again
Then, for the first time that morning, they exited the APC, near the kibbutz dining hall. At that very moment, another force dismounted near them – and one of its soldiers immediately took a bullet to the neck. "The medic came and stopped the bleeding with his finger, and I put him in the APC." Afterward, they began to move through the kibbutz on foot. There was one incident after another. Again and again they were ambushed, again and again they returned fire. "They pushed us to the limit, we had no grenades, and ammunition was running out. I replenished magazines from [the ammunition of] the wounded," he says.
Near the kibbutz kindergarten, there was a particularly fierce battle. At the height of the commotion, a sergeant first class from another platoon in the battalion stood next to him. "Suddenly I hear on his radio that one of the soldiers is wounded and needs to be extracted. I look and don't understand where he is, and then I suddenly identify him about a hundred meters from me. Insane fire was directed there," he recounts, "I thought they were doing it because they wanted to kidnap him, so I ran to him. I felt the bullets whistling past me, flying over me. One of them hit the sole of my shoe, but didn't penetrate."
When he reached the wounded soldier, Ben Simon called his name, but there was no response. "I pulled him along with another soldier to a nearby fortified shelter. I removed the front part of his vest and checked his pulse. I felt something faint. I started to massage him, and after 10 minutes I understood that was it, he was no longer with us. His hands grew cold, his eyes closed.
"I removed the back part of his vest and saw an exit wound from a bullet and large amounts of blood. I covered his face, took his personal belongings from him and apologized. Afterward, I carried him about 250 meters, to the evacuation point." His vest did not have a protective ceramic plate, Ben Simon learned later on. "He took a bullet straight to the heart, he didn't have much of a chance." Sgt. Guy Bazak was only 19. Four days later, he was buried in the military section at the Kochav Yair cemetery. "Every time I drive to the center of the country I visit him."
"It was a battle of few against many," the military investigation into the Kissufim battle concluded many months later. "The chances of the soldiers of Battalion 51 and the [kibbutz] security squad members stopping the enemy's attack were very low."
According to the investigation, the first reinforcement force, from Battalion 450 of the non-commissioned officers school, arrived there only at 1:06 P.M. Ben Simon encountered them about an hour and a half later, around the time he met Sa'ar Margolis, who had been the kibbutz's security coordinator for 11 years. About a year before the massacre, he left the position but remained a member of the security squad.
"I need a force," Margolis told him. Ben Simon did not hesitate, even though he didn't have much to offer. Two of his soldiers suffered combat shock, and another soldier evacuated them. The force under his command remained meager, and joined the force from Battalion 450 commanded by Staff Sgt. Adam Agmon. At 2:52 P.M., they departed.
"We advanced through the kibbutz and saw several bodies of militants, and then the body of an Israeli civilian," Ben Simon says. They continued to move and noticed a house consumed by fire. The military investigation revealed that it was the home of Ivan Illarramendi-Caesar and Dafna Garcovich. The fire left them no chance, and their remains were identified only about a month later.
The force continued on its way, trying to save whoever could still be saved. Next to the burned house stood the home of Kissufim's current security coordinator. "Margolis told me, 'I'll go in from here, and you from the other entrance.' Then he changed his mind: 'No, actually, the other way around.'" Ben Simon complied, and Margolis and Agmon advanced toward the stairs. "I hear the door opening, and then a burst of gunfire." Both were killed on the spot.
"I signaled to everyone to fall back because the guys from [Battalion] 450 were in shock, they still didn't understand what they had gotten into," Ben Simon says. "I started shooting at the house. I was terrified," he admits. "One of the militants came out of the house and fired bursts at me. After I was discharged, I went back there and saw the bullet impacts; to this day, I don't believe I survived it."
Non-stop shooting
The shooting did not stop, and Ben Simon realized he had to change his approach. He decided to outflank the militants through the burned house, together with one of his soldiers. "I started firing in their direction. I knelt, and then I hear the sound of something rolling, and I spot a grenade. I immediately retreated."
Ben Simon returned to the kibbutz entrance and sought reinforcements to extract the bodies. A force from the Dekel Battalion of Bahad 1 [officers training school] joined the mission. They moved to the house, killed the militants inside and carried out the bodies of Margolis and Agmon on stretchers.
Ben Simon continued to encounter militants right up until the evening. He went from one encounter to the next without stopping. Only when the sun began to set did he return to his APC and meet his soldiers. "They made several rounds of evacuating the wounded and dead; everything was full of blood." Afterward, they worked together to clear the nearby Kissufim outpost of militants.
In the days following October 7, they stayed in one of the kibbutz houses near the border. They ambushed militants who were still in the area. On October 12, the last militant was killed, and the kibbutz was cleared. The investigation revealed that about 150 militants from the Gaza Strip had infiltrated the kibbutz and outpost area. The army killed about 105 of them. The kibbutz became a memorial to the battle. "I looked around and felt my mind was messed up. The destruction remained, bodies everywhere, ash and dust."
Not the same person
In mid-October, Ben Simon and his comrades were transferred to a training base, and from there to a school in the town of Ofakim. There, for the first time, members of his family were given the opportunity to visit him. "I didn't exactly process the situation, I had responsibility for my soldiers and was required to maintain composure. I didn't express emotions, but inside I was broken."
At the end of October, when the IDF ground maneuver began, Ben Simon entered the Gaza Strip. His platoon was positioned as the spearhead force of Division 36. They operated mainly in the Rimal neighborhood in western Gaza City. "We had encounters near the sea; it felt as if the militants were emerging from the water — it was surreal." Afterward, they moved to the Zeitoun neighborhood, then to Shujaiyeh, and then to the Bureij and Maghazi refugee camps. Only at the end of December did Ben Simon go home, for the first time since October 1.
In those days, when he briefly returned to reality, he realized he was no longer the same person. The breaking point came in the evening, at nightfall. "I went for a drive with a friend in my parents' car," he recounts. "Suddenly I see a large van speeding toward me, trying to cut me off from the left. It honked at me, and everything came rushing back." Ben Simon stopped and got out of the vehicle. In his hand, he held a crowbar he had brought with him from the Gaza Strip. He approached the driver and cursed him. "I almost broke his window." A girl sat next to the driver and burst into tears. Ben Simon's friend brought him back to the car, to the passenger seat.
"After a few minutes, I asked him, 'Why are you driving?' and he looked at me with a stunned expression. 'Don't you remember what happened? Are you crazy? Do you know what you just did?' he asked, and I replied, 'Not really.'"
Afterward, his friend recounted what had happened. "I didn't believe it, at first I didn't remember anything. It was as if a demon had entered me, I wasn't myself." His friend suggested he seek psychological treatment. He initially refused, but at some point, he relented. "The therapist told me: 'You're not in a good state, you must ask to see a mental health officer.'"
Meanwhile, Ben Simon returned to the army. His brigade, Golani, left Gaza and was transferred to the northern border. "I asked to see a mental health officer, but they strung me along. My condition worsened, I had violent outbursts, I was full of rage." After his company commander refused to allow him to go for treatment, Ben Simon took his things and left, and has not returned since. "I was a deserter for a month, they called and threatened me with arrest."
Eventually, with a bit of help from officers with connections, Ben Simon met with the division's female mental health officer. "I told her everything I had been through, and she just started to cry. At the end of the meeting, she said I had PTSD." She sent him to another mental health officer, who referred him to the Taatzumot center, which provides intensive treatment for combat soldiers dealing with PTSD symptoms. "I was there for four months, and they diagnosed me with severe PTSD. My condition didn't improve, and they decided to discharge me from the army."
Ben Simon is not the only one in his platoon to be discharged early due to his mental state. "Four of us, from the team that was in the APC that morning, were discharged. That's fifty percent."
In the days following his discharge, all the traumas began to surface. "I started to isolate myself, to cut myself off from friends. I suffered from violent outbursts, from dissociative episodes. My parents couldn't provide me with a solution, but I understand them. It's hard to see your child falling apart." Ben Simon tried a wide range of treatments, but didn't stick with most of them. "I hopped back and forth between psychiatrists and psychologists, but I felt judged. I couldn't open up. The only treatment I have managed to stick with is Chinese acupuncture, it helps me."
'Feel betrayed'
At the same time he began seeking recognition for his condition with the Defense Ministry's Rehabilitation Department. About four months ago, he appeared before the medical committee. "I told them everything, but I didn't try to exaggerate," he says. A week and a half later, he was informed that he would be recognized with a 40 percent disability for 10 years. The Rehabilitation Department's new policy, revealed in Haaretz, is to minimize the granting of permanent disability status for PTSD sufferers as much as possible. Especially now.
"I felt betrayed," he says, "I didn't understand how it could be that after everything I went through, this is what they give me." Since then, he says, his symptoms have only worsened. Flashbacks return and surge, and anger swells. "I am ashamed of my country, I feel like they spat in my face. Do you really think that after everything I went through, my mental disability will disappear? I can barely leave the house, certainly not work. I'm not asking for pity, just a safety net, and some peace of mind. That's all. After everything I've given, don't I deserve that?"

At least 139 migrants dead, including some children, after boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes, UN agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:25:00 UTC
20:25:00 KST

At least 139 migrants dead, including some children, after boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes, UN agency says
NAIROBI, Oct 11 - At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations' International Organization for Migration said on Sunday.
The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock — a port town in Djibouti — during the night of October 8-9, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts.
Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. A spokesperson for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore.
"Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance," said IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities," Coissac said.
Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased.
The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment.
The migrants were heading to Yemen, with the hope of eventually making it to wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals themselves flee their country, which is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
"Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries," the IOM statement said.
FIGHTING IN ETHIOPIA
Fighting has also broken out in Ethiopia since last month in the biggest escalation of violence since the 2020-2022 Tigray war.
An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years.
"People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time," the official said.
Ethiopian migrants interviewed as part of the agency's most recent situation report on Djibouti from September 20 to September 30 said they had left their country due to difficult living conditions, including the impact of drought.
"Some migrants also reported that they were fleeing conflict and forced recruitment by armed forces," the report said.
Multiple residents of Tigray, where fighting erupted on September 23, have told Reuters that they had seen Tigrayan rebels forcibly recruit young men into the defence forces. The rebels have denied conducting forced recruitment.
The conflict has sparked fears of a return to all-out war with Ethiopia and Eritrea severing relations over alleged Eritrean support for the rebel alliance seeking to overthrow Ethiopia's government. Eritrea has denied backing the alliance.
SEVERE RISKS
The so-called Eastern Route presents many dangers, including accidents at sea, trafficking and arbitrary arrests once on land. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route, according to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project, as the number of people undertaking the journey increased by 18%.
IOM has described the crisis sparked by the fighting in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging to 200,000 from 76,000 in mid-September, according to data released by the agency last week.
More than 3,700 people have fled Yemen by sea to Djibouti as of last week, it said. REUTERS

AA Photo
Service on a new high-speed rail line running from Tekirdağ’s Çerkezköy district to the Kapıkule border crossing with Bulgaria officially began on Oct. 9, Transportation and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu has announced.
With President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in attendance for its opening, the new Çerkezköy-Kapıkule high-speed rail line is part of the Istanbul Halkalı-Kapıkule High-Speed Train Project. The line reduces travel time to 54 minutes, according to the minister’s written statement.
The high-speed service operates three round-trips. Trains heading from Çerkezköy to Edirne depart at 10:45 a.m., 3 p.m. and 7:30 p.m., while the trains in the opposite direction depart at 9 a.m., 1 p.m. and 5:45 p.m.
“Our trains serve our citizens with a total seating capacity of 411, including two seats reserved for wheelchair users,” the minister stated.
Uraloğlu noted that regional train schedules have been updated to accommodate the new line, with two daily round-trip trains now running between Istanbul’s Halkalı station and Edirne’s Uzunköprü district along the same rail corridor.
Uraloğlu noted that these regional trains depart from Istanbul’s Halkalı station to Uzunköprü at 8:25 a.m. and return from Uzunköprü to Halkalı at 3:40 p.m. Passengers traveling between Istanbul and Edirne can now easily complete their journey by transferring between the regional and high-speed trains at Çerkezköy station.

Man hurls rocks at cars from bridge over major Tel Aviv highway, then flees | Watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:17:02 UTC
20:17:02 KST

An unidentified man threw rocks from an overpass onto vehicles traveling north on Tel Aviv's Ayalon Highway on Sunday morning, damaging several cars near the Halakha Interchange. Footage captured by one of the vehicles reportedly shows the suspect dumping rocks onto the roadway before fleeing toward Ramat Gan. Police have opened an investigation.
Edward Rees, whose Tesla was struck during the incident, described the frightening moments in an interview with ynet. "I was driving north in the left lane, minding my own business. As I approached the bridge, I suddenly saw stones flying, actual rocks, toward my lane and the lane next to me. We were traveling at 80 to 90 km/h, and I didn't have time to react. I heard the rocks hitting my car. Luckily, I got off lightly."
According to Rees, a taxi traveling alongside him appeared to have taken the brunt of the rocks. "My car suffered some paint damage and a few marks on the windshield, but it didn't break. The taxi next to me probably took most of the rocks."
Rees said he initially did not realize the incident was deliberate and assumed the stones might have come from construction work nearby. Because there was nowhere to pull over safely, he continued driving and decided to examine the footage from his vehicle's cameras once he reached his destination.
"At first, I thought maybe there was construction work going on. There was nowhere for me to stop, so I told myself that since I have a Tesla with cameras, I'd check afterward to see exactly what had happened," he recalled.
"A few minutes later, when I parked, I looked at the footage and saw someone simply standing on the bridge, emptying a bag or bucket of rocks onto the traffic. As soon as he finished, you could see him start running toward Ramat Gan."
Only after reviewing the recording did Rees fully appreciate how dangerous the incident had been. "From the noise, I was certain the rocks had hit my windshield. When you see that many rocks, you think they could actually penetrate the car. Apparently, I was lucky in terms of my position and timing."
Rees filed a police complaint and plans to retrieve higher-resolution recordings from his vehicle's cameras, hoping they might reveal details that could help identify the taxi involved.
Police from the Lev Tel Aviv precinct have launched an investigation into the incident. The identity of the suspect and his motive remain unknown.
Rees expressed concern that the person responsible might attempt something similar again, potentially with fatal consequences.
"My fear is that this might have been a nationalist-motivated incident, or simply someone who could come back and do it again. Next time, it could kill someone," he said. "At 90 km/h, if your windshield suddenly shatters or a rock hits someone in the head, it could end in disaster."
He added that the experience had shaken his sense of security while driving on one of Israel's busiest highways.
"It's frightening. I'm a little afraid to drive on Ayalon now. I stressed to the police investigator who took my statement just how serious this is. Someone stood on a bridge and threw rocks at moving cars. This time, we were lucky, but next time it could end very differently."

The prime minister does not need to call an election before 2029 and has repeatedly ruled out an early poll.
The new voting legislation, first introduced under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, would allow voters to use bank cards without photographs as proof of identity at polling stations, easing restrictions introduced by the Tories in 2022.
The proposals follow longstanding concerns that the requirement to show photo ID when voting disproportionately affects young people, those on lower incomes and minority ethnic communities.
Polling published by the Guardian after the last general election suggested 6.5% of minority ethnic voters surveyed had been turned away from a polling station at least once, compared with 2.5% of white voters. The Electoral Commission separately estimated that about 16,000 people who attempted to vote in person were unable to do so because they lacked the required ID, and did not return.
Burnham was among seven Labour mayors who criticised the restrictions in 2024, comparing them to voter suppression tactics used by Republicans in the US, and describing the changes as a “brazen assault on our democracy”.
Although Labour opposed the introduction of compulsory photo ID for voting, Starmer’s government stopped short of abolishing the requirement after taking office, instead proposing to widen the forms of ID accepted at polling stations. However, the Electoral Commission has warned that accepting bank cards would make it harder for polling station staff to verify voters’ identities.
The bill also forms part of the government’s efforts to tighten political funding rules amid growing concerns about foreign interference in British elections. The Guardian revealed that ministers were planning further restrictions on political donations that could retrospectively affect the £72m given to Reform UK by the crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.
Labour MPs and trade unions have been calling for tougher safeguards against foreign donations, with some urging the government to go further by introducing limits on the amounts wealthy individuals can give to parties.
A government spokesperson said: “The bill is going through the proper parliamentary process, giving MPs and peers the time and opportunity to examine and debate its measures. These reforms will strengthen our democracy and ensure the electoral system remains secure, fair and accessible.”
The spokesperson added: “The PM has ruled out an early election.”
Ministers argue the existing rules risk preventing legitimate voters from casting their ballots. Electoral Commission research found that about 4% of people who did not vote at the 2024 general election said the photo ID requirement had been a factor.
But the watchdog also says Tory peers have accused ministers of attempting to rush through changes, while the Liberal Democrat peer Mark Pack warned about the risks of introducing significant amendments without sufficient scrutiny.

Kremlin launches hunt for top executives at European defense companies — FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:14:00 UTC
20:14:00 KST

Kremlin launches hunt for top executives at European defense companies — FT
According to Ukrinform, the report was published by the Financial Times.
The Financial Times spoke with representatives of five European intelligence agencies, who warned that executives and other senior officials at defense companies have become targets of Kremlin agents.
The newspaper also noted that plots targeting civilian sites in Europe—actions previously considered off-limits even for Russian intelligence services—are becoming part of these plans.
According to the sources, Moscow has also set its sights on executives at smaller companies, particularly those involved in manufacturing drones or their components.
A senior European intelligence official told the FT that the threat to both property and people in Europe had increased.
Several defense industry executives told the newspaper that they had stepped up their personal security measures over the past six months, following specific recommendations from government security services.
Others said they take such precautions only when traveling abroad.
The report states that Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, is largely responsible for these operations.
Intelligence officials said a key feature of Russia's approach was that the campaign did not necessarily require actual assassination attempts to achieve its intended effect.
A European intelligence official concluded that Russia's main objective remained psychological, as making people feel that they could become targets was enough to achieve the desired effect. The official added that Russia wanted people to think twice before doing business with Ukraine.
As Ukrinform previously reported, in 2024, the United States and Germany thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate the CEO of Rheinmetall.

Georgia Voll smashes quickfire ton as Aussies wrap up Bangladesh series
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11

20:13:47 KST

Australia defeated Bangladesh by nine wickets to take an unassailable 2-0 lead in their ODI series at Allan Border field.
Aussie opening batter Georgia Voll struck an unbeaten 131 off 97 balls after Sobhana Mostary had become the first woman from Bangladesh to score an ODI century against Australia.
What's next?
The three-match series concludes on Wednesday at the same venue.
Opener Georgia Voll has smashed her third ODI century in just her 15th match to secure Australia a comfortable nine-wicket win over Bangladesh and a series victory.
Earlier, Bangladesh centurion Sobhana Mostary played one of the great ODI knocks to lift the visitors to 6-220 as records tumbled at Brisbane's Allan Border Field.
Mostary, 24, made a magnificent 118 off 134 deliveries and with her captain Nigar Sultana (74no off 114) added 195 for the fourth wicket — the highest partnership against Australia in women's ODI history.
Loading Twitter content
But making a mockery of the run chase, Voll and Phoebe Litchfield added 162 off just 119 deliveries in an opening stand that combined brute strength and creativity to the maximum, setting Australia up for an unassailable 2-0 lead in the series.
Litchfield (70 off 51) played strokes all around the ground in her entertaining knock while Voll's power game came to the fore as she bludgeoned anything loose.
Voll's unbeaten 131 off 97 deliveries became the highest individual women's ODI score at the venue, breaking a record Mostary had equalled only hours earlier.
The player of the match's strong bottom hand came to the fore and she was also dominant through cover when given width as Australia coasted to victory in 28.1 overs.
Voll, 23, became the first woman to score two ODI centuries at AB Field after making 101 against India at the venue in 2024.
Mostary and Sultana's stand was the largest for any Bangladesh wicket in women's ODIs and was the foundation of the team's highest total against Australia.
It was not enough to challenge Australia but it was achieved with immaculate stroke play, tactical nous and plenty of courage.
The two Bangladesh heroes came together with their side desperate at 3-8 in the eighth over and embarked on their rescue mission with class.
Mostary brought up her fifty with a cut shot off leg spinner Alana King after driving her through cover with panache to the fence.
She earlier struck three exquisite boundaries through the offside in leggie Georgia Wareham's first over.
Mostary now holds the record for the highest all-time score by a No.5 against Australia in women's ODI history, and the best by a Bangladesh batter.
Sultana was strong off her legs, with two immaculate flicks to the fence with perfect balance a highlight. She played the perfect foil to Mostary.
Australia quick Megan Schutt (4-36) was the pick of the bowlers, including ending Mostary's epic knock when she struck her leg stump.
Veteran Bangladesh opener Fargana Hoque (0) has faced two deliveries from Schutt in this series and lost her wicket both times.
Fellow opener Sarmin Sultana (five) was trapped in front after quick-thinking wicketkeeper Beth Mooney called for DRS when bowler Kim Garth was unsure.
An inswinging yorker by Schutt accounted for Sharmin Akhter (0) and the visitors were in all sorts in the eighth over.
Australia sent Bangladesh in for the second time in the ODI series as they believed rain may have impacted the run chase.
Both sides were unchanged from Friday's opening match of the three-match series, which Australia won by seven wickets.
