My recent article in The Jerusalem Post issued a critical warning to Israeli and Western strategists: Do not jeopardize the historic, civilizational bond with the Iranian people by flirting with marginal, transnational separatist factions. Predictably, the piece provoked a flurry of angry, highly personalized reactions from anonymous quarters and regionalist echo chambers.
Rather than addressing the hard geopolitical, demographic, and historical facts I raised, these counter-arguments resorted to emotional deflection and historical revisionism. This visceral anger and the complete evasion of historical evidence, however, only serve to validate the core arguments of my thesis. To misread the reality of Iran at this critical historical juncture is a luxury neither Israel nor the free world can afford. The narrative presented by these critics is fundamentally detached from reality, completely falling apart when confronted with seven undeniable truths.
Seven undeniable truths from Iranian history
FIRST, MY critics deliberately misinterpret antiquity and my invocation of Bistun and Taq-e Bostan. I referenced these monumental landmarks in the Kermanshah province to highlight an undeniable civilizational continuity. These ancient monuments prove that for over 2,500 years, this region has been a foundational pillar and a vital core of Iranian national sovereignty and territory, not a peripheral borderland waiting to be fractured.
Second, they attempt to obscure the clear line I drew between ordinary citizens and transnational separatists, calling it a “false dichotomy.” This is a classic distortion. My article explicitly separated the patriotic majority of the population from “transnational separatist movements.” It is these transnational cults and factions that actively pursue separation, whereas the actual population remains deeply integrated into the fabric of the nation.
Third, they entirely erase the strongholds of Iranian nationalism: Kermanshah and Ilam. My critics imply that the identity of the people in the western provinces is entirely defined by the political ambitions of armed rebel groups. They conveniently ignore the demographic and ideological reality of major urban centers including Kermanshah, the most populous Kurdish city in the region, and Ilam that have historically stood as fortresses of Iranian patriotism. In Kurdish regions, the local cultural identity is recognized not as an opposition to Iran, but as the most authentic and ancient narrative of being Iranian.
Fourth, they politically exploit shared suffering, attempting to weaponize selective regional cases to paint a picture of an isolated, uniquely targeted territory. This is not a valid analytical response; it is a distortion of tragedy. The Islamic Republic’s brutal execution apparatus does not target an isolated area; it commits atrocities across the entirety of Iran. Just on Monday, October 5, 2026, the regime executed Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raeisi, two young protesters arrested during the uprisings in Isfahan. When young citizens from the heart of Isfahan face the exact same gallows, it proves that state terror is a structural affliction holding the entire nation hostage. Weaponizing this universal Iranian tragedy to legitimize the political ambitions of armed, factional groups is a grotesque deflection from a shared national struggle against a common oppressor.
Fifth, there is a telling and total silence from my critics regarding the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), its leader, and their anti-Israel legacy. This glaring omission is proof of intellectual bankruptcy. They completely evade the fact that many transnational separatist movements look up to Abdullah Ocalan as a foundational figure, despite Ocalan’s continuous anti-Israel legacy. Furthermore, they have no defense against the historical fact that the PKK operated as a proxy for the Assad regime, trained alongside armed anti-Israel Palestinian factions in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley front, and fought directly against Israel. Because certain armed groups operating in Iran are direct branches of this terrorist PKK network, my critics completely censor this history, knowing it destroys their attempt to appeal to an international audience.
Sixth, my critics deliberately rewrite the history of the 1979 catastrophe to hide their own role in Iran’s destabilization. Armed regional factions were an active part of the disastrous 1979 coalition – alongside Islamists, Marxists, and Mossadeghists – that brought down the nation. Leaders like Abdul Rahman Ghassemlou openly pledged allegiance to Ayatollah Khomeini, only to later clash over the spoils of the revolution when the Islamists turned around and purged them.
If these timed factions, disguised as political parties, truly sought a democratic, unified Iran rather than secession, why did they immediately exploit the country’s chaotic vulnerability just days after February 11, 1979, the exact day the previous regime fell and the Islamists seized power? Specifically, on February 20, 1979, a mere nine days after the revolution, they aggressively raided and looted the national army garrison in Mahabad, assassinating its commander and stealing heavy weaponry, including tanks, heavy artillery pieces, and thousands of rifles. They then marched on Sanandaj, and had it not been for the fierce resistance of the Iranian National Army’s 28th Division garrison, they would have completely captured the city.
Let us ask an honest question to an international audience: Would the Israeli government or public ever tolerate a so-called political faction that raids and captures an IDF base? Calling these militant groups “freedom fighters” is an insult to sovereign nations.
Finally, they seek to erase the historical reality of local resistance, such as the Paveh events of August 1979. They imply that armed groups have always naturally represented the collective will of the local population. History records otherwise. During that critical juncture, it was the local, indigenous patriotic population of Paveh in Kermanshah province who actively took up arms and resisted the violent, armed incursion of separatist factions. This historical event proves that the people themselves have historically been the first line of defense for Iran’s territorial integrity against armed groups.
ULTIMATELY, THE angry reactions to my piece fail to counter its core warning. By flirting with marginal, transnational separatist elements, outside powers risk alienating the patriotic majority of the Iranian public.
The true, lasting strategic asset for Israel and the West is the 2,500-year-old civilizational bond with a unified Iranian nation, not short-sighted investments in armed factions like the PKK and its branches that carry a historical legacy of hostility toward the West. We must look toward a future democratic Iran based on historical territorial integrity, national unity, individual liberty, and equality before the law.

Modi is in trouble
The CJP protests sweeping through the country have exposed India’s hollowed-out democracy.
It is said that if you pluck a chicken one feather at a time, nobody notices. That is how some people deceive themselves into believing that small wrongs will never catch up with them.
The trouble with this method is that, one fine day, the truth stands bare, impossible to ignore. This October, Indian democracy resembles a plucked chicken, stripped of its plumage, as protesters who ironically call themselves “cockroaches” swarm our streets.
A lot of feather-plucking went on for 12 years before Prime Minister Narendra Modi found himself cornered, retreating behind barricades, facing the wrath of students for whom the slow erosion of democracy has left little to lose and even less to fear.
Confronted with a major protest on October 10 demanding the reversal of a purge of the voter rolls, he went on a self-incrimination spree. His government imposed measures reminiscent of the emergency era: no trains to New Delhi, paramilitary forces deployed at protest sites, the internet disrupted.
Ahead of the demonstration, leading figures linked to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest movement – Ratna Singh, Abhijeet Dipke, Dhruv Rathee – were detained. Many other known activists, including Mahatma Gandhi’s great-grandson Tushar Gandhi, were also detained.
Regardless, demonstrators poured into the streets of New Delhi, trying to reach designated protest sites, in a scene that repeated in city after city across India. Through the day, the police played an endless game of whack-a-mole with the protesters, who kept resurfacing across the capital city, reassembling in one corner after another, driven from the designated protest sites but unwilling to disappear.
By the evening, at least 2,500 protesters and 15 journalists were detained across the city and taken to detention centres set up in various locations. Many have since been released.
These acts further erode the tenuous position Modi is in, prompting more rebuke from critics who now question his fitness to occupy the office of the prime minister. On Friday, the opposition parties, led by Rahul Gandhi, met President Draupadi Murmu and submitted to her that the government had subverted India’s democratic framework.
Under Modi’s watch, problems have accumulated like barnacles on the side of the ship. Every time he has been challenged, he has gone farther away from the democratic principles on which this nation was founded.
The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls – the last feather he plucked – was an exercise in bureaucratic fascism. There is simply no other way to frame an event that strips 130 million Indians of their right to vote.
The fact that this process helped sway elections is no longer up for debate. That the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw SIR, is not resigning – out of shame – is astonishing. Even more so now that a corruption case from 2006 against him has resurfaced.
The chaotic, angry, defiant tableaux in the streets of New Delhi and beyond represent a reckoning that has been long in the making. The young, diverse protesters are a stark contrast to Modi and his cabinet – old, humourless men, who have bet on a strategy of demonisation and exclusion to succeed. His cabinet is filled with men full of self-importance, who had, mistakenly, wagered that crimes of elected officials should be tolerated and that a country can be governed indefinitely by creating fissures and manufacturing enemies.
We have now seen what happens when breakers of the law become makers of law. Criminal behaviour has been the organising principle of the party, and together, the values of these people have defined the years that Modi has ruled India. In the process, he has presided over the shredding of the Constitution of India.
Now that all this has come back to haunt him – in the form of “cockroaches” he is unable to exterminate – Modi has turned New Delhi into a fortress and unleashed all the power he has at his disposal on unarmed protesters. This is consistent with his policy of pretending to aspire to peace but unerringly generating conflict throughout his tenure: with neighbouring nations as well as among neighbours within cities.
October 10 is just an opening salvo. Over the next few weeks, Modi’s troubles will likely deepen. The CJP has announced protests will continue. Opposition parties have said they will protest on Monday.
The “cockroaches” seem to have resolved any remaining questions regarding Modi’s utter ineptitude as prime minister. They have laid bare the hollowed-out democracy that India holds up to the world as exemplary.
As his rule draws to a close — for now, the writing is on the wall — it can be safely said that history books will cast Modi in his proper role as the man who caused an entire generation of Indians to lose all respect for the government, the army, the Delhi Police, as well as the whole structure of governance.
New Delhi is temporarily suspended in a transition between a suffocating present and a promising future. This particular scrap of time, no matter how hard, will pass.
When that dust settles, what will become of all the institutions destroyed by regulatory capture and right-wing ideology – only those on the streets today will answer. This understanding is implicit in everything the “cockroaches” do. Because the whole point of it is power to the people.

One year after Trump's Gaza ceasefire, questions remain about possible next steps - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:37 UTC
19:31:37 KST

The Gaza ceasefire took shape a year ago. In September 2025, US President Donald Trump was able to network with key Arab leaders in meetings that eventually led to a ceasefire in Gaza.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law who has played a key role in the 20-point peace plan, posted about the significance of the one-year anniversary of the ceasefire.
“One year ago today, on October 9, 2025, we reached an agreement on President Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza many believed impossible,” he wrote.
He noted how important it was to end the devastating war. He wanted an agreement that created “a path to reunite hostage families with their loved ones, bring security to Israel, relieve the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza, and build a different future for the region.”
Kushner praised the progress since October 9, 2025, when Hamas accepted Trump’s 20-point peace plan. He noted some of the milestones since that day. On October 13, “all 20 living Israeli hostages return home. Something many believed would never happen.”
He also noted how the UN backed the US plan. He didn’t mention all the important pieces that came together in the following weeks. For instance, the US-backed Civil-Military Coordination Center (CMCC) in Kiryat Gat was set up. This was set up largely by US Central Command and brought together a number of countries.
The concept was to coordinate aid deliveries and monitor the ceasefire. By January 2026, Kushner notes that the UN said: “100% of basic food needs being met in Gaza for the first time since 2023.”
In January 2026, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza was established. This is supposed to be the Palestinian technocratic government for Gaza. So far, Israel has not permitted it to operate in Gaza.
Two million civilians are still stuck under Hamas rule in around 40% of Gaza. The Board of Peace, established as part of the Trump plan, has tried to do some work on the sidelines to see what might happen after Israel’s elections. In general, the theory is that Israel won’t do anything on Gaza until after the elections.
For instance, the peace plan was supposed to see the creation of an international security force. This ISF only seems to have a few dozen personnel so far. Albania and Kosovo were some of the first to come forward.
In June, reports indicated that Morocco and Greece might help support it. Reports also indicated that Kazakhstan would be helpful. Israel, meanwhile, has ejected some countries from the CMCC due to diplomatic disputes.
On the border of Gaza, a new logistics facility called LSA Endurance has taken shape. However, a lot remains to be seen. Kushner noted that the remains of all the deceased hostages had been returned by late January 2026.
He also noted that on July 31, “Hamas signs an actionable, step-by-step framework for decommissioning its weapons, developed with the support of Nikolay Mladenov and mediators from Egypt, Turkey, Qatar, and the United States. Implementation remains a critical next step.”
The last thing on the Kushner list is a meeting on September 23 where the “Board of Peace hosts an open meeting on the sidelines of UNGA releasing the next steps in the Gaza recovery plan.”
Board of Peace efforts overshadowed by Iran war
Some of the work of the Board of Peace has been overshadowed by the war with Iran. The US administration has been sidetracked to some extent. It also has to deal with other fronts that Israel is involved with. For instance, the administration has had to help Israel in Lebanon with the Lebanese government, where the US also backs a ceasefire.
The US also tried to smooth relations between Israel and Damascus and to prevent Israel-Turkey relations from becoming a crisis. At the same time, recent reports indicate Iran is rebuilding its missile and drone program, and Hamas continues to recruit in Gaza.
Kushner noted that “There is still hard work ahead. Disarmament must be implemented, security established, essential services restored, and communities rebuilt. None of this will be easy. But we have a thoughtful plan, committed partners, and a path forward that did not exist a year ago.”
The challenge in Gaza is that it’s not clear what comes next. Arab News noted that “Reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory called for under the ceasefire plan has still not materialized.”
The report said Israel controls around 70% of Gaza. “Nothing has changed for the better; everything has gotten worse, they lie to us, it is all lies,” Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, told AFP. The AFP article is the basis for the Arab News report.
It said, “On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways that have been cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance blown-out windows gape from the facades of buildings that remain standing.” This report also said that around “82% of all standing structures in Gaza are either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026 per the UN.”
It noted that the concept of the plan was for there to be a political transition in Gaza away from Hamas rule. This has not happened. In the past, Israel has accepted Hamas rule in Gaza, and prior to October 7, 2023, there was cash entering Hamas-run Gaza from Doha.
The Hamas leadership continues to live in Qatar. As such, it’s not clear if the promised change under the Trump plan will happen.
The Arab News report and others paint a concerning picture of Gaza. People there said little has changed. While Kushner has praised the peace deal, the question is going to be what will happen next. This has always been the challenge in the past as well. Getting a ceasefire is one thing. Changing the status quo is another.
Israeli voices call to resettle Gaza Strip
Some voices in Israel’s politics have vowed to re-settle Gaza and have encouraged people to emigrate from the enclave. There do not appear to be many voices discussing how to remove Hamas or whether policymakers in Jerusalem want Hamas removed. The war largely resulted in moving people in Gaza from place to place, with Hamas hiding among them.
The most recent IDF data said that the Israeli military carried out 100,000 strikes in Gaza in three years of war. Many of these were carried out in the first months of the fighting.
The IDF also said that it eliminated four heads of Hamas military branches along with 17 brigade commanders, approximately 60 battalion commanders, and approximately 300 company commanders. Hamas only had 24 battalions and five regional brigades.
As such, it would appear that in many cases the brigade commanders and battalion commanders were eliminated twice.
The same goes for the company commanders. What this means is that Hamas replaced the ones who were killed, and then the replacements were killed. Israel also estimates it has eliminated 4,000 of the 6,000 people who attacked Israel on October 7, some of them Hamas and some of them members of other groups or civilian looters.

Under the banner of confronting America and Israel, it provides military training with an unmistakable objective: to bring war into Iran’s cities, streets, and alleyways. Islamic terrorists know neither peace nor the value of life and security.
Across Iranian cities, the atmosphere is increasingly one of war. People whisper: Will Trump launch the final attack? The country hangs like a pendulum in uncertainty, with law and order unraveling. The mullahs intensify street propaganda to drown out protest, yet a national uprising looms. The regime calls participants in its street spectacles – its “Islam Party” – fedayeen, echoing the political theater of Saddam Hussein and Muammar Gaddafi.
The Revolutionary Guards and security officials squander their days in endless meetings, terrified by the deepening crisis and sheltering behind a bankrupt, discredited government. Agriculture, industry, and production have ground to a halt. There is no coherent plan to regain control. The regime’s security calculations are unraveling.
Iranians await another war in the hope that the bloodthirsty wolf of the Islamic Republic will finally be brought down. They hope Trump will finish the job – or allow Israel to eliminate the regime’s thugs and criminals, layer by layer.
Meanwhile, the regime intensifies killings and executions, hoping to prevent economic misery, relentless inflation, soaring prices, and mounting social anguish from erupting into the “final battle.” Iran is passing through fateful days as urban repression intensifies. The regime’s ultimate nightmare is a popular uprising. A regime that kills its own people for daring to protest will stop at no crime to preserve its rule.
And yet, behind every headline about war, sanctions, missiles, and nuclear negotiations lies another Iran – the Iran of ordinary people who simply want to live. They want to raise their children without fear, put food on the table, walk their streets without repression, speak without looking over their shoulders, and grow old in the country they love.
For nearly half a century, generations of Iranians have watched their lives disappear into prisons, graves, exile, poverty, and shattered dreams. They are not asking the world to give them a country. They already have one – an ancient and beloved homeland called Iran.
They are asking for the chance to take it back. Ninety million people have waited long enough. In memory of the 50,000 slaughtered in Tehran’s streets by the Shi’ite mullahs and IRGC thugs, who cried out, “This is the final battle – Pahlavi will return!” Iran deserves to live again. “Make Iran Great Again!”
Let us hope Washington has the resolve and unwavering will to make it happen.
The writer is a Middle East political analyst. His latest book, Tehran’s Dictator, examines the theocratic era of Ali Khamenei (1989-2026). @EQFard

Palestinians have been left angry by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s decision to again postpone the long-delayed Palestinian Legislative Council elections.
Candidates who had planned to run told The Jerusalem Post and posted publicly that the two-decade absence of legislative elections shows the PA is putting the “status quo ahead of the public interest.”
Abbas announced on Saturday that the elections, originally scheduled for November 28, would be postponed until September 11, 2027, citing Israeli-imposed obstacles and arguing that Palestinian factions had agreed there was no choice but to delay the vote.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar denied the PA’s accusations, calling them “yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability.”
Though Dr. Nabil Kukali, founder and president of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion, told the Post last week that the Palestinian majority would likely understand a postponement if elections could not take place in east Jerusalem and Gaza, provided the public saw a genuine desire to hold them, New Path leader Samer Sinijlawi said the decision to postpone had been made as part of a campaign by Palestinian Vice-President Hussein al-Sheikh and Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine Deputy Secretary-General Jamil Mezher.
Reports that Sheikh sought to cancel the elections have circulated for months, with Yoni Ben-Menachem, a senior researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, saying he had been told that the vice-president had explicitly cited east Jerusalem as a pretext to cancel the vote, as Abbas did in 2021.
“These efforts disregarded the hopes of millions of Palestinians who had waited two decades and welcomed this democratic opportunity,” Sinijlawi said.
“It would have allowed them to participate in the political system by exercising their most basic right: electing their representatives to the Legislative Council and making their voices heard after years of being silenced.
Abbas's decision harmful to Gaza candidates
Sinijlawi said he found it “difficult” to view the postponement as “anything other than putting the interests of those who benefit from the status quo ahead of the public interest” and added that “the right to vote is not a favor granted by anyone. It must not remain hostage to the calculations of those who fear the people’s choice.”
Explaining to the Post how Abbas’s decision was particularly harmful to candidates in Gaza, he said that “many stepped forward” while living in tents and that they had put all their efforts into running “because they believed they could help shape a different future.”
“Their candidacy was an act of hope: a chance to move from surviving devastation to representing their communities and rebuilding their lives,” he continued.
“They now face another year of uncertainty, with no guarantee that the new date will be honored. The damage goes beyond disrupted campaigns. It undermines trust in peaceful democratic change and tells a generation that has never voted that its voice can wait again. Gaza’s emerging leaders deserve the opportunity to lead, and its people deserve the right to choose them.”
Ahmad Shadid, leader of the Phoenix list, also expressed distrust in the PA’s explanation for the postponement.
“If I were one of those behind the idea of postponing [the elections], I would have some self-respect and be honest, and tell people: ‘The Authority is in our hands. We decided to hold elections, and then we changed our minds. You can go to hell.’ But I shouldn’t act like an idiot and talk about circumstances, national dialogue, and … legitimacy, Shadid wrote.”
Postponing elections reflects 'depth of current crisis'
Majda Al-Masri, deputy secretary-general of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) and head of the Unity and Democratic Change list, wrote that “postponing elections reflects the depth of the current crisis and the inability of existing institutions to address the challenges” and called for a national dialogue to “unify efforts to confront the occupation and its plans.”
Mustafa Barghouti, head of the Palestinian National Initiative list and a former information minister in the Palestinian unity government formed in 2007, made clear he opposed the postponement and demanded on X/Twitter that the Palestinian Authority guarantee that the election will not be delayed next September again.
Despite opposing the postponement, Barghouti said he welcomed the fact that legislative and presidential elections would be held in unison and said it was necessary to review restrictions ahead of September that would “undermine the democratic right to stand for election and to vote.”
“This comprehensive national dialogue must also be devoted to developing a unified national strategy to confront the ongoing genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, as well as the war of settler terror and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and Jerusalem,” he added.

'The Prime Ministers': New book covers Begin, the ‘Altalena,’  and the October 27 election - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:16 UTC
19:31:16 KST

Baroness Thatcher poured the tea, pushed a brass tray of peppermints across the table, and asked Israeli diplomat and author Yehuda Avner to tell her about “Mr. Begin.”
It was a bright April morning in 1992, in a borrowed mansion on Eaton Square, barely a month after Menachem Begin’s funeral. Thatcher had made no bones about opposing his settlement policies, she said, but she had greatly admired his convictions.
Avner told her he thought Begin had been worthy of a second Nobel Prize.
“For what, pray?”
For securing Israel’s parliamentary democracy, he said.
Thatcher’s voice sharpened. Surely he exaggerated. Israel was universally famous for its democracy, one of the most robust in the world.
Not at the outset, Avner said.
Twice, just before independence and just after, Begin had saved the country from civil war.
In 1944, the Hagana seized Irgun men and handed them over to the British; Begin ordered his fighters not to retaliate. Not one of them did. He explained himself afterward in a ramshackle Galilee cinema, speaking over the sound of rain hammering a corrugated roof.
The Second Temple fell because Jews hated each other into civil war. There are fateful times, he told them, when the choice is between blood and tears. Against the British, blood had taken the place of tears. Jew-against-Jew, tears had to take the place of blood. God forbid that a decision of a democratically elected government should ever be defied by force.
He was talking about the Altalena – found intact on the seafloor recently.
Avner says plainly that he was not there and is familiar with the scene through eyewitness accounts years later.
Begin on the burning deck, black with smoke, flinging up his arms and shouting at his own men not to fire.
On the beach, one of the officers ordered to shell her was Yitzhak Rabin, who believed Ben-Gurion’s warning that Begin was mounting a coup and told Avner decades later that his gun crew fired the shell that set her alight. Two of this book’s four prime ministers were at opposite ends of that gun.
Thatcher had no idea, and she said so.
Avner once asked Begin what the most important thing he had done in his life was. “Twice I prevented civil war,” came his answer. That is recorded near the end of The Prime Ministers, and it is the boldest claim in 700 pages. Published in 2010, Avner’s tome is more relevant than ever.
ISRAELIS VOTE on October 27, at the end of only the second Knesset since 1988 to serve a full term – the other 13 having dissolved early.
Avner’s claim is that there is anything to vote in at all because a man twice refused to fight for power he believed was his, and then brought in the voters nobody else wanted, most of them from Arab and Asian countries with no parliamentary tradition and hardly a voice in the new state. They put him in office after eight consecutive electoral defeats.
Thatcher’s own Foreign Office had briefed her that Israel had elected a warmonger and a demagogue.
‘A Jew should never hate another Jew’
Avner never argues any of this on the page. He puts down what he saw and lets you do the rest.
In May 1967, with Egyptian divisions in Sinai, the leader of the opposition walked into Levi Eshkol’s study and asked the prime minister to stand down in favor of David Ben-Gurion.
How could Begin, of all people, ask him to make way for the man who had abused him at every turn and compared him to Hitler? “The enmity is his, not mine,” Begin said. “I live by the maxim that a Jew should never hate another Jew.”
Eshkol went to the window, looked out at picketers holding signs telling him to go, then yawned and refused in Yiddish. “These two horses cannot pull the same wagon together,” he said famously, referring to himself and Ben-Gurion.
Born Haffner in Manchester
Avner was born Haffner in Manchester in 1928, reached Palestine at 18 in November 1947, and dug trenches during the siege.
From 1963, he wrote the English-language speeches of Eshkol, Golda Meir, and Rabin, holding no party card in a country where public jobs ran through Mapai. He was in the room for much of it and scrupulous about when he was not, sourcing Golda’s confrontation with the Socialist International to her own memoir and a colleague she told of it on her return.
In June 1977, the country changed hands for the first time, and the incoming prime minister told his predecessor’s speechwriter he was keeping him.
There had to be continuity, Begin said, and the world had to see it. “This government has come to serve, not to reap.”
Avner stayed six more years. The peaceful transfer of power is not an abstraction in this book. It is the author’s employment record.
The book is also funny, and the joke is rarely where you expect.
Eshkol gets into his car one morning and asks Yankele the doorman, in Yiddish, how he is doing as prime minister. Yankele closes one eye and says the taxes are far too high. Eshkol, one leg in the car, cups a hand to his ear and spends several minutes explaining the defense budget and immigrant housing to his doorman, while his speechwriter wonders how many prime ministers ask a doorman his opinion, listen, and then try to explain themselves.
The word Carter had to ask about
Underneath it is one thing, and Thatcher walks into it. Avner tells her you cannot understand Begin without the Holocaust, that almost his whole family was murdered. In 1979, she admits that she had not really known what Auschwitz was. In the White House Cabinet Room in 1977, under a portrait of Truman, Begin told then-US president Jimmy Carter that, in the past, Jewish men had to deliver their women and children to their executioners. “We were tertiated, Mr. President.”
Carter lifted his head and asked what the word had been. Tertiated, not decimated, Begin said. Decimation is one-in-10. For the Jews it was one-in-three. He rose to his full height, banged his fist on the table, and swore an oath before the president, in the name of the Jewish people, that it would never, ever happen again.
Then Begin broke, knuckles white against the tabletop, blinking back tears, while the clock on the mantelpiece became audible and all the president’s men looked at the floor.
None of it is neutral, and Avner says so, explaining in an author’s note that he reconstructed conversations, edited speech, and thought Begin the most exceptional of the four. It shows in the Sabra and Shatila chapter, which spends more energy on the unfairness of the coverage than on the decision that put Phalangist militiamen inside those camps.
He ends where the man did.
The funeral Begin had specified: no lying in state, no guard of honor, no delegations, not even eulogies. A shroud, a prayer shawl, Irgun veterans carrying him, four kilometers of mourners on the road to the Mount of Olives.
Then, in that London drawing room a month later, Thatcher asked whether Begin had left a memoir.
No, Avner told her, and he could not explain the silence to himself, let alone to her.
What he had was the end of an old Time magazine interview, where, when the reporter rose to leave, he had turned back and asked how Begin wanted to be remembered in history. Avner repeats the answer and adds nothing: “As a decent human being, and a proud Jew.” ■
THE PRIME MINISTERS: AN INTIMATE NARRATIVE OF ISRAELI LEADERSHIP
By Yehuda Avner 
The Toby Press 
715 pages; $38

From peaceful protests to free movement: 9 directions SC issued amid CJP stir in Delhi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:30:36 UTC
19:30:36 KST

The SC directed authorities to prevent illegal detentions, restore normal Metro services and protect peaceful protests and free movement amid the CJP stir.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Sunday stepped into the row over restrictions imposed during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest in Delhi, directing authorities to prevent illegal detentions, ensure normal Metro and railway operations and protect the ability of lawyers and journalists to perform their duties. The court also ordered the removal of a notice board announcing prohibitory restrictions near its premises, saying citizens and lawyers must have access to justice.A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice to the Centre on a contempt plea alleging that authorities had violated the court's October 9 directions on public transport restrictions. The hearing came a day after more than 7,000 people were detained during a security crackdown on the planned mobilisation at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
During the special sitting, lawyers alleged that detentions and movement restrictions had extended beyond the areas covered by prohibitory orders. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, however, told the court that restrictions on October 10 covered 45 of Delhi Metro's 303 stations and that most detainees had already been released.Here are the key actions and directions from the Supreme Court hearing.
Authorities told to prevent illegal detentions
The court made clear that people assembling peacefully cannot be detained outside the bounds of the law, particularly in areas not covered by prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
"There shall not be illegal detention, save and except by procedure established by law, particularly with regard to assemblage of people beyond the area within which it's imposed," the bench said.The issue was raised by senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for RJD MP Manoj Jha. Sibal alleged that police were detaining people travelling by train and individuals outside the four-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar, where prohibitory orders were in force.
Normal Metro and railway operations to be ensured
The Supreme Court directed that Delhi Metro services should operate according to their normal schedule and asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, to ensure that the authorities concerned complied with the direction. It also called for railway services to function without a blanket prohibition, subject to lawful and necessary restrictions.The direction followed the court's October 9 order, passed after a separate petition challenged the closure of 57 Metro stations and cancellation of trains in view of the planned protest.On Sunday, Mehta said entry and exit had been restricted at 45 of the network's 303 stations on October 10, accounting for around 15 per cent of the total. Lawyers appearing before the court had alleged that the restrictions continued despite the earlier order, with some stations completely inaccessible to passengers.
Internet access must not be disrupted unlawfully
The bench directed the authorities to ensure that internet services remained undisturbed, subject to law and order requirements. It also clarified that the direction did not curtail powers available under the Information Technology Act."Internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, as per law....When we are saying internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, we are not taking away the powers under the Information Technology Act," the bench said.The court's observation sought to ensure that restrictions imposed amid the security operation did not extend to internet connectivity without lawful justification.
Free movement
The court called for free movement of people, subject to traffic regulations, and for authorities to review the need for barricades that could impede movement across Delhi.Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan urged the bench to direct the removal of barricades and restoration of services at Metro stations. Lawyers had argued that restrictions were affecting not only protesters but also other residents and commuters.The court's broader directions sought to ensure that security measures did not impose unnecessary hardship on people moving around the capital.
Lawyers, journalists must be allowed to work
The bench directed authorities to ensure that lawyers, journalists and others were not obstructed from discharging their professional duties.The direction came amid allegations that several lawyers had been detained during Saturday's protests. Senior advocate Shadan Farasat, who said he was detained by Delhi Police, told the court that he and other lawyers had faced violence."It's about citizens' right to protest. The sense I got yesterday was that we were one step away from a police state. Kindly restore citizens' right to protest peacefully in the capital. Yesterday, that right was destroyed," Farasat said.Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan also informed the bench that senior advocates Dinesh Dwivedi, Uttara Babbar and Farasat had been detained.
Section 163 notice board near SC ordered to be removed
The court directed the concerned authority to take down a notice board announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the BNSS in and around the Supreme Court premises, if it had not already been removed."We have been informed that a notice board stating imposition of Section 163 BNSS in and around the vicinity of the Supreme Court has been put up," the bench said."We direct the authority concerned to take down this board, if not already done, so that citizens as well as lawyers can have access to justice," it ordered.The direction was specifically linked to ensuring access to the court for citizens and members of the legal profession.
Peaceful protests permitted, but must remain within the law
The bench observed that peaceful assemblies must be allowed in accordance with law, particularly outside areas where prohibitory orders apply. It also reminded protesters that demonstrations must remain peaceful and should not instigate others.The hearing centred on the distinction between lawful regulation to maintain public order and restrictions that effectively prevent people from exercising their rights.In its October 9 order, the Supreme Court had said authorities could regulate Metro and railway operations but should not impose an outright prohibition on their movement. It had also asked the government to publicise transport arrangements and issue traffic advisories to minimise inconvenience.
Habeas corpus and related pleas listed for October 13
The court said petitions concerning alleged mass detentions and other connected matters would be heard alongside the main cases on October 13.One of these was a habeas corpus petition filed by senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy concerning the detention of political leaders. The bench was also hearing Jha's plea alleging disproportionate use of force, illegal detention, house arrests and harassment of protesters by Delhi Police.The allegations in Jha's petition included claims of sexual harassment of women protesters. These were allegations before the court and had not been established by the directions issued on Sunday.
The bench issued notice to the Centre on a contempt petition filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, which named Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation chairperson D Thara as respondents.The petition alleged that authorities had breached the Supreme Court's October 9 order by restricting public transport and detaining protesters on October 10.The earlier order had followed a plea challenging the closure of Metro stations and cancellation of trains ahead of the CJP mobilisation. The court had observed that notifications appeared to go beyond regulation and impose a complete ban on essential public transport.
The bench had said: "Upon our indication that a distinction exists between total 'prohibition' and the 'regulation' of metro and other train movements, the solicitor general of India has fairly agreed to impress upon the authorities to reassess such prohibitions."The court's latest intervention came as it considered allegations that the earlier directions had not been followed. It also reiterated its responsibility under Article 32 of the Constitution to protect and enforce fundamental rights.

Inside the Muslim Manosphere Policing Women Online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Mariam recently disabled Facebook Messenger. As the administrator of a Facebook group for women in the United Arab Emirates with close to 400,000 members, she’d become accustomed to receiving messages from strangers. But then came a shift in the volume—and nature—of those messages until they were impossible to ignore.
“Being the admin of this group has subjected me to all kinds of harassment,” says Miriam, who asked to be identified only by her first name because she fears online retaliation. They “either want to advise you to be holy and cover up, or they want to sexually harass you—or both.”
Mariam has run the group for more than a year. And even though intended for women, the group’s size and visibility has meant that Miriam also gets a lot of messages from men. She has received a deluge of unsolicited messages telling her how to dress, not to raise her voice or wear makeup, and to cover her hands with gloves so that no skin is visible.
“I couldn’t take it any longer. It was starting to affect my mental well-being,” Miriam says.
Many women who are conspicuous on the internet have been harassed online. That comes in countless forms, even if the same misogyny underlies it. The particular variety Miriam was subjected to stems from a section of the “manosphere” dressed in the clothes of religion—the Muslim manosphere.
At its core, the manosphere is built around male grievance and antifeminist ideology—though whether that’s entirely organic or engineered to sell supplements and other products is up for debate. Regardless, it has no shortage of subcultures to chose from: Incels, pick-up artists, men’s rights activists, and followers of the Red Pill.
Some nuances may make these groups distinct, but they largely share a common worldview: Feminism has destabilized society, women have acquired too much power, and men must reassert control. And the Muslim manosphere is no different. It’s adopted those ideas circulating through the wider manosphere and rebranded them in the language of faith.
Sarah Kaddoura, a feminist researcher and creator of the YouTube channel Haki Nasawi, examined the Arabic-speaking manosphere in a 2025 report. In her study, she describes some of the most prominent influencers, such as Jordanian relationship coach Kareem Atta’i, who posts online as Coach Kareem or Red Pill Arabic.
Atta’i packages his ideas as relationship advice, but his videos frequently frame interactions between men and women as contests for power. Atta’i’s videos, which WIRED Middle East has watched, describe violence as a means of “disciplining” women or retaliating against sexual rejection.
The Arabic manosphere does more than translate Western Red Pill content. Its creators have adapted the ideology to local anxieties around religion, masculinity, marriage, money, and social change.
Kaddoura says influencers use financial insecurity, political instability, religious identity, and fears about declining morality or social cohesion to build their audiences. Misogyny becomes an explanation for a much wider sense of frustration—and women become its most visible target.
The problem is not religious expression online but the use of religious authority—real or claimed—to legitimize misogyny, harassment, and the public surveillance of women. The Muslim manosphere is also not confined to the Arab world. Like the broader manosphere, it crosses borders, languages, and platforms.
Take prominent UK-based creator Ali Dawah, whose channel features street debates and commentary about relationships, gender roles, religion, and Western culture. In one clip, Dawah says he hates Muslim feminists “the most.” In another video, he approaches women in public and challenges them over clothing he describes as immodest.
“Dawah” is not just this YouTuber’s name. In Arabic, it means to make an invitation to someone to learn about Islam. Ali is just one of many influencers often called “Dawah Bros,” and they’re generally known for being more aggressive than offering an invitation when it comes to promoting their manosphere-esque content.
Kaddoura sees the Dawah Bros as a platform-native successor to an older variety of media figure. During the 1990s, Islamic television programs in Egypt and Saudi Arabia regularly featured sheikhs answering callers’ questions about relationships, clothing, and acceptable behavior. However, unlike television preachers, today’s influencers are not limited to scheduled broadcasts, and they aren’t only interacting with people who’ve chosen to call in.
For many Muslim women—especially those who are in prominent places on the internet—these ideas do not remain confined to podcasts or debate videos. They spill into comment sections and private messages, where strangers appoint themselves enforcers of morality.
A 2026 report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue analyzed nearly 14,000 comments directed at 40 prominent public figures and influencers on Instagram in Jordan over a 12-month period. Among comments classified as hate speech, harassment, or abusive language, 72 percent targeted women, 11 percent were classified as religious or moral harassment, and the vast majority of those comments—85 percent—targeted female influencers.
Additionally, all of the comments classified as sexual harassment were directed at women, underlining the pervasive contradictions in how women are policed on the internet—the same online environment that instructing women to make themselves invisible also subjecting them to unwanted sexual attention. That contradiction is visible in the messages Mariam has received.
The manosphere’s reach is shaped in part by the recommendation systems that determine what users encounter in their feeds. “As soon as you create an account on TikTok, YouTube, X, Instagram, and others as a male, it doesn’t take long for the algorithm to start recommending misogynistic content,” Kaddoura says.
Engagement-based systems can amplify emotionally charged and polarizing content, including manosphere videos. Content blaming women for men’s loneliness or financial insecurity can generate reactions from supporters, critics, and the women being targeted. Those interactions may increase its visibility.
That becomes even thornier when religion enters the picture. The relationship coaches and other men preaching religion online often present personal opinions as religious instruction, Kaddoura says. This can make disagreement appear immoral, and criticism can then be presented as evidence that the creator is defending the faith against hostile forces.
But how exactly a user’s behavior tips over from passively encountering the content to actively engaging with it remains an open question. Researchers can examine publicly available videos and identify influential accounts, but they have limited access to the internal data needed to trace how users move between creators and communities. This leave key questions unanswered, such as whether prolonged exposure changes their behavior.
For women such as Mariam, the technical route behind the harassment may be invisible, but its effects are not. A creator publishes a video. Recommendation systems carry it into other users’ feeds. And then, eventually, users repeat its message in women’s comment sections and inboxes. Repeat ad infinitum.
WIRED Middle East contacted Ali Dawah and Kareem Atta’i for comment. Neither responded by the time of publication.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

Year into cease-fire, promised peace never arrived for Gazans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

A year after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire took effect in the Gaza Strip, residents still living in displacement camps under near-daily Israeli airstrikes say the truce has not brought the promised peace.
Israel has reduced its attack intensity but continues strikes and now controls over 70% of Gaza. The cease-fire plan's promised reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory has not materialized.
"Nothing has changed for the better; everything has got worse, they lie to us, it is all lies," Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, said.
"Martyrs are still falling, people are still being injured, the shelling continues and we cannot even find a moment's peace from the constant buzzing of the drones overhead."
On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance, blown-out windows gape from building facades still standing.
Ahmed Jonaid, another displaced Palestinian in Gaza City, said he had hoped to return home after the cease-fire.
"We thought we would experience some happiness and return to our homes. Instead, we see ourselves suffering in refugee camps, sleeping on makeshift mats," the 51-year-old said as he carried two jerrycans of water back to his tent.
Israel's genocidal war, which broke out after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, has displaced almost all of Gaza's more than 2 million residents at least once.
With 82% of all standing structures in Gaza either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026, according to the U.N., many residents still live in tents or makeshift shelters, where lack of hygiene has led to outbreaks of disease.
Ahmed Shawan, a doctor at a hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis, said he had yet to see the cease-fire take effect.
"It has been a full year since the cease-fire was declared, yet it exists only on paper," he said.
The agreement's second phase called for a political transition away from Hamas rule, with technocrat Ali Shaath appointed head of a new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
Five countries, including Morocco, have agreed to join the International Stabilization Force (ISF) tasked with post-war preparations, but its troops have not yet started operating in Gaza.
Israel controls all entry points into the territory and continues to allow only a limited amount of aid, keeping the price of basic goods too high for ordinary Gazans like Ismail Hamouda.
The 47-year-old father, displaced from Jabalia in the north to Gaza City, listed what residents still lack: potable water, food, financial assistance.
"Here in the displacement camps, we thought that after a year of cease-fire things would improve," he said. "Unfortunately, the situation is worsening gradually. We are still displaced."

Indonesia evacuated eight orangutans after fires on Borneo
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:28:05 EEST
19:28:05 KST

Indonesia evacuated eight orangutans after fires on Borneo
Kyiv • UNN
In Indonesia, eight orangutans were moved to a protected forest after fires on Borneo. Since August, 46 animals have been rescued.
On Sunday, Indonesian authorities and conservationists reported the successful relocation of eight orangutans to a safe place after forest fires on the island of Borneo destroyed the habitat of these endangered primates, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The publication notes that Indonesia is battling the strongest forest fires in 11 years, which have mainly affected the islands of Sumatra and Borneo; the government warned that the fires could continue until November, intensifying due to the El Niño weather phenomenon.
The animals rescued between August and September included three pairs of mothers with their offspring and two adolescent males; they were removed from several different locations, according to a joint statement by the Indonesian government and the conservation foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).
"The relocation to the Batu-Nyambu protected forest is expected to give these eight orangutans a chance to return to life in the wild," the statement said.
According to the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), orangutans are great apes on the verge of extinction; in the wild, they are found only on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra (Southeast Asia), with Indonesia being home to all three recognized species of these animals. Their populations have declined due to deforestation, fires, and poaching.
The relocation operation took six hours by car, one hour by boat, and another two hours on foot; the orangutans were transported in cages secured to bamboo poles. Before the transport, YIARI specialists checked the animals' health.
According to Murlan Dameria Pane, head of the West Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency, since August the agency, together with YIARI, has rescued 46 orangutans affected by the fires.
From January to July of this year, fires in Indonesia destroyed approximately 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres) of land. Official data for the following months have not yet been released; however, according to estimates by nongovernmental organizations, the fires have since destroyed at least another 600,000 hectares of forest. Smoke from the fires caused 175,000 cases of respiratory illness in Indonesia; the haze also spread to neighboring Singapore and Malaysia, where many schools were closed on Friday due to deteriorating air quality.
Recall
As UNN reported, forest fires in Indonesia are affecting an important research area where orangutans on the island of Borneo are studied, and now threaten a renowned scientific camp—the site of one of the world's longest-running studies of wild great apes.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to "get a new leader" following Volodymyr Zelenskyy's criticism of Washington’s decision to ease Russian diesel sanctions, as Trump faces surging fuel prices ahead of midterm elections.
Trump, whose Republicans face dim prospects in next month's vote partly because of soaring energy costs, defended a deal allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets after saying Vladimir Putin strongly wanted to reach a settlement in Ukraine.
Trump accused Zelenskyy of blocking a deal with Moscow and ignoring instructions not to strike Russian refineries, while Kyiv and its European allies warned that easing pressure on Moscow would help fund the Kremlin's war.
Meanwhile, the latest Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 21 people, including children.
Trump announced Friday that he had spoken to Putin and agreed Russia would release large amounts of diesel into global markets.
Ukraine and its European allies expressed dismay, with Zelenskyy telling reporters Friday it was a "weak decision."
Asked about the criticism, Trump said Zelenskyy had disobeyed his orders not to strike Russian refineries and that the attacks risked worsening fuel shortages linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
"He better damn well stop," Trump said.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," Trump said.
Trump later said Putin was interested in ending the war.
"Russia would like to make a deal ... but for whatever reason, Zelenskyy does not want to make a deal," he told reporters.
"President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly."
The U.S. president also criticized Zelenskyy for not holding an election since Russia's 2022 invasion.
"I think he should have an election and he could have settled this thing many times," Trump said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel would only help sustain Russia's war effort.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," she wrote online.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Zelenskyy in a call.
Downing Street said Burnham also pledged that Britain would "strengthen its sanctions on Russia."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga also backed his president. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide," he said in a post on X.
On Saturday, a Russian glide bomb attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia killed 20 people, including three children, according to Ukraine's state rescue service.
"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
A Russian drone attack in the central Dnipropetrovsk region killed an 11-year-old boy, regional officials said.
Russian strikes also caused widespread power cuts in Kyiv.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had hit a "data center" used by Ukraine's military.
The diesel deal was announced as U.S., Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami in a renewed bid to end the conflict.
Ukraine's delegation was headed home on Saturday, an aide to Zelenskyy said.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said on X the talks involved "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO."
He described the discussions as "constructive" and focused on ways to "de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace."
The Kremlin said Saturday that Trump had conveyed his ideas about how to de-escalate the war to Putin during a phone call Friday.
Putin received the proposals "with understanding," the Kremlin said, without elaborating.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.

Gurdwara body files complaint against Kejriwal, AAP workers for 'disrupting' Bangla Sahib's sanctity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:26:23 UTC
19:26:23 KST

DSGMC chief accuses Keriwal's AAP of “dirty politics” over protest attempt inside Gurudwara Bangla Sahib, says "not arena for your politics”
NEW DELHI: The Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee (DSGMC) on Sunday approached the Delhi Police with a complaint against Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leaders, including party chief Arvind Kejriwal, accusing them of disrupting the sanctity of Gurudwara Bangla Sahib and spreading "misleading" videos of the incident during Saturday's anti-CEC protests.The controversy erupted after a group of protesters gathered inside the gurdwara premises while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar to demonstrate against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. Police stopped them from proceeding and detained them.In its complaint, the DSGMC alleged that AAP workers and supporters entered the gurdwara and staged protests, creating a disturbance and using the sacred premises for political purposes.
"The protesters also raised political slogans inside the sacred premises, disturbing the religious atmosphere and violating the sanctity and maryada of Guru Ghar. Such deliberate political activity inside a revered place of worship has deeply hurt the religious sentiments of the Sikh Sangat," the complaint read as per news agency PTI.
DSGMC seeks action against protesters
A delegation of DSGMC office-bearers, led by president Harmeet Singh Kalka, submitted the complaint at the office of the Deputy Commissioner of Police for New Delhi district.
The delegation also provided videos purportedly showing protesters inside Gurudwara Bangla Sahib.The committee urged the police to identify those seen in the footage and investigate who had organised and directed them to enter the premises."We request Delhi Police to identify each of these persons from the videos, ascertain who mobilised, organised and directed them to enter the Gurdwara premises, and take appropriate legal action against all those involved," the DSGMC said.The complaint further accused AAP leaders and MLAs of sharing videos on social media that allegedly presented a "distorted version" of the incident and blamed the gurdwara management."Arvind Kejriwal also publicly supported and amplified this narrative, despite the conduct of his party workers and the circumstances leading to the disturbance being visible from the available material," it alleged.The DSGMC said the incident and the subsequent circulation of "selective and misleading" videos raised concerns about a possible coordinated attempt to trigger controversy at a place of worship, hurt religious sentiments, damage the committee's reputation and gain political mileage.
Row over police entry into gurdwara
Kalka also raised concerns over the conduct of police personnel who entered the gurdwara premises to detain the protesters. He alleged that policemen accompanying Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann had worn shoes when he visited Bangla Sahib.However, Kalka clarified that the Delhi Police personnel had used a passage inside the premises to reach the protesters and had not entered the Darbar Hall, the gurdwara's main sanctum. He added that the policemen should not have entered the premises in uniform.The police, meanwhile, offered a different account of the incident.Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) Sachin Sharma said in a post on X on Saturday that the personnel had walked through a common passage used by devotees to reach the designated area where they remove their shoes before entering the gurdwara.Sharma also alleged that the video circulating on social media had been shared with "malicious intent" and assured that legal action would be initiated against those responsible.
Bhagwant Mann backs protesters
AAP leaders had alleged that the police entered the gurdwara to detain protesters who had taken shelter there.Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann also defended the protesters' presence inside Bangla Sahib in a post on X, condemning the police action.
"I strongly condemn in the harshest terms the BJP's police forcibly entering Gurdwara Sri Bangla Sahib in Delhi yesterday..." he said.Mann argued that gurdwaras had traditionally opened their doors to people in need and said protesters should have been offered shelter."If the youth of this country protesting yesterday had entered there, the principle of the Guru's house is that the sevadars would grant them shelter...," he said.The competing allegations have turned the incident into a dispute over both the conduct of the protesters and the police response, with the DSGMC seeking an investigation into the events inside the gurdwara and the videos subsequently circulated online.

The coalition also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. No further details were immediately available.
The airport remains closed after an attack there on Oct 10 killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade, amid an escalation of fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces.
Despite the airport’s temporary closure, the Saudi Energy Ministry said a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Oct 11.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Oct 11’s projectile had targeted Terminal 4 of the airport, without elaborating.
Earlier, the Houthis had said in a statement on X:
“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina.”
“We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions.”
‘Worse is yet to come,’ Houthis warn
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast in September.
Yemen’s Houthi-run foreign ministry said later on Oct 11 that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.

International energy conference still going ahead

It was not immediately clear whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to go ahead on Oct 11, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available.
Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Oct 11 until Oct 15 for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
In Oct 10’s attack, the third on Riyadh’s airport in a week, the 12 dead included 4 Saudis, 2 Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said.
Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. REUTERS

A Bailey bridge supporting construction work at the Yaru Khola Hydropower Project was also damaged, while construction materials and equipment were washed away.
The Machha Khola Hydropower Project sustained damage to its access road and the bridge connecting the project site, according to the assessment.
Nepal has witnessed multiple floods caused by landslides over the past month following the devastating floods of Aug. 26. The disaster has claimed 1,455 lives, while 5,285 people remain missing, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- At least 109 migrants, including 15 children, have died and more than 116 others remain missing after a boat carrying 350 capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Sunday.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized during the night between Thursday and Friday. IOM teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance, according to the United Nations organization.
"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives," said Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti. Among the 109 bodies recovered are 52 men, 42 women and 15 children. More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals, the United Nations migration agency said in its statement released on Sunday, adding that Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing.
Local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging dignified burials for those who died, according to the statement.
The latest boat accident is one of many similar deadly calamities that have occurred in Djibouti's Red Sea coast area. In most of these incidents, desperate East African migrants attempted to cross the dangerous route, hoping to reach the Middle East via war-torn Yemen, with the main destination being Yemen's northern neighbor, Saudi Arabia. ■

In a statement, the President's House said Zardari signed the prime minister's advice under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, paving the way for the emergency measures in the province.
The statement said the decision was taken after considering the federal cabinet's recommendation, reports from relevant institutions on the law and order situation, and the failure of negotiations between government delegations and stakeholders.
Earlier in the day, the federal cabinet, chaired by Sharif, decided to recommend the imposition of emergency and governor's rule after reviewing what it described as a deteriorating security situation and a rise in terrorist incidents in the province, according to the Prime Minister's Office.
The cabinet was briefed on the prevailing law and order situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa before forwarding the summary to the president for approval.
Under Pakistan's Constitution, Article 232 provides for the proclamation of emergency under specified circumstances, while Article 234 allows the federal government to assume certain functions of a provincial government if constitutional governance in the province cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has witnessed a surge in militant violence in recent months, prompting Pakistani security forces to intensify intelligence-based counterterrorism operations across the province. ■

DUBAI/RIYADH – Yemen’s Houthis warned airlines, travellers and airport workers on Oct 11 to stay away from Saudi airports, a day after an attack on Riyadh’s international airport killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
It was the deadliest such attack in the kingdom in more than a decade, and came amid an escalation of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi militants and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina,” the Houthis said in a post on X.
“We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions.”
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counter-offensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast in September.
Yemen’s Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said on Oct 11 that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
“Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” it said in statements carried by Houthi-run outlet Al-Masirah TV.
President Donald Trump said on Oct 10 that the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
The Saudi-led coalition said the same day that a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the kingdom’s eastern province. The coalition also reported intercepting a drone in the region on Oct 11.
International energy conference still going ahead in Riyadh
The Oct 10 attack has forced the temporary closure of King Khalid International Airport, but the Saudi Energy Ministry said that a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Oct 11.
The five-day WPC Energy Congress is taking place at a convention centre about 10km from the Riyadh airport. State TV said more than 70 ministers, 300 company executives and representatives of over 25 international energy organisations have confirmed their attendance.
It was not immediately clear whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to go ahead on Oct 11, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available.
In the Oct 10 attack, the third on Riyadh’s airport in a week, the 12 dead consisted of four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and nationals of the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi authorities said.
Two previous attacks on Riyadh’s international airport earlier in the week had killed four people and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said that airport operations were temporarily suspended pending damage and safety assessments, without specifying when flights would resume.
Separately, the Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and moved to remote learning from Oct 11 until Oct 15 for all students, teachers and administrative staff. REUTERS
