Interview: Georgian Conductor Nikoloz Rachveli on Music, Ukraine and Solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

For Nikoloz Rachveli, music has long transcended the concert stage. The Georgian conductor, pianist and composer, who has worked with musicians and orchestras across the world, made supporting Ukrainians part of his artistic and civic commitment after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
On Feb. 24, 2022, the rehearsal hall of the Georgian Philharmonic Orchestra in Tbilisi spontaneously became a gathering place for a massive show of solidarity with Ukraine. In late May 2022, Rachveli traveled to Kyiv with singer Nino Katamadze and performed in the metro, on a stage between the tracks, for Ukrainians living through the war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Since then, he has repeatedly returned to Ukraine, performing in Kyiv, Lviv, Odesa, Kharkiv, Poltava, Dnipro, Ivano-Frankivsk, Uzhhorod, Chernivtsi, Zhytomyr, Lutsk and Rivne. He has worked with Ukrainian musicians while introducing audiences back home in Georgia to Ukrainian classical music.
Today, Rachveli speaks about Ukraine as a country to which he feels connected not only through music but also through a profound sense of personal responsibility.
Kyiv Post: Feb. 24, 2022, marked the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. In Georgia, musicians rallied around you and Nino Katamadze. How did that response begin?
Nikoloz Rachveli: On Feb. 23, we had a rehearsal with the Georgian Philharmonic Orchestra. There was a sense of tension; everyone was expecting something terrible to happen. One of the orchestra musicians suggested adding a piece by a Ukrainian composer to the program. On Feb. 24, I was planning to listen to Ukrainian works and choose one.
There Will be no Breakthrough in Peace Talks, - Stefan Korshak
But early that morning, we woke up to the horrifying news. Everyone in the orchestra’s group chat was writing that something terrible was happening. We decided to gather in the rehearsal hall, if only to be together. I posted on Facebook that the doors were open to everyone.
By 10 a.m., musicians from different Georgian orchestras were already on stage. Around 800 to 900 people arrived, carrying flags and banners and bringing yellow-and-blue flowers.
We went live. Nino Katamadze came, along with other singers, soloists, opposition politicians and television crews. The rehearsal hall became the epicenter of support for Ukraine in Georgia.
We reached out to musical communities around the world and began performing the national anthems of Ukraine and Georgia. Nino sang “Chornobryvtsi” (“Black-Eyed Susans”), and we concluded with music by Giya Kancheli.
It later became clear that our gathering was the first initiative of this scale organized by an artistic community anywhere in the world. It became one of the symbols of support for Ukraine.
When did you decide that you wanted to come to Ukraine in person?
I felt that urge immediately. On the evening of Feb. 24, I was calling friends and asking what we could do. I had this impulse: “Give me a weapon. I want to fight.” The same instinct had awakened in me in 2008.
When Russia attacked Ukraine, all the unhealed wounds in Georgians opened up again. I wanted to take up arms, but my friends in the military talked me out of it.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli, Nino Katamadze, Lviv National Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra “INSO-Lviv”. (Image courtesy of Nikoloz Rachveli’s personal archive)                             
Because music can be a weapon, too.
Exactly. I focused on charity and artistic work. In early April 2022, we organized a major televised fundraising marathon and invited artists and musicians from Ukraine, including the Lviv-based INSO-Lviv orchestra and Jamala. All Georgian television channels broadcast the event.
People could donate to the account of the Embassy of Ukraine in Georgia. Across several such initiatives, we raised around $500,000.
In late May, Sofiko Chkonia, founder of Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Tbilisi, suggested organizing a trip to Ukraine. She brought Nino and me together, and we decided to go.
We discovered that Ukrainians and Georgians share a powerful, deeply rooted – almost genetic – longing for freedom. That is what makes our peoples spiritually related.
You and Nino Katamadze performed in the Kyiv metro at the time. It was a very special concert for all of us.
Looking back on my life, that concert was the most special, the most important and the most emotionally intense performance I had ever given, before or since.
Because of the security situation, we were offered the opportunity to perform in the metro. I remember Kyiv with almost no cars on the streets and restaurants and cafés closed. The management of the Fairmont hotel took us in, even though nobody was working there apart from one person who opened the doors for us. They brought us bread, and we made our own sandwiches.
Bono had performed at Maidan Nezalezhnosti metro station shortly before us. Later, our musical program took place there, too. I asked some dear Ukrainian friends who play string instruments to join us. That is how the Ukrainian-Georgian performance came together.
Our stage was between the tracks. The trains did not stop, but the drivers were asked to slow down. We could see people inside the carriages.
They recognized Nino, waved to us and made heart signs with their hands. We also performed for military personnel returning from the front and for field medical staff.
It was incredible. Nothing like that happens in ordinary life.
Later, we performed together in Lviv in support of Ukraine. We returned to Georgia and realized that we wanted to come back to Ukraine again. Since then, I have personally crossed the Ukrainian border 29 times and served as musical director for approximately 50 events.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli, Sviatoslav Vakarchuk, Jamala and Nino Katamadze. (Image courtesy of Nikoloz Rachveli’s personal archive)                             
How has the war changed your understanding of music?
My understanding has changed profoundly. But it is not just my attitude toward music that has changed. My attitude toward life itself and toward the people who perform music has changed, too.
Previously, the most important things for me were the concept of a concert, the composition and the performance. Now, the person comes first – the person with whom I create music or for whom I create it.
When you are in Ukraine, especially in Kyiv, rehearsing with colleagues who risk their lives every day, you come to rehearsal after a terrifying night and look around, wondering: Is everyone here today?
I remember a concert last year. There had been a massive attack before the dress rehearsal. That morning, on stage, I began quietly counting the children – we were rehearsing with the Shchedryk choir – to make sure that everyone who had been there the day before had returned.
Later, I heard the story of a little girl who refused to go to a shelter with her father because she could not leave her mother, who has a disability, alone. The entire family stayed at home.
There are so many stories like these. Today, I understand the word “life” differently.
Here, life means constant risk. You never know what might happen in an hour, or even in a minute. That is why I have learned to value every moment in an entirely different way.
What power does music have under such circumstances?
Just look at our concert – the closing event of Kyiv Music Fest 2026, titled “Let There Be Light,” on Oct. 3. In this bleak psychological state, music gave both the audience and those of us on stage an extraordinary, boundlessly positive energy.
                                                                                                                                                                         Closing concert of Kyiv Music Fest 2026, “Let There Be Light,” Oct. 3. The Academic Symphony Orchestra of the National Philharmonic of Ukraine, conducted by Nikoloz Rachveli of Georgia, with the Dumka National Choir and soloist Bohdana Pivnenko. (Image via Dmytro and Viktoriia Holovchenko)                             
It helps us survive, stand firm, keep hope alive for the future and stay sane. That is why I value the power of music so deeply.
Composer Giya Kancheli played a special role in your life. During a recent performance of Styx in Kyiv, you found it difficult to remain at the conductor’s podium during one of the rehearsals. What happened?
After a terrible night of shelling, I heard the Dumka choir for the first time at rehearsal. Those wonderful singers had come and were singing in my native Georgian. As I conducted, I was so overwhelmed by emotion that I lost my composure and began to cry.
The story of Styx is unique for me. When Giya Kancheli wrote the piece in 1999, he specifically added a piano part to the orchestration for me. I was 19 and in my first year at the Vienna Academy of Music. Even then, Kancheli supported me enormously and had great hopes for my future as a composer and conductor.
He insisted that orchestras invite me to perform the piano part at every premiere of Styx. So, 27 years ago, I became one of the musicians who first brought the work to life, performing it in many countries around the world.
Later, I conducted Styx myself in concert halls internationally. When you perform a piece very often, it becomes almost your own. But this time in Kyiv, I experienced every measure and every note differently. Everything felt deeper, warmer and, at the same time, more emotionally intense.
My feelings were transmitted to the orchestra musicians and the choir, and then to the audience. The performance prompted unusually prolonged applause, cries of emotion and genuine tears – on stage and in the hall alike.
You knew Giya Kancheli for many years. What was your creative friendship like?
In 2002, an idea emerged in Georgia to create a stage production based on Kancheli’s music for film and theater. I proposed new arrangements and orchestration, along with vocal, theatrical and choreographic elements.
The premiere took place at the Tbilisi Opera Theatre in 2003 and played to full houses for several consecutive days. The project introduced a new generation to Kancheli’s music. Giya often thanked me for bringing this part of his work back to life on stage and giving it a new existence.
For my career, Giya was the key person who helped me move from Georgia onto the international stage. When orchestras in other countries commissioned works from him, he recommended me to them. That is how I began conducting premieres of Kancheli’s compositions with European orchestras.
Toward the end of his life, he told me something incredibly important: When he composed music, he could already imagine it being performed under my baton, in my interpretation.
For a performer, that is the highest recognition an author of his stature can offer.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli and Giya Kancheli. (Image courtesy of Nikoloz Rachveli’s personal archive)                             
One of your main areas of work today is Ukrainian music. What are your plans in this field?
One of my main goals is to perform Ukrainian composers’ works more frequently in Georgia. At the end of November, I will conduct a concert in Tbilisi with our orchestra featuring works by Hanna Havrylets, Bohdana Frolyak, Liubava Sydorenko and other Ukrainian composers.
The Soviet Union did a great deal to ensure that almost nothing was known in Georgia about Ukrainian symphonic and chamber music. The past four and a half years have been a period of constantly discovering new Ukrainian names and compositions for me.
In Lviv, I worked with INSO-Lviv on the Genocode project, which tells the story of Ukrainian classical music through excerpts from symphonic, chamber and operatic works.
That is why I see my mission as more than allowing the war to unite us in resisting Russian imperial policy. Creativity must unite us, too.
Ukrainian audiences know and love Georgian dances and music. I want people in Georgia to know and love Ukrainian composers just as much, and to look forward to hearing their music performed. I have already organized a Ukrainian music festival in Tbilisi twice. Now I am planning a third edition.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli. (Image via Dmytro and Viktoriia Holovchenko)                             
You spend much of your time abroad. How has the political situation in Georgia affected your life and work?
Yes. The political situation in Georgia has become extremely tense. Friends of mine – artists, directors, writers and journalists – are in prison because of their active participation in protests. Among them is Paata Burchuladze, a legend of the international opera world. Unfortunately, our country is beginning to resemble Belarus under Lukashenko.
At the same time, our orchestra and concert hall remain oases of freedom, places from which free speech can still be heard, along with a handful of media outlets. But more and more musicians, including members of our orchestra, are receiving heavy fines for taking part in protests.
Democracy and Georgia’s movement toward the West have weakened considerably. Nevertheless, I still do not want to believe that members of the Georgian government are pro-Russian at heart. I think some are driven by fear of war, while others are motivated by financial interests. This part of society accounts for no more than 15 percent of our population, but unfortunately, it is the group holding the levers of power.
Still, I would like to end our conversation in a major key. We need to imagine positive scenarios. What future do you dream of for Ukraine and Georgia?
Since you mentioned the word “dream,” yes, I have one: I want Ukraine and Georgia to share a common border. (Smiles.)
It is a playful dream, but if you look deeper into history, the territories between us were once connected to both Ukraine and Georgia. Perhaps, if that happened, historical justice would be restored.
We are already neighbors and brothers in spirit. I want us to become geographical neighbors, too. (Smiles.)
Seriously, though, I dream that future generations of Ukrainians and Georgians will live peacefully and without fear, will not be afraid of their neighbors and will not have to pass this struggle on to their children.
I very much want Russia to break apart as an empire and for a democratic society to emerge there afterward. Geographically, we are neighbors, and there is no escaping that reality. That is why it is important for Russia to change not only its politics but also its mindset – to acknowledge its crimes and undergo a process of moral cleansing.
After World War II, German society underwent serious work in this regard. A country that committed the Holocaust has become a model state in protecting European values and now supports Ukraine so strongly.
Of course, it is difficult for me to imagine Russia accomplishing this. But first and foremost, it must suffer a crushing defeat. Only then will its society have a chance at moral salvation.
Ukraine had already won when the enemy failed to capture Kyiv – of course, at the cost of countless lives and thanks to its extraordinary heroes. Knowing the character of the Ukrainian people, I believe in victory to the very end, a victory that will bring Ukraine a bright future. And a bright future for Ukraine also means a bright future for my homeland.
                                                                                                                                                                         Bohdana Pivnenko, Nikoloz Rachveli, Mariana Holovko and the Kyiv Camerata National Ensemble of Soloists. (Image via Bouquet Kyiv Stage)                             
Ukraine’s victory is essential to the history of humanity and the history of religions. It must show future generations that evil can be defeated by good. Otherwise, everything on which our civilization rests will lose its meaning.
Glory to Ukraine!
Glory to Georgia!
Glory to the heroes of our two countries!

Labour has got the message – developing nations suffer most from bond market turmoil | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:11:19 UTC
19:11:19 KST

From Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless.
Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere.
Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans.
That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency.
Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south, and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.
There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.
The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis.
However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran.
Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing.
The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.”
He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries.
As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support.
“There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference.
Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge.
One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues.
Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.
The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another six small island developing states that do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. These could be offered a five-year “holiday” from the moment of the next extreme weather event they face, at the cost of a further $700m a year.
An even more expansive version would embrace another five countries, including Pakistan and Angola.
Crucially, because the international financial institutions – including the IMF and the World Bank – tend to be preferred creditors, only chipping in when other help is exhausted, the costs to them would be relatively low.
Echoing Andy Burnham’s slogan – so far confined to the domestic sphere – Matthew Martin, DFI’s executive director and the author of the plan, says: “Let’s bring hope back to the poorest countries in the world, through an ambitious but financially and politically feasible initiative, which will free up $13bn for them to spend on their climate and development goals.”
It remains to be seen how bold the government is prepared to be in setting its G20 agenda, but the groundwork is being done.
Labour trashed its reputation as a champion for international development when Keir Starmer took the axe to aid spending to pay for defence. Perhaps 2027 could be the year Burnham starts to rebuild it.

Saudi Arabia has reported 12 deaths and 309 injuries following an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, 10 October, blaming Yemen’s Houthi movement for the strike. The Saudi-led military coalition has pledged retaliation, while US President Donald Trump said Washington was considering joining military operations against the group.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said the dead included four Saudi nationals, two Bangladeshis and one citizen each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt. Several injured passengers and airport workers remained in critical condition.
The attack was the third on the airport within a week and the deadliest strike on Saudi territory in more than a decade. Previous attacks on Thursday killed several people and damaged an aircraft parked at the airport.
Reuters reported that hospitals received casualties transported by ambulances and helicopters. An eyewitness described an explosion followed by scenes of injured people lying inside the terminal. One wounded traveller told the news agency that part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed after an object crossed the sky.
Saudi authorities suspended airport operations and diverted incoming flights. A Notice to Air Missions extended the closure until 21:00 GMT on Sunday, 11 October, while officials assessed damage to airport facilities.
Kuwait Airways cancelled two flights scheduled between Kuwait and Riyadh on Sunday. Jazeera Airways also reported disruption to its services, while India's Akasa Air extended its suspension of Saudi flights until Tuesday.
Schools across Riyadh will conduct lessons remotely for one week following instructions from the Ministry of Education, AFP reported, citing an email sent to parents.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Malki described the airport attack as a war crime and promised a response under international humanitarian law. The coalition also reported intercepting a drone in eastern Saudi Arabia and a separate projectile landing near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The Houthis have not formally claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack, although their media office said the group had shut down Riyadh's airport. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree renewed warnings to airlines and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, excluding Mecca and Medina.
The attacks follow renewed fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and forces supporting the internationally recognised government. Saudi Arabia has conducted air strikes against Houthi positions while Yemeni government troops have launched operations around Taiz and territory near the Red Sea.
The conflict intensified after a ceasefire established in 2022 unravelled earlier this year. Saudi Arabia originally entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, who seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
Trump described Saturday's attack as “terrible” and said he intended to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Asked whether American forces would participate in strikes against the Houthis, Trump told reporters: “We may. We're going to look at it.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that an American citizen was among those killed and demanded an end to attacks against civilians.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the strike, stating that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law and “must cease immediately”.
UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg warned that attacks on Saudi airports threatened regional security and complicated efforts to end Yemen's conflict.
Qatar, Kuwait, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Pakistan, India and several other countries condemned the attack. Oman's government called for restraint and urged parties to avoid further escalation.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said attacks against civilian infrastructure had “no justification”, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reaffirmed his country's commitment to Saudi sovereignty and security.
The US, British, Canadian and other foreign missions advised their nationals to avoid Riyadh airport. The US embassy also introduced additional travel restrictions for government personnel using airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam.
Despite the disruption, organisers of the World Petroleum Congress and Future Investment Initiative said their events in Riyadh would proceed. Delegates received information about alternative travel routes, including journeys from Dammam.

Most long-term singles stay satisfied with their lives over 11 years, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:00:18 UTC
19:00:18 KST

New research indicates that people who remain unpartnered and unmarried generally maintain high and relatively stable life satisfaction over long periods of time, even as their sexual fulfillment and desire for a partner vary widely. By tracking different generations of singles over more than a decade, the findings suggest that there is no single way to experience a solo life. The study was published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin.
Never-married singlehood refers to the status of adults who have not entered a formal marriage and are not currently in a committed romantic partnership. For many years, lifespan theories treated romantic partnerships as a universal developmental milestone, suggesting that failing to find a mate could lead to isolation. Because of this framework, scientists often evaluated singles simply by comparing them to partnered people. But as marriage rates drop globally and solo living becomes more common, researchers have increasingly shifted their focus to investigating how individual factors like personality, age, and sexual fulfillment shape a single person’s happiness.
“As the population of single individuals grows and people are increasingly delaying marriage, there is both a rise in population as well as public and academic interest for singles, or romantically unpartnered individuals,” Elaine Hoan, a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto and lead author of the study, told PsyPost. “In light of this rise, much is unknown regarding how singles’ psychological well-being changes over time, with some individuals arguing that singles report generally low well-being across the life span.”
Recent research has begun to examine what shapes singles’ well-being. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that adolescents born in the early 2000s tend to be more satisfied with being single than those born a decade earlier. Beyond generational differences, a 2020 study found that single people who are satisfied with their sex lives tend to be happier with their single status and show less interest in getting married. Additionally, a 2021 analysis of German adults showed that singles who feel less urge to find a romantic partner tend to be happier with their lives overall.
The new study builds directly on this work by tracking how these different facets of well-being evolve together over more than a decade across multiple generations of singles. Hoan and her colleagues analyzed data from the German Family Panel, a long-running national survey of relationships and families, tracking 2,930 adults over an 11-year period between 2009 and 2021. The participants came from three birth groups: emerging adults who started the study around age 18, young adults who began around age 26, and middle-aged adults who entered around age 36.
To be included, participants had to remain never married and without a committed partner at every one of the 11 yearly surveys, so the sample captures long-term singles rather than everyone who was single at the start. Because people frequently partner up as they age, this filtering was much heavier for older groups; only 14 percent of the middle-aged cohort qualified, compared with 67 percent of the youngest.
During the 11-year period, participants regularly answered single-item questions rating four specific outcomes on numeric scales: overall life satisfaction, satisfaction with their single status, sexual satisfaction, and their desire for a romantic partner. An earlier analysis of the same data, which assumed all singles follow a single average path, had suggested that singles’ life satisfaction tends to decline over time.
By using a statistical modeling technique designed to group people with similar over-time trends into distinct categories, the researchers sought to uncover whether multiple different paths existed. They also measured participants’ income, education, physical health, and personality traits to see how these factors lined up with different well-being paths.
The researchers found that the vast majority of singles across all three age groups reported high and relatively stable life satisfaction. Roughly 90 percent of the participants in each cohort fell into a group whose life satisfaction stayed above the midpoint of the scale for the entire 11 years, though it dipped slightly over time among the two younger groups. A small minority in each age group started the study with lower life satisfaction.
Among emerging and young adults, this smaller minority’s happiness tended to improve over time, eventually catching up to the rest of their peers. Among middle-aged adults, however, the smaller group with lower starting happiness did not show the same improvement; its scores edged down slightly, though this change was not statistically significant. The authors suggest this may reflect the social pressures of midlife, when expectations around marriage and family are often strongest.
“We found that while relationship-focused outcomes, like sexual satisfaction and desire for a partner, varied more between participants, singles’ overall satisfaction with their lives remained remarkably robust,” Hoan explained. “Overall, even while singles face different romantic or sexual experiences, they generally remain quite satisfied with their lives over time.”
Satisfaction with being single showed much more variety. About 67 percent of the youngest adults reported high and stable satisfaction with their single status. Young and middle-aged adults, by contrast, split into three groups: a highly satisfied group (about 30 and 37 percent, respectively), a larger group with middling satisfaction, and a group with low satisfaction (about 12 and 18 percent).
The authors suggest this shift may reflect changing life goals, since singlehood can suit the educational and career focus of emerging adulthood, while priorities often turn toward partnership later. They also point to selection: by midlife, many people have partnered, leaving a smaller group of singles who differ widely in whether they are single by choice.
Trajectories of sexual satisfaction remained flat over the 11 years but varied widely in their starting levels. The youngest adults split into four distinct groups ranging from very low to very high sexual fulfillment. By young adulthood, the pattern simplified to two groups, with about 63 percent reporting moderate sexual satisfaction and 37 percent reporting very low satisfaction.
Interestingly, individuals with higher education levels frequently fell into the groups with the lowest sexual satisfaction. The researchers propose that intense focus on advanced educational pursuits might reduce a person’s time or interest in seeking out sexual experiences, or that people less interested in sex may gravitate toward demanding educational paths.
When looking at the desire for a partner, the data indicated that most singles maintained a moderate to high interest in finding a relationship. For example, about 47 percent of young adults fell into a high-desire category. However, a small but distinct group of singles in each age bracket reported very low desire for a partner. These individuals tended to have higher education levels and lower levels of neuroticism, a personality trait associated with emotional instability and anxiety.
Across all the measures, the groups reporting the highest life, singlehood, and sexual satisfaction generally exhibited healthier personality profiles, including lower neuroticism and higher extraversion, meaning they were more outgoing, sociable, and energetic. “We found that the trajectories with the highest well-being tended to be more extraverted, less neurotic, more highly educated, and full-time employed,” Hoan said. “These results suggest that higher socioeconomic status is an important part of supporting a thriving singlehood.”
These findings are in line with earlier work by some of the same researchers, covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that higher extraversion and lower neuroticism were linked to higher well-being among singles, though that earlier work compared singles and partnered people at a single point in time rather than tracking singles over years.
However, the new findings stand in tension with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which tracked emerging adults from age 16 to 29 and found that remaining consistently single was associated with declining life satisfaction relative to peers who partnered up. Because the current study followed only never-married singles across a broader age range of 18 to 48 without comparing them to partnered people, it suggests that most long-term singles maintain relatively high life satisfaction, even though the largest group of younger singles did show a slight decline.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Because the study tracked naturally occurring patterns, it cannot show that personality traits, education, or income cause singles to follow happier paths; these factors may simply travel together. The study also defined singlehood broadly, capturing anyone who had never married and was not currently cohabiting or in a committed relationship. This means that people who engaged in casual dating or brief romantic flings between the yearly surveys were grouped together with those who completely abstained from romance, though the authors note that removing people who briefly dated did not substantially change the results.
The study was also conducted in Germany, meaning the results might not fully translate to cultures with different social norms surrounding marriage and independence. Hoan is planning to address this limitation in future work.
“I am continuing to investigate longitudinal patterns of well-being across both single and partnered individuals, but in diverse contexts beyond WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) samples,” she noted. “Given that different cultures have strongly varying norms around singlehood, investigating singles’ experiences and how they might differ from partnered people’s experiences, across cultures is an important future direction. For instance, in India, being an unmarried woman can create daily logistical barriers, such as greater difficulty with renting apartments.”
Additionally, the oldest participants in the study were in their late forties by the end of the data collection period. Future studies will need to track singles into their sixties and beyond to see how retirement and older age shape the single experience. Finally, same-sex marriage only became legal in Germany in 2017, so “never married” carried a different meaning for gay and lesbian participants during much of the study period, and the sample included too few of them (65) to compare with heterosexual singles.
The study, “The Eras of Singlehood: 11-Year Longitudinal Trajectories of Never-Married Singles’ Well-Being Across Cohorts,” was authored by Elaine Hoan, Geoff MacDonald, and Matthew D. Johnson.

The Benefits of Prescribing Food as Medicine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

We all know that eating a healthy diet is good for us.
In fact, nutrition is one of the most powerful tools we have to prevent and manage chronic health conditions like heart disease, diabetes, and hypertension. The evidence is strong enough that the American Heart Association identifies eating better as one of Life’s Essential 8, the eight key factors for improving heart health.
So, why is it so hard for Americans to eat well?
Part of the problem is knowing what to eat as part of a healthy diet. Nutrition can feel complicated, especially when health claims can be conflicting or confusing. How much protein does one really need? What are good fats and bad fats?
But the fundamentals of a heart-healthy diet have been remarkably consistent for years: eat plenty of fruits and vegetables, prioritize healthy sources of protein, and choose whole grains while minimizing sodium, processed foods, and added sugar. This was reinforced in the most recent 2026 Dietary Guidance released by the American Heart Association.
Knowing what to eat and being able to eat that way are, however, not the same thing.
Eating a healthy diet is not simply a matter of individual choice; it also depends on whether you can afford healthier foods, which often cost more. Nearly 1 in 7 U.S. households struggled with having enough food to eat at some point in 2024, according to the latest USDA data.
Even foods that seem healthy can contain unhealthy ingredients. A salad may seem like an obviously healthy choice, yet it can contain a surprising amount of sodium and saturated fat if it has processed meat, cheese, and dressing. Since much of the sodium is already baked into our food, it is not surprising that nearly seven in 10 adults exceed the recommended intake of sodium of 2,300 milligrams per day.
As a preventive cardiologist and one of the authors of the 2025 high blood pressure guideline by the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology, I know how compelling the data are to support a low-sodium diet to manage high blood pressure. Yet every day, I see that simply recommending a low-sodium diet to patients is not enough to get them to adopt it.
What if you could get low-sodium meals delivered to manage your blood pressure just as easily as you can pick up a prescription refill for your blood pressure-lowering medication?
That is the idea behind a growing movement known as Food Is Medicine. The concept is straightforward. In addition to nutritional advice, medically tailored meals can help prevent and treat chronic diseases. In response to a congressional directive, the Department of Health and Human Services developed a Food is Medicine initiative to coordinate federal efforts and provide a roadmap for the integration of nutrition into health care.
Yet evidence gaps remain: which approaches work, for whom, and at what cost? We must answer these questions with the same rigor we expect for drugs. This is exactly what the American Heart Association’s Health Care by Food initiative, launched with support from the Rockefeller Foundation, is aiming to do. This initiative is funding the research needed to determine how to make healthy food programs in health care systems accessible, affordable, and scalable.
Some of the early evidence is encouraging. In a recent randomized clinical trial of 206 adults living with heart failure in the Navajo Nation, a meal program reduced the likelihood that patients would be hospitalized or visit an emergency department within 90 days by about 30%.
We also need to do better at teaching nutrition in medical schools. In 2026, HHS and the Department of Education announced a new initiative for medical schools to deliver at least 40 hours of nutrition education in U.S. medical schools. Because healthy nutrition is important for every patient, every doctor needs to learn and know this information.
In addition to change at the individual patient level, changing the health of our population will require changing the food environment around us.
While this may seem like a daunting task, one of the best examples of success in improving population health comes from Finland. More than 50 years ago, North Karelia, a rural region in eastern Finland, faced a cardiovascular crisis. Heart disease mortality was among the highest in the world. The problem was so severe that local representatives petitioned the government to take action.
The North Karelia project was born. Public campaigns focused on dietary changes, including replacing butter and full-fat dairy with healthier fats as well as increased vegetable and fruit intake. Food manufacturers changed their products, and schools changed what was served. Over the next several decades, coronary heart disease mortality in eastern Finland fell by more than 80% among working-age adults.
We can also learn from U.S. public-health success stories. Take the example of motor vehicle accidents. For much of the 20th century, car crashes were an enormous public-health problem. Simply urging people to drive carefully was not enough: beginning in the 1960s, the U.S. adopted a broader approach that combined safer vehicle and road design—including seatbelts and later air bags—with safety laws and enforcement. Despite a tenfold increase in miles driven, the motor-vehicle death rate fell by 90% per mile traveled between 1925 and 1997, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The need in the U.S. has never been more urgent. According to the American Heart Association’s 2026 Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics report, which my colleagues and I published this year in Circulation, poor-quality diet is one of the most common risk factors for heart disease. Moreover, poor diet contributes to millions of deaths around the world each year.
We can continue to tell people to eat healthier. And we should. But our current approach is like telling people to drive more safely while watching deadly crashes happen in cars without seat belts. Better advice alone will not be enough. To transform the health of the American population, healthy food should be something we can recommend, be able to prescribe, and deliver as part of health care.

These Midterm Races Will Decide Data Centers’ Political Fate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
From surveillance and DOGE to Big Tech money and religious extremism, the midterms have never been more WIRED. Data centers are no exception: The public has rapidly turned on them since the beginning of the year.
The opposition is bipartisan, with many Republicans making a rare break from President Donald Trump. Candidates on both sides of the aisle are trying to attack their opponents for being pro–data center (or not anti–data center enough). I’ve spotted at least five candidates who have been given the derogatory “Data Center [Name]” moniker by their opponents, in an attempt to highlight their connections to the industry. (That includes two guys named Derek/Derrick getting this treatment.)
While polling shows that pocketbook issues are likely to be top of voters’ minds, data centers are a potent-enough issue that they could swing tight races—and ultimately tip the balance of power in Congress. Here are some of the races WIRED is keeping an eye on as we approach November 3.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo in August warning that Democrat Sherrod Brown, running for Senate in Ohio, was hitting his opponent, Senator Jon Husted, so hard on data centers that it could tip the outcome of the race, calling it “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Brown has called Husted “the face of data centers in Ohio,” running ads that blame Husted for welcoming data centers to the state and driving energy bills up.
Senate Democrats have taken up Brown’s cause, torpedoing a bill sponsored by Husted and modeled after the White House’s ratepayer protection pledge, with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling the bill “toothless.”
Data centers have also seeped into many other toss-up Senate races, including in Michigan, Iowa, and Texas. But the Ohio race is still the top one to watch here.
All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, and data centers have become flash points in dozens of races across the country. Among races labeled toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, I found numerous examples of candidates running data-center-related ads:
- In Michigan’s 7th district, Will Lawrence used local opposition to data centers to help win a tough Democratic primary. Lawrence is now facing off against Republican Tom Barrett and has aired several data-center-related ads, both attacking Barrett and advertising Lawrence’s promise to “stand up to corporate power.”
- In Pennsylvania’s 8th district, Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan has run ads promising to be tough on the industry—despite holding data-center-related stocks and a previously friendly stance. His Democratic challenger, Paige Cognetti, has also run ads attacking the industry.
- In Ohio’s 9th, Democratic incumbent Marcy Kaptur has run ads railing against what she says is incumbent Derek Merrin’s history of giving tax breaks to data centers. (The ads call him “Data Center Derek.”) Merrin claims that Kaptur is misrepresenting his vote on a broader bill.
- In Wisconsin’s 3rd district, Democrat Rebecca Cooke has aired attack ads against incumbent Derrick van Orden’s history of taking contributions from data center developers, dubbing him “DC Derrick.” (Sound familiar?) Van Orden has also shot back by highlighting Cooke’s ties to the tech industry, claiming she is “responsible for covering up pristine Wisconsin farmland” with data centers.
- In New York’s 17th district, incumbent Republican Mike Lawler has aired an ad slamming Democratic opponent Cait Conley’s past statements that the Hudson Valley “needs” data centers.
At least 20 candidates in the 36 gubernatorial races have promised to enact some kind of data center moratorium if elected, according to research from Multistate. The only true hyperscale moratorium in place in the US right now was signed in July by New York governor Kathy Hochul, who holds a comfortable lead ahead of challenger Bruce Blakeman (who supports data center development).
Candidates without much daylight between them have still tried to gain the upper hand on the issue. In Wisconsin’s tight gubernatorial race, Republican Tom Tiffany has attacked Democrat David Crowley with ads calling him “Data Center David.” Both candidates say they support restrictions on the industry.
In states that have been hotbeds for data center activity, some candidates in tight races have been forced to pivot on the issue. Nowhere is this clearer than in Texas, where incumbent governor Greg Abbott has gone from welcoming data center development to putting a de facto moratorium on permits in less than a year. His opponent, Gina Hinojosa, says Abbott hasn’t gone far enough to regulate the industry.
Voters in eight states are looking at more than 30 local ballot measures around data centers. Once again, Ohio is a standout here: It’s responsible for more than half of those measures, from local moratoriums to referendums around rezoning.
What We’re Writing
WIRED science editor Brian Kahn and I got exclusive access to a startup that wants to pull water from the air using excess heat from data centers. While atmospheric water-harvesting technology has been around for a while, the startup has a unique spin. Atoco uses materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs, which won one of its founders the Nobel Prize last year. The company’s previous prototypes have all needed to be hooked up to the grid to generate enough heat to extract water from the MOFs. The new version, though, only needs waste heat from industrial facilities—like data centers—to produce water, even in arid areas.
What We’re Reading
- In Memphis, Tennessee, home of Elon Musk’s SpaceX data centers, the city council postponed a vote on a data center moratorium. Business Insider has more on the “chaotic” meeting.
- Bloomberg reports that Oracle used trucks to ship in natural gas to a data center outside Salt Lake City to keep it online for more than a year—and is considering a similar move in New Mexico, where pipeline delays have held up a big project.
- As the midterms approach, environmental groups are flooding the zone with ads about the rush to build AI infrastructure powered by fossil fuels—just as Congress prepares to debate permitting reform. Heatmap has more.

Barabak: Is there a doctor in the House? Backlash to Trump, RFK Jr. may boost their political ranks

Is there a doctor in the House? Backlash to Trump, RFK Jr. may boost their political ranks
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Anti-vax policies and erosion of the nation’s public health system have spurred hundreds of doctors and scientists to seek office.
- In Sacramento, pediatrician and congressional hopeful Richard Pan is part of that wave.
FOOTHILL FARMS, Calif. — As a California state lawmaker, Richard Pan authored some of the strongest vaccine laws in the country.
His reward — and part of the backlash, on top of death threats — was being physically assaulted outside the Capitol in Sacramento and spattered with blood thrown from the gallery.
Now, a few years removed from the state Senate and teaching health policy at UC Davis, Pan is running for Congress, in part to fight an old nemesis, the terminally misguided Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and to arrest the Trump administration’s sledgehammering of the nation’s public healthcare system.
“We need people in Congress who have the background, the training, the knowledge to basically hold this administration accountable,” Pan said last week on a baking 100-degree day in the Sacramento suburbs.
“I know what it’s like to be on the front lines,” said Pan, who spent a dozen years teaching and practicing pediatrics before being elected to the Assembly in 2010. “I’ve seen measles, right?”
In fact, his push to toughen vaccination requirements was spurred by a 2014-15 measles outbreak at Disneyland, which, at the time, was one of the largest and most significant epidemics to arise after the disease was supposedly eliminated from the U.S. in 2000.
Little did we know.
Two of the country’s top political prognosticators see Democrats likely seizing the House and possibly the Senate. The guardrails Republicans were counting on to stem their losses don’t seem to be holding.
Every action has an equal and opposition reaction, a law of physics that’s equally applicable to the realm of politics.
Pan is part of a wave of doctors and scientists running for office this November — for school boards, city councils, state legislatures, the House and U.S. Senate — owing in good part to Kennedy’s quackery and the hollowing out of such vital health and research agencies as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Food and Drug Administration and the National Institutes of Health.
The political organization 3.14 Action — its name a decimal approximation of pi — has recruited and helped elect hundreds of candidates from STEM backgrounds (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) and endorsed more than 500 of those running this year, including Pan in his race in Sacramento and in neighboring Placer and Yolo counties.
Shaughnessy Naughton, a chemist who worked on drug discovery and breast cancer research, founded 3.14 Action in 2016 after two unsuccessful tries for a congressional seat in the Philadelphia suburbs. When she started the organization, Naughton noted, there were more talk radio hosts on Capitol Hill than scientists and engineers. (Nearly two dozen doctors and nurses currently serve in Congress. More than 30 have run this election cycle.)
“There isn’t an issue that doesn’t benefit by having fact-based decision-makers, people that will go into office as problem-solvers,” Naughton said from Pennsylvania, which is in the throes of the nation’s worst measles outbreak in more than three decades. Health and Human Services Secretary Kennedy has downplayed the severity, even as the incidence of other vaccine-preventable diseases is rising.
“That’s essentially what scientists and physicians are,” Naughton said. “They are problem-solvers. and clearly our country is facing a lot of problems.”
Among those she cited was “the arsonist in charge of HHS.”
Pan has a history with Kennedy, who has long reigned as one of the country’s preeminent anti-vaxxers.
In 2015, he helped summon hundreds of demonstrators to Sacramento to protest Pan’s legislation tightening vaccination requirements. (Kennedy later apologized for using the word “holocaust” to condemn the proposed law, though he revisited the Nazi analogy during the COVID-19 pandemic.)
In 2019, Kennedy returned to Sacramento to oppose another bill Pan authored, this one tightening the rules for vaccination exemptions. Again, he was joined by an army of protesters. Tensions peaked when a demonstrator threw a cup of blood from the spectators’ gallery onto the Senate floor, halting business for several hours before the bill passed.
Pan’s opponent in November is Rep. Kevin Kiley, a conservative Republican running as an independent.
Seeking election in a Democratic-tilting district drawn under Proposition 50, the voter-passed gerrymander, Kiley has sought to distance himself from Trump and the MAGA movement, saying he would not caucus with GOP lawmakers if he returned to Washington.
Like his jury-rigged political persona, Kiley seems to want it both ways on vaccines.
Before going to Congress, while serving in the Assembly, Kiley voted against Pan’s legislation cracking down on fraudulent vaccine exemptions. He’s described vaccines as a vital public health tool, but condemned government mandates and suggested vaccination should be a matter of parental choice. He claims Pan has eroded public trust by politicizing the issue.
As for Kennedy, Kiley told the San Francisco Chronicle a lot of things “that I don’t agree with,” though he’s never called out the secretary for his cuckoo-land theories — vaccines cause autism, the fluoride in public water supplies is making Americans “stupider,” and many more — or denounced his destructive policies.
That passivity, Pan said, amounts to complicity.
“It’s not just simply a talking point,” Pan said of public health policy. “It’s reality and we need to have policy based on what’s really happening, not on some ideological conspiracy theory.”
Pan’s campaign is focused on more than vaccines and RFK Jr.
Like most Democrats, he’s made affordability a key part of his candidacy, citing higher gas and grocery prices and, inevitably, the rising cost of healthcare and the roughly $1-trillion cut from Medicaid under last year’s Big Sop To Billionaires Bill.
The super-wealthy got tax cuts, Pan told a silver-haired audience at a 55-and-older community in Roseville, while the bill will make healthcare less accessible for millions and undermine both Medicare and Social Security. Kiley supported the legislation, the centerpiece of Trump’s second term. As a doctor and state lawmaker, Pan said, he worked to expand healthcare and address the needs of his community.
“We don’t pass laws to make lives harder,” Pan said. “That’s what he’s done.”
Stepping in for a complacent Congress, Democratic attorneys general are ready to fight efforts to undermine or overturn the Nov. 3 election. “We need to stay vigilant,” says Colorado’s Phil Weiser.
Later, at a forum on Black maternal health, Pan said Trump’s attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion programs and the so-called war on woke ignores glaring disparities in the treatment of Black women versus other patients. “The data is there,” said Pan, speaking before a banner decorated with purple butterflies and the proclamation, “Black Mothers Matter.”
“The facts are there,” Pan went on. “It’s a very, very real problem and it needs to be addressed and it needs to be solved.”
He brought up, somewhat sheepishly, his campaign.
“That’s why I’m running,” Pan said, to “have another person in Congress ... who’s going to tell the administration we are not going to bury DEI. We’re not going to bury disparities. These are real problems.”
As is the assault on science, the undermining of research and the promotion of nutty nostrums by those at the highest levels of the federal government.
Hopefully, the midterm election will begin the healing process.

Mexican cartels are building luxury fleets by stealing U.S. rental cars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Operatives with the Jalisco cartel and other Mexican criminal organizations are increasingly renting U.S. trucks and cars and then driving them across the border.
- The thefts often happen in border states, with California the top target.
- Models popular among the cartels include Cadillac Escalades and BMW SUVs. Rugged trucks, such as Chevy Suburbans and Ford Raptors, are sometimes converted into mutant-tanks, outfitted with ballistic-proof steel plating, firing ports and gun mounts.
MEXICO CITY — Mexican cartels are stealing cars and trucks from U.S. rental agencies at an alarming rate, spiriting thousands of vehicles across the border each year to keep top capos in the latest model BMWs and Cadillacs.
Law enforcement agencies and companies charged with trying to recover stolen vehicles say that while much of the thefts occur in border states, cartel operatives have stolen vehicles from as far away as New York, Chicago and Miami. But California remains the top target.
Each year, about 2,000 vehicles stolen from California end up in Mexico, according to the California Highway Patrol. LAPD Sgt. Juvey Mejia, a member of the Task Force for Regional Auto Theft Prevention, said the cartels love heavy-duty pickup trucks and Jeeps.
“Anything that can drive through tough terrain to get away from Border Patrol so they can move dope,” Mejia said.
Along with Chevy Suburbans, Ford Raptors and Toyota pickups, the vehicles of choice include Cadillac Escalades and BMW SUVs, according to people whose job is to recover them. To battle rival cartels or authorities, criminal groups sometimes convert the trucks into mutant tanks, adding heavy ballistic-proof steel plating, firing ports and gun mounts.
The thefts don’t require much stealth: vehicles are rented in the U.S. by cartel operatives and then driven across the border. The exact number of vehicles is unknown.
California sees significant theft, in part, because of its restrictive privacy laws on GPS tracking of rental vehicles, according to Sharky Laguana, owner of Bandago Van Rentals based in San Francisco.
Unlike other states, California requires that rental agencies wait to turn on GPS tracking until the vehicle return deadline has passed and the renter has been contacted by the company. By then, most stolen vehicles are deep in Mexican territory.
“California allows criminals to take advantage of the fact that we are not allowed to see where the vehicle is until it’s too late,” Laguana said. The American Car Rental Assn., a trade group, said in a statement that California laws make it harder to recover vehicles.
“Members are reporting a sharp increase in rental vehicle theft from California into Mexico, where California law uniquely restricts rental fleet operators from accessing technology to protect and recover their assets,” the association said in a statement. “The result is millions of dollars in annual theft-related costs.”
Early this year, criminal groups stole 10 new Ram pickup trucks from Oakland, Los Angeles and Las Vegas airports, according to private investigators. The trucks ended up in Jalisco state in regions controlled by the violent Jalisco New Generation Cartel.
The private investigators recovered one truck with help from the Mexican army. Security forces also seized a cache of Browning and Barrett .50-caliber weapons.
In another haul this year, thieves stole six 2026 model Jeep Wranglers from Oakland and Las Vegas. Four have been recovered so far. Private investigators believe the vehicles were destined for the Sinaloa Cartel.
The same investigators received requests last week to recover a dozen Ram trucks tracked to Sinaloa and seven more in Durango state.
“For the cartel, it is the cheapest way for them to do business,” said Kevin Carter, owner of Collateral Consultants, a rental car recovery company in Texas. “There’s no sense in them buying a car when they could rent one for a few hundred bucks, and it’s theirs forever.”
Along with California, Texas and Arizona are the other top targets for Mexican criminal groups.
One tactic involves cartels hiring people in the U.S. via social media to rent a vehicle for five days, get the damage waiver that includes covering the car if it is stolen, and then leave the keys in the vehicle still parked in the rental parking lot. An operative arrives, gets in the car and drives it south to Mexico.
In other cases, thieves will rent the vehicle online or at a kiosk using a stolen identity, said Mejia, the LAPD officer. Since the pandemic, it’s not unusual for people to wear protective masks, so the renter will wear a mask to hide their identity from the kiosk camera. “They know it won’t be traced back to them,” Mejia said.
The scheme, known as huachicol fiscal, is the second-largest source of revenue for cartels, after drug trafficking.
The process for reporting a stolen rental vehicle varies from state to state, but it is often tedious. It can take three days after the vehicle has gone missing for a company to prepare a demand letter to the renter seeking return of the vehicle. Such notification is required before a vehicle can be reported stolen, and it can take another two days to send the letter by certified mail.
Depending on the state, a company might have to wait up to nine days to report the theft to police. Only then can it appear on the FBI-managed U.S. National Crime Incident Database, where stolen vehicles are reported.
More days will pass before the VIN number is registered in Mexico’s stolen vehicle database. If the car or truck was rented in one state, set to return in another state and crossed into Mexico via a third, the coordination required between three state law enforcement agencies can make timely recovery of the vehicle even more complicated.
Many vehicles are never registered in the U.S. stolen car database. Carter, from Collateral Consultants, said that of the approximately 1 million cases he has seen in his 15 years recovering rental vehicles in the U.S. and elsewhere, fewer than half made it into the U.S. database.
A vehicle is not officially considered stolen until it appears in the registry. Large rental agencies often don’t bother recovering vehicles that disappear across the border, and consider the loss the cost of doing business, Carter said.
“It’s a calculated risk to most of the big companies,” he said.
While insurance companies insure rental agencies against vehicle damage, they do not cover theft, according to Luguana of Bandago Van Rentals. Most agencies are self-insured, meaning the loss of a vehicle cuts into their bottom line, he said.
Though sometimes the target is a single vehicle, authorities have also uncovered larger theft operations.
In 2024, the Colorado attorney general’s office indicted 17 people associated with the Sinaloa Cartel, accusing them of stealing 190 new Ford F150s and luxury suburbans near the Denver airport. The cartel operatives drove the stolen vehicles, valued at nearly $10 million, to Mexico, according to court documents, and exchanged them for cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine.
In the Texas border city of Laredo, Deputy Police Chief Timothy Tubbs said he has seen a 50% increase in the theft of rental vehicles — about 10 a month.
“They have seen how easy it is to steal a rental car, and the process it takes to report it,” Tubbs said of criminal groups. And the vehicles are supporting drug trafficking into the U.S., he said. “These stolen vehicles empower the cartels,” Tubbs said. “It is another tool for them to continue their smuggling and continue their violence.”
Once the vehicles are in Mexico, operatives approach corrupt Mexican officials and change out the U.S. license plates for Mexican plates and register the vehicles on Mexico’s online car registry platform, according to car recovery experts.
Authorities install a chip that is scanned by machines along federal highways. The chips are supposed to flag stolen cars and trucks, but because the new plates are valid, the vehicles are never listed as stolen.
In the United States, stolen vehicles are far more likely to be identified, experts said, for a variety of reasons — a routine maintenance check or a scan by a highway license plate camera could trigger an alert. But once a stolen car arrives in Mexico, it essentially vanishes.
“It crosses that border, it is a brand-new car,” Carter said.
Cartels steal more cars and trucks when turf wars break out because they require more resources, one U.S. law enforcement official said. And in recent years, cartels have increasingly splintered as leaders have been arrested.
Working for the sons of cartel leader ‘El Chapo,’ a pilot known as Jando rose from drug smuggler to become the commander of the Sinaloa cartel’s air force.
One of the more dramatic examples is the Sinaloa cartel, founded by the now imprisoned Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán. His sons, known as Los Chapitos, are fighting a rival faction for control of the criminal group.
The ruthless Jalisco cartel has fought to expand its territory to Michoacán and Chiapas states, warring with groups from Baja California and fighting wars on multiple fronts as it seeks to expand its presence.
Though many stolen vehicles disappear, some are recovered. In Guerrero state last November, the Mexican army seized a Toyota TRD Pro and other vehicles loaded with high-caliber weapons and nearly half a ton of meth.
According to sources familiar with another recovery, in August a member of the Jalisco New Generation cartel went to the border city of Mexicali to pick up a tractor trailer with a 2026 Cadillac Escalade and a late-model Ram hidden inside, apparently to evade detection system until they could be outfitted with Mexican plates.
But private investigators hired to recover the Cadillac began tracking it. They asked not to identify their tracking methods to avoid tipping off criminals. The investigators notified the Mexican army, providing the license plate number.
Their tracking method allowed them to see the Cadillac was on the move, passing through toll booths and military checkpoints, but without setting off alarms. At one checkpoint, National Guard soldiers opened the trailer and, seeing a wall of hay bales, let it pass.
At the next checkpoint, however, soldiers pulled back the bales to reveal the Cadillac and the Ram. The driver said he was to be paid nearly $1,500 and admitted the cars were bound for drug lords.
Fisher is a special correspondent. This article was co-published with Puente News Collaborative, a bilingual nonprofit newsroom. Reporting for this article was supported with a grant by the Fund for Investigative Journalism.
