With Senate majority up for grabs, candidates fight for 'kingmaker' voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

With Senate majority up for grabs, candidates fight for ‘kingmaker’ voters
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Analysts predict that Democrats are on track for the House majority. Senate control is a toss-up.
- A Gallup poll found that 45% of American adults identify as political independents, a record high.
WASHINGTON — With the midterm elections just over three weeks away, the fight for control of the U.S. Senate is intensifying in battleground states, as Democrats push into red regions and Republicans pour money into key contests.
Campaigns are entering a crucial stretch for persuading the independent voters who will probably determine outcomes in swing races. Nearly all of the most competitive Senate races are in states with significant swaths of people unaffiliated with either major party — the “kingmakers” in these high-stakes midterms, said Jeremy Gruber, an independent-voting expert.
“Independent voters are going to be deciding this election in every respect,” said Gruber, senior vice president of Open Primaries, an organization that advocates for states to open primary elections to unaffiliated voters.
The urgency around courting nonaligned voters has been on display at recent debates, in ads flooding the airwaves and in the campaign money pouring into key states. For Republicans, it has become an effort to put distance between themselves and President Trump; for Democrats, it’s often a rhetorical shift toward the center and away from the far left.
In Iowa, Republican Ashley Hinson used a Wednesday night debate to emphasize her willingness to break with Trump. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is circulating a video in which he describes himself as both liberal and conservative. In Alaska, a GOP-backed ad blitz launched last week aims to persuade voters that Democrat Mary Peltola isn’t independent-minded.
Though many unaffiliated voters have made up their minds, those who remain undecided will begin making decisions soon, as mail ballots go out and early voting begins in some states.
“For Republicans who are running behind and are looking at a potentially devastating midterm election performance, what they really need to do is target the independents who lean Republican,” said Karen Kedrowski, an Iowa State University political scientist. “For Democrats in some place like Iowa ... what they need to do is make it seem safe [to independents] to vote for a Democratic candidate.”
Reflecting the complex electoral balance, most Republicans have attempted to separate themselves without naming any firm difference with the president.
Unaffiliated constituents have long been key to victory in swing states, particularly where races are traditionally decided by small margins. They have been viewed as particularly persuadable this year, as public dissatisfaction with Trump’s economic policies puts the votes of swing voters who backed him in 2024 up for grabs.
Forecasters predict that Democrats are on track for the House majority and could hold a majority of gubernatorial seats for the first time since 2010. Though Senate control remains a toss-up, Democrats’ chances are viewed by forecasters to have significantly improved since the summer.
A set of New York Times/Siena polls reported last week showed Democratic candidates for the Senate ahead in Texas, Michigan, Alaska and Ohio and neck-and-neck in Kansas and Iowa — all states Trump carried in 2024. Republicans, meanwhile, are feeling increasingly bullish about their chances in Maine, New Hampshire and Minnesota, all states that went blue in the last presidential election.
Republicans hold a significant fundraising advantage, however, and party donors are pouring money into key races, hoping the spending can cut into the Democrats’ edge. By September’s end, GOP advertisers had more than doubled their spending compared with August, outstripping Democrats, according to tracker AdImpact. Among the nine Senate races considered the tightest by forecasters, Republicans have outspent Democrats in all, AdImpact reported.
But on Friday, the Cook Political Report, a leading election forecaster, moved 18 House races in Democrats’ direction, saying that heavy ad spending by Republicans has not begun to move the needle in their favor.
Democrats view themselves as in their “strongest position yet” to win the majority, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said in a statement last week.
“In this final stretch of the election, Democrats will continue to vigorously campaign and fight for every vote across the expanded map,” Gillibrand said.
Republicans are confident about their ability to persuade voters in key states, said Bernadette Breslin, a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee.
“Republicans will defend the Senate majority across key battlegrounds that have trended reliably red,” Breslin said, “with candidates like Mike Rogers [in Michigan] and Roger Marshall [in Kansas] winning over independents by exposing their Democratic opponents’ radical, unaffordable agendas.”
Along with the decisions of independent and swing voters, the midterm outcomes could also hinge on the level of turnout within each party, analysts say. If a portion of the party faithful stay home in a given place — for instance, disillusioned conservatives in Kansas or frustrated Black Democrats in Michigan — that could swing individual races, analysts said.
The number of independent voters reached a record high this year, with 45% of American adults identifying as political independents in Gallup polling. Equal shares identified as Republicans and Democrats, 27% for each party. The trend is partly driven by majorities of millennial and Gen Z voters choosing to be unaffiliated with either party, according to Gallup research.
Such voters make up a majority in Alaska and between 30% and 40% of all registered voters in Maine, Iowa, New Hampshire, North Carolina and Ohio. They account for about 29% in Kansas and about 16% in Texas and Michigan, according to state data compiled by the Independent Voter Project.
Across recent polls, independent voters have favored Democrats and expressed dissatisfaction with Trump. In a late September poll from Emerson College Polling, 66% of independents said Trump has done worse than expected during his second term in office.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico led Republican Ken Paxton among independents by 32 points in a September poll by Texas Public Opinion Research. The Democratic candidate in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, led Republican Sen. Jon Husted by 27 points among independents in a CNN poll released Thursday.
In Kansas, where the Senate race has become unexpectedly close amid economic-driven anger with Trump, disapproval of the president’s performance among independents appears to be rubbing off on incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, the Republican seeking reelection.
Fifty-two percent felt unfavorably toward Marshall and 62% disapproved of Trump’s performance, according to a recent Emerson College/Nexstar poll.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House on Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn’t be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
In those battleground red states, that creates a tough fight for both parties, analysts said. With control of the Senate hanging in the balance, candidates are duking it out in fundraising and on the campaign trail to win every last vote.
“Both campaigns are raking in ridiculous amounts of money ... and they’re spending every penny because [they] have to,” said Wichita State University political science professor Alexandra Middlewood, referring to the Kansas Senate race. “We see that they’re really going to have to fight it out all the way to the end.”
Debates are another tool for candidates to reach independent voters, said Corwin Smidt, a political science professor at Michigan State University.
In Michigan, where the Senate candidates sparred in their first debate Thursday evening, Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee, has distanced himself from Trump twice in recent weeks, first calling for an end to the war in Iran and then releasing an ad last week denouncing the tariffs against Canada. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, meanwhile, announced a rally with former President Obama, an appeal to mainstream voters.
“They’ve got to try to both win over people who have been paying attention, but also introduce themselves to the ones who haven’t been paying attention,” Smidt said.
Winning unaffiliated voters can require a tightrope walk for candidates who are faced with the dual tasks of appealing to their party base while persuading independent constituents.
In the final stretch of the campaign, candidates seeking independent votes should telegraph a willingness to admit their party’s flaws and an understanding that voters are turned off by partisan rhetoric, said Chad Peace, legal strategist at the Independent Voter Project, which advocates for open primaries.
“They have to communicate to those folks and try to meet them where they’re at,” Peace said. “[Independents] want the campaigns of persuasion, they don’t want to hear you tell me how bad the other candidate is.”
And, Gruber said, they want to be engaged with, not ignored.
“Independent voters,” he said, “are going to be responding to those candidates and parties that actually talk to them.”

NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has registered 20 FIRs in connection with the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)-led protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, officials told news agency PTI on Sunday.The cases include charges of assaulting police personnel and obstructing public servants from discharging their duties. The protest, which called for Kumar's resignation, was met with a massive security deployment and widespread detentions across the national capital on Saturday. More than 7,000 people, including opposition leaders and activists, were detained as police erected barricades and deployed thousands of personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching Jantar Mantar. Several incidents of stone-throwing were reported, leaving more than 15 police personnel injured, including Deputy Commissioner of Police (South) Anant Mittal.
Supreme Court steps in over restrictions
Amid the fallout, the Supreme Court on Sunday directed authorities to ensure that people gathering peacefully are not illegally detained and that Delhi Metro services operate normally, subject to law and order conditions.
The bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also directed that internet services remain undisturbed and that lawyers and journalists not be obstructed from performing their professional duties.The court issued a notice to the Centre while hearing a plea seeking contempt proceedings over alleged violations of its directions concerning restrictions on metro and train services during the protest. It also ordered authorities to remove a notice board outside the Supreme Court premises announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which restricts assemblies of five or more people.
Meanwhile, CJP activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka accused the administration of imposing excessive restrictions to suppress what they described as a youth-led movement."The situation across the country right now mirrors an open Emergency. Such repressive conditions have not been witnessed since the dictatorial regime of 1975," Das said, alleging that Delhi had been turned into a "cantonment".He also criticised the closure of metro stations, suspension of train services and shutdown of markets, claiming the restrictions were inconveniencing ordinary citizens and turning public sentiment against the protest.Ranka separately condemned the police's handling of activist Abhijeet Dipke, alleging that personnel showed insensitivity while informing him of his grandmother's death.

Thousands of people were detained across New Delhi on Saturday as Indian authorities mounted a sweeping security operation to stop a protest by the youth-led “cockroach” movement demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief.
Police fanned out across India’s capital to block access to Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site, stopping buses and cars at checkpoints, erecting barricades and deploying antiriot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers along key routes.
Many demonstrators were intercepted long before they reached central New Delhi, chased away or dragged into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centres. Several movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained en route, effectively halting the rally before it began.
Authorities said they had denied permission for the gathering because the request was submitted late and insisted the measures were necessary to maintain order. Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, dismissed the protesters as “anarchic elements” staging a “flop show”.
Despite the clampdown, some protesters broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and the Election Commission of India (ECI), before being detained. “We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force,” said college student Tanya Negi, who travelled from Mumbai. “Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?”
The movement led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) emerged online in May and gained prominence through protests over exam paper leaks that led to the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July.
Its latest campaign targets the ECI’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which opposition parties say has already removed more than 130 million names from voter rolls and disenfranchised supporters.
The ECI and the government deny any political bias, but critics say the crackdown highlights shrinking space for dissent as key state polls approach.

Ukraine Ready to Halt Refinery Strikes for Energy Truce, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:54:00 UTC
18:54:00 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 11, that Ukraine is prepared to halt long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries if Russia ceases attacks against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
In a statement on Facebook reviewing weekly Russian aerial bombardments, Zelensky said halting attacks on power and utility networks is achievable immediately, but asserted that Moscow remains unwilling to de-escalate.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is feasible to stop strikes on energy today, but [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do this,” Zelensky stated.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia ceases strikes against our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be mutual and with real guarantees.”
Zelensky emphasized that Russia bears sole responsibility for the war in Europe, noting that diplomatic engagements with European leaders are scheduled throughout Sunday to coordinate additional defense packages, primarily surface-to-air defense systems and ammunition for combat aviation.
Weekly strike toll and escalating civilian casualties
Zelensky highlighted the operational scale of Russian standoff strikes over the preceding seven days, reporting that Russian forces launched approximately 1,450 guided aerial bombs (KABs), 75 missiles of various types, and more than 1,640 strike drones against Ukrainian territory.
According to the president, roughly 60 percent of the unmanned aerial vehicles deployed during the weekly barrages were high-speed, turbojet-powered variants engineered to challenge low-altitude air defense interception networks.
Zaporizhzhia Bombing Death Toll Reaches 20 as Rescue Ends
The weekly barrage produced casualties and structural destruction across multiple provinces.
Zelensky confirmed that search and rescue operations in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia concluded on Sunday morning following a Russian guided bomb strike on a residential apartment building, with the final death toll rising to 23, including four children.
In the Kharkiv region, Russian munitions struck a healthcare facility on Saturday, while overnight attacks engaged municipal civilian infrastructure, residential housing, and regional utility grids.
“I am grateful to all our emergency services, who are always alongside our people and resolving consequences after Russian strikes,” Zelensky said.
Petrochemical targeting and the energy armistice framework
Zelensky’s proposal for a reciprocal cessation of energy attacks comes amid an intensified Ukrainian interdiction campaign directed against downstream petrochemical logistics across the Russian Federation.
Overnight into Saturday, Oct. 10, Ukrainian Defense Forces conducted a repeat strike against the Samara linear production and dispatching station (LVDS) near Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region.
The critical petrochemical junction blends petroleum streams to formulate standardized export-grade Urals crude while supplying refined petroleum products to the Russian armed forces.
The attack followed an earlier precision strike on Oct. 7 that destroyed four large-capacity RVS-50000 crude oil storage reservoirs at the facility.
The interdiction of refining and transshipment nodes forms part of a wider asymmetric campaign that has also engaged deep logistical facilities, including the Yug Rusi oil terminal in Rostov-on-Don and multiple corporate data centers in Vladimir, Kaluga, and Ryazan regions.
The issue of refinery strikes has emerged as a central point of friction between Kyiv and Washington.
US officials have urged Ukraine to unilaterally halt drone strikes on Russian refining capacity to mitigate pressure on international fuel benchmarks, a request that coincided with a controversial bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin to permit Russian diesel exports onto global markets.
Ukrainian officials have consistently rejected calls for unilateral restraint, arguing that degrading Russian refining infrastructure directly restricts fuel supplies to frontline Russian military units and diminishes state revenues supporting Moscow’s war effort.
Zelensky reiterated that a suspension of deep interdiction operations can occur only within the framework of an enforceable, bilateral agreement that shields Ukraine’s domestic power and heating grid ahead of the winter season.

US Proposes Economic Incentives to Russia for Limited Truce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

The administration of US President Donald Trump has proposed several lucrative economic incentives to Russia to encourage Moscow to accept a limited ceasefire with Ukraine covering energy infrastructure or maritime corridors.
According to The New York Times, citing officials familiar with the discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity, American negotiators presented three primary commercial and financial incentives designed to induce the Kremlin into agreeing to a partial armistice ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The prospective economic package was framed by US representatives as an upfront inducement to secure a limited suspension of hostilities rather than a downstream reward following the conclusion of an agreement.
Asset unfreezing, Lukoil buyout, and Belarusian potash
The first incentive involves unlocking billions of dollars in Russian sovereign state assets currently frozen across Western jurisdictions under international sanctions.
According to officials, the proposal revives discussions regarding the release of up to $100 billion in immobilized Russian reserves.
A second incentive centers on reviving a transaction authorizing the sale of foreign assets belonging to Russian oil producer Lukoil. The multibillion-dollar deal would involve an international consortium of Middle Eastern investors, including entities with prior commercial ties to US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Third, Witkoff and Kushner revived an offer that would grant sanctions relief allowing Belarus, Moscow’s primary regional ally, to resume global exports of potash.
Trump: Putin Wants Ukraine Deal, Praises Russian Oil Supplies
Ukrainian negotiators refrained from issuing a categorical rejection of the proposals during bilateral consultations, but insisted on binding safeguards to mitigate security risks.
According to sources briefed on the talks, Kyiv demanded reciprocal dollar-for-dollar financial releases from frozen assets to support Ukrainian state defense and reconstruction, alongside ironclad guarantees of expedited military assistance should Russian forces breach any prospective truce.
Diplomatic impasse and Kremlin maximalism
The revelation of the proposed economic concessions follows a telephone consultation on Friday, Oct. 9, between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, after which Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov stated that Putin rejected resuming formal peace talks and reaffirmed Moscow’s intent to sustain military operations until all objectives are met.
Ushakov claimed that Putin told Trump that Russian forces hold the operational initiative along the front line and characterized Ukrainian resistance as futile.
The economic proposals also coincide with high-level multilateral discussions hosted by the US in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9, which brought together Witkoff, Ukrainian negotiators, and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO.
The six-hour session concluded without a breakthrough, as European and Ukrainian officials questioned Moscow’s willingness to de-escalate.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that unilateral economic accommodations to Moscow project Western weakness, asserting that the Kremlin interprets concessions as appeasement rather than an incentive to negotiate.
Sybiha stressed that only a mutually enforced, verifiable ceasefire negotiated from a position of deterrence can sustainably de-escalate hostilities and stabilize regional energy markets.

At least 15 children were among 109 migrants who died while 116 others went missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti on Oct. 8, a U.N. agency said Sunday.
Survivors said the vessel, carrying 350 people from Djibouti to Yemen, capsized north of Obock, Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said in a statement.

An attempt was made to smuggle more than 650 kg of kratom into Ukraine — what kind of substance it is and how dangerous it is
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

12:49:32 EEST
18:49:32 KST

An attempt was made to smuggle more than 650 kg of kratom into Ukraine — what kind of substance it is and how dangerous it is
Kyiv • UNN
At the Tysa checkpoint, border guards found 652.8 kg of a substance resembling kratom. The briquettes were hidden in compartments of a minibus.
At the border with Hungary, Ukrainian border guards discovered more than 650 kilograms of a substance resembling the kratom plant, which is used as a drug, in a minibus. This was reported by UNN, citing the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine.
The offenders concealed the briquettes containing the substance in compartments of the vehicle.
Details
The find was discovered at the Tysa checkpoint. During an inspection of the minibus, border guards from the Chop detachment, together with operatives, found concealed briquettes containing a plant-based substance resembling kratom. The cargo was hidden in several places: above the driver's seat and behind the passenger seats. The total weight of the briquettes, including the packaging, was 652.8 kilograms.
The border guards seized the substance, as well as the minibus, whose value exceeds UAH 255,000. Law enforcement officers were notified of the find.
For reference
Kratom is a tropical plant that grows mainly in Southeast Asia, particularly in Thailand, Indonesia, and Malaysia. Its leaves contain psychoactive substances that affect the nervous system.
In small doses, it can act as a stimulant, increasing alertness and activity. In larger doses, it can cause relaxation, drowsiness, and reduced pain sensations. Regular use can lead to dependence.
Side effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, and dizziness. In severe cases, seizures, liver damage, and respiratory depression are possible.
On November 15, 2024, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine adopted Resolution No. 1306, adding kratom leaves, mitragynine, and 7-hydroxymitragynine to the list of narcotic substances whose circulation is restricted. Therefore, the illegal transportation or smuggling of this substance may constitute grounds for criminal liability.
Earlier
In March this year, law enforcement officers in Zaporizhzhia exposed an organized group that supplied the narcotic kratom disguised as matcha tea. During the special operation, more than one ton of the prohibited substance worth over UAH 10 million was seized.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Military Police Command plans to launch an experimental program in which personnel would use 3D printers to produce drone airframes and components, with personnel from its drone company handling maintenance.
The command has budgeted funds to procure mobile, containerized 3D-printing equipment to establish a mobile production line that can be rapidly replicated at scale, Liberty Times reported. This will bolster the command’s autonomy in logistics and maintenance.
The command's current force-development priorities center on integrated reconnaissance and strike capabilities and multilayered defense.
Under plans drawn up by the defense ministry, new capabilities for defending the Bo'ai Special Zone will include mobile anti-drone systems to neutralize enemy drones, per Liberty Times. The military has also allocated funding to acquire and deploy reconnaissance drones and attack loitering munitions.
These capabilities allow military police units to conduct street-level surveillance in urban combat without exposing personnel and potentially launch precision strikes against enemy special operations forces, Liberty Times said.
The command seeks to double its force from 5,600 personnel to 11,000. It has also established air defense and drone companies within its garrison units this year.

Why are today’s children so helpless? Look at their parents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:37:47 UTC
18:37:47 KST

Why are today’s children so helpless? Look at their parents
Recently, a friend went to buy trainers for her 14-year-old and was surprised to discover that most of the suitable styles had Velcro fastenings. When she asked about proper laces, the sales assistant simply shrugged and said teenagers increasingly struggle to tie them.
We laughed and then we both went rather quiet because I remembered primary school teachers talking about first-graders who can’t dress themselves, fasten buttons, pack their things, tie their shoelaces or sometimes even manage a trip to the toilet without an adult.
And it doesn’t end with primary school as I’ve seen parents tie the shoelaces of perfectly capable 12- and 13-year-olds, carry their rucksacks and generally treat them like particularly honored guests.
I would love to adopt the traditional middle-aged complaint: “At their age, we were already…” but, unfortunately, that won’t work, because I’m one of those mothers myself.
In fifth grade, I took the tram to school alone and there was no mobile phone and certainly no parents’ group chat, so I got on the tram, travelled to school and came home. Somehow, I survived.
Now I have a child of my own, and repeating that educational experiment seems considerably more frightening. Perhaps that contradiction explains much of what’s happened to us. We want our children to become independent, but preferably in a safe environment, under CCTV surveillance, with geolocation switched on and an adult never too far away.
A British survey of nearly 2,000 families found that children today are allowed to play outside unsupervised at an average age of 10.8. Their parents had been allowed to do so at about 9.7, thus more than half of parents said they gave their children such freedom later than they themselves had received it.
Why have we become like this? After all, the 1990s can hardly be remembered as a wonderfully safe and sheltered period, yet children spent hours outside, cycled to school, went to the shops and somehow found their way home without the equivalent of an electronic ankle bracelet.
Perhaps our parents were no less worried, but they simply lacked the technology to worry about us in real time.
They couldn’t open a map and discover that their child had been standing behind the neighboring house for seven suspicious minutes instead of outside the school. A child went out to play and, for a few hours, really did disappear from the family’s field of vision.
Today, every horrific incident involving a child, even one happening a thousand kilometers away, can appear on our phones within minutes, so we know far more about these cases than our parents ever could and not necessarily because terrible things happen more often, but because now we hear about almost all of them.
Modern overprotectiveness is therefore partly an expression of adult anxiety as we want to control a world that constantly reminds us how little control we really have and our own child becomes the most obvious place to start.
Often, when we overprotect children, we are reassuring ourselves rather than them, so I feel calmer if I take my child somewhere myself, write to the teacher, check the schoolbag and know exactly where he is.
The anxiety subsides, and the brain learns a simple lesson, that if you’re worried, you should exercise more control. That creates a vicious circle: the more we worry, the less freedom the child receives. The less freedom they have, the fewer opportunities they get to demonstrate, both to themselves and to us “I can do this.”
Because we rarely see them managing alone, letting go becomes even more frightening.
Independence doesn’t suddenly arrive on an 18th birthday. It’s built through hundreds of tiny rehearsals, such as fastening your own jacket, asking a shop assistant for help, packing your schoolbag and, occasionally, forgetting an exercise book – it means walking to a friend’s house alone, encountering some minor problem and discovering that you can solve it.
How many of these little rehearsals do we cancel simply because doing things ourselves is quicker and less stressful? Well, I did exactly that with my first son, I was always rushing somewhere, so it was quicker to tie his laces, pack his things, find whatever he had lost or write to his teacher myself because at the time, this made life easier for everybody.
A few years later, when he actually needed to start doing these things himself, it was suddenly very difficult and research has repeatedly found an association between overprotective parenting and symptoms of anxiety and depression among adolescents and young adults. That doesn’t mean overprotection automatically causes psychological problems, but the likely mechanism isn’t difficult to understand, given if an adult always intervenes before a child has the chance to cope, the child gets fewer opportunities to develop a sense of competence.
Seen that way, the problem becomes considerably more serious than an inability to tie shoelaces.
Of course, civilization will survive Velcro, but the real problem begins when, confronted with any ordinary difficulty, a child’s first thought is ‘where is the adult who is going to sort this out for me?’
This isn’t because today’s children are uniquely lazy or incapable. For years, we have been teaching them something through our actions: the world is dangerous and complicated; you can’t handle it yet; give it to Mum, and she will sort it out and we do this out of love.
We want to protect them from disappointment, lateness, forgotten clothes, poor grades, unpleasant shop assistants, dangerous roads and all the other things that make up a life in which not everything works perfectly on the first attempt.
Then the child grows older and we are astonished. Why is he afraid to make decisions? Why can’t he prepare his own breakfast? Why doesn’t he know how to pack his schoolbag?
Surely there must be some middle ground between the old approach of “here’s your key, heat up your own lunch” and accompanying a healthy teenager practically as far as the changing room.
But we will never find it unless we give children the right to make mistakes, and that means patience. We have to wait while a child struggles with a zipper rather than doing it ourselves and we have to remain quietly at home instead of racing to school with the exercise book they forgot.
I tell myself this every day, that perhaps a parent’s job isn’t to make a child’s road completely smooth, but gradually to teach them how to walk along a bumpy one.
Otherwise, one day we may discover that we protected our children brilliantly from all of life’s shoelaces, only to find that sooner or later they’ll still have to learn how to tie them themselves.

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Biggest Oil Storage Hub in Europe Again, Leaving Four Giant Tanks Destroyed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:37:04 UTC
18:37:04 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russia’s Biggest Oil Storage Hub in Europe Again, Leaving Four Giant Tanks Destroyed
Ukrainian forces struck Russia’s largest oil storage facility in Europe once again overnight on October 10, continuing a series of retaliatory attacks on the Samara oil hub, where four massive storage tanks were destroyed in an earlier strike.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff on October 10, the latest operation targeted the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station near the settlement of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region. The extent of damage from the new attack is still being assessed.
The General Staff also confirmed that a previous strike on October 7 destroyed four RVS-50000 oil storage tanks and triggered a large fire at the facility. Each tank is designed to hold approximately 50,000 cubic meters of oil.
The Samara facility serves as a major collection, storage, and blending hub for Russian crude oil. It receives supplies through pipelines from Tatarstan, Western Siberia, and other oil-producing regions across Russia.
At the station, crude oil with varying sulfur concentrations is blended to produce Urals, one of Russia’s main export oil grades. The facility also supports the logistical needs of the Russian military, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.
The latest strike came just hours after US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Vladimir Putin on October 9 to allow millions of tons of Russian diesel onto US and global markets, easing sanctions on Russian energy exports.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the decision, calling it “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” according to Reuters on October 9. He emphasized that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities are a response to Moscow’s continued attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

Pakistan: President puts Khan stronghold province under emergency rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:37:00 UTC
18:37:00 KST

Pakistan: Khan stronghold province put under emergency rule
October 11, 2026
Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday announced that the northwestern Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule, effectively removing power from former Prime Minster Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
The imposition of emergency rule comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.
Current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif proposed the move, which Zardari signed into order on Sunday.
The suspension of regional government was justified under constitutional articles that allow the central government to confront security threats and give it sweeping powers in emergency situations.
Sharif's government claims regional authorities have not done enough to curb Islamist violence in the province.
Why is Pakistan's government taking control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?
Last Sunday, thousands of Khan's supporters began to make their way from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.
Organizers had declared their intent to rally hundreds of thousands more along the way in hopes of bringing about Khan's release from prison.
Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence in Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.
Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, was ousted from office in April 2022 after losing a no-confidence vote.
He has been in prison since August 2023.
Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023. Khan rejects the charges as a politically motivated plot to keep him away from power. He remains a popular political figure in Pakistan.
Khan's supporters claim that the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.
Pakistan has seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks.
The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

Inside Ukraine's world of naive art — and the Gunia aesthetic it inspired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:35:30 UTC
18:35:30 KST

A cat's fur for a brush, crushed petals for paint, and an eye for beauty — as it turns out, that's all some Ukrainian artists needed to make some of the most distinctive paintings of the 20th century.
"Naive My Love," a new coffee table book by French publisher Assouline in collaboration with Ukrainian fashion and design brand Gunia Project, celebrates the bold colors, imaginative motifs, and deeply personal visual language of Ukrainian naive and folk art.
The book's visuals stand on their own, but they are accompanied by texts that trace the origins of naive and folk art, along with short biographies of about 40 self-taught Ukrainian painters and sculptors, featuring examples of their painting, embroidery, carving, and other decorative arts.
While naive and folk art overlap in themes, they differ in motivation and technique — folk art is rooted in communal traditions passed down through generations, while naive art is typically created by self-taught artists expressing a highly personal, individual vision.
As "Naive My Love" points out, these works — created by Ukrainians for their own enjoyment — stood in quiet defiance of socialist realism, the only form of art officially sanctioned in the Soviet Union for those hoping to build a career. Their personal, heartfelt creations offered an alternative to the state-prescribed aesthetic, expressing individuality and resistance through art.
The most famous of all the Ukrainian naive artists is Maria Prymachenko (1909-1997), whose storied life in Kyiv Oblast inspired much of her work: she walked with a cane after contracting polio as a child, survived the Holodomor, raised her son alone after his father died fighting in World War II, and lived through the Chornobyl nuclear disaster.
Her art is most memorable for its saturated colors and fantastical beasts. The book includes paintings such as "The Beast of War," a massive, snarling brown beast that takes up most of the canvas. However, beneath the beast is a red flower hiding in plain sight — a reminder that even when terrible events seem to dominate day-to-day life, beauty still finds a way to exist in the world.
Artist Polina Raiko's (1928-2004) work, which became more widely known through Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, is also featured in the book. At 69, Raiko began painting the walls inside her home in Oleshky to cope with a series of family hardships — the colorful doves and angels that adorned her walls represented her desire for inner peace.
"I was working in my garden, got tired, painted a dove, and rested. It was joyful. It was like I wasn't alone. I looked and looked at it — could I have really done that? No. But I did. I couldn't believe myself. And I was so, so joyful in my soul," Raiko said of her work, as quoted in the book.
The house soon attracted the attention of locals and people from across Ukraine, and it was eventually designated a national heritage site. However, Raiko's one-of-a-kind house was almost completely destroyed in the summer of 2023 after Russia blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant dam, flooding Kherson Oblast and neighboring southern regions.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it almost impossible to evacuate safely.
It was only a matter of time before Gunia, as a brand, released a book about art. As they describe in the book, objects such as a rushnyk — a traditional embroidered cloth that is personalized in every home — can shape and inspire new directions in product development. That's why expeditions are crucial for the brand's designers: they help them better understand and reinterpret Ukrainian folk art, giving age-old traditions a fresh, contemporary twist.

Yemen's Houthis warn passengers not to use Saudi airports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:35:00 UTC

Saudi Arabia: Second strike hits Riyadh airport
Published October 11, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was struck by an "unidentified projectile" for the second time in two days on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
"King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement, adding that it "resulted in injuries, and the assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities are still under way."
Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki also said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available.
The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."
A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.
Sunday's strikes came as Riyadh airport remained closed following an attack on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured over 300 more — the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade.
On Sunday, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed that one of its citizens died after being wounded in Saturday's attack.
"It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today," read a statement posted on social media. "We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased."
Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia
The latest Houthi strikes also came just hours after the rebel group warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports.
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted.
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Why are Saudi airports being targeted?
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks?
The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."
The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.
The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.
The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.
While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.
How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."
Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.
On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."
Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.

‘He was merely a journalist’: Family demands accountability for Palestinian reporter’s death (VIDEO)
The family of Palestinian journalist Muhammad Abdel Aziz al-Najjar, who was killed in an Israeli strike in southern Gaza, has demanded accountability from the Israeli military, accusing it of killing an innocent man whose family depended on him for survival.
Al-Najjar was killed on September 30 in an Israeli drone strike in the Mawasi al-Qarara area, north of Khan Yunis, according to Palestinian media. Local sources said the attack came as Israeli forces continued shelling and firing across Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement with Hamas reached a year earlier.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) admitted to killing al-Najjar, but claimed he was a member of Hamas’ military wing and took part in the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel that sparked the war. An IDF spokesman, cited by Israeli media, accused him of plotting attacks against Israeli troops and civilians and “working to rebuild Hamas’ military capabilities.”
His family’s account, however, differs greatly. In an exclusive interview with RT on Saturday, they described him as a journalist and religious teacher. His father, Abdelaziz, said al-Najjar worked as a field correspondent for Holy Quran Radio and was also a Quran teacher, preacher, and imam at the Ibad al-Rahman Mosque.
“I hold the Israeli army fully responsible for his death… He has done nothing wrong,” his mother, Asmehan, said. She described Muhammad, the eldest son, as the family’s backbone, saying his death has left them without the person they relied on for everything.
His brother, Alaa al-Najjar, said Muhammad held the family together through war and displacement.
“There is a massive void now,” he said. “He was the one who always kept the family united. We have lost a brother so dear that only God knows the depth of that loss.”
Al-Najjar was the 263rd Palestinian media worker killed since Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
International press freedom and human rights groups have condemned Israeli attacks on journalists in Gaza and Lebanon, accusing the military of deliberately targeting media workers and demanding accountability.
In February, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) said Israel was responsible for two-thirds of the record 129 journalists and media workers killed worldwide in 2025.
In March, RT correspondent Steve Sweeney and cameraman Ali Rida Sbeity narrowly survived a missile strike less than 10 meters from their position in southern Lebanon, suffering shrapnel wounds. Israel denies that it deliberately targets journalists, insisting its operations are directed against Hamas and other armed groups.
Al-Najjar’s killing comes amid Israeli strikes and gunfire across Gaza despite last October’s ceasefire, which the Palestinian authorities have accused Israel of violating. The Gaza Health Ministry says at least 1,431 Palestinians have been killed and 5,026 wounded since the agreement, bringing the overall toll since October 2023 to more than 74,000 dead, including at least 21,000 children, and 175,000 wounded.
Al-Najjar’s father told RT the ceasefire has brought more fear than safety: “Since the ceasefire, we have not felt more secure at all. We thought it would bring safety, but rather fear and worry have increased.”

“We always respond in mirror-like fashion,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, following the Sasovo strike. “You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can’t share all the details.”
Russia has struck several Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure facilities over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv, in an apparent effort to disrupt the country’s connectivity and digital commerce.

Eerik-Niiles Kross: The true impact of Trump and Putin's diesel deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

Eerik-Niiles Kross: The true impact of Trump and Putin's diesel deal
The agreement's economic impact will likely be minimal, while its moral and political consequences could be far more lasting and extremely damaging to the U.S. in the long run, writes Eerik-Niiles Kross.
Under an alleged diesel deal reached by phone between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, Russia is expected to supply the global market with an initial 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November, then 1 million metric tons and, later, another 3 million metric tons "if possible." A total of 4.8 million metric tons of diesel has been promised.
At first glance, this seems like a large quantity. However, the actual impact depends on how quickly the fuel can be delivered and how much of it represents genuinely additional supply to the global market.
The U.S. consumes approximately 16 million metric tons of diesel per month, most of it domestically produced. The first promised shipment of 300,000 metric tons therefore represents less than 2 percent of one month's U.S. consumption. The 500,000 metric tons promised for November amounts to about 3 percent.
The entire promised 4.8 million metric tons would equal roughly 30 percent of one month's U.S. consumption, but no deadline has been set for its delivery and much of it may never reach the U.S. at all. If those 4.8 million metric tons were indeed delivered to the U.S. over the course of a year, for example, that would amount to 400,000 metric tons per month or 2.5 percent of U.S. consumption. It is ridiculous to assume that this could actually affect fuel prices in the U.S.
Still less is this a quantity that could fundamentally reshape the global fuel market over the longer term.
Another important consideration is that the diesel promised by Russia may not be — and most likely is not — newly produced fuel. At least some of it has already been produced and is sitting in storage facilities or export pipelines. Bringing this fuel to market could temporarily increase supply. However, if Russia simply sells fuel originally intended for existing customers to new buyers instead, total global supply will not increase at all.
Meanwhile, Trump's main objective in reaching the agreement, at least according to his own statements, is to lower fuel prices. The conclusion must be that Trump either hopes releasing Russian diesel onto the market will have a psychological effect and influence markets, intends to further ease sanctions on Russian oil exports or has simply allowed the Russians to pull the wool over his eyes. All three possibilities are rather depressing.
Agreement far more significant for Putin
Russia produced approximately 85 million metric tons of diesel in 2025, of which around 61 million metric tons was summer-grade diesel. Successful Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have significantly reduced production in 2026. At the same time, the Russians are facing a familiar seasonal problem: Winter always catches Russia by surprise. In winter, northern regions need cold-resistant diesel, but refineries that have been damaged and require repairs are unable to switch production quickly enough, if at all.
As a result, Russia may simultaneously face a surplus of summer-grade diesel and a shortage of winter-grade diesel. The summer-grade fuel must either be exported or stored. Once storage tanks are full, refineries have to cut production, further worsening Russia's fuel supply situation.
Putin therefore stands to gain considerably more from this deal than the relatively insignificant increase in export volumes might suggest. The temporary easing of U.S. sanctions allows Russia to sell fuel that would otherwise occupy storage capacity, leaving nowhere to put newly produced fuel. Refineries can now continue operating, generating additional export revenue.
Whether the Russians can actually deliver the promised quantities is another matter. According to various estimates, Russia exported approximately 27 million to 40 million metric tons of diesel in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026, seaborne exports had fallen to around 190,000 barrels (this may be an optimistic estimate from our perspective and does not appear to be based on complete statistics, but no better figures are currently available) or 26,000 metric tons, per day. That represents an 80 percent decline from the beginning of the year.
Thus, delivering the first 300,000 metric tons should not pose an insurmountable problem, provided sufficient stocks are available. The 500,000 metric tons promised for November is also feasible in principle.
However, exporting the entire promised 4.8 million metric tons at the current rate would take approximately six months. Even that assumes Russia diverts all its existing export volumes to the U.S. to fulfill the agreement. If Russia wanted to deliver those quantities in two months, for example, exports would have to roughly triple from their current level. That should be impossible, at least without restoring refinery capacity, particularly assuming Ukrainian attacks continue.
Trump can, of course, announce that he has brought millions of metric tons of additional fuel onto the global market and taken steps to lower prices. As we saw, his post to that effect on Friday drove oil prices down by more than 4 percent.
An actual, sustained decline in prices, however, requires that the promised fuel actually reach the market and that the shipments represent additional global supply rather than simply a redirection of existing exports — for example, diesel going to the U.S. instead of Brazil. A one-off shipment could affect prices for days, perhaps weeks, but it certainly would not resolve a longer-term shortage. Ultimately, I do not see the price decline Trump is hoping for materializing either in the U.S. or on the global market.
The most important effect of the agreement is political and psychological
The biggest weakness of the diesel deal is its striking asymmetry. As usual, the Russians have already gotten what they wanted, while the U.S. has received promises that are unlikely to be fulfilled. So far, Russia has had to do essentially nothing that was not already in its own interests. On the contrary, Russia has effectively received U.S. approval to continue destroying Ukraine's infrastructure.
The U.S. Treasury Department has already issued a sanctions exemption allowing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel until April 7, 2027. The exemption is not conditional on the promised deliveries actually taking place and contains no quantitative limit. This means Russia is already benefiting from sanctions relief, regardless of whether Putin can or even intends to deliver the 4.8 million metric tons of diesel promised to Trump.
Russia's contribution to the deal consists of a promise to sell its diesel fuel. Not to give it away, not to provide it as humanitarian aid, but to sell fuel on the global market that Russia itself has a vital interest in exporting. Putin has gained an opportunity to earn additional revenue and mitigate the impact of Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil industry.
Russia has made no known reciprocal commitment to stop attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, scale back military operations or make concessions in peace negotiations. Instead, Trump has pressured, if not outright threatened, Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure.
The moral problem with the agreement is colossal. For years, Western countries have sought to restrict Russia's energy revenues in order to reduce its ability to wage its war of aggression against Ukraine — yes, sometimes hypocritically, but they have made the effort nonetheless.
Europe and the U.S. have largely been united on this issue. Now the U.S. president is opening up a new opportunity for the Russians to sell fuel and presenting it as a step that serves the interests of the global economy and American consumers. At the same time, he has previously threatened third countries that buy Russian petroleum products with sanctions — India, for example, as recently as a short while ago — and Congress has just passed the so-called Lindsey Graham bill, which would make it possible to impose effective sanctions on Russia.
Trump's deal stands in stark contradiction to all of this. The Russians are being rewarded for destroying Ukraine's infrastructure with an opportunity to earn additional revenue and portray themselves as the saviors of the global energy market.
For Putin, this is an important political and psychological victory in any case. He can demonstrate both to his domestic audience and internationally that the policy of isolating Russia is unsustainable and that even the U.S. needs Russia's help. What is more, Russia has achieved this outcome without making a single concession in Ukraine. I would call that a 4-0 victory for Putin...
For Ukraine, the message is particularly damaging. Ukraine has taken enormous risks to damage Russia's refining industry and thereby weaken the aggressor's economic and military capabilities. It is depressing to recall the damage Ukraine itself suffers every day in this context. And now our principal ally is helping to alleviate, at least in part, the economic consequences of precisely those attacks that have so far been one of Ukraine's main tools for putting pressure on the Russians. Meanwhile, the Russians continue attacking Ukraine's power plants, heating systems and energy infrastructure and murdering civilians.
You can bet that Russia will use the promised diesel deliveries as a tool of political pressure. If Trump starts linking lower American fuel prices to the operational capacity of Russian refineries, Putin will say Ukraine is to blame and that Trump should make the Ukrainians stop attacking them. Trump already seems to be following this logic — or, more accurately, this absurdity. The result is a situation in which the aggressor continues destroying Ukraine's energy infrastructure while Ukraine is pressured to abandon attacks on the aggressor's energy infrastructure.
The agreement also creates problems for relations between Europe and the U.S. The European Union has sought to reduce its dependence on Russian energy and restrict the revenues flowing into Russia's war economy. The U.S., and Trump in particular, has spent years lecturing Europe for continuing to buy Russian petroleum products. Now he is blatantly disregarding all of that.
The U.S. sanctions exemption does not, of course, invalidate European sanctions, but it makes maintaining a common sanctions policy more difficult. Operating Russia's shadow fleet will become cheaper, insurance companies may begin insuring tankers carrying Russian cargo again and so on. All of this has implications extending well beyond diesel.
European companies must continue complying with EU restrictions while the Americans allow the Russians back into the market. It is reasonable to expect European oil companies to start pressuring their governments to make similar concessions.
U.S. credibility has taken a serious blow in both Europe and Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has already criticized the deal, understandably and as the only possible response. The only people in Europe who might be celebrating are Putinist right-wing forces such as the AfD.
Against this backdrop, the economic benefits of the agreement for the U.S. are uncertain, to put it mildly. Its impact on U.S. gasoline prices is even more indirect than its impact on diesel prices and is likely nonexistent. Russia, meanwhile, gains an opportunity to expand its customer base, reduce the discounts it offers, earn export revenue and ease storage problems at its refineries. Fortunately, this deal will not resolve Russia's own shortage of winter-grade diesel or restore production capacity damaged by Ukrainian attacks.
So there we have it. Trump gets to promise cheaper fuel, which will not actually help him, while Putin has already secured tangible sanctions relief.
There is probably a longer backstory to all of this. According to an October 10 report in the Financial Times, U.S. representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukrainian negotiators in Miami that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Ukraine did not stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure. The Ukrainian delegation cut its visit short. In other words, the U.S. is threatening to end the last significant form of assistance it still provides Ukraine while simultaneously providing direct assistance to the aggressor.
The agreement's economic impact will be modest at best and probably minimal. Its moral and political consequences could be far more lasting and extremely damaging to the U.S. in the long run. It undermines the credibility of sanctions, puts Ukraine under pressure and deepens divisions between Europe and the U.S.
Ultimately, this is another Sputnik-style spin operation. During the coronavirus pandemic, Putin marketed a vaccine around the world that did not work and that Russia was unable to produce in sufficient quantities, creating the impression that Russia was coming to the rescue of those in need. Now, in a single stroke, he has eased his export difficulties, demonstrated that Western sanctions do not hold up and dealt a blow to America's reputation.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Houthi airport attack forces swift rethink of Trump’s new 'Blame Ukraine' strategy
Patrick Wintour
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Saturday.
It was to blame what he described as “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – on the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying his attacks on Russian oil refineries were the cause. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.

‘She was swaying, zoning out’: UK pets poisoned in record numbers by illicit drugs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:30:22 UTC
18:30:22 KST

A record number of pets are ingesting recreational drugs and requiring veterinary care in the UK, figures shared with the Guardian reveal.
Last year, the UK’s only emergency poison centre for animals received its highest ever number of calls involving animals poisoned by cannabis, cocaine, magic mushrooms and nicotine, and it is on course to do so again this year.
The centre runs two emergency phone lines, the Veterinary Poisons Information Service (VPIS) for vets and the Animal PoisonLine (APL) for owners.
Pet owners are reporting that dogs in particular have poisoned themselves by finding and eating the vomit or faeces of a drug user, or abandoned food laced with drugs. Others have been poisoned after swallowing discarded nicotine gum, vaping fluid or other recreational drug products.
Dr Nicola Robinson, the VPIS head of service, said: “It’s quite remarkable what dogs decide to eat. Cats think before they eat, so there are far fewer cases of cats [being poisoned] than dogs.”
In 2025, there was a 42% increase in calls to toxicology specialist helplines involving recreational drugs and nicotine, from 445 calls in 2024 to 633. This exceeded a 26% increase in total calls to the VPIS and APL over the same period.
“We’re very busy at the moment, so I expect we’ll have a record year again this year,” Robinson said.
On average, the poison centre receives a call a day about an animal that has ingested recreational drugs, and it is dealing with 87% more cases than it did in 2021. The greatest numbers of calls concern nicotine products and cannabis.
Robinson said cannabis was a growing problem. “It’s amazing how many pets get it in a public place – in an alleyway, a public park or even in quite rural places like the woods.”
The dog insurer Waggel has seen a rise in the number of cannabis claims owners have made over the past five years. “Highly food-motivated breeds like labradors, golden retrievers and beagles are most at risk,” said Aimee Warner, a Waggel vet.
Pamela Wesson, 72, no longer lets her dog Lola off the lead in Mill Road cemetery in central Cambridge, a Victorian burial ground that is now a wildlife haven.
Lola, a jack russell crossed with a pug, used to run into bushes and come out licking her lips having eaten something she shouldn’t have. “I’d have a little yucky laugh with the other dog owners nearby: ‘Oh no, there she goes again,’” said Wesson. “I certainly wouldn’t say that any more with a light heart.”
On Christmas Eve 2023, Lola darted into some bushes and emerged “looking guilty”, said Wesson. “Very soon after that, at home, her legs started sliding out from under her and then she collapsed. I thought she was going to die.”
She rushed Lola to the emergency vet, who diagnosed toxin ingestion. Police have seized class A and B drugs during patrols of the cemetery, and Wesson suspects Lola – who made a full recovery after an expensive overnight stay – was poisoned by eating residues of drugs in human waste.
“The cemetery is a beautiful place to walk – it’s soul-enhancing, if you ignore the drawbacks,” Wesson said. “But it’s incredibly dangerous, what some of these people do. If Lola had died I would have been heartbroken.”
Robinson recommends that any animal poisoned by a recreational drug is immediately taken to see a vet. “I would not recommend owners waste time calling us on the Animal PoisonLine. Go to the vets and let the vet ring and get treatment advice if they need it,” Robinson said.
Poisoned on Ben Nevis
Christina Bluhme and her son Magnus were nearly at the top of Ben Nevis when they noticed their six-year-old labrador, Tokyo, was behaving oddly. “She started losing her weight bearance on her hind legs – her legs kind of went [from] under her,” she says. “She was swaying, zoning in and out.”
They decided to turn back, fearing the normally agile dog had suffered a stroke while climbing Britain’s tallest peak. But Tokyo refused to move. “She just lay down and was completely lifeless.”
Bluhme, a 50-year-old dog trainer from Surrey, tried to carry the 24kg dog down the mountain but was unable to get very far.
In desperation, she called the emergency services and discovered a team from Lochaber mountain rescue were already descending the 1,345-metre (4,413ft) summit after rescuing a hiker. Alerted to the dog’s plight, they rushed Tokyo down the mountain on a stretcher.
A senior emergency vet who was waiting in a nearby clinic saw that the dog was exhibiting signs of having digested a neurotoxin and a call to the VPIS confirmed this. “She had every symptom,” Bluhme says. “She couldn’t control her bladder, she was drifting in and out of consciousness, her body temperature was really low, and when the vet took her temperature, we could actually smell the cannabis she was digesting, coming from her behind.”
After being treated with activated charcoal to absorb the cannabis in her gut, Tokyo made a full recovery. The vet’s bill, which included an overnight stay, came to £1,121, which was settled by Bluhme’s insurer, Petplan.
After appearing on ITV’s This Morning to talk about what happened, Bluhme was inundated with hundreds of messages from people with similar experiences, she says. “It’s opened my eyes to a problem that’s just crazy.”
On social media, people have made jokes about Tokyo experiencing a high on a high or getting munchies on the mountain, which Bluhme has tried not to read. “It’s really not funny. It’s a real problem.”

How the 2026 Super El Niño and Climate Change Are Related
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

The tropical Pacific has seen heat build for months as a “super” El Niño takes shape.
A climate phenomenon that forms every few years, this year’s iteration of El Niño has been on a tear of daily records and is forecast to reach unprecedented strength this winter. While it’s characterized by hotter-than-normal waters in the eastern tropical Pacific, El Niño is a global problem.
It’s fair to wonder how another global problem is interacting with El Niño: climate change, driven by burning fossil fuels. While a hotter climate begetting a hotter El Niño might seem like a done deal, “I have more questions than I have reactions” to what’s happening, says Christopher Callahan, a climate researcher at Indiana University. In other words, the relationship is still an area of active research—and this year’s event could provide vital insights.
El Niño’s added ocean heat affects the atmosphere, causing weather patterns around the world to shift. Consider it kind of like a domino run, where one tile starts a chain reaction. Such a major slug of heat in the Pacific will act more like a shove then a light flick on the atmosphere, and the resulting shifts in weather are expected to be generationally intense.
The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is forecasting 100 percent odds of an extremely strong El Niño through December and above 80 percent odds it stays that way through February. Data shows this El Niño has already set multiple all-time daily heat records including a recent peak of 3.4 degrees Celsius.
NOAA issues its El Niño forecast as a three-month rolling average, and the agency predicts heat could peak at 2.7 degrees Celsius above normal for the period from October to December. (It’s not out of the question that heat could surpass 3 degrees Celsius, though.) If the forecast holds true, it would smash the previous record of 2.4 degrees Celsius, which was set during the 1982-1983 event.
How Is Climate Change Impacting El Niño?
There is a growing body of evidence that climate change is likely playing at least some role in influencing El Niño. The magnitude and frequency of the phenomenon has increased over the past 60 years, says Francisco Estrada, coordinator of the Climate Change Research Program at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, and so has the variability and how the effects are distributed around the world. He says there shouldn’t be a debate framed as a choice between a “natural El Niño” and an “El Niño caused by climate change” but rather as an interaction between the two processes.
“You can’t separate El Niño from global warming—they’re inextricably linked,” he explains.
Modeling also indicates that El Niño is likely to strengthen as the planet warms, though Callahan notes that many models struggle to accurately represent long-term temperature trends in the eastern tropical Pacific. That can give researchers some pause, but there’s also other evidence that climate change is juicing El Niño.
“The majority of climate models say that El Nino amplitude shall go up in a warming climate, and all of our paleoclimate records say that we're currently in a more active period of El Niño than the last several 1,000 years,” Callahan says.
Research published in August uses data collected from ancient coral, and provides that 1,000-year glimpse Callahan mentions. (He wasn’t involved with the study.) The scientists found an uptick in El Niño amplitude that neatly mirrors when humans started pumping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, though they didn’t attempt to attribute the shift to climate change.
This year’s El Niño will provide another data point to help researchers suss things out.
How Is El Niño Impacting Climate Change?
But as Callahan notes, there’s also an important question about how El Niño is layering on top of climate change.
“Even if climate change has not made the event itself stronger, even if the [sea surface temperature] anomalies are totally natural, the presence of those SSTs in a climate that has been changed by global warming might produce unprecedented impacts,” he says.
El Niño’s impacts on weather—known as teleconnections—are well known, from increasing the odds of drought in the Amazon and Indonesia to juicing precipitation in the Southwest US and lowering the odds of Atlantic hurricanes.
Such an extreme event layered on top of climate change doesn’t mean teleconnections get thrown out the window, though. In fact, some of them may be even more intense.
“We can no longer place as much confidence in the knowledge we’ve gathered from data regarding how El Niño manifests in terms of weather and climate in different parts of the planet,” says Estrada.
What El Niño Means for Climate Risk
From a risk perspective, Estrada believes it’s important to understand how the two phenomena interact and how that combination will affect societies.
He and Callahan’s main concern is not merely whether this El Niño will be the most intense on record but rather the combination of an exceptional event with a climate that has warmed significantly.
“Surprises are the last thing you want when you’re trying to manage risk,” Estrada says.
Callahan’s work shows that the impacts of El Niño on society are extreme, with the most severe events knocking off trillions of dollars from the global GDP. Ecosystems also suffer greatly, particularly coral reefs, which are facing a mass bleaching event.
Given this scenario, the United Nations and other international organizations have called for urgent adaptation measures to safeguard the well-being of the at-risk populations and ecosystems. Some places are already doing that: California preemptively declared a state of emergency last month.
“El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world. Impacts will hit even harder, travel even farther, and cross borders with devastating speed,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said last month.
Additional reporting by Brian Kahn.
