Brittas said the CJP leaders had been treated worse than hijackers. (PTI)
NEW DELHI: CPM Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas on Sunday got into a heated argument with Delhi Police personnel as they attempted to detain him amid a political row over the detention of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) chief Abhijeet Dipke and other party leaders.Brittas, along with CPM MP A A Rahim, had criticised the police action against Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were reportedly detained aboard their flight from Mumbai after it landed at Indira Gandhi International Airport on Saturday.
Speaking to reporters in Delhi, Brittas said the CJP leaders had been treated worse than hijackers or people accused of major financial scams.“The central government is doing all this because they are scared. The police could have arrested them once they come out of the airport. They could not have escaped from inside the airport. There was no need to detain them from inside the plane,” he said.Brittas also condemned the action against journalists, alleging that several were detained or prevented from reporting on the protests, PTI reported.He accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah of taking such measures to protect Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Rahim alleged that several CJP activists and protesters who resisted restrictions on the demonstration at Jantar Mantar or objected to the removal of their phones were “brutally tortured”.Dipke, Ranka and Das were released on Sunday after being produced before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) Court at Delhi Cantonment Police Station.Delhi Police said the three were preventively arrested under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) on October 10 and produced before the court on October 11.The police said the three were released after furnishing a surety bond of Rs 50,000, with a condition to maintain peace and good behaviour for one year.CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also confirmed their release, saying it was subject to an undertaking to maintain public order. “Condition - no breach of peace for one year,” she posted on X.Before his release, Dipke had alleged in a video posted on Instagram that Delhi Police personnel entered his flight to detain him and his associates after they landed in Delhi.“So, you can see that Delhi Police is entering the plane to arrest us. They are all entering the plane. We just landed. All the Delhi Police officers are standing in the aisle. They are trying to arrest us from inside the plane. The entire Delhi Police is getting on the plane. This is the fear of Narendra Modi...Not even Indira Gandhi did this during the Emergency. All we wanted to do is a peaceful protest, and they are picking us up from the flight like we are criminals,” Dipke said.The detention of the CJP leaders came amid a major security clampdown in Delhi on Saturday. Delhi Police detained protesters, activists and political leaders at multiple locations, including along routes leading to Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned to hold a demonstration.
The party and opposition groups have been demanding Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police had denied permission for the gathering, and many protesters were detained before they could reach the proposed venue.More than 7,000 protesters were detained at multiple locations, according to the details provided. Several opposition leaders, including former chief ministers Arvind Kejriwal, Mamata Banerjee, Pinarayi Vijayan and Manik Sarkar, were also detained while attempting to join the protest.

Jointly organized by UNAM's Confucius Institute and the Global-South China-Africa Research Center, the fair connected Chinese enterprises operating in Namibia with local talent, particularly Chinese-language learners and Namibians who had studied in China.
For UNAM graduate Soin Ndalimbililwa, who arrived with her curriculum vitae and an HSK Chinese proficiency certificate, the event offered a chance to put her language learning to practical use.
"It is a great opportunity for students as well as fellow young people who are still job-seeking to build relationships and connections which will result in employment," she told Xinhua.
The participating enterprises, including private and state-owned companies, represented sectors such as mining, manufacturing, tourism, road construction and logistics. Company representatives introduced their businesses and outlined employment opportunities, internships and graduate training programs that could lead to permanent positions.
For those still studying, the fair also offered an opportunity to learn about potential employers and prepare for the transition from university to the workplace.
UNAM student Leroy Nangolo said he was surprised by the number of Chinese enterprises operating in Namibia and offering employment opportunities.
"I am still absorbing it. This platform is good to learn and make connections for the future when we start job hunting," he said.
Beyond recruitment, company representatives highlighted opportunities for local employees to develop professional skills through working alongside their Chinese counterparts.
Fabianus Shilongo, human resources superintendent at GMS Namibia Mining Services, said the company employed more than 550 Namibians working alongside Chinese colleagues.
Chinese staff were sharing their expertise with local employees to facilitate skills transfer, he said.
Angela Naobes, from UNAM's Directorate of Student Affairs, said the fair strengthened the link between education and employment by bringing together academic learning, language proficiency, cultural understanding and career opportunities.
"Your commitment to connecting talent with industry demonstrates the importance of collaboration between education institutions and the private sector in preparing our young people for the future," she said.
Liu Dianbo, Chinese director of the Confucius Institute at UNAM, said the event sought to translate the outcomes of Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah's July visit to China into concrete action.
He also described Chinese-language learning as a bridge to opportunity and encouraged more Namibians to enroll at the institute. ■

World Insights: Thriving exchanges add new momentum to China-Botswana partnership
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:27:38 CST
18:27:38 KST

by Xinhua writer Guo Chunju
GABORONE, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Botswanan President Duma Gideon Boko will pay a state visit to China from Oct. 12 to 17 at the invitation of Chinese President Xi Jinping, as the two countries seek to deepen cooperation in trade, investment and people-to-people exchanges.
In January 2025, Xi and Boko exchanged congratulations on the 50th anniversary of diplomatic ties, expressing confidence in the prospects for closer cooperation. In September 2024, the two countries elevated their bilateral ties to a strategic partnership. Beyond these diplomatic milestones, cooperation between both countries has taken shape in projects ranging from energy and mining to education and health care.
IMPROVING LOCAL LIVELIHOODS
Chinese-invested companies have maintained steady cooperation with Botswana for years, covering areas such as infrastructure, energy and mining, bringing tangible benefits to local communities.
Water infrastructure projects have helped improve access to essential services across Botswana. The Thune Dam, constructed by Chinese companies, supplies water for domestic and agricultural use, with its water resources integrated into Botswana's North-South Water Carrier system. Other projects, including water supply and sanitation works in Maun and the Boteti region, are also helping improve local water services.
Meanwhile, the Digital Delta Data Center is strengthening Botswana's digital infrastructure and supporting the growth of its digital economy.
Cooperation in energy and mining is creating further opportunities for development. The Jwaneng 100 MW Solar Power Plant project has officially commenced operations, helping to ease Botswana's electricity shortage and strengthen the country's energy security. Meanwhile, the Khoemacau Copper Mine Expansion Project is expected to boost production and generate employment opportunities.
The establishment of the Mining Centre of Excellence at Maun Technical College with the support of Botswana's Ministry of Higher Education also helps equip young people with practical skills tailored to the needs of the mining industry, linking vocational training more closely with local employment.
Beyond economic development, cooperation has also extended to healthcare and education. The teaching hospital at the University of Botswana School of Medicine in Gaborone supports medical care and training, while four China-aided primary schools have improved learning conditions for local children, contributing to the development of Botswana's basic education system.
EXPANDING TRADE, DEEPENING COOPERATION
Economic and trade cooperation between China and Botswana is mutually beneficial and enjoys broad prospects. Bilateral business trips and engagements have become increasingly frequent, with continued exchange between the two sides.
From May 1 this year, China extended zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties, bringing significant benefits to Botswana's premium products, such as beef and citrus. "This important initiative opens new opportunities for Botswana to expand its exports, strengthen trade and deepen our economic cooperation with China," said Botswana's Minister for State President, Defense and Security Moeti Mohwasa.
Two-way trade between China and Botswana reached 1.222 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, an increase of 21.3 percent year on year, and rose by 58.6 percent to 852 million U.S. dollars in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, official statistics showed.
In January 2021, the two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for cooperation on the Belt and Road Initiative, making Botswana the 46th African partner country to join the initiative.
In 2025, the two countries signed a MoU on promoting the implementation of the Global Development Initiative, and Botswana joined the Initiative on International Trade and Economic Cooperation Framework for Digital Economy and Green Development. These bilateral agreements provide new opportunities, expand cooperation into new sectors, and open up new prospects for China-Botswana practical cooperation.
Many Chinese business delegations have visited Botswana to explore market opportunities, while Botswana's officials and think tank representatives have praised the achievements of Chinese modernization following visits to China.
Viewing China as "a constant friend and a reliable development partner," Botswana seeks to learn from China's achievements in improving people's living standards and poverty alleviation, as the southern African country pursues its own development agenda, seeking investment, partnerships, and alignment between development strategies.
BRINGING PEOPLE CLOSER
People-to-people exchanges have brought the two peoples closer through cultural, educational and community activities, including "Chinese Bridge" competitions, film festivals and medical outreach programs by Chinese medical teams.
The Confucius Institutes at the University of Botswana in Gaborone and the Botswana International University of Science and Technology (BIUST) in Palapye in central Botswana run programs on promoting Chinese language education and cultural exchange.
"By learning the Chinese language, our students gain a key to unlocking opportunities in a rapidly globalizing world," said BIUST Vice Chancellor Otlogetswe Totolo, describing the institute as a platform for cultural exchange, academic collaboration and closer friendship between Botswana and China.
The growing popularity of the Chinese language and culture among the people of Botswana has helped strengthen people-to-people ties and deepen bilateral friendship, while more Botswana people are looking forward to opportunities to visit China.
"The relationship between Botswana and China has grown steadily over many decades, bringing cooperation for many, many years of mutual interests," said Botswana's Minister of International Relations Phenyo Butale.
Over the years, bilateral partnership in the health sector has continued to flourish. Since 1981, 18 successive groups of Chinese medical professionals, comprising more than 600 experts in total, have traveled thousands of miles to serve in Botswana. They have become an integral part of Botswana's healthcare system, providing specialized medical care to local communities and strengthening bilateral cooperation.
"Their dedication has significantly improved access to specialized healthcare, enhanced the quality of medical services, strengthened the capacity of our healthcare system, and ultimately contributed to improving the health outcomes of our people," said Tshepo Machacha, acting permanent secretary of Botswana's Ministry of Health.
Machacha himself has received traditional Chinese acupuncture therapy. He said traditional Chinese medicine has enriched Botswana's healthcare system.
"This serves as a practical demonstration of how cultural exchange and medical cooperation can directly improve patient care while strengthening medical understanding between the two nations," he said. ■

At least 139 migrants dead, more than 84 missing after boat capsizes off Djibouti
At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, died and 84 remain missing after a boat carrying 350 people capsized off Djibouti en route to Yemen, the International Organisation for Migration said on Sunday.
At least 139 migrants were killed after a boat sank off the shores of Djibouti overnight on October 8-9, a UN agency said Sunday.
An earlier statement indicated an initial toll of 109 dead including 15 children, with some 116 missing. The updated figure accounts for the discovery of a further 30 bodies, with a total of 84 individuals remaining unspoken for.
Survivors said the vessel – which was carrying 350 people from Djibouti to Yemen – capsized north of the Djibouti town of Obock, according to a statement from the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), whose teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency aid.
"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives," said Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, in the statement.
Read moreDjibouti President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh wins sixth term in office
He said IOM teams were on the ground alongside Djiboutian authorities to provide emergency aid.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and then to reach Gulf countries.
Among the bodies recovered were at least 52 men, 42 women and 15 children – nine girls and six boys – the statement said.
More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals.
"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," the IOM said.

A ‘Cold Fish’ Who ‘Never Made Eye Contact’ – Former UK PM on Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:24:00 UTC
18:24:00 KST

Former UK Prime Minister Theresa May reflected this week on her encounters with Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, changes in the White House media environment, and what she believes those changes meant for President Volodymyr Zelensky’s explosive exchange with Trump in the Oval Office in February 2024.
May was interviewed at the Henley Literature Festival in the UK on Oct. 8, as part of a special recording of The Independent’s political podcast “In the Room,” which examines what really goes on inside the rooms where decisions are made.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Reflecting on her time in Downing Street, May said of Putin, “Once a KGB man, always a KGB man,” reiterating the words she used in a Sky News interview on July 30, 2026, in which she also said “it cannot be business as usual with Russia.”
Recalling in the Henley podcast what it was like to come face-to-face with global leaders and sit across the table from Putin at Group of 20 (G20) meetings, she said Putin “wouldn’t make eye contact with anybody” and was a “completely cold fish.”
“As prime minister, you meet other world leaders and you have to take them as you find them,” May said.
“In Putin, I will say, once a KGB man, always a KGB man. He was a completely cold fish and one of the things I noticed particularly at G20 meetings when we were all sitting around the table was, he just wouldn’t make eye contact with anybody. He was sort of like this the whole time, but obviously we had very limited relations with Russia post Salisbury, and we’d had fairly limited relations before.”
Trump: Putin Wants Ukraine Deal, Praises Russian Oil Supplies
May’s remarks referred to Russian military intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia, who were found slumped on a park bench in Salisbury, England, after being exposed to the Novichok nerve agent. The UK government concluded in September 2018 that the poisoning – which the Skripals survived but which led to the death of Salisbury resident Dawn Sturgess – was “almost certainly” approved by the Russian state.
May added that she had always been “a bit of a Russia hawk” during her tenure as Home Secretary and said that the UK “hadn’t properly” responded to the killing of Alexander Litvinenko, which was always “hanging over” relations.
Litvinenko was a British-naturalised Russian defector and former officer of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) who was poisoned with polonium-210 in late 2006 and died as a result in a London hospital on Nov. 23 that year.
On Trump and the White House media machine
Turning to Trump, May remarked jovially, “I think I’m probably the only world leader whose hand he’s held,” referring to her official visit to the White House on Jan. 27, 2017, when the two leaders walked along the White House Colonnade. As reported at the time by UK newspaper The Guardian, the gesture “surprised” British officials and prompted a flurry of international media coverage.
May went on to say that – in her view – Trump is “different” in his second term from his first, appearing to link this to changes in both the conduct of traditional set-piece meetings and the people surrounding the US president.
“I think he was able to have four years when he was out of office, thinking about what he really wanted to do and about who he wanted to have around him,” May said.
“There were some very key people around him in the first administration who were old hands if you like – some would say the establishment – who sort of knew about the way that most of these relations were conducted.”
May described Oval Office meetings for which leaders would traditionally be briefed to “say warm words,” for example about “strengthening the relationship,” after which cameras would be ushered out of the room and a private meeting would begin.
May then likened more recent meetings during Trump’s second term to “a TV show” and expressed disappointment with the way Zelensky was treated during his fiery Oval Office encounter with Trump on Feb. 28, 2024.
“It’s a TV show now as we saw sadly with the way President Zelensky was treated on the first visit… the cameras are in there during this… they’re able to ask questions so it’s an entirely different environment.”
The February 2024 verbal clash between Trump and Zelensky erupted over ceasefire terms, the management of the war, a paused rare-earth minerals deal, and demands from the US administration for more “gratitude” from Ukraine for US military aid.

18:23:05 KST

Former White House Middle East adviser Brett McGurk has offered a behind-the-scenes account of the prolonged negotiations to free Israeli hostages held by Hamas in Gaza, describing a diplomatic process repeatedly derailed by new demands, political disagreements and developments on the battlefield.
In an interview published by The Sunday Times on Saturday, McGurk discussed his forthcoming book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, which examines the efforts of American negotiators to secure the release of those abducted during the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
One of the most devastating setbacks came in August 2024, when negotiations appeared close to producing an agreement involving a ceasefire, the release of hostages and Palestinian prisoners and measures to ease restrictions on movement in Gaza.
Those hopes collapsed after Israeli forces recovered the bodies of six hostages murdered by Hamas in a tunnel beneath Rafah: Alex Lobanov, Almog Sarusi, Carmel Gat, Ori Danino, Hersh Goldberg-Polin and Eden Yerushalmi.
McGurk recalled learning of their deaths from then-CIA Director William Burns. He subsequently advised President Joe Biden that meaningful progress was unlikely while Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar remained alive.
The killings reinforced his assessment that the negotiations could not succeed without a fundamental change in the circumstances on the ground.
Netanyahu's competing objectives
McGurk, who served in senior Middle East policy positions under several American presidents, described the hostage crisis as the most difficult diplomatic challenge of his career.
He said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pursued two objectives throughout the war: securing the hostages' release and preventing Hamas from retaining control of Gaza.
Those priorities were not always compatible, complicating American attempts to broker an agreement. “I always found him extremely confident in his assumptions,” McGurk said of Netanyahu. “If you try to tell him he’s seeing it wrong, it’s tough to make that case.”
McGurk nevertheless rejected the argument that Netanyahu's decisions were driven exclusively by political survival. He portrayed the Israeli leader as deeply convinced of his own assessments and difficult to persuade when American officials disagreed with him.
The former envoy reserved particularly sharp criticism for Hamas, accusing the terrorist organization of repeatedly obstructing negotiations.
He pointed to the breakdown of the first temporary ceasefire in December 2023, when Hamas failed to release additional female hostages as anticipated. Accounts of sexual abuse subsequently provided by released captives raised further concerns about the treatment of women held in Gaza.
According to McGurk, Hamas also complicated negotiations by failing to provide reliable information about the hostages it was prepared to release.
He argued that international discussion of the war often focused heavily on Israeli military operations while paying insufficient attention to Hamas' responsibility for the conflict and its continuation.
Sinwar's strategy and the civilian toll
McGurk said Sinwar had spent years preparing for a confrontation with Israel, including the development of an extensive underground tunnel network that presented major operational challenges for the Israeli military. In his assessment, Sinwar hoped the October 7 attack would provoke a wider regional conflict that could threaten Israel's existence.
Although that broader objective was not achieved, McGurk acknowledged that the war had seriously damaged Israel's international standing. He also expressed frustration over the inability to establish arrangements that would have allowed Palestinian civilians to escape the fighting in Gaza.
Drawing on his experience with military campaigns against Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, McGurk noted that large numbers of civilians had been evacuated from combat zones in previous conflicts.
In Gaza, however, residents had few options for escaping the fighting.
He argued that temporary evacuation arrangements should have been explored alongside enforceable guarantees allowing displaced Palestinians to return to their homes.
McGurk acknowledged the historical sensitivities surrounding Palestinian displacement, particularly the experience of refugees from the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, but maintained that civilian protection should have received greater attention.
How Biden and Trump officials worked together
McGurk also credited cooperation between the outgoing Biden administration and President Donald Trump's incoming team with helping advance the negotiations.
Following Trump's victory in the November 2024 presidential election, McGurk began coordinating with Steve Witkoff, who would become Trump's Middle East envoy, and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and former senior adviser.
By that stage, the regional balance had changed significantly. Israeli forces had killed Sinwar, dealt major blows to Hezbollah in Lebanon and struck Iranian military capabilities.
McGurk believed those developments created an opportunity to renew diplomatic efforts. He said coordination between the two administrations proved essential, despite the deep political divisions in Washington.
“We wouldn’t have been able to get the deal without the two teams working together,” McGurk said.
The first hostages released under the resulting agreement returned on Biden's final day in office in January 2025. Subsequent releases took place under Trump, with the remaining hostages returned in October 2025.
McGurk described the cooperation as an example of bipartisan coordination on a critical foreign policy issue.
The unresolved future of Gaza
Despite the end of the war and the return of the hostages, McGurk warned that the underlying political and security problems remain unresolved.
Hamas has been severely weakened but has not disappeared as an armed organization. Gaza continues to face extensive destruction and humanitarian hardship, while Israeli forces retain a military presence in parts of the territory.
McGurk sees only a limited path toward lasting stability, one requiring Hamas to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw and a new Palestinian governing structure to emerge. He stressed that the October 7 attack fundamentally changed Israel's approach to threats along its borders.
“What you need to appreciate is that, after October 7, Israel will never allow threats to gather on its border again,” McGurk said.
In his view, Israel will not permit Hamas to rebuild its military capabilities or allow Hezbollah to reestablish a large armed presence near its northern communities.
Although McGurk acknowledged grounds for criticizing some Israeli military decisions, he argued that preventing another October 7-style attack remains a legitimate security objective.
He also rejected growing calls in American political circles to distance Washington from Israel, maintaining that close engagement offers the United States greater influence over Israeli decision-making than isolation or punitive measures.

British startup develops 100-mile strike missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:22:02 UTC
18:22:02 KST

- British startup Cody Aerospace & Defence unveiled the Badger Mk1 strike missile, with a 70- to 100-mile range and up to 100 kg warhead.
- The missile is in design, the company is raising pre-seed funding, and it targets development maturity within 18 months to two years.
Cody Aerospace & Defence, a British company founded in February, has unveiled its first product, the Badger Mk1 ground-launched strike missile, along with plans for a factory to build it and a goal of replenishing stockpiles in under a year.
The company announced the missile at the Apex Europe defense show in London this week. It says Badger Mk1 will fly 70 to 100 miles (about 110 to 160 km) and carry a warhead of up to 100 kg (220 pounds), and that it is aimed at NATO members and allied armies as a ground-to-ground indirect fire weapon. The missile would launch from a converted ISO shipping container, sold together with radar and fire control so a customer buys a complete system.
Badger is still in the design phase, and Cody is raising pre-seed capital. Founder Henry Price told the UK Defence Journal the company wants to bring the missile to development maturity, including testing, within 18 months to two years, using seekers, rocket motors and guidance systems bought off the shelf from existing suppliers. Cody has not announced any customers, a unit price or test dates.
Cody also announced Ordnance One, the factory where it plans to build Badger. The company says the plant would also produce other companies’ and countries’ weapons under license. It has not said where the factory will be built or how much it will cost.
Price, who spent 15 years at large defense contractors and their main suppliers before founding Cody, said the company’s pitch rests on stockpile numbers.
“If you look at the problem statement of seven to ten days of stockpiles on the shelf for the UK in intensive warfare, and three years to replace it, that’s all we need to solve,” said Price.
He said Cody is aiming for a replenishment cycle of under a year once the missile is in production, compared with the roughly three years he says it takes to replace stocks bought off the shelf from the United States. He added that U.S. defense orders carry priority ratings that generally put American customers first, which he said can stretch delivery to four or five years. Cody also plans to add an interceptor missile to the same container launcher “a couple of years” after Badger, giving one vehicle both strike and air defense roles.
Price said Cody is lining up British suppliers for explosives and rocket motors, but acknowledged that rare earths and composites depend on supply chains Europe does not fully control. He said a fully British supply chain would cost three to four times as much, according to suppliers.
“I want engineers to be delivering capability, not managing obsolescence,” said Price.
He also argued that NATO should standardize rocket munitions so any similar-sized round can be fired from different allied launchers, and said Cody’s software and fire control will be open source.
The UK government has been trying to rebuild weapons stocks since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Price said the Defence Investment Plan set aside £11.1 billion (about $14.8 billion) for stockpiles and that Cody wants to help the Ministry of Defence spend it more efficiently. Another British startup, Cambridge Aerospace, has already moved from founding to a Ministry of Defence order for its Skyhammer interceptor in less than two years.

EU finalizes plans for tighter visa restrictions on Russians — Politico
Politico reported this in an article, according to Ukrinform.
The move is intended to strengthen the European Union's protection against hybrid attacks.
EU officials told the publication that the European Commission is preparing to present relevant proposals early next year. A group of countries, including Poland, Sweden, and Estonia, has pushed for stricter visa rules for Russian citizens, particularly former participants in the war against Ukraine.
Last year, Russian citizens were issued approximately 478,000 tourist visas to the Schengen Area. A significant proportion were multiple-entry visas, allowing holders to cross the border repeatedly without having to apply for new documents each time.
Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer warned that the system poses a threat to European security amid an increase in acts of sabotage, arson, and other forms of hybrid warfare organized by Moscow.
"It's obvious I think for everyone that we have vulnerabilities in our system that can be used by our enemies. As far as I understand things, the Commission is preparing a proposal that, according to what I have heard, should be launched in January next year. From a Swedish point of view, we would love to see it even earlier," Strömmer said.
Other EU countries plan to raise the issue at the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting on Monday, October 12, and propose additional restrictions on Russian diplomats in the European Union.
As Ukrinform previously reported, in September, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said the bloc was preparing new measures targeting the Russian economy, including its shadow fleet. The EU was also discussing further restrictions on Russian diplomats' movements, visa bans for former combatants, and a review of its tourist visa policy for Russian citizens.

Rare Northern Lights display seen over Switzerland

Rare Northern Lights display seen over Switzerland
Sporadic sightings of the Northern Lights were reported in the Swiss night sky on Saturday evening. Although the lights were faint, they could be seen clearly, meteorologist Daniel Gerstgrasser wrote in a post on X.
The natural spectacle could be seen on several MeteoSwiss webcams. The Northern Lights are caused by heightened solar activity. Large quantities of electrically charged particles are ejected from the Sun and can reach Earth within one to five days, according to MeteoSwiss.
More
Strong solar storm brings Northern Lights in Switzerland
The charged particles are deflected towards the poles by the Earth’s magnetic field. There, they collide with oxygen and nitrogen molecules in the atmosphere, creating the characteristic light displays. During periods of particularly intense solar activity, the Northern Lights can also be visible from Switzerland.

Germany rejects Trump demand, 'fully supports' Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

Germany rejects Trump demand, 'fully supports' Zelenskyy
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
What you need to know
- Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin 'fully supports' Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
- The gesture of solidarity came in response to Donald Trump's calls for new leadership in Ukraine
- Friedrich Merz's CDU gathers for leadership meeting addressing electoral free fall
- The German government has said it will continue working with EU partners on Russia sanctions
- Ex-Chancellor Gerhard Schröder faces criticism for attending Putin's birthday
Read below for a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 10, and Sunday, October 11.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Deutsche Bank CEO: Political extremism putting off foreign investors
Christian Sewing, CEO of Deutsche Bank, Germany's biggest, warned that the growing strength of both the far right and the far left is spooking foreign investors.
Sewing told the tabloid Bild that recent election victories for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and post-communist Left Party "pose a significant risk for Germany and should not be downplayed."
The Deutsche Bank boss said it mattered little that the elections were on the state and local level. "You can't expect a foreign investor to immediately draw a distinction between a state government and Germany as a whole," he said.
"It's seen as Germany as a whole and I think that from an investor's point of view, that's understandable."
Some economists say the AfD is creating an atmosphere that will drive away much needed skilled labor as well as foreign investors.
The Left Party, meanwhile, won victory in Berlin promising to expropriate residential property companies' holdings to lower housing costs in the German capital.
"Whether it's Saxony-Anhalt with the AfD or what's happening here in Berlin," said Sewing, "it's anything but conducive to economic growth. And it's anything but investment-friendly."
Sewing said Chancellor Friedrich Merz must get on with carrying out reforms and reviving the economy, saying, "That is the only response we have to the far-right and far-left extremists in this country."
Foreign Minister Wadephul: 'Germany fully supports' Zelenskyy
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Sunday made clear that Berlin stands with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, rejecting US President Donald Trump's calls for his replacement.
Germany will "fully support the president as he carries out his difficult duties," said Wadephul at his party's two-day CDU leadership conference.
On Friday, after a long phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump announced a deal that would see sanctions on Russia eased dramatically and allow Moscow to export millions of barrels of diesel, thus pumping much needed cash into Russia's economy.
On Saturday, Trump called for Zelenskyy's removal and again sought to pin blame on the Ukrainian president — not his own Iran war — for high global oil prices.
Germany is the biggest EU donor to Ukraine, and an advocate for tighter sanctions and increased pressure on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.
Berlin responded to Trump's oil scheme by stating that it would not be lifting any Russian sanctions.
On Sunday, Wadephul responded to the second point, making the case for "consistency and clarity" in terms of support for Ukraine.
"We don't need less pressure on Putin to force him to negotiate," said the German diplomat. "We need more," he added. "That is what this moment requires and that's what this government stands for."
Merz's CDU huddles to find way out of electoral free fall
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will kick off a two-day leadership meeting on Sunday to plot a path out of the electoral crisis the party finds itself in after three dismal state elections.
The 25-member leadership meeting was called after the CDU — until now one of Germany's two largest popular parties — failed to even clear the 5% hurdle to enter Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature. The stinging loss, which Merz himself described as "a disaster," represented the first time in the party's history that it was booted from a statehouse.
The CDU has been struggling to hold off the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and has been thrust into an identity crisis due to the rate at which it is losing voters to the party.
In one of the summer's other elections — in Saxony-Anhalt — the CDU dropped nearly 20 percentage points, getting clobbered by the AfD, which racked up over 40% of the vote.
This weekend's meeting is designed to address voter dissatisfaction with the CDU-led governing coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD), as well as looking at possible long-term solutions to the party's electoral death spiral.
Faced with this new electoral reality, leaders will reportedly look at the potential policy consequences of the party's losses, reconsidering whether to push on with much-needed reforms to the healthcare and retirement systems, for instance.
Party leaders will also grapple with the fundamental question of how to deal with the AfD in the long run, namely, whether to maintain the party's "firewall" policy rejecting any cooperation or to work with the anti-immigrant rightwing populists in hopes of remaining relevant.
Speaking with Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper ahead of the pow-wow, Hesse State Premier Boris Rhein said leadership, "has to deal with all of the issues that are important to everyday citizens: Cost of living, security, immigration and jobs."
This blog is on pause
We are pausing our coverage for now. Join us again on Sunday morning for more coverage of the German news and analysis.
Germany rejects proposed EU budget, calls for greater cuts
Germany swiftly rejected a proposed new budget for the European Union that was put forward on Saturday.
Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, put forward a budget of €1.826 trillion ($2.046 trillion) for the next seven years — a reduction of around €159 billion compared to the European Commission's original proposal of nearly €1.985 trillion.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget cuts should go further.
"The size of the new proposal is no basis for an agreement," Merz said.
"The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the main burden of financing," he added.
Germany is the largest net contributor to the EU budget. It and other net contributors including the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland all want the next budget to be slashed by hundreds of billions of euros.
But the second-largest net contributor to the EU budget, France, has instead argued that the 27-member bloc needs a more generous budget in order to overcome new challenges.
'Ragebait' named Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year
The Langenscheidt publishing house on Saturday named "ragebait" as Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year during the Frankfurt Book Fair.
Ragebait is social media content designed to draw people in by making them angry with provocative claims, lies, or outrageous opinions, thereby driving up clicks and interactions.
Langenscheidt, Germany's best-selling dictionary publisher, organized an online poll with 1 million young people taking part in this year's competition.
Ragebait took 36.5% of the vote, with runners-up including the terms "peak," meaning the best of the best, and "crashout," meaning when someone loses their cool.
Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions
Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.
"The federal government has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.
"The federal government remains committed to the decisions on sanctions against Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.
Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.
Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.
A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."
"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.
Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.
In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.
The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.
However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.
Ex-Chancellor Schröder criticized for Putin birthday visit
The appearance of Germany's Russia-friendly former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder at President Vladimir Putin's birthday party earlier this week has drawn criticism in Germany.
Franziska Brantner, the co-leader of Germany's Green party, called on Schröder's Social Democrats (SPD) to revisit revoking Schröder's party membership.
"Russia is now even attacking us in Germany with hybrid attacks. Schröder hasn't learned anything from this. A new approach needs to be put on the table," she told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.
"Schröder is celebrating Putin's birthday with him, while civilians in Ukraine are once again dying as a result of Russian attacks. This is politically unacceptable," said Brantner.
Anything less than expulsion from the party would be "a disastrous signal, not only to Ukraine but also to the people and their safety in our country," Brantner added.
The SPD's Hubertus Heil, who served as Germany's labor minister from 2018 to 2025, also criticized Schröder.
"The warm embrace between Schröder and Putin in Moscow deeply outrages and disturbs me," Heil told the Tagesspiegel.
Celebrating with a "dictator" whose "murderous imperialism causes horrific suffering every day" is "unjustifiable under any circumstances," he said.
Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.
"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands,
Schröder's business and personal ties to Russia have drawn controversy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, but he fended off calls at the time by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.

A post from an Instagram account appearing to be linked to the protests that had promoted the demonstrations said people had "been squeezed by rising house prices and the cost of living" for years.
Thousands of people gathered in Lisbon and Porto on Saturday to protest rising living costs and housing prices.
The protests, which were also planned in Aveiro, Braga, and Funchal, were organised by a platform named "You can't live like this anymore," and saw demonstrators chanting about wages and holding signs with messages such as "this salary isn't enough to live on."
Others lifted placards bearing slogans such as "I want to move out of my parents' house before I'm 50."
One attendee at the Lisbon march, Teresa Fonseca, told the Lusa news agency that she had taken inspiration from similar recent protests in Spain.
"I saw on Instagram that this protest was going to take place, so I came. Enough is enough. This country is getting worse and worse, and now we need to leave our homes and take to the streets to make our voices heard, just as the Spanish did," she said.
A post from an Instagram account appearing to be linked to the protests that had promoted the demonstrations said people had "been squeezed by rising house prices and the cost of living" for years.
"We spend our lives working and exhausting ourselves just to make our wages last until the end of the month, to cope with rising fuel prices and basic living costs, and to avoid losing our homes," it said.
"We can’t go on living like this!" it added.
'Let’s do it like they do in Spain'
Some protesters, like Fonseca, seemed to be seeking to emulate recent events in Spain, where housing protests broke out following the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who later died.
One group in Porto - where around 1,500 demonstrators reportedly turned out - stood next to a sign reading "let’s do it like they do in Spain."
In Spain, Maricarmen's case served as a launch pad for further demonstrations against the country's housing crisis and heaped pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's government.
The Spanish government proposed new emergency housing legislation as pushback mounted, but it failed to pass, prompting Sánchez to call a snap general election for late November.

The U.S. Ambassador to Mongolia, Richard Buangan, delivered the closing remarks for the event, looking ahead to the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Los Angeles. Italy and the U.S. virtually passed the baton from the 2026 Milan-Cortina Winter Games to the LA28 Summer Games.
                                    
The webinar offered important food for thought thanks to contributions from exceptional guests: Marco Ragini, the Italian head coach of the Mongolian national soccer team, who spoke about nurturing young talent and the prospects for soccer’s growth in Mongolia; Mongolian cyclist Jambaljamts Sainbayar, fresh off his splendid bronze medal at the Asian Games; and Alberto Zatta, secretary general of the Italian Chamber of Commerce in Mongolia, who highlighted the synergies between sports, innovation, and business, including sports infrastructure and the role of the private sector in this area.

Foreign online studies not enough to meet Estonia's compulsory education requirement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Foreign online studies not enough to meet Estonia's compulsory education requirement
Children under 18 living in Estonia must attend an Estonian school to fulfill compulsory education requirements, even if they are enrolled in a foreign online school, the Ministry of Education has said.
At an information seminar for local governments and schools, the Ministry of Education announced that all children under the age of 18 who have moved to Estonia, with certain exceptions, must fulfill their compulsory education requirement at an Estonian school. Attending online classes at a foreign school does not exempt them from this obligation.
The Tartu city government's education department asked the ministry which legal provision the requirement was based on as the Education Act does not explicitly establish such a rule.
Marika Peekmann, a senior expert at the Ministry of Education, said the requirement stems from the combined provisions of the Education Act and the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act.
"The law does not provide for the possibility of considering the compulsory education requirement fulfilled for a person residing in Estonia solely on the basis of enrollment in a foreign educational institution. This is also supported by the objectives of the compulsory education reform, the obligation of local governments to monitor compliance with compulsory education requirements under the law and so on," Peekmann said.
She added that accepting enrollment in a foreign school as fulfilling the compulsory education requirement for children living in Estonia would raise the question of why the law links compulsory education to residence in Estonia in the first place.
"The central idea of the compulsory education reform is that local governments monitor and ensure the education of young people living in Estonia. If enrollment in a foreign school or participation in an online school were sufficient, local governments would have no real way of verifying whether a student is actually studying, how much they are studying, whether the instruction meets the required educational standards or whether their studies are continuing without interruption," the senior expert said.
According to Peekmann, this would create a gray area in which compulsory education requirements would formally be met, but the state would have no real overview of a young person's educational progress.
"The Estonian state cannot automatically assess the legal status of a foreign school, the standard of its curriculum, how instruction is actually organized or whether learning outcomes are being achieved," she explained.
Peekmann said the problem is particularly acute in the case of foreign online or alternative educational institutions, as the state would have no clear basis for determining which forms of foreign education meet the objectives of compulsory education and which do not.
The ministry's senior expert said the aim of the compulsory education reform was not merely to ensure that young people receive some form of education, but also to reduce school dropout rates and the number of young people who are neither studying nor working.
"Achieving this objective requires students to be monitored within the Estonian education system, their educational progress to be recorded in the Estonian Education Information System (EHIS) and support measures to be made available when necessary. In most cases, this is not possible with foreign educational institutions," Peekmann noted.
Starting this academic year, the Ministry of Education extended compulsory education to the age of 18, meaning that students who complete basic school must continue their education at an upper secondary school, vocational school or in preparatory studies. The compulsory education requirement does not apply to the children of foreign diplomats.
--
Editor: Karin Koppel, Marcus Turovski

Attorney-general bars Ben-Gvir from prison visit videos, recordings

The meeting itself took place against the backdrop of Ben-Gvir’s policy of tightening the conditions of confinement for security prisoners, which he has pursued since taking office, as well as his efforts to advance the death penalty for terrorists.

Former A-G Avichai Mandelblit ends testimony in Netanyahu trial over investigations authorization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:01:29 UTC
18:01:29 KST

Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit testified Sunday that investigators carried out serious actions in the cases against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu without his approval. He said he had wanted the main investigative steps reviewed, but had not expected to approve every police action.
“There were things I did not approve, including serious things,” Mandelblit told the Jerusalem District Court.
Mandelblit, who approved investigations into Netanyahu and later decided to indict him in Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000, was called by the defense. Netanyahu’s lawyers argue investigators exceeded the scope of Mandelblit’s approvals and that some actions began without the consent required by law. The prosecution says he authorized the investigations, including orally, and that the defense is mischaracterizing those approvals.
The testimony is expected to continue Monday. The defense has requested five further days, from October 18 to 22.
The central dispute is what Mandelblit approved and how those decisions were recorded.
Basic Law requires A-G consent for investigation against prime minister
Under Basic Law: The Government, an investigation of a sitting prime minister requires the attorney-general’s consent. The prosecution relies on Justice Ministry meeting records and a memorandum from Mandelblit to show that he approved opening the investigations.
The defense says the records do not establish the required approvals or show that police stayed within their scope. In 2021, the judges rejected a defense request to dismiss the indictment on this ground, but criticized the lack of separate written authorizations.
Mandelblit said he closely supervised the investigations because they involved a sitting prime minister, but was not informed of every police action. He wanted the main steps reviewed because of the case’s sensitivity and the need to balance gathering evidence with protecting the office and dignity of the prime minister. Police, he said, can be “like runaway horses” in pursuing suspicions. But the law did not require him to approve every action, and he said he had not tried to manage the police team.
Defense attorney Amit Hadad cited testimony from former senior investigator Koresh Barnur, who said every action in the case had been approved by the attorney-general. Mandelblit said that was inaccurate and agreed that some actions he had not approved were serious.
One example was a wiretap targeting Natan Eshel, a close Netanyahu associate. Mandelblit said the surveillance should have been brought to him because it was sensitive. When he learned of it, he demanded it stop unless investigators had information connecting Eshel personally to an offense. He said he told investigators to consult him in advance about similar steps.
Mandelblit also addressed a controversial police tactic involving Nir Hefetz, a former Netanyahu aide who became a state witness. Investigators arranged a chance encounter between Hefetz and a woman close to him while he was in custody, intending for him to learn that police knew personal details about him. Mandelblit said he had not known about the tactic beforehand and called it “improper and wrong.”
He said he considered whether to investigate the conduct immediately, but decided against questioning the officers and witnesses while the case was underway, fearing that bringing them together could affect the proceedings. Instead, he told his staff to examine documents related to the incident. He said he did not know that prosecutor Yehudit Tirosh had attended a meeting where the tactic was discussed and would have expected to be told.
Hadad also asked what Mandelblit knew about pressure on state witnesses. Mandelblit said he had not been in the interrogation rooms and did not know what pressure investigators had put on Hefetz. Hadad raised claims that investigators tried to get Or Elovitch, the son of Shaul Elovitch, Netanyahu’s co-defendant in Case 4000, to persuade his father to replace his lawyer. Mandelblit said it was unacceptable for an investigator to tell a suspect to change lawyers.
Mandelblit said investigators had to seek his consent to open an inquiry into a suspicion involving the prime minister, and return to him if a new suspicion emerged. An investigation, he said, had to be based on a specific suspicion, not a personal impression of the prime minister.
On Case 1000, the illegal gifts affair, Mandelblit rejected Hadad’s claim that he had not authorized investigators to look into cigars and champagne. He said he had approved examining whether Netanyahu received benefits from businesspeople, including wealthy figures abroad. Asked about businessman Arnon Milchan, Mandelblit said he did not remember refusing to investigate gifts from him. He said the wording investigators used when cautioning Milchan as a suspect went beyond what he had approved.
Mandelblit denied knowing investigators had acted without his approval
On Case 4000, the Bezeq-Walla case, Mandelblit said he had approved examining whether actions by then-Communications Ministry director-general Shlomo Filber were connected to Netanyahu. He denied knowing that investigators had taken steps in the case without his approval. The defense challenged whether the meeting records supported his account.
Mandelblit also rejected the suggestion that Case 4000 had been essential to his decision to indict Netanyahu. He said each of the three cases independently justified an indictment and that he viewed them as connected in reflecting a pattern of conduct. He acknowledged that he may earlier have hoped the inquiries would not produce evidence warranting charges, but said he had to approve examining a suspicion once it arose.
The trial, which began in May 2020, combines three cases. In Case 1000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu and his family received gifts from wealthy businessmen. Case 2000 concerns recorded conversations between Netanyahu and Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon Mozes about a possible exchange of more favorable coverage for Netanyahu for steps to curb rival Israel Hayom.
In Case 4000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu advanced regulatory measures benefiting Bezeq in exchange for favorable coverage on the Walla news site. Netanyahu denies wrongdoing. He faces charges of fraud and breach of trust in Cases 1000 and 2000, and bribery, fraud and breach of trust in Case 4000.
Netanyahu arrived after the testimony began and said, “The truth is coming to light.” He left before the afternoon session resumed, and Mandelblit continued testifying in his absence.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, former Israel Bar Association head Efi Nave and MK Tali Gotliv also attended. Gotliv, who recently moved from Likud to Otzma Yehudit, shouted at Mandelblit as he entered the courtroom.
At the hearing’s opening, Mandelblit complained that a journalist had confronted him outside court and made claims he could not answer. Kan 11 journalist Ayala Hasson denied his account and said she had approached him politely.
Prosecutor Yehonatan Tadmor called testimony by a former attorney-general “exceptional,” warning that questioning a prosecutor could become a means of personal attack or expose internal discussions. The prosecution had not opposed Mandelblit’s testimony because of the unusual circumstances and the dispute over whether he authorized the investigation, Tadmor said.
Justice Minister Yariv Levin called Mandelblit’s appearance “disgraceful” and said it showed that the case against Netanyahu had been fabricated. He called for the trial to be canceled before the election and for a commission of inquiry into law-enforcement officials.
Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

Hegesth plan to publicly livestream Nidal Hasan execution draws bipartisan, UN condemnation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:00:43 UTC
18:00:43 KST

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the December 3 firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan has drawn objections from the UN, Republican and Democratic lawmakers, and the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, while the Trump administration has not made a final decision on the broadcast.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers and wounded 32 others at the Fort Hood military base in 2009. A Defense Department official announced that his execution would be livestreamed.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told podcaster Jack Posobiec aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday.
Hegseth separately told Real America's Voice that Hasan was "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers - as it should be.” Asked about any final requests from Hasan or contact with US President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming the execution would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture.”
A Pentagon spokesperson said Monday that Trump had approved Hegseth’s recommendation. Trump said Friday that Hasan deserved execution by firing squad but did not address livestreaming at the time. Speaking to reporters Friday evening, he said the administration would decide on the broadcast.
Vice President JD Vance also questioned whether it would happen, saying, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.” He said he would not watch.
The last public US execution was Rainey Bethea’s 1936 hanging. Hasan’s execution would be the US Army’s first execution of a soldier since World War II and the first death penalty imposed on an armed service member in 65 years.
Public executions only done in Iran, Afghanistan over last year
Of the more than 2,700 executions recorded in 17 countries last year, public executions occurred in just two. Amnesty International documented 11 such executions in Iran in 2025 and six in Afghanistan.
Republican lawmakers joined the criticism. Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said public executions belong to “oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan,” while Georgia GOP Rep. Austin Scott said “live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Republican Sen. John Curtis warned against turning executions into “bloody spectacles,” while Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut called the proposal “disgusting” and “medieval.”
The president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plan a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”

Surgeon faces deportation as Home Office revokes refugee status for Syrians

18:00:22 KST

A Syrian plastic surgeon is facing deportation from the UK after the Home Office revoked his refugee status, declaring it is now safe for him and his family to return to their home country.
Despite Foreign Office guidance advising against all travel to Syria because of the “volatile” security situation, the government has classified it as a safe place for refugees to return to.
Although some European countries are strongly promoting voluntary return to Syria, the Home Office’s decision to actively remove refugee status for Syrians is thought to be the first of its kind in Europe since the fall of the Assad regime.
The surgeon, who fled the Assad regime and arrived in the UK in 2016, now lives in London with his wife and six children, three of whom are studying at university. He is understood to be one of the first Syrian refugees in the UK to have his refugee protection cancelled.
The move is believed to be the first time the Home Office has cancelled refugee protection for a particular nationality, and thousands of Syrians settled in the UK are likely to be affected.
“I am so shocked by the Home Office’s decision to withdraw refugee protection,” the surgeon said. “I brought my family to what I considered to be a safe place. We have integrated well but now my refugee status has been cancelled.
“I worked as a plastic surgeon in Syria, converted my medical qualifications here so that I am registered with the General Medical Council to work as a doctor here. I am currently working in a GP surgery but am hoping I will be able to continue my practice as a plastic surgeon soon.
“I don’t believe Syria will be a safe place for me to return to. I was targeted by certain radical groups in Syria who are still operating there. They are capable of doing many things to me. And I don’t believe that the current Syrian government would be able to protect me from these groups.
“I have heard of a few other families who have also had their refugee status taken away from them on the same basis as me – the Home Office says Syria is now a safe country for us to return to.
“After I received the letter from the Home Office I delayed telling my family because I wanted to protect them from sadness for a few more days. But now I have given them the news. Like me, they are all in shock and are only just starting to absorb this. My three older children are all studying at university: one is doing neuroscience, another cybersecurity and a third pharmacy.
“It’s unsafe for all of us to go back to Syria. By revoking our refugee status the Home Office is depriving us of the right to live our lives.”
The Home Office letter states: “Your refugee status has been ceased. Although officials accept that the situation in Syria remains ‘complex’ they consider that changes in Syria are so significant that your fear of persecution and serious harm can no longer be regarded as well founded.”
The technical term is “cessation” of refugee status. The UN’s refugee agency, UNHCR, in its most recent guidance about the safety of Syria, found that governments should not be returning refugees there.
It said: “UNHCR calls on states to refrain from implementing cessation exercises until such time as the situation in Syria has seen significant improvements in overall stability.”
Foreign Office guidance states that the security situation in Syria “remains volatile” and adds: “Fighting and violence may occur around the country and is highly unpredictable. This includes artillery and airstrikes.” The guidance also states that there is a humanitarian crisis in Syria including lack of infrastructure, water, sanitation and health services.
The family’s solicitor, Manini Menon of Duncan Lewis, said: “It is regrettable that the home secretary has seen fit to target Syrian refugees and their families as part of her pledge to reduce net migration figures. This is a cynical and unprecedented step which will have devastating consequences for a group of people who have rebuilt their lives in the UK with considerable effort, contributing to their communities and putting down roots here.
“The evidence in relation to Syria is clear: the circumstances in the country do not allow the home secretary to lawfully conclude that they have stabilised to the extent that refugees can be safely returned there.”
The Home Office said: “Britain will always provide protection to genuine refugees, and we will never return anyone to danger. When it is safe for someone to return to their home country, they will be expected to do so. We continue to work closely with governments around the world to develop and maintain returns agreements, including with Syria.”

Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

Humankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.
Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.
While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity – existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating, global proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima, how much longer can our luck hold?
Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putin recently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time, Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacks deep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.
Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US is upgrading its nuclear arsenal of 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing a lucrative deal with Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.
Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’s status as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim, whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit, is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow – which, at this rate, there may not be.
Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spending reached nearly $3tn last year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paper published by the non-partisan Arms Control Association (ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.
The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too, is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and others advances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.
If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.
- Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator
