After RAF Fairford incident, how big a threat to the UK is Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:00:21 UTC
18:00:21 KST

Britain may have been only peripherally involved in the bombing of Iran that Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu started, but in the past fortnight it has become clear that Tehran wants to pose a threat inside the UK in response.
In the aftermath of the confused incident near RAF Fairford, western officials are weighing up whether to warn publicly that Iran now has US military targets in Europe on its mind, such as the air force base in Gloucestershire.
That could come even though there remains British scepticism about Iran’s capability to pull off a drone raid on a secure facility far from Tehran.
What is already accepted by MI5 is that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has sought to coordinate and promote the targeting of the Jewish community in the UK and Europe, starting from March with a string of arson attacks directed at synagogues and similar sites.
That is itself a significant step up from the regime’s longstanding campaign of assassination plots and threats against critics overseas, tasks the IRGC has traditionally hired criminal gangs to carry out.
Exactly what happened at RAF Fairford remains unclear, though Iran may have gained something from it for very little. A week later, last Sunday, a worried US decided to withdraw the 12 B-1 bombers it had stationed there, with leaks to US media suggesting there was a fear of a Ukraine-style drone attack.
What is known is that five men from London drove up in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, one of whom called 999 as they did so. All five were arrested in Whelford, a village next to the airbase, only to be released on police bail a day later when no explosives were found or discernible plot discovered.
Two more men have been arrested on suspicion of terror offences, and released on police bail. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part, and on Thursday the Met police chief, Mark Rowley, said “you will see more progress on this investigation”.
RAF Fairford is an exposed site, with plane spotters easily able to get up close enough to photograph and track the forward-deployed US B-1 and B-52 bombers, which with permission from the former prime minister Keir Starmer were taking off to make attack runs into Iran in the spring and early summer.
“Iran has a track record of planning and carrying out attacks especially on opponents of the regime in the UK. Given the use of Fairford by US bombers, it’s only prudent to assume that they would see an interest in attacking a wider range of targets, whatever their involvement in the Fairford incident,” said Lord Ricketts, a former UK national security adviser.
Dr Antonio Giustozzi, a terrorism specialist with the Royal United Services Institute, suggests the drive to the village was “a feint” where individuals, who may have been unwitting, were sent “to hint at what could happen”. But he is sceptical that Iran could pose a real military threat to Fairford or elsewhere.
As for attacking Fairford, piloting first-person view drones of the type used in Ukraine is a skill requiring several days if not weeks of training, while an operation on an airbase would probably take months to prepare. “I doubt that Iran could bring in military-grade explosive to the UK; the last people to do so were the IRA,” Giustozzi said.
A genuine attack on RAF Fairford or similar would almost certainly be a one-way mission ending in capture or even death, which it would be it hard to recruit for. But despite the low risks, the US chose to withdraw the B-1 bombers, which cost $300m (£225m) each, as a precautionary move. It was “an operational decision to reduce the risk”, Rich Knighton, the head of the UK armed forces, said on Thursday.
This week, a US congressional research report counted that 81 US military planes, helicopters or drones had been destroyed or damaged in the Iran war, including several struck on the ground at bases in Saudi Arabia and Jordan, a reminder that Iran fought back more effectively than the US acknowledged. The value of lost aircraft and air defence systems is estimated at $1.9bn and $3.3bn respectively.
Meanwhile, Trump, desperate to lower oil prices, has set back any future attack on Iran until after the US midterm elections in early November. But regardless of other justifications for the US withdrawal from RAF Fairford, and the police investigation – which has yet to lead to any charges – the wider Iran threat in the UK is now elevated.
A week ago, two Iranian nationals, Salam Ahmadyan from Liverpool and Rahman Salehi from Salford, were charged with terror offences, accused of trying to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade chlorine powder bomb.
Prosecutors told a magistrates court on Saturday the pair were in contact with a third party, believed to be in Iran, who directed them and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. A trial at the Old Bailey has been scheduled.
Early in May, the US indicted Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, 32, an Iranian-Iraqi dual national, accusing him of promoting and coordinating 18 arson and other low-level terror attacks against Jewish and US sites in the UK and Europe during March and April 2026. He was, the US authorities said, a commander with Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi group long backed by the IRGC.
The following month, in a Manhattan courtroom, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty and said he was “a prisoner of war”. He faces a terrorism trial, accused in one instance of participating in an arson attack on a synagogue in London via a FaceTime video call. Though nobody was killed in the campaign, al-Saadi is accused of telling an associate that he was engaged in “psychological warfare”.
The group al-Saadi is accused of running, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia (HAYI), also claimed credit for the firebombing of four Jewish community ambulances in north London in postings on social media. Four people pleaded guilty to arson in the case in August, in an attack that caused an estimated £1m of damage. Sentencing and a full airing of the facts in court are not due until next year.
Jonathan Hackett, a former US marine and intelligence specialist, says the threat in the UK and Europe will endure because Tehran believes it serves a purpose, though it will alter depending on who becomes responsible after al-Saadi. “The psychological effects alone are certainly important; the goal is to create a wedge between the US and its allies,” he added.

California’s Tallest and Most Iconic Trees Are Getting Heatstroke
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

This story originally appeared on Vox and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
A grove of coast redwood trees is a forest of forests. Individual trees can live for thousands of years, and as they grow, their canopies develop mats of soils and ferns, creating something like a second forest floor hundreds of feet above the ground.
These elevated ecosystems are home to creatures like the wandering salamander, which can spend its entire life cycle on top of a single tree, and the marbled murrelet, a seabird whose nesting habits were a mystery until one day in 1974, when a tree-trimmer stumbled upon a nest 150 feet above the ground. Sometimes a stray seed—a sitka spruce or oak or even another redwood—finds its way up a massive redwood and grows into another tree entirely, nestled among the branches of a giant.
For millennia, redwoods have been the anchors of this incredibly stable ecosystem; they can even survive wildfires that devastate other tree species. They’ve also been the source of plenty of human inspiration and drive millions of dollars to California’s tourist economy. But like other living things, they aren’t immune to warming temperatures, and it turns out these trees have a particular weak spot.
A new study from researchers at the University of California, Davis, using measurements taken twice a month for two years, found that coast redwood leaves essentially dial down their photosynthesis during periods of extreme heat. This means trees are slowing their “breathing” and “eating” because they can’t cool down fast enough when temperatures rise. It’s a problem that’s only going to get worse as climate change continues to drive global temperatures up, and it raises urgent questions about the future of these iconic trees and the layers of life that live on and around their shadow-dappled lengths.
To understand what’s happening to the redwoods—and what that may mean for the species that rely on them—first we need to take a quick foray into tree anatomy. Trees use the pores in their leaves, stomata, to do two things: take carbon dioxide in, and let water out. Open stomata mean the tree is “breathing” in carbon dioxide and photosynthesizing, but probably also letting water out. Closed stomata mean the tree is conserving water but also slowing down its photosynthesis, since it isn’t taking in any carbon dioxide.
“Because leaves are a physical, light-absorbing object, they heat up just like asphalt would in the sun,” said Lily Klinek, a PhD student at UC Davis who was the lead author on the study.
“They’re heating up faster than the air around them,” she said. “And one way that they can cope with this is by opening their stomata and allowing water to transpire out of the leaf, which is kind of like the way that humans sweat. When water evaporates off our skin, it cools us down, and it’s the same for leaves. But they can only really do that if they have enough water to lose.”
Klinek and her colleagues studied coast redwoods in Mendocino County, near the southern part of their range, where the researchers used specialized instruments to measure whether or not individual leaves were photosynthesizing. During heat waves, they found, coast redwoods hit a point where they can’t cool down fast enough, and they just keep their stomata closed. While that saves water, it also means the tree isn’t taking in more carbon—which means it’s not “eating” or building up energy stores it can use to keep growing.
This may sound like a technicality of tree physiology. But it could have a big impact on these forests, creating a vicious cycle where trees don’t have enough carbon stored to replenish their leaves in the future, which means they won’t be able to photosynthesize as efficiently, which will starve them even further, repeating until trees eventually die. And while this sort of behavior has been observed in tropical trees, it’s the first time anyone has studied how coast redwoods respond to the same heat stress.
“The term people use is carbon starvation,” said Chris Still, a forest ecologist at Oregon State University who didn’t participate in the study. “Leaves can be expensive to build for a plant.”
Most of the redwoods in California and the Pacific Northwest nowadays are new-growth forests planted in the last couple of centuries. That means the trees are relatively hungry, like growing adolescents, compared to their old-growth cousins, so they need to suck in lots of carbon dioxide to grow taller.
Redwoods are also incredibly good at storing carbon. Thanks to their bulk and long lives, they store more carbon dioxide per acre than any other forest in the world. “Not only is it negative feedback on the climate system itself, with less carbon sequestration from these trees and forests, but the trees themselves are going to obviously not grow as big,” said Anthony Ambrose, a plant physiological ecologist and co-founder of the Ancient Forest Society. So even if the trees survive, they might not have as much space for fern and soil mats, which means less habitat for the creatures that live in them, and they may not grow as tall as they once used to, which could hurt them in another way.
A central threat to these trees, Klinek explained, is that in addition to the heat stress, they may also lose a crucial source of hydration and protection: Coast redwoods have an intricate relationship with the fogs of their native Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. The trees are so tall that their canopies reach high into fog layers, where they can sip water directly from the sky. The fog also shades the trees from the sun and helps coast redwoods create their own microclimate, which is why these forests are noticeably cooler than the areas adjacent to them. But warmer oceans and drier air are making fog more sporadic, which means the trees are missing a crucial source of relief from heat that is only getting more intense.
“It’s kind of a double whammy,” said Todd Dawson, a plant ecophysiologist at the University of California Berkeley, who also didn’t participate in the study. “They’re running out of water and also getting this heat stress,” he said. “They’re used to living in a very narrow temperature range of 8 to 27 degrees Celsius (about 46 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit). California, like everywhere, has been getting long periods of much warmer days than we’ve ever experienced, and now the fog, which is normally kind of like an air conditioner, has also declined between 30 and 40 percent.”
These temperature swings also impact the organisms living high up in the trees. “If they experience really excessive heat throughout the summer,” Ambrose said, “then the soil mats and ferns will probably dry out much faster. And then those salamanders and birds might not be able to live there. So we’ll see cascading effects through the whole ecosystem at that point.”
Klinek said, the trees seem to be doing okay after the heat passes; while the leaves she and her team looked at over their two-year study didn’t acclimate to the heat, they also didn’t lose their capacity to photosynthesize after the heat passed. While that’s a bit of hopeful news, it doesn’t reduce the urgency of the need to better understand the impact of climate change on these trees, and to reduce the warming itself.
“Right now the temperatures are coming back to normal in the fall and winter and letting the trees recover,” Klinek said. “But in five or 10 years, if temperatures are even hotter and heat waves are even more frequent, we don’t really know if there would be a recovery.”
For now, the salamanders and seabirds still have their homes high atop the coast redwoods. But we’re a part of the redwoods’ larger ecosystem too, even if we don’t live near them—they, like all trees, are key to keeping our planet hospitable. The trees Klinek studied have the potential to live for more than a thousand years. The question is if we’ll let them.

Sybiha stated that external criticism only demonstrates that Zelensky is performing his duties effectively, emphasizing that the Ukrainian head of state retains broad public support.
To facilitate the Russian fuel shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was granted three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which established mandatory statutory sanctions and tariffs on purchases of Russian petroleum.
The agreement was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were engaged in multilateral consultations with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami.
Zelensky described the Miami talks as a “smokescreen” for bilateral economic concessions to the Kremlin, noting that granting Moscow market access generates revenues that sustain Russian military operations.
Under the administration’s proposed diplomatic framework, Washington has asked Kyiv to halt drone attacks on Russian refineries to stabilize energy benchmarks. However, the proposal does not include a binding condition requiring the Russian military to suspend missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s power and heating infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials have stated that Kyiv will not suspend its asymmetric interdiction campaign against Russian refining installations without an enforceable, mutual energy ceasefire that protects Ukrainian utilities ahead of winter.

China wants private firms to lead key tech breakthroughs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:55:34 UTC
17:55:34 KST

- China’s Communist Party Central Committee and State Council issued guidelines with 19 measures to accelerate core technology breakthroughs and scientific self-reliance, Xinhua reported.
- The guidelines call for full implementation of the “AI Plus” initiative and give national laboratories and capable private firms larger roles in major projects.
China’s Communist Party leadership and the State Council have issued new guidelines laying out 19 measures to speed up breakthroughs in core technologies, expand the use of artificial intelligence across industry and make the country more self-reliant in science and technology, state news agency Xinhua reported on Oct. 9.
The guidelines are built around what Beijing calls “new quality productive forces,” a phrase Chinese leaders use for growth driven by advanced technology and innovation rather than by heavy investment and cheap labor. The 19 measures fall into five areas: scientific and technological innovation, linking research more closely with industry, new development approaches, institutional reform and talent development. Xinhua did not publish the full text, and it did not say how much funding is attached to the measures.
The document calls for faster breakthroughs in what Beijing describes as key core technologies and for strengthening key manufacturing supply chains. It gives national laboratories a leading role in organizing major state science and technology projects and calls for capable private companies to take the lead on some major national technology tasks, a role usually held by state-backed institutes and state-owned enterprises.
“The new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation has opened up broad prospects for developing new quality productive forces. Seizing this historic opportunity requires moving faster to achieve greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology and raising innovation capacity across the board to maintain strategic initiative,” said Wang Shengxiao, a researcher at the Party School of the Communist Party of China Central Committee.
On artificial intelligence, the guidelines call for full implementation of the “AI Plus” initiative, which aims to apply AI across traditional industries, and for faster innovation in AI and other digital technologies. They also call for systems to monitor technology, give early warning of risks and respond to emergencies so that AI remains, in Xinhua’s words, safe, reliable and controllable. Other measures cover national data infrastructure, digital manufacturing clusters, green manufacturing and the country’s energy transition.
The guidelines tell officials to balance self-reliance with opening up and to coordinate development with security. They also urge measures to avoid “involution-style” competition, the term Chinese officials use for destructive price wars among companies in crowded sectors, and they encourage foreign venture capital firms and international standards bodies to operate in China.
China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, covering 2026 to 2030, names the development of new quality productive forces as a key strategic task. The plan’s outline lists 28 major projects tied to that goal, about a quarter of the 109 major projects in the plan, focused on industrial competitiveness, emerging industries, cutting-edge technologies and innovation capacity.
“New quality productive forces are primarily driven by transformational technological breakthroughs, which bring profound changes to how innovation is organized, industries evolve and resources are allocated,” said Liu Zhenzhong, a researcher at the Institute of Industrial and Technological Economics of the National Development and Reform Commission. “These changes require deeper reforms to reshape institutional frameworks and remove obstacles to development.”

Houthis defiant after deadly Riyadh airport strike: ‘We’ll keep attacking, don’t fly there’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:55:25 UTC
17:55:25 KST

Yemen's Houthi rebels vowed Sunday to continue enforcing their declared air blockade of neighboring Saudi Arabia, hours after a Houthi missile exploded at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing 12 people and wounding 309. 
The rebels renewed their warnings to airlines and passengers as the Saudi capital's main airport remained closed following the unprecedented attack. In an official statement Sunday morning, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned airlines, airport employees and passengers against using Saudi airports or airspace, saying they "serve as theaters of operations for our forces."
In his statement, Saree declared that the Houthis remained determined to enforce the rules they had announced: "Airport for airport, blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation, until our objectives are achieved." He also accused Saudi Arabia of bearing responsibility for the consequences of any failed attempts to intercept missiles launched by the Houthis, urging the public to take the group's warnings seriously. Saree said the Houthis regarded all areas of Saudi Arabia as potential theaters of military operations, except Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities. His comments followed accusations by Riyadh last month that the Houthis had fired a missile toward Mecca, the destination of the annual Muslim pilgrimage and home to the Kaaba, one of Islam's most sacred sites. The accusation portrayed the rebels as threatening Islam's holy places.
Hours after Saturday's missile attack, flight operations at King Khalid International Airport remained suspended. A source in the Saudi aviation industry told AFP on Sunday morning that the airport was still shut. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported on X that the closure had been extended by another 24 hours, until midnight between Sunday and Monday, Israel time.
According to reports from Saudi Arabia, the Houthi missile exploded in the area housing Terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights. The dead reportedly included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Sudanese and a Palestinian. Many of the 309 people wounded were reported to be in serious condition. Reports Sunday morning indicated that hospitals in Riyadh remained filled with casualties from the attack. The strike was the deadliest attack on any Gulf Arab country since the war with Iran began in February.
According to Western sources, information collected following the attack indicates that the missile struck without any advance warning and that no sirens sounded before the impact. The deadly attack came just two days after an earlier Houthi strike on the same airport, in which at least one passenger aircraft, empty at the time, was hit. Three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in that attack. Several additional attacks targeted airports in Riyadh and the southern Saudi city of Abha earlier last week, killing three more people. The series of attacks marks a new peak in the escalating confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which has intensified in recent weeks alongside renewed fighting inside Yemen between the rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Saudi Arabia has supported those government forces with extensive airstrikes on Houthi-controlled territory.
On Saturday, President Donald Trump said the United States could join the fighting and assist Saudi Arabia in conducting strikes against the Yemeni rebels, although he emphasized that no decision had yet been made. Trump subsequently described the Houthi attack on Riyadh as "a terrible thing" and "unacceptable." United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres expressed "deep shock" over the airport attack Sunday morning. Germany also condemned the strike, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described it as "a dangerous escalation."
The Houthis have intensified their attacks on Saudi cities in recent days, increasingly targeting airports as part of a campaign to disrupt the kingdom's aviation industry and effectively close its skies. The rebels say the campaign is retaliation for Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions in Yemen. At the beginning of last week, the Houthis warned international airlines not to operate in Saudi airspace, declaring it an operational zone for attacks against the kingdom. They said they would not accept responsibility for the consequences if airlines continued to fly there.
The renewed confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia began in July, ending a four-year lull in Yemen's civil war. That conflict erupted in 2014, with Riyadh subsequently intervening in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. The latest escalation began after the Houthis attempted to break the air blockade imposed on them by Saudi Arabia, against the backdrop of an intensifying war involving Iran, their regional ally. Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid territorial offensive, capturing strategic coastal areas in southwestern Yemen overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The territorial gains strengthened their position along one of the world's most important maritime shipping routes. The Houthis had already demonstrated their ability to attack shipping in the Red Sea using long-range missiles and drones, but their advances on the coast gave them tighter control over movement through the strategic passage. Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea and Suez Canal shipping route between Europe and Asia, carrying approximately 12% of global trade.
Its strategic importance, particularly for Saudi Arabia, has increased dramatically because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula during the war with Iran. Early last week, Yemeni government forces aligned with Riyadh launched a major ground offensive aimed at driving the Houthis from their newly captured territory and regaining control of Bab el-Mandeb. Saudi Arabia has provided extensive air support for the operation, including heavy bombardment of Houthi-held areas. Reports indicate that pro-Saudi forces have advanced in the area surrounding the strait, although the extent of those gains remains unclear. The Houthis dispute claims by Yemen's internationally recognized government that its forces have already recaptured Bab el-Mandeb, leaving control of the vital waterway contested as the fighting escalates on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula.

Taiwan, Japan urged to deepen semiconductor and defense technology ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:50:48 UTC
17:50:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan and Japan should deepen cooperation in semiconductors, AI, and defense-related supply chains to strengthen economic security and counter pressure from China, experts said Sunday at a forum in Taipei.
The 2026 Taiwan-Japan Future Technology Forum was hosted by the Indo-Pacific Strategy Think Tank and the Japan Institute for National Fundamentals on Sunday at the Chang Yung-fa Foundation in Taipei, per CNA.
Participants included former Japanese Ground Self-Defense Force Chief of Staff Iwata Kiyofumi, Indo-Pacific Strategy Think Tank Executive Director Yaita Akio, former Minister of Economic Affairs Wang Mei-hua (王美花), and Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), director of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research’s Division of Defense Strategy and Resources.
Yaita said Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine had underscored the geopolitical risks facing Taiwan and Japan, highlighting the need for the two sides to move beyond traditional friendship and exchanges toward creating shared economic and technological value.
Taiwan brings strengths in semiconductor manufacturing, while Japan has a strong foundation in scientific research, advanced materials, and production equipment. Combining those capabilities could help both sides develop more resilient supply chains, he said.
Wang said Taiwan occupied an important position in the artificial intelligence industry, spanning chip design, servers, data center infrastructure, and AI models. Few places have such a comprehensive supply chain, she said, adding that Taiwan should recognize the value of its industrial capabilities.
However, Wang also highlighted questions about competition between open-source and proprietary AI models, including whether inexpensive Chinese-developed models could accelerate adoption while raising concerns about cybersecurity, data security, and trust. These issues could have significant implications for Taiwan’s technological development.
Turning to semiconductors, Iwata described Taiwan and Japan’s industries as mutually dependent, with Taiwan specializing in advanced chip manufacturing and Japan supplying critical materials and production equipment.
Without Taiwan’s advanced semiconductors, Japan’s automotive, consumer electronics, and defense industries would face difficulties, he said. Conversely, Taiwan’s chipmakers rely heavily on Japanese materials and equipment, making the two economies’ industrial capabilities complementary, per CNA.
Iwata said the two sides should also consider how to protect these supply chains against economic coercion and excessive dependence on China.
On security, Iwata pointed to Yonaguni Island, Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, about 110 kilometers from Taiwan. Taiwan and Japan occupy strategically important positions along the first island chain, which is central to regional security planning.
He said Taiwan’s location near the Bashi Channel, between Taiwan and the Philippines, also gives the island strategic importance for regional maritime routes and military operations.
Iwata argued that Taiwan-Japan defense cooperation should initially focus less on major weapons transactions, such as fighter jets and missiles, and more on dual-use components, materials, and modules that serve both civilian and military purposes.
He said Taiwan and Japan should reduce strategic vulnerabilities by avoiding excessive dependence on China for defense-related production and by building more reliable industrial partnerships. He added that a stronger foundation in parts, materials, and manufacturing could create opportunities for future cooperation as regional security concerns grow.

Russia shelled five regions of Ukraine: at least 21 people were killed and dozens were injured. Residential buildings and infrastructure were damaged.
Russian forces shelled Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv regions. At least 21 people were killed in the shelling, and dozens of civilians were injured, including children, UNN reports, citing the regional military administrations.

The highest number of casualties was recorded in Zaporizhzhia region. According to the regional military administration, 20 people were killed and another 37 injured as a result of Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia district.
The occupiers launched 904 strikes on 51 settlements in the region. In particular, they carried out 27 airstrikes, used 616 drones of various modifications, shelled settlements 35 times with multiple-launch rocket systems, and launched 226 artillery strikes. According to Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, energy workers are working to restore power.
In Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russians attacked four districts of the region more than 20 times with drones and artillery. According to Regional Military Administration Head Oleksandr Hanzha, six people were injured, including two children.
In Dnipro, apartment buildings, food warehouses, and cars were damaged. Four people were injured, including two eight-year-old children. One girl was hospitalized.
In the Zelenodolsk community of Kryvyi Rih district, a private house and infrastructure were damaged. In the Dubovykivska community of Synelnykove district, a residential building was damaged and one person was injured. In Nikopol district, Nikopol, the Marhanets, Chervonohryhorivka, and Pokrovske communities came under fire. A private house and a fire station were damaged there, and a man was injured.
In Kharkiv region, Kharkiv and nine settlements in the region came under Russian strikes over the past day. According to Oleh Syniehubov, Head of the Regional Military Administration, six people were injured, including a 14-year-old boy.
In Kharkiv, three women aged 42, 53, and 63, as well as a 46-year-old man, were injured. Another 32-year-old woman suffered an acute stress reaction. A 14-year-old teenager was injured in the village of Khotimlia in the Staryi Saltiv community.
Russian forces attacked Kharkiv's Kholodnohirskyi, Slobidskyi, and Kyivskyi districts. A civilian enterprise, a medical facility, and a cargo truck were damaged. In other settlements in the region, private houses, outbuildings, warehouse premises, and power grids were damaged.
In Kyiv region, four people were injured as a result of Russian attacks over the past day. According to the Regional Military Administration, 37 civilian and infrastructure facilities were damaged.
The greatest damage was recorded in Obukhiv and Bucha districts. In particular, 18 facilities were damaged in Obukhiv district, including 12 private houses, an apartment building, a production facility, and a car. Two people were injured.
In the Bucha district, 11 sites were damaged, including residential buildings, warehouses, a retail establishment, and infrastructure. One person was injured. In the Boryspil district, a private house, a solar power plant, vehicles, and an infrastructure facility were damaged. There is also one injured person there.
In addition, damage was recorded in the Vyshhorod and Bila Tserkva districts.
Emergency and municipal services are working at the sites of the Russian strikes. The aftermath of the attacks is being addressed, damaged buildings are being surveyed, and the final scale of the destruction is being determined.

How Effective Is Ukraine’s Air Defense? September Data Reveals the Answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:41:17 UTC
17:41:17 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
How Effective Is Ukraine’s Air Defense? September Data Reveals the Answer
Ukraine’s air defense and military aviation countered tens of thousands of Russian aerial threats in September 2026, including ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and various types of attack drones, providing a picture of the scale of Ukraine’s efforts to protect its airspace.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force on October 10, Ukraine’s Defense Forces destroyed more than 4,700 aerial targets and neutralized over 48,000 additional tactical-level drones throughout September.
The reported results included the destruction of 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, and eight Zircon missiles. Ukrainian forces also intercepted six Iskander-K cruise missiles and six Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles.
Russian-made Shahed drones accounted for a significant portion of the reported interceptions. Ukrainian forces destroyed 2,722 Shahed-131/136 drones and 1,935 Shahed-238 drones, bringing the combined total to 4,657.
In addition, the military reported destroying 86 S8000 Banderol weapons, 1,009 reconnaissance drones, and 719 Lancet loitering munitions.
Ukraine’s Air Force also maintained extensive aviation operations throughout the month, conducting more than 1,600 sorties. Approximately 1,300 were dedicated to fighter air cover, while more than 250 involved strikes against Russian targets and aerial support for Ukrainian ground forces.
Although the figures demonstrate the scale of Ukraine’s air defense operations, they do not provide an overall interception success rate. The Air Force did not specify the total number of Russian aerial weapons launched during September, making it impossible to determine what percentage was successfully intercepted or neutralized from these figures alone.
As Russia continues to expand its use of faster jet-powered drones, Ukraine is adapting its air defense capabilities to counter the evolving threat. More than 12 Ukrainian-made Sky Sentinel automated anti-drone turrets have already been deployed across Kyiv, with the systems successfully intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, including the Geran-5.

Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:39:17 UTC
17:39:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12 people and injures over 300
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country's main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
A Saudi-led coalition blamed Saturday afternoon's attack on the Houthis. It was the latest of several in the past week at King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, and marked the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter, and the attacks have sent up oil prices and rattled markets.
Following the attack, US President Donald Trump said Saturday he was weighing whether the United States would join Saudi strikes against the rebels.
Airport operations were suspended Saturday. Authorities later extended the closure until at least 9PM. Sunday, according to Flightradar24.
Also on Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 91 Yemenis were killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said 60 percent of those killed were women and children.
Mix of nationalities killed at Saudi airport 
The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the injured.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.
The Egyptian man was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flybas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera New television.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels.
The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies, including the United States, to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.
Shortly after the attack, Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. "We may. We're going to look at it," he said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Trump said later Saturday that he planned to speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a "fully-fledged war crime" and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier on Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the war on Iran. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key US ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognised government.
Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.
Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theatre for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group, and Pakistan International Airlines suspended flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

North Korea planted mines that hit South Korean troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:38:36 UTC
17:38:36 KST

- South Korea’s military and the UN Command concluded North Korea deliberately planted mines south of the border that wounded three South Korean soldiers on Sept. 21.
- President Lee Jae Myung drew criticism for calling the blast an “unfortunate accident,” while troops removed the remaining North Korean mines on Oct. 5.
South Korea’s military has concluded that North Korean troops deliberately planted the land mines that wounded three South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarized Zone last month, and it has removed the remaining mines, but President Lee Jae Myung’s description of the blast as an “unfortunate accident” has drawn sharp criticism at home.
The explosion happened on Sept. 21 in the western sector of the DMZ, in an area patrolled by the South Korean Army’s 25th Infantry Division. Two of the three soldiers were seriously injured. On Oct. 5, after a joint investigation with the U.S.-led United Nations Command, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said the blast was caused by North Korean resin anti-personnel mines planted south of the Military Demarcation Line, the actual border inside the DMZ. The UN Command recognized the mines as a violation of the 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement.
Investigators matched fragments taken from the wounded soldiers with a North Korean resin mine previously recovered from the Imjin River, and they found one more North Korean mine about 1 meter (3 feet) from the second blast site. The resin mines are made of plastic, which makes them harder to find with metal detectors. The JCS said two mines exploded and that soldiers saw a third, unexploded mine as they withdrew.
South Korean troops entered the area with specialized equipment on Oct. 5 and destroyed the North Korean mines at about 12:51 p.m., the JCS said. Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul called the operation effectively unprecedented in the history of the DMZ and a resolute response. On Oct. 8, JCS Chairman Gen. Jin Yong-sung told lawmakers he regarded the blast as a North Korean provocation and said the military would review further response measures.
Lee, who visited the wounded soldiers at the Armed Forces Capital Hospital, did not directly name North Korea in his Oct. 1 Armed Forces Day speech. He referred to the soldiers injured in an “unfortunate accident” and said he would keep working to reduce military tensions and restore dialogue with Pyongyang. His spokesperson later said the remark was meant to comfort the injured troops.
The opposition People Power Party seized on the wording. Party leader Jang Dong-hyeok faulted Lee for not assigning blame to the North, and lawmaker Lim Jong-deuk called the president’s stance submissive. Members of Lee’s Democratic Party noted that the mine removal was the first operation to clear North Korean mines planted south of the demarcation line and that the previous government of Yoon Suk Yeol took no major action after North Korea began fortifying the border in April 2024.
Criticism has also come from columnists. In an Oct. 7 column in the Chosun Ilbo, Yang Sang-hoon argued that Lee’s approach has gone further than earlier Democratic Party governments in accommodating North Korea, and he suggested that Pyongyang could try to use the case in which Lee is accused of involvement in illegal payments to North Korea as leverage. Yang said he did not wish to speculate that the case was driving Lee’s policy. Lee was indicted in 2024 over Ssangbangwool Group’s alleged transfer of $8 million to North Korea and has denied wrongdoing. His trials were suspended after he took office.

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Retail gasoline prices in Cambodia continued to surge on Sunday while diesel saw a slight drop, according to the latest Ministry of Commerce announcement.
From Oct. 11 to 21, the price of regular gasoline will rise 3.8 percent to 5,350 riels (1.31 U.S. dollars) per liter, up from 5,150 riels (1.27 dollars) during the previous 10-day period. Conversely, diesel prices fell 1.7 percent to 5,550 riels (1.36 dollars) per liter, down from 5,650 riels (1.39 dollars).
Driven by the Middle East conflict since late February, regular gasoline and diesel prices in the kingdom have so far jumped by 38.9 percent and 44 percent, respectively, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
To cushion the economic impact, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet said on Wednesday that the government has injected nearly 500 million dollars in subsidies to curb rising fuel costs and stabilize electricity prices. He affirmed that these subsidies will remain in place as long as global fuel markets remain elevated.
The Southeast Asian nation relies entirely on imported petroleum and diesel, as its offshore oil reserves remain unexploited.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said that soaring energy costs are hitting local logistics and manufacturing.
"This surge is driving domestic inflation and eroding consumer purchasing power, with food and agricultural products taking the hardest hit," he told Xinhua. ■

European Commission will propose visa restrictions for Russians in January, Politico reports
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:36:00 EEST
17:36:00 KST

European Commission will propose visa restrictions for Russians in January, Politico reports
The European Commission is finalising plans to tighten visa rules for hundreds of thousands of Russians who visit EU countries as tourists every year, aiming to strengthen the EU's defences against hybrid attacks.
Source: Politico, citing EU officials, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The EU representatives said the European Commission plans to put forward the proposals in the new year after a group of countries, including Poland, Sweden and Estonia, pushed for stricter visa rules for Russians, including former combatants who fought against Ukraine.
Last year, Russian citizens were issued around 478,000 Schengen tourist visas, a significant proportion of which were multiple-entry visas.
Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer believes this system poses a threat to European security amid growing concerns about acts of sabotage, arson and other forms of hybrid warfare sponsored by Moscow.
"It's obvious I think for everyone that we have vulnerabilities in our system that can be used by our enemies. As far as I understand things, the Commission is preparing a proposal that, according to what I have heard, should be launched in January next year. From a Swedish point of view, we would love to see it even earlier," Strömmer told Politico.
Strömmer welcomed the "progress" and "growing support" for introducing a stricter visa regime for Russians.
Other countries plan to raise the issue at the Foreign Affairs Council meeting on 12 October and propose additional restrictions on Russian diplomats in the EU.
Estonia has proposed a complete ban on entry to the EU for former members of the Russian armed forces. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said there are around 650,000 of these former combatants, and they would be banned from entering "person by person".
However, he said a tougher approach across the EU is vital for its security.
"I think a large number of these ex-combatants will come, supported by the Russian secret services, to Europe. And they will take over our organised crime and they will be heavily weaponised and supported by Russia to commit terror attacks or attacks against our societies. So this is very serious," the Estonian foreign minister stressed.
After an initial decline in the number of Russian citizens receiving visas to travel to the EU, "the numbers are not going down anymore", said European Commissioner for Migration Magnus Brunner.
"We urge the member states there to do a better job and to give less visas … to Russian citizens," he said.
"You never know who these tourists actually are," he said. "So that's why we urge the member states to decrease the number," Brunner added.
Background:
- In September, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that EU member states could tighten controls on the movements of Russian diplomats within the Schengen Area, ban visas for former Russian combatants and reduce the number of tourist visas issued to Russians.
- On 12 October, the EU Foreign Affairs Council will discuss the possibility of introducing additional restrictions on the movements of Russian diplomats between EU member states, potentially including a complete ban on leaving the country in which they are accredited.

U.S. Army drills drone defense in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:33:54 UTC
17:33:54 KST

- U.S. Army SGT STOUT and Sentinel radar crews trained with AH-64 Apaches in a live-fire counter-drone exercise at Grafenwoehr, Germany, on Oct. 5.
- The exercise focused on passing real-time targeting and early-warning data between ground sensors and aircraft to counter unmanned threats.
U.S. Army air defense crews in Germany fired live rounds at aerial targets alongside AH-64 Apache attack helicopters during Operation Skyfall II, an exercise built around sharing drone-tracking data between ground radars and aircraft.
The training took place on Oct. 5 at Grafenwoehr Training Area in Bavaria, according to U.S. Army photos released from the event. Crews from the 5th Battalion, 4th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, part of the 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade, operated SGT STOUT air defense vehicles and Sentinel radars, while Apache crews from the 12th Combat Aviation Brigade flew in the same exercise. The U.S. Army said the goal was to train crews to pass real-time targeting and early-warning information between ground sensors and aircraft to counter unmanned aerial threats.
SGT STOUT is the U.S. Army’s Stryker-based Maneuver Short-Range Air Defense system, built to travel with armored and mechanized units and protect them from drones, helicopters and low-flying aircraft. Its turret carries Stinger missiles, Hellfire missiles, a 30 mm cannon, a machine gun and its own radar. The Sentinel is a mobile radar that detects and tracks low-flying aircraft and drones and feeds that information to air defense units.
The 5th Battalion, 4th Air Defense Artillery Regiment was the first U.S. Army unit to receive SGT STOUT, getting its first systems in April 2021 and becoming fully equipped in late 2022. The U.S. Army has since fielded the vehicle to battalions at Fort Sill, Oklahoma; Fort Hood, Texas; and Fort Bragg, North Carolina.
Linking air and ground sensors lets a unit spot a drone with one system and engage it with another. A helicopter flying above treetops can see targets a ground radar may miss, and a ground radar can cue a helicopter crew toward a threat before they see it themselves.
The U.S. Army is also working on lighter short-range air defense for units that do not operate Strykers. Its next version, M-SHORAD Increment 4, is planned as a pallet-mounted system that can be loaded onto light vehicles, and General Dynamics Land Systems is showing a version on a Ford Ranger pickup at this week’s Association of the U.S. Army meeting.

Authorities in Pakistan have announced a state of emergency in the northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

The provincial governor will take charge with an advisory council, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad, adding that the arrangement will initially be in place for six months.
The move comes as the PTI has been preparing for a march on the capital, Islamabad, to demand the release of Khan, who has been in jail for more than three years but still commands widespread popularity across the country.
The march was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed until October 4 to allow talks between the government and the PTI leadership to take place.
The government, however, said it would not allow the march to enter the capital and has been preparing for weeks to prevent the arrival of PTI demonstrators in Islamabad. It has erected barriers using shipping containers to block main access routes to the capital.

Excavations resume at ancient Tyana Roman Baths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

AA Photo
Excavations have resumed at the Roman Baths in the ancient city of Tyana, located in the town of Kemerhisar in Türkiye’s central province of Niğde’s Bor district, following a 20-year hiatus.
The work, conducted under the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Heritage for the Future Project, aims to identify earlier phases of the baths and uncover associated structures, such as a palaestra (an exercise area or courtyard) or a gymnasium (a center for physical and intellectual education).
Archaeologists also hope to uncover evidence of cultural activity dating to well before Roman rule.
Osman Doğanay, head of the Tyana Excavation Team and a professor in the Department of Archaeology at Aksaray University’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences, told state-run Anadolu Agency that excavations at the Roman Baths had resumed after a two-decade hiatus.
Doganay noted that at least two other baths are believed to exist in the ancient city beyond the complex currently being excavated, adding that efforts to locate them would begin.
Tyana was a major metropolitan center in Cappadocia during the Roman period, and the baths under excavation were built by Emperor Caracalla in AD 213, he said.
“Changes were also made to the structure of these baths during the reigns of emperors who succeeded Caracalla. We can confirm this with certainty,” Doğanay said.
Excavations at the baths began in 2002 and continued for four years, uncovering numerous remains and artifacts. Researchers have since established the structure’s layout and confirmed that it was a public bathhouse, he said.
Located on the southern slopes of Tyana Mound, the baths were positioned to receive the greatest amount of heat, Doğanay said.
He added that archaeologists believe the complex received a significant portion of the water carried by aqueducts from the Roman Pool, citing water pipes discovered during excavations between the pool and the baths.
HH Bronze Age layer discovered beneath baths
Doğanay said the primary objective of the current excavation season was to identify earlier phases of the bath complex. Much of the work this year has focused on clearing layers of rubble and debris from the site.
Test excavations extending nearly 2 meters below the surface revealed that the baths had been built over a Bronze Age layer, he said.
“In our upcoming work, we will uncover all the sections of the baths and determine whether structures associated with sporting activities, such as a palaestra and a gymnasium, are present.
“At the same time, we expect to find important evidence of the city’s cultural heritage dating to periods long before the Roman era,” Doğanay said.
He added that measures were being taken during the excavations to protect the structure.
The team also hopes to make the historic Roman Baths a new regional tourist attraction.
“There is no comparable bath complex of this kind in the Cappadocia region. As part of our efforts to promote Tyana as a destination for tourism and contribute to the regional economy, we are working to include the Roman Baths in visitor routes through the ancient city and establish the complex as a destination in its own right,” Doğanay said.

The Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response Sunday after a strike at Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people, wounded hundreds, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in over a decade.
The coalition blamed the Iran-backed group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a "full-fledged war crime" that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.
The attack came during an unprecedented wave of Houthi strikes on the kingdom since a truce in the group's long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unraveled in July.
The spiraling violence has raised the possibility of a wider escalation, with U.S. President Donald Trump signalling Washington could join military action against the fighters.
One passenger said they witnessed a strike in the airport's domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the witness said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
Four Saudi citizens were among those killed in the attack, as well as two Bangladeshis, one U.S. citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement.
It said some of the 309 wounded were in serious condition.
Operations at the airport were suspended following the attack and authorities said damage assessments were ongoing.
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency situation," a medical source said.
Two doctors told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that several pilgrims headed to Mecca were among the wounded.
Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month.
Parents in the capital received emails Sunday, citing an order from the education ministry, saying "all schools in Riyadh will switch to distance learning for the entire week".
"The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia ... which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime," coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.
Earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted missiles targeting Saudi Arabia and destroyed launch platforms.
The Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the airport Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not immediately take responsibility for any new strikes Saturday.
Saturday's attack was the deadliest in the kingdom since May 2015, when a suicide bombing by the Daesh terrorist group killed 21 worshippers in a Shiite mosque in the eastern Qatif governorate.
The civil war in Yemen flared back to life in July after a four-year, U.N.-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015 and is now being drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbor's conflict.
Asked Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, Trump said: "We may."
He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in the kingdom "not acceptable."
U.S. media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for U.S. military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies were banning their staff from using the airport "over the next week."
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the "heinous attack" and reaffirmed Islamabad's commitment to Saudi Arabia's security under their defense pact.
The latest attack came on the eve of Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season, which begins this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas the group captured last month around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counteroffensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab el-Mandeb area – a key choke point for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Two Renoir paintings stolen in France recovered: mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:29:52 UTC
17:29:52 KST

Two paintings by French master Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been recovered a month after they were stolen from a museum in southern France, the town’s mayor has said.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and managed to escape with two works by the French impressionist painter, abandoning two others as they fled.
“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer.
“Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”
There has not yet been any statement from the police and Masson did not give any details regarding where the works were found or their condition.
The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum’s tree-lined grounds, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, Masson said at the time of the robbery in early September.
The theft took place in just a matter of minutes, shortly before 6 a.m. 
A source close to the probe told AFP earlier this week that police had arrested five people as part of the investigation.
According to Masson the museum alarm and police sirens forced the burglars, which he described as “well equipped and well informed” about the museum, to hurry.
They made off with a portrait titled “Madame Colonna Romano” and the depiction of a woman at a well called “Jeune femme au puits,” his office said.
The paintings dropped during their escape include “Madame Pichon” and “Coco lisant,” a portrait of Renoir’s young son Claude reading.
The police said at the time of the robbery that it was clear that they were not first-time offenders, and that they had scoped out the premises before the crime.
The Renoir Museum lies a half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir’s last home before he died aged 78 in 1919. Its collection comprises nine paintings by Renoir, according to the museum.
It also includes several sculptures by him, as well as objects and furniture that belonged to the painter, such as his easel and wheelchair.

Musk’s post marks the latest in a series of public criticisms directed at the Ukrainian head of state.

Zelensky has gone too far
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 10, 2026
Trump’s remarks and criticism of refinery strikes
Musk’s comments align with a public defense mounted by Trump on Saturday regarding a bilateral commercial diesel agreement reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking to reporters roughly a month before the US midterm elections as retail diesel prices approached $6 per gallon, Trump blamed Ukraine’s long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries for causing disruptions across international energy and agricultural markets.
“He wants to make problems for the world, for our farmers with diesel,” Trump told reporters, arguing that Zelensky had prolonged the war unnecessarily.
US Envoys Witkoff, Kushner May Visit Russia Soon
“Zelensky could have settled this war many, many times, but he chooses not to,” Trump said, renewing his calls for political change in Kyiv. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US president’s calls for a leadership transition in Kyiv drew a rebuttal from Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who affirmed on Sunday that only the Ukrainian electorate holds the legal and sovereign authority to determine national governance during wartime. Sybiha stated that external criticism only demonstrates that Zelensky is performing his duties effectively, emphasizing that the Ukrainian head of state retains broad public support.
Trump’s comments followed his announcement on Friday, Oct. 9, of a commercial arrangement with Putin under which Moscow agreed to deliver over 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, scaling up to 1 million tons in subsequent phases through 2027.
To facilitate the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary sanctions waiver running through April 2027.
The diesel deal was announced while a Ukrainian delegation was engaged in multilateral security consultations with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami. Zelensky described the Miami talks as a “smokescreen” for bilateral economic concessions to the Kremlin.
Under the framework promoted by the administration, Kyiv has been urged to unilaterally halt drone interdiction operations against Russian oil refineries to stabilize fuel benchmarks.
However, the proposal contained no reciprocal condition requiring the Russian military to halt missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s power and heating infrastructure.
Officials in Kyiv have reiterated that Ukraine will not suspend its asymmetric campaign against Russian refining installations without an enforceable, mutual energy ceasefire.
Ukrainian lawmakers and foreign policy officials have emphasized that degrading Russian downstream energy hubs remains necessary to constrain fuel supplies for Russian military operations and diminish state revenues funding the Kremlin’s wartime budget.

Will the Coalition move towards the right or centre?

Dimitar Paskov: The Bulgarian scientist who pioneered a treatment for polio

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:25:31 UTC
17:25:31 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
BG contribution
Dimitar Paskov: The Bulgarian scientist who pioneered a treatment for polio
His development of Nivalin earned him international recognition and helped pave the way for a medicine still used today
Sunday 11 October 2026 10:35
Sunday, 11 October 2026, 10:35
PHOTO Facebook / BNT
Font size
At the height of the polio epidemics that swept through the world in the 1950s, a Bulgarian doctor received what seemed like guidance from above – an insight that would offer hope to children facing lifelong paralysis.
According to a widely told story, he noticed a sudden improvement in the condition of a young girl who had drunk water from a glass of snowdrops standing on her bedside table in hospital. From this apparent coincidence came an idea that would help bring about an important advance in the treatment of polio-related paralysis, thanks to a medicine called Nivalin.
PHOTO Pixabay
The story of the remarkable Bulgarian doctor Dimitar Paskov begins on 18 October 1914 in the village of Gorno Brodi, near what is now the Greek city of Serres. After the First World War, Aegean Macedonia remained outside Bulgaria's borders, and his family, along with hundreds of thousands of refugees, decided to settle in Sofia.
In 1940, Dimitar Paskov graduated from the Faculty of Medicine at Sofia University and became a doctor in the village of Byaga, in southern Bulgaria. Four years later, he found himself at the front, tending to wounded Bulgarian soldiers. There he earned a reputation as “a universal favourite among soldiers and officers, helping everyone and always having a kind word for all”.
After the Second World War, he chose a career in science and travelled to Leningrad, determined to lay the modern foundations of Bulgaria's school of experimental pharmacology. There he met traditional healers and worked alongside medical specialists conducting research into animals and plants.
Paskov’s book on Nivalin and its applications.
PHOTO Knizhen Pazar
On returning to Bulgaria, Paskov became head of the Department of Pharmacology at the Higher Medical Institute in Sofia. His knowledge of the country's wealth of medicinal plants – a wealth which, he believed, was surpassed only by that of the Himalayas – helped him make his great breakthrough in 1956. His research into plants containing galantamine, including the common snowdrop (Galanthus nivalis) and the summer snowflake (Leucojum aestivum), led to the development of Nivalin, a medicine based on this naturally occurring alkaloid.
“After consuming cooking oil adulterated with machine oil, I fell ill and went blind. I travelled to Vienna, Brussels and London in search of a cure, but without success. I heard that in Bulgaria there was a professor who treated blindness like mine with a medicine derived from snowdrops. I arrived in Bulgaria blind and returned home able to see with both eyes. Three words I shall never forget: snowdrop, Nivalin, Paskov,” the Frenchwoman Marcella Goetz wrote in her diary.
PHOTO mu-sofia.bg
While the medicine was gaining recognition around the world, a bitter campaign was unfolding against Dimitar Paskov in his own country. He was accused of plagiarising the achievements of “great Soviet science” – possibly, according to accounts of the controversy, under Soviet pressure to ensure that the discovery remained Soviet intellectual property. Although Academician Sergei Anichkov, under whom the Bulgarian scientist had defended his doctorate, acknowledged Paskov's contribution to the development of the medicine*, a series of reprisals followed. Paskov was dismissed from his leadership position at the Institute of Experimental Medicine and resigned from the Higher Medical Institute.
Meanwhile, the man who had become the target of envy and intrigue in his own country was winning international recognition for his pioneering contribution to Nivalin, a Bulgarian medicine developed using locally sourced plant material. In 1961, French television broadcast a film about the scientist and his medicine. He was also invited to lecture at the Sorbonne.
A year later, the University of Bologna published Paskov's first work, Pharmacology and Clinical Application of Nivalin. Shortly afterwards, he published a monograph, translated into Italian and Russian, in which he described his research in detail. The work also became a model textbook of experimental pharmacology.
Undoubtedly, his greatest honour was the international Ennio Award for scientific achievement, presented to him in Naples and described as the equivalent of a medical “Oscar”.
PHOTO Pixabay
Dimitar Paskov died in 1986, leaving humanity a medicine whose active ingredient remains in use today. Galantamine is now used particularly in the symptomatic treatment of Alzheimer's disease, while Nivalin has also been employed in treating various neurological and neuromuscular conditions.
His legacy also includes some 120 scientific papers in pharmacology, a textbook for doctors and medical students, 20 inventions and a number of medicinal preparations based on Nivalin. Those who believed they owed their recovery to him expressed their gratitude in many ways. There were even press reports of a newborn girl being given the name Nivalina.
Voted “Person of the Century” by the people of the town of Peshtera, the scientist was laid to rest amid a sea of snowdrops. Thousands came to bid him farewell, lining his final path with the delicate, fragrant flowers whose medicinal properties had helped him bring hope to people suffering from paralysis far beyond Bulgaria's borders.
PHOTO Pixabay
* Although galantamine had previously been isolated and studied by Soviet researchers. Paskov's pioneering pharmacological work, alongside that of his Bulgarian colleagues, helped turn the substance into Nivalin, a medicine used in treating neurological and neuromuscular disorders, including paralysis associated with polio. - Editor's note.

English editor: E. Radkova

Riyadh vows response to airport attack, US weighs involvement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:22:21 UTC
17:22:21 KST

Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country’s main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility in a televised speech for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's international airport that killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Yemen's Houthis on Sunday renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports, saying the warning should be taken seriously and that the kingdom "bore responsibility for failed interceptions".
Indian national injured in Riyadh airport attack dies
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian national injured in the attack at Riyadh's international airport had died.
"We are in touch with the family and will provide all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains," the embassy said in a post on X.
The Indian national's death adds to the death toll from the attack at Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, which killed 12 people according to initial reports and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest such strike on Saudi Arabia in over a decade.
Netanyahu condemns 'horrific' attack on Riyadh airport
ICC fugitive Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday condemned the "horrific terrorist attack" on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia a day earlier.
"I condemn in the strongest possible terms the horrific terrorist attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh," Netanyahu wrote on X, adding that he extended Israel's "deepest condolences" to the families of the victims.
Houthis claim responsibility for Riyadh airport attack
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility in a televised speech for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's international airport that killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
A blast was heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Sunday, AFP journalists reported, a day after Iran-backed Houthi forces attacked the city's airport, killing 12 people and wounding hundreds.
AFP journalists heard a powerful blast in central Riyadh but the cause was not immediately clear.
France on Sunday called on Palestinian leaders to go back on their decision postponing legislative elections to next year.
The delay "deprives the Palestinian people of their right to democratically express themselves at the ballot box" for the first national elections in two decades, the French foreign ministry said in a statement.
Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday pushed back the legislative vote, which had been scheduled for November 28, to September next year, alongside a presidential poll.
Russia condemns Riyadh airport attack, calls for diplomacy
The Russian Foreign Ministry said on Sunday that it condemned the attack on Riyadh airport, Russian news agency Interfax reported.
The situation in the Middle East can only be resolved through diplomatic means, while taking into account the interests of all countries in the region, the ministry said.
France condemns 'heinous attack' by Houthis on airport
France on Sunday condemned the "heinous attack" by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis a day earlier on Riyadh's international airport and stressed "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
France, which is already lending troops and military equipment to Saudi Arabia, "will continue to remain by its side in its defence of its territory and its infrastructure", a foreign ministry statement said, calling on the Houthis to cease their attacks.
Saudi embassy in Kuwait organises buses for repatriation
The Saudi embassy in Kuwait on Sunday said it was organising buses to transport its citizens back to the kingdom after their flights were cancelled following attacks on Riyadh airport.
"The embassy said it would provide buses to transport Saudi citizens wishing to return to Riyadh whose flights had been cancelled, provided they have proof of a cancelled flight booking," read a statement posted online by the embassy.
UAE stands in solidarity with Saudi after airport attack
The United Arab Emirates said on Sunday it stands in solidarity with Saudi Arabia after the deadly attack on Riyadh's airport, and expressed support for "all measures" to safeguard the kingdom's security.
The UAE foreign ministry in a statement denounced the "flagrant violation" of Saudi Arabia's sovereignty. It "reaffirmed the UAE's full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its support for all measures aimed at safeguarding the kingdom's security and stability".
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the "lethal attack by the Houthis”, adding he is "shocked" by the attack.
"Attacks on civilians & civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," Guterres wrote on X.
I am deeply shocked by & strongly condemn Saturday’s lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which reportedly killed 12 people & injured hundreds of civilians. Attacks on civilians & civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately.
Iraq on Sunday condemned the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport, warning that it endangered "regional security and stability" and calling for an end to hostilities.
"Iraq calls for a comprehensive cessation of military operations, to spare civilians and the peoples of brotherly countries the consequences and repercussions, and to ensure that civilian facilities are protected," the Iraqi prime minister's spokesman Sabah al-Numan said in a statement.
Iranian authorities have executed a man for killing a police officer who was run over by a vehicle during clashes four years ago, the judiciary said Sunday.
The country has ramped up executions since the outbreak of the Middle East war in February and since anti-government protests erupted late last year.
"The death sentence for the killer of Reza Ehterami, a police officer serving in Iran's police emergency unit, has been carried out," the judiciary's Mizan Online website cited local prosecutor Aref Akbari as saying.
