Isaias threatens US Southeast with floods, tornadoes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:13:17 UTC
15:13:17 KST

Four people died in the southeastern United States as post-tropical cyclone Isaias threatened flooding and tornado risks Saturday as it moved northward after making landfall on Florida's Gulf Coast.
Isaias roared ashore late Friday as a Category 2 hurricane near the resort community of Destin, packing sustained winds of 105 miles (165 kilometers) per hour before weakening overnight, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said.
It was the first hurricane of an Atlantic season tamed by a historic El Nino weather phenomenon, and the first hurricane since 2024 to hit the US mainland.
In Mary Esther, a coastal community near Destin, Matt Howard said he was fortunate the storm weakened ahead of landfall.
Despite losing power and having his neighbour's metal shed crash into his backyard, "overall, we were okay," he told AFP.
"We hunkered down, got in the center of our house, and did all the things you're supposed to do, and luckily came out on the other side," he said.
Officials reported at least four deaths related to the storm, including two from trees falling on homes -- one near Pensacola in Florida and another in Birmingham, Alabama.
AFP reporters saw overturned vehicles, downed trees and power lines, and numerous buildings with damaged roofs.
Coastal streets were largely deserted after mandatory evacuations.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis warned of hazards from floodwater and downed power lines, urging residents not to run generators indoors after a man was found dead in a garage.
Around 440,000 customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia lost power, while the US authorised the release of up to four million barrels of reserve crude oil.
Flood risks
A major flood threat remained as the storm headed northward and inland. The NHC warned that some areas could see upwards of 10 inches (25 centimeters) of rain.
"Considerable flash flooding and landslides are also possible across the Southern Appalachians," it warned in a briefing.
The threat was particularly worrying in the mountains of North Carolina, where communities are still recovering from hurricane Helene of 2024.
That storm made landfall in the same Florida region as Isaias, but remained at tropical storm strength as it moved northward, dumping record amounts of rainfall into the mountains and leading to deadly flooding.
Isaias's late arrival this season is largely due to an El Nino of historic strength.
El Niño creates strong wind shear over the Atlantic, weakening storms, while reducing shear in the Pacific and allowing hurricanes to intensify.
The Pacific has already seen several hurricanes reach Category 5 strength, as weakening post-tropical cyclone Rachel approached Baja California and Hurricane Simon threatened western Mexico.

War update: 221 clashes on front line over past day, fiercest fighting in Pokrovsk and Huliaipole sectors
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in its update as of 8:00 on October 11.
The enemy launched one missile strike and 73 airstrikes, dropping 255 guided aerial bombs. In addition, Russian forces deployed 8,444 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,553 attacks on settlements and Ukrainian military positions, including 45 using multiple rocket launchers.
Russian artillery shelled multiple settlements in Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces aviation struck one Russian UAV command post.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, Ukrainian forces repelled three Russian assault attempts. Russian troops launched four airstrikes using 11 guided aerial bombs and carried out 171 shelling attacks on Ukrainian positions and settlements.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukrainian units repelled 10 Russian attacks. Russian forces attempted to advance near Starytsia, Vovchansk and Vovchanski Khutory, as well as toward Radkivka.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces made one attempt to improve their positions by launching an assault near Nova Kruhliakivka.
Attempts to break through Ukrainian defenses were repelled in the Lyman sector, where Russian troops launched 10 attacks near Nadiia, Novoiehorivka, Novoselivka, Lyman and Dibrova.
In the Sloviansk sector, Russian forces launched six attacks near Ozerne and Kryva Luka, as well as toward Pyskunivka and Mykolaivka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, the enemy conducted no assault operations.

In the Oleksandrivka sector, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.

In the Dnipro River sector, Ukrainian defenders repelled one Russian attack.
No signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected in the Volyn and Polissia sectors.

'Kicked him, covered his head and hit him again': Israeli daycare aide sentenced to 10 years for abusing 8 infants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:09:55 UTC
15:09:55 KST

The Central District Court in Lod sentenced Roan Abd al-Hay, a daycare assistant at Sigal's Kindergarten in Hod Hasharon, to 10 years in prison Sunday after she was convicted of 277 violent offenses against eight toddlers aged eight months to a year and a half. The court also ordered her to pay 450,000 shekels in compensation to the children's parents, to be divided according to the harm suffered by each child, and imposed suspended prison sentences.
Abd al-Hay was convicted in April of abusing children under her care between May and July 2023. The convictions included nine counts of abusing a helpless minor, 146 counts of assault causing bodily harm to a helpless minor and 122 counts of aggravated assault.
Among the incidents detailed in the verdict, Abd al-Hay kicked a toddler lying on a mattress, struck him forcefully on the head and back, covered his head with a blanket and pressed him against the mattress before hitting him again. In another incident, she violently shook a toddler and later threw her onto another child, turning away as both cried.
The court also convicted her of psychological abuse of the toddlers in her care, citing their prolonged exposure to violence and their inability to defend themselves.
During sentencing hearings, parents described the lasting consequences of the abuse. One mother told Judge Michal Barak-Nevo that everyday situations, including medical appointments and collecting her children from daycare, continued to trigger anxiety. She said she suffered from post-traumatic stress and that the ordeal had affected her ability to work and care for her family.
"Today you no longer enter my home, but you still enter my nightmares," she told Abd al-Hay.
Another mother said her son continued to suffer from nightmares, hoarded food and displayed fears associated with bathing and hot water, nearly three years after the abuse.
"Many professionals told us, as soon as we began treatment, that he wouldn't remember, but his body would remember. His body remembers," she testified.
Prosecutors had sought a 14-year prison sentence, arguing that Abd al-Hay had not accepted responsibility or undergone meaningful treatment. Her defense attorney disputed that claim, citing her young age, lack of a criminal record and prospects for rehabilitation. Abd al-Hay herself previously expressed remorse, telling the court: "I'm very sorry, and I know that saying sorry cannot erase the trauma, what they went through."
In her sentencing remarks, Judge Barak-Nevo addressed parents who had expressed guilt over failing to recognize the abuse. "You could not have known," she wrote, noting that Abd al-Hay had made an excellent impression on them and that they had checked the daycare and received positive recommendations.
"Do not blame yourselves," the judge told the parents. "There is no reason to."

US forces strike cargo ship attempting to breach Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:04:29 UTC
15:04:29 KST

Ahmet Salih Alacaci
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
US forces struck and disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after its crew allegedly ignored repeated warnings and attempted to breach Washington's naval blockade against Iran, the US military said.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said a fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, disabling its propulsion system.
The military said no crew members were harmed in the strike. The vessel had previously departed an Iranian port and was attempting to transit regional waters when it was intercepted, according to CENTCOM.
The incident came amid the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, which Washington resumed on July 14, two days after Iran said it had again closed the waterway following the resumption of US attacks on July 8.
CENTCOM said four commercial vessels have been disabled and 135 ships turned away during three months of enforcement.
US forces have also destroyed 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' (IRGC) oil transportation network over the same period, the command said.
Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said Sunday that a tanker caught fire after being struck on its port side by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. The crew was reported safe.
The IRGC said late Saturday that an oil supertanker had struck a naval mine and exploded while attempting to leave the strait through an unauthorized route.
It was not immediately clear whether the UKMTO and IRGC reports concerned the same vessel or whether either incident was connected to the US strike on the Ocean Molica.
CENTCOM warned commercial vessels to comply with blockade instructions and urged crews operating in the Gulf of Oman and near the Strait of Hormuz to monitor maritime notices and maintain communication with US naval forces.
Tehran has also warned that it could target vessels that use routes other than those designated by Iranian authorities or try to transit the strait without permission.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28 that has killed more than 3,000 people, according to Tehran. Iran retaliated with attacks that killed Americans and Israelis before a ceasefire was reached in April.
The US subsequently carried out additional strikes on Iranian sites amid stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran, despite the signing of a framework agreement in June.
Talks have remained deadlocked due to disagreements concerning navigation through the strategic waterway.

Following that call, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state media that Putin reiterated Moscow’s intent to sustain military operations until all Kremlin objectives are fulfilled, rejecting the resumption of formal peace negotiations.
Ushakov claimed that Trump instructed American officials to relay the diplomatic positions articulated by Moscow directly to the Ukrainian government.
Diplomatic outreach following Miami consultations
The prospective trip follows multilateral consultations convened by the US in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9. The leaders of India’s Cockroach movement accused the Narendra Modi government of declaring “war with its own citizens” and vowed to continue with their protest after being released from police detention, as anti-government unrest rocked Delhi for a second day.
The three leaders of the youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) were taken into custody on Saturday when thousands were detained by police as authorities went to extreme lengths to prevent young people taking to the streets to protest.
By Sunday morning, a magistrate had ordered that the three CJP leaders, Abhijit Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, be released on the condition that they would not “breach peace” for a year.
In a social media post soon after his release, Dipke, CJP’s founder, pointed his criticism directly at the prime minister. “Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said.
Saturday’s protest was called by the CJP alongside student groups and civil society leaders to demand the resignation of India’s election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of an “assault on democracy” by overseeing an exercise that has deleted 130 million names from India’s electoral roll.
Kumar is accused of implementing the voter roll revision to help Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) entrench its power and to disenfranchise minority groups such as Muslims who are not traditionally part of the BJP’s voter base.
Those who attempted to take part in Saturday’s demonstration were ruthlessly obstructed by a security crackdown, in which more than 25,000 police barricaded roads and the internet and public transport were shut down. More than 7,000 people were taken into police custody, many before they had even reached the protest site in the centre of the capital.
Despite the heavy-handed police response, it was still an unprecedented display of dissent against the powerful Modi government, which has been notoriously intolerant of any political opposition or criticism over its 12 years in power. Several senior opposition leaders were among those who tried to protest and were detained.
By Sunday, the centre of Delhi still resembled a high-security fortress, with roads blocked by barricades and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary still deployed. Supreme court judges have ruled that the government must restore internet and reopen the capital’s metro stations.
Small groups of students and Cockroach supporters, many freshly released from police detention, again attempted to demonstrate in Delhi and were detained.
Among those taken into custody for a second time was the student leader Neha Bora, whose repeated defiance in the face of the police crackdown has made her a figurehead of the movement.
In a video she posted on social media after she was picked up by Delhi police, Bora showed a detention bus with metal grilles over its windows and four small “jail-like” compartments secured with latches.
She said six to eight protesters were crammed into each of the compartments, leaving little room to breathe, and that male protesters were subjected to verbal abuse and physical violence.
“So many troops, so much police presence, so much violence, abuses targeting mothers and sisters, caste-based slurs – why?” Bora said in the video. “Simply because you want to protect a thief, Gyanesh Kumar.”
Marching alongside Bora was Surbi Yadav, 20, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, who said police detained her on Saturday morning. She accused police personnel of dragging her, injuring her arm and leg.
“They treated us like animals. They pushed us into a bus and took us to a sports facility that had been turned into a detention centre,” Yadav said, while showing scars on her arms. “The police kept misbehaving with us on the way and warned us against taking part in the protests.”
Yadav was released on Saturday evening. By Sunday afternoon, she was back on the streets with other students, holding a placard She vowed to return the following day and keep protesting until their demands were met.
“We are not afraid any more. The government and the police will have to understand that,” she said. “They can use as much force as they want to silence us, but it will be futile. In fact, it will only backfire. Every day, more people are turning against this government because of the way it is treating protesters.”
At a press conference on Sunday afternoon, the CJP leaders Das and Ranka condemned the police and government for turning Delhi into a “war-like situation” and reiterated their message of defiance that “this fight is on”. They added that it was no longer just about Kumar but also targeted at Modi and his home minister, Amit Shah.
“The state is at war with its own citizens,” Das said. “An atmosphere of fear has been created in country, it’s clearly being done to save one person. We want to ask Modi and Shah, why are you trying to save Gyanesh Kumar?”
There was no response from Modi to the accusations by the protesters. However, the BJP’s spokesperson, Gaurav Bhatia, said earlier that the voter roll revision was a legitimate exercise to remove dead and illegal voters and refuted any political interference.
“These are baseless allegations being levelled by an irresponsible opposition,” Bhatia said. “The claim that democracy is being destroyed and that the constitution is being undermined has no basis and not an iota of evidence.”
The weekend’s protests had drawn support from the leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, who has accused the Modi government of “vote chauri” or vote cheating through the voter roll revision. Gandhi was detained twice last week as opposition parties attempted to hold a protest in central Delhi calling for Kumar to resign.
“Mr Modi does not understand that the game is over,” Gandhi said on Saturday. “We will ensure that Modi pays for the crimes he has committed against the country.”

The eye has a hidden cleanup system scientists never knew existed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:01:54 UTC
15:01:54 KST

The eye has a hidden cleanup system scientists never knew existed
Scientists have uncovered a hidden waste removal system in the eye that could transform how we understand and treat blinding diseases.
- Date:
- October 11, 2026
- Source:
- University of British Columbia
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a hidden cleanup system at the back of the eye that drains fluid and waste through a previously unknown pathway. The surprising finding, demonstrated in mice, could open the door to new treatments for glaucoma, macular degeneration, and other causes of blindness.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown cleanup system at the back of the eye, revealing a hidden route that allows fluid and waste to escape into the body's lymphatic system. The discovery challenges long-standing assumptions about how the eye functions and could eventually lead to new approaches for treating serious conditions that cause blindness.
Glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, and several other major causes of permanent vision loss are associated with the accumulation of fluid, metabolic waste, and inflammatory material in the back of the eye. Until now, researchers have struggled to explain exactly how this sensitive region removes unwanted substances.
A team from the University of British Columbia (UBC) and the University of Toronto has identified a previously unrecognized drainage route called the posterior ocular lymphatic outflow, or POLO pathway. The system appears to carry fluid and waste away from the back of the eye and into the lymphatic network, which helps the body maintain fluid balance, remove waste, and support immune defenses.
The finding, demonstrated in mice, offers scientists a new way to investigate how the eye protects its delicate tissues and what happens when waste removal is disrupted.
"The retina is one of the most metabolically active parts of the body, constantly generating byproducts that need to be cleared," said Dr. Neeru Gupta, professor and head of UBC's department of ophthalmology and visual sciences. "This discovery helps explain how the eye flushes this waste and promises to transform how we think about and treat a range of eye conditions."
A Hidden Eye Drainage System Could Open New Paths to Treatment
The retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye, requires substantial energy to convert incoming light into signals the brain can interpret. This constant activity produces metabolic byproducts that must be removed to keep the surrounding tissues functioning properly.
When fluid and waste accumulate, they can contribute to conditions that damage the eye. Glaucoma, macular degeneration, and other retinal disorders are associated with changes in fluid regulation, cellular waste buildup, tissue stress, and inflammation.
Age-related macular degeneration alone affects approximately 2.5 million Canadians, highlighting the potential importance of understanding the processes that keep the retina healthy.
The newly identified POLO pathway suggests that the back of the eye has a natural mechanism for moving unwanted material out of this vulnerable region. If scientists can determine how that mechanism works and whether it can be strengthened, it could provide a new target for therapies designed to protect vision.
"This gives us a whole new framework for understanding these diseases and a potential target for therapeutics," said Dr. Gupta. "The question now is: How can we enhance or exploit this cleanup system to treat or even prevent disease."
A Discovery That Challenges More Than a Century of Assumptions
For over 100 years, scientists generally believed that the eye lacked the lymphatic drainage systems found in nearly every other organ.
The lymphatic system consists of vessels and tissues that collect excess fluid, transport certain waste products, and help coordinate immune responses. It works alongside the blood circulatory system to maintain healthy conditions throughout the body.
The idea that the eye was largely separate from this network began to change in 2009, when Dr. Gupta and Dr. Yeni Yücel identified a lymphatic-related drainage route in the front of the eye.
They named it the "uveolymphatic" pathway, providing evidence that the eye had previously unrecognized connections to the body's fluid clearance mechanisms.
Dr. Yücel, a professor and director of ophthalmic pathology at the University of Toronto, continued investigating the possibility that similar pathways might exist elsewhere in the eye.
Despite that earlier discovery, the back of the eye remained relatively unexplored. This was a particularly important gap because the retina and surrounding tissues are affected by some of the most serious diseases responsible for permanent vision loss.
"The retina is responsible for vision and it's also where many of the most serious vision-loss diseases occur," said Dr. Yücel. "Understanding how this part of the eye maintains a balanced environment and flow of materials is critical."
Scientists Trace a Secret Cleanup Route Behind the Retina
To investigate how fluid leaves the back of the eye, the researchers combined several advanced imaging methods in mice, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and microscopic examination.
They placed fluorescent tracer molecules into a narrow space at the rear of the eye. Because these molecules could be detected as they moved, the scientists were able to follow the fluid's path and determine where it traveled.
The results revealed tiny lymphatic vessels in the choroid, a thin, blood vessel-rich layer located beneath the retina. The choroid plays an important role in nourishing the outer retina, but lymphatic vessels had not previously been established in this region.
The team observed fluid moving from the back of the eye into the surrounding orbital tissues, which occupy the space around the eyeball. Within minutes, the tracers reached nearby lymph nodes, connecting the eye's newly identified drainage route to the body's broader lymphatic system.
This provided evidence that fluid from the back of the eye could enter an active drainage pathway rather than remaining confined within the eye.
"Because lymphatic vessels in the choroid were thought not to exist, the team used multiple techniques to demonstrate both their presence and function," added Dr. Yücel, a pathologist-scientist at St. Michael's Hospital. "We were surprised to see such a direct route for fluid to leave the eye and connect with the lymphatic system. It suggests the back of the eye has an active clearance pathway, which could play an important role in removing fluid, proteins and inflammatory material that build up in disease."
Could the Eye's Cleanup System Help Prevent Blindness?
Although the discovery offers a new explanation for how fluid and waste may leave the back of the eye, important questions remain.
The experiments were conducted in mice, and further studies are necessary to establish how the POLO pathway functions in humans. Researchers also need to determine whether changes in this drainage system contribute to eye disease and whether its activity can be safely modified.
If those questions can be answered, the pathway could eventually offer several possibilities for treatment.
One approach might involve developing therapies that improve fluid clearance, potentially reducing the buildup of substances associated with inflammation and tissue damage. Another possibility is using knowledge of this drainage route to improve how medications are delivered to structures deep within the eye.
Understanding the system may also help researchers investigate how pressure, inflammation, and fluid movement interact in conditions such as glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration.
These applications remain potential future developments rather than established treatments. Nevertheless, the discovery gives scientists a new anatomical pathway to study and a possible explanation for processes that have remained poorly understood for decades.
"This is a foundational discovery that shows the eye is not as closed a system as we previously thought," said Dr. Gupta. "It gives us a new map, a new mechanism and a new set of questions to explore."
The findings were published in the scientific journal Translational Vision Science & Technology.
The research was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Glaucoma Research Society of Canada, Henry Farrugia Ophthalmology Research Fund, Canadian Space Agency, Dorothy Pitts Chair, Stephen M. Drance Chair, Thor and Nicky Eaton Research Fund, and Canada Foundation for Innovation Leaders Opportunity Fund.

Teen revolt or revolution? The student protests threatening France's presidential race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:00:35 UTC
15:00:35 KST

French students' grievances include long school days, overcrowded classrooms, outdated facilities and teacher shortages. Their anger has resonated across Europe, with students in Belgium and Italy also staging protests.
Three weeks into France’s student protests, questions are mounting over whether the demonstrations will fizzle out or evolve into a broader social movement.
The protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September, before rapidly spreading nationwide. Dramatic images of students climbing the iconic column at Paris' Place de la Bastille on Thursday managed to capture audiences worldwide.
The scenes carried historical weight given that the square stands on the site of the former Bastille fortress and state prison, stormed by Parisians on 14 July 1789 in a defining moment of the French Revolution.
After its demolition, the Bastille became a lasting symbol of the triumph of regular citizens against political oppression. Taking to X on Thursday, hard-left France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon declared that the Bastille had been "retaken."
A range of student grievances lie at the heart of the movement, including long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down schools and teacher absences. Their anger has resonated with young people across Europe, with students in Belgium and Italy also staging protests in recent days.
Could the student movement grow into something broader?
Another day of protests, backed by student and trade unions, is scheduled for Tuesday, 13 October. Meanwhile, a separate demonstration against the cost of living crisis and rising fuel prices — planned before the student movement erupted — is scheduled for 17 October.
There is speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike. For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.
If student protests converge with wider social unrest, France could potentially face scenes reminiscent of May 1968. In recent weeks, many students have brandished banners referencing these historic demonstrations, which saw student protests escalate into a nationwide general strike.
At the time, several million workers joined the demonstrations, bringing the country to a standstill, but also sparking major wage negotiations. The movement also triggered a political crisis, prompting General de Gaulle, then France's president, to dissolve the National Assembly and call snap legislative elections in June 1968, in which his supporters secured a parliamentary majority.
Regardless, May 1968 left an indelible mark on France by dismantling rigid post-war social hierarchies. The demonstrations helped advance civil, student and labour rights, permanently embedding a tradition of mass protest into the nation's political identity.
France's tense political backdrop
At present, France's minority government is struggling to secure parliamentary support for its 2027 budget, as opposition parties resist proposed austerity measures. The country's public finances are squeezed, with the government projecting the public deficit to reach 5.4% of GDP for 2026, among the highest level in the eurozone.
The deepening cost-of-living crisis, driven largely by high fuel and energy prices, has intensified public frustration. The economic pressure on households has heightened social tensions across the country, less than six months away from the country's presidential elections — amid a highly fragmented political landscape.
According to a poll by public polling firm Ifop, carried out between 25 and 29 September, the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen (35%) is currently leading for the first round, followed by Edouard Philippe (15%) and Jean-Luc Mélenchon (14%). Under these projections, the second round would see a Le Pen-Philippe face off. Other projections have predicted a Le Pen vs Mélenchon scenario for the second round.
A movement which shows no sign of abating
Despite Education Minister Édouard Geffray's announcement on Thursday that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed nationwide to schools facing teacher shortages, public anger shows little sign of abating. Geffray said the measure would likely cost “tens of millions of euros” for 2026.
Unions have criticised the plan as a short-term fix, warning that available substitute teachers may not match schools' needs in terms of specialisms or location. In cases where no replacement is available, classes may still go uncovered, while substitute teachers may be assigned support duties until a matching vacancy arises.
“We need to look at the details, because we have to be careful with this figure that has been thrown around," Jean-Rémi Girard, a teacher and president of the national union of schools and higher education (SNALC) told Euronews.
From the onset, students have been supported by teaching unions, as Girard pointed to a system in "crisis."
"We are increasingly struggling to replace teacher absences, French classrooms are among the most crowded in Europe, classrooms aren't properly equipped during heat waves. These are things we already know."
"The starting point is that the school system is in crisis, and it has been for a long time."
Major trade union federations in France have also rallied alongside students. Following Thursday's protests, the CGT, one of the country's largest trade unions, highlighted a range of demonstrations, some of which were unrelated to the student movement, declaring: "The struggles are multiplying, and the balance of power is shifting!"
Parallels with past student protests in France
Paolo Stuppia, professor of sociology and politics at Sciences Po Paris, drew parallels between the current demonstrations and past social movements in France, citing a range of movements including May 1968.
"It’s not new for students from the suburbs to rally around demands that are specific to them, and then for those demands to be taken up by other secondary schools located closer to the city centre."
For Stuppia, the fact that students from private schools have also participated in blockades marks a new departure for student protest movements. Many observers were also surprised that students from the Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas, which is viewed as having a conservative student body, staged a blockade on Thursday.
Nevertheless, Stuppia warned that the movement's momentum could be impacted by upcoming school half-term holidays in France.
"When there’s a two-week school break, it becomes harder to get a movement going again afterwards, because everything has been on hold."
A movement which has expanded in response to police violence
While many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by sideline riots and clashes with law enforcement authorities. According to figures shared by France's Ministry of Justice on Friday, there have been 6,877 arrests since the beginning of the movement, with 86% involving minors.
The scale of arrests is striking compared with those made in the initial weeks of the yellow vest movement in 2018, which saw 4,596 people placed in police custody during its first month.
Rights groups have condemned police brutality following a wave of shocking injuries to students.
Outrage has grown over cases including a 15-year-old schoolboy who lost his left hand to a police stun grenade, a 16-year-old partially blinded by a rubber bullet, and a 14-year-old who suffered a shattered jaw and lost multiple teeth after being struck by a tear gas canister. The incidents are under internal investigation, with a total of 24 currently being conducted by the French police disciplinary body.
A United Nations spokesperson declared on Friday that the organisation was concerned about the situation in France, calling for demonstrations to remain peaceful and for the use of force to be proportionate.
Meanwhile, according to authorities, 761police officers and gendarmes have been injured since the beginning of the protests. Across the country, several schools have been damaged, burned or ransacked. In some cases, rioters have infiltrated the demonstrations.
For Stuppia, the level of police repression in recent weeks was "unprecedented" since May 1968 protests.
Meanwhile, Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author with Paolo Stuppia of "Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation", said police brutality has helped draw adults into the movement.
"Adults [trade unions and parents] have been marching alongside students, but have also intervened through contacting lawyers and magistrates, in response to violence and possible human rights violations."
However, she said that there was also a portion of the adult population which viewed the protests with "disdain" and "dismissed or discredited" them.
Increasingly politicised protests
In a TV address on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalised, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults.”
He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles.” France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” Lecornu said.
The government, joined by right-wing and far-right opposition parties, has accused Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party of exploiting and manipulating young people for political gain. Mélenchon has maintained that while his party supports the movement, it is not organising the protests and wants them to remain peaceful.
Ahead of the protests which took place on 5 October, the hard-left France Unbowed party hailed the fact that “student, secondary school, trade union and professional organisations" were "converging across the country."
For Becquet, although certain political leaders have been accused of “instrumentalising” student protests, secondary school students are on the whole able to distinguish between genuine political support and attempts to exploit the movement.
"There are people who have no particular interest in the movement, as you can see. Some are on the left, while others think 'well, this could be useful to us.'"
"Because of the way things work, and the way young people are treated — how they are dismissed and criticised — it ultimately creates opportunities for political intermediaries."
She warned that the protests could evolve into a broader social movement, given that frustration over school conditions reflect deeper anger about inequality across French society.
"There are inequalities at all levels, with gaps widening between different social groups."
"Given the rising cost of living, and the fact that working-class people already face numerous daily challenges, such as long working hours and commuting distances, in terms of social inequality, we are at a critical point."
Students share protests 'firsthand' on social media
Student demonstrations have spread rapidly across the country in part because footage of the initial demonstrations staged in the Paris suburbs went viral on social media.
According to Olivier Ertzscheid, senior lecturer in Information and Communication Sciences at the University of Nantes, social media allows students to organise themselves, but also to document protests firsthand from the ground.
"Social media allows them to document reality, to provide firsthand accounts of what is happening, both when things go well and when, unfortunately, they do not. Police investigations are now open, and social media images can be used as evidence, or at least play a part in the legal process."
Ertzscheid said that social media is also actively fostering a sense of connection and shared identity among protesters, which drives momentum.
"It is a way of building a sense of group identity and expressing one’s social connections, including their political awareness or at least civic engagement. This notion of young people's sense of belonging and social interaction is at play here, and these are very important in an age where the use of social media is so widespread."
Given that a large proportion of young people in France and across the world rely on social media as their main news source, the medium has also played a role in informing their perception of the protests, as well as the government's response.
Ertzscheid said there are no "hard and fast rules" governing how protests might evolve in coming weeks.
"Whatever happens next with this movement, we know that the media and social networks will act as echo chambers. By itself, no social media platform — however powerful it may be — is strong enough to trigger a movement. But these platforms are certainly helping with visibility and allowing students to get organised very quickly."
He described several different "converging" agendas ahead of upcoming protests in France, stating that "it is possible, that all these different starting points for anger or discontent could eventually converge. But equally, it is entirely possible that the student movement will fizzle out.”

‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:00:18 UTC
15:00:18 KST

New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election.
Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week.
The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell, but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come.
The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills, a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000.
Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.”
Housebuilders have been among the biggest donors to the Conservative party, though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit.
Simon McWhirter, the chief executive of UKGBC, said: “The housebuilding industry has spent years preparing for the introduction of the FHS, investing in skills, supply chains and new products. Reversing course would … risk slowing progress towards building the homes that people want and need.”
Badenoch’s housebuilding plans are only part of a torching of the Tories’ green policies. Despite the crisis of sewage and farm pollution in the UK’s rivers and beaches, and the dramatic drop in wildlife, the party would abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England.
The party’s U-turn on environmental issues and net zero was contrary to what voters wanted, said Robbie MacPherson, Kennedy scholar at Harvard University and the former head of the UK’s all-party parliamentary group on climate. “No winning political strategy, after years of fossil fuel-driven energy price spikes and a summer of climate breakdown, can include environmental regression.
“Voters won’t reward politicians who want to kill employment opportunities, spurn economic growth and fail to keep Britain safe.”
While the Conservatives spent their party conference burning their green credentials, an equally unexpected U-turn came from the Green party, which resolved last weekend to abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear power.
Although the party would still prioritise renewable energy, Green MPs could now support new reactors, in recognition of their potential role in low-carbon generation.
Paul Dorfman, Bennett scholar at the University of Sussex and the chair of the Nuclear Consulting Group thinktank, said: “The Green party has taken a wrong turn on nuclear and this will lose them significant grassroot support and votes.
“With 20-plus-year construction times, repeated delays and huge cost overruns, new nuclear diverts scarce resources from faster options. Renewables, storage, efficiency and stronger grids can deliver much more for every pound spent.”
The battle between the Green party and the Labour party in this week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection is likely to be repeated during the general election, where the Greens could be the main challengers in urban Labour strongholds.
Responding to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “Abdi-Wali has shown that voters are putting their trust in Labour, but the Green party increased its share of the vote and remains a serious challenger. As extreme heat becomes a regular threat and droughts extend for much of the year, concern about climate change is on the rise and cannot be ignored.”
At Labour’s conference, Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature. He announced a publicly owned body to invest in the energy grid, alongside the privatised National Grid, which has been criticised for slow progress on upgrades. There was also a nod towards localised support for nature with a community fund for planting 500,000 trees across England.
McCarthy said: “Voters will be comparing Labour with other parties that have a clear plan to lower energy bills and tackle the climate crisis rather than with the fantasies of the Conservatives and Reform. Labour has a clear plan but needs to deliver it – starting with a full-throated rejection of any scramble for fossil fuels in the North Sea.”
The decision on the future of the Rosebank and Jackdaw drilling sites was reportedly postponed for the byelection, and McCarthy said it would “truly define this government’s legacy on climate”.
Failure to recognise and tackle the damage caused to the UK by a summer of record heat and drought would prove costly, campaigners warned. A record El Niño weather system is brewing, super-charged by global heating and likely to bring heatwaves, droughts and floods to key agricultural areas, pushing millions into hunger and raising food prices globally.
Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “With El Niño bringing a wetter and stormier winter season to the UK, we desperately need to see some parties getting back in touch with reality. The government must translate its words into action that delivers for people and the planet.”

‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentially
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:00:18 UTC
15:00:18 KST

You’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your Google calendar. There’s an entry for a meeting that you must have completely forgotten. The note that pops up when you click on it says you’ll be reviewing a project and includes a link to more details. Confused, you follow it to find out more; the website you land on asks for logon details, and you provide them.
Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank, or another institution.
Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”.
The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar.
It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder.
“Calendar apps, such as Google Calendar, can add invitations automatically without users even accepting them,” Wescott says. “So scammers don’t even need you to open an email.”
And while you may not look twice at one from someone whose name you do not recognise, when something turns up in your calendar you may treat it differently. “It can create a borrowed credibility by showing up in the same place as your dentist appointment or a weekly 1:1 with your boss,” he says.
Max Gannon, an intelligence analysis manager at the cybersecurity company Cofense, says some scammers are using legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, making them look more convincing to the recipients, and to security software.
“That makes it really hard to block,” he says. “Even AI-backed blockers struggle.”
If you set up something to filter out invitations from these platforms, he says “that would also block any legitimate meeting invitations”.
What it looks like
You will receive an email and see an entry in your calendar. The titles vary: examples seen by the Guardian include fake meetings, notifications of voicemail messages, and software renewals.
Wescott says this is standard. “We typically see stuff like ‘New voicemail received’, ‘Payment receipt confirmation – $298.99’, ‘PayPal unusual activity’ warnings, ‘Your auto-payment will be processed within 24 hours’, and invitations to bid on a contract,” he says.
Gannon says the invitation could look like it has come from within your company. “If they want to they could make it look like an internal invitation,” he says. “They can customise the content, may be adding the logo of your company.”
The event description will typically contain a link, or a phone number.
Wescott adds: “Either they want you to click a link to a fake login page like Microsoft, Google or PayPal, and enter your password, or to call a ‘support’ number to cancel a charge that never actually happened.”
Until you click on this, or make a call, you are not compromised. The scammers do not have access to everything in your calendar – they are just trying to lure you to a place where you will hand over your details.
As Wescott says, “it sounds familiar to typical phishing, it’s the same technique, just using a different delivery method”.
What to do
Don’t panic if you see an unexpected meeting or reminder in your calendar. Treat it as you would an unexpected email and don’t click on the link.
“My number one advice is people just need to be paranoid,” Gannon says. “It doesn’t matter if the invitation has come from someone two desks down, you’ve got to be suspicious of everything.”
Wescott advises turning off automatic accepting. In Google Calendar you can go into settings and opt to only accept invitations from known senders, or when you have accepted.
He adds: “Don’t click ‘decline’ on suspicious invites as it can tell the sender that your address is ‘live’. Instead, delete or report it as spam/junk.”

Healing waters: 10 of the best spa towns in Europe for a restorative autumn break
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:00:18 UTC
15:00:18 KST

Mariánské Lázně, Czechia
In 2021, Unesco designated 11 historic spa towns across Europe as one transnational world heritage site, recognising their “exceptional testimony to the European spa phenomenon, which gained its highest expression from around 1700 until the 1930s”. This was the original wellness tourism, and these grand health resorts include Bath in England and the town of Spa in Belgium, as well as the west Bohemia spa triangle of Karlovy Vary, Františkovy Lázně and Mariánské Lázně.
Of that trio, Karlovy Vary is the most well known and within a day trip of Prague, but Mariánské Lázně is arguably the prettiest. The town offers three natural healing traditions: mineral springs, carbon dioxide springs known as Maria’s Gas, and therapeutic peloids (mud and clay). Czech nationals are still prescribed weeks-long spa stays to recover from surgery, severe illness or chronic conditions, but anyone can check into the Nové Lázně hotel (doubles from €234 B&B, including spa access), a canary yellow neo-renaissance confection built in 1896 that faces the central park.
Its spa is a trip back in time: baths surrounded by marble columns and intricately decorated treatment cabins, including one built for King Edward VII, who visited nine times. Join tourists and locals drinking the waters from special porcelain cups while walking along the colonnades, and don’t forget to pair it with a spa wafer – large, thin, crispy confections with sweet fillings such as hazelnut or chocolate. It’s not all virtuous.
Bad Kissingen, Germany
Germany is home to about 350 designated spa towns, including three of the Unesco Great Spa Towns of Europe: celebrity favourite Baden-Baden, quiet riverside Bad Ems and elegant Bad Kissingen in Bavaria. The latter’s striking architecture is arguably the most interesting of the three, much of the central spa district having been rebuilt by star German architect Max Littmann in the early 20th century. This includes the grand fountain hall, with its stained-glass roof, where Brunnenfrauen (fountain women) dispense different mineral waters from bronze pipes, and the huge basilica-style Wandelhalle, where the town’s spa philharmonic orchestra performs several times a day.
Music has always been part of the spa experience – the Staatsbad Philharmonie Kissingen holds the world record for the most concerts performed in one year (727!) – and the beautiful art nouveau-style Regentenbau houses one of the best concert halls in Europe.
The modern KissSalis Therme (from €19 for two hours) on the southern edge of town is the main public bathhouse today, with indoor and outdoor thermal pools, mud treatments and various – clothing-free – saunas.
At the more classical end of the spa spectrum, the Grand Hotel Kaiserhof Victoria (doubles from €209 B&B, including spa access) sits next door to the Wandelhalle on the town’s Kurgarten. The water used in the spa here is pumped up directly from the brine spring, while the inhalation room has a wooden graduation tower covered in knobbly salt deposits, which mimics the healing effects of mineral-rich sea air.
Bad Wildbad, Germany
Deep in the north of the Black Forest, this spa town offers ways of immersing in nature beyond soaking in waters from the thermal springs. Rising above the town, Sommerberg (meaning “summer mountain”) will get pulses racing. A funicular railway whizzes visitors to the top, the starting point for hiking and biking routes. For more heart-pumping views, the accessible Treetop Walk (€12.50) spirals above the dense pine trees to an observation tower 40 metres up, with a tunnel slide back down the middle for extra thrills, while the Wildline suspension bridge (€9.50) – with its 380-metre walkway – arches over the Enz valley for maximum views.
Back in town, there are two thermal baths to dip into: the modern Vital Therme, where those with joint and back problems are prescribed movement therapy and spa treatments (€14 for three hours); and the historic Palais Thermal, where the pools are surrounded by marble pillars, statues of Venus and Moorish tiles (€21 for three hours). Mokni’s Palais Hotel is connected to the Palais Thermal building, meaning guests can pad over in their bathrobes (doubles from €183 B&B, including access to the spa).
Bagnoles-de-l’Orne, France
Local legend has it that, after many battles, the medieval lord Seigneur Hugues de Tessé freed his faithful warhorse Rapide in Normandy’s Andaines forest to live out the rest of its days in peace. Much to the nobleman’s surprise, the horse later returned to him stronger and full of life, then led his master to the warm, sulphurous waters of Bagnoles’ spring. Centuries later, a spa resort sprang up so the Parisian bourgeoisie could also tap into this fountain of youth, with belle époque villas laid out on the shores of a lake in the middle of the forest (today, it’s also handily less than an hour and a half from the ferry at Caen for British wellness seekers).
That belle époque quartier was the vision of local politician Albert Christophle, whose former hunting lodge on the edge of the village is now the very lovely five-bedroom Château du Gué aux Biches (doubles from €195 B&B).
This summer, its Danish owners, Klaus Bentin and Soren Rasmussen, added a new restaurant in the old kitchen, serving up smørrebrød (open sandwiches).
The hotel has a partnership with the nearby spa at B’O Resort, meaning Klaus or Soren will line up your treatments, and there are bicycles to borrow so you can pedal a couple of kilometres over for that clay body wrap or hydromassage.
The surrounding forest is crisscrossed with hiking, biking and trail running routes. In autumn, take things more meditatively by going mushroom foraging among the more than 1,700 varieties sprouting from the Andaines forest floor.
Bad Gastein, Austria
This genteel town in the Hohe Tauern Alps was built on water; indeed, a roaring waterfall cascades right through the middle of it. The healing reputation of its radon-rich waters, which bubble up from the town’s thermal springs, saw grand hotels built in the 19th century to house the emperors and aristocrats, writers and thinkers (Sigmund Freud among them) who came to be cured of their ills.
The fashion for “taking the waters” trickled away, but in recent years there’s been something of a revival, with a clutch of new hotels opening. The Cōmodo (doubles from €188 B&B) is one of them, a slick spot refashioned from a 1960s sanatorium. Bedrooms look out over the valley and mountains, as does the thermal water-filled indoor pool. There are several public fountains where you can still drink water straight from the source (warm, slightly salty and metallic tasting), but perhaps more palatable is to soak at the brutalist Felsentherme public bath complex with its numerous pools (€40 for a day pass).
Just as warming – but with fewer health benefits – is a bowl of Kaspressknödelsuppe (beef broth with cheese-infused dumplings) at the cosy cabin of Schafflinger Alm (soups from €4.50, mains from €17) after a bracing hike through the forest or carving up the Schlossalm-Angertal-Stubnerkogel ski area, where the season kicks off in late November.
Piešťany’s Spa Island, Slovakia
Just before crossing the Colonnade Bridge to get to Piešťany’s Spa Island, there’s a statue of a man breaking his crutch, symbolic of the healing powers of the town’s thermal waters and sulphurous mud, harnessed on this enclave of wellness in the Váh River. The first simple wooden bathhouses were built on the island in 1778, but the opening of the Thermia Palace hotel and its Irma Balneotherapy House in 1912 turned it into a health resort.
Further hotels and spas are dotted between the trees and become increasingly concrete and functional as you get further from the bridge.
The Thermia Palace is still the fanciest option, with a raft of treatment programmes in the spa, from extensive diagnostics and lab tests to mud packs and pools (doubles from €210 half-board, including spa access). The blue-black goop is applied all over the body at a toasty 45C and left for about 10 minutes before being unceremoniously hosed off.
Outside, the spa park also feels restorative, with lily ponds, fountains and free-roaming peacocks.
In town, Elektrárňa Piešťany is a former power plant turned cultural centre that feels surprisingly vital, with film festivals and rock concerts, while the strikingly brutalist House of Arts hosts chamber orchestras and tango music trios.
Rogaška Slatina, Slovenia
This town in eastern Slovenia is famed for Donat Mg, one of the world’s most magnesium-rich mineral waters, traditionally consumed for its digestive benefits. The company now sells millions of bottles of the stuff each year, but here at the source you can sip it for free from the fountains in the Pivnica Drinking Hall – although its salty, fizzy, metallic flavour is something of an acquired taste.
Like other towns of its ilk, Rogaška attracted the great and the good of Europe in the 19th century, and its confection of architecture is testament to that. A short stroll away from the drinking hall, through immaculately clipped gardens, the butter-yellow Grand Hotel Rogaška is straight out of the town’s golden age (doubles from €198 half-board include spa access). Bedrooms are traditional, but the spa has all the bells and whistles, from carbon dioxide baths and mineral water inhalations to reflexology and magnetotherapy.
Somewhat fittingly for a town famous for its drinking water, Rogaška is also known for its glassware – and visitors can tour the Rogaška crystal factory (€12) to see the glass-blowing in action before buying glasses for their Donat Mg from the on-site shop. The surrounding wooded hills are the place for autumn walks.
Salsomaggiore Terme, Italy
In Emilia-Romagna’s so-called “food valley”, not far from Parma, this small spa town will help balance out some of that indulgence. Last year, the Italian thermal brand QC Spa of Wonders reopened the beautiful art deco-style Terme Berzieri, where the gilded interiors – all frescoes, mosaics, majolica and stucco – are as much of a draw as the salty spring waters, rich in iodine and bromide (five-hour spa sessions from €62). There’s the usual thermal attractions, as well as a sauna cinema and infinity rooftop pool, while treatments in wooden barrels nod to the area’s winemaking.
Try some of those wines at the Cantina Il Poggio vineyard in the hills outside Salsomaggiore, which produces a range of styles including the local sparkling Malvasia di Candia Aromatica (tastings from €30). Continue the tastings with a visit to a parmigiano reggiano producer, such as Caseificio Ugolotti (tour and tasting €23), before picking up some ham from Parma’s famous La Prosciutteria. Stop for a roast pork sandwich at legendary panini place Pepèn, before feasting your eyes on the Pilotta Palace complex with the Galleria Nazionale, Palatine Library and Farnese theatre, while the opulent Teatro Regio hosts the annual Verdi festival in October. The organic agriturismo Case Zucchi, about a 10-minute drive from Salsomaggiore, makes a suitably foodie base, with bedrooms named after herbs and the breakfast table piled with fresh bread, eggs, ham, cheese and fruit each morning (doubles from £104 B&B).
Caldas de Monchique, Portugal
High in the Serra de Monchique mountains, surrounded by cork oak and eucalyptus forests, the whitewashed hill town of Monchique offers a slower-paced autumn escape than the nearby Algarve coast. Its cobbled streets are lined with craft shops, ceramic workshops and simple taverns serving chouriço (smoked sausage) with a small glass of medronho (fruit brandy). In a wooded valley below town, the spa village of Caldas de Monchique is little more than a handful of 19th-century buildings around a shaded square and park, where you can drink slightly warm spring water from the public fountain.
Wallow in the alkaline waters a little longer at Caldas de Monchique Villa Termal Spa Resort (doubles from €84, thermal water circuit £17 for 90 minutes).
The spa offers hydro rituals including a Vichy shower, massage and bath, or thermal water circuits around the pools, sauna and Turkish baths, before a dip in the outdoor pool.
Afterwards, the 1692 restaurant, with its stained-glass windows, dishes up bacalhau à Monchique (salt cod stuffed with chouriço and ham). It’s not far from here to Fóia, the highest mountain in the Algarve at 902 metres. It’s worth the walk to the summit for the views, or hike on a further 2½ miles (4km) to the Barbelote waterfall, which cascades over a rocky cliff face in the wetter months.
Chaves, Portugal
There’s a little run of spa towns in the north of Portugal near the Spanish border, a curative route through Pedras Salgadas, Carvalhelhos, Vidago, Carlão and Chaves.
In Chaves, the waters are some of the hottest in Europe, coming out of the ground at a scorching 76C. The Romans built a large therapeutic bathing complex here, that was only rediscovered by accident in 2006 when work began on an underground car park. Now, the free Museu Termas Romanas de Chaves allows visitors to explore the pools and soaking baths, perfectly preserved thanks to an earthquake in the 4th century that sealed them for millennia.
To take the waters today, head to the Aquae Salutem Thermal Complex (€30 for 90 minutes), a circuit of outdoor pools, saunas, steam and showers that opened in 2025.
About half an hour down the road, the Pedras Salgadas Spa and Nature Park sits on the fringes of one of the other small spa towns. The owners have built 18 eco-houses and treehouses on stilts (doubles from £171 B&B, spa access additional £17 per room) among the pine trees at the source.
Guests can do a spot of forest bathing before dipping into the spa – redesigned by one of Portugal’s most famous architects, Álvaro Siza – for a thermal water hydro-massage, or wander between the pink spring pavilions in the park. Pedras Salgadas is also a popular, naturally sparkling mineral water brand.

Animals and their people: country shows across the UK – in pictures

Animals and their people: country shows across the UK – in pictures
Photographer Irina Werning, who grew up in rural Argentina surrounded by animals, has spent the summer photographing animals and their people at county and agricultural shows across the UK, from Essex and Kent to Surrey, Gloucestershire and Buckinghamshire, a project she began in Argentina.
‘As animals become less visible in the countryside, I’ve turned to agricultural shows – places where people still gather to see and celebrate them. For the past four years, I’ve photographed these fairs in Argentina and the UK, exploring our changing relationship with animals. I see them as a kind of Darwinian theatre, looking for moments when humans and animals unexpectedly mirror each other’

Nearly seven years after announcing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would be indicted, and a decade after disclosing that a preliminary examination into his affairs was underway, former Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit arrived Sunday at the Jerusalem District Court to testify in Netanyahu's corruption trial.
Mandelblit entered the courthouse accompanied by two police officers and court security personnel. Netanyahu also arrived for the hearing, which took place just over two weeks before Israel's October 27 election.
Among those attending the testimony were Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and Efi Nave, the former head of the Israel Bar Association who was defeated in the Likud primaries. It was the first time Sa'ar had attended a hearing in Netanyahu's trial.

Mandelblit, appearing as a defense witness, is expected to face questions from Netanyahu's attorneys, Amit Hadad and Noa Milstein, focusing primarily on whether he authorized investigative actions taken against the prime minister and whether police carried out certain steps without his knowledge or approval.
The question of authorization has become a central issue in the defense's challenge to the investigation. Netanyahu's lawyers argue that some investigative actions were conducted without the necessary approval from the attorney general, while prosecutors maintain that the investigative steps were lawful and properly authorized.
At the defense's request, Mandelblit was summoned to testify over seven nonconsecutive days. However, it remains unclear whether the judges will allow the full seven days, as questioning concerning the attorney general's authorizations may require less time than the defense has requested.
Mandelblit's testimony is expected to focus on decisions made during the investigation that ultimately led to the criminal charges against Netanyahu, including the scope of the approvals he granted police and whether investigators exceeded those authorizations.

Trump’s trade wars sting US manufacturers ahead of midterms
- Trump’s tariffs and trade fights are raising costs for US manufacturers, especially aluminium and steel firms, as midterms near.
- Ohio businesses say higher duties, transport costs and Canada tensions are hurting sales, hiring and expansion plans.
- Industry leaders warn the policies may help some firms, but overall they are causing uncertainty, lost customers and wider economic strain.
AI generated
NORTH JACKSON, Ohio – For Doug Rende, who runs an aluminium product manufacturer in the US state of Ohio, President Donald Trump’s tariffs have meant millions of dollars more in annual costs – and the Iran war has made shipments even more expensive.
Rende is chief executive at Shapes, one of many American producers smarting from Trump’s economic policies as midterm elections approach.
“Frustrating would be one word,” Rende said. “I think that we’re sensing a lack of trust in not only the administration but also the governmental process, the role of Congress to rein in executive power,” he added.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has wielded executive authority to slap tariffs on various products and countries. Besides aluminium, the duties hit the steel and automotive industries too, while US trading partners face additional tariffs that vary by country.
Even as some American manufacturers have benefited as their foreign competitors encounter higher barriers, others struggle with ballooning costs and persistent uncertainty.
Trump’s spiralling trade fight with Canada and war with Iran have only deepened worries.
Grievances over his trade policies are among fault lines that Democrats hope will work in their favour as they push to flip control of the Senate and House of Representatives in November’s vote.
Tough to cope
Rende’s company in North Jackson, Ohio, makes and distributes aluminium building products used in fixtures like fences.
Trump’s tariffs on aluminium have climbed steadily, from 10% during his first presidency to 25% and then 50% in 2025.
“This year alone, it’s upwards of US$4.5 million (S$5.8 million) to US$5 million in additional costs,” Rende said. “There’s only so much that the end consumer is willing to eat,” he added. “So, we absorb a healthy portion.”
These added costs include steeper transportation fees, as fuel prices have surged with the US-Israel war on Iran. Surcharges are “upwards of US$6,500 per container” of goods from suppliers, Rende said.
As a result, he has paused recruitment for new jobs while investing in more robotic assembly.
Sam Miller, another Ohio manufacturer who makes kitchen and bathroom products, has been hit on both fronts in Trump’s trade wars, paying tariffs on imported materials from Asia while finding it harder to expand into Canada because of trade tensions.
“It’s been difficult for businesses to manage,” Miller said from his factory floor in Warren as a machine hummed nearby, cutting countertop material. “I do think that there will be a shift away from Republican views.”
Although Miller received refunds after the Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s duties, the US leader has since reinstated many of them.
Tariffs add to the strain
Deteriorating US-Canada ties add to his challenges, with Washington and Ottawa slapping tariffs on each other’s products after trade negotiations collapsed in August.
“We’re selling into Canada and it is particularly straining on both us and our customers,” Miller said.
He originally planned on opening a distribution facility in Canada in 2026, but progress has slowed.
Guy Coviello, president of the Youngstown Warren Regional Chamber, said he is monitoring tariffs, the Iran war and immigration very closely.
These are a “mixed bag” for firms but negative overall, said Coviello, whose business group has some 3,000 members.
Some firms have lost customers or had to downsize, he said.
Canada is also Ohio’s biggest export market, with a third of Ohio’s exports going to the country.
“Where it gets even more complicated is that there are some goods that go back and forth across the border multiple times,” he said.
The Iran war adds to the stress, raising freight costs and hitting aluminium supplies due to drone attacks in the Middle East.
With a lack of new US aluminium smelters, Coviello said: “We are all for tariffs for critical items such as defence and medical industry.”
But he added: “We have to be careful when you’re talking about products that are not crucial and are not available in the US.” AFP

Feature: A Fijian village's fight to restore life beneath the waves
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:54:18 CST
14:54:18 KST

A young man plants coral fragments in Naidiri, Fiji, Oct. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Bai Yongquan)
By Xinhua writers Guo Xinhui, Bai Yongquan, Liu Xiaoyu
SUVA, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Beneath the turquoise waters off Fiji's west coast, a remarkable transformation has been unfolding.
Along a stretch of coastline once scarred by widespread coral bleaching, vibrant reefs are recovering, fish are returning, and a small fishing village is offering a lesson in community-led climate action.
In Naidiri, a village of just 147 residents, years of collective effort have helped revive nearly 10 km of degraded coral coastline, capturing international attention.
Earlier this week, during a ministerial preparatory meeting for the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in Fiji, the country officially launched its first National Action Plan for Coral Reef Conservation 2026-2031.
Covering more than 6,000 square km, Fiji's coral reefs sustain island livelihoods, support marine biodiversity and protect coastlines from storm surges, said Sivendra Michael, the country's Permanent Secretary for Environment and Climate Change.
Naidiri's fishers began noticing rising sea temperatures in the 1990s, villager Joseva recalled.
About a decade ago, a powerful El Nino event compounded by global warming triggered severe mass bleaching. Within months, more than 70 percent of the nearby corals had bleached, turning the reef into what Joseva described as an underwater graveyard.
Fish stocks plunged, while the weakened reef offered less protection against storm surges. Village elders warned that without action, the community could disappear within decades.
In early 2020, fishers, elders and young volunteers formed a community restoration team. They established coral nurseries in sheltered waters, collected surviving, potentially heat-tolerant corals, cut them into fragments and transplanted them onto damaged reefs.
"This is a struggle measured in years, against currents and an unpredictable climate," said Manoa Duwai, a Naidiri villager who leads the project.
Several times a week, villagers took boats offshore to tend the corals, facing strong currents, algae growth and unpredictable weather.
A brief marine heatwave in late 2021 caused renewed bleaching, destroying much of their progress.
Yet the villagers continued. Women recorded water temperatures and coral growth, elders shared traditional marine knowledge, and younger residents carried out underwater restoration, Duwai recalled.
By 2023, signs of recovery emerged. Corals survived in the nurseries, while butterflyfish, damselfish and groupers returned to the restoration areas. As the reef regained its capacity to absorb wave energy, storm impacts eased and local fish catches gradually improved.
An underwater survey in 2025 found that live coral cover had returned to a healthy level, according to villagers. For residents, seeing fish swim among colorful coral branches marked the return of a marine ecosystem once feared lost.
Duwai has since shared the village's experience in Australia, Canada, Sweden, South Africa and elsewhere.
In November 2025, the Naidiri Marine Biodiversity Park, established by local villagers, received the 2nd OceanLove Innovation Award at the Blue Economy World Congress.
The village's story has gained renewed attention during Fiji's Pre-COP31, highlighting how local communities can contribute to climate action through sustained efforts to protect the ecosystems on which they depend.
"While many places are still debating the costs of action, Pacific islanders have long been diving beneath the waves, writing the most vivid and heartfelt answers to global climate governance," said Inia Seruiratu, the Pacific Ocean Envoy for COP31. ■
A young man holds coral fragments ready for cultivation in Naidiri, Fiji, Oct. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Bai Yongquan)

The IDF said residents could maintain their normal routines and that no special Home Front Command instructions had been issued. Nevertheless, many members of the local rapid-response teams activated Saturday evening in communities near the Lebanese border remained on duty as the searches continued.
During the night, security forces also investigated additional suspicions, including a possible infiltration from the sea near Nahariya. Those concerns were subsequently ruled out.

Ben-Gvir denies the allegations, maintaining that he had arrived in the area to attend the memorial service and was merely on the sidelines of the confrontation.
The officer also testified that shouts of "You are Nazis" were directed at police during the incident.
