Estonian Artists' Association's charity auction brings in record-breaking €2.3 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:41:00 UTC
14:41:00 KST

Estonian Artists' Association's charity auction brings in record-breaking €2.3 million
The Estonian Artists' Association (EKL) charity auction concluded with total sales of €2.3 million, the highest amount ever recorded for a single art auction in Estonia.
A total of 159 works were sold, representing 98 percent of the 162 works put up for auction.
Thanks to the auction, the association will be able to repay the losses incurred through a fraud scheme ahead of schedule, while all remaining proceeds will go toward supporting Estonian artists and the country's art scene, EKL said.
According to EKL President Maarin Ektermann, the auction's results exceeded all expectations.
"When planning the auction, we didn't dare hope it would cover the entire €700,000 loss, as art auctions are unpredictable. That's why we cut the association's expenses and looked for other ways to free ourselves from the debt burden. But thanks to the people who decided to purchase treasures from the art collection and donated works, showing such strong support for the artists and the association, we can now repay our obligations ahead of schedule and develop plans for how best to support our members and Estonia's art scene," Ektermann said.
The partial sale of the art collection was an exceptional step that could only be taken once in this form.
"We knew from the outset that this was a one-time decision. That's why it was important to us to organize a public auction where everyone would have an opportunity to acquire works from the collection, with starting prices as low as €100," Ektermann said. "Together with experts, we selected the works very carefully to preserve the integrity of the collection. Far fewer works went to auction than we had originally planned, which made the result all the more surprising."
Jaanus Samma, who coordinated the artists' donations, said the artists who donated their works to the auction deserve special thanks.
"Not all the works could even be included in the auction and those remaining will be offered for sale at a separate exhibition in EKL's galleries at the end of the year," Samma said.
Historic records
The auction raised €23,500 on the first day and €786,400 on the second, while 80 works from the third day's selection of paintings, sculptures and applied art sold for a total of €1.5 million.
On Saturday, Tiit Pääsuke's "Lapi kakk" fetched the highest price of the day at €185,000.
The highest hammer price of the entire auction went to Jaan Elken's painting "Juhikabiin," which sold for €205,000. This is the highest price ever paid at auction for a work by a living Estonian artist.
Ludmilla Siim's "Rõdu" set a new auction record for a work by an Estonian female artist, selling for €150,000. Olev Subbi's "Keskpäev" sold for the same amount, setting a new auction record for the artist.
Art market expert Tiina Määrmann said she was particularly pleased that the works' art historical significance was positively correlated with their market value.
Where will the proceeds go?
The auction proceeds will primarily go toward covering losses incurred as a result of the fraud scheme in the spring, including repaying a loan. A portion of the proceeds will also be paid to artists: the creators of works sold from the association's art collection or their heirs will receive 5 percent of the hammer price, while artists who recently donated works will receive 15 percent.
"Although the resale royalty rate under the Copyright Act drops to 3 percent for more expensive works, we will pay the creators of works sold from our art collection 5 percent regardless of the hammer price," Ektermann said.
The association will use the remaining proceeds in accordance with its statutes, which stipulate that EKL's mission is to support Estonian artists and the country's art scene. The management board will submit proposals on how to use the funds to the association's council and some of the money will be allocated to developing the art collection and making it more accessible to the public.
"We want decisions to be made openly and together with our members. We hope to present more detailed plans at the extraordinary general assembly on November 16," Ektermann said.
The Estonian Artists' Association, in cooperation with Eesti Kunstioksjonid OÜ, held an extraordinary art auction from October 8 to 10, offering 162 works from the association's collection and recent donations by artists. The selection ranged from paintings and graphic art to photographs, sculptural objects and textile art. The association selected the works together with an expert committee comprising art historians, critics and art market specialists.
The association organized the auction to cover losses caused by financial fraud. On May 15, 2026, the association discovered that nearly €700,000 had been transferred out of its bank accounts as part of a criminal scheme.

The game at Tainan Asia-Pacific International Baseball Stadium drew a sellout crowd of 23,500, setting a single-game attendance record for the playoff challenge series, per CNA.
The Lions entered the game facing elimination after losing Friday’s opener 4-1. The Brothers, who earned a one-win advantage by winning the second-half championship, had taken a 2-0 lead in the series under the league’s postseason format.
Saturday’s victory extended the series to a third game. The teams are scheduled to meet Sunday at Taichung Intercontinental Baseball Stadium, the Brothers’ home field.
The game was tense from the opening inning, with Lions starting pitcher Jordan Balazovic escaping a bases-loaded jam in the first without allowing a run. Balazovic settled in after the shaky start, holding the Brothers scoreless through six innings. He threw 107 pitches, allowing five hits, striking out five, and walking three to earn the win and the game’s MVP award, per CNA.
Chen helped preserve the shutout with his defensive work at shortstop. In the bottom of the fifth, he singled, advanced to second, and later scored on a sacrifice fly by Chiu Chih-cheng (邱智呈) after an infield hit by Lin Hung-hsien (林泓弦).
The Lions’ bullpen protected the narrow lead, with Jackson Stephens (獅帝芬) pitching two scoreless innings before Chung Yun-hua (鍾允華) closed out the game.
Uni-Lions captain Chen Chieh-hsien (陳傑憲) also made history during the game. After collecting two hits in Friday’s opener to reach 20 career postseason challenge-series hits and tie former Lions player Kao Kuo-ching (高國慶), Chen recorded another single Saturday to set a new challenge-series hits record, according to CNA.
Lin Chia-wei (林佳緯), who entered as a substitute, extended his postseason challenge-series hitting streak to nine games with a single in the eighth inning. The Uni-Lions once again face a must-win game to advance to the Taiwan Series against regular-season champions the Wei Chuan Dragons.

This year’s Bruges Christmas market will look very different. After six years, the black containers – which were criticised for their ‘cold appearance’ – are being phased out. They are making way for new stalls made from traditional materials with a contemporary design. The city is investing 1.8 million euros in new structures.
“As everyone knows, last year was the last time the black containers were used,” explains Minou Esquenet, alderwoman for Work and Enterprise. “We set out to find a completely new concept. The result is these wooden huts. For the front, we’ve opted for a traditional wood colour, and for the edges, sides and rear, a darker shade.”
“A major advantage of these huts is that they are fully equipped with LED lighting and electricity connections. The roof can be removed, and they can then be folded up, which makes stacking them much easier,” said the alderwoman. “Incidentally, these stalls are not just intended for the Christmas market. They can also be used for events at other times of the year.”
A new shelter, a new name
“As this is a completely new product, specifically designed for Bruges, we’ve also come up with a new name. We settled on ‘Bruges Kaban’, written and pronounced in the ‘Flemish way’,” laughs the alderman.
‘Cabane’ is the French word for cabin or hut.
Price tag
Bruges has spent 1.8 million euros on 95 new stalls. “The expected lifespan is 10 years. Anyone using them will have to pay a rental fee. That way, we’ll recoup part of the costs.”

How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:35:09 UTC
14:35:09 KST

How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election
Israel’s election appears less a demand for change than a further entrenchment of the jingoism that surged after October 7, 2023.
As Israel entered the final month before its October 27 election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a chilling warning to share.
Israel’s enemies, he said on September 29, were plotting an attack on the country before the vote. Without providing any evidence, he then quickly referred to continuing attacks by Israeli troops in the Gaza Strip, where he said they had killed more than 100 “terrorists” in recent weeks.
That link drawn by Netanyahu – between the genocidal war on Gaza that began after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks, the upcoming elections, and Israel’s national security – was not coincidental, say analysts.
Netanyahu’s insistence that he alone can secure Israelis from a range of threats they face from across the country’s borders, they say, lies at the heart of his re-election campaign, even as his alleged failures during the attack three years ago and in securing the quick release of captives have offered his opponents ammunition.
When a Flydubai flight packed with Israeli passengers on their way from Dubai to Tel Aviv a day after his recent warning nearly crashed after a co-pilot attacked his pilot with an axe in the cockpit, Netanyahu was quick to seize on the incident to argue that he is still man for the country’s top job.
Polls suggest that he faces a stiff test in what is the first general vote since the 2023 attacks, which led to the killing of 1,139 people in Israel and triggered the genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, where Israeli have attacks have since killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
Three years later, the war has become inseparable from the domestic debate over Israel’s direction while also accelerating a political shift to the right – with once-fringe positions on Palestinians now very much the mainstream view.
Few embody this transformation more than Israel’s far-right financial Minister Bezalel Smotrich, sanctioned by a number of Western countries and known for his incendiary and racist language and policies towards Palestinians.
In one of his characteristically inflammatory statements, Smotrich told Israeli outlet Ynet late last month that the Israeli army should “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and “do there what we did in Gaza”.
Less than two weeks later, Smotrich’s electoral ally Moshe Feiglin added fuel to the fire.
“The enemy is Gaza, not Hamas”, he told the Jerusalem Post, calling for the annexation of the besieged territory after the election. “The baby that will be born tomorrow in Gaza will do exactly the same,” he said, in reference to the 2023 attacks.
Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar said these are not “stray comments” from marginal figures but an electoral message from power-seeking politicians aimed at portraying Palestinians as “not a people with rights, but a demographic and security problem to be expelled, conquered or destroyed”.
He added: “The frightening reality is that the coming election risks becoming a competition not over whether Palestinian life should be protected, but over who can promise to erase it most aggressively.”
‘This is madness’
Following October 7, the younger generation in particular slid rightwards, said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.
He said the forces driving Israel to the right had been gathering for decades.
“The trend toward the right began after the Yom Kippur War in 1973, but it has intensified dramatically since October 7,” Bregman told Al Jazeera, referring to the bloody 19-day October War, or the 1973 Arab-Israeli War – a conflict between Israel and a coalition of Arab states led by Egypt and Syria.
More recently, the far right has been emboldened through electoral politics as part of Netanyahu’s government since 2022 – the most right-wing government in Israeli history.
Another outspoken cabinet member alongside Smotrich is Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right provocateur who has previously been convicted of inciting racism and of supporting a terrorist organisation.
“Netanyahu’s greatest mistake – among many – was bringing figures like Ben-Gvir and Smotrich into his coalition,” said Bergman. “By doing so, he legitimised them as influential forces in Israeli politics.”
Ben-Gvir has been so cemented into Israel’s political system, he has hopes pinned on becoming the next Israeli defence minister, the analyst pointed out.
“This is madness. But that’s contemporary Israel,” said Bergman.
Analysts also pointed out that several parties running, including ones that are currently in power and a number that are challenging the current coalition, all advocate for the expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza, as one of the examples of the shift to the right.
Omar Baddar, director of Palthink for Strategic Studies, said the messaging from across the Israeli political and military spectrum in the lead-up to the election shows that there is “a consensus” to continue the attacks on Gaza, where nearly 1,500 have been killed since a “ceasefire” last year.
“They’re using the threats to get more votes,” he said, pointing out to what he described as the radicalisation of the society.
With the election approaching, added Baddar, Israeli leaders are seeking to undo one another: “Who[ever]’s more radical is more likely to get more votes.”
As Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher from inside Israel, writes, “what it means to be ‘right-wing’ in Israel today is above all to take a harder line on Palestinian national claims, security and territorial control.”
He adds: “On security and the Palestinians, a large part of Jewish Israeli politics already works from assumptions that would have been treated as right-wing a generation ago: Deep suspicion of a sovereign Palestinian state, a high tolerance for prolonged military control, and a stronger insistence on Jewish sovereignty as the starting point rather than one value among others.”
Observers and rights groups say the disparity is even evident in the electoral process. A prominent politician and Palestinian citizen of Israel, Sami Abu Shehadeh, has been forced to withdraw from the election over his remarks about the Gaza war, while Israeli far-right leaders have remained untouched despite their violent rhetoric against Palestinians.
Netanyahu’s security credentials endure
Recent polling indicates that the events of October 7 are top of mind for Israelis, who also have questions about who was responsible for the security failures of that day.
Just last month, reports surfaced indicating that Netanyahu had received two separate warnings about an imminent Hamas attack in 2023, from Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, and United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Netanyahu’s two main rivals in the race for prime minister have cited the alleged warnings to call the prime minister “unfit” to remain at the helm of the country.
But Netanyahu has denied suggestions that he had been forewarned about the attack, and the reports do not appear to have had a significant effect on opinion polls.
While October 7 represents a profound rupture in Israelis’ sense of security, public trust in the Netanyahu government had already been badly shaken by its controversial judicial overhaul, introduced when the prime minister’s current coalition first came to power, said Mairav Zonszein, an Israel-Palestine analyst at the International Crisis Group based in Tel Aviv.
Despite these breaches of trust, the Israeli leader retains support.
“Israelis in general still see Netanyahu as kind of the guy on security. And more to the point, they don’t really see an alternative,” Zonszein told Al Jazeera.
A June survey by Mitvim – the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies found that the Israeli public supports its government’s military and security solutions, and rejects resolving the Palestinian issue and ending the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory. This is the case even while it has been concerned about international isolation and the decline of Israel’s international standing since the beginning of the genocidal war on Gaza, the survey reported.
Yet Israelis are also increasingly war-weary, even as they back the use of more force. Its troops – stretched between six fronts of war in the last few years – are bearing the brunt of this fatigue in Israeli society.
Israel’s Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday that nearly 30,000 soldiers and security personnel are facing psychological trauma since the war.
The ministry said its rehabilitation department’s budget has increased by 88 percent over the past three years to 10 billion shekels ($3.3m), with the majority supporting treatment for mental health conditions and post-traumatic stress disorder.
As Israel expands, the two-state solution fades
Still, Israel in recent months has been more and more vocal about its expansionist vision, with officials brazenly stating the goal of “Greater Israel”. The claim for the conquest is based on a biblical verse (Genesis 15:18-21).
For decades, Israel has ignored international law in its continuous occupation of Palestinian and Syrian land, and has shown little respect for its neighbours’ sovereignty, occupying more land in Syria, as well as in Lebanon in more recent years.
According to Najar, the political economist, the “complete dehumanisation” of Palestinians as evidenced during the campaign reveal that Gaza “is being presented to Israeli voters not as a catastrophe or a crime for which there must be accountability, but as a blueprint to be repeated elsewhere”.
In southern Lebanon, where Israel has been carrying out near daily attacks and and has occupied large swathes of land, residents have told Al Jazeera they expect little to change even if Netanyahu is defeated in the election.
Netanyahu’s main political challenger, Gadi Eisenkot – head of the Yashar party and former army chief of staff – is the father of the so-called Dahiyeh Doctrine, and is just as hawkish about expansion. That doctrine, since Israel’s war with the Lebanese group Hezbollah in 2006, calls for the use of huge force, even against civilian infrastructure, as a deterrent against enemies and was deployed in Israel’s recent wars, particularly in Beirut’s southern suburbs.
If it were up to Eisenkot, the Lebanon front of war would have never scaled down: He has accused Netanyahu of bowing to US pressure to halt operations in Beirut, and has insisted that the military should be able to attack Hezbollah anywhere in Lebanon.
For Israelis still reeling from the events of October 7, Eisenkot could fill the security void many are feeling, said Zonszein.
“They really … see the world as kind of very hostile towards them, the world not understanding what they went through on October 7, and [therefore why] the need to have these security buffer zones in Lebanon, in Syria, and Gaza,” she said.
A two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict is therefore out of the question, said the analysts – and has not even made a blip of an appearance in campaigning before the election.
The idea first emerged during the Oslo Accords more than 30 years ago, which set out a negotiating process aimed at resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, predicated on the belief that the creation of a Palestinian state alongside Israel was imperative to forge peace.
But since the Oslo process began in 1993, the number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank has ballooned from about 260,000 to more than 700,000, embedded deep inside West Bank areas that would be needed for a contiguous Palestinian state.
“The concept of a two-state solution is currently irrelevant and likely will remain so for another decade or two, if not longer,” said Bergman. “It is unlikely to become a reality in the foreseeable future, as no Israeli leader can propose it to the Israeli public after the events of October 7.”
The only way it could regain prominence is if there is substantial international pressure, including severe sanctions on Israel, and a non-violent intifada, or an uprising by Palestinians, he said.
The outright rejection of Palestinian statehood has simply become much more “acceptable”, said Zonszein.
“There’s several parties who advocate these views, whereas there isn’t a single Jewish Zionist Party that puts the need for a two-state solution or a Palestinian political process at the forefront,” she said.
Taken all together, Israel’s election appears less a demand for change than a further entrenchment of the jingoism that surged after October 7, 2023.
“[There’s] more and more movement towards more military force, more need for pushing the borders … out of a lot of fear that another October 7 could happen,” said Zonszein.

Riyadh airport attack kills 12, injures 309
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:33:00 UTC
14:33:00 KST

AP Photo
Yemen's Houthis threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and airspace on Oct. 11, urging passengers not to travel after a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people and injured 309.
The group stopped short of claiming responsibility for the Oct. 10 attack but said the kingdom's airports could be targeted, excluding those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," Military Spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X.
The attack was Saudi Arabia's deadliest in more than a decade and marked an escalation in Yemen's war. Riyadh supports the internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who captured stretches of the Red Sea coastline in a rapid offensive last month.
The group intensified attacks on King Khalid International Airport and other targets in Saudi Arabia over the past week. Three people were also killed in attacks on the airport on Oct. 8.
A spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed the Iran-backed group for the Oct. 10 strike, calling it a "full-fledged war crime." A diplomatic source also attributed the attack to a Houthi missile.
The coalition said it would respond. Houthi media reported on Oct. 11 two Saudi strikes had targeted Yemen's Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate.
A U.N. special envoy and several world leaders condemned the Riyadh attack. U.S. President Donald Trump called it "not acceptable" and said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," he said at the White House.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said the dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and one citizen each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Some of the 309 injured were in serious condition.
A Western diplomat based in Riyadh told AFP the official injury count appeared to give an incomplete picture of the aftermath and did not seem to include people with minor wounds.
Airport operations remained suspended into Oct. 11, a senior aviation source told AFP. Flight tracking service Flightradar24 said the closure had been extended until 2100 GMT.
A second aviation source involved in overseeing flights to Riyadh confirmed operations had stopped "until further notice." Radar and communications equipment had been damaged, according to information available to the source, who said the runways also needed assessment.
A passenger told AFP they witnessed a strike in the domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the passenger said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies advised their citizens to avoid the airport. Several embassies were barring staff from using it over the following week, a senior Western diplomat told AFP.
The Saudi-led coalition also reported a projectile had fallen near Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on the evening of Oct. 10.
The U.S. Embassy said on Oct. 11 its staff in the kingdom would need permission to use airports in Dammam and Jeddah. A similar requirement had been introduced for Riyadh days earlier.
The attack led health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said. Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month, according to emails sent to parents and seen by AFP.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the strike a "dangerous escalation." Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the "heinous attack," while Jordan described it as "brutal."
The attack was the kingdom's deadliest since May 2015, when an Islamic State suicide bombing killed 21 worshippers in the eastern Qatif governorate.
It also came ahead of Saudi Arabia's convention and entertainment season. Riyadh hosts a busy calendar of events, including an investment conference attended by foreign leaders and business executives.
The WPC Energy Congress opened in Riyadh on Oct. 11 after being delayed by the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war in February.
Saudi Arabia has led an international coalition supporting Yemen's government militarily since 2015. Military sources told AFP on Oct. 10 Saudi-backed government forces were advancing against the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key passage for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping, in areas the group captured last month.
The Houthis said they had repelled the advance. Yemen's government announced a counteroffensive last week to retake Houthi-held territory.
Claims by the opposing sides could not be independently verified because of rapidly changing conditions and limited access for journalists.

 and Ashutosh Ranka on the condition that they do not engage in any "breach of peace for one year", the party's legal affairs head Ratna Singh said.

The CJP leaders are set to hold a press conference at 2pm on Sunday.
Delhi Police detained them from their flight shortly after they landed in the national capital on Saturday to protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Delhi Police said it had registered more than 20 FIRs over attempts to forcibly hold a protest on October 10.
The cases include charges related to disturbing law and order, obstructing government work and assaulting police personnel. Four people have been detained in connection with the cases, police said.

Traumatised Panamanians begin recovery from 7.7-magnitude earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Traumatised Panamanians begin recovery from 7.7-magnitude earthquake
- Residents in southern Panama began cleaning up after a 7.7-magnitude quake, with no reported deaths but widespread damage, fear, and more than 100 aftershocks.
- People in Chitre and other hard-hit areas slept outdoors or in schools as homes, roads, and power lines were damaged, and 30 people were treated for minor injuries.
- President Jose Raul Mulino declared a state of emergency to speed up up to US$100 million in aid, while the US pledged rapid support and airlift assistance.
AI generated
CHITRE, Panama – Residents near the epicentre of a major earthquake in southern Panama began cleaning up on Oct 10, traumatised by the previous day’s strong shaking that left widespread damage but so far no reported deaths.
“This is something we’ve never seen before. We weren’t prepared for this kind of event,” said Aldulfo Quintero as he cleared debris from a store in Chitre, about 250km south-west of Panama City.
The 41-year-old said he has a “great fear” that a new earthquake could strike any moment.
After the initial 7.7-magnitude quake around midday on Oct 9, more than 100 aftershocks have been recorded, some as strong as magnitude 6.0.
Like many others in Chitre, the capital of hard-hit Herrera province, 28-year-old Yakshuri Castillo chose to sleep outdoors due to fears of another quake.
She said she “went into shock” when the first quake struck.
In Macaracas, also located in Herrera province, 68-year-old retiree Javier Jimenez said he had to sleep at the town’s school.
“We can’t live like this,” he said, adding that his house entrance was covered with broken tiles from the roof.
“Everyone is afraid because the earthquakes are constant, we don’t dare to return,” he added.
Dozens of homes were damaged in the city, whose 66,000 residents were still without electricity on Oct 10.
The epicentre of the initial quake was registered by the US Geological Survey (USGS) about 60km away, near the border of Herrera, Los Santos and Veraguas provinces.
Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica.
State of emergency
Strong shaking in Panama City, more than 200km from the epicentre, sent people pouring into the streets from the capital’s numerous high-rise buildings.
While no deaths have been reported from the quake, about 30 people have been treated for minor injuries.
Officials are still assessing the damage in remote areas. Several communities have been cut off due to roadways damaged by the quake.
“The disaster we are facing is massive,” Panamanian president Jose Raul Mulino said upon arriving in one of the affected areas.
His government declared a state of emergency on Oct 10, a move that will speed up procedures to manage “up to US$100 million (S$128 million)” in humanitarian aid, according to Presidency Minister Juan Carlos Orillac.
The US, which counts Panama among the members of President Donald Trump’s new “Shield of the Americas” initiative, has pledged rapid support.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X on Oct 9 that he was “closely monitoring” the situation, with his office “rapidly mobilising resources and personnel to assist”.
The top US military commander in the region, Francis Donovan, has “directed immediate support to help the people of Panama, including on-the-ground support from rotary-wing aircraft...and the airlift of key personnel and supplies into the country,” US Southern Command said in a statement on Oct 10.
The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake in 2026 in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela’s Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August. AFP

Three days of unsettled weather — rain, colder temperatures and frost are returning to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Rain, heavy precipitation in some regions and colder temperatures are expected in Ukraine in the coming days. Frost of up to 3° is possible in the west.
Rain is returning to Ukraine, along with colder weather and, in some places, frost on the soil surface, UNN reports, citing the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center.
Unsettled weather is expected over the next three days: moderate rains, with locally heavy rains on October 11 in most western regions and on October 12 in Chernivtsi, Khmelnytskyi, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr and Kyiv regions; in the east, and on October 12–13 in the west of the country, there will be no precipitation
The wind is expected to be southerly, shifting to northwesterly, at 5–12 m/s.
Temperatures will be 6–14° at night; on October 12–13, 1–6° above zero in the west of the country, with frost of 0–3° on the soil surface; 18–25° during the day, and tomorrow in the western regions, on Monday and Tuesday across Ukraine, except for the south and east, 10–17°.

India court orders release of 'Cockroach' movement leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:28:00 UTC
14:28:00 KST

India: 'Cockroach' leaders vow new protests after release
Published October 11, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
What you need to know
Here are the latest developments from India on Sunday, October 11:
- The CJP said leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were ordered released after nearly 24 hours of detention
- Indian media reports cite Delhi Police officials as saying thousands of detained protesters were released
- The CJP called for a fresh protest on Sunday
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
India's Supreme Court orders no illegal detentions
The Supreme Court passed a slew of directions as it held a special Sunday hearing over restrictions and detentions by Indian authorities to stop demonstrators from reaching Jantar Mantar in New Delhi for Saturday's protest.
The court ordered that there should not be any illegal detentions of people gathering peacefully, "except by procedure established by law, particularly with regard to assemblage of people beyond the area within which it's imposed."
The court was referring to Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law that prohibits any form of assembly or protest and had been enforced in key parts of Delhi ahead of the protest.
Peaceful assemblies must be allowed in accordance with law, especially outside areas where prohibitory orders under Section 163 were in force, the court said.
The Supreme Court ordered that a notice board concerning the imposition of Section 163 in the area around its complex, should be taken down so there is "no apprehension regarding access to justice."
It also ordered the restoration of Delhi metro and railway services, unless regulations were required to be imposed, keeping in mind disturbance to public order.
The top court went on to add that lawyers and journalists should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties, after Saturday's police action saw several lawyers and journalists being detained along with the protesters.
How has the BJP reacted to the protests against India's election chief?
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) says that protests over alleged voter list manipulation are an attempt to "create a highly dangerous and serious situation in the country."
The party has denounced the CJP and the INDIA bloc of opposition parties as "anarchists".
"Right now, there's a race in the country to prove who is how big an anarchist," BJP National President Nitin Nabin said on Saturday, adding this included Rahul Gandhi's 'INDI alliance' and the leaders of the "Cockroach" movement
These sentiments were also echoed by BJP MP Bansuri Swaraj at press briefing on Sunday.
"It seems a competition in creating anarchy is emerging between Arvind Kejriwal and Rahul Gandhi. Whether it is the Aam Aadmi Party or the Congress, the country's revered voters have rejected both. Having failed to secure power through the people's mandate, they are now looking for excuses for their defeat," Swaraj told reporters.
CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke railed against Modi in a post on X, shortly after the activist leader was released from detention on Sunday.
"Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India," Dipke said, while calling the Indian leader as a "coward" and "bully."
Modi was in Tamil Nadu's capital Chennai on Sunday for a series of engagements, including laying foundation stones for development projects estimated to be worth over 130 billion Indian rupees. He has yet to directly address the latest CJP protests this weekend.
CJP issues fresh appeal for peaceful protests
CJP co-convenor Saurav Das called on people from across India to again protest in a peaceful manner.
"This demonstration is still on," Das said as he spoke about reported protester detentions taking place for a second day.
"We are not going to move back, we appeal to all Indian citizens that you will have to fight. You will have to come out on the streets. Wherever you are, you will have to do a peaceful demonstration," he told a press conference.
"This system cannot go on like this. This system is broken. This system is corrupt… and this system only works in the service of two people," Das said, going on to name Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah.
The CJP's Ashutosh Ranka said peaceful protesters who wanted to demonstrate at a designated protest site were picked up.
"The fight has just begun…Modi and Shah should feel ashamed for treating this fight like a war," he said.
CJP leaders hold press conference after release from preventive detention
"Cockroach" protest movement leader Saurav Das told reporters at a press conference in New Delhi that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is putting India in a "civil war-like situation,"
Das spoke to reporters hours after he was released from detention along with co-leaders Abhijeet Dipke and Ashutosh Ranka.
Ranka and CJP legal head Ratna Singh were also present at the press conference.
Das accused the police of "arriving like mafia dons" and "abducting" them on Saturday when they were detained from a plane upon landing in New Delhi.
He alleged they were not allowed to meet their lawyers while in detention.
New protest arrests reported in Delhi
More detentions are being reported in New Delhi as India's election protest appears to be entering a second day.
Several protesters were seen marching towards the protest site in Jantar Mantar in images circulating on Indian media.
News agency ANI reported that some people were detained at the inner circle of Connaught Place, close to Jantar Mantar, where student and youth organizations of opposition parties were protesting.
Meanwhile, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which is organizing protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, shared a series of videos on X, alleging fresh detentions.
"Detain us, arrest us, do whatever you can! We will not be intimidated. This is just the beginning. We will continue fighting until all our demands are met," the CJP’s Ajinkya Shinde said on X.
India slams UN human rights body's statement on detentions
India on Sunday rejected remarks by the United Nations Office for the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) that called on Indian authorities to immediately release "arbitrarily detained" people during Saturday's protest.
"We are concerned by reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today's large-scale demonstrations in Delhi," the OHCHR said in a statement on Saturday.
"All those arbitrarily detained must be immediately and unconditionally released."
India's Foreign Ministry called the UN office's concerns "unwarranted" and said that they "constitute an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs" of the country.
"India is the world's largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media," the ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
"As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to the maintenance of public order and safety. Our law enforcement authorities act strictly in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for the redressal of any grievances."
The ministry went on to accuse the UN human rights agency of having an "approach of extreme selectivity" on public positions.
The ministry said it had noted that "violent responses to protests" in India's neighborhood have gone "uncommented, as indeed have law enforcement actions in its own vicinity."
The statement accused the OHCHR of "double standards" which it continued to say "only erode the credibility" of the body and "contribute to the loss of faith in multilateralism."
What is the latest on the protests?
The CJP is set to hold a press conference in New Delhi at 2 p.m. local time (8.30 am UTC) today, the group said Sunday.
Meanwhile, it is yet to be seen if a fresh protest in New Delhi will take place. On Saturday evening, temporary protest leader Ajinkya Shinde had called for new demonstrations.
Earlier on X, Shinde said that a protest was scheduled in Mumbai at 4 p.m. adding that more cities "will follow."
As of early afternoon in Delhi, there were no signs of any major gathering of protesters around the Jantar Mantar site in the center of the city.
On Saturday, Mumbai too saw a series of detentions at a protest against the chief election commissioner over alleged electoral roll irregularities.
According to reports, around 600 protesters were detained and later released. The detainees included Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of India's independence icon Mahatma Gandhi, and Bollywood actor Imran Khan.
Why do protesters want election chief Gyanesh Kumar to resign?
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) started as an online satirical movement and sprung to the mainstream as a pressure group in July after forcing the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's then education minister amid massive youth-led demonstrations.
Now the CJP movement has Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in its crosshairs.
Here is a ten-point breakdown of the controversy surrounding the top election official:
- The protests concern a contentious, nationwide voter-verification exercise — called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — which began last year. Around 130 million names have been removed so far from electoral rolls under the process.
- Kumar heads the three-member Election Commission of India (ECI) overseeing the SIR process.
- Last Month, The Indian Express newspaper published a report alleging differences within the ECI over decisions related to the SIR.
- According to The Indian Express, Kumar's two fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over a 10-month period regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data, but their concerns were allegedly not taken into consideration.
- The report said that in one objection, one of the commissioners complained that the ECI had acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
- The report sparked a political storm with protests calling for Kumar's resignation, allegedly for undermining the poll body's credibility.
- The ECI has maintained that all its decisions were lawful, saying that differing views were a routine part of the decision-making process.
- Kumar is yet to address the allegations against him.
- Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large number of minority voters.
- They accuse Modi's BJP party of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains and question the ECI's independence. The ECI says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and helps prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
The CJP is not the only group calling for Kumar's resignation.
India's bloc of opposition parties, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, has been carrying out a sustained campaign against Kumar in recent days, including organizing its own protest marches.
'Cockroach ' leaders released on condition of 'no breach of peace' for a year — reports
Cockroach Janta Party leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were released from detention on condition that they made "no breach of peace for one year," according to reports citing the movement's legal head, Ratna Singh, on Sunday.
In a post on X cited by the AFP news agency, Singh said the three had been released on the condition that they make "no breach of peace for one year."
News agency ANI reported the Delhi Police as saying the movement's leaders were placed under "preventive arrest" on Saturday, and that a bail bond of 50,000 rupees (€ 460) was filled for "maintaining peace and good behavior for a period of one year."
YouTuber Dhurv Rathee released from detention
Social media influencer Dhruv Rathee, who was detained from his Gurugram residence on Saturday morning ahead protests in Delhi, was released overnight, reports said.
Reuters news agency cited an anonymous Interior Ministry official as saying that Rathee was released on condition that he would not take part in any further protests.
On Friday night, Rathee had uploaded a video of himself standing in front of New Delhi's iconic India Gate, where he called out the elaborate restrictions authorities had put in place to counter the protests planned by the Cockroach movement.
Supreme Court holds special Sunday hearing on protest curbs, detentions
A rare Sunday hearing is set to take place in India's top court over a contempt petition against a set of transportation restrictions during a large-scale protest in New Delhi a day earlier.
The petition accuses authorities of closing metro stations despite a Supreme Court order against a complete shutdown of public transport ahead of the protest.
On Friday, authorities had ordered the closure of more than 50 metro stations and canceled many trains bound for two major railway stations in the capital in a bid to keep protesters from heading to central Delhi.
But the Supreme Court later directed the government to not completely stop train services and said that there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
The court was also scheduled to hear petitions challenging the detentions of thousands of protesters, Cockroach Janta Party leaders and political leaders from India's opposition parties.
'Cockroach' leaders ordered released from detention, party says
An executive court in Delhi has ordered the release of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and other leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the youth-led movement said on Sunday.
The three were detained ahead of a large protest in Dehli on Saturday and appeared in court earlier on Sunday after being in detention for nearly 24 hours.
Earlier, the CJP had alleged the leaders were being detained at an undisclosed location and did not have access to their lawyers.
On Saturday evening, the CJP issued a fresh call for a march to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Sunday.
"We're not backing down! We will march to Jantar Mantar again tomorrow," Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's interim protest leader, said at a press conference.
The exact number of demonstrators detained during the protest could not be immediately verified.
Shinde told reporters that over 15,000 people, including students, had been detained across India.
The Hindu newspaper, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that 2,500 demonstrators were detained in Delhi on top of 1,000 people picked up in overnight preventive measures ahead of the protest.
Indian media reports cite Delhi Police as saying that all detainees had been released later on Saturday.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's Studio in New Delhi, bringing you the Sunday edition of the India news blog.
We are continuing our coverage of the intensifying election protests in India over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
Here's a quick recap of what went down on Saturday:
Dramatic scenes unfolded in the streets of the capital of the world's largest democracy on Saturday as authorities tried to thwart a protest called by the "Cockroach" movement calling for the resignation of India's election chief.
Thousands of youth protesters were detained and hauled away in buses as parts of Delhi were locked down with a mammoth deployment of police and paramilitary personnel, who essentially outnumbered the demonstrators.
Mobile internet services were suspended in central Delhi in a rare move for the key power district, while dozens of metro stations were closed.
Police cited violation of a ban on the protest as basis for the mass detentions. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and student organizations supporting the demonstration maintain that they did not need permission, citing protesting as a fundamental right.
The three main faces of the CJP — Founder Abhijeet Dipke, Co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka — were detained onboard a plane as soon as they landed in New Delhi for the protest.
Meanwhile, four former chief ministers of Indian states were also briefly detained during the protest, amid the opposition parties stepping up their calls for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Stay tuned as we bring you more.

The petition accuses authorities of closing metro stations despite a Supreme Court order against a complete shutdown of public transport ahead of the protest.
On Friday, authorities had ordered the closure of more than 50 metro stations and canceled many trains bound for two major railway stations in the capital in a bid to keep protesters from heading to central Delhi.
But the Supreme Court later directed the government to not completely stop train services and said that there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
The court was also scheduled to hear petitions challenging the detentions of thousands of protesters, Cockroach Janta Party leaders and political leaders from India's opposition parties.
'Cockroach' leaders ordered released from detention, party says
An executive court in Delhi has ordered the release of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and other leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the youth-led movement said on Sunday.
The three were detained ahead of a large protest in Dehli on Saturday and appeared in court earlier on Sunday after being in detention for nearly 24 hours.
Earlier, the CJP had alleged the leaders were being detained at an undisclosed location and did not have access to their lawyers.
On Saturday evening, the CJP issued a fresh call for a march to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Sunday.
"We're not backing down! We will march to Jantar Mantar again tomorrow," Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's interim protest leader, said at a press conference.
The exact number of demonstrators detained during the protest could not be immediately verified.
Shinde told reporters that over 15,000 people, including students, had been detained across India.
The Hindu newspaper, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that 2,500 demonstrators were detained in Delhi on top of 1,000 people picked up in overnight preventive measures ahead of the protest.
Indian media reports cite Delhi Police as saying that all detainees had been released later on Saturday.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's Studio in New Delhi, bringing you the Sunday edition of the India news blog.
We are continuing our coverage of the intensifying election protests in India over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
Here's a quick recap of what went down on Saturday:
Dramatic scenes unfolded in the streets of the capital of the world's largest democracy on Saturday as authorities tried to thwart a protest called by the "Cockroach" movement calling for the resignation of India's election chief.
Thousands of youth protesters were detained and hauled away in buses as parts of Delhi were locked down with a mammoth deployment of police and paramilitary personnel, who essentially outnumbered the demonstrators.
Mobile internet services were suspended in central Delhi in a rare move for the key power district, while dozens of metro stations were closed.
Police cited violation of a ban on the protest as basis for the mass detentions. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and student organizations supporting the demonstration maintain that they did not need permission, citing protesting as a fundamental right.
The three main faces of the CJP — Founder Abhijeet Dipke, Co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka — were detained onboard a plane as soon as they landed in New Delhi for the protest.
Meanwhile, four former chief ministers of Indian states were also briefly detained during the protest, amid the opposition parties stepping up their calls for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Tennessee execution survivor Christa Pike released from hospital, returned to prison

14:19:30 KST

Death row inmate Christa Pike was released from a US hospital on Saturday and sent back to prison, where she will continue receiving medical care following her botched execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said.
Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years, said attorneys Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the Tennessee Office of the Post Conviction Defender in a joint release.
Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke "angry and confused" in the hospital this week with a long recuperation ahead after surviving the attempted execution on September 30, her lawyers said on Wednesday. They previously believed she could be brain-dead.
Tennessee executions halted after Pike's failed lethal injection
Pike, 50, had been taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.
A Tennessee judge this week ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to their failed attempt to execute her, a development one of her lawyers called the "first of many steps to preserve and enforce her constitutional rights."
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look into the botched execution of Pike and a similar failure involving Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines.

Middle East conflicts, energy supplies, to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:19:15 UTC
14:19:15 KST

Finance officials from around the world will gather in Thailand this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest energy supply shock ever, and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.
The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held outside of Washington for the first time in three years.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be notably absent, dispatching two senior officials in his stead while he handles some "domestic engagements," a US official said.
His decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 major economies, which the US leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine's battle against Russia's invasion, and the US move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that while global growth had held up better than feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, shutting off some 20% of the world's oil, pressures were building again. Soaring diesel prices, rising fertilizer costs, and a looming "super" El Niño weather effect that experts say could lead to 450,000 heat-related deaths are hitting at once.
Group of Seven countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from US President Donald Trump, who wants lower gasoline prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Trump announces diesel deal with Russia
Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of US sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of the war on February 28, but industry executives say the amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fueling pressure on prices.
Banga said the Bank was not revising down its global forecasts at the moment, but was keeping a close eye on developments. "The real thing is not just El Niño by itself; it's the combination... What's happening to fertilizer prices? What's happening to energy costs? What's happening to debt? It's that put together that creates its own challenges," he said. "And I think that will call upon all of us to be far more careful on what we prepare for in the coming months."
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva issued a similar warning in her traditional curtain-raiser speech previewing the meetings, telling the audience, "Winter is coming."
The IMF has signaled little change to its forecast of 3% global growth in 2026 and may slightly raise its forecast for next year. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia's invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.
IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.
Growing public debt leaves developing countries heavily vulnerable
One major headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden, which is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressure. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and will exceed 100% of GDP before 2030.
Advanced economies, led by the United States, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, El Niño, and lack of investment in AI, which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.
Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Interest payments already exceed 10% of revenue in developing countries on average.
Early in the COVID crisis, G20 leaders announced a suspension of debt service payments for the poorest countries, but G20 diplomats said there is little appetite for such action now, as high debt levels and political pressures pose bigger hurdles this time.
Many lower-income countries worry about new IMF recommendations for loan programs that call for fewer, but deeper, reforms as a condition of approval, a change many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.
"Countries are already cutting their expenditures because their debt payments are going high and because of the IMF conditionality," said Iolanda Fresnillo, who works on debt justice for Eurodad. "We fear that this review of conditionality policy is just going to make things worse."
Kenya, she said, had avoided a debt restructuring by cutting public expenditures and trying to raise taxes, but the changes sparked significant protests, especially by the young.
The IMF risked losing credibility unless it acknowledged the severity of the crisis facing many developing countries.
"As long as they continue with the governance structure that they have, they are becoming less and less relevant," she said.
Flight routes to Bangkok often route through the Middle East, posing immediate security challenges to the 10,000-plus travelers descending on Thailand's bustling capital city of 9 million residents following recent attacks on Saudi airports.
Previous IMF-World Bank meeting took place after Oct. 7
The last off-site annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank took place in Morocco just days after the October 7 massacre.
Three years later, the link between national security and international finance is clear, although finance officials at the time dismissed the Hamas attack as not an economic issue, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council.
"Obviously there have been massive global ramifications," he said. "What we're currently experiencing with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has a direct connection with what happened three years ago."
Policymakers needed to become more agile in responding to geopolitical crises in an increasingly interconnected world, Lipsky said. "They have to be proactive, and they have to recognize that they don't live in the world they used to."

Hundreds of protesters marched through Toronto’s downtown core via Yonge Street Saturday afternoon, chanting more loudly as additional people joined the demonstration. “We will honor all our martyrs, all our children, sons and daughters!” and “In my lifetime I will see Palestinians living free!” the crowd yelled in unison.
Separated by metal barricades and police officers, a much smaller group of counterprotesters waving Israeli and Iranian flags stood at the southern end of Sankofa Square, where the demonstrators gathered before the march to mark the third anniversary of the war in Gaza.
Trailing behind a white Ford F-150 equipped with speakers, protesters at one point shouted, “Overthrow the Epstein class,” a slogan referring to disgraced Jewish financier Jeffrey Epstein to decry the global elite and call for the ultra-wealthy to be stripped of power. Tensions briefly flared when a man wearing a Turning Point Canada sweatshirt confronted a group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators.
Otherwise, the protest was largely peaceful. Toronto police said that one individual was arrested at the demonstration after being recognized by officers as someone wanted in connection with an unrelated incident.
The protest was part of a broader international wave of demonstrations, with the Israeli Ministry for Diaspora Affairs counting 17 protests in Canada planned for Saturday through Wednesday, including in Montreal and Ottawa.
Demonstrators included Jews, Israelis critical of Zionism
The demonstrators included Jews and Israelis who are highly critical of the prosecution of the war in Gaza and Zionism as a whole. “I went to school in Haifa, and I saw how Palestinians are treated,” said pro-Palestinian protester Shlomit, 65, who didn’t provide a last name due to concerns for her safety. “I grew up in a very Zionist family, but being in Israel actually changed my mind about things.”
Shlomit said she had mutual friends with Vivian Silver, a Canadian-Israeli peace activist who was murdered on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas attacked Israel, launching the Gaza war. She said she was emotionally impacted by Silver’s death, and believes the kind of work like Silver’s was critical to building peace between Israelis and Palestinians.
“I knew all these people who were connected to [Vivian]. She was a peace activist, and what happened to her was distressing to me,” said Shlomit, who wore a pin labeled “Jews Against Occupation.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney mentioned Silver in a statement on Wednesday, the three-year anniversary of Oct. 7 itself. “Canada unequivocally condemns Hamas, which must play no role in the future governance of a demilitarised Palestinian state,” read Carney’s statement. “We stand steadfastly with the Israeli people in their pursuit of a safe and secure Israel as part of a two-state solution.”
The statement continued by commemorating the Canadian lives lost to the Hamas attack, mentioning Silver and eight others. “We remember them for the lives they lived and the people they loved – and we honor the families and friends who continue to mourn their loss. May their memory be a blessing,” he said.
Other demonstrators expressed solidarity with issues beyond the Middle East. Caelen Leizer-Romalis, 24, was attending the protest as part of the Revolutionary Communist Party. “We have an obligation as Canadians to stand up to imperialism,” said Leizer-Romalis, who is Jewish. “In order to liberate the people of Palestine, we need to liberate the workers here as well.”
Pro-Israel demonstrators carried Iranian flags
Despite being outnumbered, pro-Israel demonstrators - all of whom carried either an Iranian flag or a picture of the last shah of Iran before his ouster in the Iranian Revolution of 1979 - waved their flags as “Tel Aviv” by Omer Adam blasted from a boombox.
Mahya Tayabi, 38, decided to come to the protest to demonstrate unity between Israel and Iran. “I’m Persian, but I love Israel. I love Jewish people. Bibi and the IDF helped my country,” said Tayabi, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by his nickname. As Tayabi spoke, the boombox switched to playing an EDM beat featuring the lyrics “Ayatollah Khamenei is dead!” Israel and the United States killed the ayatollah at the beginning of the war on Iran that they launched in late February.
The Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs expressed concern regarding the weekend’s protests.
“Canada’s Integrated Threat Assessment Center has warned about the consequences of turning a blind eye: when targeting of the Jewish community becomes frequent and normalized, it can push susceptible individuals toward violence. Events praising the ‘resistance’ responsible for the October 7 atrocities, as communities gather to mourn the murdered, demand moral clarity from civic leaders about what is acceptable in our society.”

Israeli expat recounts destruction, home collapse in magnitude 7.7 Panama earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:18:50 UTC
14:18:50 KST

As a magnitude 7.7 earthquake shook Panama on Friday, Israeli Nurit Goren Elfant and her family felt lucky to be outside as their house, like many others in the area, collapsed.
Speaking to N12 News on Saturday, Elfant described the destruction and damage caused by the quake and subsequent aftershocks, some reaching up to magnitude 5.8.
“It happened a few minutes before one in the afternoon. It was something you can’t even imagine,” she recounted. “The ground shook at a level you don’t see in movies, and for 13 consecutive hours, there were tremors every few minutes. We were lucky to have been outside when our house was destroyed.”
Much of southern Panama was cut off from the internet in the aftermath of the quake, including in the coastal town of Playa Venao, an area where Elfant told N12 many Israeli families live. Only those who have access to satellite internet have been able to connect to the outside world.
“Some of these families lost everything,” Elfant continued, describing the experience of her fellow Israeli expats. “Everything completely collapsed.”
A tsunami warning sends families to higher ground
A Tsunami warning was issued during the tremors, leading to many of the families moving to higher ground in the mountains. Elfant’s family returned to lower ground earlier than others, but some of those who stayed got stuck in the mountains due to roads being blocked with debris and bridges collapsing.
Elfant told N12 that Israeli families were among those stuck up on the mountain on Friday afternoon as Shabbat approached.
A community that comes together
The Israeli community managed to organize a Shabbat meal despite the conditions.
"The rabbi of the Chabad house went up to the mountain; they took the food they had left at the Chabad house and what they could salvage from the supermarket, which was completely destroyed, and they set up an impromptu Shabbat meal there and a big kiddush for the entire Jewish community," Elfant said.
"I think there were over 200 people there. They stayed to sleep outside there. They are still without water and electricity, so we don't know what's happening to them."
Elfant’s family has been able to help some neighbors with two buses they previously converted into homes. "Because a bus can absorb shocks, we sleep in it and let other families live with us. Right now, five families live here on our farm. We have solar electricity, but there is no electricity in Vanu and the entire area," she explained to N12.
According to N12, the water supply in the area has been severely damaged, and people have little access to potable water. "Our well, which is 42 meters deep, has completely mixed up and is mainly producing basalt," says Nurit. "Because of the tremors, all the water tanks that people had for emergencies were flooded. We had a three-cubic-meter water tank that exploded."
To drink water, Elfant said she and her family will have to collect water from a stream or rainwater and boil it. They hope to get through the next month and rebuild their home.

Flooding in Nepal destroyed homes and bridges; authorities announced an evacuation
Kyiv • UNN
A landslide blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, causing flooding in five districts of Nepal. Homes and bridges were destroyed; no casualties have been reported.
On Sunday, Nepalese authorities urged local residents to move to safer locations after a powerful flood on a river in the central part of the country destroyed several homes and infrastructure facilities; no casualties have been reported so far, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
According to the authorities, a landslide (not involving water) in the village of Chumnubri (Gorkha District, approximately 100 km west of Kathmandu) blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, causing flooding downstream.
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River. It flows downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse in August caused a catastrophic flood that claimed the lives of 1,457 people, while thousands are still considered missing.
Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after a deadly flood02.10.26, 13:56 • 8942 views
"We have asked residents living along the riverbanks downstream to evacuate and ensure their own safety," said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, head of the Gorkha District administration.
Mishra said the flood swept away several homes and two suspension bridges, and also damaged a hydropower facility.
National disaster response services warned residents living along the river in Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flooding.
"Please help ensure the timely relocation of people from dangerous areas to safe places and facilitate search-and-rescue operations as needed," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in a social media post.
Officials said rescuers from the army and police had already arrived at the scene and were monitoring the situation from a helicopter.

Farming and solar power are competing for land. Can agrivoltaics solve the problem?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:02:20 UTC
14:02:20 KST

Agrivoltaics could help to prevent farmland abandonment by protecting crops and boosting income. But some say the solution ignores the real problems.
As the sun moves westward across the sky in Murcia, Spain, solar panels capture its rays while sheltering diverse crops, from bell peppers to wine grapes and dragon fruit.
Known for its agriculture and abundant sunshine, this southeastern region is exploring whether, rather than competing for land, farming and solar energy can coexist peacefully.
“Agrivoltaics is the integration of food production with renewable energy production,” explains Silvia Tomasi, Senior Researcher at Eurac Research. This entails installing photovoltaic panels above, in between or at the margins of agricultural production, she adds.
A 2023 study estimated that Europe has the potential to generate 25 times its current electricity demand via agrivoltaics, also known as agri-PV.
Yet solar power is fraught with its own environmental and social costs. Requiring more land than other energy sources to generate the same amount of electricity, it has sparked conflicts over land use, especially in rural areas.
“Agrivoltaics has great potential: both economic benefits and environmental ones,” Tomasi says. “But then it’s always a matter of how the technology is implemented and who really benefits.”
Governments and Big Tech turn to agrivoltaics
The idea of turning southern Europe into a solar powerhouse received a high-profile endorsement in January, when Elon Musk said sparsely populated areas of Spain and Sicily could theoretically generate enough solar power for all of Europe.
Big Tech has already caught on. In southern Italy, Amazon and Apple have signed contracts to purchase power from large-scale agrivoltaic projects with a combined capacity of over 150 megawatts – enough to meet the yearly needs of roughly 100,000 Italian households.
Europe is also funding the shift. The EU-funded AGRISOL project intends to invest €1.9 million in agrivoltaics projects, including in Italy and Spain, while Italy alone has secured €1.7 billion in state aid for the initiative.
“For now, [agrivoltaics] is just a minimal contribution,” says Angelo Gentili, national secretary of Legambiente, Italy’s largest environmental organisation. “But if it expands, it will represent a big impulse for decarbonisation goals.”
Managing the impact on crops and land
EU and national rules increasingly require agriculture to remain a meaningful part of land where solar panels are installed. In France, projects must maintain at least 90 per cent of crop production compared to locally determined reference yields. In Italy, at least 70 per cent of the area must remain dedicated to agriculture.
Experts say not just any combination of solar and agriculture should qualify. “More than a definition, what we really need is a classification,” says Pilar Flores, who coordinates an EU-funded agrivoltaics project at the Murcian Institute for Agricultural and Environmental Research and Development (IMIDA). She says protecting agriculture should drive all classifications: “The key is to ensure there’s minimal loss [of arable land].”
Why use farmland rather than empty or abandoned land in the first place? Flores says the requirements are similar: relatively flat and near the grid. Unused land may also hold ecological value. “It’s not just a simple calculation of how much free land is left,” she says.
How agrivoltaics can benefit farmers
In some cases, agrivoltaics have been found to improve water-use efficiency, protect crops from extreme weather and increase the productivity of land. Solar installations can also help farmers face climate change. “Excessive rainfall and heat have heavily damaged agricultural fields, pushing farmers to abandon farmland,” says Gentili. “Agrivoltaics represent a great instrument to avoid land abandonment and profit gaps for farmers.”
Panels cast shade that can reduce evaporation, help soil retain moisture and offer relief to farmworkers and grazing animals. They can also protect crops from hail. Farmers can use the energy to power their own operations and sell any excess to the grid, or rent the space above their fields to energy producers.
But the benefits are not guaranteed, Flores warns. “All these opportunities are sometimes discussed as if they always happened, but it depends on the agrivoltaic system used and the specific characteristics of the site.” In Murcia, her team found that water-stressed peppers grew better under solar panels than well-watered ones. “You have to analyse each case and each location,” she says.
But who really benefits from agrivoltaics?
Not all farmers are convinced. To Fabrizio Garbarino, president of the Italian farmers’ union Associazione Rurale Italiana, agrivoltaics fail to address the root problems farmers face. “Agrivoltaics are taking advantage of the farming sector crisis in Italy while we should actually focus on real solutions for preventing farmland abandonment,” he says. “To me, this just sounds like a shortcut.”
Startups representing larger companies, including data centre developers, are hounding farmers for their land, he says. “Even if the energy produced is good, we’re taking away [farmers’] land to support businesses that require a lot of energy.”
Big Tech firms say agrivoltaic power-purchase agreements help them reach net-zero targets. But a PPA does not necessarily mean that the electricity from a particular solar farm physically supplies a particular company facility, and the exact carbon footprints of AI data centres remain opaque.
A 2025 study co-authored by Tomasi, based on expert interviews across four European regions, found that the benefits of agrivoltaics can favour large-scale farmers, landowners and investors over smaller farmers and local communities. It also found that excluding residents and ecosystems from decision-making can deepen existing power imbalances.
High upfront costs and grid connection queues mean large projects backed by multinationals tend to dominate the sector. A 2025 review by the Italian newspaper Today.it found that about 86 per cent of the roughly €775 million in government funds for agrivoltaic projects went to large-scale projects, including ones owned by foreign multinationals.
In September, a new agrivoltaics project financed by an Israeli company in Tuscany sparked widespread outrage and raised concerns over who gets to profit.
Tomasi says local communities must have a voice to ensure a just transition. “Big investors going into places they really don’t know anything about, with a top-down approach… and getting the economic benefits from the renewable energy generation side of agrivoltaics… shouldn’t be labelled as agrivoltaics, from my point of view.”
‘Agriculture should not be a secondary concern’
Flores says administrations can help by offering farmers funding and giving agrivoltaic systems priority access to the grid.
There is also the question of what kind of agriculture the income supports. To live up to the environmental promise, one study has noted, “the type of agriculture funded by the rental income from agrivoltaics should not be a secondary concern”. Instead, the author argues, this rent could subsidise agroecological practices or help farmers transition away from industrial farming.
Agrivoltaics has the potential to be mutually beneficial to farmers and the renewable energy sector. It can help protect farmland, support farmers facing climate change and contribute to Europe’s decarbonisation goals. But it also risks becoming a greenwashing opportunity, a crutch for unsustainable farming practices, or a way of meeting growing corporate energy demand on arable land. On its own, it is not a silver bullet. Much depends on how the systems are designed, who owns them and, ultimately, who benefits.
“The goal of agrivoltaics is to protect farmland and the entire ecosystem; that’s the philosophy,” says Flores. “We have to be able to distinguish that from other interests.”
Reporting for this story was made possible by the Magma Environmental Reporting Fellowship.
