US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott for antitrust violation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:59:00 UTC
12:59:00 KST

US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott
October 11, 2026
The US Department of Justice announced on Saturday that it is investigating whether the White House press pool's decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month, violated the nation's anti trust law.
Group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law, spokesperson Emily Covington said.
"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," she said.
The networks under the scrutiny are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, criticized the administration's decision to investigate.
"The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access," Zamora said on X. "The public's right to know depends on that access."
Why is Trump's press pool under investigation?
On September 21, a pool of five broadcasters ceased presidential coverage after the Trump administration barred news networks CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying covering the president was a "privilege, not a right."
As a result, the five television networks suspended coverage in protest and refused to provide replacement program.
The news outlets also sued the administration, accusing it of violating free speech and free press rights under the First Amendment of the US Constitution and pursuing retaliation over their coverage.
On September 24, the White House reinstated their press credentials after a US district Judge ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate and restore" their access.
The president has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and clashed with reporters during interviews.
The White House press pool is a roating group of news outlets which cover the president and accompany him on official duties.
CNN is one of the five news organizations, along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBS, that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the cost of covering the president and take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
The White House press pool has now become a proxy for a fight over press freedom.

Tsai urges democratic cooperation, says Taiwan offers more than chips
Unknown

03:54:35 UTC
12:54:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former President Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) called for greater international cooperation with Taiwan, saying the country can contribute to regional peace and democratic resilience beyond its semiconductor and technology industries.
Speaking at a forum titled “Taiwan Beyond the Headlines: How Taiwan Builds Resilience Through Democracy,” Tsai discussed political polarization, the value of restraint in leadership, and Taiwan’s role in strengthening international cooperation, per Liberty Times.
A day earlier, Tsai delivered an address at a VIP dinner for the Stanford DEFCON 2026 Technology & National Security Conference. Her talk covered Taiwan’s asymmetric defense, indigenous submarine program, semiconductor industry, and drone supply chains.
The Hoover forum focused more closely on democratic resilience and political cooperation. Former US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Larry Diamond, scholars, researchers, and Stanford students attended the event.
Tsai began with a lighthearted reflection on her political career, noting that some people had described her as “boring” during her presidency. She argued that restraint can be valuable in an era when provocation often attracts more attention than measured leadership.
This approach, she said, was particularly important when balancing Taiwan’s security needs with the search for common ground necessary to sustain democratic progress.
When discussing Taiwan, people often ask why the country matters, Tsai said. An equally important question, she added, is what Taiwan can contribute to the broader democratic community.
“Taiwan can offer more than just semiconductors and technology,” she said, pointing to the country’s experience in protecting elections, maintaining public trust, and fostering cooperation between government and civil society.
Cooperation with Taiwan would not simply help the country but also strengthen a broader system of peace, trade, technological development, and democratic cooperation, she argued. “Taiwan is ready to participate in this joint effort,” she said.
Tsai said the international order was undergoing a profound transformation but stressed that external threats and coercion would not weaken Taiwan’s determination to engage with the world and contribute to the international community, per Liberty Times.
She also cautioned against defining Taiwan solely through the risks it faces, arguing that the country should be recognized for its democratic achievements and contributions to global cooperation.
Tsai concluded by emphasizing the need for leaders and societies to work through disagreements, exercise patience, and seek common ground. Although such an approach might appear boring, she said, the ability to show restraint and cooperate across differences is precisely what leadership requires in a polarized political environment.
After the forum, Tsai visited Startup Island Taiwan, a startup hub in Palo Alto, California, where she met with young entrepreneurs and discussed technology and innovation. She emphasized the human dimension of technological development and joked that she had not asked artificial intelligence for help while serving as president, drawing laughter from the audience.

The performance marked the third year of Taipei 101’s National Day fireworks celebration, with organizers expanding the production and increasing the drone fleet from 500 last year to 600 this year, per CNA.
Before the fireworks began, three mascots entertained the crowd: Taipei City Government’s Bravo Bear, Taipei 101’s Damper Baby, and Taishin Shin Kong Financial Holding’s Richart. The mascots posed for photos with spectators, adding to the festive atmosphere ahead of the main event.
Chia thanked Taishin Shin Kong Financial Holding for sponsoring the show for two consecutive years, saying the partnership allowed the public to enjoy a performance combining technology, art, and creativity while celebrating Taiwan’s National Day, per CNA.
Taipei 101 also scheduled a three-night exterior light show from Friday through Sunday under the theme “A Smart Partner,” featuring illuminated messages and laser beams. In recent years, the landmark skyscraper has become a backdrop for large-scale public displays of Taiwanese cultural identity on important public holidays.

Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:41:58 UTC
12:41:58 KST

Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
Medical services in Taiz risk shutting down as fuel, medicines, and supplies run alarmingly low under Houthi blockade.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has warned of an “imminent health and humanitarian catastrophe” in the besieged city of Taiz, in the country’s southwest, as the Houthis continue their siege and “obstruct essential supplies”.
Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said in a statement on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.
It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”.
Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said.
It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid.
It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities.
“Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said.
Renewed siege
The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast.
Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre.
The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed.
The renewed siege took shape in early October.
The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.
Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October.
Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.
He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced.
Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58).
“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.
The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organization have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril.
“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization.

Earlier on Oct. 11, Yandex Cloud reported power disruptions in an availability zone identified as being located at the company's data center in Vladimir.
"There are power interruptions in the ru-central1-a availability zone. The team is working to resolve the issue," the company said in a statement published on its official Telegram channel.

Russian independent media outlet ASTRA reported that Yandex Cloud experienced power disruptions at its Vladimir data center following warnings of a drone attack in the region. Ukrainian monitoring channels also circulated images purportedly showing a fire near the facility.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the images or the extent of damage at the facility or to any of the Yandex apps or services.
The latest incident follows two drone strikes that Yandex has publicly acknowledged.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing it to suspend operations completely. Yandex said it could not yet determine when the facility's equipment could be restored.
A second strike on Oct. 9 damaged the company's data center in Kaluga, disabling several modules and potentially disrupting services.

On Oct. 10, Yandex updated its user agreement to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations.
The reported attacks come amid an expanding campaign of Ukrainian long-range strikes against infrastructure inside Russia.

Hurricane Simon strengthens into Category 4 storm as it takes aim at Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:28:31 UTC
12:28:31 KST

Hurricane Simon lashes Mexico's Pacific coast, pounds resorts and vulnerable towns
Hurricane Simon's eye remains just off Mexico's Pacific coast, but the Category 4 storm's most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall. This could mean Simon maintains its extremely dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 150 mph.
That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for U.S. tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.
At daybreak, Simon was centered about 110 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow 6 mph. A senior hurricane center specialist, Phillipe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico was the most likely place for landfall.
"Simon is very close to the coast of Mexico this morning," Pappin told The Associated Press on Sunday.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."
Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 10 to 20 inches of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas.
On Saturday, ahead of the storm's arrival, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows. Few were walking the streets under overcast skies.
"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."
The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge "along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall." The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do Saturday. "I just don't know what to expect."
Unlike the Atlantic, which saw just its first named hurricane of the season this week with Isaias, the Pacific season has been very active. Simon's arrival comes on the heels of Polo, which slammed Mexico last week as a Category 2 hurricane before reaching the southwestern U.S. and bringing heavy flooding to the region.

Czech opposition retains Senate majority after elections
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:50 CST
12:26:50 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Czechia's opposition parties will retain their majority in the Senate after securing five seats outright in the first round of elections for the upper house of parliament, according to preliminary results released early Sunday.
The five winners include candidates from the Christian Democrats, the Mayors and Independents and other opposition parties.
Under the Czech electoral system, one-third of the 81-member Senate, or 27 seats, are contested every two years. Candidates must win more than 50 percent of the vote in their respective constituencies to secure a seat outright in the first round.
The three main opposition groups hold 37 of the 54 seats not up for election. With five more seats secured in the first round, the opposition has ensured a majority of at least 42 seats, leaving Prime Minister Andrej Babis' ruling coalition in the minority.
In the nationwide municipal elections also held on Friday and Saturday, independent candidates and local groups won the majority of local council seats, while Babis' ANO party led in several major regional cities. ■

HANOI, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam's real estate bond issuance reached 149.5 trillion Vietnamese dong (about 5.7 billion U.S. dollars) in the first nine months of 2026, surging 126 percent year on year, local media outlet VnEconomy reported Sunday, citing rating agency VIS Rating.
The average interest rate on newly issued real estate bonds stood at around 11.4 percent, up 110 basis points from the same period last year, according to the report.
VIS Rating expects property bond issuance to remain high as developers face refinancing needs for 167 trillion Vietnamese dong (about 6.52 billion U.S. dollars) in bonds maturing in the fourth quarter of 2026 and in 2027, alongside funding requirements for major development projects.
Meanwhile, the Vietnamese government has introduced measures to encourage affordable rental housing and greater private-sector participation, including land-use fee exemptions, infrastructure support and land allocations for rental housing projects. ■

Descendants of Doolittle Raid participants visit Shangrao, China's Jiangxi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:33 CST
12:26:33 KST

A descendant of a rescued Doolittle Raid participant (R) hugs a descendant of a Chinese villager who took part in the rescue in Shangrao, east China's Jiangxi Province, Oct. 10, 2026. The Doolittle Raid, planned and led by U.S. Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle on April 18, 1942, was an air raid on Japan as a retaliation for the attack on the U.S. Pearl Harbor.
After the raid, 15 planes heading for an airport in Quzhou ran out of fuel and crashed in various localities in east China.
Chinese villagers risked their lives to rescue the parachuting airmen and helped them evacuate to safety. Of the 75 airmen aboard the planes, 64 were rescued by the Chinese people. However, many locals were suspected of sheltering the Americans, and some were tortured or even killed by Japanese soldiers.
In China, the Doolittle story has long been regarded as a symbol of the friendship forged between the Chinese and American peoples during their joint fight against fascism.
On Oct. 10, 6 representatives of descendants of the Doolittle Raid participants visited Shangrao to view a historical exhibition, revisit rescue sites and pay tribute to the Chinese people who rescued American airmen 84 years ago. (Xinhua/Zhou Mi)

Australia's Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility closes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:21 CST
12:26:21 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility closed on Sunday, with some residents asked to relocate about 100 km south of the Northern Territory capital.
The 400-bed YiSSA facility, which had been operating at capacity with a waiting list, provided temporary accommodation for people experiencing homelessness, residents from remote Aboriginal communities visiting Darwin for medical treatment and families escaping domestic violence, according to local media reports.
The Northern Territory government has established a smaller replacement facility in Batchelor, about 100 km south of Darwin, with capacity for around 150 people.
The closure has raised concerns over access to health, legal and other support services that are concentrated in Darwin.
Danila Dilba Health Service said about 250 of its clients had YiSSA registered as their address and warned that some could face difficulties continuing to access services after the closure.
The Northern Territory government has said medically vulnerable residents would not be relocated to Batchelor without arrangements for continued access to necessary care.
The government previously rejected a joint funding proposal from the federal government to keep the Darwin facility operating.
The government has said the Batchelor site will provide transitional accommodation as well as emergency evacuation capacity during extreme weather events. ■

China retains world junior badminton team title after dramatic final against Malaysia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:20 CST
12:26:20 KST

Team China poses on the podium during the award ceremony after winning the final against Malaysia at the BWF World Junior Team Championships 2026 in Cairo, Egypt, Oct. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
CAIRO, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- China successfully defended its title at the Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Junior Team Championships on Saturday, defeating Malaysia 2-1 in a dramatic final that saw both teams battle through three closely contested sets.
The Chinese team won the opening set 55-46 before Malaysia fought back to take the second 55-53. China then regained control in the deciding set, winning 55-45 to lift the Suhandinata Cup.
The final was closely contested, with China recovering from 43-50 to level the second set at 52-52 before Malaysia held on to force a decider. China built an early lead in the third set through women's and men's singles and maintained its advantage despite Malaysia's late challenge.
China's coach Guo Zhendong credited the team's balanced strength across all five disciplines and praised the players' composure under pressure.
"In the deciding third game, we had a clear advantage in the singles events and managed to build a substantial lead. Although Malaysia narrowed the gap by several points during the women's doubles, our players managed to withstand the pressure and ultimately defend our title," Guo said, adding that the experience of handling pressure in closely contested matches would benefit their future development.
Feng Yilang, an 18-year-old Chinese player who competed in mixed doubles, acknowledged feeling nervous during the opening two sets but said he became more confident as the final progressed.
"In the third game, I was able to relax more and play with greater confidence. My performance was better than in the first two games," Feng said.
His teammate Wei Yueyue, also 18, who competed in women's doubles, identified "team unity" as the key to China's victory.
"Whenever we face difficulties, there is always someone who steps up. That's what makes our team so united," she said.
Malaysia's team manager Vincent Chin praised his players' determination despite the defeat, saying they fought until the final set.
"We are happy that we got a silver medal in the team event, but we are looking for the gold medal in the individual event," Chin told Xinhua, expressing optimism about the upcoming individual championships.
Thailand and Indonesia shared the bronze medals after losing their semifinals to China and Malaysia, respectively.
Looking ahead to the individual championships, which begin Monday in Cairo, Guo said the Chinese team would review its performances and allow the players time to recover before preparing for the different technical and tactical demands of the five disciplines.
"We will continue to give our best and strive for strong performances in the individual events," he said. ■

Shahar Nevo's double life as Bar-Ilan math professor accused of plotting massacre - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:17:20 UTC
12:17:20 KST

For more than two decades, Prof. Shahar Nevo built an extensive career in the world of mathematics: he graduated with honors, published dozens of studies, and taught generations of students at Bar-Ilan University.
Until this week, his name was known mainly in the hallways of the math department and among those who took his courses in calculus and analysis. His online presence consisted mainly of scientific articles, course pages, exams, and lecture summaries, with no interviews, public statements, or social media presence.
However, this academic career now exists under the shadow of a severe indictment: the 60-year-old professor is accused of preparing to execute an act of terrorism, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice. According to the indictment, he planned an attack for more than three years, with the aim of killing hundreds of Israeli Arabs.
Academic Background and Research Career
Nevo was born on October 12, 1966. He began his academic path at Tel Aviv University in 1984 and, three years later, completed a bachelor's degree in mathematics. In 1992, he moved to Bar-Ilan University, where he completed a master's degree in 1995 and a Ph.D. in 1999. He completed his master's studies summa cum laude, earning the Dean's Prize in 1996, and his doctoral dissertation was also praised. He wrote his research under the supervision of Prof. Lawrence Zalcman, an expert in complex analysis, and the two maintained a professional connection through the joint studies they published.
Upon completing his Ph.D. in 1999, Nevo joined the tenured academic faculty at Bar-Ilan. He started as a lecturer and, over the years, advanced through the ranks to Associate Professor in the Department of Mathematics.
According to his official profile, he specializes in complex analysis, operator theory, and matrices of rational functions.
Over the years, he accumulated 51 academic outputs, including 40 published papers. His research activity continued uninterrupted into recent years: in 2023, he co-authored a study with Zeev Shem-Tov published in the Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications, and in 2024, he published another study with Tomer Menaket.
Concurrently, he maintained long-standing international collaborations, including a series of publications with the German mathematician Jürgen Grahl from the University of Würzburg, alongside participation in conferences in Israel and abroad.
In 2012, he was among the organizers of an analysis session at the Israel Mathematical Union conference and even lectured there, and in 2017 he served as a visiting researcher at the School of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Sydney in Australia.
Teaching Activity and Personal Profile
Alongside his research, Nevo remained an integral part of the teaching framework at Bar-Ilan. Traces of the courses he taught have been scattered online for over a decade - from exercise sheets and exams to lecture summaries prepared by students; in 2023, for example, a document titled "Summary of Infi 4 Course based on lectures by Prof. Shahar Nevo" was uploaded to the Math-Wiki website.
In the last academic year, he continued to lecture as usual. In the university's schedule, he is registered as a lecturer in the courses "Mathematics for Chemists C" and "Infinitesimal Calculus 4," and even appears as an academic advisor to students on the department website. The most recent retake exam (Moed B) for the calculus course took place on September 1 of this year, just weeks before his arrest.
Outside of academia, almost no public information exists regarding Nevo's personal life. According to the details of the case revealed in prosecution documents, he lives alone in Petah Tikva and holds a firearm license.
An examination of his past highlights the near-total absence of any non-professional dimension: despite decades at the university, dozens of studies, and generations of students, his digital footprint consists almost entirely of pure mathematics.
Online, an old personal website remains on the Bar-Ilan University server, including a curriculum vitae, a list of publications, and contact details, alongside various academic and professional profiles. Meanwhile, no public social media accounts can be definitively attributed to him, nor are there any past interviews or opinion pieces.
Even on the "Dargo" website, where students typically review teaching staff, a page exists under his name, but it has no reviews. His official page on the Department of Mathematics website, last updated on June 9 of this year, displayed him as Prof. Shahar Nevo and detailed his research areas before it was removed from the internet.
At Bar-Ilan University, officials quickly disavowed the veteran faculty member. Following the filing of the indictment, the institution stated that they "condemn and is shocked by the acts attributed to the lecturer," clarifying that he would be suspended immediately pending the conclusion of proceedings. Concurrently, his name was removed from the university's lecturers page.
The Terror Plot Details
According to the indictment filed by the State Attorney's Office to the Central District Court in Lod, the 60-year-old lecturer, a resident of Petah Tikva, planned to execute an extreme plan - which he conceived over several years out of an ideological motive. The defendant named his plan after an acronym for "Am Ya'ase Transfer" ("The Nation Will Execute a Transfer").
The Central District Attorney's Office attributes to the defendant in the indictment the commission of security offenses of preparation to commit an act of terrorism under the Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice, and is requesting that the court detain him until the conclusion of legal proceedings against him.
From the indictment filed by attorneys Roy Reis and Tomer Steinberg of the Central District Attorney's Office, it emerged that against the backdrop of the "Operation Guardian of the Walls" riots and later, with greater intensity against the backdrop of the Swords of Iron war, the defendant decided to plan and carry out numerous terror acts simultaneously, and to cause the deaths of many hundreds of Arab Israeli citizens, including Bedouins, throughout the entire country, including Arabs residing in east Jerusalem and the West Bank.
The plot was intended to cause their flight and permanent deportation to the territories of Jordan, Lebanon, and the Gaza Strip.

Gidi Dar’s Legend of Destruction, the movie that depicts the Jewish revolt against Rome and the destruction of the Second Temple through images, is now available for digital purchase in the US on platforms including Apple TV, Google Play, and Prime Video.
The English-language version features Oscar Isaac, Evangeline Lilly, Elliott Gould, Billy Zane, and Marilu Henner. It was directed by Dar, who has made such acclaimed films as Ushpizin and Eddie King, and it was written by Dar and Shuli Rand.
The two have collaborated frequently, and their upcoming film, The Wedding Entertainer (The Tale of Moishe Badhan), had its world premiere at the Tribeca Festival this year.
Legend of Destruction brings ancient Jerusalem to life through 1,500 original paintings by David Polonsky (who also worked on Waltz with Bashir) and Michael Faust.
The story follows Ben Batich, voiced by Isaac, an idealistic young man who joins the zealots rebelling against Rome, driven by anger at corruption and inequality. As the revolt that began in 66 CE descends into civil war, his pursuit of justice turns into fanaticism, helping the Romans to destroy the temple and retake control of Jerusalem.
Lilly voiced Queen Berenice, Gould played Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, Zane portrayed rebel leader Bar Giora, and Henner voiced Batich’s mother.
Film draws on The Jewish War, Talmudic legends, and historical research
Drawing on Josephus’s The Jewish War, Talmudic legends, and historical research, the film explored how a divided society can bring about its own downfall.
“By stripping away the illusion of 24 frames per second, we invite the viewer’s mind to fill in the gaps, creating not just motion, but emotional depth,” Dar said of its unusual visual approach.
Isaac said he quickly stopped noticing that the images were still paintings: “I felt like I was watching Gladiator.”
Lilly described the film as “a warning signal for the modern world.”
More information is available at legendofdestruction.com

Abbas delays elections until 2027, Palestinian democracy demands genuine reform - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:17:05 UTC
12:17:05 KST

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas postponed legislative elections on Saturday, replacing the November 28 vote with a promise of presidential and parliamentary elections on September 11, 2027.
His decree cited Israeli actions and deteriorating conditions across Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.
The difficulties facing election organizers are substantial. Gaza is devastated, Hamas remains armed, and movement restrictions complicate preparations. Those conditions require serious practical arrangements.
Abbas also owes Palestinians an explanation of how another postponement will produce a political system capable of holding its leaders accountable.
Palestinians last elected a president in 2005 and a legislature in 2006. Abbas’s presidential mandate expired in 2009. An entire generation has reached adulthood without choosing its national leadership.
Responsibility for that prolonged failure rests heavily with the Palestinian leaders who have retained power throughout it.
Palestinians need accountable leadership, Israel needs reliable security
Palestinians deserve the opportunity to replace their rulers peacefully. Israel also has an interest in credible Palestinian institutions that can maintain security, implement agreements, and exercise authority over armed factions.
Building such institutions requires sustained reform, enforceable rules, and leaders prepared to accept limits on their power.
Hamas’s victory in the 2006 legislative election and its subsequent violent takeover of Gaza must inform any discussion of another vote. The organization responsible for the October 7 massacre cannot acquire a legitimate claim to govern while retaining its terrorist infrastructure.
Its weapons threaten Israeli lives and the freedom of Palestinians to organize, campaign, and disagree.
Participation should therefore require renouncing terrorism, recognizing Israel, accepting existing agreements, and dismantling independent armed forces. These obligations must apply equally to every faction and be verified in practice.
Candidates running under alternative labels must face the same scrutiny when evidence establishes organizational ties to armed groups.
Eligibility rules should be published in advance and subject to independent review. Their enforcement must rest on documented conduct, with a fair appeal process protecting peaceful challengers from arbitrary exclusion by incumbents.
A credible election also requires an independent electoral commission, accessible voter registration, impartial courts, and protection for journalists and opposition candidates.
Voters must be able to criticize the Palestinian Authority without fear. Parties must commit to respecting the results and allowing future elections, including when their own hold on office is threatened.
Abbas must set clear reform deadlines ahead of September 2027 elections
Abbas should publish a timetable for those reforms, with deadlines that can be assessed before September 2027.
Preparations for polling and international monitoring should proceed alongside transparent public finances, scrutiny of security institutions, and action against incitement.
Public funds must be subject to safeguards preventing their use to reward or encourage terrorism.
These changes will face resistance from those whose influence depends on patronage, secrecy or coercion. International partners should make clear that another postponement carries political consequences.
Donors should condition support for governing institutions on measurable progress, with humanitarian assistance protected so ordinary Palestinians are spared the cost of their leaders’ failures.
Countries recognizing Palestine must demand accountable governance
Governments that have recognized a Palestinian state have a particular responsibility to insist on these standards. Their diplomatic commitments should be followed by scrutiny of how Palestinian institutions operate. Recognition creates no guarantee that a government respects its citizens, controls its territory, and intends to live peacefully alongside Israel.
Israel has responsibilities too. Its government should work toward practical arrangements for voting, election observers, and necessary movement, consistent with protecting Israeli citizens.
Specific restrictions should be justified by concrete security needs and reviewed when circumstances change. Facilitating credible Palestinian government can serve Israel’s long-term interests.
Jerusalem voting arrangements will require careful negotiation. Security concerns must be addressed through workable procedures, while Palestinian leaders must demonstrate that they are pursuing solutions in good faith. Progress on electoral independence, financial transparency, and political freedoms can begin immediately, even while difficult logistical questions remain unresolved.
The new election date should carry obligations that can be checked throughout the coming year. Abbas should face regular public scrutiny over what has changed, which commitments remain unmet, and who is responsible. Palestinian civil society deserves access to that information and space to challenge official explanations.
Palestinians need accountable leadership, and Israelis need reliable security.
Elections conducted within a reformed political system can advance both interests. The months ahead should be used to establish the freedoms, safeguards, and enforceable commitments that give a future vote meaning.

Tens of thousands of pro-Palestinian demonstrators turned out across Europe on Saturday, as activists marked three years of war in Gaza with rallies and marches in cities from London to Rome and Berlin.
According to Israel’s Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, 357 pro-Palestinian protest events were scheduled across 39 countries from the beginning of October through Wednesday, with Saturday expected to be the day with the largest number of protests. The United States had the highest number of expected demonstrations across the two-week period, followed by Spain, Britain and Australia.
In the UK on Saturday, thousands of demonstrators marched through London, wearing keffiyehs and waving Palestinian flags. The Palestine Solidarity Campaign claimed that more than 250,000 people took to the streets of London in support of Palestine, though the figure was not independently verified by JTA.
“Today we’re marching for Palestine in London to mark three years of Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people and demand our government go further to sanction Israel for its crimes. Britain must stop arming Israel now,” the group wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
Footage posted by the Palestine Solidarity Campaign showed thousands of demonstrators marching through the British capital, waving Palestinian flags.
Police, counter-protestors present
Local police imposed restrictions on the march to “minimize the risk of serious disruption to communities.” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Carl Galvin was quoted in British media as saying that “Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”
He added that police would use their powers to require anyone deliberately concealing their identity with a face covering in the protest area to remove it.
British media also reported that a counter-protest organized by Stop the Hate was taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside the Metropolitan Police headquarters.
Across the Irish Sea, more than 10,000 demonstrators gathered in Dublin for a march in support of Palestine, according to RTÉ. The broadcaster reported that it was the 21st nationwide demonstration since the war in Gaza began in October 2023 and that more than 160 Irish civil society groups supported the march.
On the European continent, Italian media reported that marches and demonstrations were taking place in around 50 cities, including Rome, Milan, Turin and Naples. The wave of demonstrations was organized by several pro-Palestinian groups under the slogan “The End of the Genocide.” Sky TG24 reported that Swedish activist Greta Thunberg was present at a demonstration in Naples.
'From the river to the sea' chanted throughout Italy, Europe
Footage from Rome, Bologna and Turin showed thousands of protesters marching with signs and Palestinian flags. Some signs read, “From the river to the sea,” while another large banner read, “Against genocide, war, Zionism, and all complicity.”
Farther north, more than 1,000 demonstrators took part in a protest in Berlin, according to Die Welt. The demonstrators gathered outside the Chancellery in the afternoon, chanting “Free Palestine, free Palestine” and “F–k you, Israel.”
A smaller counterdemonstration took place across from the march, with participants waving Israeli flags and calling to “Free Berlin from Hamas,” the newspaper reported.
Berlin police had announced plans to deploy approximately 1,400 officers, including personnel from several other German states and the Federal Police.
In Switzerland, around 1,000 people gathered in Zurich to protest the war in Gaza. Swiss public broadcaster SWI reported that demonstrators observed a minute of silence during the march, which took place under a substantial police presence.
More demonstrations are expected around the world in the coming days to mark three years of war in Gaza. Several protests are scheduled to take place across the United States over the next 24 hours, while large demonstrations are expected in Australia on Sunday. A series of protests is also planned in Latin America in the coming days.
Earlier this week, the third anniversary of Oct. 7, 2023, was marked, commemorating the day Hamas led an invasion into southern Israel, killing approximately 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. Large pro-Palestinian demonstrations were held around the world that day and in the following days, including at numerous locations across the United States.

The US Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of the US president, Donald Trump, last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.
A spokesperson for the department said group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” they said.

Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC.
The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports – a type of free speech, pillar of American democracy.
Last month’s developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump’s efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive.
On 19 September, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico and MS Now from entering the building, revoking their credentials. The White House said covering the president was a “privilege – not a right”.
CNN, MS Now and Politico sued over the days-long ban. It was lifted after a judge handed the three news organisations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday.
Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed. The broadcasters in the pool share the costs of covering the president, take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ regional director of the Americas, on Saturday criticized the administration’s decision to investigate.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”

Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:06:35 UTC
12:06:35 KST

Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
Researchers in Vienna have built the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, bringing scientists closer to a new era of ultra-precise timekeeping.
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- Vienna University of Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists in Vienna have achieved a major breakthrough in timekeeping by creating the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a technology that could eventually surpass even the most precise atomic clocks. Instead of relying on electrons in atoms, the clock uses the tiny nuclei of thorium atoms, which are far less sensitive to outside disturbances.
- Share:
Scientists have reached a major milestone in the quest to build an entirely new kind of clock. After decades of research, a team in Vienna has developed the world's first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a device that could eventually measure time with far greater precision than today's most advanced atomic clocks.
Unlike earlier prototypes, the new nuclear clock can maintain its own stability without depending on a conventional atomic clock. Researchers have demonstrated that it can operate steadily for more than 24 hours without intervention.
The achievement represents an important advance in precision measurement, also known as metrology. By using atomic nuclei as exceptionally stable references, nuclear clocks could eventually allow scientists to measure time and other physical quantities with levels of accuracy that existing technologies cannot reach.
Why Thorium Holds the Key to Nuclear Clocks
The breakthrough relies on an unusual property of thorium atomic nuclei that scientists have investigated for decades.
Atomic nuclei can exist in different energy states, but moving between those states typically requires enormous amounts of energy. Thorium is a rare exception. Two of its nuclear energy states are separated by an unusually small energy gap, making it possible to trigger a transition between them using laser light.
This property is crucial because it allows researchers to control the energy state of a nucleus with a laser, something that is not possible in the same way for most other atomic nuclei. Scientists can then use this extremely precise transition as a reference for measuring time.
A major breakthrough came in April 2024, when researchers led by Prof. Thorsten Schumm at the Institute of Atomic and Subatomic Physics at TU Wien, working with a team led by Prof. Ekkehard Peik at PTB Braunschweig, identified the long-sought nuclear transition experimentally. They demonstrated for the first time that laser beams could excite thorium nuclei.
Further progress followed in the fall of 2024. The researchers connected their thorium excitation apparatus to a conventional optical atomic clock, demonstrating that the nuclei could serve as a highly precise timekeeping reference.
Although this established the basic principle of a nuclear clock, one essential capability was still missing: the ability to maintain its own accuracy independently.
Scientists Build a Nuclear Clock That Stabilizes Itself
"What you really want is a self-stabilizing nuclear clock," explains Prof. Thorsten Schumm. "The basic idea is simple: you have a laser and you have thorium. The laser changes the energy state of the thorium nuclei, and the thorium nuclei are used to stabilize the frequency of the laser."
To make this possible, the researchers developed a system built around a special crystal containing thorium atoms, manufactured at TU Wien. A laser shines onto the crystal, interacting with the thorium nuclei inside.
The laser's light oscillates at a particular frequency, providing a regular rhythm that can be used to measure time. However, even tiny changes in the surrounding environment can interfere with that rhythm.
"The oscillation of this laser light can be used for timekeeping, but the laser frequency can shift slightly from time to time, for example due to temperature fluctuations," explains Thorsten Schumm. "For high-precision measurements, you therefore need a mechanism to keep the laser frequency exactly stable, so that the clock continues to tick with precisely the same rhythm."
Traditional atomic clocks solve this problem by using the energy transitions of electrons in atoms as a stable reference. The Vienna team has now demonstrated that the nuclei of thorium atoms can perform the same function.
The mechanism works because thorium nuclei absorb laser light only when the light has precisely the correct frequency. If the laser begins to drift away from that frequency, the amount of light absorbed by the nuclei decreases.
The system detects this change and automatically adjusts the laser to bring it back to the correct frequency. This continuous feedback keeps the clock operating at a consistent rate, without requiring a conventional atomic clock to maintain its stability.
For the first time, scientists have demonstrated a self-regulating nuclear clock that can function independently.
A Clock With an Error of Just One Second in 30 Million Years
The potential advantage of nuclear clocks comes from the extraordinary properties of atomic nuclei.
"The great advantage of the new nuclear clock in Vienna is that, if you use atomic nuclei rather than atoms, much higher precision is possible in principle," says Thorsten Schumm.
Atomic nuclei are more than 10,000 times smaller than atoms. Because of their extremely small size, they are much less affected by external influences that can disrupt precise measurements.
This resistance to environmental disturbances makes nuclear energy transitions especially promising for ultra-precise timekeeping.
To evaluate their prototype, the researchers measured its performance over the course of a day. The nuclear clock achieved a relative precision of approximately 10 to the power of minus 15, equivalent to an error of roughly one second over 30 million years.
That figure describes the clock's measured precision rather than an actual test lasting millions of years. Nevertheless, it illustrates the remarkable accuracy the researchers have already achieved with an early prototype.
The new clock is not yet as precise as the world's leading optical atomic clocks, which remain the benchmark for high-performance timekeeping.
"This is not yet at the level of the world's best optical atomic clocks, but for a first prototype it is a fantastic result," says Thorsten Schumm.
The Next Step Toward Even More Precise Timekeeping
The researchers believe their nuclear clock has considerable room for improvement. By using more powerful lasers and developing higher-quality thorium crystals, they hope to substantially increase its precision.
These upgrades could eventually allow nuclear clocks to outperform existing atomic clocks and establish a new standard for measuring time.
The implications extend beyond simply building a better clock. More accurate timekeeping can also improve the measurement of other physical quantities, providing researchers with increasingly sensitive tools for investigating the fundamental properties of nature.
For now, the Vienna team's achievement demonstrates that a long-pursued scientific concept can operate as a self-sustaining timekeeping system. With the world's first self-stabilizing nuclear clock now running independently, scientists have taken an important step toward a future in which time can be measured with unprecedented precision.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Vienna University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- L. Toscani De Col, T. Riebner, I. Morawetz, F. Schneider, N. Sempelmann, J. Schlachet-Lépinay, F. Schaden, M. Bartokos, G. A. Kazakov, K. Beeks, B. Gerstenecker, M. Pimon, S. Lahs, A. Hellerschmied, T. Lercher, H. Denker, J. Premper, A. Niessner, M. Matus, M. Čížek, O. Číp, V. Lal, G. Zitzer, V. Petrov, J. Tiedau, M. V. Okhapkin, E. Peik, T. Schumm. A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop. Nature, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11084-4

House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:05:49 UTC
12:05:49 KST

WASHINGTON -- Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking Russian oil purchases, challenging President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as lawmakers warn the move could help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.
Fitzpatrick (Republican-Pennsylvania), co-chair of the House Ukraine Caucus, announced on October 10 that he would introduce the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick wrote on X. “It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly.”
Representative Don Bacon (Republican-Nebraska) has agreed to co-sponsor the bill. A Democratic sponsor had not been identified.
A discharge petition can force a House vote without approval from the relevant committee or House leadership if it secures 218 signatures.
The effort faces time constraints: Congress is not scheduled to resume voting for several weeks, and the current congressional term ends in January. Any bill would also need Senate approval and could face White House opposition.
Fitzpatrick invoked former President Ronald Reagan's approach to confronting Moscow and reaffirmed congressional support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has again criticized.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine. Russia is squarely to blame,” Fitzpatrick wrote, adding that Congress and the American people stood behind Zelenskyy “until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
Republicans Question Sanctions Reversal
The proposed legislation reflects concern among some Republicans that easing Russian energy restrictions could undermine pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Representative Michael McCaul (Republican-Texas), the former chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that lifting sanctions could “fund the Kremlin's war machine -- emboldening more violence and destruction.”
He cited the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The law authorizes the president, under specified conditions, to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian energy. McCaul said it gave Trump leverage over Russia and China to help secure a negotiated end to the war.
Senator Lisa Murkowski (Republican-Alaska) urged Trump to use those authorities instead of allowing Russia to earn more from diesel exports.
“We can discuss Russia's return to global energy markets once the war is over, but in the meantime, we need to cut off everything fueling it,” she wrote on social media.
Democrats Cite Existing Oil Ban
Democrats and former officials have also pointed to the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has met specified conditions, including withdrawing from Ukraine, recognizing Ukrainian sovereignty and posing no threat to NATO.
The law passed the Senate 100-0 and the House 413-9 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Former Representative Tom Malinowski, also a former top State Department official, urged Democratic leaders to use the law's expedited procedures to challenge the administration's decision.
“Under this law, House and Senate Democratic leaders can introduce a ‘Joint Resolution of Disapproval’ to prevent the purchase of Russian oil, which Congress then has to vote on in an expedited manner,” Malinowski wrote on social media.
“Schumer and Jeffries should do so ASAP,” he added, referring to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Whether the 2022 law applies to the latest arrangement remains a key question as the administration's temporary authorization for Russian diesel exports faces scrutiny.
Advocates Warn Of Damage To Sanctions
Daniel Balson, advocacy director at Razom for Ukraine, told RFE/RL that Trump's decision undermined the purpose of the sanctions legislation passed weeks earlier.
“Three weeks ago, Congress passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. This bill was designed to force other countries to lower their Russian energy dependence. President Trump's recent decision just increased our own,” Balson said.
He urged lawmakers to challenge the move to protect Ukraine and the credibility of congressional action. Although he had not seen Fitzpatrick's bill, Balson said pro-Ukraine advocates would pursue “any and all legislative avenues” to oppose the decision.
Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who generally votes with Democrats, said in a statement that the agreement would offer little relief to American consumers while benefiting Russia.
Citing administration figures, King said the deal covered 300,000 tons of diesel for October and 500,000 tons for November -- roughly equivalent to a day's diesel consumption in the United States.
“This so-called deal with Russia will do little for America and much for Vladimir Putin as he seeks to sustain his murderous campaign on Ukraine,” King said. He called the agreement “a fraud.”
Trump Again Calls For Zelenskyy To Be Replaced
Trump on October 10 renewed his attacks on Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should hold an election and replace its president with a leader willing to reach an agreement with Russia.
“Well, I think he should have an election. And he could have settled this thing many times,” Trump told reporters.
Earlier, Trump had said Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.” He also demanded that Kyiv “damn well stop” attacking Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has targeted to disrupt Moscow's war economy and fuel supplies.
Trump blamed Zelenskyy for failing to secure a settlement, a claim at odds with Kyiv’s position that any agreement must protect Ukraine’s sovereignty and with lawmakers’ calls to maintain pressure on Moscow. Trump also portrayed Putin as eager for peace and praised the release of Russian oil onto global markets.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia's war economy is terrible,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
Trump's remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhya.
Zelenskyy has said elections cannot be held under martial law and amid the security risks created by Russia's invasion. Ukrainian officials have also cited the need to ensure soldiers and displaced citizens can participate in a credible vote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha issued a statement late on October 10 backing the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy "leads our nation in a time of war -- a war for independence, freedom, and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support," Sybiha wrote on X.
EU Rejects Easing Pressure On Russia
European officials criticized the diesel agreement, warning that additional Russian energy revenue could help sustain the war.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians over the past two days and that Moscow had intensified hybrid attacks against EU member states and NATO allies.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't,” Kallas said, adding that EU foreign ministers planned to announce a major new round of sanctions on October 12 targeting people and organizations supporting Moscow's war effort.
Germany also reaffirmed its commitment to existing sanctions and said it would work with European partners on further measures.
A spokesman for Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Berlin stood by its restrictions, while government spokesman Stefan Kornelius reiterated support for Ukraine. Economics Minister Katherina Reiche also backed the EU sanctions packages.
Germany's Fuels and Energy Trade Association said it did not expect the agreement to have a major effect on petrol-station prices.

Could Thai durian export duty mean higher prices, higher quality in China?
Proposed levy part of a draft bill aimed at establishing a fund for research and ‘sustainable’ development of the sector
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
A Thai government proposal to charge export duties on durians, a major cash crop, could raise prices for the fruit in China – its primary market – along with the quality, analysts said.
Thailand’s draft bill to establish a fund for research and “sustainable” development of the durian sector would include the collection of fees, the government’s public relations department said last month.
Southeast Asian media outlets and agricultural publications have tipped the export duty to be as high as 2 baht (5 US cents) per kilogram.
That extra cost could be passed on to Chinese supermarkets, analysts said. China consumed more than 90 per cent of the world’s durians, HSBC analysts said in a report published in 2023.

Akhilesh shares video of alleged harassment during Delhi crackdown
NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav on Sunday took a swipe at the BJP over alleged incidents of harassment and violence against women during the crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi, which was brought to a halt with thousands of people detained, including several political leaders.The protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar was effectively reduced to a story of restrictions, detentions and containment, with Delhi Police enforcing security measures ahead of the proposed showdown.
Akhilesh shared a video on X purportedly showing multiple incidents in which women were allegedly harassed and assaulted by men dressed in civilian clothes. Targeting the ruling BJP, the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister wrote: “The country's capital, drowned in shame! This is the truth of BJP's 'honoring women.' Disgraceful!”
Mamata-led Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra also shared a video, directly targeting the RSS. She wrote: “What’s worrying in this video is not that RSS goon Raman is assaulting women. What is worrying is Delhi police is telling him to go & ensure camera is off.”
Saturday’s proposed protest at Jantar Mantar was met with a massive security deployment, with around 35,000 police personnel mobilised. Security restrictions, including metro service curbs and internet shutdowns, were also reported as authorities moved to prevent the demonstration from escalating.
The heavy police presence and surveillance in the national capital curtailed the protest before it could gain momentum.CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained shortly after arriving in Delhi by air.Several other leaders, including former chief ministers Arvind Kejriwal, Mamata Banerjee and Pinarayi Vijayan, were also detained amid the crackdown.

Saudi-led coalition vows ‘firm’ response after 12 killed in attack on Riyadh airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:52:41 UTC
11:52:41 KST

Tarek Chouiref
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen vowed early Sunday to respond “firmly” to an attack on the main airport in the capital Riyadh, which authorities said killed 12 people and injured 309 others.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki blamed Yemen’s Houthis for the Saturday attack on King Khalid International Airport, saying it targeted one of the passenger terminals and killed and injured both travelers and airport workers.
Al-Maliki said the attack constituted a war crime under international humanitarian law and customary rules.
He said the coalition’s Joint Forces Command would respond “firmly” and in line with international humanitarian law.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said early Sunday that the fatalities included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, and one citizen each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine, and Sudan.
The authority said 309 people were injured, including some in critical condition, and were getting treatment at hospitals.
The attack also caused material damage, which authorities said they were still assessing.
Operations at the airport were temporarily suspended on Saturday while officials assessed the damage and verified the safety of its facilities.
The attack came in the wake of recent Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and other facilities.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ramzi Mahmud and Tarek Chouiref
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
The Israeli army destroyed four Palestinian homes in northern and central Gaza late Saturday in airstrikes that also damaged dozens of nearby buildings, according to witnesses and sources.
An Anadolu correspondent said Israeli warplanes struck three homes in Gaza City and another in Deir al-Balah after evacuation warnings were issued for residential areas.
Witnesses said residents got evacuation orders by phone, triggering panic and forcing dozens of families to flee.
Sources said the strikes targeted homes in Gaza City’s Shujaiya, Al-17, and Rimal areas, as well as a home belonging to the Al-Buhaysi family in Deir al-Balah.
The four homes were destroyed, while dozens of surrounding houses and buildings were damaged, said witnesses.
A fifth Israeli airstrike hit empty agricultural land near Salah al-Din Street, east of Deir al-Balah.
No casualties were reported, according to preliminary information from sources.
Medical sources said Israeli drone strikes earlier Saturday in Gaza City killed five Palestinians and wounded several others.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000, according to Palestinian figures.
The war has also destroyed 90% of the enclave's infrastructure, Palestinian figures have shown.
Israeli violations of a ceasefire deal have killed more than 1,470 Palestinians and wounded over 5,180, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres late Saturday "strongly" condemned a Houthi attack targeting the main airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, which claimed at least 12 lives and injured hundreds of civilians.
"I am deeply shocked by & strongly condemn Saturday’s lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which reportedly killed 12 people & injured hundreds of civilians," Guterres wrote on US-based social media company X.

The suspension has disrupted flights, with passengers advised to check with airlines before heading to the airport. Kuwait Airways also canceled Saturday service to Riyadh and return flights, citing the airport’s closure.
The attack comes amid heightened tensions following Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and facilities in recent days.

Interest payments to IMF and World Bank to cost Ukraine $27.94 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:40:14 UTC
11:40:14 KST

MOSCOW, October 11. /TASS/. Ukraine will have to pay the IMF and the World Bank $27.94 billion in interest on its debt until 2061, according TASS calculations based on data from the Finance Ministry.
As part of the repayment of the body of debt to the international financial institutions, Ukraine will have to pay 59.7 billion euros ($66.93 billion), $21.3 billion, and 9.4 billion units of special drawing rights to the IMF by 2061 (SDR is a conditional unit used in settlements with the IMF, calculated on the basis of a basket of the five currencies. At the moment its exchange rate is $1.35 per 1 SDR, so Ukraine owes another $12.69 billion). The total amount that Kiev will have to repay on the principal debt to the international financial organizations stands at $100.92 billion.
Taking into account the principal debt and interest, Ukraine will have to pay the IMF and the World Bank $128.86 billion. These amounts will increase, and payment term will be postponed, as Kiev continues to build up its foreign debt fast.
Ukraine’s total state and state-guaranteed debt amounted to 9.603 trillion hryvnias, or $215.55 billion as of August 31. According to TASS calculations, each Ukrainian owes $8,622 based on a population of 25 million. If we assume a population of 22 million, the debt amounts to almost $9,800 per capita. There are no exact statistics on Ukraine’s population at present, but Social Policy Minister Denis Ulyutin put it at between 22 and 25 million.

‘Blatant attack on press freedom’: Journalists’ bodies condemn detention of journalists at Delhi protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:31:15 UTC
11:31:15 KST

A protestor being dragged towards a detention bus during Jantar Mantar 2.0 on October 10 in Delhi
NEW DELHI: Four journalists’ organisations on Saturday expressed concern over the detention of journalists covering protests in Delhi demanding chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, saying the incident raised serious questions about press freedom.The Press Club of India (PCI), Indian Women’s Press Corps (IWPC), Delhi Union of Journalists (DUJ) and Delhi unit of the Kerala Union of Working Journalists (KUWJ) said journalists were targeted while documenting the police action. In a joint statement, they alleged that reporters carrying valid press identity cards were taken away and that some had their phones and reporting equipment confiscated, news agency PTI reported.
The organisations termed the action a “blatant attack on the freedom of press” and demanded the immediate release of all detained journalists.Reporters taken to detention centres, equipment seizedAccording to the statement, journalists covering Saturday’s protests were put on buses and taken to locations including Chhatrasal Stadium and Chanakyapuri police station, alongside hundreds of protesters detained by the police.
The organisations said reporters were filming the detentions when police personnel took them into custody, despite their displaying press cards. They also cited complaints that officers refused to acknowledge their journalistic credentials, with some allegedly remarking, “Everybody claims to be a journalist these days.”The statement further alleged that official reporting phones belonging to some of the detained journalists were taken away.‘PIB accreditation cannot determine who can report’The four bodies also objected to the Delhi Police’s reported insistence that only journalists accredited by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) could cover the protests.“Press freedom in India cannot be conditional on PIB accreditation. A large section of digital and independent media does not have PIB cards, yet they are recognised press under the law,” they said.The organisations said they had flagged the issue in a memorandum to the Delhi Police commissioner earlier in the week. However, they alleged that the concerns and recommendations raised in the representation had not been addressed.They sought an inquiry into the role of senior police officers who allegedly directed the detention of journalists even after being shown their press identification cards. Their demands also included the return of seized equipment, a public apology from Delhi Police and an assurance that reporters would be free to cover demonstrations without interference.
They also said the restrictions, coupled with the detention of journalists, undermined the ability of the media to report on public protests and question institutions.
“Preventing journalists from doing their job, detaining them without reason, and creating a fortress-like situation in the capital with 22,000 police and paramilitary, closed metro stations and unprecedented internet shutdowns, to stop peaceful questioning of institutions is reminiscent of a fascist state,” the statement said.
Priyanka Jaiswal has four years of experience in digital journalism, news agency reporting and video production. Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

New HK$122 million lifeguard outsourcing contract sparks public spending concerns
Firm awarded new contract to supply services at six pools despite failing to provide required staffing on seven occasions previously
A controversial decision by Hong Kong authorities to award a lifeguard and first aid services contract worth more than HK$122 million (US$15.6 million) to a company previously found to have failed to provide the required staffing at swimming pools has sparked concerns over whether public funds are being used prudently.
The department outsourced services at six public swimming pools in September 2024 in a trial scheme to tackle long-standing lifeguard shortages, awarding two contracts worth a total of HK$75.9 million to Spotlight Enterprises for two years of services.

Interview: ITTF chief Sorling regards WTT China Smash as flagship event
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:28:35 CST
11:28:35 KST

by sportswriters Li Chunyu, Su Bin and Yue Ranran
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- As the World Table Tennis (WTT) China Smash returned to Beijing's Shougang Park for a third consecutive year, International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF) President Petra Sorling praised the event as a flagship and a model from which other organizers can draw inspiration.
"Among all events in the WTT calendar, China Smash here in Beijing is really important and special for us," said Sorling on Saturday. "Our athletes like it a lot, and we have good support from the fans. We are also proud to be a sport that can be played on the highest level in the capital city. It's more than just table tennis."
Shougang Park, home to the Winter Olympic venue Big Air Shougang, has developed into a popular sports and tourism destination amid its preserved industrial heritage.
"I was here for the Winter Olympics in 2022 when I saw skiers making their different loops in the sunshine," Sorling said. "I was so impressed for how this park was converted, combining modern architecture together with a former industrial area. I'm very proud that we can use the Olympic legacy for table tennis, not only once but every year."
At the foot of Big Air Shougang, less than one kilometer from the China Smash competition venues, a Smash Park was set up with catering services and sports activities. Visitors could watch matches live on big screens and meet table tennis stars at autograph sessions.
"The Smash Park itself is a good example. A family can come to have a picnic and meet with friends. It's a way to bring out the events to the community, not only for the few with a ticket inside but a bigger crowd. I even tried to see if we can do something similar at the Olympics," Sorling said.
The ITTF president said the China Smash offered lessons for other organizers in areas ranging from community engagement to player services.
"The China Smash is a presentation. It's about how to build the Smash Park with the community. In terms of the care of the players, they have everything close around. The players can walk and don't have to transport themselves," she further explained.
Running from October 1 to 11, this year's China Smash coincided with China's National Day holiday from October 1 to 7, bringing the tournament into the wider holiday atmosphere.
"If possible, to have an event during a holiday is a big advantage. This is a chance for family to come together and really enjoy. We have a calendar, and to schedule everything is not always easy. But when we can do it like here during a holiday and festival season, it is the best," Sorling noted.
The draw and opening ceremonies also incorporated Chinese cultural elements.
"Within the venue, when you are at the table, it looks the same. But like the draw ceremony, it was held in such an iconic and historical place, adding cultural aspects of music, dancing and some painting," Sorling said. "It helps us to learn more about each other and experience more than just coming to another place and play table tennis."
"The draw ceremony was not only for the ones who are here, but also followed by millions of viewers around the world. So it's a good way to showcase, and I believe that many would like to come when they see this beautiful video from the draw ceremony," she added.
Even after the holiday, the tournament continued to attract spectators with its latter stages, while the China Youth Smash, featuring more than 100 young players, ran from Friday to Sunday.
"For the young players here, it means a lot. Myself and CTTA (Chinese Table Tennis Association) president Wang Liqin went to meet with the players and speak with them. We asked them about their dreams and how we can do better for them. They dream of one day being here as a senior player. It is actually a very important educational tool to bring the youth closer to the senior level of players," Sorling said.
Sorling said the presentation of the sport beyond competition itself was increasingly important to the success of WTT events.
"What I can say in the landscape also as an IOC (International Olympic Committee) member is that sport today is about entertaining. It means that we can't only focus on the match itself. It has to be presented in a way that the younger audience want to come and like to be part."
At the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, table tennis will feature six events, including the newly introduced mixed team competition alongside men's and women's singles, men's and women's doubles, and mixed doubles.
"For a very long time, table tennis had four medal events until the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. We feel like the athletes deserve more chances to win medals, and we also know that it's very difficult to get a new discipline and a new medal event to the program. The mixed doubles was an easier choice for us back at the Tokyo Games, then we had five medal events," Sorling recalled.
"We were innovating around that, then it became a Mixed Team World Cup with a new playing format. It's a little bit faster as we are counting the set. We felt immediately that this was appealing for the young audience and the fans. Then, we started to inform and inspire the IOC of this new innovation," she said. "I'm very excited about LA28 when we will be the racket sport with the most medal events."
This year marks the ITTF's 100th anniversary, and Sorling said the federation would continue to innovate and adapt through new concepts and technologies.
"We are thinking of and working every day to improve and make our sport relevant for the next generations to come. What table tennis looks like in the next 100 years is something that we are working on. Here we are really happy to listen to the athletes and our fans - 'What do you want? How can we do better'?" ■

LONDON, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Saturday reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky amid tensions between Washington and Kiev over a U.S.-Russia agreement on diesel supplies.
