More than 70 stranded as Solomon Islands ferry drifts for days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
23:45:59 UTC
08:45:59 KST

Dozens stranded at sea after Solomon Islands ferry engine fails
In short:
A Solomon Islands ferry was travelling between the remote islands of Anuta and Vanikoro when its engine failed on Friday, about 100 nautical miles from its destination.
Aircraft from Australia and New Caledonia have dropped supplies and equipment for the boat with more than 70 passengers onboard.
A Panama-registered bulk carrier reached the ferry on Sunday morning and began transferring water and food.
More than 70 passengers have been stranded aboard a drifting ferry in Solomon Islands waters since Friday, as an international operation scrambles to get supplies to the vessel.
The ferry was sailing between the remote islands of Anuta and Vanikoro in Temotu Province when its engine failed on Friday, leaving it adrift at sea.
A Panama-registered bulk carrier reached MV Awka on Sunday morning and began transferring water and food, passenger John Tua said.
The Solomon Islands Maritime Authority told the ABC there are 74 passengers and 16 crew on board.
Mr Tua, a nurse with the provincial government, said the engine was overheating when it broke down about 100 nautical miles from its destination.
"Everyone is OK, no-one panicked, passengers were calm … we're just waiting for the rescue ships to come,"
he said.
While the seas have been mostly calm, Mr Tua said the ship had also experienced rough swells.
A distress call was issued on Friday, with the Solomon Islands enlisting help from the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) and New Caledonian government.
An AMSA spokesperson said its Cairns-based rescue jet made several drops of critical items including food, water, medical supplies and communications equipment.
A French aircraft from New Caledonia was first on the scene on Saturday, dropping life rafts and desalination equipment.
"The urgent need was water. We've run out of water onboard … the ship's water supply was used to cool the engine down when it was heating up," Mr Tua said.
"We have lots of brown coconuts on board to drink, but our water is finished."
A Temotu provincial government statement said: "The latest information indicates that the passengers on board MV Akwa now have access to essential supplies, including drinking water, food, and medical provisions delivered through the air and sea supply operations."
On Sunday morning, the Panama-registered bulk carrier Sunnine 3 reached the vessel early and began transferring water and food, which was live-streamed online by Mr Tua.
Loading...
Passengers have stayed in touch with families using the ship's Starlink internet, while Mr Tua has been the main source of news for worried relatives.
Temotu Premier Stanley Tehiahua said a police patrol boat was on its way from Honiara.
"To all relatives, families and friends anxiously awaiting news of their loved ones, we recognise the emotional distress and uncertainty you are experiencing," he said in a statement.
"We call on everyone to remain calm, united and prayerful during this difficult time,"
Mr Tehiahua said.
The ABC has requested comment from the Solomon Islands Maritime Safety Administration and the country's Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.
The incident comes four weeks after the inter-island ferry MV Matui sank in rough seas in neighbouring Vanuatu with more than 50 people onboard. Two people have since been confirmed dead, 14 have been rescued while 39 others remain missing.
There have been calls for Australia and New Zealand to invest more in maritime safety, including from Peter Nuttall, technical adviser for the Micronesian Centre for Sustainable Transport at the University of the South Pacific, who told the ABC after the Matui sinking that Australia could easily invest in better vessels for the Pacific.
"We could have built 40 to 60 safe, brand new, low-carbon ferries for the same budget as we've spent on 20-something patrol boats, several which have already been scrapped," Dr Nuttall said.

Ukrainian Armed Forces strike on Russia’s missile disposal center may have affected the Kremlin’s strategic programs - Defense Express
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:44:37 EEST
08:44:37 KST

Ukrainian Armed Forces strike on Russia’s missile disposal center may have affected the Kremlin’s strategic programs - Defense Express
Kyiv • UNN
The strike on the missile disposal center in the Nizhny Novgorod region may have affected Russia’s arsenal and space projects. The extent of the damage is unknown.
Ukrainian forces struck the Center for the Elimination of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles in the area of Syrovatikha, Nizhny Novgorod Region, Russia, overnight on October 9. Despite its name, the facility may have played an important role not only in disposing of old missiles, but also in supporting Russia's strategic missile arsenal and ensuring space programs. This is stated in an analysis by Defense Express, reports UNN.
Details
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the enterprise was involved in the production chain for explosives and rocket fuel components. The center was established in 1991 on the basis of a military unit that had previously been engaged in the neutralization and dismantling of missiles.
In the 1990s, the facility disposed of intercontinental ballistic missiles that remained in Russia after the collapse of the USSR. In total, 448 missiles of the R-36 and UR-100N UTTKh types were eliminated there במסגרת international strategic arms reduction agreements.
How the center is connected to the "Satan" missiles and satellite programs
Later, the enterprise acquired additional functions, including maintaining the technical condition of R-36M missiles, known as "Satan" or RS-20 "Voevoda." According to estimates cited by Defense Express, as of 2024 Russia had 34 such missiles.
In addition, the center was involved in the Dnipro program, which provided for converting intercontinental ballistic missiles into space launch vehicles. Although the program was officially closed in 2015, the enterprise continued to participate in supplying liquid-fuel components for other launch vehicles.
Analysts note that such technologies are significant for Russian satellite projects, including "Bureau-1440" and "Yamal," which are viewed as attempts to create their own satellite communications systems similar to Starlink.
Defense Express emphasizes that the strike on this facility is important given its possible role in Russia's rocket and space industry. At the same time, the extent of the enterprise's damage and the actual impact of the strike on Russian programs remain unknown.

- The US announced new sanctions on the ICC hours after Pillay won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, and the court said the move attacked international law.
- Israel, Netanyahu and Trump condemned the award and the ICC, while the Nobel committee’s choice drew sharp political backlash.
AI generated
OSLO – The winner of 2026’s Nobel Peace Prize, judge and former UN rights chief Navi Pillay, on Oct 10 called sanctions announced by the US on the International Criminal Court (ICC) “unheard of, unacceptable”.
“There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague,” she said via video link from Nuremberg during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo.
She also lamented that “there are hundreds of staff who feel they are under threat”.
“Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable,” the 85-year-old South African lawyer said.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee on Oct 9 announced that Pillay, who once sat on the ICC, was 2026’s recipient of the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize.
Both the US, whose leader Donald Trump has long coveted the award for himself, and ally Israel condemned her being awarded the honour.
Hours after she was named the laureate, the US announced new sanctions against the ICC, provoking swift condemnation from member states and the United Nations.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he described as a “rogue court”, escalating a long-running campaign by Trump’s administration against the Hague-based tribunal.
‘History will judge’
The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that “history will judge this moment”.
In addition to serving on the ICC, Pillay was the UN human rights high commissioner from 2008 to 2014 and she headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which found in 2025 that genocide was occurring in Gaza. The body does not speak on behalf of the UN.
Israel has rejected the COI’s findings, calling them “distorted and false”. The country’s Foreign Ministry said the award legitimised “anti-Israel hatred”, adding that it thought that Nazi propagandist Joseph Goebbels must be “applauding from hell”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the awarding of the prize to Pillay showed the Nobel committee had “lost its moral compass” by honouring “a bigot”.
Trump, who in September called on ICC member states to quit the court, labelled the committee’s choice “a disgraceful and embarrassing decision”, telling a rally of his supporters in Syracuse, New York he had “never heard of” Pillay. AFP

The AI boom is reshaping the global debt market: companies are borrowing trillions of dollars despite high interest rates
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:40:40 EEST
08:40:40 KST

The AI boom is reshaping the global debt market: companies are borrowing trillions of dollars despite high interest rates
Kyiv • UNN
In the United States, corporate bond issuance reached $1.69 trillion, largely driven by AI financing. SpaceX and Broadcom are preparing new multibillion-dollar borrowings.
Technology companies investing in the development of artificial intelligence are changing the rules of the global debt market. Despite higher borrowing costs, they are ramping up bond issuance to finance data centers and chip purchases. In 2026, the volume of U.S. corporate bond issuance has already reached $1.69 trillion, Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to the agency, this is approximately 30% more than during the same period last year. At the same time, the average bond yield increased by 1.2 percentage points, reaching 5.97%. More expensive borrowing usually restrains companies, but the rapid development of AI has disrupted this pattern.
Technology giants are counting on substantial future profits from artificial intelligence. In particular, OpenAI expects its annual revenue to reach at least $70 billion by the end of the year. At the same time, investors fear that the market will struggle to absorb such a volume of new debt obligations.
Technology companies are preparing new multibillion-dollar borrowings
According to Bloomberg, Elon Musk's SpaceX is negotiating to raise $40 billion to purchase Nvidia chips. Meanwhile, Broadcom is working on financing AI chips for OpenAI and raising about $60 billion for projects involving Anthropic and other companies.
Hyperscalers' capital expenditures are expected to total about $1 trillion next year, which means that the issuance of artificial intelligence bonds will not slow down despite higher interest-rate conditions
Experts warn that large-scale borrowing by technology companies could increase financing costs for other businesses. In particular, U.S. corporations issued only $11.4 billion in bonds last week, instead of the expected $25–30 billion, indicating caution among traditional borrowers.

On Saturday, however, he attacked Zelensky just hours after another deadly Russian bombardment, which killed 20 people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump was asked about Russian attacks that have only intensified and that this week killed dozens more civilians in two particularly deadly strikes. Rather than criticize the Kremlin, even indirectly, he turned his anger toward Zelensky.
"I advise (the Ukrainians) to find a new leader who can make a deal, because he actually could have made many deals, but for some reason he makes none," Trump said. “This is a war that should never have started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to find a new president.”
Trump announced the agreement to release Russian diesel onto global markets after a phone call with President Vladimir Putin, in an effort to bring down fuel prices that have been weighing heavily on Americans ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
In his remarks Saturday, Trump also criticized Zelensky for refusing his appeals to halt Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries. Those strikes contributed to a severe fuel crisis in Russia over the summer and forced Moscow — normally a major fuel exporter — to temporarily halt diesel exports in order to preserve supplies for domestic consumers. The move helped drive up diesel prices, alongside another increase caused by the war with Iran.
“We said, ‘You can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem,’” Trump said. “He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel, because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel around the world,” Trump said.
“And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel,” Trump added. “He better damn well stop.”
Zelensky has yet to respond to Trump’s criticism, which appears to mark a return of the severe rift between the two leaders last year. That crisis began with the “shouting summit” at the White House in February, which ended with Zelensky being thrown out after refusing the U.S. president’s demand that he compromise in negotiations with Russia — a demand Trump was then pushing as part of an effort to fulfill his campaign promise to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours.
That crisis also led to a temporary halt in U.S. intelligence assistance to Kyiv, but the dispute was later resolved and the two leaders patched things up and met several times afterward.
Earlier this year, Trump even praised Kyiv’s campaign of drone attacks on targets deep inside Russia, aimed at making Russian civilians feel the effects of the war and thereby pressuring Putin to seek an agreement to end it.
But those attacks have also targeted oil refineries, contributing to the current surge in global diesel prices. Trump, concerned about the impact on Republicans’ already difficult prospects of retaining control of Congress in the midterms, has been pressing for the strikes to stop.
As early as the middle of last month, Trump announced what he described as an agreement between Kyiv and Moscow under which both sides would stop attacking energy facilities. Neither side confirmed such an agreement, however. Zelensky made clear that he would halt attacks on oil facilities only if he received guarantees that Moscow would do the same.
In recent days, Russia has instead stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities, including strikes on energy facilities that have forced Ukraine to announce planned power outages just before the freezing winter. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have also continued without letup.
Trump surprised observers Friday when he announced the agreement allowing Russian diesel exports to the United States and other countries.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Russia would immediately provide more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia would provide another 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” he added.
Soon afterward, the United States lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Russia itself lifted restrictions Saturday morning that it had imposed over the summer on diesel exports because of domestic shortages caused by Ukrainian attacks.
The agreement marks a significant reversal after years of U.S. pressure on Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It came only a month after Trump signed a sweeping sanctions law targeting Russia, aimed in part at curbing its ability to profit from oil exports that help finance the war.
Ukraine reacted angrily to the agreement, which was announced as U.S. and Ukrainian representatives were holding talks on the war. Those talks were interrupted after the announcement. Zelensky described the deal as “a weak decision by strong partners” and warned: “Gifts to Putin, such as weakening sanctions, will not end the war. Russia will ‘repay’ concessions on diesel with more terror.”
Hours after the agreement was announced, Russia continued its attacks on Ukrainian cities. In one strike on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, at least 20 people were reported killed, including three children, after glide bombs hit a residential complex.
“Today, Russia said ‘thank you’ for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelensky said. “Last night provided further confirmation that Russia sees every easing of pressure on it as a signal that it can supposedly continue fighting and continue dropping bombs on cities. Different messages need to be sent.”
Images from the scene showed buildings completely destroyed. Authorities said Russia struck several locations in the city simultaneously in the early morning hours.
At least 18 more people were wounded. Reports said one of those killed was a 6-year-old girl. Her grandfather, Anatoly Chumny, was seen crying over her body, which had been covered with a white sheet after rescue workers pulled her from the rubble. Reuters reported that another resident’s leg was trapped in the debris and that he screamed in pain as rescue workers tried to free him.
“If the Russians have money, they will be able to keep fighting us,” said Natalia Malysheva, 49, whose parents were critically wounded in the attack and later died at the hospital after being pulled from the ruins. “How many lives have been lost here? How many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?”
Kyiv was also hit by waves of drones Saturday. Dramatic footage circulated from the city showing a drone exploding at a kindergarten, as a passerby standing nearby ran away moments before the impact.

Number of Germans who change their minds about refusing military service grows

BERLIN, October 11. /TASS/. The number of Germans withdrawing their applications to refuse military service is growing amid the conflict in Ukraine and changes in the security situation, the RND editorial association quoted a representative of the Federal Office for Family and Civil Society (BAFzA) as saying.
According to its information, the Cologne-based office received 570 applications to renounce the status of a conscientious objector in the first eight months of the year. Forecasts say this figure could increase to 855 for the entire year, which would significantly exceed the 781 applications received last year. In 2023, the agency recorded 536 such applications, and in 2024 - 626.
A representative of the agency said that to withdraw an application, it is sufficient to send a signed statement in a free form to BAFzA.
"If the application for conscientious objection to military service is withdrawn or the status is revoked, the applicant is no longer legally considered a person who has refused military service. In the event of a resumption of conscription, as well as in the event of a threat of aggression or in wartime, they are again subject to unlimited military duty," she explained.
Earlier, BAFzA said that the number of applications for conscientious objection to military service is also growing and at a much larger scale - by the end of August, 12,102 such applications were received. This is already more than three times higher than the figure for the entire of 2005, when 879 applications were submitted.
The reasons for withdrawing refusals to perform military service are similar. Janosch Dahmen, a Bundestag deputy from the Green Party, explained his decision to withdraw the application to the fundamental changes in the European security policy. The parliamentarian noted that, despite his unwillingness to use weapons against people, he acknowledges the change in external conditions. According to Dahmen, the protection of the state and free society in the event of an attack by external forces cannot remain solely the responsibility of third parties.
On January 1, a law on a new model of military service came into force in Germany. It requires young people to undergo a medical examination and restores military registration. Recruitment into the Bundeswehr is currently on a voluntary basis. According to the new law, adult males are required to fill out a questionnaire about their physical fitness and readiness to join the armed forces. Filling out such questionnaires for women is voluntary. Mandatory military conscription in Germany was abolished in July 2011, after which the country transitioned to a professional army. Currently, the number of Bundeswehr personnel stands at 186,400.

Military reserves may be needed for pontoon crossings over the Dnipro in Kyiv – Defense Express
Kyiv • UNN
Reserve crossings could compensate for up to half of the capacity of Kyiv’s bridges. They require additional military pontoon systems.
To establish reserve pontoon crossings over the Dnipro in Kyiv, additional sets of military engineering equipment may be needed, since the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ existing assets are already being used to support combat operations at the front. At the same time, deploying pontoon-bridge units from the front line could create problems for military logistics, Defense Express reports, citing military engineering specialists, writes UNN.
Details
Against the backdrop of regular Russian attacks that damage bridge infrastructure, the capital is considering the possibility of creating alternative crossings over the Dnipro. The relevant ministry, the Recovery Agency, the military, and the city authorities are planned to be involved in implementing the project. The reserve routes are intended to provide up to half the capacity of Kyiv’s bridges, which are used by up to 600,000 vehicles daily.
According to expert estimates, constructing a single continuous crossing over the Dnipro could require between two and four complete sets of pontoon-bridge equipment, depending on the river’s width and the use of additional earthen embankments. In narrow areas near Kyiv, the Dnipro is approximately 400–600 meters wide.
Will pontoon equipment have to be taken from the front?
A Defense Express source familiar with the work of the military engineering forces said that, before the full-scale invasion, the Ukrainian Armed Forces had slightly more than 20 battalions equipped with pontoon-bridge sets. Since 2022, these units have been actively providing crossings and logistics support in various areas of the front, while some of the equipment has been lost.
It is likely that, if it really comes to building pontoon bridges across the Dnipro, reserves will have to be found. Pulling PMP sets from the entire front line does not look realistic. The equipment for constructing pontoon crossings is held by the troops and is already carrying out combat missions
Experts identify the purchase or acquisition of additional pontoon-bridge sets from international partners, particularly Poland or France, as one possible solution. At the same time, information about the availability of corresponding reserves in Ukraine is not being disclosed.
Defense Express emphasizes that even if the necessary equipment is available, operating such crossings would require constant military control. Pontoon bridges are more vulnerable to damage than permanent structures, while organizing civilian traffic would require additional security measures and a clear division of responsibility between the military and the capital’s authorities.

Scientists discovered bacteria in people from Africa and South America that may have been transmitted from common ancestors
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:27:37 EEST
08:27:37 KST

Scientists discovered bacteria in people from Africa and South America that may have been transmitted from common ancestors
Kyiv • UNN
Scientists discovered more than 1,200 species of intestinal bacteria. Some of the microorganisms may have been passed down to humans from common ancestors.
American scientists have discovered a remarkable similarity between the gut bacteria of two Indigenous peoples living on different continents. The study suggests that some microorganisms may have accompanied humanity for thousands of years, passing from generation to generation during ancient migrations. The University of California, Santa Barbara, reports this, citing a study published in the journal Nature, UNN writes.
Details
Scientists from the University of California, Santa Barbara, and Stanford University studied the gut microbiome of the Tsimané people, who live in Bolivia, and the Hadza people, whose members live in Tanzania and maintain a traditional hunter-gatherer way of life.
In the gut microbiomes of the populations studied, scientists identified more than 1,200 species of bacteria. At the same time, more than 60% of these species are rare or entirely absent in people living in industrialized societies.
Ancient bacteria may have traveled around the world with humans
What particularly surprised the researchers was that the gut microbiomes of the two peoples turned out to be similar despite significant differences in diet. The Hadza consume the meat of wild animals, fish, fruit, and other gathered foods, whereas the Tsimané diet contains more plant fiber, including plantains, rice, cassava, and maize.
This made us wonder whether there really is a core set of bacterial and other species that traveled with the ancestors of the Tsimané during their migration around the world
To test this hypothesis, the scientists analyzed the genetic characteristics of bacterial DNA and used the rate of mutation accumulation to estimate when the bacteria of the two populations diverged from common ancestral lineages. The results indicated a connection dating back thousands of years.
The analysis shows strong evidence that their ancestors, and probably all of us, had these same bacteria long ago
According to the scientists, the findings help provide a better understanding of the history of the human microbiome and how changes in lifestyle and diet may have affected the diversity of gut bacteria in modern populations.

Davyd Aloian / Photo: NSDC

Ukrainian arms manufacturers risk losing international markets due to new export rules
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11

Ukrainian arms manufacturers risk losing international markets due to new export rules
Kyiv • UNN
Resolution No. 875 requires a 20% advance payment before authorization to export weapons. Manufacturers are calling for the rules to be changed due to the loss of foreign customers.
Government Resolution No. 875, which was intended to give Ukrainian defense companies broader access to the international arms market, has failed to deliver the expected results over the past three months. One of the main obstacles has been a mandatory advance payment amounting to 20% of the value of an export contract. Ihor Fomenko, head of the Federation of Employers of Ukraine "FRU Defense," said this in an interview with Defense Express, UNN reports.
Details
According to Fomenko, the resolution adopted on July 1 contains a number of provisions that complicate the conclusion of international contracts. In particular, companies must pay 20% of the deal's value before receiving an export permit, creating financial risks and making Ukrainian products less competitive.
Indeed, the biggest problem with the resolution today, in my view, is precisely the obligation to make an advance payment in the form of a 20% fee on the deal, and to do so before its implementation begins in order to obtain a permit
Defense companies propose changing the rules
The head of the association, which includes more than 700 defense companies, proposes reducing the export fee depending on the type of product. For armored vehicles and other weapons that the Ukrainian army purchases in insufficient quantities, he proposes a rate of 1–3%, while for drones and electronic warfare systems – 5–7%. At the same time, payments should be made after the contracts are fulfilled.
Fomenko cited export geography restrictions as another problem. Instead of defining a list of countries to which Ukrainian weapons may be sold, he proposes establishing a list of prohibited destinations so as not to lose markets in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
According to the representative of the defense industry, Ukraine is already losing potential customers. In particular, just six months ago, countries on the Arabian Peninsula were actively interested in Ukrainian interceptor drones, but these opportunities could not be used because export rules had not been regulated. Subsequently, demand for the systems in question declined due to technological development.
Fomenko called on the government to suspend Resolution No. 875 or certain of its provisions until financial and economic calculations are carried out and amendments are introduced. He warned that further restrictions on exports could lead to the loss of engineers, technologies, and production competencies within Ukraine's defense-industrial complex.

What's the latest on the storm?
Two of the deaths were in Florida, while the other two were in Alabama.
The storm originally made landfall on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida. It is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.
Florida, Alabama and Georgia have all declared states of emergency due to the storm. According to PowerOutage.com, over 500,000 customers are without power in Florida and Alabama.
The Florida Division of Emergency Management said approximately 5,000 Florida National Guard soldiers and airmen have been "activated to support impacted communities."
The storm brings heavy rainfall and powerfall winds, bringing the risks of flooding and tornadoes. It has ripped the roofs off buildings and downed trees in its wake.
Storm moving into West Virginia
The storm has weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and is moving over the southern US states of Tennessee and Kentucky into West Virginia, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
In its latest update, the NHC warned of possible flash and urban flooding and said "landslides are possible across the Southern Appalachians." It also warned of wind gusts along with additional power outages and downed trees.
In addition, swells from Isaias will continue to impact much of the Gulf coasts of the US, Mexico and western Cuba, and are "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions." NHC said a couple of tornadoes are also possible across eastern Georgia and the Carolinas.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon has hit Category 4 strength as it barrels towards Mexico's Pacific coast, where it is expected to make landfall on Sunday. The storm is expected to impact Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for American tourists.

In the U.S. state of Montana, the warning area for a powerful winter storm has been expanded. The storm could bring up to 76 centimeters of snow to some mountainous areas. Forecasters are also warning of wind gusts of up to 80 km/h and hazardous conditions on roads, the U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to the updated forecast, the heaviest snowfall is expected in the Bob Marshall Wilderness area, where the snow cover could increase by nearly 76 centimeters. In the East Glacier Park and Northern High Plains areas, 25 to 50 centimeters of snow is forecast, while wind gusts could reach 80 km/h.
The warning covers the communities of Browning, East Glacier Park, St. Mary, and Babb, as well as Logan Pass. According to meteorologists, the heaviest precipitation is expected in mountainous areas south of U.S. Highway 2.
Forecasters raised snowfall projections
The National Weather Service also expanded the warning to the Snowy and Judith Mountains in central Montana. There, 15 to 30 centimeters of heavy, wet snow and wind gusts of up to 72 km/h are forecast.
In the city of Great Falls, the snowfall forecast was raised to 18–36 centimeters, although 13–28 centimeters had previously been expected. Up to 36 centimeters of snow could fall in the Bozeman Pass area, while 30 to 46 centimeters is forecast in the highlands near Butte.
Difficult weather conditions are also expected on key transportation routes, particularly near Rogers and Macdonald passes. The combination of heavy snowfall and gusty winds could significantly reduce visibility and make driving difficult.

Live: Drivers and teams make final preparation for Bathurst 1000

Bathurst 1000: Anton De Pasquale runs out of fuel on last lap, Brodie Kostecki and Todd Hazelwood win
A shattered Anton De Pasquale has said he knew his hopes of winning the Bathurst 1000 "were cooked", moments before his car ran out of fuel while leading on the final lap.
Brodie Kostecki and Todd Hazelwood took full advantage of De Pasquale's misfortune, securing a victory for Dick Johnson Racing that they appeared to have blown earlier in the race.
The number 18 car, by Team 18, appeared to have played a blinder late in the race when De Pasquale held a big lead in the final laps.
But his team urged him to "maximum fuel save" as the chequered flag neared.
A late safety car with five laps to go, the only one of the race, appeared to have potentially saved Team 18 and secured De Pasquale and co-driver Lee Holdsworth a famous win.
But the number 18 ran out of fuel on the 161st and final lap, allowing Kostecki to breeze by in the number 17 car and claim the most dramatic of victories.
"Once I knew how much fuel short we were, I knew we were cooked," De Pasquale said in the aftermath of his dramatic final lap.
"Very disappointed. We had a really good day, and the chequered flag was 6km away.
"The car was amazing at the back end of the race, where we wanted it; everything went our way, until it didn't."
De Pasquale and Holdsworth had driven a wonderful race on Sunday, and were in a fight with the number 10 Matt Stone Racing entry of Zach Bates and Aaron Seton for the race lead late.
Team 18 had saved fuel well at Mount Panorama and took the lead of the race after the final pit stop, with Matt Stone Racing having the fuel pump in their number 10 car for 15 more seconds than their rivals.
But Team 18 got their sums wrong and were pleading with De Pasquale to save fuel with less than 10 laps remaining.
"I can't believe it. I didn't know we were so close on fuel, or what happened," Holdsworth said after watching from the garage as his teammate was left helpless in a spluttering car.
"Massive disappointment. I've got no words."
Kostecki and Hazelwood were in control of the Bathurst 1000 for much of Sunday, but their second-to-last pit stop was slow and dropped them from the lead to fifth.
Kostecki roared in the final laps, and then was gifted the chance to win when the late safety car was deployed.
"We executed so well up until that second-last pit stop with the brake change," Kostecki said.
"But, like I've always said, the mountain chooses the winner.
"We definitely had the fastest car today — so super proud of everyone … this Ford Mustang was on rails."
Dick Johnson was holding back tears in the DJR garage, while those from Team 18 were left devastated.
"That's amazing," an emotional Johnson said after the race.
"I tell you what, I want a couple more before I fall off the perch."
Will Brown and Scott Pye were second for the Triple Eight team, while Matt Stone Racing's pole sitters Zach Bates and Aaron Seton were third.
Bates and Seton were able to snag a tremendous third place, but will leave Mount Panorama with the knowledge they would have won the race had the safety car never come out.
On the third-last lap, Bates was pushed wide by Kostecki into the final corner for second, and Will Brown was able to take advantage to relegate Bates to fourth, before Team 18's fuel drama.

Palestinian president postpones elections until late 2027

Palestinian president postpones elections until late 2027
October 11, 2026
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has postponed legislative elections for almost another year, according to a decree issued on Friday.
Abbas had previously scheduled legislative elections for November 28, and presidential elections for early next year. Now both elections have been pushed back to September 11, 2027.
They would be the first Palestinian elections in more than 20 years.
Why are Palestinian elections postponed?
In his decree, Abbas cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" as the reason for the postponement of "free, fair and inclusive elections."
He pointed to Israeli settler violence, military attacks and restrictions of movent in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, as well as Israel's continued withholding of tax revenue.
In Gaza, where Israeli strikes continue after three years of war, the decree cited "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions," the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces and a lack of progress towards reconstruction, among other issues.
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded to the news on X, calling the decree "yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability."
A commitment to hold elections
Abbas had committed in writing to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that elections would be held as part of France's recognition of the State of Palestine last year.
The delay comes just weeks after Abbas reaffirmed this commitment to hold elections in November when he delivered a video address to the UN General Assembly.
Abbas has governed by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009.

At least 12 killed, more than 300 hurt in strike on Saudi airport, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:51:34 UTC
07:51:34 KST

At least 12 people killed, more than 300 injured in strike on Riyadh airport, Saudi officials say
At least 12 people, including one American, were killed and 309 others injured in a strike Saturday on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, according to Saudi officials.
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said those killed included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis and one person each from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Those injured were receiving treatment at several hospitals, officials said in a social media post. Several people were in critical condition.
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the airport, which is the country's main international airport.
A Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed Saturday afternoon's attack on the Houthis. The attack was the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh — and it marked the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
The Saudi kingdom has faced an extraordinary series of assaults on the new front in the Iran war that has opened up involving the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
President Trump said earlier Saturday he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
"We may. We're gonna look at it," Mr. Trump told reporters when asked about the possibility. "We just found out about the recent attack [on the airport]. So we'll make a decision — we move very quickly."
"The United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.
A State Department spokesperson told CBS News the Trump administration is in close contact with its "Saudi partners."
The Houthis have not yet claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike. However, the Houthis did claim attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. In Saturday's strike, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
In a statement posted to social media, Hans Grundberg, United Nations special envoy to Yemen, called Saturday's strike a "dangerous escalation" that poses "a grave threat to regional security."
Riyadh airport operations have been suspended
Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.
Flights were diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the U.S., Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry, hours after the latest one, was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Though the Houthis have told The Associated Press and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged on the ground, with no passengers on board.

Asked again whether the US would intervene, he said: “You’re gonna find out… We have communication with the Houthis, and we’ll see what happens. But what they did was very bad.”
The remarks came after a Houthi strike on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital killed 12 people and injured another 309, according to updated figures released on Sunday by Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). The dead included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign nationals, among them an American. Some of the injured are in critical condition.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack, one of several targeting Saudi airports in recent days. Speaking exclusively to RT, senior Ansar Allah official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti said the strikes were intended to force Riyadh to accept a “comprehensive and permanent peace” and end the war and mutual blockade.
The renewed fighting comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have launched a major offensive to retake territory seized by the Houthis, including strategic areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Saudi-led coalition said on Friday that it launched “large-scale operations” against the group, destroying 136 military targets, according to the spokesman.
Trump’s remarks suggest a potential shift in the US position. In September, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman repeatedly sought US military assistance against the Houthis, but Trump ultimately backed away from authorizing strikes despite preparations for an operation, according to the New York Times.
Washington has reportedly continued to provide Riyadh with intelligence and other non-combat support, but direct US strikes against the Houthis would open another front in the regional conflict.
In March 2025, Trump ordered weeks of US air and naval strikes against Houthi positions, targeting missile launchers, radar installations, and other military infrastructure in an attempt to halt attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. The campaign ended abruptly in May under an Omani-brokered ceasefire after the Houthis agreed to stop targeting US vessels.
In September, Trump claimed that the Houthis contacted Washington, seeking to avoid another confrontation with US forces, saying the group “would much prefer not having us involved.” Ansar Allah denied making contact.
The latest escalation comes amid the broader regional conflict triggered by the US-Israeli war against Iran in February. The Houthis have expanded their control along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, threatening a crucial shipping route that Saudi Arabia increasingly relies on for oil exports amid disruptions to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Ukraine, which long kept its weapons at home, is now clearing its arms makers to sell abroad. Its Commission on Export Control has granted 18 Ukrainian companies permission to send their finished weapons abroad and has processed more than 400 export applications, with over 90% approved, the National Security and Defense Council says, citing commission head Davyd Aloian.
Ukraine now produces far more weapons than it can afford, with defense production growing from about $1 billion a year at the start of the invasion to a projected $55 billion in 2026.
The exports are reportedly conducted under the Drone Deals framework that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy unveiled in April, which allows controlled sales of surplus weapons to partner countries while the Defense Ministry and General Staff retain first claim to everything the front needs. Some categories already run up to 50% beyond what Ukraine can use or finance.
From a stalled commission to 18 approvals
The commission’s work had been halting. It resumed in February after an eight-month freeze and issued the first permits then, and its updated membership has been working since, Aloian notes.
Building partnerships abroad
Aloian framed the goal as scaling Ukrainian technology rather than one-off deals. The state wants domestic producers to expand abroad while partners get working solutions, he says, and is open to dialogue with the defense industry to fix problems as they arise.
Earlier, an industry group that represents more than 400 companies warned in September that the mechanism was choking. A new 20-to-30% fee on export permits priced Ukrainian goods out of the market, it said, and a joint-production program had stalled with hundreds of foreign bids pending.
Euromaidan Press cannot verify whether the Commission on Export Control has taken the issue into consideration.
The council recently met a UK Defense Ministry delegation to discuss closer cooperation, including a Drone Deal, an anti-ballistic coalition, and joint production, Aloian adds. Reaching foreign markets enables producers to attract new orders and investment, scale up, and build long-term partnerships.

WHO says no plague case registered after Russian lab worker’s death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:34:29 UTC
07:34:29 KST

WHO says no plague case registered after Russian lab worker’s death
The WHO says the lack of a confirmed diagnosis remains a key uncertainty, with no sign of ongoing transmission.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has said it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a laboratory worker at a Russian plague research institute and that no case of plague has been registered.
Russia’s state health regulator told the WHO that tests on the worker and people who had been in contact with her were negative for the dangerous pathogens they tested for, the United Nations health agency said in a statement on Saturday.
Her contacts still showed no symptoms, and no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been found, the WHO added.
“Based on the information provided… WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker,” it said.
What happened?
The worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and stoking public health fears on social media.
Russian media named her as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, in the Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Pneumonic plague, a lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas, was suspected early on.
The governor of neighbouring Buryatia said the woman had “died, maybe of the plague”.
Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said she had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.
Russian authorities said the worker was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body. They say post-mortem tests did not detect plague.
On Thursday, Russia said it had completed health checks on all her contacts and had given the WHO all the information.
A local official said on October 6 that 60 percent of those placed in quarantine had already been released.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus asked Russia on Wednesday to respond to media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. Russia dismissed the reports as “false information”.
The United States has also called on Russia for transparency.
Global health officials have been extra alert to deadly pneumonia cases of unknown cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading, fatal respiratory illness in China.
The cause of individual pneumonia cases often cannot be determined.

EU imports record 12.18 million tons of Russian Arctic LNG in nine months, 9.5% more than year earlier — research group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:32:44 UTC
07:32:44 KST

Europe keeps buying record amounts of Russian gas even as it plans to punish its war machine against Ukraine. The EU ports took in a record 12.18 million tons of Russian liquefied natural gas from January to September, 9.5% more than in the same period of 2025, according to a study by the German group Urgewald based on Kpler tracking data.
Europe spent about 7.88 billion euros on that Russian gas in nine months, revenue that helps fund a war Russia wages with daily missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities. The flow continues even as the EU prepares its largest-ever package of sanctions against Russia’s military industry.
The gas comes from Russia’s Yamal project, which sent 167 cargoes to EU ports over the nine months, roughly one every 1.6 days. Europe took 85% of the project’s recorded deliveries by volume, remaining by far its biggest market, Urgewald reports.
Europe’s share grew even as Yamal’s worldwide deliveries fell 1.3%, so the EU absorbed a larger slice of Russia’s Arctic output. In September alone, EU ports received 792,440 tons worth an estimated 818 million euros, nearly three-quarters of it going to France.
Washington could pull the plug by 18 October
The imports run up against a looming US decision. The Trump administration has until 18 October to complete its first review under the Lindsey Graham sanctions act, signed into law on 18 September, which allows Washington to sanction this gas trade at any time, the group notes.
However, after the US allowed Russian diesel to enter the US and global market, the decision will likely remain stalled.
Originally, the law covered Yamal’s leadership, foreign vessels that knowingly carried Russian LNG, and foreign ports that serviced US-sanctioned ships. Yamal depends on specialized Arc7 ice-class tankers and on nearby European ports where they can unload and quickly return, so closing that route would make the Arctic trade far harder to sustain.
Europe’s own ban is still months away
The EU’s measures so far have barely dented the trade. A ban on short-term LNG contracts took effect in April and has had no visible effect, while the full import ban under long-term contracts only starts on 1 January 2027, Urgewald says.
Every month of largely uninterrupted trade means more revenue for Russia while Ukraine suffers daily attacks, sanction campaigner Sebastian Rötters says. The next EU package should close the remaining loopholes, above all those keeping the Arc7 tanker fleet running.

Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:30:34 UTC
07:30:34 KST

The northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening.
Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis.
The Met Office said sightings could continue during clear skies until Tuesday.
Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland.
The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic storms interacting with the upper atmosphere.
Sightings will remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies, the Met Office said.
Aurora displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is emitted at various wavelengths, creating colourful displays in the sky.
According to the Met Office, the sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at bout 1m mph.
The forecaster said: “When these particles interact with Earth’s magnetic field – especially when the solar wind’s polarity is opposite to Earth’s – they are funnelled toward the magnetic poles.
“As these energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy in the form of light. Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.”
Last year, experts said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.

Spain and Greece refuse to give Ukraine Patriot missiles nearing expiration

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

Spain and Greece refuse to give Ukraine Patriot missiles nearing expiration
This was reported by The Telegraph, according to Ukrinform.
The newspaper notes that Spain and Greece have some of the largest stocks of interceptor missiles in Europe, which Ukraine urgently needs to defend against Russian attacks ahead of winter. President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Ukraine needs between 300 and 360 such missiles to repel Russian attacks over the winter.
NATO and EU officials are trying to persuade Athens and Madrid to transfer Patriot PAC-2 missiles to Kyiv whose shelf life is nearing its end.
According to available data, Greece has at least 200 PAC-2 missiles, whose estimated 23-year shelf life is due to expire soon.
It is not known how many such missiles are held by Spain, but last month the Spanish foreign minister said Madrid would provide Ukraine with five interceptors.
EU High Representative Kaja Kallas said during talks in Ireland last month: “We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine.”
Allies are trying to determine how to help Greece and Spain make such a decision. According to a diplomatic source cited by The Telegraph, it would make sense to provide Ukraine with at least those interceptors whose shelf life is due to expire soon.
Patriot interceptors have a defined shelf life during which the manufacturer guarantees their reliability and effectiveness. Once that period expires, the missiles must undergo recertification.
Around 95% of the Patriot interceptor missiles Ukraine receives are provided through a NATO-backed program under which European countries finance missile purchases directly from the United States. However, the war in Iran has caused a global shortage of interceptors.
According to media reports, U.S. stocks of Patriot missiles may stand at fewer than 1,700 units. At the same time, there are doubts over whether the Pentagon is prepared to continue replenishing Ukraine’s stocks while U.S. forces are engaged in combat operations against Iran, the publication says.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 24, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced an agreement to provide Ukraine with a package of missiles for Patriot systems, but did not specify which country the agreement had been reached with.

Yemeni government’s military says its forces advancing against Houthis
Saudi-backed forces say 1,150 Houthis killed in operations against the Iran-aligned group over the past 24 hours.
The military of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has killed hundreds of Houthi fighters in targeted operations over the past 24 hours.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemeni government forces, said at least 1,150 Houthis were killed in almost 2,000 targeted operations across the country as part of operation “Dawn of Yemen”.
He said the army had destroyed Houthi ammunition dumps and at least 180 combat, transport and supply vehicles operated by the Houthis, adding that ground forces “continued to advance their assault”.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the information.
An attack on King Khalid International airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, on Saturday killed and injured several people and led to flights being cancelled.
When asked if the United States would join strikes against the Houthis after the attack, President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he “will make a decision soon”.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen on Saturday, said the Houthis had yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack.
But the Iran-backed group has warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target.
Mawry said the Houthis were preparing to fight the war on multiple fronts, including against the participation of international actors, such as Pakistan.
“The Houthis say that if Pakistan engages in any military activities against them on behalf of Saudi Arabia, then they will be treated in the same fashion as the Saudis are currently being dealt with,” Mawry said.
There are plans to launch ballistic missiles towards Pakistan and attack Pakistan-flagged vessels in the Red and Arabian seas, he added.
“The fighting is spreading on multiple fronts, but it is a situation that will keep escalating,” Baraa Shiban, an associate fellow in international security and Yemen expert at the London-based Royal United Services Institute think tank, told Al Jazeera, adding that the violence will not be “dying down” anytime soon.
“There is no mediation happening this time – there [are] no regional or local mediators that are able to cool down the situation,” he said.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea.
Battles are now raging around the strategic southern Yemeni cities of Mocha and Dhubab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb.
The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides claim control of the shipping lanes.

Anxiety treatable, but 83% of affected did not get help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:08:48 UTC
07:08:48 KST

Whenever Thane businessman Shekhar travels to south Mumbai for a meeting, he sets off over three hours early. This is because he plans his route carefully to ensure he is never more than five minutes from a hospital in case he "suffers a heart attack while driving".Karthik (32), an IIM graduate with a high-powered marketing job, dreads routine meetings. "There is this heaviness in my stomach and my legs seem leaden. It's a paralysing fear that stays until the meeting is over," he says.Shekhar and Karthik (names changed) have anxiety disorders, a group of conditions that can turn ordinary journeys, workplace interactions and social situations into emotional ordeals.
The invisible burden
National Mental Health Survey, conducted by National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) across 12 states between 2014 and 2016, found that 2.57% of adults had an anxiety disorder at the time of assessment.Around 83% of those affected were not receiving treatment, while nearly 60% experienced disability of varying severity, according to the study published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 2022."Anxiety disorders are frequently under-recognised and inadequately treated. Stigma surrounding mental illness and a lack of awareness contribute to the problem," said psychiatrist Dr Kedar Tilwe of Fortis Hospital, Mulund.
Child psychiatrist Dr Kersi Chavda said anxiety can take many forms, from social anxiety and academic stress to persistent, intrusive thoughts.In children, it may manifest as school refusal. Among adolescents facing examinations, anxiety can also present as headaches, body aches or backaches.Social anxiety is another concern, said Dr Chavda. The pressure to appear perfect, amplified by curated virtual lives on social media, can intensify the fear of being judged or found wanting.
When the body's alarm won't switch off
Everyday anxiety is a normal response to uncertainty or danger. An anxiety disorder involves persistent or disproportionate fear that interferes with daily life.A senior psychologist from a civic hospital linked anxiety to the body's built-in alarm system. The alarm is meant to respond to a threat, but sometimes it reacts to a gust of wind as though an intruder were approaching.Psychiatrist Dr Harish Shetty said, "Crowded trains, inadequate sleep, workplace demands, educational pressures, financial worries and concerns about personal safety can keep people in a state of heightened stress."Weakening support systems and reduced emotional connectedness may also be contributing, said Dr Shetty.
Life in the slow lane
In adults, panic disorder can be accompanied by agoraphobia - fear of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable if a panic attack occurs.
"Patients may avoid bri-dges, crowded trains, flights or traffic jams. Some will not travel without their spouses or may turn down promotions or jobs that require them to venture beyond familiar surroundi-ngs," said Dr Tilwe. As a result, he added, it's a life lived in second gear: not ready to take up new challenges as one prefers to stick to known schedules.
It's treatable
Anxiety disorders are treatable, but a trained physician is needed to recognise the problem. Treatment depends on the type and severity of the disorder and may involve psychotherapy, medication or both. "A person with a severe anxiety disorder may need counselling along with medication for up to six months to be able to cope," said Dr Tilwe.Dr Shetty recommends attention to sleep, time management, breathing exercises and meditation. Doctors said reducing excessive caffeine and smoking would help some people manage symptoms.

Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh airport attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:07:00 UTC
07:07:00 KST

Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh strike
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.
"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.
Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.
At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."
Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Coalition vows to respond
On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government accused the Houthis of carrying out the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The coalition vowed to respond "decisively."
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki described the attack as a "war crime" and vowed the coalition "will respond decisively to this terrorist attack."
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the attack on Riyadh's international airport "not acceptable."
He also told reporters that he will speak with Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
When asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States strongly condemns recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, confirming that an American citizen was killed in the strikes.
"These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law," Guterres said. "These attacks must cease immediately."
What do we know about the Riyadh attack?
A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.
The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."
Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."
What did the Houthis say?
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.
However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.
In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."
When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."
Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week
Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.
Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.
Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.
The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.
The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Understand, don't just hear out a child in conflict with law: CJI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:04:42 UTC
07:04:42 KST

NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant Saturday said a child in conflict with law must not only be heard but also be understood, since few young people can speak up for themselves before the police or any authority.Speaking on 10 years of the framing of Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, Kant said very often, the child in conflict with law today was, only a little earlier, a child in need of care and protection whom we did not reach in time and that should be kept in mind while dealing with them.
"Our answer to such a predicament is restoration, not retribution. The Act presumes everyone below 18 to be innocent of any criminal intent, treats institutional care as a last resort, encourages diversion from formal proceedings, and prefers counselling, community service, and probation to confinement, while promising a fresh start. These choices flow from the Constitutional philosophy discernible from Articles 15(3) and 39 and also from the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which looks to the young assuming a constructive role in society. The 2015 Act thus makes a wager that a child given a second chance is far more likely to become a productive member of society than one branded as a criminal," he said.Supreme Court judge, Justice B V Nagarathna, who is heading SC's Juvenile Justice Committee, said adults have a duty to understand the anxieties of children. "We cannot be dismissive of their concerns, lest they feel alienated and rejected. The true measure of a society and its elders lies in how they deal with their children. We must ensure that we do not fail on that count. All children are ours and their distress is our distress too," Nagarathna said.

Luna provided no specific evidence that the Ukrainian president is deliberately obstructing the negotiation process. Her claim about Zelenskyy's actions is a political assessment, not an established fact.
It is also unclear from the congresswoman's message whether she was referring to new American proposals or terms that had already been discussed. She did not disclose details regarding possible security guarantees, territorial issues, or other provisions.
Additionally
Anna Paulina Luna has previously made critical statements about Ukraine on numerous occasions. In particular, in July 2025, she accused President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of allegedly banning the Orthodox Church and threatened to halt American military aid. In January 2026, the congresswoman also claimed that Orthodox Christians were allegedly being persecuted in Ukraine. Roundup: Türkiye tightens social media rules for children under 15
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:00:45 CST
07:00:45 KST

ANKARA, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye is tightening regulations on children's access to social media, with new rules requiring platforms to prevent users under 15 from accessing their services amid growing concerns over cyberbullying, online harassment and young users' safety.
The regulation, published Saturday, introduces new obligations for social media platforms, including age verification and measures to block underage account creation.
The measures will take effect on Nov. 1, following legislation passed by parliament in April to strengthen safeguards for minors online.
Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas, who played a key role in introducing the restrictions, has repeatedly warned that social media platforms treat children as commercial assets, stressing the government's responsibility to protect young people from potential online harm.
According to a 2024 survey by the Turkish Statistical Institute, 91.3 percent of children aged six to 15 in Türkiye used the internet, while 66.1 percent used social media.
Experts say exposure to inappropriate content and cyberbullying have become major concerns for parents and educators.
Asli Goral, an independent accountant whose 14-year-old son uses digital platforms, said monitoring children's online activities had become increasingly difficult.
"Despite our best efforts, it is literally impossible to regulate his activities across multiple social media platforms," Goral told Xinhua, describing tighter controls as necessary.
She said online harassment reports at her son's school have risen in recent years.
The new rules place greater responsibility on platforms to verify users' ages, prevent underage access, provide age-appropriate services for older teenagers, offer parental-control tools, and safeguard personal data.
They stipulate that existing accounts must undergo age verification, with platforms required to complete the process by March 31, 2027.
Meanwhile, the rules extend to online gaming, requiring appropriate age ratings for all games, and unrated games may only be offered to adults under the highest age-classification category.
Ankara-based education expert Zeynep Taskin said protecting children online requires a comprehensive approach that combines regulation with education and cooperation among families, schools and technology companies.
She said effective protection also depends on whether children can report abuse safely and whether platforms respond promptly.
"Parents and educators play an important role in helping children recognize online harassment, protect their personal information and seek assistance when they encounter threatening or humiliating behavior," Taskin said.
Analysts say the effectiveness of the new framework will depend in part on how age verification is implemented. Platforms will need to establish reliable methods of verifying users' ages while minimizing the collection and retention of sensitive personal data.
Türkiye's move comes amid broader international efforts to strengthen online protections for children. Australia has introduced a minimum-age requirement for social media use, while several European countries have debated or pursued age-based restrictions and additional safeguards for younger users. ■
