Trump seethes that no one knows her; Navi Pillay has rattled US and Israel anyway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:12:44 UTC
02:12:44 KST

Trump seethes that no one knows her; Navi Pillay has rattled US and Israel anyway
TEHRAN — Within hours of Navi Pillay being named the Nobel Peace Prize laureate, the American president had shared a post calling her a hater of America and Israel, and his secretary of state had sanctioned an entire international court. Israel summoned Joseph Goebbels.
Nobody had to explain what the 85-year-old South African jurist did to earn this. The reactions did it for her.
The Nobel deserves no reverence here. Oslo handed its peace medal to Henry Kissinger in 1973 while American bombers pounded Indochina, to Barack Obama in 2009 before drone strikes became his signature, and to Aung San Suu Kyi, who later stood before the ICJ to defend Myanmar’s generals against a genocide charge.
The prize launders power so reliably that a laureate who prosecutes it is the anomaly. Pillay needed no committee to vouch for her.
From Clairwood to Rwanda
Pillay was born in 1941 in Clairwood, a working-class Indian neighborhood of Durban, South Africa. Her father drove a bus. Neighbors raised the money for her law degree at the University of Natal. She clerked for ANC lawyer N.T. Naicker, whose house arrests pushed her into court early.
White firms refused to hire her, so in 1967 she opened her own practice, the first non-white woman in Natal to do so, in a profession that barred her from judges’ chambers and white-only law libraries.
In 1973 she won Robben Island prisoners, Nelson Mandela among them, access to lawyers and law books. When police detained her husband, she won an order forbidding his torture and sent sworn affidavits to anti-apartheid groups at the UN, which pushed the world toward a Convention Against Torture.
Then came Rwanda. She was the only woman on the tribunal’s bench for its first four years, later its president, and co-authored the 1998 Akayesu judgment, the first to hold that rape can be an act of genocide and that propaganda alone can amount to incitement.
The ICC followed, then the UN human rights office from 2008 to 2014. She now sits as an ad hoc ICJ judge in the same Myanmar genocide case.
The verdict on Gaza
In 2021 she took over the UN commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory. Its September 2025 report found Israel had committed four of the five acts listed in the Genocide Convention, with intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza, and that President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former war minister Yoav Gallant had incited it.
It asked whether genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference from the pattern of conduct, the standard the ICJ applies, and found that it was.
Israel’s stated aims of “self-defense, defeating Hamas and recovering hostages” explained little of what it documented, she told Middle East Eye, because most of those acts had no military objective she could see. Gaza’s Health Ministry now counts more than 74,000 dead.
Pillay made a point Western governments dislike hearing. Nobody has to wait for The Hague. The Genocide Convention binds every state to prevent the crime, she argued, and those still shipping weapons and jet fuel to Israel risk complicity.
She also warned that Trump’s Gaza plan, which sidelines Palestinians and leaves Israel in security control, ignores the ICJ’s ruling that the occupation must end.
Trump rants, Israel smears, Washington sanctions
Trump did not congratulate her. Hours after the announcement he reposted a message saying the committee had “shamed itself beyond repair” and calling Pillay “an unabashed hater of America and Israel.”
Late Friday, after a rally in Syracuse, he posted her photograph and wrote that she got the prize “over the Great United States of America, whose Representative, ME, settled eight Wars.” No one had ever heard of her, he added, except that she “hates Israel.” It was an “indelible stain” on Norway.
In a follow-up he insisted, “I settled 8 WARS, am close to ending or settling 2 more.” His tally counts the June 2025 war on Iran, which U.S. bombers joined in illegal strikes on civilian sites. In July he told reporters 15 million people had been beheaded in the Congo war, roughly four times the usual death estimate.
He has also launched an illegal campaign of aggression against Iran, beginning on February 28. The war has killed civilians in repeated attacks, including at least 155 people, mostly children, in the Minab school massacre; at least 21 in U.S. strikes on Lamerd; and five more near a wedding in Kuhestak, where 67 were wounded.
He also invaded Venezuela earlier this year. Last year’s laureate, the Venezuelan María Corina Machado, handed Trump her medal, a gesture the Nobel Institute says does not change the official award.
Washington’s real answer to Pillay winning the prize came the same day. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court itself, the next step in a campaign to dismantle it “brick by brick.”
The U.S. had already sanctioned its president in August. The goal is no secret. Officials want the arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant dropped. The ICC condemned the move and welcomed her prize.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry called the prize “the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice” and said Goebbels was “applauding from hell.” Netanyahu, himself wanted by the court, issued his own rebuke.
Support came quickly elsewhere. UN chief António Guterres, rights chief Volker Turk, ICC President Tomoko Akane and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa all hailed her. Hamas’s Bassem Naim called the prize a message that “humanity still resists the forces of evil targeting international justice.” Amnesty’s Agnès Callamard, beside her in Nuremberg, noted she is a former ICC judge while Washington tries to destroy the court.
Pillay learned the news at the Nuremberg Forum and told applauding supporters that if they kept clapping, she “may share this prize with Trump.” Then she turned serious, warning of a world where “power rather than law determines whose suffering matters.”
Washington and Tel Aviv have spent two years trying to bury her report. The prize has handed it a bigger stage, whatever the committee’s record.

Three elections on the horizon
TEHRAN – Three elections loom: Israeli Knesset elections, the U.S. midterms, and Palestinian legislative elections.
Each will unfold amid ongoing wars, domestic crises, shifting public opinion, and mounting international pressure. But not every election can reshape the political landscape in a region burdened by wars, divisions, and international shifts.
As for the Israeli regime, the contest appears to be between Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot. In the United States, the focus is increasingly on President Trump’s ability to pursue his agenda without greater constraints from Congress. In Palestine, the question is whether the Zionist regime will allow Palestinians a democratic choice and strong international representation.
The Israeli elections scheduled for October 27 are taking place, for the first time, after three years of genocidal war in Gaza. Those three years have been marked by major security, political, social, and economic crises within the Zionist regime. All of these issues pose challenges for Netanyahu, making it difficult for him to secure another government.
However, the opposition camp may also face a major challenge in successfully forming a stable government. The equation within the regime’s political landscape remains uncertain for either side, despite opinion polls favoring Eisenkot. Leading a political camp in terms of votes does not, by itself, give it the ability to determine the outcome. What matters is the ability to form a bloc of 61 seats in the Knesset.
Netanyahu could lose the election without losing his grip on power if he succeeds in forming a new coalition. Likewise, his political opponents could emerge on top without possessing the keys to forming a cohesive and strong alternative government.
The failures of Netanyahu’s coalition are also substantial: the cost of the illegal wars he has waged against Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran; the internal divisions over judicial issues and military conscription; and the damage to the regime’s image internationally.
One important aspect remains at the forefront: if Netanyahu leaves the political scene, that does not mean the regime will abandon a right-wing fascist ideology. The region is facing an extremely quasi-Nazi Israeli right giving way, perhaps, to a camp that is only marginally less extreme. Netanyahu may be replaced as prime minister, while the political and security structures that produced the same policies remain in place, with Eisenkot, another criminal, taking center stage.
In the United States, the real electoral battle will be over the limits of presidential power. The congressional midterm elections are approaching on November 3 and will determine all seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the seats in the Senate. If the Democratic Party regains control of either chamber, or both, Trump will face a Congress with greater capacity to exert influence and oversight in two important areas: federal spending and legislation.
Here, an important issue arises: If the Democratic Party succeeds, how will it deal with the Zionist regime amid the shift taking place within the party’s supporters? Observers argue that reducing the matter to the assumption that a Republican defeat would automatically mean a decline in U.S. support for the regime would be a superficial reading.
U.S. foreign policy is not made by Congress alone. The president and lobby groups retain broad political powers and tools for managing America’s relations with the regime.
Yet what could realistically change? Analysts believe a change in the composition of Congress may raise the political cost of certain U.S. policies relating to the regime. This would come on the backdrop of public opinion shifting amid the U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza.
Such a shift has already begun, particularly among younger people, university students, and other segments of American voters. At that point, the elections would not represent a sudden turning point, but rather one stage in a longer process that could redefine the boundaries of the U.S.-Israeli relationship.
In the Palestinian case, the ballot box is the most important and sensitive of the three. Legislative elections, originally scheduled for November 28, 2026, have now been postponed until September 11, 2027, when presidential elections are also set to take place. The delay extends an electoral freeze that has left Palestinians without legislative elections since 2006 and presidential elections since 2005. The two votes would mark a significant moment in Palestinian political life, offering a long-overdue opportunity to renew the leadership's mandate amid deep divisions and mounting public frustration.
Palestinian elections face a fundamental question that goes beyond who will win and who will lose, particularly amid reports of political challenges and alliances now taking shape. The more important question is: Can Palestinians conduct an electoral process in a political geography that is enduring a genocidal war, settler terrorism, and Zionist occupation?
The success of any Palestinian election should not be measured by opening polling stations and announcing the results. It begins with ensuring that elections are held free of Zionist terror and occupation. The reason cited for the reported delay is “that the anticipated political, security and economic conditions, on which the scheduling of the legislative elections for 28 November, 2027 was based, have not materialized.” This is hardly surprising.
Some analysts argue that there is an opportunity for Palestinians that goes beyond simply electing a new legislative council. It is an opportunity to rebuild a new political compact based on reforming the institutions of the Palestine Liberation Organization, redefining the role of the Palestinian Authority, uniting Palestinians at home and abroad, and developing a clear national strategy for confronting the occupying regime.
To do that, Palestinians need genuine global recognition and representation. As of last week, that was supposed to be the case. Now the Zionist regime is trampling on this too.
This is where the three elections intersect. Netanyahu may lose without the regime’s policy changing its treatment of the Palestinians. The Republican Party may lose control of one of the chambers of Congress without U.S. military support for the regime coming to an end. And the Palestinian people may proceed without a new political map emerging.
The U.S. and Israeli elections will produce little for Palestinians and the wider region. Recent history demonstrates that sustainable peace cannot be achieved by a change of policymakers in Washington or Tel Aviv.

US sanctions the entire ICC to shield American and Israeli war criminals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:11:12 UTC
02:11:12 KST

US sanctions the entire ICC to shield American and Israeli war criminals
TEHRAN — The United States placed the International Criminal Court under sanctions on Friday, October 9, dropping any pretense that its quarrel was limited to individual judges and prosecutors.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the measure in a video statement that left little room for interpretation. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” he said.
Rubio called the tribunal a “rogue court” and promised to “ban transactions” with it, “cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
He said Trump “will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” then told allies who sit on the court while relying on American troops for their defense to “rein in the court.”
A blacklist with a clock attached
The Treasury Department added the court to its list of Specially Designated Nationals. All property the ICC holds in the United States is blocked, and no one under American jurisdiction may supply it with funds, goods, or services.
The court has about 900 staff. Banks, insurers, and software vendors that keep serving it now risk penalties, and since banks tend to over-comply with sanctions, the real damage could exceed the legal text, up to exclusion from dollar transactions.
Washington attached a 180-day general license covering maintenance of operations, with narrower carve-outs for cloud and software services, the pension plan and detainees.
The State Department says the window exists so member states can show “meaningful progress” on “fundamental U.S. concerns,” and that it can be adjusted if they fail. Critics see an ultimatum with a calendar.
The court prepared for this, swapping Microsoft for Germany’s openDesk, dropping insurer Axa and paying staff months ahead. More than 90 percent of its processes had relied on U.S. technology. Mark Kersten of the University of the Fraser Valley warned that “the worst-case scenario has come about.”
Diplomats at the court’s annual assembly said in December that the administration had pressed it to drop its investigations in Palestine and Afghanistan, and to amend the Rome Statute so nationals of non-members, meaning Americans and Israelis, could never be prosecuted. The assembly refused, though it did not name Washington.
Condemnation and political messages
Hours earlier, the Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a South African jurist and former ICC judge who oversaw the 2025 UN report concluding that Israel’s actions in Gaza constituted genocide.
The committee said judges and institutions of international law are “under political attack.” Law professor William Schabas called the prize “a kind of polite endorsement” of that report. “There’s often a political message lurking behind the award of the Nobel Peace Prize, and I think this year is no exception,” he said.
The ICC called the sanctions “an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order” and warned that “the Court cannot stand alone.” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply alarmed,” and rights chief Volker Turk called the measures “unacceptable.”
Human Rights Watch’s Philippe Bolopion said the aim is to “destroy” the court and “shield U.S. and Israeli officials from facing charges.” Amnesty International said this “existential attack must fail.”
Israel cheered. “Thank you for your leadership,” Netanyahu wrote, calling the ICC “a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide.” The charge comes from a man the court wants arrested.
Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan said they “regret and strongly disagree.” Belgium’s Maxime Prevot said “Europe must act” and urged activating the EU Blocking Statute, which would bar European firms from complying with the sanctions.
Palestinian rights groups say similar calls have gone unanswered since April, calling that “complicity through inaction.”
The warrants behind it
The trigger came in November 2024, when judges issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former War Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, chiefly the use of starvation as a method of warfare.
Neither Israel nor the United States belongs to the court. The ICC has long held that crimes committed on the territory of a member state, Palestine included, fall within its reach whatever the suspect’s passport says.
Washington’s second grievance is Afghanistan, where an inquiry could touch CIA torture at secret sites in Romania, Lithuania and Poland. The court has deprioritized that strand since 2021 and has never sought to prosecute an American.
That has not slowed the campaign. Executive Order 14203, signed February 6, 2025, opened the way. Sanctions fell on 13 ICC officials, among them half of the 18 judges and former prosecutor Karim Khan, then on UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese in July 2025 and on the Palestinian groups Al-Haq, Al Mezan and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights in September.
Last month Trump told the UN General Assembly the court was an “evil group of people” and demanded that members withdraw.
A 2002 law, nicknamed the “Hague Invasion Act,” authorizes the president to use “all means necessary and appropriate” to free certain Americans and allied personnel detained by the court. The threat of force has thus been enshrined in U.S. law against a tribunal that has never prosecuted a U.S. citizen.

Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:10:29 UTC
02:10:29 KST

Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital after surviving Tennessee’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday.
Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement.
“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”
Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalized after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday.
But in a shocking turnaround, on Thursday her lawyer said that she was “up and walking” – though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much.
Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. Witnesses present in the chamber said that “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol.
There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors.
Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic.
Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17.
Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18.
After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.
Tennessee’s top prison official has announced his resignation.
Meanwhile, the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. And Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, on Friday canceled a planned lethal injection execution in the state.
But they continue elsewhere.
For instance, the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of former army psychiatrist Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations.
Donald Trump on Saturday said Hassan “was vicious – he was violent” and that he would “make a decision” about the plans to livestream his execution.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show,” the president remarked. “Because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

UK Greens' deputy leader Mothin Ali warns of rising racism in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:10:26 UTC
02:10:26 KST

Breadcrumb
'England is my home': Green Party deputy leader Mothin Ali warns of rising racism in Britain
"A message to Suella: I'm Brown, I'm Muslim, but I'm as English as a Yorkshire cup of tea."
That was the message Green Party Deputy Leader Mothin Ali delivered to former Home Secretary Suella Braverman at his party's annual conference last week, challenging the increasingly hostile rhetoric surrounding immigration, race and British identity.
For Ali, a British Bengali politician whose parents migrated to the UK in the 1960s, the debate over who belongs in Britain is deeply personal.
Speaking to The New Arab on the sidelines of the conference, he warned that rhetoric from senior politicians was creating an environment in which racism and racial violence could become increasingly normalised.
"I think it's really important for Black and Brown people, who are born here, raised here, part and parcel of this country, to be able to feel like they belong here," he said.
"I think what Suella Braverman did was particularly egregious because what she was describing was a creation of othering, and it's something that she's consistently done whether as Home Secretary or now in Reform," Ali added, referring to her anti-migrant stance.
"We can't allow high-profile people to just get away with saying that kind of rhetoric without being challenged."
Ali also called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to treat racism and racist violence as a national emergency.
"We have a crisis of racism in this country," he said.
'Where do I belong?'
Ali drew comparisons between the current political climate and the racial violence experienced by South Asian communities in Britain during the 1970s and 1980s.
"The fact is, I belong in this country. This country, I know no other home. England is my home. If I can't be treated as English and called English, then where do I belong?" he questioned.
"Okay, my blood is from somewhere else. But how far do we go back, because ancestrally, if we keep going back and back and back, we're all going to come back to the same person."
He recalled the killing of Altab Ali, a young Bengali textile worker murdered in a racist attack in east London in 1978, whose death became a turning point in the British Bangladeshi community's struggle against racism.
Ali fears that increasingly inflammatory political rhetoric could encourage a return to the hostility experienced by earlier generations.
"We're seeing videos pop up regularly of young men, particularly from African descent, who are being targeted when they go to the park, and that's just not acceptable," he said.
"We saw a group of people chase the Pakistani cricket team around because they thought they were immigrants. I mean, that's just disgraceful behaviour."
The Green deputy leader, who was elected to the position in 2025, argued that tackling racism required more than condemning individual incidents of abuse.
"I want to create an equal society in Britain and across the world. People should be able to live free without feeling like they're second class to someone else," he said.
Divisions over Zionism and Palestine
Ali also addressed the divisions surrounding the Green Party's "Zionism is Racism" motion, which was adopted at the conference by 1,022 votes to 813.
The motion, which defines Zionism as a racist settler-colonial ideology, exposed disagreements within the party, with senior figures including fellow Deputy Leader Rachel Millward expressing concerns.
Ali, a longstanding advocate for Palestinian rights, supported the proposal and argued that the debate needed to be understood in the context of Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza.
"Let's think about the context. The context is genocide. We're talking about a context where a classroom full of kids are being blown to bits every single day," he told The New Arab before the vote.
The motion marked a further shift in the Greens' position on Israel and Palestine, following the party's 2024 decision to formally recognise Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide.
"At that time, [the 2024 motion] was radical, but it shifted the political dial, it shifted the political discussion, and it made it okay for even people within the Green Party to refer to what's happening in Gaza as genocide," Ali said.
He argued that defining Zionism more explicitly would allow for a clearer political debate.
"If we have a clear definition of our terms, then we can have an argument based on that," he said. "The motion has defined what it's calling racist. If someone has different beliefs to that, then obviously they're not covered by that definition."
Despite supporting the motion, Ali acknowledged that he and Millward held different views on the issue.
"If [Millward] has a slightly different opinion to me on a subject, that's fine and the same applies the other way. I've got a different opinion to her, so she's okay with that as well," he explained.
Following the vote, the party's five MPs, leader and co-deputy leaders issued a joint statement pledging to "continue to work to ensure that the Green Party is an anti-racist party in every way".
Ali dismissed suggestions that the disagreement should prevent senior party figures from working together.
"Sometimes we win votes, sometimes we lose votes, but whatever happens, we have to get up and carry on and work together because our ultimate goal is the same," he said.
"I think people are trying to create division. Now what I want to do is try and create unity. My priority is making sure that we can have the united front and work together."

Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to Tennessee prison
Pike survived two doses of lethal-injection drugs on September 30, renewing scrutiny of capital punishment.
Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital and returned to a Tennessee women’s prison after surviving the US state’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said on Saturday.
The 50-year-old is back in the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she had been incarcerated for 30 years. She had been in hospital since September 30 when officials administered two doses of pentobarbital in an attempt to execute her.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer.
Her lawyers said she was continuing to receive medical care in prison and that they would monitor her recovery. They also expressed gratitude to the first responders and medical team who treated her.
The failed execution has drawn attention to the US death penalty as a separate controversy unfolds over the military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan. The former army psychiatrist was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. His execution is scheduled for December 3.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement on Thursday of the livestream drew criticism, even from some supporters of capital punishment. Vice President JD Vance questioned on Friday whether it would happen and said he would not watch. In a social media post, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the proposal “beyond disgusting”.
Archbishop Paul S Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, also condemned the plan, calling it “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death”.
In Tennessee, however, Pike’s failed execution has not prompted Republican legislators to reconsider capital punishment. Instead, some have discussed alternative methods, including the electric chair and firing squads.
Support for the death penalty in the US has declined from its peak in the 1990s. Ten states have abolished capital punishment since Pike was sentenced in 1996, but executions continue nationwide.
Thirty people have been executed in the US this year, with eight more scheduled, mostly in Texas and Florida.
A Pew Research Center poll in July found that about two-thirds of US adults considered the death penalty morally justified for people convicted of murder. But roughly six in 10 said it did not deter crime, while about seven in 10 said there was some risk of an innocent person being executed.

Sistan and Baluchestan, which borders Pakistan and Afghanistan, is a strategically important southeastern province where Iranian security forces have repeatedly confronted armed groups and cross-border security threats. Iran has long stressed the importance of strengthening border security alongside development, public services and engagement with local communities.
Eftekhari’s responsibilities in cultural and social affairs placed her in direct contact with residents and community groups. Iranian officials have highlighted such engagement as an important part of efforts to strengthen public trust and social cohesion, particularly in remote areas.
The bombing has prompted senior Iranian officials to call for a thorough investigation and accountability for those responsible. Their messages also underscored that attacks on security personnel and public servants would not deter the authorities from pursuing security measures or efforts to address local communities’ concerns.

The tunnel idea echoes a Cold War-era proposal for a “Khrushchev-Kennedy Bridge” linking the two countries. Republican Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna released declassified Soviet files on the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy this week. The 350-page collection included material on the proposed bridge.
Dmitriev first proposed the tunnel two months after Putin and Trump met in Alaska in August 2025 to discuss efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict. The summit marked the first top-level direct contact between Moscow and Washington following the escalation of the conflict.

The RDIF is ready to participate, he said, citing the fund’s role in building a rail bridge linking Russia and China.
Earlier this year, Dmitriev announced that the fund had signed an agreement to continue designing the tunnel, with further steps expected by the end of the year.

The attack on Sunday targeted a Yandex facility in Vladimir Region, around 180 km (112 miles) northeast of Moscow. The site also houses Galushkin, one of the company’s three supercomputers used for AI development. The strike damaged the data center’s infrastructure and forced a shutdown, Yandex said on Telegram.
“The infrastructure of Yandex’s data center in Vladimir was damaged as a result of a drone attack, and the data center’s operations have been completely suspended. Some Yandex services are unavailable to users,” the company said.
No injuries were reported. Emergency crews and Yandex engineers worked to assess the damage and restore services. The company urged cloud customers to activate alternative disaster-recovery plans.
The attack forced Yandex Cloud into emergency operation, with outages affecting banks, online marketplaces, delivery services, retail apps, pharmacies, fitness clubs, and the website of St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport, according to media reports.
In a later update, Yandex said access to some of its services, including Alice AI assistant, Search, Maps, Taxi, and Mail, was gradually being restored.
This was the third attack on a Yandex hub in four days, amid intensified Ukrainian strikes on civilian infrastructure in Russia. Yandex’s data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Region sustained serious damage in an overnight attack on October 7, forcing it offline. A facility in Kaluga Region, around 150 km southwest of Moscow, was damaged in a drone strike on Friday.
The attacks come amid mounting US criticism of Kiev’s strikes on Russia, particularly against oil refineries. US President Donald Trump lashed out at Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky on Saturday, accusing him of rejecting peace deals and worsening global diesel shortages by ignoring warnings against targeting Russian refining infrastructure.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump said.
His remarks followed a phone call with President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in which the two presidents agreed on measures to ease the global fuel crisis. The US Treasury temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports in exchange for Russia releasing 300,000 metric tons to global markets immediately and another 500,000 next month to ease the fuel crisis. Tech billionaire Elon Musk later backed Trump, writing on X that Zelensky “has gone too far.”
Zelensky said on Sunday that Ukraine would continue its strikes until a ceasefire backed by “real guarantees” is secured. Later in the day, Trump claimed on Truth Social that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, urging both sides not to violate it. Neither country has publicly confirmed the terms of the purported agreement.
Russia has rejected the idea of freezing the conflict without addressing the root causes, arguing that a temporary ceasefire would only give Ukraine time to rebuild its military and resume the hostilities. Putin recently warned that Kiev faces a “catastrophic scenario” by attacking Russian economic and civilian infrastructure.
In response to the attacks, Russia has stepped up strikes on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, telecommunications infrastructure, mobile operators, and data centers, disrupting internet access, digital television, and other services. During the latest overnight strikes, Russian forces said they hit the Tenet data center in Odessa, on Ukraine’s Black Sea coast. Moscow maintains that it only targets Ukrainian military facilities and infrastructure that supports Kiev’s war effort.

Breadcrumb
At least 139 migrants dead, including some children, after boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes
At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations International Organisation for Migration said on Sunday.
The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock, a port town in Djibouti, during the night of 8-9 October, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts.
Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. An Ethiopian government spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore.
"Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance," said Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities," Coissac said.
Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased.
The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment.
The migrants were heading to Yemen, with the hope of eventually making it to wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals themselves flee their country, which is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022. 
"Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries," the IOM statement said.
Fighting in Ethiopia
Fighting has also broken out in Ethiopia since last month in the biggest escalation of violence since the 2020-2022 Tigray war.
An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years.
"People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time," the official said.
Ethiopian migrants interviewed for the agency's most recent situation report on Djibouti from 20 September to 30 September said they left their country because of difficult living conditions, including the impact of drought.
"Some migrants also reported that they were fleeing conflict and forced recruitment by armed forces," the report said.
Multiple residents of Tigray, where fighting erupted on 23 September, have told Reuters that they had seen Tigrayan rebels forcibly recruit young men into the defence forces. The rebels have denied conducting forced recruitment.
The conflict has sparked fears of a return to all-out war, with Ethiopia and Eritrea severing relations over alleged Eritrean support for the rebel alliance seeking to overthrow Ethiopia's government. Eritrea has denied backing the alliance.
Severe risks
The so-called Eastern Route presents many dangers, including accidents at sea, trafficking and arbitrary arrests once on land. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project, as the number of people undertaking the journey increased by 18 percent.
IOM has described the crisis sparked by the fighting in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging to 200,000 from 76,000 in mid-September, according to data released by the agency last week.
More than 3,700 people have fled Yemen by sea to Djibouti as of last week, it said.

Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi's government was stifling dissent.

Ten of thousands urge EU for climate action at Brussels demonstration

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11

Ahead of a major UN summit, thousands of protesters marched through the streets of Brussels demanding greater action to combat climate change.
Tens of thousands of people marched Sunday through the Belgian capital Brussels to the EU's headquarters to demand greater action to combat climate change ahead of a major UN summit.
Record heatwaves across Europe this month have raised concerns about the impact that man-made climate change is having on the continent.
Delegates from around the globe will gather in the Turkish resort town of Antalya next month for the annual COP gathering.
But expectations are low that the meeting will yield any major breakthroughs, as the United States under Donald Trump has disengaged from the process and momentum is waning in Europe.
Sunday's protest was organised by Climate Coalition, in collaboration with other groups, including Groen, Flanders' green political party.
Climate Coalition listed five key demands, including the phasing out of fossil fuel subsidies and taxing the fossil fuel sector, more green spaces, a fair climate transition, more support for citizens and businesses to move away from fossil fuels, and more international co-operation in fighting climate change.
President of the Green Party in Flanders and Brussels, Aimen Horch, told Euronews that the demands have remained unchanged, however the sense of urgency has never been greater.
Belgium, like many other European countries, has experienced unpredented spike in excess deaths during the extreme heatwaves that swept across the continent this summer.
"People actually died from the heat. They felt that the conditions of their homes made it impossible to sleep at night. They saw the wildfires in the High Fens, one of the country's most important nature reserves, and saw that the government did nothing," Horch said.
Many demonstrators at the march, including Horch, voiced their frustration at politicians' lack of action, as climate goals appear to be losing priority on the political agenda, with many governments scaling back their ambitions.
"We have to fight in the European Parliament and here in Belgium to make sure climate stays on top of the agency, because the urgency is not gone. The heatwaves are not gone. The impact of climate change on people's daily lives is not gone.
Police put the number of participants at the march — the latest in a series to be held in Brussels — at 45,000. The organisers estimate roughly 60,000 people attended.
"There is a great deal of concern among the population, not just among the protesters today", said economist Etienne de Callatay, as he attended the march.
"The extreme heat we experienced this summer is something everyone was aware of. Politicians shouldn't be afraid of electoral repercussions if they take courageous measures on environmental issues."
Aurore Schreiber, who works for a development cooperation NGO, said she had attended with her family "so that politicians wake up and hear the citizens' message".
"We need to listen to the demands of young people and the most vulnerable", she said. "We need greener, fairer supply chains that take into account workers' issues and wages".
EU's low expectations for COP31
After having its hopes dashed for a more ambitious deal last year in Brazil, the European Union is setting its sights low for next month's COP31.
With climate sceptic Trump withdrawing the United States from the negotiations, international efforts to combat global warming had already taken a battering.
But now the situation looks even less promising as surging energy prices have put major oil and gas producers in a position of strength that makes them less likely to want to discuss phasing out fossil fuels.
The EU insists it remains the global leader on climate action and is the principal international donor in the field.
But the bloc arrives at the COP having recently watered down its own environmental legislation.
As it struggles to compete with China and the United States, Brussels has been on an increasingly business-friendly push.
The most recent example last month was the commission proposing to postpone the implementation of a law targeting methane — an extremely polluting greenhouse gas — by one year, from 2027 to 2028.

IAI to unveil new tactical radar that seeks out low-flying drones at US's AUSA military expo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:46 UTC
02:15:46 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) announced on Sunday that it will unveil a new radar solution that can detect low-flying drones from its position suspended high above the ground.
The system, known as POINT@AIR, brings long-range radar detection and persistent surveillance to a compact, highly mobile aerostat platform. The unveiling was made at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, taking place this week.
The radar’s elevated position extends its line of sight beyond terrain and other ground-level obstructions, supporting earlier detection of low-altitude threats, while enabling forces to adapt surveillance coverage as mission requirements evolve.
In that sense, a heavy focus will be on anti-drone defense, an area where Hezbollah exposed IDF weaknesses during the 2026 conflict, leading to significant IDF losses.
The system will not replace MMR radar technology and other radars which are primarily focused on long-range detection, but will supplement them in certain specific areas where the threats, such as drones, are evolving.
Persistent operation, rapid relocation capabilities
Designed for persistent operation and rapid relocation, the system can operate without reliance on permanent infrastructure and can detect and track multiple aerial, maritime, and ground targets.
This is one of the new major issues, given that enemy threats have become more unpredictable regarding where and how they will attack from.
It supports multiple missions simultaneously, prioritizes targets according to operational requirements, and interfaces with command-and-control systems to contribute to an integrated operational picture, signaling the continued move toward greater integration of AI and the full network of sensors.
IAI's CEO Guy Bar Lev: 'Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense'
Guy Bar Lev, president and CEO of IAI, said, “Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense. The more persistent and comprehensive that view becomes, the better equipped forces are to understand what is unfolding, anticipate threats and act with confidence. IAI is increasingly developing next-generation capabilities that expand the boundaries of situational awareness and provide our customers with greater visibility, flexibility and time to respond.”
Dror Bar, CEO of ELTA Systems and EVP at IAI: “POINT@AIR reflects a fundamental shift in how persistent surveillance can be delivered - bringing sophisticated radar capabilities to an elevated platform that is smaller, more mobile and adaptable to the mission. Our goal was not simply to reduce the size of an existing solution, but to rethink what an aerostat-based radar could achieve. By combining advanced AESA technology, long-range detection and 360-degree coverage in a compact configuration, POINT@AIR gives operators the ability to establish persistent awareness where fixed infrastructure may not be practical.”
Based on the proven ELM-2083 radar family, POINT@AIR incorporates advanced Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) technology, with electronic scanning in both azimuth and elevation combined with mechanical rotation to provide 360-degree coverage.

Israel’s next leader should be chosen by Israelis, not Washington - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:36 UTC
02:15:36 KST

Israel owes an enormous debt of gratitude to the United States – to Democratic and Republican administrations, to president Joe Biden for standing beside us after the horror of October 7, to President Donald Trump for confronting Iran and advancing the Abraham Accords, to Evangelical Christians who have defended the Jewish state when others abandoned it, and above all to the American people.
Yet gratitude must never become submission, because Israel’s prime minister must be chosen by Israelis in Jerusalem, not by a president, donors, or political strategists gathered at Mar-a-Lago.
Trump has said that staying out of Israel’s October 27 election would be appropriate. He has also suggested that he might endorse someone. More recently, he shared an article highlighting a poll favorable to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc.
That may not constitute a formal endorsement, but in a close election, it is political intervention by suggestion. Our country is not a client state, an Evangelical political project, or a Trump-branded Middle Eastern property. Gaza is not an empty beachfront awaiting luxury towers, and Israel is not a corporation whose controlling shares belong to foreign patrons.
We are a sovereign democracy whose citizens bury the dead, send children to war, and live with the consequences.
Trump understands the power of uncertainty. By saying that he may endorse a candidate without naming one, he encourages every Israeli contender to seek his approval. Netanyahu can present himself as Trump’s natural partner. His challengers must assure Washington that they will protect the alliance.
Trump gains leverage before casting a single political coin. This is not merely affection for Netanyahu. Trump values loyalty, public credit, and the image of being the decisive dealmaker. He sees diplomacy through transactions, leverage, and visible victories.
That approach can produce breakthroughs, as the Abraham Accords demonstrated. But nations are communities of memory and responsibility, not properties to be acquired, redesigned, and branded.
Netanyahu understands this theater. For years, he has used photographs, speeches, and meetings with American presidents to reinforce the argument that only he can manage Israel’s most important alliance. His message is familiar: Without me, Israel will be isolated. Without me, Washington will turn away. Without me, the country is unsafe.
That is not democratic confidence. It is manufactured dependency. Israel’s future also cannot be managed by a narrow diplomatic circle embodied by Netanyahu’s longtime confidant Ron Dermer, despite his experience.
Dermer helped cultivate American and Gulf relationships. But diplomacy conducted mainly through leaders, billionaires, investment channels, and palace intermediaries leaves ordinary citizens outside the room. Israel needs institutions, public accountability and many voices, not one prime minister, one emissary, and one foreign patron.
Gadi Eisenkot's political rise
The rise of Gadi Eisenkot exposes the weakness of that argument. Israelis themselves have presented another credible leader: a former military chief with decades of security experience, personal sacrifice, and a reputation for sobriety. Recent polling has placed Eisenkot’s Yashar Party near or ahead of Likud, and one survey showed him leading Netanyahu as the public’s preferred prime minister.
Americans do not have to support Eisenkot. Trump does not have to like him. Evangelical donors do not have to agree with every decision he may make. But they must respect the possibility that Israeli citizens, after October 7, want a different kind of leadership less theatrical, less divisive and more accountable.
Trump should promise not to endorse a candidate. American political organizations and major donors should show the same restraint. They may support Israel and advocate for their beliefs, but money, access, and presidential prestige should not select its government.
Israeli candidates must also stop campaigning as applicants for American approval. They should tell voters what they will do about security, diplomacy, living costs, national service, social inclusion, and the failures of October 7. Their mandate must come from Israelis.
The next government should protect the American alliance as a relationship between democratic nations, not political personalities. Israel worked with Biden despite disagreements. It can work with Trump without surrendering its independence. Institutional alliances endure; personality arrangements collapse.
Eisenkot should make this principle central to his campaign. He can thank Trump for his contributions, honor Evangelical friendship, and recognize Biden’s support during Israel’s crisis while stating clearly that no outside leader will receive a veto over Israeli democracy. That position is not anti-American. It is the foundation of an alliance between equals.
I write as an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American who loves both countries. America taught me the importance of constitutional government and peaceful transfers of power. Israel taught me that Jewish sovereignty carries responsibility.
Those lessons lead to the same conclusion: Friends may advise, assist, and disagree, but citizens must decide. Israel’s election belongs to the nurse in Jerusalem, the reservist returning from Gaza, the struggling family in Beersheba, the Arab teacher in Nazareth, and the Ethiopian-Israeli mother whose children serve a country that still too rarely allows her community to represent it.
My teacher, Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, z”l, expressed this principle clearly: “Whoever governs in Israel does so only under the authority delegated by God on the one hand, the people on the other.” That covenantal principle applies equally to domestic politicians and foreign benefactors. Israel’s democratic authority comes from its people, not from Mar-a-Lago, royal palaces, billionaires, or political donors.
President Trump may be Israel’s friend. Evangelical Christians may be among Israel’s most loyal supporters. President Biden and millions of Americans deserve our gratitude.
But none of them is Israel’s kingmaker. Let the citizens of Israel choose. If they choose Gadi Eisenkot, Washington should respect that decision.
Israel’s future must be decided in Jerusalem, not at Mar-a-Lago.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

When I was 19, my father and I took my rabbi, Sinai Adler, to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington because the rabbi was a survivor, and he refused to believe that the American government kept a permanent exhibition in which it admitted it could have interrupted the machinery of Auschwitz and chose not to.
He needed to see the admission with his own eyes. The gallery held a US War Department letter explaining the decision not to bomb the rail lines and a reconnaissance photograph of the camp taken from an American bomber. That photograph was made 17 days after Rabbi Adler had been brought through the gate.
As we walked out, my father tried to lift him. The halls were thick with school groups, and most of the children were not Jewish, which my father offered as proof that the world had learned something and that the next generation would not repeat the crime. Rabbi Adler answered that they were only coming to study their mistakes and to learn how to do it better the next time.
Years later, in a study hall in Israel, a student told him that German visitors were standing at the back of the room. They had come, they said, to see the miracle of the Jewish state. Students argued that these Germans had not been alive during the war and that six decades had passed. Rabbi Adler had them removed from the campus.
Those two scenes can be filed under trauma if you want an easy label. Rabbi Adler was a careful reader and a disciplined mind, and the conclusions he drew did not begin in shock.
He returned again and again to the Talmudic teaching that Esau hates Jacob. He treated that line as an operating instruction. Gentiles will persecute Jews, and a Jew who forgets that fact is unprepared for what history holds.
I hear the same complaint about Israel that I have heard for years. If only the country explained itself more clearly, if only the press operation were sharper, the world would grant the benefit of the doubt and perhaps even real support, especially after the massacre of October 7.
The evidence offered for that hope is the long stretch of Western backing that Israel enjoyed through most of its first seven decades. There were breaks in that pattern.
The West changes how it treats Israel
US President Dwight D. Eisenhower threatened Israel over the Sinai campaign of 1956. France embargoed arms on the eve of the Six Day War. Boycott campaigns gathered in universities and unions. Still, until about three years ago, the West as a bloc treated Israel as a partner more often than as a defendant.
The hope that better public relations will restore that climate misreads the record. Rabbi Adler and the sages were right about the ground under our feet. Antisemitism is the baseline we can count on. Support is the exception.
A common theory holds that the goodwill of those first decades was an aftershock of the Holocaust, a period in which even polished antisemites understood that Europe had gone too far and that open annihilation had become embarrassing.
That aftershock never erased the double standard. Friends still applied rules to Jerusalem that they would not apply to themselves. The pockets of hostility were the older pattern showing through the courtesy. The courtesy has worn off. The Holocaust survivor bump has ended. Baseline antisemitism has returned. We can argue about the date it faded.
But its end is no longer in dispute.
Support from Evangelical Christians is the large exception that still holds, and it grows out of their theology rather than out of a sudden affection for Jewish power.
Other help arrived from sources that were moral and strategic at once. US president John F. Kennedy approved weapons sales. US politician Henry M. Jackson tied aid for the Soviet Union to the release of Jews who wanted to leave. American president Richard Nixon ordered the airlift that kept Israel standing in the Yom Kippur War.
Those acts matter, and we should remember them with gratitude. They do not rewrite the longer pattern. Not all the gentiles hate us all of the time, but most gentiles will hate us most of the time. History is stubborn on this point for anyone who finds the sentence extreme.
Zionism began because that pattern would not dissolve. For two thousand years millions of Jews absorbed hatred and exile as a condition of life and waited for gentile mercy to improve.
Early Zionists first trusted emancipation and the Enlightenment to repair the Jewish situation from outside. When the repair failed, they concluded that the Jewish people needed a state of their own, a place that could shield them from persecution, let them work at full capacity, and for many restore a life of sanctity in their own land.
At eye level from Rabbi Adler’s seat in his study sat a set of Mishna books that he liked to take down for guests. The volumes had been printed in Berlin in 1936, three years after Hitler took office and three years before the first mass killings.
The publisher added an introduction that explained away the Mishna warnings about trusting gentiles. Those laws, the introduction said, belonged to an ancient world in which pagans hated Jews. The German gentile of the present was the most refined man civilization had produced. Jews could rely on him and did not need to apply the old suspicion. The books were still on the shelf when the refined men began the work the introduction had declared impossible.
The belief that Jews can talk the nations into permanent friendship treats 20 centuries of evidence as a public-relations problem. “Never again” was not coined to fund a better press office.
It was coined to remind Jews what happens when they rest their survival on the goodwill of people who have already shown them the limit of that goodwill.
The museum photograph, the German visitors at the back of the hall, and the Berlin Mishna of 1936 belong to one argument. Learn the baseline. Build as if the exception will not last. Keep the state strong enough that the next improvement in gentile technique never gets its laboratory.
The writer is a Zionist educator at institutions around the world and recently published a new book, Zionism Today.

Iran at the threshold, Israel outside the room - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:11 UTC
02:15:11 KST

One justification for war with Iran was that time was running out. Tehran, Israelis were told, was “racing” toward nuclear weapons, “a step away” from a bomb.
Yet Iran has been near the nuclear threshold for years. Its distance from a weapon has never depended solely on centrifuges, enriched uranium, or the time needed to produce fissile material. US intelligence assessed that Tehran had acquired capabilities bringing it close to the threshold but had not decided to cross it. A crucial barrier was political.
Six months into the war, it is difficult to say that barrier has strengthened. Nuclear facilities have been damaged, but subsequent US intelligence assessments do not indicate a significant increase in the time Iran would need to produce a weapon.
Questions remain about its enriched uranium stockpile, while discussion in Iran about crossing the threshold has become more open. The war has also opened a front in the Strait of Hormuz and increased Israel’s diplomatic costs, particularly in the United States. Whether it has made Israel safer from nuclear threats remains unclear.
The only effort in the past decade that successfully imposed agreed, monitored, verifiable limits on Iran’s nuclear program was diplomatic. The 2015 agreement dramatically reduced its enriched uranium stockpile, restricted enrichment and centrifuges, and introduced extensive monitoring.
The International Atomic Energy Agency and Western intelligence assessments found Iran compliant with its core nuclear commitments. Missiles, proxies, and other security issues could – and still can – be addressed separately.
When the Trump administration withdrew unilaterally in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions, the IAEA was still verifying compliance. Iran began exceeding the limits afterward. Israel’s push for US withdrawal, followed by the shift from diplomacy to war, demands a sober assessment of this strategy’s costs.
A low-risk diplomatic option remains largely unknown to Israelis. Since 2019, regional states have gathered annually at UN headquarters in New York for the Conference on the Establishment of a Middle East Zone Free of Nuclear Weapons and Other Weapons of Mass Destruction. Its seventh session takes place this November. Iran and the Arab states participate. Israel is invited but stays away.
Israel has long argued that disarmament cannot be separated from regional security; that arrangements must be developed by regional states with their consent; and that states cannot relinquish capabilities considered essential while remaining in conflict with their neighbors.
It has rightly opposed focusing exclusively on its nuclear capabilities while ignoring missiles, chemical and biological weapons, and other threats. These concerns remain relevant.
They do not, however, require postponing disarmament discussions until peace, recognition, normalization, and extensive confidence-building measures have been achieved. Arab states see this approach as an endless series of prerequisites before weapons of mass destruction reach the table.
Peace, confidence-building, arms control, and disarmament can advance in parallel. War only increases the need for communication, escalation prevention, monitoring, and agreements.
Changing the regional landscape
Participation in November would not require Israel to relinquish weapons attributed to it, join the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), abandon nuclear ambiguity, or accept a future treaty in advance. The conference operates by consensus: regional states participate, and decisions cannot be imposed on Israel.
Several longstanding Israeli demands are therefore already met. If Israel wants missiles, delivery systems, escalation prevention, regional security, and confidence-building on the agenda, it should make those demands inside the room.
Participation could itself build mutual confidence. Israel would discuss weapons of mass destruction directly with its neighbors without committing to an outcome. Arab states and Iran would have to accept Israel as a full, equal negotiating partner.
This would not constitute normalization: states conditioning full relations on ending the occupation and reaching an Israeli-Palestinian settlement could retain their positions. But accepting Israel as a legitimate participant would matter to a country that has long insisted recognition and regional relations are essential to disarmament.
The United States also stays away. Alongside its own reservations, Washington has linked its absence to incomplete regional participation and Israel’s opposition to the format.
An Israeli shift could enable an American one. The government formed after October’s elections could invite Washington to join it in November. After months of confrontation with Iran, this would be a significant diplomatic gesture without advance commitments to disarmament, NPT accession, or an unwritten treaty.
There are precedents. Israel participated in Arms Control and Regional Security talks with Arab states in the 1990s and consultations on a weapons of mass destruction conference in 2013–2014; Iran attended one meeting.
Beginning in 1980, Israel joined the UN General Assembly consensus supporting a nuclear-weapon-free Middle East for over two decades, while retaining reservations about how to achieve it. Attending November’s conference would revive a tradition of raising objections and demanding conditions while continuing to talk.
Meanwhile, the regional landscape is changing. Saudi Arabia is expanding its civilian nuclear program and security alliances, including the Mecca Agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan. Iran is reconsidering its nuclear future, and another confrontation remains possible.
Burying one’s nuclear head in the sand does not preserve freedom of action. It leaves others free to shape the reality Israel must confront.
The next government should arrive in New York with Israel’s security interests, reservations, demands, and proposals – and ask Washington to join it. It need not commit to disarmament. Entering the room does not endanger Israel’s security. In today’s regional reality, remaining outside requires an explanation.
The writer is a guest writer at the Mitvim Institute and an advocate for eliminating nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction from the Middle East. She is the founder and executive director of the Middle East Treaty Organization (METO).

Two remembrance days in memory of October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

One peculiarity of the State of Israel is the large number of formally celebrated remembrance days.
Remembrance days around the world frequently commemorate events connected to wars, joyous events (such as victories), or tragic events (such as the Holocaust).
One could argue that the multiplicity of remembrance days in Israel reflects the multiplicity of wars and tragic events that befell the Jewish people in general, and the Jewish state in particular, since biblical times and more specifically during the last 85 years.
The most recently added remembrance day – that commemorating the atrocities of October 7, 2023, and their aftermath – is unusual, in that despite the general agreement in Israel that the day should be marked, there are politically based disagreements as to how the commemoration should take place.
The differences, between those who support the government and those who support the opposition, are over who is directly responsible on the Israeli side for October 7, and whether more could have been done by the government to save at least some of the 41 hostages captured alive and returned dead.
Opposition spokesmen and some of the families who received their dear ones in plastic bags blame Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for this tragedy and for allegedly caring more about his political survival than the fate of the hostages.
Netanyahu and his supporters argue that this criticism is unfair and libelous and fails to take into account broader national security interests.
As a result, for the past three years there have been two separate commemoration ceremonies.
Two October 7 commemorations
The first one is organized by the state on 24 Tishrei, two days after Simchat Torah, which in 2023 occurred on October 7. This ceremony is called the Remembrance Day for the Fallen of the Swords of Iron War.
This year it occurred on Monday, October 5. The ceremony, which was held on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem and was attended by President Isaac Herzog, Netanyahu, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, Supreme Court President Isaac Amit, and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, was divided into two parts.
The first part was a state memorial for the casualties of the IDF and other security forces on October 7, and the three-year war that followed. The second part was a state memorial for the civilians who were massacred in the Gaza border communities on October 7, and civilian hostages killed after that in the Gaza Strip.
The second ceremony, held on October 7 in Tel Aviv’s Yarkon Park – the National Memorial Ceremony of October 7 Families – was organized this year by the Kumu movement.
Kumu is a nonpartisan organization of bereaved families, founded in 2024 by Yonatan Shamriz, whose brother Alon was one of three Israeli hostages who managed to escape their captivity in December 2023 but were accidentally shot by IDF forces in Gaza who failed to identify them.
Though Kumu is nonpartisan, it does not conceal the fact that it holds the government responsible for what happened on October 7. It is also critical of the fact that Netanyahu has so far failed to take personal responsibility and has avoided setting up any sort of inquiry committee to investigate who is responsible for Israel having been caught by surprise, and for some of the failures that followed.
The ceremony drew an audience of about 50,000, with no government representatives. Though the leaders of the five main Jewish opposition parties – Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan – were present, none of them participated officially.
The two hosts of the ceremony were actress Shani Cohen and former hostage Eli Sharabi, whose wife and two daughters were murdered by Hamas terrorists on October 7, after Eli was abducted from his home in Kibbutz Be’eri to Gaza. His brother Yossi was abducted to Gaza on the same day, but was killed while in captivity, apparently during an IAF attack on the area where he was held.
At the ceremony, survivors and bereaved family members briefly told their stories, while Cohen and Sharabi added commentary. Well-known Israeli singers also participated. It was a highly emotional event, but Sharabi distinguished himself by managing to keep a straight face throughout and concealing his emotions.
It should be noted that the National Memorial Ceremony was broadcast in full and in real time on Channels 11, 12, 13, 15 and 99. Channel 14 was the only Hebrew news channel that did not broadcast the ceremony.
During the ceremony, Channel 14 broadcast its program The Patriots, as usual.
Every once in a while, in the course of the ceremony, I switched over to Channel 14 to see whether it would show a modicum of respect for the feelings of the bereaved families and avoid attacking those attending the ceremony.
But, alas, these were false expectations. The panel members were their usual nasty, insulting, mocking selves.
One of the regular panelists stated that the supporters of the bereaved families of those killed as hostages, who could allegedly have been saved had the government acted differently, are hypocrites who don’t give a damn about the hostages, and are only interested in bringing down Netanyahu.
I expected the program’s host, Yinon Magal, to call the panelist to order in honor of the day. But he said nothing, and his facial expression indicated that he was pleased by the remark.
Then I suddenly remembered that the previous morning, on his talk show together with Ben Caspit on Radio 103fm, Magal had mentioned the names of 13 of over 282 contributors to a Hebrew book published in 2024, with a picture of Netanyahu on its cover, titled “Mr. Depriver – the heritage of he who abandoned the hostages.”
Yinon said of the 13: “All the names I have mentioned shall be remembered eternally in disgrace, on a pillory. These are the most despicable persons living in the State of Israel, who falsely accused Benjamin Netanyahu of a blood libel.”
Eleven of the names mentioned were of returned hostages, or of relatives of hostages who had perished in Gaza. They included Shamriz.
Magal finally apologized for mentioning the hostages, but the damage was done.
What are the chances of the two ceremonies being united next year? Well, that depends on who wins the election in two weeks.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.
